A Promise Has to Be Kept by the Whole Organization

Unit 3: Professor Das Narayandas teaches Market-Facing Functions. The final session: a summary of the unit's concepts, with Starbucks Korea as the optional reading. Over this unit I wrote pre-class pieces on five of Das's cases: Olay, Belden, Bajaj Finance, Equitable, and Starbucks Korea. Each one stopped at a multiple-choice question. In the last class he didn't teach a new case. Instead he pulled three weeks of material into a single thread: Find your own market. Staple yourself to the customer's journey. Make a promise, then have the whole organization — people, processes, AI and compensation — keep it together. In the final few minutes, he talked about himself. After class, I wrote one line in my notebook: Put a purpose in your business, make promises and keep them. This piece follows the order of the class: what Das said, what I jotted down in class, and what I thought of on my own. Here goes — enjoy: Whoever you promote is who your organization becomes The classroom we met in is what HBS calls the Big Room. Das opened by explaining what the room is used for: about a hundred tenured professors gather here to decide who gets tenure and who doesn't. The review report is written by a committee of three tenured professors. The committee spends four months interviewing dozens of peers and experts in the field, and writes a report of about twenty pages — something like a case. Everyone reads it, discusses it in this room for ninety minutes, and then votes: yes, no, or abstain. He asked: which one is the worst? Abstain. Four months of preparation and ninety minutes of discussion, and you still can't decide — either the case itself is flawed, or something hasn't been said out loud. In a professional services firm, the most important decision is whom to promote. Whoever you promote is who your organization becomes. Put the wrong person in this room and they will slowly take apart the institution's character. When someone isn't promoted, the mood in the room is far heavier than when someone is. Getting to review takes about nine years. Saying no means admitting that eight to ten years of investment have come to nothing. So the decision can't be driven by emotion; it has to be calm and objective, and it can't stray from your own culture. This was the setup for the day's last topic: good talent only gets more expensive. At the end of the day, he talked about compensation. Don't say you're small — go find your biggest market The summary began with MAM — My Addressable Market. Never say you're a small player in a big pond. Saying that isn't modesty; it means you haven't understood yourself. When someone in your organization says "we're not big enough," ask them to show you which market we are the biggest in. Then go fight there. Be the 900-pound gorilla in that space: you set the rules, and the game is played your way. He said that, compared with some of the other people he has taught, what the people in this room lack is resources. So you have to get the maximum return from every resource in your hands. He doesn't buy the venture-capital line of "go global, go fast." Win on your own turf first, and you earn the right to make your turf bigger. Don't tell me what you do — tell me what your customers go through To win on your own turf, you have to make every customer a hero. How? The same line he's repeated all unit: staple yourself to the customer's journey. The phrase comes from a 1992 HBR article, Staple Yourself to an Order, written by several of his colleagues. Back then, what you stapled yourself to was an order; today, it's the whole journey — from the moment the customer first feels the pain, to consumption, to everything after consumption. He told the story of Intuit. Co-founder Scott Cook watched his wife manage the household accounts. She used a checkbook, writing out checks one by one and recording each entry — a real hassle. This was the dot-matrix printer era, and Intuit's first software was a small program to help households write checks. Later they discovered that many buyers of this home software were small businesses. That made no sense: running a business takes a general ledger and financial statements. At first they assumed users had filled in the registration forms wrong. Only when they stapled themselves to these small business owners' daily routines did they see it: the accounting software on the market had been written by accountants, for accountants. Small business owners had good ideas and plenty of passion, but they didn't come from business backgrounds, let alone accounting. Asked whether he understood the general ledger, one owner replied: which World War II general was he? If you don't staple yourself to the customer's journey, you'll miss opportunities that no one else can see either. Insight isn't only about new products. Friction in the processes customers go through to deal with you is also opportunity. Break your business down into individual processes and see clearly where the people are and where the machines are. Friction mostly comes from manual steps; automating them doesn't mean cutting people — it frees them to do other things. Then he made a request: from today on, when we meet again, he doesn't want to know what business we're in. He only wants to hear two things — what our customers are going through, and how they experience us. Before class, I wrote in my Bajaj Finance piece: Customer-centricity means the customer can walk into the next product on their own, rather than waiting for a team they can't reach to push it. This class moved that line one step earlier: before the customer can walk in on their own, someone first has to walk the whole path with them. A brand is a promise; making it and keeping it are two jobs Das recast Keller's brand pyramid in his own words: a brand is a promise. First look at what you promised; then at how the customer responds; finally at what kind of relationship they want with you — an emotional embrace, or an efficient business handshake. Different businesses, different answers. A leader therefore has two jobs: one is to take part personally in making the promise; the other is to make sure their people keep the promises already made. He also put in a fair word for sales. He's done sales himself and likes it; he just doesn't want us to treat sales as the tip of the spear. A promise has to be kept by the whole organization; sales is only one link. Always putting sales on the highest pedestal tells everyone else in the organization, again and again: you're not good enough. That isn't true. When he got to the two customer interfaces, the "bow tie" and the "diamond," he made a point of correcting us: the diamond isn't a sales team, it's a customer-promise team — mobilizing the whole company's resources to deliver the experience promised to the customer. This approach is more expensive. So don't do it defensively; only do it where revenue can grow faster than cost. Perhaps twenty or thirty percent of the business is still better done one transaction at a time. Being customer-centric doesn't mean being obsessed with every customer. Saying no to an order isn't saying no to the customer. An order you know you can't do well will just become your reputation. Promises need boundaries — you wouldn't ask a neurosurgeon to look at your toe. Before class, I wrote in my post-class notes on Olay: The promise can change; looking down on customers can't stay. This class filled in the other half: you can make a high promise, but it has to have boundaries. A new uniform doesn't make you a new role From a box-selling supplier, to a value-added partner, to a strategic advisor — whether B2B, B2C or professional services, the climb is hard. A new uniform and a few new talking points won't turn you into a solutions provider. You may need different people. He posed a question. Three account managers: one holds the bottom tier, selling standard products and competing on price and performance; one works at the top as a strategic advisor; one is in the middle, doing a bit of everything. The customer says only one can stay to manage the whole relationship. Whom do you keep? The bottom-tier one matters most — he's the one earning today's money. But when he looks up at the top tier, he thinks: too far, too complicated, I have to go out hunting every day. He can protect today, but he can't build tomorrow. The top-tier one loves long dinners and talking about the industry five years out; when the grunt work comes, he feels it's someone else's job. The middle one isn't good at either end, which is why he's in the middle. He described an experiment he'd been part of. A diversified financial services company assigned an account manager to each of its top hundred clients — a third from the bottom tier, a third from the middle, a third from the top. Two years later they looked at sales, and only one variable explained the results: where the manager originally came from. Wherever they came from, that's the category they sold more of. Cross-divisional, "one firm" selling didn't happen even once — and the compensation had in fact already been adjusted. If there's one person in the organization willing to step out of their comfort zone, it's you. Don't count on anyone else. Many colleagues like to say you should turn every employee into an entrepreneur; he disagrees. If someone has the same risk appetite as you, they should start their own company — or walk in and tell you: no base salary, give me 35% commission. In professional services, the problem is harder. Top-tier clients listen to only two kinds of people: those with gray hair, or rocket scientists. McKinsey relies on gray hair — having seen a lot. BCG took another path and called itself the rocket scientists: the experience curve and the growth-share matrix both came from there. The middle tier relies on deep industry knowledge. Many professional services firms complain that clients don't respect them. Das said that's because you've never built credibility at that level. Making promises isn't enough; you have to keep them. Before class, I wrote in my Belden piece that beneath the three hard problems lay one question: How can a channel system designed to sell parts make room for selling solutions? This class gave a colder answer: the system has to change, and the people may not be the same people anymore. Build steps to the moon, and draw the guardrails in plain sight Coming back to Equitable, he said he doesn't sell any particular methodology. For an organization to keep innovating, it needs five things: Goals: everyone's goals feed into the company's goals Voice of the customer: put out a minimum viable product first, and keep the customer in the room Guardrails: drawn by the leader, and drawn in plain sight Agility: not just the IT department's job — the whole company iterates quickly Skills: look at skills, not titles Lots of people talk about moonshots. Das said your job is to build the organization a staircase to the moon. Goals can stretch people, but don't break them. Don't write moonshot goals into basic performance reviews and pay. Give a realistic goal first, then ask the person: by your own reckoning, what's your moonshot? If they hit it, reward them publicly. Guardrails were what he talked about most. Some things can be declared "not open for discussion" — say a family business says "we manage the finances ourselves" — and that's perfectly fine, as long as it's said clearly and applies to everyone equally. A week earlier, in this same room, he and his colleagues had discussed how to bring AI into HBS teaching, and they spent the first fifteen minutes drawing the guardrails: anything outside the guardrails, they don't do. Inside the guardrails, shorten the distance between decision and action. He has seen plenty of bosses with a stack of documents on their desk, flipping page after page without reading, signing at the bottom. That's also why he had us read Starbucks Korea: seven people had signed off before that incident. Each one signed assuming someone else had read it. One more signature doesn't mean one more layer of management. The last item is skills. Don't tell him you have three VPs and four AVPs; tell him what skills you have on hand. He admitted this one is the biggest threat to HBS itself — an institution that has always been proud of its titles. My class notes Take the moonshot, but build the steps to the moon. Whatever you do, set goals. Stretch people, but don't break them. Set realistic goals, ask them, let them take the moonshot — and reward them in PUBLIC!! People love to be recognized. Align people with the org's goal. Discuss the guardrails (you have to!). My Thinking Counting skills, not titles — that's the future of organizations. One step further: if a skill can be done by AI, there should be an AI officer responsible for that part. Take us as an example: much of the work of a CFO and HR can be done by AI. Take reviewing people: administrative and cashier arrangements still need humans, but analysis and feedback can be done entirely by AI. — Provided, that is, we have the data. Before class, I wrote in my Starbucks Korea and Equitable pieces, respectively: Make reviews correspond to real responsibility. Everyone knows what they're judging, and knows whom to go to when they spot a question. Adding signatures can't replace that. Who qualifies for the 100% must be spelled out clearly. Looking back now, those two lines say the same thing: draw the guardrails in plain sight, and put responsibility on specific people. Sixty percent human judgment, thirty percent machine prediction, ten percent left to the machine Next he talked about AI, then compensation. Before AI, he made a point of saying: this is a businessperson's take, not a technical one. He divided a leader's decisions into three types, and left us homework for next year: Descriptive: the machine provides historical data, and humans decide. About 60% Predictive: the machine predicts outcomes, and humans decide. About 30% Prescriptive: humans set the rules, and the machine decides on its own. At least 10% Descriptive: stop making decisions in Excel We all grew up in Excel. He put it bluntly: if you're still making decisions in Excel two years from now, you've fallen behind. Use AI, check it for hallucinations, but use it. The real skill is visualization. Watch how your people spot patterns — the next generation reads charts differently from us. Don't compete with AI; collaborate with it, and let it lay out the patterns in a way everyone can understand. When uncertainty is high and the world is changing too fast, you still have to rely on intuition. Prescriptive: once the machine decides, stop second-guessing it His example was his wife's Tesla. He sits in that car and never touches the steering wheel — his wife won't let him. So what's left for the person? Giving direction. Humans set the objective function: maximize profit today, or minimize inventory. The machine executes. What suits the machine are decisions that are tiny individually, but where each one isn't quite precise enough. Over many repetitions the gap becomes large — dynamic pricing on store shelves, for example. He has a new HBR article: many companies have just wrapped their existing organization in a shell of AI, and then measure only usage — how many tokens were consumed. An employee asking AI where to go for dinner also counts as usage. Usage is not adoption. Predictive: don't fall in love with accuracy When previous OPM participants showed him their dashboards, nine out of ten featured customer churn. Churn is a lagging indicator — the customer has already left. A better metric is "customers at risk of churning": when a customer who accounts for 20% of revenue starts flashing red, everyone mobilizes to save them. Data scientists pride themselves on prediction accuracy, and the easiest way to raise accuracy is to strip out the fuzzy gray zones. But a businessperson sees two kinds of cost: false positives bring wasted effort, false negatives bring missed opportunities. Don't fall in love with accuracy; keep your eyes on wasted effort and missed opportunities. Models should be built by the business people and the data people together. My class notes Descriptive analytics: the machine provides historical data. Learn to use AI analysis instead of Excel — Excel is linear. Once the machine makes a decision, do not second-guess it. Execute. False positive: the machine says do it, but you shouldn't — wasted effort. False negative: the machine says don't, but you should — missed opportunity. Leaving money on the table: the model should not chase 100% accuracy. Take out the outliers, and you will be just normal. My Thinking We should let AI run processes. We should also pay attention to where AI has surprised us, and where AI is helping us make decisions. AI isn't just processes and scheduling; it also makes decisions. An AI-native organization relies not only on AI's automation, but also on AI's judgment. In my own work, AI can help me assess and screen clients, and help me follow up with them. At the same time, keep AI in check. When AI steps onstage, go back to the start of the journey Das said this is the other reason he had us read Starbucks Korea: AI is moving from backstage to onstage. Think of a business as a performance. Descriptive and predictive analytics are both backstage; if something goes wrong, there's still time to catch it. Dynamic pricing is already at the edge of the curtain. Generative AI and agents stand directly in front of the customer: writing content for you, talking to customers on your behalf. Onstage, a single small mistake by AI can destroy all the credibility you've built up in the market. Onstage AI needs someone watching it 24 hours a day. The letting go we talked about earlier shouldn't be applied to decisions that directly affect customer relationships — there, you don't get a second chance. A classmate asked: as more and more of our customer interactions are with AI agents, how do we keep our promises? Das's answer: go earlier in the journey. Be with the real customer before they hand their instructions to an AI agent, closer to the trigger point. When he was in sales, he used to tell his team: if we can't get ourselves written into the customer's requirements spec, this deal is over. That's even truer today. Write yourself in while human emotion is still part of the decision. Once the decision is handed to an agent, the agent uses cold, rational evaluation, and we may no longer have a chance. Staple yourself to the customer's journey, not the AI agent's. My class notes Left side (backstage): allow for what we just discussed. Right side (onstage): you will not get a second chance at a first impression. How to keep our promises: the agent has to be taught by the customer. Get closer to the people, go through the customer's journey. Human emotions still need to be involved. If the machine makes the decision, don't make the user take the blame When he got to prescriptive analytics, he first told a story, and said he'd come back to it at the end. When UPS launched its routing algorithm ORION, it piloted it with drivers first. The drivers said: it's unbelievably good — it only arrived yesterday, and it knows my route better than anyone. Das added: have you ever tried telling a London cabbie he took the wrong route? He'll ask you to get out. When people that proud say an algorithm is better than they are, they mean it. But after the full rollout, adoption didn't take off. Most drivers were overriding the algorithm's routes. The problem wasn't the algorithm. If the algorithm succeeds, who gets the credit? Not the driver. If the algorithm fails, who gets punished? The driver. If I'm going to carry the blame when things go wrong, I'd rather keep my own hands on the wheel. So they quietly used the system "with the brakes on." According to Das, what UPS did next was simple: it stopped measuring on-time rates and customer satisfaction, and looked at just one thing — how often you followed the machine. Late? Fine. Something went wrong? Fine. Adoption happened almost overnight. People are afraid of being held responsible for someone else's mistakes, even when that "someone else" is a machine. After covering AI stepping onstage, he came back to this story and placed it on a chart from his HBR article: every decision raises two questions at once — who makes the decision, and who is accountable for the outcome. The UPS drivers landed in the most troublesome box: the machine decides, the human takes the blame. This isn't a new problem. ERP was supposed to let headquarters see the whole organization, but plant managers were still evaluated on their own plant's performance, so the production schedules sent down from headquarters went straight into the trash. Ask for good data, and people will give you numbers that make it look good. When the machine decides and the machine is accountable, it's like walking a dog: if the dog relieves itself on the sidewalk, the owner cleans up. Machines make mistakes, so each machine needs a designated owner — the people who designed it, who hold the keys to update it. They clean up, not the people who use it. Everyone loves to say "human in the loop." He said, don't make the user the human — make the designer the human. He mentioned Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, who had visited the school a few weeks earlier: there are a few numbers on the dashboard that even he can't touch; he can only tell the people who own the system: we missed, something went wrong somewhere, go fix it. Das told this to the CEO of a consumer goods company, who said it was impossible — the whole reason I exist is to turn these knobs every day. There's another box that's the reverse: the human makes the decision but blames the machine — the dog ate my homework. Last week he met a group of Wall Street traders complaining that their quant models were inaccurate. When they went back to check, it turned out they had been overriding the models themselves all along. My class notes AI can inform you to make better decisions. Become more fluent with AI, so it gives you better visualization to make decisions. Machines make mistakes. But if you still blame people — watching people's necks — you will be stuck. Make the designers the human in the loop, or the human on the loop for the rules and regulations. Before class, I left a question at the end of my Starbucks Korea piece: When AI makes output faster and cheaper, where are we going to put human attention? This class gave a concrete answer: on the rules and the exceptions, and on who cleans up after something goes wrong. You set the rules, and the organization will game them The last topic was compensation. There are only two clean approaches: pay for behavior, or pay for outcomes. Pay for behavior, or pay for outcomes Paying for behavior: the example is the person behind the McDonald's counter. You don't hold them responsible for store traffic; they only need to do two things well: smile, and when a customer buys a burger, ask whether they'd like fries. There are two preconditions: you know clearly which behaviors lead to results, and you can see those behaviors — hence the camera above the counter. People paid this way look after both the company and the customer, and think long-term. They say: "Let's do this together." Paying for outcomes is for when you can't articulate the causal link between effort and results — you can only measure the results, so you pay commission on results. People paid this way look after themselves first and value the short term. They say: "I delivered the results; leave me alone." Two axes, four boxes The horizontal axis: can you measure effort? The vertical axis: can you link effort to outcomes? Both high: high base, low commission — pay for behavior Both low: pay for outcomes You know what works, but can't see what people are doing: train first, then pay for outcomes You can see the effort, but don't yet know which actions work: learn first, then pay for behavior In the third box, most companies use a hybrid — a bit of base, a bit of commission. Das said that's not a good idea. Manage invisible effort with training first, then motivate it with pay. Build your own sales methodology, and no one goes to the front line until they've passed the training. First teach them how to fish and how to bait the hook, then let them live by their skill. Many companies are afraid people will leave once they're trained, so they don't train. But as long as they're still working for you, one trained person beats an untrained team running around out there. The fourth box is common in the digital world, where every action is recorded. The task here is learning: use AI and the data you have to learn how customer behavior is changing, and once you've figured it out, move boxes. When you think about compensation, always think about control at the same time. He calls this the two Cs: control and compensation. One page, five questions He has little patience for complicated compensation plans: the more the consultants charge, the more complicated the plan; the more complicated the plan, the harder it is to execute. A compensation system is best explained on a single page. He recommended five questions, which he said a colleague taught him (the handout credits Ian Larkin): 1. What good behaviors will this system produce? 2. What bad behaviors will it produce? 3. Do the good far outweigh the bad? 4. How can you reduce the bad — through culture, through training, for example? 5. How much does reducing them cost, and is it worth it? On the second question, he repeated a line from the previous two units: your job is to design the rules of the game, and your people will game the rules. Never assume you're smarter than your organization. He closed with three assumptions about people: people take care of themselves first; their risk appetite differs from yours; and they're always calculating which takes less effort — going along with you or working against you. My class notes Build your company's methodology. Don't only focus on compensation — also focus on control!! Do not let your salespeople go before you train them!!!! Have the most intensive training; do not let them train themselves. Start with training, then move to outcome-based compensation. Digital world: it's easy to measure. The world has changed. START BY LEARNING, then move to behavior-based compensation. Always focus on minimizing the effort people need to understand their compensation!!! "Design the rules of the game, and your people will game the rules!! Do not ever operate under the assumption that you are smarter than others." People will first take care of themselves. They will always measure the cost. My Thinking We need to think through how to design incentives for sales — not only for external sales partners, but for our internal sales team too. Before class, I wrote in my Belden piece: People follow the compensation plan, not the strategy speech. This class completed the second half: people follow the pay, and they also follow the loopholes you didn't design for. So list the bad behaviors as carefully as you list the good ones. To whom much is given, much is expected When he finished, he said this was the first time he had taught the whole unit in this version. He'll teach it once more in the spring, then write the book. In the remaining few minutes, he said he wanted to move his relationship with us from "yelling at you, being tough on you" to something more like friends. He talked about himself. He was smart from a young age; no exam could stump him. Things came too easily, and that brought other things with it: a touch of arrogance, and no sense of purpose. He always assumed that everything he got was simply his due. Then his elder son was born. It was the first adversity in his life that he couldn't handle. It was his wife who carried everything, searching everywhere for help for their child. Within a year, they decided to leave India to find a better environment for their son to grow up in. Going abroad for a PhD wasn't because he wanted to be a scholar; it was the family of three's way out. That's why he calls himself an "accidental academic." A marketing professor who did his PhD in a windowless room and never met a single customer. When he graduated, people suggested he go to a research university; they chose Massachusetts, because it was the best place for their child to grow up. In his early years in the US, his only thought was getting tenure, to give his family a sense of security. For that, his wife raised the children almost single-handedly. He said he has made many mistakes. If he could do it over, the one thing he'd most want to change is this: to be a more present father, and a more present partner. He is learning to do that now. Finally he said: life is hard. You are all very fortunate; life has given you a lot. Much is expected from those to whom much is given. To whom much is given, much is expected. He said his two sons have taught him a great deal. After Class What I most want to remember from this class: Think through and design every part of the business: know where you stand, and know what value you bring to others. Knowing where you stand is MAM — the space where you write the rules. Knowing what value you bring to others is the promise — what the customer goes through, and how they experience you. Each of my five pre-class pieces for this unit stopped at its own multiple-choice question. This wrap-up class put them back on a single map: the customer's journey, the promise made, the customer-facing interface, AI's decision rights, and how incentives work. What kind of empowerment does a transformation need

Unit 3, Professor Jeff Polzer, Leadership: The Transformation of Mudo. A founder hopes his company can keep running without him, and still waits every day for the sales figures. Mudo's transformation took place while both of these wishes were alive at once. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Mustafa Taviloğlu founded Mudo in 1964, starting with a small record and gift shop and gradually moving into apparel, furniture and home goods. He had a gift for spotting trends, and deep business relationships. Many of the key decisions in the company's growth came from his intuition and drive. As the company grew, this reliance on one person began to strain. Managers were used to taking orders, and cross-functional coordination was weak; his son Ömer had been with the company for years, and father and son wanted professional managers to run the business, with the next generation taking on the chairman's role. They chose to keep family control and drive the reforms themselves. In March 2012, Accenture partner Barış Karakullukçu became CEO. She knew systems and organizational change well, but had no direct experience running a retail business. The company had more than two thousand employees at that point, and its merchandise, store formats, logistics and management relationships were all complex. The apparel business faced more and more competitors, and its original value-for-money proposition and positioning had eroded. Furniture sold relatively well in large dedicated stores, but when placed in mixed apparel-and-home department stores, it was constrained by display space, storage and logistics. The two kinds of customers also had completely different purchase cycles. The new CEO overhauled the information systems, supply chain, performance management and team. Complaints fell from about 200 a month to 20. The head of home goods cut redundant merchandise and adjusted pricing and delivery; from 2012 to 2014, home goods EBIT went from a loss of 5.7 million lira to a profit of 7.7 million. Over the same period, apparel EBIT fell from a profit of 10.7 million to a loss of 1.6 million. By the end of 2014, professional management had gained some authority, and budgets were getting tighter and tighter. The founder still wanted to open 50 new stores over the next three years; the CEO's analysis supported only a few of them. What she had to answer was how, in the next phase, to make the organizational improvements truly show up in business results. My Thinking The transformation needs to be evaluated piece by piece The progress in home goods and the decline in apparel need to be acknowledged at the same time. The former's EBIT improved by 13.4 million lira; the latter's worsened by 12.3 million. Calling it either "a successful transformation" or "a failed transformation" flattens the very difference most worth understanding. My own judgment is that this CEO made changes worth keeping, but has not yet delivered on her promise of economic results. Backing her to continue doesn't mean accepting a self-assessment of nearly full marks; holding her accountable should also acknowledge the constraints imposed by the business cycle and the way shareholders make decisions. Professionalization has to reach everyday decisions Authority is only real when everyday behavior acknowledges it. A new org chart can show a chairman, a CEO and business heads, but if employees still receive instructions that bypass their superiors, they'll keep guessing whose word counts more. Late in the case, the CEO and her team handle about half of decisions on their own, about 40% require consultation with the son, and the remaining 10% still need the father's approval. These changes are meaningful, and they also show that professionalization is still under way. What needs to be spelled out further: which issues can be challenged, when discussion ends, and who owns execution once a decision is made. The founder's experience deserves to be translated Good governance should make experience usable by others. For someone who created a company, giving up decision rights doesn't mean ceasing to care about it. His ability to see opportunities doesn't disappear with a change of title, either. I would keep his observations on merchandise, trends and locations, ask him to explain the signals behind his judgments, and then have the team validate them. That's more constructive than simply treating intuition as an obstacle. At the same time, when validation doesn't support an investment, the rules must allow the company to say no. The successor's caution needs an outlet Prudence without a standard of evidence can turn into endless waiting. Ömer explains his conservatism by the fact that he once bore the consequences of bad decisions. Understanding this is what keeps a governance conflict from being reduced to a clash of personalities. My own leaning is to agree up front on what information is needed, how big a loss is tolerable, and when a decision will be made. The chairman needs to keep overseeing, and also needs to let the team act once the information is sufficient. Trust is sometimes built by jointly acknowledging uncertainty. The next phase should reduce the number of simultaneous changes What a company spends isn't only project budgets, but also its limited management attention. Launching 50 projects in the first 18 months shows the force of the reform; still running a large number of projects afterward may also mean resources are spread thin. The late arrival of the apparel head is a timely reminder that building support systems and fixing commercial problems need a sensible sequence. I would first make cash, apparel merchandise and conversion, home goods shrinkage, and store-format economics the core tasks. For new stores not yet committed, hold off on taking on further obligations, and compare store by store the cost of continuing, adjusting, renegotiating the lease or exiting. Marketing can be tested on a small scale, but the merchandise has to be good enough to hold the customers it draws into the store. Takeaways for Arcus42 Responsibility needs matching decision rights. When someone is asked to be accountable for results, they should also be clear about what they can decide, and which questions need to be decided jointly. Passing on experience has to land on specific judgments. Rather than asking the team to imitate the founder's style, explain which signals a judgment looked at and which options it discarded. Process metrics need to connect to service outcomes. Better processes have value, and they also need to be checked continually for whether they reduce customers' confusion, waiting or repeated confirmations. Priorities mean being willing to pause some things. When every project is important, it's hard for managers to truly protect the most important work. Carrying a few things all the way through to results is an organizational capability too. Before Class My pre-class choice is to keep the CEO, narrow the next phase's mandate, and hold off on large-scale, unvalidated store openings. At the same time, get the father, the son and the professional managers to form a clearer shared agreement on authority. A company can carry on its founder's heart and effort, and it also needs, gradually, to gain the ability to make good decisions without him. This is a personal study analysis of a course case; the figures and people's circumstances refer to the period described in the case. It does not assess the current state of the companies or people involved. The sequence of actions in the text reflects my personal pre-class judgment.
Giving an old craft new meaning

Unit 3, Professor Jeff Polzer, Leadership: Jean-Claude Biver (A): The Reemergence of the Swiss Watch Industry. Once timekeeping became cheaper and more accurate, the mechanical watch had to answer anew why people would still need it. Biver's story is about an old craft regaining its meaning — and about a forceful leader running into his own limits. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Quartz technology transformed watchmaking. It was more accurate, used fewer parts and lent itself to mass production. The Swiss mechanical watch industry took a heavy blow, and many companies and craftsmen lost their place. Biver, who had worked at Audemars Piguet and Omega, came to believe that the future of the mechanical watch could be built on craftsmanship, history and emotional value. In 1982, he and watchmaking partner Jacques Piquet bought Blancpain, a brand that had been dormant for years. The team sought out craftsmen, turned an old farmhouse into a workshop, and held firm to mechanical watchmaking, low inventory and made-to-order production, making the brand's history part of both the product and the way they worked. In its first year, the company sold 97 watches for revenue of US$75,000; five years later, it was selling about 3,000 watches a year, with revenue of US$9.4 million. Biver didn't just reach out to consumers; he also built relationships with industry leaders, collectors and craftsmen. Old skills began to be valued again as capabilities worth cherishing. Alongside the business's success, the team also had to deal with his emotions. He could be generous, passionate and quick to recognize others' contributions, but he could also fly into rages and publicly berate employees. A personal marital crisis further affected his work. After selling Blancpain in 1992, he soon found that wealth was no substitute for the meaning that a team and a mission had given him, so he asked to return to the Swatch Group. Hayek had him take on the revival of Omega at the same time. Biver repaired the brand's messaging and, through a long-term partnership with Cindy Crawford and the Bond films, reconnected its heritage with contemporary consumers. From 1995 to 1999, Omega's revenue grew from US$350 million to more than US$900 million, with the group's resources also supporting the turnaround. A serious illness in 2000, changes in his family, and a shift in his role within the group brought him to another choice. During a leave of absence, Hublot emerged as a possible new opportunity, but the company was still losing money, and its owners were worried about his management style. His past achievements did not make the decision about the next chapter of his life for him. My Thinking After technology changes, value has to be explained anew Biver found the reasons why mechanical watches were still worth buying. Craftsmanship, history, aesthetics and identity can add up to a kind of value distinct from cheap, precise timekeeping. My own take is that this requires the product to deliver on it. Without craftsmen, manufacturing and a consistent experience, history becomes mere packaging. Nor can we conclude from this that every old technology can be reborn; whether customers care, and whether they'll pay, still has to be tested. Consistency has to run through every business choice Brand messaging only has real power when it can coordinate design, production, distribution and communication. At Blancpain, the workshop, the sense of limited supply and the mechanical promise all reinforced one another; at Omega, history, product lines and long-term partnerships achieved consistency in a different way. This also explains why you can't simply copy the same playbook. The scarcity logic of a small brand and the scaled revival of a group brand draw on different resources. What can be learned is how decisions are organized around a single customer promise. A personal vision needs complementary capabilities to carry it Craftsmen, partners, employees and institutional resources all took part in the success. Biver's way of expressing ideas and rallying people is easy to remember, but Piquet's craftsmanship, Hayek's backing, and the group's manufacturing and distribution mattered just as much. I'd be wary of writing an industry's revival as a story of a single hero. Swatch's quartz products and industry consolidation are part of this history too. Only by understanding these conditions can we see how an idea travels from persuading others to reliable delivery. High standards and harmful behavior need to be judged separately Business success doesn't prove that rage is a necessary condition. Employees in the case describe passion and generosity, but also humiliation, threats and fear. Both kinds of evidence deserve to be taken seriously. My own judgment is that you can keep intense debate about ideas while clearly opposing harmful ways of treating people. An apology without a change in behavior can hardly give employees stable expectations. The more a leader has achieved, the more they need someone who can calmly voice disagreement. The next venture has to be compatible with life as it is now Selling the company didn't automatically bring fulfillment, and starting over won't automatically solve every problem. At the end of the case, Biver has to weigh the meaning of the work, his family, his recovery and the real authority he'd have. I'd support him in exploring the new opportunity, but only after spelling out the commitment, the role and the boundaries. Hublot is very small and still losing money; he can't assume it will work again just because he once revived a brand. For someone who has already proven what he can do, allowing himself to choose on his own terms may be harder than continuing to prove himself. Takeaways for Arcus42 When tools change, explain anew what people are worth. The judgment, explanation, trust and accountability clients need have to be visible in concrete service, not just in an abstract narrative. Let the promise discipline the delivery. However we express ourselves externally, we need corresponding information and action internally to back it up. Every inconsistency raises the cost of understanding. Pair storytelling with the ability to verify. People who can articulate a direction and people who can find holes and check facts should support each other. A good story needs someone to keep checking it. Protect disagreement even after success. When a leader has often been right in the past, the team more easily stops questioning. Keeping dissent sayable protects future judgment. Before Class My pre-class judgment is that what's most worth learning from Biver is his ability to rediscover value, build community and coordinate action. The behaviors that harmed employees should be left clearly in the reflection. For a craft to endure, it needs someone to reinterpret it, and also people willing to calmly keep doing it well. This piece is a personal learning analysis based on the course case. The people's experiences, business figures and management descriptions are limited to the period covered by the case, and no assessment is made of the current situation of the people or companies involved. Judgments of behavior are my personal pre-class views.

Unit 3, Professor Frances Frei, Operations & Technology: Shohei Ohtani: Achieving the Dream. A teenage boy writes down an enormous dream — and also writes down tidying his room, thanking people, and building lower-body strength. What draws me to Shohei Ohtani's goal chart is exactly this span: a distant wish, carefully placed into the life right in front of him. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Shohei Ohtani grew up in a sporting family in Iwate Prefecture, Japan. His father had played baseball and also coached him. After practices and games, father and son exchanged little notebooks, writing down what had gone well and which movements needed work. A mistake didn't end in frustration; it was turned into something that could be described and practiced again. In high school, his coach Hiroshi Sasaki had players write down goals and introduced the Harada Method. At the center, Ohtani put becoming a rookie coveted as a first-round pick by multiple teams; around it he laid out eight categories of conditions — body, control, mentality, speed, breaking balls, character, luck and more — and then wrote out 64 concrete actions. The chart included strength and technique, but also respecting umpires, caring for equipment, tidying his room and reading. The question it tried to answer went beyond any single game: if I want to become that kind of player, how should I train today, how should I live, how should I treat other people? Career choices also played a part in reaching the goal. Ohtani originally wanted to go straight to the U.S. after high school, but the Nippon-Ham Fighters offered him a path that let him both pitch and hit. He chose to stay, and only later moved to Major League Baseball. The goal persisted; the route did not unfold exactly as the teenager's list had it. The case records his remarkable achievements, and also his adjustments. In 2024, unable to pitch after surgery, he shifted his focus to hitting and baserunning and reached the goal of at least 50 home runs and 50 stolen bases in a single season. The exhibits record 54 home runs that year; in 2025 it was 55. By the end of the case, he had won four MVPs and two World Series titles. These results are astonishing, but what's more worth discussing in class is how to understand the relationship between goals, daily actions, environment and opportunity — without turning a success story into a success formula. My Thinking A goal needs to explain today's actions A useful goal changes how you allocate your attention today. The goal chart breaks a distant wish into supporting conditions, and then into behaviors you can practice. It makes "wanting to be better" concrete. My own understanding is that the most important part of the chart is the reasoning connecting each action to the goal. If you can't say why something helps, filling in every box won't add any sense of direction. Conversely, a plain but well-grounded action may be more worth sticking with than a very complete plan. Reflection makes repetition more than repetition The little notebooks father and son exchanged built a feedback loop long before the prettier chart came along. They didn't just record results; they described his control, his swing and his mistakes, so that experience could be preserved in words. It reminds me that doing something consistently is not the same as consistently learning it. You need to put expectation and reality side by side to know what to keep and what to change next time. If a record is reduced to counting completions, it can hardly serve that purpose. The right environment can protect an unusual ability The Japanese team's offer to develop him as both pitcher and hitter is a crucial condition in this story. If an organization only allows one standard path, then however hard an individual works, they may have to give up another ability too early. My own inclination is to write the choice of environment into the goal plan as well. Whom you learn from, under what kind of evaluation you work, what feedback you can get — all of these affect whether an ability can grow. Willpower matters; the environment deserves to be chosen just as carefully. Character has value, and winning is still uncertain Respect, consideration and caring for your surroundings don't need winning as their only justification. They may help with emotional steadiness, cooperation and sustained commitment, and they have value beyond performance. I wouldn't read "luck" as meaning that doing good inevitably brings good results. Losing a game says nothing about a person's character, and outstanding results don't automatically prove moral worth. Bringing daily habits into your goals can make a person more whole; turning them into some mystical cause of winning or losing goes too far. Serious pursuit includes revising the path Changing his focus for the season after an injury shows that adjusting and persisting can happen at the same time. In 2024 Ohtani concentrated on hitting and baserunning, keeping his demand for excellence while accepting that he couldn't pitch at the time. If all 64 actions become equally urgent tasks, they may eat up too much attention. I'd rather treat the chart as a whole to be tested, and choose a small number of actions from it for the current period. Every so often, look back at the purpose, the evidence and the costs, so the path can be updated. Takeaways for Arcus42 Broad commitments need observable behaviors. Diligence, transparency and reliability in our service should translate into checking information, explaining and following up — not just stay as adjectives. Look at outcomes and process evidence together. A good result may contain luck; a disappointing result may still contain the right actions. A review needs to keep both layers of information. Feedback should come before large-scale repetition. If repetition brings no correction, scale only multiplies the same error. We need to know first what is worth continuing. Values shouldn't shift with short-term returns. Respect, integrity and being clear about what we don't know are worth holding to, even when they don't immediately produce a nice-looking number. Before Class My pre-class choice: high goals, a few actions for the current period, continuous review. In borrowing this method, I'll keep its ability to bring aspirations into daily life — and keep the right to revise the path. You have to look up to see the light in the distance, and still look carefully at the next step beneath your feet. This is a personal study analysis based on a course case; athletic results and events are as described in the case for its time period. It does not treat a single success story as causal proof that the method works, and does not constitute training or health advice.
Count checking as part of efficiency

Unit 3, Professor Frances Frei's Operations & Technology course, AI-First Snack. This time, the prep material isn't a long case about a company. The professor gave us three questions: how I like to use AI, how it will change business over the next 6–18 months, and how I want employees to use it. Something I've been working on lately happens to make a good starting point: using AI to connect my Harvard readings, the professor's questions, bilingual Q&A, my own thinking, the articles and their illustrations. The process has become more complete, and it has also made me increasingly clear about which steps can't be skipped just because an answer appears quickly. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary This is an in-class exercise. The professor asked us to download the data files handed out during the course onto our laptops before class, and to use them in class together with our preferred LLM. I don't have the files yet, so at this point there are no data findings to report; preparation should start from the questions, my experience of using AI, and how to test things. The first question is about personal and professional use. What it asks for isn't a list of tool names, but an account of what AI actually helped with in real tasks. For me, learning and writing have already become one connected process: understand the source text, respond to the questions, then express my judgement. The second question stretches the timeframe to the next 6–18 months. Technology changes fast, but changes in business only become visible through specific work. Faster first drafts and easier search — whether they really improve delivery still depends on checking, rework and handoffs between people. The third question turns to teams. One person occasionally getting a good result and many people reliably completing the same kind of task are two different capabilities. Leaders need to provide suitable tasks, time to practise, quality standards and support when exceptions come up. So my pre-class preparation falls into two parts: sorting through the personal experience of using AI that has already happened, and putting forward testable ideas about the future. The latter are not yet actual business results, and shouldn't be taken as plans already carried out just because they're written in the first person. My Thinking A complete process is worth more than one beautiful answer Turning a reading into a summary is convenient; combining it with the professor's questions, discovering where the evidence is thin, and then practising explaining it in another language — that's where the value gets concrete. In this process, AI can offer candidate structures, compare explanations, help with expression, and also help generate illustrations and previews. Once the different steps are connected, the outputs are easier to keep using. But being connected doesn't mean being automatically right. If a denominator is misread early on, the error may be written up more clearly and more beautifully later. The longer the process, the more the key facts need to be traceable back to the original material. Checking time is part of efficiency too If a first draft goes from an hour to ten minutes, but you then spend an extra hour finding sources and fixing errors, you can't judge the overall improvement by those ten minutes alone. The times here are just an example to show how the calculation works, not my measured results. What I want to measure is the full cycle: drafting, checking, revising, communicating, until the recipient can actually use it. The quality bar has to be the same as well. You can't compare the speed of unreviewed output with work that used to be delivered complete. A truly meaningful improvement is getting the whole thing done faster without any drop in reliability, or doing it better for similar effort. Even the most fluent answer can't decide for me what to believe When preparing a case, AI can supply arguments for several options at once. When they all sound plausible, personal judgement actually matters more. I still have to ask myself: which arguments come from the source text, and which are inferences? If one assumption changes, does the conclusion change? Which cost am I willing to bear? When challenged in class, can I explain rather than just repeat? The outcome of learning can't be judged by the thickness of the document. If the article is finished but I can't clearly state the most important disagreement, the understanding still isn't complete. Employee adoption needs room for practice and feedback The change I'd like to see is people being able to use AI around real tasks: state the goal first, provide the right context, check the output, and know how to proceed when unsure. That takes deliberate arrangement, not just an instruction that "everyone has to use it." You can start with one repetitive task, provide examples, have people who know the business practise together with people willing to experiment, and then compare quality and total time on similar tasks. Failure cases are just as worth showing. How an error was caught helps a team build judgement more than a pretty screenshot does. If employees worry that admitting a problem will make them look like they can't use the tool, learning may stay on the surface. For the next six to eighteen months, start with testable hypotheses I don't want to write my expectations of AI as firm predictions. It's more appropriate to pick a few working hypotheses: which repetitive processing can be reduced, which explanations can come sooner, and which exceptions still need a person to catch them. Start with one process that has clear boundaries, measure the baseline first, then look at the results with AI assistance. Keep the instructions, examples and checks that work; if the effect falls short, adjust or stop. Scaling should happen after the method has been proven useful. The number of times a tool gets used can rise quickly, but service capability has to be built up one delivery at a time. Takeaways for Arcus42 Define value from specific tasks. First say whose problem you're solving and what it is, then decide which part the tool takes part in. With a clear scope, results are easier to evaluate. Keep evidence and judgement separable. Mark in the output which parts are factual basis, which are inference, and which are not yet verified, so the recipient can understand how strong the conclusion is. Keep checking and exception handling in the process. Even after speed improves, it still needs to be clear who confirms which results, and what situations need escalating. Form a shared method through small-scale trials. Record the practices that work, the conditions under which they fail, and the fixes, so experience can be reused by others instead of living only in one person's chat history. Direct people's time towards more valuable judgement. The point of reducing repetitive work is to leave more attention for understanding, relationships, explanation and taking responsibility. That needs to be validated by actual results. Before Class When I bring the data files into class, I want to first confirm what each row represents and how each metric is calculated, and only then look at what conclusions the tool gives. This also corresponds to one expectation I have of using AI: form candidates faster, check the basis more clearly, and decide more carefully what I ultimately want to say and do. This piece is my pre-class thinking for an in-class exercise; the data files have not yet been obtained, and it contains no actual in-class analysis results. The content about business and employees consists of general methods and ideas about the future, and does not represent processes or results already implemented by any organisation.
Leave the other side a way to follow through

Unit 3, Professor Kevin Mohan's Negotiations: Thirteen Days — A Memoir of the Cuban Missile Crisis. Before reading about the Cuban Missile Crisis, I was inclined to think of it as a contest of wills: whoever backs down first loses. Reading the memoir alongside its foreword, that view stopped being enough. Both sides had the capacity to cause enormous destruction, and neither could guarantee that every step would stay fully under control. The truly hard part was protecting your vital interests while still leaving the other side choices it could accept and actually carry out. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary In October 1962, the United States discovered that the Soviet Union was deploying nuclear missiles in Cuba. Neither earlier intelligence assessments nor Soviet assurances had led the US to expect this. Once the new evidence emerged, Kennedy faced not only a weapons threat, but also public commitments, domestic pressure and relations with allies. The Soviet Union and Cuba had their own fears. The Bay of Pigs and US activities aimed at the Castro regime left Cuba worried about another invasion; Khrushchev saw the missile deployment as a way to protect Cuba and change the balance of power. Understanding these motives doesn't mean accepting the secret deployment and the deception, but it does explain why both sides described their own moves as defensive. The US advisers weighed an air strike, an invasion and a naval quarantine. An air strike was direct, but couldn't guarantee eliminating every weapon and might provoke retaliation elsewhere. A quarantine preserved time and room to adjust, but construction on the island continued, and contact at sea could also spark conflict. No option could eliminate the risk. Kennedy chose the quarantine, combining it with military preparations, allied support and negotiation. After a US reconnaissance plane was shot down, the pressure rose sharply, yet he still didn't let retaliation happen automatically, and kept searching for an arrangement that would remove the threat. In the end, the public terms — withdrawal of the missiles from Cuba and a guarantee not to invade Cuba — together with a private arrangement on the missiles in Turkey formed the backdrop to the resolution. Schlesinger's foreword explicitly fills in the secret exchange that the memoir plays down. The crisis was defused, but not without a price, nor did it mean that everyone affected took equal part in the decision. My Thinking The appeal of the first move can hide the disaster of the fourth The temptation of an air strike lies in its directness. Find the weapons, destroy the weapons — it looks like a clear-cut problem. But as long as some weapons remain undiscovered, as long as Soviet casualties would provoke a response, as long as Berlin or Turkey could become the next flashpoint, the problem no longer stays in Cuba. The value of a move has to be judged after factoring in how the other side will respond. This is also the part that's easy to miss in business decisions. Raising prices can improve today's gross margin, cutting staff can reduce today's costs, tough contract terms can increase today's protection. But customers, employees and partners will all respond. However good the numbers from the first move look, they're no substitute for thinking through what happens next. Keeping options open requires concrete execution arrangements A quarantine isn't a gentle label. Warships, submarines, pilots and commanders on the scene are all in motion, and any local incident could change the situation. Kennedy cared about whether ships had time to turn around, whether messages had actually been delivered, and whether an individual incident was enough to trigger retaliation. Whether a strategy can stay limited depends on these seemingly minor execution conditions. So-called flexibility, without authority to pause, channels for information and conditions for review, is likely to remain just a wish expressed in a meeting. Conversely, giving the other side a little time to react has a cost too: construction on the island won't wait. Keeping options open has to go hand in hand with observation and judgment. Dissent needs to feed into the decision, not stay outside the meeting room Among the advisers there were hawkish positions and differing judgments. The president was sometimes absent, so that discussion would be less swayed by authority; different groups had to produce complete plans, not just say what they were for. What interests me more is how this disagreement was used. Once a plan was challenged, it had to answer for its implementation conditions, the opponent's likely response and its possible costs. The argument shifted from positions to testable assumptions. Someone was still responsible for the final decision. Allowing disagreement doesn't mean waiting forever for consensus; the leader's responsibility is to make sure key information gets through, and then to take on the judgment with incomplete information. Beyond the public story, there was a real exchange Reading only the main text, it's easy to remember the US responding to the earlier letter, and the line about not making trades under pressure. The foreword, however, makes clear that the secret arrangement on the missiles in Turkey is a part that can't be ignored. This adds a layer of caution to how I think about "winning a negotiation." The public narrative may emphasize firmness, while the actual agreement depended on mutual adjustment. To judge an outcome, you need to know what each side really gave up and what it kept. Private communication can reduce the pressure of public posturing, but it can also leave those affected without a say. Secret deals in history can't be taken as a direct justification for bypassing authorization in business. What's more worth learning is spelling out the terms within your real authority, and checking that the commitments are consistent with one another. A good deal has to be one the other side can deliver on A concession that can't be explained internally is hard to sustain. Leaving your opponent their dignity isn't just a courtesy; it also affects whether they can follow through. Kennedy avoided publicly claiming credit after the crisis ended, which was consistent with his limited aims all along. What mattered was that the danger came down, not making the other side admit defeat in front of the whole world. The memoir still reflects a participant's perspective, and a successful outcome can't erase chance and the unknown. Information disclosed later showed that the world at the time was more dangerous than the decision-makers knew. An ending like this is worth studying, and worth approaching with humility. Takeaways for Arcus42 First define the problem everyone needs to solve together. If each party only defends its position, it's easy to overlook the losses that all sides actually want to avoid. Write down the goals and constraints first, and only then will you know which terms can be adjusted. Put your preferred option through a reverse test. Those who back a decision should also spell out the circumstances in which it would fail. The more popular a judgment, the more it needs someone to challenge it seriously. Spell out authority to pause and escalate in advance. When new evidence emerges, who can stop an action and who can change a commitment can't be left to guesswork in the moment. Clear authority makes execution steadier. Extend the deal into delivery. Who approves, who implements, how completion is confirmed, how delays are handled — all of these should be part of the arrangement. An agreement is only worth something if the other side can actually deliver on it. Preserve the dignity that cooperation requires. Hold firm on your vital interests, while avoiding humiliation that raises the other side's cost of following through. This is a practical judgment in a long-term relationship. Before Class The question I want to bring to class: when time is short, information is incomplete and the other side is also under internal pressure, how does a leader know whether to keep up the pressure or to change the shape of the agreement? My preliminary answer from this case is to shift attention from posture to process: whether the facts are being updated, whether reactions are controllable, whether the terms are clear, and whether the other side still has a path it can actually follow. These are pre-class reading notes and personal reflections, written on the basis of the assigned historical materials and not yet discussed in class. The business parallels drawn here are general methods, not mechanical analogies to the historical situation, and do not concern the internal affairs of any organization.

Unit 3, Professor Das Narayandas, Market-Facing Functions, Starbucks Korea’s Tank Day: When the Machines Forgot. This was an optional reading. The professor didn't ask us to prepare formally or give us case questions; he just asked us to look at the main text and the first exhibit if we had time. After reading it, what stuck with me wasn't that AI wrote an inappropriate piece of copy, but an organisational phenomenon the case describes: the content went through approval by several people, yet nobody stopped it in time. The process seemed to have been completed, but no judgement actually took place. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary As the case tells it, on 18 May 2026 Starbucks Korea launched a "Tank Day" promotion for a large-capacity stainless steel tumbler. The team used AI to help brainstorm the language, hoping to convey the tumbler's capacity, toughness and memorability, but didn't fully consider what the date and the wording meant historically in Korean society. 18 May is tied to the commemoration of the Gwangju Democratization Movement; and an onomatopoeic expression in the slogan reminded some people of the official cover-up language from another historical event. To the creators it may have been product language; to the people receiving it, it was not a combination that could be understood apart from history. According to the reports and company statements cited in the case, the approval chain involved seven managers, and some approvers reportedly never opened the attachment. The materials don't include the full prompts or operating logs, so we can't conclude that the tool created all the content on its own, let alone simply divide responsibility equally among everyone. What we can see is that this organisational process failed to identify the problem. The campaign was halted quickly, but the screenshots had already spread. The case then describes the apology, personnel changes, the public reaction and investigations, and stores nationwide closing early for training in historical and social sensitivity. A marketing decision made at headquarters ended up affecting the store staff who face customers. The first exhibit places AI applications within the broader marketing system: from identifying needs, designing products and setting prices, to reaching customers, selling, service and fulfilment. That perspective widens the problem. What a company has to judge isn't just whether the copy is good, but what each decision AI takes part in ultimately promises the customer. My Thinking Meaning appears where words meet context Taken on its own, a word can mean strong; placed within a certain date, a certain language and a certain shared memory, it can evoke something entirely different. That kind of shift is hard to capture exhaustively with a "banned words list." Reviewers need to know where, when and to whom the content will appear. Looking at material divorced from where it will be published is like inspecting only the parts of a sentence without seeing what people will finally read. AI can help find associations and list potential issues, but asking another model about the same passage doesn't automatically amount to independent judgement. The person responsible still has to understand the audience, and be able to admit what they don't know. The number of approvers is no substitute for reviewing the content Seven names sounds very safe. But if everyone assumes the person before them has already checked, a signature can become merely the act of passing information along. I'd start by asking: what exactly is each approver responsible for judging? Did they see the final version? Did they have enough time? When they're unsure, can they pause the launch? The answer isn't necessarily to add more layers. A more effective setup might be to have one clearly responsible person check the entire campaign, and, when local culture, factual claims or other sensitive conditions are triggered, bring in someone with real knowledge and authority. When generation gets faster, attention can become the constraint Going from a few lines of copy to dozens of candidates can help a team explore, but it also adds to the screening work. If the volume of what gets published grows accordingly while review time stays the same, people's attention gets spread thin. This isn't a quantified causal conclusion the case offers, but a management risk it helped me see: the drafting time a tool saves isn't necessarily the net time the process saves. Verification, rework, coordination and after-the-fact repair all have to be counted too. I'd rather ask whether the team can deliver results that are just as reliable, or more reliable, in less time. Higher output alone doesn't prove the work has improved. Training has to make it into the next real decision Training in historical and social sensitivity matters. But if, after the training, approval still just means clicking "agree," and the pressure to launch is still greater than the room to raise questions, the same structure may remain. Knowledge needs a place to be used. For example: campaign materials that clearly list the date, region, audience, final copy and visuals; someone who checks those combinations; a quick channel for raising doubts; a record of what was changed and why. Repair can't fall on the front line alone, either. Whoever decided on the campaign should take part in explaining and changing things. Store staff need support, not to bear headquarters' mistakes alone in front of customers. The customer journey is longer than one ad Exhibit 1 reminded me that AI can also affect prices, offers, service replies, inventory planning and delivery promises. Customers don't necessarily distinguish which team or tool these outputs came from; what they encounter is one and the same brand. So evaluation can't stop at clicks and conversions. Were the promises kept? Did returns and complaints rise? Were exceptions handled properly? When customers come back, is the experience consistent? A reply can be very fluent and a promotion very attractive, but if the capability and accountability aren't there behind them, efficiency at the front can turn into disappointment further down the line. Takeaways for Arcus42 Let the factual basis follow the expression. Next to every important claim you should be able to find its source and the conditions under which it applies, so fluent prose doesn't make uncertainty disappear. Check the final draft in the recipient's context. Look not only at whether the words are accurate, but at how they'll be understood at a specific time, in a specific relationship and setting. Make review match real responsibility. Everyone knows what they're judging, and who to go to when they have a doubt. Adding signatures is no substitute for that. Keep the human ability to handle exceptions. Standard processes can improve efficiency, but when there's a contradiction, emotion or an important promise, you need people who can catch the problem. Count quality and rework as part of efficiency. How much time you saved has to be looked at alongside how much extra checking, correcting and communicating you did; only then can you judge the real gain. Before Class What I'd like to keep discussing is this: when AI makes output faster and cheaper, where are we going to put human attention? My initial choice is to put it on meaning, evidence, exceptions and promises. Tools can help with drafting, but an organisation still needs someone who has truly read the thing and is willing to take responsibility for the final decision. This piece is a study summary based on an assigned HBS reading. Related events and reports follow the case's account, and no judgement is made on subsequent investigations; the governance suggestions are my personal pre-class thoughts and do not represent classroom conclusions or the internal practice of any institution.
Management Control: A Letter from Prison
Time is part of the facts too

Unit 3, Professor Eugene Soltes's Control course, A Letter from Prison. The contracts were real, the products were delivered, and the cash came in. So one manager came to believe that booking revenue a few days early was fundamentally different from the more sensational financial scandals. This case makes you see again that time itself is part of the facts. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Computer Associates was an enterprise software company. Stephen Richards joined the company's sales force in 1988 and rose all the way to head of worldwide sales. High growth, high targets and high pay accompanied his climb, and the company lived under constant pressure from quarterly results. Under the accounting treatment of the time, as the case describes it, once a software licence contract met conditions such as signature, delivery and reasonable assurance of collection, the licence fee could be recognised all at once in that quarter. A customer might buy a term running several years, yet a signature a few days late would change which quarter the entire licence revenue landed in. Customers, too, gradually learned to wait for better terms at quarter-end. Some managers stretched the quarter operationally, booking contracts signed after the quarter closed as if they belonged to it. The deals could be real; the periods were not. In Q2 of FY2000, correctly recorded revenue was about US$1.047 billion, and another roughly US$558 million was recognised early; reported earnings per share were US$0.60, just above the market expectation of US$0.59 — stripped of the improper recognition, they would have been US$0.05. After media questions and regulatory investigations surfaced, the company's initial internal investigation did not reveal the full picture. A further independent investigation found the evidence in documents and electronic records that had been left out. The case also describes executives misleading the investigation, and the head of internal legal later admitting to directing this behaviour. Richards pleaded guilty in 2006 and was sentenced to seven years in prison. In 2008, he wrote from prison to Eugene Soltes, then a student, explaining the targets, incentives, recognition for performance and managerial pressure he had faced. He also wrote that managers often find themselves in grey areas. The professor's questions therefore have two layers: how serious was the conduct, really; and if the same numbers had been reached using the flexibility the accounting standards allow, would the judgement change? Finally, we have to answer what we would do if we stood in that position, and what consequences we would be willing to bear. My Thinking A few days' difference can change the whole picture of the business Which quarter revenue belongs to affects how others understand a company. In this case, the misattribution made a result that fell well short of expectations look as though it had just beaten them. What it changed was the performance investors saw. My own judgement is that the fact that the deals were ultimately real cannot offset the fact that the reporting at the time was not. Nor should the total recognised early be called stolen cash or investors' total losses. Criticising a behaviour clearly also requires staying accurate about the numbers. Understanding the pressure doesn't require cancelling the responsibility The mechanics of pressure are worth understanding, and the choices individuals made also need to be seen. Richards describes how analysts' expectations found their way into internal targets, then were passed down to teams through the organisational structure, incentives and management style. That is an important explanation. Another point in the letter struck me: beyond money, recognition for performance and self-identity can also exert enormous force.
