When "always delivering" becomes part of who you are, admitting to missing a target even once can become extraordinarily hard. A control system that only watches bonuses may miss this quieter driver. The same numbers call for asking how they were formed Reasonable accounting judgement and deliberately changing the facts should be evaluated separately. If an estimate is supported by evidence, applied consistently and properly disclosed, it can't be deemed wrong simply because it helped hit a target. But legality alone can't answer every management question either. Postponing valuable R&D might raise current-period profit while weakening the future; a barely defensible accounting treatment can also make it hard for readers to see how the business is changing. I would look at the facts, the basis for the judgement, the transparency and the long-term value together, rather than only at the profit on the bottom line. Controls have to hold when the target is about to be missed The real test happens on the last day, not on the day training is completed. If everyone knows the date can't be changed but no one can bear the consequences of missing the target, the rules will keep getting reinterpreted. I would record signing, revenue recognition and collection separately, preserving the real dates and the original evidence. For requests that fall outside the normal process, I would provide a channel that allows independent review. That the internal investigation failed in this case is also a reminder: handing a problem to someone with a formal title does not automatically mean it has been handled independently. The right choice should also spell out its cost Refusing to extend the quarter could mean smaller bonuses, pressure on the share price, even losing your job. If the classroom answer is just "I would stick to my principles," it skips the genuinely hard part. My own choice would still be to keep the real dates, report the actual shortfall, and push for independent review. At the same time, I would fix forecasting and incentives so the company can face the business issues of late-signed contracts and customers' quarter-end bargaining. Accepting the short-term cost doesn't guarantee an immediate reward; it simply lets subsequent decisions be rebuilt on credible information. Takeaways for Arcus42 Conclusions should be traceable to the information available at the time. Original sources, dates and the reasoning process are the foundation for later review. You can't use answers learned afterwards to rewrite the uncertainty of the moment. Allow people to report honestly that something isn't done. If a team can only report good news, it may gradually shift its energy to maintaining the appearance of completion. Only real progress can support planning the next step. Dissent needs a usable path. When the person who sets the targets also decides all the evaluations, doubts are hard to voice in full. Someone needs to be able to hear the problem independently. Metrics should be examined at the level of behaviour. Every seemingly clear number encourages certain choices. Besides asking whether the target was met, we should also ask what people gave up in order to meet it. Before Class My pre-class judgement is that this was a serious distortion of reporting. Genuinely reasonable accounting choices deserve a different assessment; practices that mislead about the facts can't be lightly glossed over just because the deals eventually happened. Reliable records preserve, for the future, a starting point that doesn't need to be explained over and over. This piece is a personal study analysis based on the course case and the letter in it. The facts and accounting context are limited to the period of the case, and nothing here constitutes current legal, accounting or investment advice. It does not cite the preface to Paper to Practice , which was assigned separately and has yet to be obtained.
How to grow without losing the brand's reason for being

Unit 3, Professor Juan Alcácer's Strategy course, Golden Goose: Reshaping Luxury. A company that sells distressed sneakers has grown to hundreds of millions of euros in revenue. The next question is how to keep growing while holding on to the reason customers wanted to walk in the door in the first place. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Golden Goose was founded in 2000, bringing together the handcraft of Venice, Italy, with the laid-back style of California. It started out making lifestyle apparel; what really drove the business's expansion was the Super-Star sneaker, launched in 2007. Its shoes look like they've already been worn. Scuffs, fading and wear become part of the design. Traditional luxury often emphasizes carefully preserved perfection; this brand tries to make it easier for people to wear its products into their own lives. A shoe doesn't have to look brand-new forever to be cherished. Its later development didn't rely on one aesthetic alone. Private equity shareholders came in one after another, and the organization built out functions such as HR, merchandising, marketing and legal. From 2017 the company accelerated its rollout of directly operated stores and brought e-commerce operations in-house. Starting from six directly operated stores, it reached 215 stores by the end of 2024. In 2019 the brand began offering Co-Creation. Customers choose details together with in-store artisans, turning a pair of shoes into something personal to them. Later it added repair, re-creation, resale and recycling services, and also set up an academy to train artisans. Meanwhile, CRM data was used for site selection, product recommendations, customer outreach and inventory allocation. According to the case exhibits, 2024 revenue was €654.6 million, with sneakers still contributing about 87% of sales. The company already has ready-to-wear, accessories and kidswear, but there's no obvious answer yet for where the next stage of growth should come from. There are three paths ahead: 1. Expand existing stores, adding more sneakers and co-creation services; co-creation starts at about US$150, and needs floor space as well as skilled artisans. 2. Strengthen ready-to-wear and accessories; existing customers know the brand, but whether they're willing to extend that affinity to other categories is something only purchasing behavior can answer. 3. Keep entering new geographies; a standard store costs about US$500,000 to US$600,000 to open, and the company requires payback within two years and a target store EBITDA margin of 30%. My Thinking What customers buy is more complete than a pair of shoes Product, artisans, stores and customer data together make up the customer experience. The distressed look is easy to see; the service and learning capabilities behind it are far less visible. Customers take part in creating, sales staff carefully gather feedback, and the company then uses that information to adjust products and stores. None of these moves exists in isolation. A small number of classic styles provides recognizability, co-creation provides variety, direct retail provides relationships, and data lets those relationships continue. My own understanding is that to judge whether an advantage can be copied, you have to look at whether competitors can organize the whole set of activities. Imitating a look and building a consistent experience are two jobs of very different difficulty. Experiences can scale; people's attention has to be cultivated More floor space is easy to put in a budget; more skilled, patient people takes time. The more popular co-creation becomes, the more artisan capability, waiting times and variation in quality deserve attention. The academy is an important investment because it gradually turns craftsmanship that used to depend on individuals into a capability the organization can sustain. But training shouldn't be imagined as an assembly line that churns out people immediately. And a customer feeling understood isn't the same as a sales associate getting through the full standard script. Replication should happen at the level of quality standards, training and ways of working together. How each individual expresses things still needs room. Each new category needs one more reason to buy Liking a brand doesn't mean being willing to buy everything the brand puts out. A sneaker customer might admire a jacket, but won't necessarily choose it at the same price point. Ready-to-wear means new design judgment, size assortments, inventory structure and returns risk. Seeing revenue grow and immediately treating it as a mature second growth curve makes it easy to overlook the resources that growth is consuming. My inclination is to keep experimenting and use existing customers to test real conversion. Full-price sell-through, repeat purchases and inventory turns are closer to the answer than "customers know we make ready-to-wear too." As revenue moves forward, watch profit and cash too The quality of growth has to be judged from the relationships between different financial statements. In the case, 2024 revenue grew about 11.5%, but EBIT fell slightly; inventory also grew faster than revenue. This doesn't directly prove the company has a problem. Store openings, organizational investment and product preparation can all temporarily affect profit and inventory. But it reminds me that a new round of growth can't just hand in a revenue report card. Store EBITDA margin also can't stand in for the cash payback period. Leases, fit-outs, training and inventory all have to be paid for by someone in the end. Deepen existing commitments first, then decide where to extend I would first expand co-creation in stores where demand is already clear, then selectively enter new geographies. Keep ready-to-wear and accessories to small-scale tests, rather than rolling out all three paths at full scale at once. That means accepting a slower pace of diversification and continuing to carry the concentration risk of the sneaker category. But the benefit is that the company can judge more clearly where new revenue is coming from, which costs have to grow alongside it, and which capabilities can genuinely be replicated. If bigger stores only bring higher rents and longer waits, co-creation should stay where it fits. If the incremental cash, experience and repeat purchases all hold up, keep expanding. Takeaways for Arcus42 Let clients help define the outcome. The value of participation is that it helps both sides understand needs and trade-offs more accurately. Personalization on display only becomes meaningful when it enters actual decisions. Let information change the next interaction. Recording client preferences is only the beginning. It should change when you reach out, how you ask questions, and where people focus their attention. Count people's capacity as part of growth. Before adding services, look at who will do the new work and how much judgment and communication it requires. An increase in the number of services can't automatically be treated as an increase in service capacity. Re-validate the reason with every extension. Existing trust gives a new service a chance to be understood, but in the end it's still the client who decides whether it deserves to exist. Before Class My pre-class choice is to deepen first, then replicate. As a business grows, it needs to keep checking: have the details that made customers want to come closer grown along with it? This piece is based on the HBS assigned case, for my own pre-class learning and management reflection. Figures follow the basis of the case exhibits; judgments stay within the case context and do not constitute investment advice regarding any company involved.
How customization becomes a repeatable business

Unit 3, Professor Juan Alcacer, Strategy: Breezm: Innovative 3D-Printed Eyewear. A pair of glasses you wear on your face every day can have the right prescription, a great look, and a badly balanced weight all at the same time. Breezm starts from this very specific discomfort and tries to reorganize how glasses are made and served. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Park had worked at an eyewear brand and knew consumers and retail; Sung moved from finance and investment banking into manufacturing, and noticed that glasses are small and relatively high-value — possibly a good fit for 3D printing. Combining this with Humax Optics' manufacturing experience, the two spent a year on research and founded Breezm in South Korea in 2017. What they care about is fit. Traditional frames are produced first, and consumers then choose from a limited set of sizes; Breezm wants to put facial measurement before production. Customers book an appointment, come into the store for a scan, eye exam and consultation, choose a style, and then an optometrist fine-tunes the fit before the order goes to the factory. In 2018 the team tested demand with ten pop-up stores, then opened its first permanent store. As the business grew, the company turned fitting adjustments that used to take a professional designer one or two hours into work an optometrist can do in about ten minutes after one day of training. Technology began to change the division of labor in delivery. The product changed too. Polymer frames are 3D-printed; when it came to titanium products, the team found printing too expensive, so it switched to laser cutting and proprietary hinges. Customers end up waiting about ten to fourteen days to pick up their glasses, and the company offers a forty-five-day guarantee for returns, exchanges or remakes. By 2022 Breezm had eight stores and sold about fifteen thousand pairs of glasses over the year. The exhibits show revenue of US$4.448 million, up about 55% from the year before; but the operating loss also widened to US$2.901 million. The factory had idle capacity, and the stores still required a lot of consultation time. The two founders want the company to break even in 2024 and go public in 2027. There are three options in front of them: 1. Optimize the existing Seoul operation, improving equipment and store efficiency. 2. Replicate stores in other Korean cities, expanding domestic scale. 3. Go overseas, looking for bigger markets and different willingness to pay. The Korean market is about 1.4% of the global eyewear market, so the overseas opportunity is genuinely tempting. The question is whether the next growth map can be carried by the current way of delivering. My Thinking The value of customization has to land in how the glasses wear Customers pay for a better fit; the technology's job is to deliver on that promise. The pressure on the bridge of the nose, the length of the temples, the position of the lenses — these are all differences you can feel in everyday use. My own take is that the strategic clarity most worth keeping at Breezm is the switch to laser cutting when metal printing didn't make sense on cost. It was willing to change the technology to keep its promise to customers. This also reminds me that when evaluating an innovation, you need to ask: which hassle for the user has actually gone down? Equipment can be bought; coordination takes time to grow Breezm's advantage lives in the links between measurement, fitting, manufacturing and feedback. Similar printers can be bought, and material suppliers may serve competitors too, but getting optometrists to do the right fitting faster requires software, training and hands-on experience working together continuously. The 1,200 measurement points in the case can easily become the hero of the technology narrative. What I'd rather dig into is whether this data reduces remakes, whether it makes the next customer more comfortable, whether it helps new staff become competent faster. Only when it can answer these questions does accumulating data gradually become an operating capability. Gross margin hasn't yet answered whether the company can make money Gross margins of about 60% and continuing losses can coexist. Breezm has to pay not just for materials and manufacturing, but also for consultation, R&D, marketing, stores and management. In 2022, SG&A was US$4.475 million, slightly more than full-year revenue. The early total frame cost in the exhibits is also worth reading closely: the US$313 includes manufacturing, R&D and SG&A, and can't all be called manufacturing cost. Mixing frame prices from different periods, revenue per complete pair of glasses and total unit cost would build the expansion discussion on the wrong numbers. My own inclination is to first break out, by store and by product, the contribution after deducting the real service and customer-acquisition costs. A busier factory doesn't automatically mean a healthier company. Replicate the operating results first, then the store count I'd first give Seoul a time-boxed operating test. Can appointments smooth out busy and quiet periods? Can digital fitting raise qualified deliveries per optometrist hour? Will the remake rate rise with volume? Can another team achieve the same results? Once these questions are answered, replicating one store in another Korean city becomes a meaningful test. Without first defining the operating results to be replicated, the number of stores opened can easily become a good-looking but incomplete metric. The overseas opportunity is worth keeping, and also needs to be proven on its own A bigger market needs to be validated separately from customers being more willing to pay. The US eyewear market is far larger than Korea's, but local service, customer acquisition, prescription and return costs will change too. Moving Korea's gross margin to the US and multiplying it by a bigger market size is not an overseas plan. I'd run low-cost overseas demand research in parallel, looking for groups clearly bothered by standard frames. If paid commitments and local service trials show better economics, then adjust the expansion sequence. Choosing to optimize first may cost you a step; that cost should be acknowledged, not packaged as risk-free prudence. Takeaways for Arcus42 A customized service needs a result you can explain. I'd rather ask which errors of judgement, rounds of back-and-forth or missed information the service reduced. The more complex the delivery, the more you need to spell out the improvement the client actually gets. Standardization can protect personalization. Information gathering, basic checks and process records can be reused. That's the only way to save people's time for the questions that are truly different for each family. Data should record outcomes. Having more material doesn't mean having better judgement. Only by recording how advice was understood, carried out and corrected can it help the next engagement. Before replicating, test the dependence on individuals. If a service can only be done by the founder personally, scaling up will keep squeezing the same person's attention. You need to first verify whether others can do work of equal quality within clear boundaries. Before Class My pre-class choice is to validate the quality of the Seoul operation first, while keeping a small-scale overseas exploration going. For customization to become a repeatable business, different customers need to get the right result, and different teams need to deliver it at an affordable cost. Once a pair of glasses fits a face, the next question only begins: how do you make that fit happen, reliably, many more times? This article is a personal study analysis based on a course case; the figures and business situation refer to the period described in the case. It does not constitute an investment judgement on, or an assessment of the current operations of, the company concerned. The expansion sequence and testing suggestions in the text are my personal pre-class views.
Saying clearly the things that are hard to talk about

Unit 3, Professor Christina Wing's Unspeakable: Unspeakable: The Taboo Topics We Avoid and How to Talk About Them, and Note on Difficult Conversations in the Family Enterprise. Some arrangements make perfect sense on the day they're written down. Many years later, they're still sitting there in the documents, while people's lives have moved on somewhere else. This session's two readings are about how those changes can be seen, and how they can be put into words. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary The introduction to Unspeakable opens with an email after a funeral. Luis Garcia founded a successful dry-cleaning business and gave his family a comfortable life. He was thoughtful about many things and prided himself on treating people fairly. But there were a few topics he never wanted to discuss: money, succession, and the fact that one day he would be gone. Whenever his children tried to bring them up, he'd say there was still time, and that they could figure it out themselves later. A few days after the funeral, the three children received an email from a lawyer they'd never met. The attachment laid out their father's arrangements: control of the business went to the elder daughter, the family home to the son and his wife, and the remaining assets into a trust that benefited all three children but came with quite a few restrictions. Everyone was surprised, and each believed they understood what their father had really intended. The trouble was, they couldn't point to a single conversation they had all been part of that explained why these decisions were made. The will had been written twenty years earlier. Back then, the elder daughter lived near her father and was well placed to take over the business; the son had just started out in education, with a modest income, and needed the stability a house would bring; the younger daughter's finances were shaky, and her father hoped to protect her through restrictions. Put back in that moment, the arrangements had their reasons. But twenty years on, the elder daughter had moved out of state, and the son had also left the area and become an accomplished professor. The younger daughter — the one who had originally worried her father — ended up staying on to work in the business and living at home to care for her ageing father. Life had changed, but the arrangements stayed frozen in the past. The original considerations were never revisited, and the father never worked out together with his children what would count as fair now. According to Wing's account, within a year the three children were no longer speaking to one another. She notes in the book that some names have been anonymised. The problem in this story has a clear time span: a decision that was reasonable at the outset became hard to understand in a reality that went twenty years without an update. The accompanying HBS note grounds this theme in concrete methods: tell the other person the topic of the conversation in advance, build a shared understanding, stay objective, and agree on next steps at the end. It offers three sample dialogues — on succession, inheritance and a family prenuptial agreement — and lists questions the next generation of a family can ask. The prep question the professor left us is very direct: think of a conversation you've been putting off, and write down who it's with, why you haven't had it, and what the waiting is costing. My Thinking Silence robs a decision of the chance to be updated The three Garcia children understood the same arrangements differently because the realities they were each holding had already diverged. Who stayed in the business, who took on the caregiving, who needed support — the picture twenty years ago and twenty years later was not the same. If those changes are never put on the table, a single document ends up carrying several people's mutually incompatible expectations. A decision needs reasons, and it also needs someone to recheck whether those reasons still hold. The same goes for succession plans, partnership roles and key appointments in a company. My own take is that maintaining an arrangement requires someone to keep questioning its premises. Does this person still want that job? Is the person who originally took on the risk still bearing the same risk? When the facts change, does everyone know where to raise an adjustment? Paper can preserve a decision. Understanding has to keep happening between people. Consideration means giving the other person a chance to choose Maya, in the introduction, is a star employee at a consulting firm. Her manager considers her indispensable, and clients often ask for her by name. When a more senior role opens up, everyone assumes she'll get the promotion. But she has been back from parental leave for only six months. Her baby often fusses and cries, and she looks exhausted. Her manager thinks adding responsibility now would make things harder for her, and also feels family matters are too private to ask about — so, without discussing it with her, gives the opportunity to someone else. When Maya later asks about it, her manager says they assumed she didn't want to take on such a role right now. She admits she might well have said no. But she's shocked that she was never even asked. A well-meant judgement can still take away someone's chance to make their own decision. What's worth talking through here is what the role requires, what she herself wants, and what support she'd like to have. How much of her private situation she chooses to share can be left up to her. My own take is that consideration should leave room for asking. We can have our observations and guesses, but we also need to give the other person room to correct them. Being willing to face a problem also means leaving room for the unknown This session has a premise worth probing: not every conversation that hasn't happened yet is stalled because someone is afraid to speak up. Sometimes we're willing to face the problems we can already see, but don't yet know that another problem exists. Steve, in the HBS note, is in exactly that situation. He's 29, has worked in private equity, and is about to start business school. He has always assumed he'll take over one day. His mother, however, believes he loves his work outside and doesn't want to join the family business. She herself was once required by her father to join the company, so she wants to give her son more freedom. His mother also has another successor in mind: John, who already works on the company's sales team. But she has never asked John whether he wants to take over, either. And so three people's futures rest partly on understandings that have never been confirmed. Being willing to talk about what you know needs to go hand in hand with another ability: discovering what you don't know. For example: "I've always assumed you want to stay on — is that right?" Or: "Is there any part of this that I haven't thought of but that matters a lot to you?" My own take is that candour also includes uncertainty about your own judgement. Only if you're still willing to make room for new information after stating your position can a conversation change what you understood before. Once it's raised, agree on who takes the next step Steve's conversation with his mother doesn't settle on the spot who will take over. The progress it makes is more concrete: in two weeks, get the third-generation members together to find out what each of them wants; Steve drafts the invitation email, his mother sends it, and she has her assistant book the meeting room. This part deserves attention. Many important issues have already been raised, and have even drawn the response "we should find time to talk about this properly." But who will organise it, what information is needed, and when to pick it up again still have no answers. After you speak up, the issue still needs to enter a process that can keep moving forward. The HBS note's three steps map onto exactly this. First, build a shared understanding. Explain why you want to talk and what you hope to clarify, and make it clear you're willing to hear the other person's view. The material suggests that, ideally, you give at least 24 hours' notice so the other person can prepare. Second, stay objective. Stick to facts that can be confirmed, and avoid presenting guesses as the other person's motives. When emotions run too high, you can pause and give both sides time to regroup. Third, agree on next steps. Restate what each of you heard, which questions now have answers, which still need information, and who will do what next and when you'll talk again. My own inclination is that a first conversation can aim for just one small piece of progress that both sides agree on. The cost is accepting that you may not get a final answer this time, and committing time to follow up. But it gives a huge, daunting problem somewhere you can actually start. Explaining the rules in advance reduces personal misunderstandings In another example in the HBS note, Crystal is about to get married. Her father suddenly calls her into his office and hands her a stack of prenuptial agreements that she and her fiancé need to sign. Her first feeling is that her father doesn't trust her partner. Only as the conversation goes on does she learn that this is a uniform family arrangement, and she just happens to be the first in her generation to marry. The father is talking about family rules; the daughter hears a verdict on a specific relationship. That information gap puts the conversation on the defensive from the very start. The later a rule is explained, the more easily it's taken as an ad hoc judgement about a particular person. How family members join the business, what their pay is based on, how things are adjusted when performance falls short — these run into similar problems. Explaining rules in advance doesn't mean the rules are necessarily reasonable. They still need to be explained and discussed, and they need to accommodate differing opinions. It's just that when the discussion happens before a specific person is asked to accept a particular outcome, everyone has a better chance of seriously understanding the rule's purpose and its costs. Takeaways for Arcus42 Treat the questions that haven't been clarified yet as part of the work. Even a fully organised set of materials may still fail to answer what a particular family member really cares about. In discussions, you can separate confirmed facts, each party's understanding, and the questions still to be clarified, so the follow-up work has a clear point of entry. Give the people affected a chance to speak. A well-meant interpretation one person makes on behalf of others needs to leave room for the people themselves to add to it or correct it. Who takes part in which round of discussion should also match the issue and the wishes of everyone involved. Let tools help with follow-up; let people carry the communication. In an AI-native way of working, technology can help organise information that people have agreed may be recorded, flag to-dos and track progress. Opening up sensitive topics, understanding emotions, and making the final decisions still require the people involved and the right professionals. When recording next steps, also record the disagreements that remain. The end of a meeting doesn't mean everyone has reached the same view. Writing down clearly where there is agreement and where there isn't yet lets the next conversation pick up from where things really stand. As life changes, recheck the premises of your arrangements. Family members' wishes, responsibilities and circumstances change. Building in regular opportunities for discussion helps existing arrangements keep up with reality; where specific legal, tax or investment matters are involved, the relevant professionals need to be part of the judgement. Before Class In this session, I want to keep pressing on two questions: how do you discover the problems you haven't yet realised exist? And when an issue has been raised but no arrangement has taken shape, how do you get everyone willing to move it forward together? My pre-class vote goes to one concrete standard: by the end of a conversation, our understanding of the next step should be clearer than when we started. This piece is a pre-class discussion based on the introduction to Christina Wing's Unspeakable and HBS 624-044, Note on Difficult Conversations in the Family Enterprise . The Garcia and Maya stories appear on pages 1–4 of the introduction; Steve, Crystal and the conversation methods are on pages 2–7 of the HBS note. Some names have been anonymised by the original author. The extended reflections here are my personal understanding and do not constitute legal, tax or investment advice.
What kind of shareholders does growth need?

Unit 3, Professor Martin Sinozich's Finance course, Mercado Bitcoin: M&A, IPO, or Series B?. When a startup finally reaches the point where capital is chasing it, it also starts facing another question: once the money comes in, who decides how the company grows? Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary On April 10, 2021, Mercado Bitcoin chairman Roberto Dagnoni had less than a day to decide. The company was preparing an IPO, two large banks were in acquisition talks, and SoftBank had just sent over a US$200 million investment offer valid for 24 hours. A few months earlier, he had still been running around trying to close a much smaller round. Mercado Bitcoin, or MB, was founded in Brazil in 2013 by brothers Gustavo and Mauricio Chamati. The original business was simple: let customers buy and sell bitcoin with the local currency, the real. In the early days they faced the same choice again and again — should limited money go into product first, or into security first? The brothers chose security: they paid for audits, built their own trading platform, and did customer identity verification and record-keeping voluntarily while regulatory requirements were still incomplete. When the market rallied in 2017, the company's revenue for the year exceeded US$24 million, customers approached 871,000, and staff grew from 8 to 85. The founders also realised the next stage would need different experience. They brought in Dagnoni and Reinaldo Rabelo, who had worked at the Brazilian exchange B3, to add governance, compliance and financial-markets experience. The trough that followed in 2018 showed the team the other side of expansion: revenue fell, expenses rose, the EBITDA margin dropped to about 33%, and headcount was cut in half. The experience didn't make them give up. Management broadened its goal to financial market infrastructure, using 2TM as the holding platform, and gradually built out wallets, custody, asset tokenisation and other financial services. In 2020 the company had revenue of about US$21.25 million, EBITDA of about US$8.1 million, and 2.125 million users by year-end. Yet its first outside funding still took about a year: it eventually raised almost US$20 million at a pre-money valuation of US$64 million. The audit the investors required covered both the financial statements and verification of the customer assets in custody. A few months later, the market heated up fast. MB wanted to expand into more Latin American countries and Europe, acquire small companies, recruit technical talent and add products, with plans to grow the team from 200 to 750. Early shareholders also wanted to cash out part of the wealth that had been concentrated in the company for years. Veteran investor Hélio Seibel often reminded everyone at board meetings: “If you only have one option, then you have no options.” Now Dagnoni finally had three options in front of him, each with a different price tag: 1. IPO: list in Brazil, expected to raise US$220 million to US$350 million, at a valuation of US$1.1 billion to US$2 billion. The company would enter the public markets and start bearing the pressure of continuous disclosure and market pricing. 2. Bank M&A: two banks wanted a controlling stake, at valuations of up to about US$1.5 billion. The banks could offer distribution, regulatory experience and organisational support, but earn-out payments tied to future performance and put/call rights on the shares were still under discussion. 3. SoftBank Series B: US$100 million into the company as a zero-coupon convertible note, plus another US$100 million to buy existing shares. The secondary shares would trade at a US$1.5 billion valuation; the convertible would later convert at a 20% discount, with a pre-money valuation cap of US$2 billion and an 18-month term, plus preferred shares, a board seat and IPO price-protection arrangements. My Thinking With a big round, first work out whose pocket the money goes into US$200 million easily becomes a single, complete impression. But in this deal, the new money that actually supports building the company is US$100 million. The other half goes to the existing shareholders selling their shares. Both parts have value. The company needs money for technology, compliance and new markets; the founders and employees may also need to reduce the risk of having their personal wealth overly concentrated. A moderate amount of liquidity can sometimes make founders more patient operators. The problem comes from letting one total stand in for two budgets. The company has to answer how much money the most important capability-building ahead requires; the shareholders have to answer how much willingness to share the risk they keep after taking cash off the table. My own take is that a financing plan needs to explain both where the money goes and how the benefits are split. Mix the two together, and it's easy to mistake a deal that satisfies some shareholders for one that has given the company enough money to grow. Valuation must be read together with rights The banks' US$1.5 billion, the IPO's US$1.1 billion to US$2 billion, and SoftBank's US$2 billion cap look on the surface like a single question of which is biggest. In reality, they buy different rights. The banks want control; what they're buying is access to new markets and future synergies. Public shareholders buying into a listed company will keep watching revenue, profit and governance. What SoftBank offers is a combination: buy existing shares now at one price, and later convert the new money into preferred shares through a protected mechanism. The US$2 billion cap limits the investor's conversion price. If the next round values the company at US$2 billion, the 20% discount means this new money converts at the equivalent of a US$1.6 billion pre-money valuation; if the next round is only US$1 billion, under the same simplified mechanism, it's US$800 million. It does not protect a US$2 billion floor for the founders. On top of that, the IPO ratchet compensates the investor in certain scenarios where the listing is priced unfavourably. The case doesn't disclose the exact formula, so the extra dilution can't be calculated precisely; but it will affect how common shareholders view a future listing. My own inclination is to first get clear on whether the discount, the preference and the IPO compensation are stacking protections, and only then push for a better-looking valuation. The fine print in the contract will decide who takes the weight first the next time the market turns. Growth forecasts need to be tested against a downturn MB's customer acquisition metrics look great. In 2020, the estimated customer lifetime value was US$138.70 and customer acquisition cost was US$9.30; in Q1 2021, the two became US$77.15 and US$3.99. LTV/CAC rose from about 15x to about 19x. The ratio improved, but the estimated value of each customer fell. Acquisition cost fell even faster, making the overall metric look better. That should prompt management to keep asking: will these customers keep trading, will they use other services, and will they stay once the market cools? The revenue mix is also worth breaking down. In 2020, about 52% of revenue fell in the Services-Exchange category — trading, custody, OTC and so on; about 46% fell in the Financial category, which includes a range of activities such as treasury and float. Not all revenue can be treated as stable, recurring fees. The case's 2025 revenue target is about US$822 million, nearly 39 times 2020. Over five years, that implies a compound annual growth rate of about 108%. Meanwhile, some of the segment forecasts in the exhibits have inconsistent definitions and need further checking. My own take is that even after raising big money, the budget must still be executable when the market cools. Spending on security, custody and compliance is hard to shrink in step with trading volume. 2018 already taught the team that lesson once; capital should give them more room the next time things contract. The banks' distribution advantage needs to be priced together with control CEO Rabelo supported taking the bank acquisition seriously, for very practical reasons. The company needs to work with regulators, needs top talent, and needs customers to feel safe keeping their assets in custody. A bank's experience and distribution could help, and its existing customers could become an entry point for new business. These capabilities have economic value. If you compare financing options only on valuation and dilution, you underestimate what a strategic buyer contributes. Capabilities a team would take years to build itself can sometimes be gained by joining a bigger system. But the banks also need control. MB had hoped to become financial infrastructure serving many kinds of institutions; once inside one bank, its product priorities, partners and pace of innovation would all be shaped by the parent's goals. The distribution synergies promised in an acquisition also need concrete resource commitments and execution plans before they materialise. My own take is that before choosing a strategic buyer, you need to be clear about which capability the company lacks most. If the gap is mainly distribution and regulatory organisation, a bank may be a good fit; if the core opportunity lies in independently connecting more institutions, the cost of handing over control is higher. I would choose the Series B and accept the cost of its terms My pre-class vote is Series B, with the IPO second and bank M&A third. That includes the strict premise the professor set: assume all three offers are final, and my choice can't rest on a renegotiation that is sure to succeed. So the reason can't simply be that a bank merger is too slow, or that the IPO might fail. What I value is that the Series B offers US$100 million for the company, US$100 million of liquidity for existing shareholders, and room to keep building the platform independently — all at once. For a team in the middle of broadening its revenue sources and governance capabilities, that combination is attractive. The case against is just as strong for the IPO: the company might raise more money and also have tradable stock for future acquisitions. If it's confirmed that the necessary investment over the next phase significantly exceeds US$100 million, and the IPO could fill that gap, it could well be the better choice. But the case has no complete cash flow budget, so you can't claim MB must immediately spend money on the scale of a full IPO. I would put core technology, security and compliance first, and arrange cross-border expansion, acquisitions and new products into a sequenced plan. The cost of the Series B is that common shareholders have to accept more conditional allocation of rights. The 20% conversion discount, preferred shares, the IPO ratchet, and a possible future down round could all affect the value the founders and employees keep. A high valuation also raises expectations for growth in the next stage. I am willing to bear these costs at this stage, but they need to be laid out clearly in front of the board. Choosing a shareholder is also choosing how you'll talk things through in hard times. Takeaways for Arcus42 This case made me think that a business built on long-term relationships can also start by asking a few more specific questions when choosing capital. First, turn trust into a process that can be audited. Trust needs records and clear responsibility behind it. Why an important judgement was formed, and on what information, should hold up when looked back on later. Second, choose shareholders around the decisions ahead. Shareholders take part in the company's pace, governance and trade-offs. Before signing, you can talk through a few difficult scenarios and see whether both sides can understand each other's judgement. Third, discuss company funding and founder liquidity separately. Both deserve serious attention, and each has its limits. Only by laying them out clearly on the table can you see which problems a deal really solves. Fourth, match the speed of growth to organisational capability. Money can buy talent and systems, but shared judgement still has to be formed through the work. Every new commitment should come with matching responsibility and the capacity to deliver. Fifth, check how rights are allocated on the downside while times are good. A friendly atmosphere at the negotiating table is precious; clear terms matter just as much. Spelling out disagreements that might arise in future is itself part of the partnership. Before Class Before class, I vote for the Series B, and the line I agree with most is: valuation must be read together with rights. This piece is a pre-class discussion based on the HBS case Mercado Bitcoin: M&A, IPO, or Series B? ; the main data are from pp.5–13 of the text and Exhibits 5, 6, 8 and 10; the case notes that some details have been altered. 2025 figures are management forecasts, and the conversion figures in the text are simplified illustrations of the mechanism, not the final contract or actual deal outcome. The judgements are limited to the case's decision context and do not constitute investment or legal advice.
Who takes the helm after you sell the equity

Unit 3, Professor Martin Sinozich's Finance, GeBBS Healthcare Solutions: Did You Ever Have to Make Up Your Mind?. This is the story of a founder walking into a sale process for the third time. The two offers are very close, yet they lead him, his family and his team towards different futures. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Nitin Thakor saw the rise and fall of a family business early on. His father ran a computer monitor business, which later closed. In 1997 he founded GeBBS Consulting in the US, handing American software development projects to teams in India to execute. The company reached US$20 million in revenue at one point; after the dot-com bubble burst, client demand slowed. He cut costs, returned the company to profitability, and started rethinking how his next company should be built. His reflections were concrete: he had taken on clients without clear industry boundaries, lacked intellectual property of his own, and competed mainly on price. In 2005 he and his father founded GeBBS Healthcare, focusing the business on back-office services for US healthcare. Hospitals have to deal with different insurers' rules, medical coding, billing and denial appeals — work that affects revenue and requires specialist knowledge. GeBBS provided these services with skilled professionals in India, starting as a subcontractor to large outsourcing firms and gradually serving hospitals directly. The company also kept options open for clients. Technology systems, workflows and delivery locations could all be adapted to the client. For clients wary of offshore delivery, a US team served them first, and once trust was built, part of the work was moved overseas. This FlexSource model lowered the barrier to a first engagement. Once inside a client, the company gradually expanded the scope of its services. In 2010 GeBBS had revenue of about US$8 million and EBITDA of about US$2.8 million, and received a US$20 million acquisition offer. The deal fell apart at the final stage. By 2012 revenue had grown to US$11.6 million, and Thakor invited investment banks to pitch for a sale. The bankers' feedback was remarkably consistent: the management team wasn't strong enough, there was no differentiated technology, no marquee direct clients, the service relied too heavily on labour-cost arbitrage, and the company depended too much on the founder himself. The valuation expectation at the time was about US$30 million. He decided to keep investing. At the end of 2013, Milind Godbole — MG — joined to run the India business. He came from a much larger company, and agreed to come on two important conditions: his equity would vest within about five years, and the founder would genuinely delegate. The company then filled out its sales and operations teams, developed the iCode technology platform co-designed with clients, and won hospital-system clients such as Memorial Sloan Kettering and Johns Hopkins. By FY2018 revenue had reached US$49.3 million, with adjusted EBITDA of about US$10.76 million; the share of revenue from direct clients rose from 31.5% in FY2015 to 58.3%. The third sale process reached out to 185 potential buyers and received 17 preliminary indications of interest. By November 2018 the choice had narrowed to two. Thakor had been building and running companies for thirteen straight years, and most of the family's wealth was still in the company; the team wanted to take the company to US$300 million in revenue. He had to decide, all at once, how much the family should cash out, who the company needed for its next stage, and how much power he was willing to hand over. 1. Regimental Technologies: an enterprise value offer of US$150 million for the whole company, aiming to acquire 100%. Of this, US$120 million would be paid at closing, and the other US$30 million depended on revenue and profit targets over the next three years. 2. ChrysCapital: an enterprise value offer of US$145 million for the whole company, acquiring up to 80% of the equity, with the founding family retaining a minority stake and continuing to take part in running the business and in the next exit. 3. Stay independent: keep 100% of the equity and current control, and bear the investment for future growth, operating risk and the uncertainty of another sale on their own. My Thinking The low valuation in 2012 handed the company its to-do list The five problems the bankers raised all point to the same thing: whether the company could turn the business it already had into a capability that keeps running after a buyer takes over. Profit belongs to the current period; valuation also depends on whether that profit can be sustained. When a company's clients, delivery, sales and product decisions are all tightly bound to the founder, the buyer has to bear the risk of that key person leaving. Clean books are certainly valuable, but they aren't enough to remove that dependence. After Thakor brought in MG, the truly hard move was pulling his own hands back from day-to-day operations. He used to go to India six times a year to manage the business; later he had to give the new leader room. A manager's ability only becomes the company's ability once it enters real decision-making. My own take is that preparing for a sale can be a very useful organisational check-up. Put yourself in the buyer's shoes for a while and look: why do clients stay, what does the team base its decisions on, and what would happen if the founder were away for a month? The quality of revenue changed, and growth got a new explanation GeBBS's transformation isn't just revenue growing from US$11.6 million to US$49.3 million. From FY2017 to FY2018, direct client revenue rose from about US$14.1 million to US$28.8 million, while channel revenue fell from about US$21.2 million to US$20.6 million. The growth in this period came mainly from expanding direct client relationships. The company got closer to its clients' problems, and had more opportunity to provide multiple services. The way iCode was developed is also worth noting. The company had earlier tried to develop its own technology, without much success; later it insisted on having clients take part in development, using software to solve specific work problems. Once technology becomes part of the service process, the client relationship has a chance to move gradually from buying cheap labour to jointly improving the business. But this still doesn't make GeBBS a software company. It still needs a lot of people to deliver, and channel partners may become competitors of its direct sales. FY2018 gross margin was about 42.2%, against a US healthcare IT industry benchmark of about 51.6% given in the case. This shows technology has brought differentiation, and also reminds us that in valuation we still have to take its cost of service seriously. Break each offer into the money you can get and the risk you still carry US$150 million versus US$145 million — a difference of just US$5 million. The real difference lies in the terms. Regimental's US$30 million earn-out is paid out over three years based on performance. After negotiation, the schedule was moved from back-loaded to front-loaded: US$15 million, US$7.5 million and US$7.5 million. Even assuming all of it is achieved, using a 12% discount rate purely for classroom calculation and assuming payment at the end of each year, this portion has a present value of only about US$24.71 million, or about US$144.7 million together with the upfront payment; in reality you'd also have to factor in hitting the targets, escrow, claims and taxes. The operating authority you keep after a sale affects how much of the sale price you actually end up realising. If headquarters changes budgets, staffing, client arrangements or cost allocations, the original team may still carry responsibility for the numbers without the decision rights it used to have. This was exactly MG's concern. ChrysCapital's US$145 million is the enterprise value of the whole company. In a simplified scenario — zero net debt, working capital delivered as agreed, ignoring adjustments such as an incentive pool — selling 80% corresponds to consideration of about US$116 million, and the retained 20% is worth about US$29 million on the same basis. The latter is still risky equity with no immediate liquidity; it can't be treated like a bank deposit. The two arrangements leave the founder holding risk in different ways: one is payment tied to future performance, the other is continuing to own equity in the company. What needs comparing is the size and duration of each risk, and how much he himself can influence it. A fair valuation needs growth, and also needs the profit to come back as cash Based on the last-twelve-months adjusted EBITDA of US$12.1 million in the case's term sheet, the two offers come to about 12.4x and 12.0x. Using the earlier FY2018 adjusted EBITDA, they come to about 13.9x and 13.5x. A different denominator makes the offers look different. This company has real growth and has been through multiple rounds of market bidding, so both offers have a reasonable basis. Still, growth is absorbing cash. FY2018 adjusted EBITDA was about US$10.8 million; after deducting the increase in working capital and capital expenditure, the pre-tax cash flow listed in the case was only about US$4.8 million. The future profit in a valuation has to make it through collections, reinvestment and taxes before it becomes distributable cash. When revenue grows quickly, receivables can also grow quickly. Simply multiplying profit by a multiple misses this tied-up capital. My own judgement is that both offers are in a range worth closing at, but that doesn't mean the company has one precise fair price. Whether you believe in the next stage of growth, how much reinvestment it needs, and at what risk rate future cash should be discounted all change the answer. I lean towards the PE option, while acknowledging that control has passed What attracts me about ChrysCapital is that it fits fairly well with what the company needs next: industry experience, operating partners, a healthcare network, and a track record of taking businesses to a larger scale. MG had already worked with it, and the way the two sides got along during negotiations offers a bit of a reference too. For the family, cashing out most of its holding reduces excessive concentration of wealth; for the team, retaining a minority stake still gives a chance to share in future growth. My pre-class choice is to sell 80% to ChrysCapital, and to write management authority and minority shareholder protections into the agreement. This choice has a clear cost. On the seven-person board, ChrysCapital holds four seats, Thakor two, plus one independent director. The chairman title won't change who holds the majority of seats. Continuing to take part in running the business has to be made concrete in specific rules on budgets, personnel, acquisitions, financing and exit. The financing terms also need checking. The body of the case describes the PE option as a debt-free deal, but the exhibits list US$35 million of borrowing, and suggest it could be held by the buyer's holding company and repaid with dividends the buyer receives. Their impact on the company's cash and the family's equity needs to be clarified before signing. Summing it up with the word "debt-free" would hide an important difference. Staying independent is attractive too, but the family's concentration risk, the founder's fatigue, management's equity vesting and the capability gaps for the next stage won't disappear automatically as revenue grows. Keeping all the equity is also a choice that comes at a cost. Takeaways for Arcus42 First separate the family's life goals from the business's growth goals. That the business still has room to grow doesn't mean the family must keep the vast majority of its wealth in it. When discussing an exit, you need to look at future opportunities, the degree of wealth concentration, and the time the family wants to have, all at once. Gradually turn key people's judgement into capability that can be passed on. Client trust, work records, team roles and decision processes need to support others in picking up the work. A founder's value also includes keeping the organisation's quality up when they aren't in the room. Technology investment needs specific users and specific problems. GeBBS's approach of co-developing tools with clients is very instructive for professional services. First understand the difficulties in real work, then judge which steps are suited to standardisation and which still need human judgement. When discussing a partnership, pin power down to specific matters. Shareholding, board seats and titles provide the outline; rules on budgets, personnel, data, financing and exit determine how the partnership actually works. Both sides should be clear about what they can decide, and how disagreements will be handled when they arise. Translate every offer back into time and conditions. Payment at closing, deferred payments, incentive equity and retained equity each pay out differently. Only by taking them apart can a family see which risks it still carries after the deal. Before Class My pre-class vote goes to ChrysCapital: cash out most of the family's holding, keep a stake in the next stage of growth, and accept that majority control has been handed over. The judgement I'm bringing to class: choosing a buyer is also choosing how you will work and live in your next stage. This piece is a pre-class discussion based on HBS case 820-041 and its exhibits; historical figures, forecasts and deal terms all refer to the case setting, and the analysis does not use the outcome of any later transaction. Calculations are classroom exercises, not investment, legal or tax advice.
How much public responsibility can a company take on?

Unit 3, Professor Carrie Elkins, Global Markets, “A Marshall Plan for Africa”: James Mwangi and Equity Group Holdings. A bank that began by keeping small savings safe for farmers ended up at the table where East Africa’s regional development is debated. The capabilities it built along the way gave that ambition a foundation; the speed at which the ambition grew pushed its responsibilities further out, too. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary The story begins with a tin can hidden beside a banana tree. James Mwangi’s mother had no bank account. She kept her savings under the mattress, and when that felt unsafe, she put them in a tin can and buried it. Mwangi grew up in rural Kenya; his father died during the independence struggle, and his mother raised seven children on her own. He sold firewood and vegetables, kept studying on scholarships, and later became an accountant and a bank executive. He learned early on that people with meagre incomes also plan every day’s money with great care. Kenya became independent in 1963. The inequalities in land and employment formed under colonial rule did not disappear with independence. The early government supported market development, GDP grew fairly quickly for a time, and it invested in education, but population growth and concentrated incomes meant prosperity did not reach households evenly. Later, the political and economic environment deteriorated further. The poverty rate cited in the case rose from 45% in 1992 to 57% in 2000. These historical figures are a reminder that how an economic system distributes opportunity finds its way into very concrete daily lives. In 1993, Peter Munga, founder of Equity Building Society, approached Mwangi. At the time, the institution had been declared technically insolvent, non-performing loans made up 56% of its book, and it had about 12,000 customers. Mwangi accepted a 94% pay cut and remortgaged his house to put money in. The problem he set out to solve was how a failing institution could serve people banks had never taken seriously. He started with savings. He removed hurdles such as minimum balances, improved withdrawals and the service experience, trained staff, and went to rural markets to teach people about finance. As the team recalls, their competitor back then was: “We were competing with the mattress.” A bank had to beat the mattress first before it could earn a family’s trust. Small amounts, high frequency and unstable incomes became the real-world conditions for product design. Later, automation cut processing time from about 30 minutes to 5; customers built a savings record first, and only then did the bank offer credit. Head of legal Mary Wangari Wamae drove the licensing and compliance work. Equity became a commercial bank in 2004, listed in 2006, and received an investment of about US$178.7 million from Helios in 2007. Capital made channel expansion possible. Agent outlets, basic mobile banking and digital systems were gradually connected. Equity went through cooperation, competition and renewed cooperation with Safaricom, and also expanded into neighbouring countries. By 2021, the group had 16.2 million customers, 337 branches and 61,061 agent outlets across six countries. Its pre-tax profit for the same period was about KSh 51.88 billion; serving small customers had become a business model at scale. Equity Group Foundation, meanwhile, used the same network to run programmes in education, healthcare, entrepreneurship training, agriculture and social protection. The case exhibits report about 47,000 scholarships and training for about 392,000 micro and small enterprises. These are programme outputs reported by the institution, and still need to be judged separately from long-term improvements in people’s lives. During the pandemic, Mwangi organised local production of personal protective equipment; the experience made him believe even more firmly that a company can coordinate a wider range of social capabilities. In 2022, Equity launched the Africa Recovery and Resilience Plan and signed a memorandum of understanding with the East African Community. The plan links six pillars — agriculture and extractives, manufacturing and logistics, trade and investment, micro and small enterprises, social and environmental, and technology — and proposes a US$6 billion financing framework. The case exhibits set targets of 100 million online customers and 5 million borrowing businesses by 2025, and 50 million direct and indirect jobs. These figures are the plan’s commitments, not achievements already delivered. The choice in front of Mwangi is therefore more complicated than “to grow or not to grow”: 1. In going from 16.2 million group customers to 100 million online customers, can channel expansion be matched by the corresponding service and risk-management capabilities? 2. Within the US$6 billion financing framework, who actually puts up the money, and who bears the credit, maturity and cross-border risks? 3. How will the 50 million jobs be created and verified, and who decides which people and which industries get opportunities first? My Thinking Reducing poverty means making growth reach actual people My previous prep, on India, was about how a country’s development capacity turns into a better life for the majority. With Equity, that question arrives at a bank’s counter. Kenya’s early growth after independence was not slow. The case also points out that in the later years of Kenyatta’s rule, the poorest 40% of households received about 9% of total income, while the richest 10% received almost half. Put the numbers side by side and you can see the gap between growth and distribution. Whether a person can go to school, save, run a business and cope with illness determines whether they can take part in growth. Government scholarships helped Mwangi escape poverty, which also shows that the public sector once provided real opportunities. Regulatory opening, public education and private innovation need to connect with one another, not cancel one another out. In Development as Freedom , Amartya Sen puts people’s actual choices and capacity to act at the centre of the development debate. For this case, that lens is very concrete: whether a family, beyond meeting sudden expenses, can start planning for a slightly more distant future. My own understanding is that poverty-reduction policy needs to ask which paths growth travels through. Schools, jobs, accounts and markets — each one can carry opportunity further, or bring it to a halt. Saving lets a family slowly come to own a tomorrow Mwangi’s understanding of his mother shaped the order in which Equity provides services: first give money a safe, convenient place to go, then gradually build a credit relationship. According to the case, customers had to show six months of savings history before the bank would offer a corresponding loan. This process lets the bank build a basis for judgement, and also helps customers build up a small cushion. For people who buy fuel every day and pay for transport every day, the balances are small, but the way they manage money is meticulous. Savings give a family some room to manoeuvre; credit needs future income to carry it. Both can be valuable, and the order and the conditions of use change the outcome. Without orders or stable conditions for production, a loan may simply add another bill that has to be paid next time. This model has its own limits, too. People who cannot put aside even a little may first need social protection, health support or basic services. Financial institutions should see their situation, rather than deleting them from the development conversation because they can’t be extended credit. My own inclination is to use whether something expands a person’s choices as the test. The tin can didn’t hold much, but it may have been the first space a family set aside for tomorrow. Empathy has to enter the cost structure to serve more people Understanding customers is only the starting point. Equity’s story holds up because the team kept reworking the cost of service. Cutting processing time from 30 minutes to 5 means customers queue less, and it also means the same resources can handle more transactions. Agent outlets and mobile channels brought many small transactions closer to customers. A high-volume, low-margin model needs these concrete moves to hold it up. An institution’s goodwill ultimately has to be delivered through processes, people and capital. Warui took part in customer education, Wamae drove the legal and organisational transformation, investors supplied capital, and the regulatory system allowed new channels to emerge. Mwangi’s ability to bring these capabilities together is the part of his leadership worth learning from. Nor did he fix any competitive relationship in place. Safaricom could be a partner or a rival; when there was a conflict over customer relationships, Equity found other routes, and later they worked together again. The mission provides direction; the specific methods are still tested by reality. My own understanding is that only when empathy enters the cost structure can it extend beyond the circle the founder can serve personally, so that many more people actually receive the same treatment. The results of social programmes have to be verified in people’s homes Equity plugged education, healthcare and enterprise training into its commercial network, and the design is appealing. When customers have skills, good health and buyers, financial services are more likely to create value; the commercial network, in turn, can help social programmes avoid duplicated effort. But the same number can carry different meanings. How many businesses were trained is a delivery record; whether those businesses survived, whether their profits improved, and whether families took on less dangerous debt are results at another level. Once service coverage expands, we still need to see whether lives have become more stable. The Kenyan poverty rate cited in the case fell between 2009 and 2021, but that alone cannot prove how large Equity’s contribution was. The government, other financial institutions, mobile payments and families’ own efforts were all part of it. The 2021 FinAccess survey by the Central Bank of Kenya and other institutions measures access to formal finance and usage of banking services separately, at 83.7% and 44.1% of adults respectively. This is also a reminder that access to financial services, using a bank account and escaping poverty need to be measured separately. I would look at two sets of results at once: whether the bank’s risk and operations are sound, and whether customers’ businesses and lives have improved. When one set looks great and the other stays silent for a long time, further questions are needed. When public responsibility expands, accountability must expand with it I support the direction of the regional plan. Agriculture needs processing, processing needs logistics, and businesses need orders, skills and capital. Organising these conditions together has a chance of removing constraints that a single loan cannot solve. But I would vote to approve a phased version. 100 million online customers and 50 million jobs have already pushed the task into cross-border coordination. The success of the existing bank provides a starting point for the new plan; the next step still requires proving new capabilities. When a company gains more public influence, it also needs to accept clearer public accountability. Who decides where resources flow, who can raise objections, and who bears the losses of failure cannot rest solely on trust in one leader. I would start with a small number of value chains that have clear buyers and reliable partners, spell out financing maturities, currencies and loss-sharing, have specialist institutions carry out specific projects, and let the board and public partners retain independent review rights. For services of a public nature, it should also be considered how people outside the bank’s customer base can get access to opportunities. This would sacrifice some speed, add coordination costs, and might even require giving up some short-term returns. But what depositors, borrowers and taxpayers can bear is the condition for the plan to be sustainable. Ample liquidity does not mean equally ample capital to absorb losses. The further a bridge extends, the more reliable supports it needs. Equity is well suited to be an important builder, but the sharing of public responsibility needs to be designed in from the very first span. Takeaways for Arcus42 What this case offers are a few methodological reminders about service and trust. First, understand the decisions the client actually has to make. Equity started from how families save and pay. The lesson for family services is to put the specific people, responsibilities and constraints first, and only then discuss what tools are needed. Second, let technology improve delivery, and let people own judgement. Automation can reduce repetitive work and lower the cost of service. Explaining uncertainty, understanding the circumstances of different families, and taking responsibility for important judgements still require clear people and clear accountability. Third, when coordinating capabilities, write down the division of labour. A complex problem often needs several kinds of professional expertise. Who makes recommendations, who executes and who verifies should be understandable; professional or licensed work should be handled by appropriately qualified professionals. Fourth, measure whether clients are more able to act. The number of documents and meetings alone cannot prove value. Whether agreements are understood, whether actions are completed, and whether problems surface in time are closer to the real change a service brings. Fifth, let trust gradually become an organisational capability. Reasons, commitments and conflicts of interest need to be recorded, and there need to be paths for independent review and for voicing disagreement. Trust built on personal relationships can be preserved for longer through these everyday arrangements. Before Class Before class, my vote goes to a phased approach. Equity already has a starting point that is trustworthy enough, and it also needs to build new constraints for its greater public impact. What I agree with most: however much public responsibility a company takes on, it needs to build a matching capacity for accountability.
