Valuation starts with asking who the buyer is

Unit 3, Professor Martin Sinozich's Finance — The Trade Sale Process, class discussion of Nantucket Nectars: The Exit. Before class, I focused on whether Nantucket Nectars should sell, and to whom. In class, the professor laid out the financial statements and played recordings of the two founders looking back. The question gradually became more specific: does a company's value belong to the company itself, or to the buyer who happens to need it right now? Here goes — enjoy: Growth first has to get past cash flow Class opened with the two founders' passion. It's easy to see passion as a strength: they went years without drawing a salary, kept putting money back into the company, insisted on product quality, and were willing to do the selling and stock the shelves themselves. But passion has another side. Insisting on quality can squeeze margins; and if a company depends too much on its founders, buyers will worry about whether the team can keep growing after they leave. A founder's passion can light the fire, but it can't substitute for operating capability that can be handed over. At this point the professor brought the discussion back to the statements. Revenue was growing, but cash was tight. Inventory tied up roughly two months, and receivables grew along with sales. Not all of the products the company had sold had yet turned into money collected. One classmate suggested the company could keep raising money and sell later, once profits and distribution were built up. Others pointed out that financing isn't free, and the management team might not deliver on its growth projections. The professor's judgement came down to two things: whether the growth story holds up, and whether the cash can last long enough to deliver on it. The growth on the income statement may be consuming the cash on the balance sheet. For a growing business, inventory and receivables aren't accounting details; they're the everyday constraints that decide how much longer it can keep running. Valuation models set the anchor; competition sets the price The case gave two very different valuation scenarios: about US$34 million to US$58 million as a standalone business; about US$106 million to US$176 million once a strategic buyer's growth, procurement and distribution synergies are added. The wide gap in between is the value a buyer might create. The professor rebuilt a discounted cash flow model. Raise the discount rate and the valuation falls; change the assumptions on growth, margins or working capital and the result moves too. The class also compared precedent acquisitions and public company valuations, but didn't treat any one multiple as the right answer. A DCF helps the seller know what they're negotiating about; only bidding makes the buyer say how much they're willing to pay. The distinction matters. When several companies come asking at the same time, whether you can line them up into an orderly competition is a separate thing from the valuation formula itself. The model helps set the floor and lets the seller know what a lowball offer means; the competitive process gives different buyers' synergies a chance to make it into the price. The class also discussed the role of investment banks. A bank doesn't just produce a valuation table; it can find the right buyers, maintain confidentiality and run the process, so founders don't have to run the company while personally saying the price things that damage relationships. This time, Nantucket Nectars' founders didn't hire a bank. They were faced with an unexpected rush of buyers, and with help from lawyers they kept the competition going themselves, one phone call after another. The professor reminded us that this kind of starting point is rare. Many companies never get seven buyers calling them unprompted. The value a buyer brings also brings integration costs In class, we went back and forth comparing Ocean Spray, Pepsi and Triarc. Pepsi had the strongest distribution and scale, and in theory could open up the most markets; Ocean Spray could provide fruit sourcing capability, and also needed single-serve distribution and a young brand; Triarc knew the beverage business well, but already owned brands like Snapple, and integrating distribution could damage Nantucket's existing relationships. The more synergy a buyer can create, the more the target may be worth; but how that synergy is realised also determines what the founders will lose. What the two founders worried about wasn't some abstract "big-company culture," but very concrete things: whether the product would be reformulated for margin, whether existing distributors would be replaced, whether employees and the brand story would be merged into an unfamiliar system. In the recording played in class, the founders said they ultimately chose Ocean Spray because it understood the juice business and genuinely understood product quality. They felt Pepsi wouldn't push the price high enough, while Triarc would make employees feel they were betraying the original culture. In the end, Ocean Spray promised to let Nantucket operate relatively independently. Retained equity needs an exit written into the contract Ocean Spray bought 80% at a company valuation of about US$80 million; the two Toms together kept 20%, and Egan exited entirely. The founders kept running the business, taking some cash while keeping the possibility of future upside. But a minority stake doesn't equal control. A few years later, Ocean Spray's management changed, and the new leadership decided to sell the business. The founder recalled that, relying on a five-year clause in the original agreement, he negotiated with the new management over the price of the retained stake, and rejected the compromise they proposed. The class transcript doesn't spell out all the details of the later deal; what is certain is that the deal relationship had changed, and the contract became one of the few bargaining chips left in the founders' hands. This gave me a new understanding of the pre-class discussion about the "second bite of the apple." Keeping a minority stake lets you keep participating in the future; but without a clear pricing mechanism, sale conditions and dispute resolution, it can also become a piece of paper you can't cash. Your future options have to be written into the contract before the deal. Deal timing is where buyer demand meets seller readiness The session ended by returning to a simple fact: buyers can suddenly need a business because the market shifts, and they can also redo the math on a deal because management changes. Ocean Spray at the time needed distribution capability and a young brand. Several strategic buyers were also chasing New Age beverages. Later both the industry and the company changed, and cultural promises couldn't stop the business from changing hands again. There's luck in timing, but preparation can make luck more useful. A seller needs to know how long the cash will last, whether shareholders can agree, where the business's standalone value lies, and also think clearly about whether they want to stay on. Only then, when a buyer knocks, can they negotiate price, structure, and life after leaving. My own take is that selling a business is like answering two different questions: how much the market is willing to pay for it; and what the founder is willing to give up for that price. No valuation model can answer the second one for you. After Class Before class, I leaned towards the two Toms selling to Ocean Spray through a competitive process and keeping a minority stake. The actual deal discussed in class was close to that judgement, and its outcome filled in a part the pre-class model hadn't finished: the five-year clause in the contract later became the founders' basis for negotiating with the new buyer. Companies keep moving forward, and the people who own them change too. So what you keep when you sell isn't just a percentage of equity, but also what you'll still be able to say and do when the future changes. A review of the class case; the valuation and deal information in this piece is compiled from the Nantucket Nectars case and the transcript of the class recording, and does not constitute investment advice.
Focus and delivery in a crisis

Unit 3, Leadership: Lisa Su and AMD. Why does a company that once made excellent products end up in trouble? And how does the person who takes it over reorganize the capabilities that still exist into a path that actually works? Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary AMD's early opportunity came from customers' need for a second source of supply. IBM didn't want to rely on a single trusted source for a critical processor, which gave AMD an important way into the PC industry. It could offer customers choice while working with the software ecosystem that already existed. [1] But AMD's history also includes moments when it defined products itself. The Athlon, which began shipping in 1999, and later the products that reached 1 GHz, proved its engineering strength. The Opteron, launched in 2003, let customers upgrade to 64-bit computing while continuing to run their existing 32-bit software. Compatibility protected customers' past investments, and also opened the door to new technology. [2] [3] [4] Opportunity came with bigger commitments. In 2006 AMD completed its acquisition of ATI, at an announced transaction value of about US$5.4 billion, taking out a US$2.5 billion term loan for the deal. Graphics capability came into the company, and so did pressure on cash and debt. In 2009 AMD spun off its wafer manufacturing business as GLOBALFOUNDRIES, beginning to change the way it carried the cost of manufacturing. [5] [6] Meanwhile, its products ran into competitiveness problems. Contemporary benchmarks of the FX-8150 in 2011 showed that single-threaded performance dragged down the experience in some applications and games. Having more technical ideas doesn't automatically mean customers get better results. [7] By the time Lisa Su took over as CEO in October 2014, the company already had some foundations worth keeping: the CPU team was being rebuilt, the semi-custom game-console business already had customers, and the manufacturing spin-off had long been completed. Keller had returned in 2012, and the use of AMD chips in Sony's and Microsoft's new generation of consoles had been announced in 2013. What she inherited was a set of capabilities and commitments that needed to be reconfigured. [8] [9] [10] The quarterly snapshot around the time she took over: cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of about US$938 million, and total debt of about US$2.2 billion. The traditional Computing and Graphics segment was under pressure, while the Enterprise, Embedded and Semi-Custom segment was profitable. Not all the debt was due immediately, and these figures can't be converted directly into "how many months it can survive"; what they suggest is that room for allocating resources was already limited. [11] Freezing time at this point, I'd frame the choices in front of her as three questions: 1. With limited cash, which spending do you stop first, and which capabilities do you protect? 2. How do you set the order of investment among CPUs, GPUs and the existing customer businesses? 3. How do you get employees, customers and the board to jointly accept a plan that will take years to prove itself? My Thinking Technology that once led needs an organization that keeps delivering AMD's early history shows that technical capability can change a company's position. Customers are willing to seriously consider a challenger because it offers concrete value — performance, compatibility, supply choice, or reasonable cost. But a lead doesn't last. Whether the next-generation product comes out on time, whether the software is ready, whether suppliers can cooperate, whether customers are willing to adopt it again — all of this requires the organization to keep delivering. My own understanding is that a technical breakthrough has to be caught by a whole set of delivery capabilities. Technology opens up possibilities; the organization makes sure those possibilities still hold the next time, and the time after that. Cash buys time for long-term technology If I put myself in 2014, I'd look first at cash flow, payment commitments and R&D milestones. A new processor's development cycle doesn't suddenly get shorter because there's a new CEO. Stopping some work might bring expenses down. But if what gets stopped is exactly the key capability the next-generation product needs, the company just gets smaller without gaining any new reason to compete. My choice would be to put the short-term cash plan and the long-term technology plan on the same table. For the businesses that can contribute resources today, assess how much time they can buy for tomorrow; for the technologies tomorrow's hopes rest on, require progress that can be checked today. There's only so much time in the hourglass. The leader has to decide which things are worth letting it run out on slowly. Focus needs a real stop list CPUs, GPUs, embedded, game consoles — every direction comes with an opportunity story. The problem is that every opportunity takes up engineers, management attention and customer-support capacity. If I were Lisa Su, I'd make high-performance computing the main direction, review the core R&D already under way, and maintain the valuable existing customer businesses. Projects off the main line would need stronger customer evidence, tighter investment limits, and clear stopping conditions. Focus ultimately shows up in resource allocation. Who gets the best team, who gets continued budget, who has to stop — that's where strategy actually happens. My own inclination is to pursue fewer directions and accept some opportunity cost. This choice carries risk too: the bet becomes more concentrated, so it needs staged validation all the more. Acknowledging what your predecessors built is how you put resources in the right place Looking back at a success story, it's easy to rearrange the whole history around one person. The change in manufacturing model, the return of key talent, the winning of important customers all seem to have happened only after the new leader arrived. AMD's timeline reminds me that a successor's first job is to judge what's already in hand. What's truly valuable, what needs continued investment, and what — even though a lot of money has gone into it — should be stopped. Accurately acknowledging what the organization has built helps keep the people who actually do the work. A CEO can bring new decisiveness, and also needs to respect the people and the work that make those decisions possible. My understanding is that part of leadership lies in organizing what's been built up across different teams into a direction everyone is willing to share responsibility for. Trust has to be rebuilt through round after round of delivery After the strategy is announced, the truly fiddly work begins: performance misses targets, validation hits problems, customer requirements change, the supply chain needs coordinating. I'd give every major product a clear owner, and have R&D, sales and operations face the same set of facts together. When problems come up, first get the real situation into the meeting, then discuss responsibility and remedies. The earlier bad news is reported, the more choices the team has. My first three steps would be these: get a clear picture of the facts and the cash, concentrate resources, and then deliver on commitments one by one. The three move forward in parallel, and within the first 90 days there should be visible changes in plans, accountability and how things are validated. The long-term direction deserves patience; specific projects need testing. Only by doing both well at once do employees have a reason to keep investing themselves, and customers a reason to give you another chance. Takeaways for Arcus42 What this case gives me is a few reminders about how to build an organization. First, be clear about the core capabilities worth building up over the long term. A service may bring in immediate revenue, but also look at whether it improves judgment, delivery quality and client trust. Before a new opportunity comes in, check how it relates to that capability. Second, give experiments a budget, and an end condition. Leave room for new ideas, while agreeing on when to review them and what evidence is needed to continue. The team's attention needs to be allocated carefully too. Third, protect the work that short-term reports can't yet fully reflect. Knowledge curation, quality review and developing people all take time. Protecting them also means explaining how they improve delivery, and continually checking on progress. Fourth, turn client commitments into a shared working standard. Who's responsible, when it's due, how it's signed off — all of this needs to be clear enough. Getting problems to surface early is usually worth more than explaining them afterwards. Final Thoughts Before class, my vote goes to this line: leadership in a crisis means making limited resources support a path that can keep delivering. What kind of capital growth needs

Unit 3, Professor Martin Sinozich, Finance: Creating the First Public Law Firm: The IPO of Slater & Gordon Limited. A law firm can carry its clients' costs up front and only get paid once the case succeeds. But when it wants to offer that service to more people, who bears the cost of waiting? Slater & Gordon's IPO plan brought something rather inconspicuous in professional services out onto the table — time needs capital too. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary In 2007, an Australian law firm was preparing to become the world's first publicly listed law firm. Slater & Gordon, or S&G, was founded in Melbourne in 1935 and started out handling workers' compensation claims for unions and working people. By the time of the case, it had nearly 400 staff, more than 140 lawyers, and 21 offices across six states. Decades of serving individuals had given it a brand, a referral network and around 30,000 phone inquiries a year. Personal injury litigation contributed about three-quarters of its core revenue. The key promise of this business: “No Win—No Fee” If the case doesn't succeed, there's no legal fee. Clients thereby get legal services they might otherwise not have been able to afford; the firm, for its part, has to screen cases, advance disbursements, and bear the risk of not getting paid. A typical case in the study lasts 6–24 months, with a typical fee of around A$15,000. The success rate on personal injury cases taken on recently was about 95%, but that rests on past screening and execution capability. Book revenue and cash collection move on different timetables. Based on work progress, expected fees and the probability of winning, the firm recognizes part of the revenue before a case ends, creating a work-in-progress asset, WIP. In one successful case in the exhibits, the firm spends A$4,250 in each of the first three periods and only receives A$17,250 in the fourth, including reimbursement of advanced costs. The final pre-tax profit is A$4,500, after A$12,750 had been advanced along the way. S&G wanted to bring this capability to a bigger platform. Since 2002 the firm had consolidated eight smaller firms; the four acquired in the most recent year cost a combined A$9.3 million and were expected to contribute more than A$8 million in revenue in FY2008. Small firms faced increasingly complex legal and administrative requirements, while a consolidator had the chance to share brand, client acquisition, systems and professional resources. The catch: on top of the purchase price, new cases have to be funded on an ongoing basis. The existing shareholders' ability and willingness to put in more money were limited, debt financing was constrained by cash flow and collateral requirements, and the business changes proposed by private equity investors were not accepted. Regulatory changes in Australia at the time opened the door to outside ownership. S&G planned to issue shares at A$1 each for a total deal size of A$35 million, of which about A$17.3 million would go to existing shareholders selling shares, A$2.3 million to issuance costs, and the remaining roughly A$15.4 million to reducing net debt. Listing would free up financing capacity, but it wouldn't turn the entire proceeds into new cash for the company. Facing this deal, the case's fund manager, Gloria Rosen, has to answer three questions: 1. Between a historical success rate of about 95% and a long collection cycle, how much value does this business model actually create? 2. Can acquisitions and an IPO let professional capability be replicated sustainably, while upholding the duty to the court and putting clients first? 3. Discounted at an 11% cost of capital, what is this company worth, and is A$1 per share worth buying into? My Thinking The profit is recognized, but the cash may still be on its way S&G's business combines legal services, case selection and funding advances. Clients hand part of the fee risk to the firm; the firm uses its judgment to decide which cases to take, and then uses capital to fund the wait. The A$4,500 pre-tax profit on a successful case can't be treated directly as value created today. Using the single-case model from the course materials, with six-month periods and an 11% discount rate, a case certain to succeed has an NPV of about A$1,408; using 95% as the model's success probability, and handling losing-case losses and taxes as the model does, the expected NPV is about A$890. If each period is stretched to nine months, the NPV of a successful case drops to about A$701. As time passes, the profit on the books doesn't disappear, but the price anyone is willing to pay for it today changes. My own take is that with businesses like this, you have to ask three questions together: do the cases have economic value, is revenue recognition reliable, and when will the cash come back? Growing volume amplifies all three at once. Faster growth can also mean a deeper funding gap. The value of acquisitions comes from how they're run afterward A brand can bring in cases, unified systems can cut duplicated work, and more cases can diversify some single-case risk. Professional resources can be shared too, giving previously independent small teams better support. These are all places where consolidation can create value. But buying a law firm with revenue isn't the same as buying free growth. The buyer pays the purchase price and also takes on the working-capital needs of the new business; lawyers leaving, local client relationships drifting away, or a drop in case quality during integration can all erode the expected returns. The base-case model in the course materials assumes A$10 million a year in acquisitions in 2009–2011, at 1.2 times the acquired revenue. When I set future acquisition spending to zero and kept everything else the same, enterprise value fell from about A$151.0 million to about A$144.2 million. In the model, this set of future acquisitions creates incremental value of about A$6.83 million. The model supports the consolidation strategy, but it doesn't give it unlimited margin for error. As scale grows, good targets may get pricier and management distance may lengthen. Every deal still has to answer: after paying the price, are the operating improvements left over enough to cover the capital invested? The case for listing has to rest on the funding cycle S&G's need for financing has a clear business basis: it needs to pay for acquisitions, and it needs to carry the time between putting money into cases and getting it back. Equity capital has no fixed maturity or repayment requirement, and public shares can also provide employee incentives, liquidity for shareholders and currency for future deals. The corresponding costs are just as concrete: issuance and ongoing disclosure costs, dilution of existing shareholders, the market's demands for short-term results, and more management attention diverted to capital markets. Equity also requires a return; its cost doesn't vanish just because there's no interest bill. To back a company's IPO, you first need a clear view of what the money is for. Of this IPO's A$35 million deal size, nearly half goes to existing shareholders selling shares. Giving long-term shareholders liquidity is reasonable in itself, but investors can't count the entire amount as a cash reserve for future growth. According to the course model, free cash flow for 2009–2011 totals about negative A$21.64 million. Reducing net debt frees up some financing room, but further growth still needs a workable funding plan. For an entrepreneurial company, deliberately slowing growth should stay on the menu too. The financing approach has to support the company's operating rhythm. The boundaries of professional judgment must be written down before the capital arrives When law firm clients buy services, they often struggle to judge professional quality independently, and they also have to hand over sensitive information and trust the lawyer's judgment. So conflicts arise between shareholders' pursuit of returns and professional duties, and these need to be explicitly dealt with. In the case, S&G wrote the order of priority into its offering arrangements: duty to the court comes first, then duty to clients, and then the company's other obligations and shareholders' interests. This was the arrangement in the case at the time, and it can't be directly extrapolated into a rule for every country and every professional services firm. The capital structure can change, but responsibility for professional judgment must not become blurred. If whether to take a case, when to settle and whether to keep investing are all driven by short-term profit metrics, what shareholders end up buying may be eroded client trust. My own leaning is to support, conditionally and where the rules permit, public ownership of professional services firms. The conditions include professionals retaining the necessary judgment, a board that can handle conflicts of interest, disclosure that lets investors understand business quality, and incentives that don't look only at short-term revenue. Accounting firms also face their own constraints, such as audit independence, and can't simply copy the law firm's answer. Whether A$1 a share is worth buying depends on whether the assumptions hold Using the professor's specified 11% WACC and the course model's base-case assumptions, enterprise value is about A$151.0 million. Subtracting post-issue net debt of about A$5.4 million gives equity value of about A$145.6 million; divided by about 107.78 million shares, that's about A$1.35 per share. The number is attractive, but it also has obvious dependencies: the present value of the terminal value accounts for about 83% of enterprise value. The model uses a 24% EBIT margin, whereas the case's historical margin in 2006 was about 17.8%, and the 2008 forecast only reaches about 24.2%. Future efficiency gains have to be delivered by operations. Holding everything else constant, if the margin falls to 20%, the per-share value is about A$0.96. If organic growth also drops to 5%, the margin to 22%, and the acquisition multiple rises to 1.5 times, the per-share value is about A$0.90. An offer price below the base-case valuation doesn't eliminate operating downside. If I put myself at the IPO decision point in the case, my in-class choice is: participate conditionally, and in a small way. The conditions are confirming the quality of WIP, the ability to finance the expansion period, and the priority of professional duties in actual governance. The price I accept is that the headroom shown by the base-case valuation could be eaten up by changes in margins, collection times or acquisition costs. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading this case, I thought about how professional services handle the relationship between growth, cash and trust. What can be borrowed here are a few operating principles. First, look at delivery, revenue recognition and cash collection separately. Each answers a different question. Growth planning has to look not only at what has been done for clients, but also at when the investment happens and when the money comes back, leaving enough slack for the wait. Second, distill service standards into reusable capabilities. As scale grows, what can be shared is process, knowledge and quality management. Professional judgment still needs clear ownership, and more clients or more revenue can't substitute for evidence of delivery quality. Third, match the time demands of capital to the service cycle. Long-term relationships require continuous investment. When choosing a financing approach or a growth rate, put the time by which capital expects a return on the same sheet as the time it takes the service to actually create value. Fourth, settle the order of decision-making before conflicts of interest arise. When client interests, professional responsibility and business goals meet, an organization needs to know who decides, on what basis, and how it's documented. The clearer the boundaries, the more a partnership can rest on expectations everyone understands. In Closing Before class, my vote goes to this line: the capital growth needs must be able to wait until value turns into cash. How development can reach the many

Unit 3, Professor Carrie Elkins, Global Markets, India: The Path to Development. A country that can already land on the Moon, export software and build a digital payments system at enormous scale still has to answer a plain question: how do these capabilities turn into a life that most people can actually live? Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary The case opens with two different lives on the same day. In the Delhi heat, a white-collar worker with a fever orders food delivery from home and sees a doctor remotely; medicine can be delivered to his door. A delivery worker who is just as sick finishes his shift, walks to the nearby public clinic, and finds the outpatient service suspended. Technology has connected the two of them in the same transaction, but healthcare and social protection still keep them apart. To understand that distance, you need a longer time frame. The ancient India of the case once connected the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia and China through monsoon trade and the exchange of knowledge. Later, the East India Company moved from trade to taxation and rule, and the colonial administration put order, revenue and the export of resources at its center. Gaps in industry, basic education and public health, together with an elite bureaucracy, became the starting point of the independent nation. Independence in 1947 came with Partition and mass migration. The new country had to solve not just economic problems but how people of different religions, languages and castes would live together. The 1950 Constitution established a democratic republic, and the first national election faced 176 million eligible voters, nearly 85% of whom could not read. Amid widespread poverty, India chose universal suffrage, and it kept and reshaped the administrative system it had inherited. Economically, the government built industry through planning, state-owned enterprises and import substitution, pushed agricultural reform, and set up research institutions and elite engineering schools. Food production and technical capabilities accumulated, but companies' entry, expansion and product choices were bound by layer upon layer of licenses. The case quotes Rahul Bajaj recalling the judgment of the ministry in charge: "There is no demand for more than this." Judgments about demand were often made in advance by the approvers, on the market's behalf. At the same time, there were gaps between research, university teaching and industrial application, and basic education and healthcare remained weak. The 1991 balance-of-payments crisis forced India to change how it developed. Foreign exchange reserves were enough for only a few weeks of imports, and Prime Minister Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh pushed through reforms of the exchange rate, trade, foreign investment and industrial controls. Software and business process outsourcing then expanded rapidly, and companies gained access to much larger markets and capital. But success didn't travel down the same road to everyone: workers lacking the skills and language were hard-pressed to enter high-value-added services, and many remained in agriculture or informal urban work. Digital public infrastructure began to change some of the costs. Aadhaar digital identity, bank accounts, mobile communications and UPI instant payments were gradually linked up, with successive governments continuing to build them out. According to the case, electronic identity verification cut the cost of onboarding a customer from about $15 to $0.25. A small customer who once wasn't worth serving might, as a result, enter formal financial and commercial networks. But the pandemic also showed that progress in registration, payments and coordination had not closed the gaps in healthcare and job security. Viksit Bharat 2047 writes the next stretch of road as a national vision: to become a developed, high-income country by the centenary of independence, growing the economy from about $4 trillion in 2025, as listed in the case, to $30 trillion, while improving manufacturing, exports, green development and public services. The three questions the case leaves are therefore linked: 1. Going from $4 trillion to $30 trillion, how do you keep creating new productive capacity for 22 years? 2. With informal employment still at 88.3% in 2024, how do you make growth bring more stable, more productive jobs? 3. While pushing for speed in policy execution, how do you preserve the ability to spot mistakes, respond to different groups and change direction? My Thinking History explains the choices — and reminds us to choose again India's attachment to economic self-reliance has concrete historical roots. Having lived through external control and the extraction of resources, it's understandable that a new nation would want its own food, industry, research and technological capabilities. The problem is that institutions built for one historical stage change their function in another. Protection can help capabilities get started, and can also let incumbents avoid competition for a long time. An approval system for managing scarce resources may later become a system that limits new supply. 1991 matters because India was still the same India; after the policies changed, companies had a different room for action. That makes explanations like "culture determines growth" or "population is destiny" look too convenient. My own understanding is that history is most useful in helping us tell apart which capabilities are worth keeping and which arrangements need to end. The openness of ancient trade, the technical accumulation after independence, the later digital public systems — all can become foundations for the next stage. They don't need to come bundled with every layer of the old restrictions. Development means bringing more people to where productivity is In the case, the unemployment rate in 2024 was about 4.1%, while the informal employment rate reached 88.3%. The two numbers don't conflict. A person can work every day while earning very little, lacking protection, and having no chance to build up skills and capital. Leaving agriculture does not automatically mean entering more productive work. Walking from the fields to the city may lead into a factory, or may just mean scraping by in a different place. That's also why I'm reluctant to simply pit services against manufacturing. Services include software, but also logistics, tourism, healthcare and business services; manufacturing can absorb labor, but can also be highly automated. What really needs comparing is: what skills these industries require, how many people they can take in, whether they can raise real incomes, and whether companies have the conditions to keep growing. My own inclination is that India needs to keep its edge in high-skill services while laying down more upward paths suited to people's actual skill levels. The demographic dividend has to pass through schools, transport, health, childcare and employers before it reaches individuals. The efficiency of digital systems needs real services to catch it e-KYC dropping from about $15 to $0.25 is a substantial change. It alters the economics of serving small customers, and lets scattered small-scale transactions be connected. But identity can be verified online; a doctor can't exist only on a list in a system. Courses can be sent to a phone; a child still needs someone to help them learn to read. The ASER rural survey cited in the case shows that in 2024, among fifth graders, 48.7% could read a second-grade-level text and 30.7% could do division. This isn't a statistic for all children nationwide, but it's enough to point to a gap in foundational learning. Access is a precondition; outcomes still have to be delivered. An education system should be judged by what was learned, a health system by whether people got timely and effective care, digital finance by whether it helped business owners improve their real livelihoods. My own understanding is that technology can amplify existing capabilities, and it also shines a brighter light on the gaps in services. Once it has connected the roads, we still need people, organizations and professional skill to deliver what needs to be delivered. $30 trillion needs to be broken into several different report cards Going from $4 trillion in 2025 to $30 trillion in 2047 means growing 7.5-fold, implying a nominal compound annual growth rate of about 9.6% in dollar terms. This is my own calculation from the case's target, and it doesn't mean real GDP must grow 9.6% a year. Prices and exchange rates will both change the dollar size of the economy. More importantly, total economic size, the high-income threshold and broad improvement in living standards need to be tested separately. The World Bank's income classification is based on GNI per capita, and macro income crossing the threshold can't stand in for judgments about education, healthcare and job quality. If I had to pick a side before class, I would vote against "on the current path, the full set of goals will be fully delivered by 2047." The conditions for India to keep getting richer are strong, but most workers entering high-productivity jobs, public services becoming reliable, research results entering broad production — these changes still need more solid mechanisms. This judgment also has conditions that could change it: if learning outcomes, real incomes, female labor participation, growth-stage companies and the quality of local services all improve together for several years running, I would raise my expectations of the goals being met. They can help us judge whether growth has a broader foundation. I would give priority to foundational learning, primary healthcare, labor-intensive exports, small-business expansion and climate adaptation. The cost is that certain subsidies and showcase projects would have to give way, and the results of reform may arrive more slowly than a single election cycle. Execution capacity and the capacity to correct need to be built together The relationship between democracy and economic growth is hard to sum up in a straight line. India experienced low growth under democracy, and also accelerated growth through reform while keeping elections. A regime-type label alone can't explain the change from before to after. Elections, the media, the courts and public debate can make problems visible and give policies a chance to change. In 1977 voters replaced the government that had declared the Emergency; the turnover in 2004 also suggested that macro performance doesn't necessarily equal how enough people feel about their lives. What these show is a correction mechanism; they can't be taken directly as precise causal proof about GDP. Democracy can also suffer from short-term handouts, obstruction by vested interests, and majorities excluding minorities. Discussing these flaws is necessary; at the same time we should ask: once power is more concentrated, how are misjudgments discovered, how do those harmed make themselves heard, and how are policies unwound? Speed of decision only becomes development capacity when it's tied to quality of decision. A society needs a government that can get things done, and also institutions through which real feedback can enter decision-making. My own inclination is to build public service capacity and accountability together. The differences among India's states, and the local nature of basic education and health, mean that the center's vision ultimately has to pass through many concrete institutions before it becomes part of people's daily lives. Climate pressure will play out in these places too: how long outdoor workers can work, whether the fields have water, whether cities can keep basic services running in extreme heat. Takeaways for Arcus42 What this country case gives me is a few reminders about organizations and technology. Nations and companies differ in goals, power and responsibilities; what can transfer is a way of looking at problems. First, measure completing an action separately from creating value. A report finished, a process automated, only shows that an action took place. The better question is whether the people being served understand their situation better, and are more able to make judgments. Second, give expertise the chance to be used by more people. The outstanding abilities of a few need to reach everyday work through training, a shared language and review. Whether knowledge can be passed on and tested determines how much responsibility an organization can take on. Third, keep a channel open for dissenting views to enter decisions. Clear responsibility helps action; keeping assumptions visible and reviewing them helps correction. Everyone agreeing quickly doesn't, on its own, prove the judgment is right. Fourth, let the time technology saves go back into human judgment. Once AI makes drafting and organizing more efficient, we still need to see whether verification is more thorough, understanding deeper, and relationships between people tended to more carefully. High Tech, High Touch has to be delivered in these concrete steps. Final Words Before class, I cast my vote for this sentence: the quality of development depends on whether more people gain the ability to improve their own lives. $30 trillion can be a signpost in the distance. The road leading to it has to be built, stretch by stretch, all the way to people's feet. These are my personal pre-class study notes. The ASER indicators come from a rural survey; 9.6% is my own estimate of nominal dollar growth based on the case's target. The income classification method follows the World Bank WDI Sources and Methods. The judgments on development and the organizational analogies are my personal thinking and do not constitute investment or policy advice.
Why paper compliance couldn't stop the window dressing

Unit 3, Professor Eugene Soltes, Control: Lehman Brothers and Repo 105. In another class the same day, Frances Frei asks whether service is something you design. This class asks about control — the audit firm, the law firm, management: what role did each of them play? In this story, every piece of paper is in order. What's missing is the number behind the paper. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary May 2008: Matthew Lee had been at Lehman for fourteen years. He was a senior vice president in the finance division, responsible for the balance sheets of more than a thousand legal entities worldwide. He read the company's Code of Ethics over and over: if you discover a possible violation, you have a duty to report it immediately; good-faith reporting will not be met with retaliation. He hesitated for a long time. After seeing a lawyer, he decided it was his duty. On May 16, his letter reached the controller, the CFO and the chief risk officer. It made six points: at month-end there was roughly US$5 billion of net assets on the books that no one was really managing; there were billions of dollars of accounts worldwide that didn't reconcile; there were billions of dollars of inventory that, at current market prices and at the volumes they held, probably could be neither bought nor sold. The systems couldn't keep up with the expansion. The finance function in Mumbai might be efficiently distributing wrong numbers. Some senior internal audit staff were not equipped for a job that had become complicated. The words "Repo 105" did not appear anywhere in the letter. About two weeks later, his boss called him in: you've been laid off, as part of a larger downsizing. No other reason was given. He fought it, then accepted a severance agreement with a confidentiality clause. Lehman went bankrupt in September, and he never received all the money in the agreement. The audit firm said afterward that the company had investigated the letter itself and reported to the audit committee in July, concluding that the allegations were unfounded and there were no material issues. The firm's own review was never finished — the company no longer existed. Lehman was founded in 1850, one of Wall Street's oldest and, at one time, most profitable investment banks. In 1984 it was sold to Shearson/American Express; in 1994 it went independent through an IPO. Richard Fuld, a former trader, became chairman and CEO. Its historical strength was fixed income. Investors worried that its fixed-income exposure was too large, so the firm diversified: fixed income fell from 55% of revenue in 1995 to 39% in 2007. In the mid-2000s it deliberately pursued faster growth, shifting from a low-risk brokerage model to a high-risk banking model — the balance sheet went from "passing through" to "holding on." From 2004 to 2007, assets grew by roughly US$300 billion while equity grew by only US$6 billion. The high profits came from riskier things: packaging and trading exotic mortgage-backed securities. In 2007, it posted record revenue of US$19.3 billion and profit of US$4.2 billion. Fuld said: Smart risk management is never putting yourself in a position where you can't live to fight another day. It had no retail deposits to fall back on; it relied on short-term loans that were constantly rolled over. Once creditors panicked, the funding would stop. In 1998, when Long-Term Capital Management nearly collapsed, rumors were already going around that Lehman was finished. Fuld quelled that crisis of confidence at the time, and it came to be seen as the defining moment of his career. In March 2008, Bear Stearns, equally highly leveraged, collapsed. Since mid-2007, analysts and rating agencies had been watching investment bank leverage. After Bear Stearns, it became an urgent task: the market had to see leverage coming down. CFO Erin Callan said she was fighting hand-to-hand combat against the rumors. On March 18 she told the earnings call: we have deliberately brought leverage down; net leverage is 15.4x, versus 16.1 at year-end. On June 2, S&P cut its rating from A+ to A, while still praising its strong funding and liquidity profile. Less than a week later, Lehman pre-announced its first quarterly loss since going public, US$2.8 billion, replaced its CFO, and announced its third equity raise of the year, US$6 billion. The new CFO said: gross leverage has fallen from 31.7 to 24.3, net leverage from 15.4 to 12; the right leverage for now is in the low double digits; we will run the business conservatively. Not everyone believed it. Hedge fund manager David Einhorn had been shorting the stock since July 2007, and was especially skeptical of the published leverage numbers — about 40x on tangible equity, and holding things that should never have been levered at all. By June 2008, Lehman was the most heavily shorted investment bank on Wall Street. In August it cut 1,500 jobs. Over the first eight months the stock fell 73%. On September 10 it reported another loss, of US$3.9 billion. Three days later, the president of the New York Fed called Wall Street together and made it clear the government would not bail it out. That weekend, there was no buyer. On September 15, Lehman filed for bankruptcy. Its assets exceeded US$600 billion. The largest in American history. All its peers used repos for short-term funding. An ordinary repo is borrowing: a 2% haircut, the assets stay on the balance sheet, and cash and liabilities rise together. The accounting standards are clear: with collateral between 98% and 102%, you retain effective control and can't treat it as a sale. Lehman invented Repo 105: raise the haircut to 5% or 8%, claim that it had surrendered control, and therefore book it as a sale. Treated as a sale, assets on the balance sheet go down, the cash received pays off other liabilities, equity stays the same, and leverage appears to fall. The case includes an illustrative table: the same US$5 billion, treated as financing, leaves net leverage at 17.6 after paying down debt; treated as a sale, it drops to 15.6. From Q4 2007 to the end of Q2 2008, this practice cumulatively reduced net assets by more than US$138 billion. Usage ramped up in the days before reporting periods. It used US$24.5 billion at the end of 2006 and US$50.4 billion in Q2 2008. It was never publicly disclosed. In the financial statements it was folded into the derivatives notes. Readers couldn't see that the company was obliged to repurchase tens of billions of dollars of securities within a short period. American law firms refused to characterize this as a sale. The British law firm Linklaters would, under strict conditions — the securities had to be located in the UK, and the transactions had to be done under English law. So American securities were transferred to an affiliate in London, made the round trip, and were transferred back after the reporting date. From mid-2007, what the market watched shifted from revenue to the balance sheet. Chief risk officer Madelyn Antoncic had already been urging caution at the executive committee in late 2006. In 2007 she was sidelined — whenever a tense risk topic came up, Fuld had her leave the room along with the deal team. When traders found that sticky assets were hard to sell, and didn't want to sell them at a discount, they could "rent the balance sheet": use Repo 105 to move inventory off temporarily and still hit their net leverage targets. In March 2008 Fuld appointed veteran Bart McDade as "balance sheet czar." McDade wanted traders to be disciplined. In an email he wrote: another drug we [are] on. His position: sell the inventory. To those in power, Repo 105 counted as shrinking the balance sheet. Lehman took its laundered ratios to the three rating agencies to argue that it shouldn't face negative action. Repo 105 was nowhere in the materials. The New York Fed and the SEC didn't know either. The audit firm had audited Lehman's books since it went independent in 1994. Over ten years its fees exceeded US$185 million, and for seven straight years Lehman was one of its fifteen largest clients. In 2001 Lehman showed its internal accounting policy to the engagement partner, hoping to use Repo 105. The audit firm approved it. An internal memo from 2001 put it bluntly: this treatment lets Lehman net down its balance sheet. Lehman initially said the program would be capped at US$20 to 30 billion. In 2007 it started exceeding the cap. The new controller told the engagement partner: usage spikes at every quarter-end; the rationale for treating it as a sale is legalistic and form-driven. The audit firm still felt comfortable with the treatment under the standards. Its own workpapers defined materiality as: a 0.1 move in net leverage, which typically corresponded to US$1.8 billion. US$50.4 billion was 28 times that threshold. Lee's letter reached the audit firm. The engagement partner immediately told the chair of the audit committee and insisted that management inform regulators. The committee chair asked them to meet Lee and report back every allegation that came up in the investigation — whether or not it was in the letter. The interview was on June 12. On the spot, Lee added something that wasn't in the letter: at the end of Q2, Lehman had used Repo 105 to take US$50 billion of fixed-income securities off the balance sheet, and put them back a few days later. The next day, the engagement partner briefed the audit committee. He did not mention Repo 105. At the July 8 meeting, and at the July 22 meeting where internal audit reported "no material issues found," he stayed silent. On July 10, the audit firm issued an unqualified review report on the quarterly filing. Less than a month after the interview. The audit committee never knew about Repo 105, never knew American securities were being sent to the UK to do it, and never knew that its scale and quarter-end timing had been raised as a problem. The audit firm's CEO later gave an interview. In the end, he said, we feel good about the work we did at Lehman. These repos probably would only have changed leverage from 31x to 32x. Lehman would still have been the bank with the third-highest leverage. Beyond the case, Soltes has us read two other things. One is a letter he received from prison years ago: Stephen Richards, former global head of sales at Computer Associates, served seven years for recognizing contracts two or three days early. In the letter he wrote that executives spend most of their lives in the gray, and that it is a dangerous place. The other is the preface to his new book. The title already states the whole argument: Designing Process Versus Measuring Outcomes. Compliance programs often fail not for lack of effort, but because they measure effectiveness by process inputs — was the training completed, was the policy signed — rather than by whether behavior actually changed. The three questions in front of this class: 1. If you were a Lehman investor, how would you assess the risk of this business? 2. Why did Lehman use Repo 105? 3. Which institutions, if any, bear responsibility for the use of Repo 105? How would you improve those institutions? My Thinking Investors shouldn't look at net leverage, but at what keeps this company alive I wouldn't start with the 12.1x they quoted publicly. I'd first ask: how would this company die? It had no stable retail deposits. It rolled over short-term loans every day. The 1998 rumors had already shown how fast this kind of funding can collapse. Once Bear Stearns fell in March 2008, this was no longer a hypothetical enemy. Then look at what was sitting on that thin layer of equity. That record profit in 2007 came from high-margin mortgage-backed securities it held itself. Fuld said never put yourself where you can't fight another day. The balance sheet said the opposite. Lee put the internal version in his letter. US$5 billion extra at month-end that no one was managing. Billions in accounts that didn't reconcile. Billions in inventory that couldn't be sold at market prices. These aren't footnotes. This is the risk: a business that lives on confidence, funds itself overnight, and sits on sticky valuations. Einhorn had been short since July 2007. He might not have been able to name Repo 105. He picked the right target — the published ratio, and what lay beneath it. By June, it was the most shorted investment bank. On June 2, S&P was still praising its liquidity profile; a week later the company pre-announced its first quarterly loss since going public. My own take: a ratio that's only true on the reporting date isn't a risk metric — it's a press-release metric. The investor's scorecard really has just three lines: what keeps it alive, what it holds, and the governance of that number. Repo 105 is the evidence for the third line. Even if you couldn't yet name it at the time, the first two lines were enough. Repo 105 wasn't financing; it was a drug for the market's benefit Ordinary repos could already provide funding. What they wanted wasn't cash. They wanted the net leverage number to come down, without having to sell sticky assets at their real prices. From mid-2007, the market stopped watching revenue and started watching the balance sheet. Fuld made McDade czar. The businesses were ordered to shrink the balance sheet, to avoid a downgrade. McDade wanted them to sell inventory. The traders couldn't sell, or didn't want to eat the discount. So they rented the balance sheet: move things off for a few days, use the cash to pay down debt, leave equity untouched, and the printed ratio comes out lower. McDade gave it the right name — another drug. To those in power, this dose counted as shrinking the balance sheet. The accounting trick was small and specific. An extra 3 points of haircut bought a "sale." The illustrative table in the case writes the cosmetics in two figures: 17.6 becomes 15.6. Then they hid the product. The sentence American law firms refused to write, they went to London to buy. American securities took a round trip through the London affiliate and were transferred back after the reporting date. The dose rose from US$24.5 billion to US$50.4 billion. Across the last three quarter-ends, US$138 billion in total. Ramped up in the days before the reporting date. Laundered ratios taken to the rating agencies. The term nowhere in the materials. My own leaning is that the motive has to be stated plainly. This wasn't clever financing. It was window dressing under pressure. Richards wrote about the same slippery slope from prison: once you start managing the number, change the procedure even a little and you and the whole organization are exposed. Lehman's "little" was the extra 3 points, plus an opinion letter from London. After that, every quarter needed a bigger dose. By the time the form passes, the function has already failed The headline of this class is the audit firm, the law firm, management. I won't just single out one villain. This system let the form pass and let the function fail. Management first. They designed the drug, upped the dose, never disclosed it, and took the numbers to the rating agencies. McDade at least called it a drug while in the room. The risk officer had already been shown the door. The law firm was the ticket. American lawyers refused to call this a sale. A legal opinion like that isn't a control. It's a ticket that makes the form stand. The audit firm approved the policy and knew as early as 2001 that its purpose was to net down the balance sheet. They still didn't know the three syllables of Repo 105. You can't oversee a number no one has told you is synthetic. My own take: no single institution invented this lie. Each one stamped its own small slice of the form, so no one owned the function. Measure compliance by process inputs — training completion rates, policy sign-offs, whether a hotline exists — and every box on the paper gets ticked. Lehman had all of it. A Code of Ethics that required reporting and promised no retaliation. An independent audit committee. A Big Four auditor. An opinion letter from a Magic Circle law firm. Lee did exactly what the paper said. The result: laid off, gagged, and after the bankruptcy, never fully paid. In the book he writes about a gap that matches this letter. Ask employees whether they'd report misconduct if they saw it, and more than 90% say yes. Ask whether they actually reported it in the past six months, and it usually drops below 50%. Forty percentage points. Many compliance programs pretend this gap doesn't exist. Lee was one person inside that gap. In one quarter, legitimate revenue was inflated by 53%. Announced earnings per share were US$0.60; without the accelerated recognition, only US$0.05 was left. He too had comfort letters from a Big Four firm. He too had an investigation by the in-house general counsel that found nothing. Until the board brought in a different law firm, which recovered 23 boxes of missing documents and dug up the emails. In the letter he wrote: one minute you're doing an outstanding job, the next minute you've crossed an imaginary line. The world isn't black and white. Executives spend most of their lives in the gray. My own take is that the gray isn't somewhere you visit. It's where the quarter gets closed. The person who can create what Soltes calls uncomfortable dissonance — someone outside the inner circle who can still kill the deal — is the control. Antoncic was that person, and she was shown out of the room. Lee was that person, and he was laid off. The person on the audit team who wrote down reputational risk had their email stop at a manager. If that person can't survive the quarter, the rest of the program is paper. Improving these institutions doesn't mean writing another version of the code. It means changing what they count as success. Once you take the drug away, is the number the CEO quotes on the earnings call still the same number? Is the person who says it isn't still at the table? Those two things are the outcomes. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading this case, what comes to mind isn't one investment bank's bankruptcy. It's how any well-written set of controls can turn into window dressing on reporting day. First, having a code doesn't mean anyone dares to speak. Lehman's paper required reporting and promised no retaliation. Measuring training, sign-offs and whether the hotline exists can't measure Lee being laid off two weeks later. There are only two outcome metrics for speak-up: the person is still here, and the facts reached the table they should have reached. Second, a number that's only true on reporting day isn't risk control. Portfolios, proposals, progress — anything that only gets tidied up in the three days before a report, first ask McDade's question: are we selling inventory, or are we on drugs? The story we tell externally should still be the same story once you strip out the last three days' maneuvers. Third, legal opinions should state the purpose, not just whether something can be done. The sentence American lawyers refused to write was the most useful risk-control opinion of the day. Go buy one in another jurisdiction that will write it, and the form will stand. The question for the buyer is: if the only purpose of this move is to make some statement look good, do we still do it? Fourth, the committee needs to hear the ugly sentence. Setting out the right chairs — independence, expertise, executive sessions — isn't enough. When information is being filtered, oversight is already over. The standard materials should include a mid-quarter versus quarter-end comparison, and every "the form passes" opinion currently in use. If an auditor says a letter looks bad on its face but shouldn't lead to material issues, that sentence is itself the problem. Fifth, once the gray becomes well-trodden, you need an outsider. Richards wrote that it is a dangerous place. Don't pretend the world is black and white. There has to be someone who doesn't get shown out of the room, who is allowed to say "legalistic, form-driven" out loud. If control serves only the form, it becomes part of the window dressing. Final Thoughts Before class, the line I identified with most was "another drug."
