Unit 3, Professor Juan Alcacer's Strategy course, KLog.co – Charting the Course of its Future. The last one, Axel Springer, was an old company selling off newspapers it loved in order to buy a new world. This one runs the other way: a Chilean freight forwarder keeps its old business as a cash cow, builds the new world into a lock, and then asks — should the next dollar go into making that lock deeper, or into planting five new flags? Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Santiago, December 2023. Janan Knust holds an espresso and stares at the mural by the headquarters entrance. The mural tells KLog's first eleven years, and the staff are proud of it. He hopes there will be room on it for the next eleven. The company is no longer the impulse of that day in 2012 at the dinner table. His father ran logistics for fish exports and asked him to meet the people from Kerry Logistics. His father turned down the Chinese side's proposal, and he cut in: I'll represent you in Latin America. When KLog started out, it was simply Kerry's broker in Chile. By 2023 it provided both freight and software to more than 1,500 importers and exporters across Latin America: the forwarding business handled 13,834 shipments a year, its home-built SaaS reached US$500,000 in annual recurring revenue just over a year after launch, and it had always been profitable and never raised outside money. Several term sheets were already on the table. He kept asking himself the same set of questions: keep growing on our own cash, or take the first outside money? How should resources be split between forwarding and software? Would each decision damage the layer that makes KLog KLog? Knust's path doesn't look like a freight forwarder's. Born in Israel, with dyslexia and ADHD, he was cut from his football team at 17, went to Switzerland to study hotel management, and worked his way up from dishwasher to head of food and beverage at high-end hotels worldwide. He brought the hotel industry's obsession with service into an industry that doesn't put the customer at the centre. For the first three years, the brand and the relationships were there; the numbers weren't. The debt owed to Kerry piled up to the edge of bankruptcy, and he flew to China to secure a line of credit. As he later put it: good relationships aren't enough in a low-margin, highly commoditised industry; the new principle had to be "who we are," not "what we do." Freight forwarding is structurally unattractive. Global logistics is worth about US$10.7 trillion; forwarding itself about US$176 billion, growing at a compound rate of around 4.1% a year over the next five years. DHL has 6%, Kuehne + Nagel 4%, and small players together hold 60%. In Knust's words: barriers to entry are basically zero; anyone can do it. Customers use different forwarders for different routes and choose the cheapest. The industry's average cost of sales is 82%, and EBIT is 5%. Documentation is still almost entirely paper. The pandemic turned that into an accident: if the bill of lading can't get through, the cargo just sits there. Freight rates, meanwhile, turned everyone's revenue into a rollercoaster — the industry was +30% in 2021 and -11% in 2023; KLog's own revenue per shipment crashed from US$7,819 to US$2,764. He decided not to do it the way the industry does. In 2017 he kept Álvaro Serrano, CTO of a company he had invested in, and built a platform from scratch, first for internal use: purchase orders, instant quotes, sailing schedules, tracking, documents. At the end of 2020 Serrano said he couldn't go on — six developers, almost all in their first jobs, and no product, design or marketing. They wrote a plan to "make technology the main value proposition" and kept him. Customers began voting with their feet. A purchasing manager at a large Latin American home-goods retailer said: we switched to KLog because the platform adapts to how we operate; with anyone else, one change takes forever. The CEO of a Chilean sports distributor said: beyond the freight, what we like is that we can track, store documents, see historical costs, compare prices, and still talk to an account manager. One feature of the platform matters more than the feature list: customers can add shipments moved by other forwarders too. Documents are centralised even when KLog isn't the one moving the box. To get people to move in first, they created K4All — ship one load with KLog within a window and the platform is free. Software-only customers pay by container volume. The platform also comes with fully transparent quotes and a three-click Book & Pay, so sales can be bypassed. The information asymmetry traditional forwarders feed on was dismantled by KLog itself. The pandemic was an unexpected validation. Freight rates soared, and importers often didn't know where their cargo was. The technology investment proved right in the chaos, and revenue was lifted to about US$80 million. Flexport was at one point valued at US$8 billion, and Nowports at US$1.1 billion. Knust knew the tide would go out. He strengthened his team, opened offices in Peru, Bolivia and Mexico, and hired a Mexico CEO from Rappi. He met investors and got term sheets, but in the end decided to keep rolling on cash. He later said that bootstrapping this way kept them clear-eyed about costs. By 2023, the report card was split. Revenue fell from a peak of US$78.1 million to US$38.8 million, with US$50 million budgeted for 2024. Volumes were still growing: full containers rose from 5,256 TEU to 14,718, a three-year compound rate of 41%; the number of transactions grew 35% in the very year revenue per shipment was cut in half. Overall customer churn fell from about 55% in 2017 to about 40% — still typical of the industry. But once customers got onto the platform, retention followed a different curve: about 80% or more, back to 100% by year seven; for those not on the platform, it dropped to 51% in year one, and only about 20% remained after five to seven years. In mid-2023, platform users were only 26% of active customers. Forwarding had a gross margin of about 22% and an operating margin of about 11%; SaaS had 90% and 35% — and only US$500,000 of annual recurring revenue. The culture was written down as AFIRE: fun, focus, discomfort, resilience, learning. Knust says culture has been the single most important success factor so far. Hiring deliberately avoids people from the forwarding industry; at the same time, he has known most of his senior executives since he was three. The office has a nap area, on-site massages and draught beer. Four things in front of him, and US$15 million of cash over two years. Geographic expansion — Brazil, Colombia, Panama, plus China and Miami — about US$20 million; the digital platform plus a SaaS sales team, about US$12 million; trade credit, inventory finance, payments and insurance, about US$11 million; adding a CMO, a CRO and a chief of staff, about US$2 million. About US$45 million in total. The illustrative term sheet is US$50 million at a US$200 million pre-money valuation, a 1.5x liquidation preference, the right in year seven to redeem or force a sale, and a board seat with veto rights over audit and compensation. Sitting at his desk, Knust has to answer: 1. Is freight forwarding an attractive industry? 2. What is the latest version of KLog's model? Does it solve the industry's problems? 3. What is its competitive advantage, and can it be defended? 4. Where is this growth curve strong, and where is it weak? 5. Should it go deep next, or go wide? 6. Should it use outside money to pay this bill? My Thinking Freight forwarding is unattractive — and that is exactly where this case starts In Alcacer's strategy course, the first question is almost always about the industry itself. Answer it with "forwarding is growing, so it's attractive," and the next five answers all go off course. Zero barriers to entry, zero switching costs, price is the product, average EBIT of 5%, and the top two players together hold only 10%. Big companies already negotiate directly with the shipping lines. What decides revenue is often not skill but freight rates — KLog's own revenue per shipment can halve within a year. Unattractive is not a reason to stay out; it is a reason not to scale up this industry as it is. My own take is that strategy in an industry like this isn't "we move boxes better than anyone else," but "we make it hurt when customers leave." That pain isn't in lower freight rates. Anyone can copy freight rates. The boldest move is dismantling the information asymmetry you live on Traditional forwarders live on three things: relationships, negotiation, and customers not being able to see clearly. KLog put its quotes on the table and added three-click booking, so its own salespeople can be bypassed. That isn't a product manager's feature. It's an old advantage that a founder chose to give up. In the short term it looks like tearing down your own brokerage; in the long term what it buys is trust — and that forked retention chart. The same thinking shows up in one more place, which is easy to dismiss as merely "open-minded": the platform lets customers add shipments moved by other forwarders. A forwarder that builds its own booking tool is competing for a button; one that becomes the place where the customer's documents and history live is competing for memory. "Customers will stay and keep letting KLog move their boxes, because competitors are still moving boxes with pen and paper." Knust's line puts two things together: the one moving the boxes is still the forwarder; what makes people not want to switch is the system. My own take is that once the old information rent becomes a stranded asset, the earlier you give it up, the cheaper it is. Give it up too late, and someone else will give it up for you — and walk off with the memory. The moat isn't the software; it's software and forwarding growing up in the same system Serrano didn't stay because of the technology itself. In his own words: technology alone isn't enough. The platform grew up together with the operations team, and what employees use is what customers use. That's why customers say other people's tools are thin and rigid, and one change takes forever. The culture is written down as a layer alongside the software. The two words in AFIRE I care about most are discomfort and learning. The first forbids the company from relaxing just as things start getting easier; the second forbids relying on cleverness and improvisation. Add one hiring rule: deliberately don't hire from the forwarding industry. This three-piece set — live operations, one shared system, and a culture that is still filtering — can't be copied by copying a feature list. Copy a single screen, and the big forwarders are already doing it; Flexport acted that out at a far higher valuation. It isn't finished, either. Only 26% of active customers live on the platform. US$500,000 of annual recurring revenue, backed out using the case's average software revenue per customer, means roughly twenty-some paying accounts. K4All's free tier is lifting retention, but the software company hasn't been born yet. My own inclination is to treat "moving in" as the strategic metric first, rather than ARR. If 26 becomes 60, the nature of the forwarding book changes; if 500,000 becomes 5 million while 26 stays at 26, nothing changes. Revenue halved while volumes kept growing: a report card and a warning Read only revenue, and KLog looks like it's shrinking: US$78.1 million down to US$38.8 million. Read only 2021, and it looks like a tech company that ought to be worth US$200 million. Both readings are wrong. Volumes are growing, customers are growing, prices per shipment are collapsing. In 2023 transactions were +35% and revenue per shipment -60%. This is a company taking share in an ugly industry, with its income statement torn open by a freight-rate chart. The 2024 budget of US$50 million and 15,000 shipments is a recovery, not a moonshot. The warning is on the other side. Overall churn is still about 40%. The four cultures haven't fully grown together — Serrano almost left in 2020, technology is replacing manual work, and Knust can already see that "if we don't grow exponentially, our people will run out of work." He has known most of his senior executives since he was three: at two hundred people that means speed; when you need to add marketing, a head of revenue and a whole credit function, it's a blind spot. The geography is still thin, weighted heavily to Chile. AFIRE and draught beer can't be exported as a toolkit. Make the platform sticky enough first, then go into Brazil The four-item menu adds up to about US$45 million, against US$15 million of cash over two years. The platform plus the team is US$14 million, which fits in their own pocket. Brazil, Colombia, Panama, China and Miami are US$20 million, and fintech is US$11 million; those don't fit. I would spend the cash on the first two. Push geography back, and when the time comes, go in with the software first, not the warehouses. Put fintech on hold — trade credit is a third business, they have only just survived a 60% drop in revenue per shipment, and there is no reason to start lending at this point. The growth menu is not four equal items. The ordering is the capital structure. The cost is clear: in São Paulo, for a while, they will look smaller than rivals who have raised money. The other path costs more: before 26 turns into 60, turning yourself into a more respectable regional forwarder — on someone else's clock. DHL and K+N grew by buying the local top students. KLog shouldn't copy that path before it has something those top students don't. I wouldn't sign this term sheet US$50 million at a US$200 million pre-money valuation, 20% dilution. A 1.5x liquidation preference, the right in year seven to redeem or force a sale of the company, and a board seat that holds audit and compensation in check. On 2023 revenue, that's about 5x. Even valuing the software at ten times annual recurring revenue, it's worth only a few million. The investors are underwriting a forwarding book that has just been cut in half, plus a story. The case itself says it: the Flexport kind of hope has cooled. The useful part of fundraising, they've already had once. The process got the company understood and left relationships behind, and they didn't take the money. In the boom, that was right. After the tide went out, if growth means only the platform and the team, it is still right. My own take is that outside money is only for a moat that cash can't cover. In this round, KLog's cash can cover the moat. What the terms would rewrite is precisely the moat — how people get paid, what gets measured, and what kind of story must be told in year seven. The next panel of the mural shouldn't be in someone else's handwriting. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading this case, what came to mind wasn't shipping containers, but any company that sells both "service" and "system" at once: the old business pays the bills, while the new system decides whether the customer will still be there tomorrow. First, ask whether the industry is attractive before asking whether you should grow the way it does. In an industry with low barriers, price wars and customers who can leave any time, expanding territory just replicates churn. The first job of strategy is to change how much it hurts to leave, not to open a few more doors. Second, what you're really competing for is the customer's memory, not the booking button. If a system can only hold what you yourself sold, it's still a forwarder's website. If a system can hold what happened to the customer elsewhere, it starts to become the source of truth. When a person leaves and the customer follows, it's often because the memory still lived in that one person's head. Third, give up the old information rent voluntarily. Not being able to see clearly is the source of profit for many intermediary industries. Lay it out in the open and in the short term it looks like you're dismantling your own sales; don't, and someone will do it for you. Stickiness is the new profit; opacity is a stranded asset. Fourth, rank the growth menu; the ranking is the capital structure. Four things that all look right will, added together, force a term sheet that rewrites your culture. Do first the thing that makes it hurt for customers to leave. If your cash can cover the moat, don't buy someone else's calendar for the sake of more flags. Fifth, culture is strategy only while it is still filtering. Words on the wall, plus "we don't hire veterans of this industry," make a filter. Words on the wall, plus finding the next hire only among people you know, plus an outside compensation committee, make an atmosphere. Sixth, whether fundraising is right isn't about whether you raise, but whether the money covers the layer cash can't. Going through a full round and then setting the terms aside can be the most valuable stretch of all. Raise when you should; when you shouldn't, the process itself is already enough. Final Words Before class, the line I agree with most is: "The growth menu is not four equal items. The ordering is the capital structure." Global Markets: The Atlantic and OpenAI
Should content be sold to the models?

Unit 3, Professor Carrie Elkins, Global Markets: The Atlantic and OpenAI. The last piece asked whether the silicon shield is a protection or a weak spot. This one swings the camera from wafers to a magazine. What gets taken for training here isn't production capacity — it's sentences. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary In March 2024, The Atlantic announced a two-year partnership with OpenAI. OpenAI got a licence to use the magazine's content to train its models and answer queries; the magazine got licensing fees, priority access to the technology, and a place inside the tech giant as a "premium news source." CEO Nicholas Thompson cared about more than the money: he saw a potential traffic channel, and a chance to "help shape the future of AI." The newsroom exploded. Staff wrote an open letter to Thompson and editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg: AI cannot replace journalists, and no outlet that still wants to live up to this magazine's century-and-a-half of standards can allow that to happen. Editor Damon Beres called it, in the magazine's own pages, "a devil's bargain." Jessica Lessin, founder of The Information, used the same pages to argue that these deals amount to settling without suing — trading hard-won credibility for a bit of cash, with a counterparty that undervalues you while building products plainly meant to replace you. From day one, the magazine was more an American idea than a good business. In 1857, a circle of abolitionist intellectuals — Emerson, Longfellow, Holmes — founded it in Boston to talk about slavery, and about the tensions pushing the nation towards civil war. It went on to publish Hemingway and Einstein, and early work by Mark Twain and Henry James. Former editor Cullen Murphy put it this way: it advances something you could call "the American idea." Culturally indispensable, it rarely won on the books. In the 1990s it could lose US$500,000 a year. In 1999 David Bradley bought it for US$10 million, and reportedly poured in more than US$100 million after that. The magazine still lost US$4–8 million a year. Only when he started running it like a startup — digital advertising rising from 9% to 45% of revenue, expansion into events and consulting — did it turn a US$1.8 million profit in 2010. His children didn't want the magazine. He began looking for an exit. In 2017, Laurene Powell Jobs, Steve Jobs's widow, bought 70% through Emerson Collective for more than US$100 million. Her net worth at the time was about US$18.2 billion. Bradley told staff she had always been at the very top of his list: Emerson was already investing in serious journalism for its own sake. She described the magazine as a critical mission at a critical moment — equality, the American idea, American culture, and this wonderful and often messy experiment in democracy. The collective is named after Emerson. The organisation itself, though, is pure Silicon Valley: an LLC rather than a traditional foundation, with venture capital, activism and philanthropy at the same table. She promised not to touch the editorial side, while hiring heavily: headcount grew by about 30%, a paywall went up, the typography was redone, and the whole company was pushed to use technology more deeply. Bradley said at the time that The Atlantic's core strength was not operating at the technological frontier. She said: it should be. Expansion was expensive. Profits of roughly US$10 million a year when she took over turned back into losses. In March 2020, even as subscriptions rose, the magazine laid off 17% of its staff. In late 2020, former Wired editor-in-chief Nick Thompson became CEO. His mandate: dig out of the hole and build a business that could sustain itself. He inherited a US$20 million deficit. He immediately raised subscription prices by 50% and launched a dynamic paywall that targets readers by their likelihood to convert. Goldberg moved the magazine away from daily news towards fewer, more deeply reported stories. By 2024 the magazine was profitable again, with more than 1 million subscribers and US$100 million in revenue, nearly two-thirds of it from subscriptions — up from less than half. Under Thompson it won three Pulitzers. The October 2024 issue, its cover almost free of headlines, won ASME's best cover the following year. One story led to the resignation of the then-head of CNN; one cover story helped exonerate a wrongly convicted man. In Goldberg's words: We treat it almost as an ideology, an idealism — what we make is worth paying for. Over the same stretch, OpenAI turned the tech industry upside down. ChatGPT launched in 2022 and passed 30 million users in two months. Microsoft's investment reached US$14 billion. Models need oceans of text. Believing that scale converts directly into performance, AI companies tested the limits of copyright and swallowed the internet whole. In one study, ChatGPT-4's hallucination rate approached 30%. In December 2023, The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft: in Common Crawl, a "copy of the internet," Times content alone accounted for 16 million records. GPT-3 through GPT-4 were reportedly trained on 45 TB of data, roughly a 3.7-billion-page Word document. The Times demanded the models be destroyed and sought statutory damages of up to US$150,000 per article — for pieces that typically license for about US$10. OpenAI pleaded fair use and argued that no single source contributes meaningfully to training. By May 2025, some 40 copyright cases were pending. The rulings split: one judge held that training a competing product on another party's case summaries was not transformative; another held that Anthropic's use of 7 million books was. Anthropic still settled in September 2025 for US$1.5 billion, about US$3,000 per book — the largest settlement in US copyright history. Thompson chose a different road from the Times. He acknowledged that the large models had plainly scraped without permission, and then did the maths: there's a whole range of ways to get paid, so put what the other side offers on the same scale as the cost of suing and the damages you might win. The exact terms were not disclosed. OpenAI was signing deals at a furious pace, and industry estimates of annual fees ran from several million to US$50 million — News Corp at US$250 million over five years, the Financial Times at US$5–10 million a year, Axel Springer at US$25–30 million over three years. By April 2025, OpenAI had partnered with 20 news publishers covering more than 160 outlets; across publishers and AI companies there were roughly 72 licensing deals in total. Thompson said the magazine would not become overly dependent on AI traffic; it would keep telling stories in the best way it could, and then distribute them as hard as possible. He also said: if content like The Atlantic's goes into these models, the world will be a better place. Powell Jobs has never spoken publicly about the deal. She kept her promise not to interfere with editorial. When Goldberg was mistakenly added to a classified Signal group discussing war plans, she stood by her editor. But her interest in AI is public. Emerson has invested in several AI startups, and she played a key role in the roughly US$6.4 billion hardware partnership between OpenAI and Jony Ive, a longtime friend of the Jobs family. In 2025 she and Ive made a rare joint appearance. Ive said that innovation has unforeseen consequences, some wonderful, some harmful, and that he still feels responsible. She picked up the thread: we now know unambiguously that certain technologies have dark uses — but that was a sideways result. The case stops at the table, just before renewal. Google's AI Overviews have already cut click-throughs to outside sites by more than 34%; chatbots have replaced search for more than 25% of Americans. The news industry is planning for "search zero." Yet The Atlantic is hiring: 30 editors in the first half of 2025, at salaries of US$200,000–300,000. Most of its peers are cutting. Is this just one of the few self-sustaining outlets hiring by the old logic, or has she seen another layer — that the people building models need writers? Trained only on synthetic data, models may collapse. Is the partnership between writers and AI companies the key to both sides surviving economically, or is it accelerating the replacement of journalism and pushing creativity towards something flatter? The four questions in front of Carrie Elkins: 1. What is the ideas economy? How does it reshape the world business leaders operate in? 2. Why did Laurene Powell Jobs and Emerson Collective buy The Atlantic ? 3. Should The Atlantic partner with OpenAI? 4. What would continuing the partnership mean for the magazine's journalism, and for the wider landscape of ideas? My Thinking The ideas economy puts a price on an original sentence The ideas economy is not a new industry. It is the market that produces, distributes and prices original thought. Journalism, literature, science, argument — and everything a society uses to decide what is true, what is worth paying for and what is permitted — all live inside it. It has three layers. Production is the work of scarce people: a magazine 168 years in the making, a novel thirty years in the writing, an investigation that can make someone resign and bring a wrongly convicted man home. Distribution used to be print, then the open web, then the search box. Now it is also a chatbot that can answer without ever sending the reader back to the source. Capture is who gets the money. For most of The Atlantic's life, capture was weak. In 2024 the income statement finally held up — US$100 million in revenue, nearly two-thirds from 1 million paying subscribers — and just then a new buyer appeared: model trainers who treat the archive as fuel. Business leaders already live in this market. Regulation, talent, customers, even whether they are allowed to keep operating — all of it sits downstream of other people's sentences. Consultants who use models outperform those who don't overall, but the gains go mostly to those with low baselines, and the variance in team output gets flattened. The case cites a 2025 MIT study: ChatGPT users showed the lowest brain engagement and later slid into copy-and-paste. People who treat the model as a free intern are quietly thinning out their own judgement. My own reading is that what's truly new in this Global Markets class is not that a magazine and a lab signed a deal. It's that the way ideas cross borders has changed. They used to travel as printed matter and as graduates. Now they also travel as tokens in a training run. Whoever sets the price of those tokens — licensing, litigation, or fair use marked down to zero — is writing the trade rules for knowledge work over the next decade. What she bought was an American idea, not an income statement The 2017 acquisition can't be explained by the US$1.8 million profit of 2010, nor refuted by the US$20 million hole that came later. Bradley paid US$10 million in 1999, poured in more than US$100 million afterwards, and was still losing US$4–8 million a year before he got to that US$1.8 million. For someone then worth about US$18.2 billion, paying more than US$100 million for 70% was a stewardship cheque. Her words at the time: a critical mission at a critical moment. The collective is named after Emerson. The first page of the case is Emerson himself — the poets and inventors unlock our chains. Buying the magazine that Emerson's circle founded is the most literal way to fund that sentence. She did two things that don't easily sit in the same room. She promised not to touch editorial, and kept that promise. At the same time she ran Emerson like a startup, told each unit to disrupt its own field, and, when Bradley said The Atlantic wasn't a tech company, answered: it should be. In 2020 her orders to Thompson changed again: dig out of the hole, build a company that can sustain itself. A mission without a going concern is a subsidy. A going concern without a mission is just another website. She has always wanted to hold on to both. The OpenAI deal is where those two wishes can no longer live in separate rooms. My own reading is that what she bought was never an IRR. She bought the right to have a voice at the level of ideas. The renewal question isn't whether this deal makes money. It's whether the voice is still there, and at what price it is being sold. Sign — but don't renew on the same contract The first deal is a pricing exercise, not a marriage. Thompson's sentence is the right frame. The models plainly scraped without permission. There's a whole range of ways to get paid. Weigh what the other side offers against the cost of suing and what you might win. With the archive already inside GPT-3 and beyond, that is the only grown-up arithmetic. The financial case for signing is clearer than the open letter admits. The Atlantic had only just climbed out of a US$20 million hole. The cluster in Exhibit 3 that looks most like it — the FT at US$5–10 million a year, Axel Springer at US$25–30 million over three years — amounts to 5–10% of annual revenue. Enough to pay for most of the 2025 hiring round. Litigation is not free. The Times spent US$10.8 million in the first year, and still has no ruling. A magazine that has only just turned profitable, with 1 million subscribers, shouldn't volunteer to be the test case that funds a decade of discovery. The "don't sign" side is real too. A hallucination rate near 30% can stain a brand that has only just made "worth paying for" true. Cheap licences may be funding the very product that means readers never have to arrive. Google's summaries have already taken more than 34% of referral clicks. Sharper still is the owner's own position: Emerson's AI portfolio and Ive's hardware mean she has to be able to show that the renewal terms were negotiated as if she had no other chip on the table. My own choice: renew, on terms written by the seller. Sell training and retrieval separately. Ban verbatim regurgitation; accept only clickable citations. If the Times or the next big settlement raises the floor, reopen the deal. Never let AI referrals become a significant acquisition channel. Keep suing those who don't pay — they later sued Cohere, which shows they can already tell a counterparty from a free rider. Take the owner's other bets out of the terms. The cost of renewing blindly is the sentence Lessin has already written, in The Atlantic, to The Atlantic. The cost of walking away is spending money the way the Times does, without the Times's balance sheet. Sell the past to pay for the next investigation Goldberg has in fact already built the strategy along the way. They left daily news for fewer, deeper stories. Daily news is the first thing chatbots replace. Investigations that make someone resign, that bring a wrongly convicted man home, are what models can't originate and what subscribers will still pay for. Licensing out the archive while thickening the newsroom is internally consistent. Sell the past; raise the price of the next original piece. Thirty editors in the first half of 2025 at US$200,000–300,000 is not a billionaire's mood of benevolence. It's a bet that human reporting is a scarce input. The question at the end of the case and this bet are the same sentence — whether labs need writers to keep their models from collapsing. The medium-term risks are on the same page. If models answer with a smooth paraphrase and a dead link, subscribers won't come. Incentives inside the magazine will quietly tilt towards getting cited by models: shorter explainers, fewer year-long investigations. The hiring wave becomes a content farm with nicer furniture. A hallucinated "Atlantic" claim isn't a traffic problem; it's a reputational problem dressed in the magazine's own typeface. My own leaning: the money has to go back to the writers for this deal to be worthy of the reason she bought the magazine. A quiet, permanent feed for the models is not. Models will flatten the marketplace of ideas — unless someone can say no By April 2025, OpenAI had 20 publishers covering more than 160 outlets. Across the industry there were roughly 72 licensing deals. That sounds like a market. It's only a market for those who can afford a Thompson. The passage in the case on novelist Min Jin Lee is the other half. She spent thirty years writing books, gave up a legal career, and then discovered that models had stolen her stories. If the going rate is a seven-figure cheque for the mastheads and zero for everyone else, there will only be fewer of the next books that take thirty years to write. Adobe's verifiable attribution on creative work helps with credit. It doesn't create a living. Creativity research is the layer business leaders will feel even if they never buy a magazine. AI beats all but the very best humans at divergent thinking. Stories written with it help weaker writers more, yet as a group they come out more alike. Consultants get better together, and more alike together. ChatGPT users get lazier. The Four C model separates everyday little-c creativity from the steam-engine kind of Big-C creativity. The former will be automated and homogenised. The latter will become more valuable, and harder to sustain — if the distribution layer no longer sends readers or royalties back. My own reading is that Powell Jobs doesn't owe the labs a cheap corpus. She owes the next Emerson a world in which new ideas still have someone who pays for them. Renewing without terms betrays that sentence. Walking away, and letting fair use stay marked at zero for everyone smaller than the Times, betrays it too. Someone who sits in both rooms at once has to set a price the other rooms can copy. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading this case, what comes to mind isn't one magazine's renewal, but any company that writes judgement into systems: the archive is already within a model's reach, and the pricing rules don't exist yet. First: once knowledge is in the system, the live question is licensing, not purity. Meeting notes, family archives, proposal drafts — all of it will become trainable text. Training, retrieval and generating sentences for clients to read are three different things; don't fold them into one checkbox. Second: people own the judgement, models handle the rest — and the rest can't face the client directly. The Atlantic used its paywall to protect those 1 million subscribers. What a family office has to protect is that layer in the room. The model can draft. What the family is still buying is a judgement a person is willing to sign. Third: don't hand distribution to a platform a second time. Publishers first handed their readers to search, then watched summaries take more than 30% of their clicks. Internal systems can be queried. They can't become the place where a client "discovers they have a problem." Fourth: whoever sits on both sides owes the weaker side a process. An owner can love technology and also love an institution of ideas. When both sit in the same chequebook, a renewal can't run on vibes. Recusal, disclosure and an independent person reviewing the terms are cheaper than explaining afterwards. Fifth: the new buyer's money has to go back to the scarce people. The deal only holds up because The Atlantic turned the partnership fees into a round of well-paid editors. If platforms pay for process knowledge, the fees should flow back into the quality of judgement, not into a leaner team. In Closing Before class, the line I agree with most is: "Sign, and renew — but not on the same contract."
Is the silicon shield a protection or a weak spot?

Unit 3, Professor Carrie Elkins, Global Markets, Taiwan, Semiconductors, and a “New Cold War”? The previous piece asked why compliance that's complete on paper can't stop window dressing. This one pulls the camera out to an island, a strait and a chip. The shield in this story is the most advanced wafer in the world. The question is whether the shield becomes a bullseye first. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary In autumn 2021, Tsai Ing-wen addressed the world in Foreign Affairs . Sorties by military aircraft into the air defence identification zone were at a record high. The defence minister judged that by 2025 the other side of the strait would be able to take military action at the lowest possible cost. She wrote: if Taiwan were to fall, the consequences for regional peace would be catastrophic. She also knew that ideals often dissolve in international relations, so she offered another reason — TSMC, and the semiconductor industry more broadly, are a “silicon shield.” Chairman Mark Liu told 60 Minutes that the whole world needs Taiwan's high technology, and so no one will let war happen in this region. Yet Beijing and Washington were both pouring in money, trying to break their dependence on Taiwan — and on each other. Some began calling this a new Cold War. Semiconductors were never something the market grew on its own. In 1947, Bell Labs built the transistor. The Pentagon put up money, set standards and built plants. Antitrust action by the Justice Department forced AT&T to open up its patents. Venture capital grew Fairchild and Intel in the Stanford Industrial Park. Moore's Law became the metronome. In the 1970s, the US moved packaging and testing to places including Taiwan; Japan's MITI coordinated R&D and subsidised loans, and its share rose from 28% in 1978 to 46% in 1986, while the US fell from 55% to 40%. Washington did not go on “trusting the market.” It threatened anti-dumping action, slapped tariffs on US$300 million of Japanese electronics, and set up SEMATECH with fourteen companies. The US went on to win in design, not in wafers. In 2019, 38% of global semiconductor value added was still in the US, as was 74% of EDA and core IP. What it lost was the most advanced fab. Taiwan chose a very narrow slice. Land reform, export processing zones and vocational schools got the people ready first. In 1990, 30% of university students studied engineering. ITRI was founded in 1973 to do applied research, and over twenty-seven years it fed roughly 12,000 engineers into industry. Its electronics research institute bought an already outdated 7-micron process from RCA, achieved yields higher than RCA's own US plant, and then spun off UMC. In 1985, Morris Chang put down the phone. He had spent twenty-five years at Texas Instruments, had watched the cost of building a fab roughly double every five years, and had seen a crop of fabless design companies start renting other people's capacity. The premier had asked him to lead this effort. His judgement was: don't build yet another chip company that does everything itself. Use state capital to build a pure-play foundry that only manufactures for others — no design of its own, no brand of its own. He signed with Philips, brought in technology only nine months behind the frontier, and founded TSMC. Within a year, more than forty design companies sprang up in Hsinchu. In 1992, AMD's CEO was still saying real men have fabs. In 2009, AMD sold its fabs. By 2020, TSMC held half of global foundry capacity. In 2019, 92% of logic wafer capacity below 10 nanometres was in Taiwan. In 2014, Beijing switched to a bigger industrial policy. After the Snowden affair, the leadership concluded that core technology could not be in other people's hands. Xi Jinping's words in 2016: Core technology is our greatest lifeline; having core technology controlled by others is our greatest hidden danger. The National Integrated Circuit Industry Development Guidelines set an investment target of US$150 billion. Made in China 2025 wrote a ten-year self-sufficiency rate of 70%. From 2014 to 2018, 86% of state equity support for semiconductors worldwide came from China. Government ownership of SMIC rose from under 15% to over 45%. The toolkit also included forced joint ventures, US$35 billion a year in outbound M&A, and talent programmes. The scoreboard was mixed. In the first ten months of 2020, about 200 new semiconductor companies were registered every day. SMIC announced 7 nanometres. Tsinghua Unigroup walked into bankruptcy. Chinese-owned firms still produced only 5.9% of the chips China used. Huawei's Mate 60 took domestic components from 29% to 47% — real progress, but still without the extreme ultraviolet lithography machine that only the Netherlands in the whole world can make. Washington rewrote Beijing from “responsible stakeholder” to strategic competitor. Export controls, the extraterritorial reach of the foreign direct product rule, and investment screening expanded to minority stakes, step by step removed Huawei from TSMC's customer list — it had been the second-largest customer after Apple, contributing more than 15% of revenue, and after it left, Huawei's own revenue fell by roughly a third. In September 2022, National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan said: we used to only need to stay a generation or two ahead; now, for advanced logic and memory, we must maintain as large a lead as possible. Mitt Romney, once a critic of industrial policy, turned to backing the CHIPS and Science Act : US$278 billion authorised, over US$52 billion for semiconductors. The Boston Consulting Group calculation cited in the case is that US$50 billion in subsidies would lift the US share of output only from 12% to 14%. Morris Chang called it an expensive exercise in futility. TSMC still went to Arizona, planning to invest US$40 billion, at a local construction cost roughly four times Taiwan's. He said that if a machine breaks at 1 a.m., in the US it gets fixed the next morning; in Taiwan it's fixed by 2 a.m. He also said: globalisation is almost dead, and free trade is almost dead. On the island, the silicon shield theory was being used at the same time. In 2020 Taiwan was the world's twenty-second-largest economy. Exports often exceeded half of GDP, 40% of them semiconductors, and China absorbed 44% of exports. It was the economy with the second-highest exposure to global value chains. Compulsory military service had been cut to four months, which some called summer camp. Military spending fell from about 5% of GDP to about 2%. Roughly half of respondents said they were willing to defend the island, and most believed they would never really have to fight and could count on the US. In 2020, US$8.1 billion bought 66 F-16s. Analysts would rather see a porcupine: anti-ship, anti-tank and air defence, for a war of attrition the island could survive. In the winter of 2024, Lai Ching-te won the presidency. After his victory he said that Taiwan's semiconductors are a shared asset of the world, and he hoped everyone would treasure them. The silicon shield narrative lives on. The case ends with a question: is it alive and well, or dying a hard death? The three questions in front of Carrie Elkins: 1. How have the government policies of the US, Taiwan and China each shaped the semiconductor industry? 2. How should Taiwan navigate US–China tensions? Are semiconductors a protection, or a vulnerability? 3. Does this competition mean a deglobalising world? If so, what are the consequences? My Thinking Three countries' industrial policies grew three different capabilities Semiconductors are not the spontaneous order of a free market. They are capabilities selected by policy. US policy built an open knowledge system and then outsourced the factories. The Pentagon and antitrust provided the first push; venture capital provided diffusion; the counterattack on Japan preserved design. Today the most valuable US chip companies often have no fabs of their own. Nvidia hands its products to TSMC. CHIPS's US$52 billion is an attempt to buy the factories back. A bill can buy back concrete; it can't buy back the work culture of someone coming to fix the machine at 2 a.m. Taiwan's policy chose one segment and cut all the way down. Not design and brands — a pure-play foundry. ITRI, Hsinchu, Philips technology only nine months behind, government stakes of up to 49% — all for this one segment. Apple, Qualcomm and Nvidia look the way they do today because someone took on the manufacturing risk. A developmental state doesn't “develop electronics” in the abstract. It picks the slice it can do, and avoids the one it can't. China's policy is bigger, broader and more urgent. A US$150 billion target, 70% self-sufficiency, 86% of the world's state equity support. Money can pile up 200 new companies a day; it can pile up the Mate 60's 47%. It hasn't yet piled up stable advanced yields. An advanced chip takes about 700 process steps. Only if every single step is right does the final product hold up. Subsidies can be written into documents. The discipline of 700 steps can't. My own understanding is that industrial policy isn't a switch. It's a choice: at which segment of the chain are you actually prepared to become irreplaceable to the whole world? The silicon shield is both an amulet and a bullseye 92% is a number that changes the calculus of war. In 2019, 92% of logic wafer capacity below 10 nanometres was in Taiwan, and the remaining 8% in South Korea. Only three companies in the world could make 5 nanometres. A conflict that lands on this island wouldn't be a local war. Phones, the cloud, cars and model training would all stop together. In that direction, the shield is real. The same set of numbers is also drawing a bullseye. Both sides are spending money so that they no longer need this 92%. Beijing writes it as 70% self-sufficiency. Washington writes it as export licences and a fab in Arizona. With every piece of equipment installed, the sentence “this chip can only be made in Taiwan” becomes a little less true. Huawei once contributed more than 15% of TSMC's revenue, and it left not because of the market but because of a list. China still absorbs 44% of Taiwan's exports. Pineapples have already been used once, as a rehearsal for sanctions. My own inclination is that being irreplaceable is not the same as being safe. A moat looks like an amulet — until the neighbour decides the moat is a threat. Then the moat becomes their reason to come over. Tsai Ing-wen and Mark Liu cast TSMC as security policy. That made sense in 2001, when the term silicon shield was first coined — back then nobody could really afford the price of getting out. The new fact of the 2020s is that both sides have decided they can. The sharpest layer should stay on the island Taiwan shouldn't pick just one of “stay” or “move out.” What it should do is build a portfolio. The most advanced process nodes, and the yield know-how that only Hsinchu can really explain, stay on the island. That's the genuinely scarce leverage. CHIPS money can buy a fab; it can't buy the feel that keeps all 700 steps stable. Arizona can exist, and should — the fourfold construction cost is an insurance premium paid to the US Congress and US customers, its purpose political entanglement, not cost. Morris Chang has already said the unpleasant part out loud: globalisation is almost dead, so you still have to go and build. Just don't move the frontier along with it. The day it moves is the day the shield expires. Nor can the shield go on serving as the navy. Four months of compulsory service, units only about 80% staffed, military spending down to about 2% of GDP, and then US$8.1 billion spent on fighter jets — this is a rich island using a foundry in place of defence. The porcupine the analysts describe isn't pretty, and it won't lift market cap. But it is the second line that has to be added once the shield starts to depreciate. Politically, the polls in the case are clearer than any slogan. What most people want is the status quo, not an immediate move to either end. After Hong Kong, the island's elections have already given one answer. Ambiguity here isn't weakness. It's the product the middle has already bought. My own choice: keep the sharpest layer, pay an expensive American premium, reshape the military into something that can survive, and gradually bring down the 44% of exports going to a single counterparty. Every step is expensive. The other path is more expensive — a shield that both sides are making obsolete, sitting in the same typhoon track. This isn't deglobalisation; it's permission being weaponised Deglobalisation would grow three complete stacks: the US designing, manufacturing and supplying its own equipment; China able to survive without Dutch lithography machines and American software; and a third stack in between that sells to no one. That world isn't in the case. What's in the case is: wafers are still crossing the sea, software is still being licensed, talent is still flying. In 2023, China's imports of chips and equipment were still near record highs. Nvidia didn't leave; it modified its cards to sit just below the threshold. The Netherlands and Japan followed with controls, not by bringing factories home. The US still makes more than 70% of design software. The only company that can make EUV lithography machines is still in the Netherlands. What has changed is permission. The foreign direct product rule claims jurisdiction over chips that contain “no American atoms.” Investment screening can review a Korean company with almost no US footprint. A single entity list can make your second-largest customer disappear within a quarter. My own understanding is that the globalisation of atoms is still running. The globalisation of permission is being rewritten. Those are two sentences. The first explains why a conflict on this island would still bring the world to a halt. The second explains why both great powers feel that, given time, they can care a little less. Morris Chang says globalisation is almost dead. What he's describing is the gates. Not the road. The bill will land on mature nodes first Even without full deglobalisation, the price is already being paid. Arizona's fourfold construction cost will sit inside every phone and every server, or inside a fiscal subsidy that can't be cleanly carved out. When every capital pours money into the easiest segment of the chain, mature nodes end up in oversupply — TSMC's CEO already said on an earnings call in 2024 that too much mature-node capacity may have been built. The truly scarce things — EUV, yields, the discipline of 5 nanometres — will stay scarce for longer. The old model put manufacturing risk on one specialist island so a hundred design companies could iterate. Three half-finished islands will waste capital on concrete instead of on the next nanometre. Families, carmakers and cloud providers will start maintaining two bills of materials. One that can get into this side, one that can get into the other. This isn't two planets. It's two sets of passes for the same road. My own understanding is that the word deglobalisation is too big, and too convenient. It makes people think the world is splitting into three blocs that don't deal with each other. The more accurate picture: the road is still there, the checkpoints have multiplied, the premiums have gone up, and the checkpoints will move once more just after you think you've already diversified. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading about this island that wrote its chips into a shield, what came to mind wasn't whether we should talk about geopolitics, but whether we've been treating concentration as an amulet that expires. First, being irreplaceable is not the same as being safe. One fab holding 92% looks like a moat. Moats can also become bullseyes. A family that puts its operating company, its listed entity and its living expenses all in one place is a scaled-down version of the same story. Second, what makes you rich doesn't necessarily keep you safe. Cash flow isn't a navy. A listed company isn't defence policy. When your core business becomes someone else's reason to make policy, you need a second line that doesn't make money — structure, liquidity, jurisdictions you can switch between. Third, permission is now a due diligence item. Clients, licences and listing venues can vanish within a quarter because of a list. Before asking what an asset is worth, ask: if permissions change, can it still be serviced, sold, and handed to the next generation? Fourth, diversification depends on whether the underlying risk is the same. Ten products with six identical exposures isn't a portfolio. Two bills of materials, two custody locations, two settlement currencies — that's when it starts to look like a portfolio. Things that look globalised are often just different brand names on the same chain. Fifth, don't bet on which capital wins the tech war. A government can spend US$52 billion to move output share by two points. A family can't spend money like that. Our job is to make sure the family can still function under any outcome. The premiums will be expensive. Expensive, because the shield is depreciating. Final Thoughts Before class, what I agree with most is this: “the silicon shield is turning into a bullseye faster than it can go on being a shield.”

Unit 3, Professor Frances Frei, Operations & Technology: Commerce Bank. The last piece, on Spyder, asked how ownership rewrites a company's value. This one asks something else: is service excellence designed, or improvised on a Friday afternoon? The story takes place on Halloween 2002 — at a bank that calls its branches stores and its customers fans, and that has just let its managers juggle in the lobby. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Halloween 2002, Cherry Hill, New Jersey. A pumpkin, a Dalmatian and a masked Zorro run past Deborah Jacovelli's office door. This is Commerce University, Commerce Bank's full-time training centre. The giant letter C outside the door has been draped in a cape. Jacovelli is the dean here. She has seen plenty of things that don't look like a bank, but one thing this year still unsettles her: a pilot headquarters has just launched, called Retailtainment. Branch managers are free to experiment on Friday afternoons with ways to entertain waiting customers. Free hot dogs, guitarists, jugglers, someone in a letter-C costume on roller skates. Some stores have already had incidents. A hot dog cart caught fire, a juggler got burned, and it made the local news. Vernon W. Hill II opened this community bank in southern New Jersey in 1973 with US$1.5 million. His judgement was blunt: the world doesn't need another me-too. With no capital and no brand, he had to find a point of difference. For nearly thirty years after that, Commerce made no acquisitions, opening its own stores into Pennsylvania, Delaware and New York. Hill called branches stores, and benchmarked against Starbucks and Home Depot, not the bank next door. He asked: how does Starbucks get you to pay US$6 for a cup of coffee? The retail experience. Since 1990, the stock had risen twentyfold. CFO Douglas Pauls has a line on the cover of the case: The hardest thing about becoming a big bank is not becoming a big bank. The hard part isn't growing up. It's growing up without turning into a big bank. The industry at the time was working a different problem set. Deposits and loans were both treated as commodities. From 1998 to 2001, industry deposits grew by about 19% in total, with loans running at nearly 90% of deposits; the outsized growth of the big banks came almost entirely from acquisitions. Banks tiered customers by profitability, and satisfaction stayed chronically low — 79% of credit union members were "very satisfied," against just 53% at retail banks. Attrition could run as high as a third of customers a year; even the best lost 15%. Of those who left, 34% did so because of fee surprises, poor service or errors, 34% because they moved beyond the branch network, and 15% because somewhere else was more convenient or open longer. Electronic channels had low marginal costs, and most banks actively pushed people away from the teller window to self-service: with advertising, with rewards, occasionally with penalties — US$3 to use a teller. Commerce turned that whole logic on its head. Stores opened 7:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. on weekdays, and on weekends too; busy drive-throughs could stay open until midnight. There was also a 10-minute rule: open 10 minutes early, close 10 minutes late. There were only four kinds of checking account, and opening one came with a gift. Hill said other banks, because branches are expensive, push people out and onto the web — "You can't find a successful retailer that survives by pushing people where they don't want to go." Their model was to make every channel the best it could be, and assume you'd use them all. The result wasn't just deposits growing far faster than the industry — up 37.5% in 2001, against 5.1% for the industry — but online usage of 34%, higher even than Wells Fargo. The average store had 40,000 visits a month; busy ones had 100,000. A McDonald's gets about 25,000. What they sold wasn't loans; it was core deposits. Hill said a bank's value isn't in its loan book, it's in the money that didn't come for the rate. Commerce was usually the lowest-rate payer in its markets, often by 50 basis points. Asked why they'd opened a new account, 3% of customers said for the highest rate; 62% said for service and convenience. Competitors fought over the 3%; Commerce fought for the 62%. Its expense ratio looked ugly as a result. Hill's reversal: a low expense ratio is a negative, not a positive — banks with low expense ratios are disinvesting in their own business every day. Money saved didn't go to the bottom line; it went back to customers. Switching ATM contracts saved several million, which they used to abolish card fees company-wide; in New York, when someone else's machine charged you US$1.50, they refunded it. Loans were a supporting act. The loan-to-deposit ratio was 45%, against 87% for the industry. The policy was one sentence: no deposits, no loans. The loan officer was the store manager. At some point you'd have to come into the store to sign — and that was the moment to persuade you to bring your deposits over too. Stores were built as replicable machines. Built from scratch for about US$1 million: white brick, black metal roof, black-and-white marble, lollipops and dog biscuits. Hill said, we know every screw in the model. Payback took 12 to 18 months; the industry needed three years. When it rained, staff walked customers to their cars under umbrellas. They gave away 300,000 pens a month. A phone next to the ATM connected to the call centre. Online, you could see both sides of your cheque the next day. When other banks began refusing large amounts of coins or charging for them, Hill spent US$10 million on the Penny Arcade — coin-counting machines. In 2001 they handled 750,000 transactions and took in US$71.7 million in coins, free to customers and non-customers alike. Falese called it Marketing 101: once they're in, keep doing it. WOW was an operating system. In 1994, nine people wrote the SMART principles: say Yes to customers, make everyone feel looked after, keep your promises, know how to recover, think like a customer. Commerce University had 41 full-time staff. New hires went through Traditions, which taught smiling, handshakes and greetings — "smile with your teeth." For 40 positions in Manhattan, they interviewed 2,000 people. There were 14,000 mystery shops a year; saying "may" instead of "can" cost you points, and raises depended on the scores. Kill a stupid rule and you got US$50. Trainer John Manning told a roomful of bank officers: we hire wack jobs. You're all wack jobs. Your responsibility is to go out and find more. Retailtainment was the next step in 2002. Competitors had started copying the basic service. Washington Mutual entered New York with its "un-bank": roving tellers, kids' corners, no desks. Dutch ING opened café-style branches in Manhattan. Bank of America was experimenting with televisions in the queue. Pauls said: we need the next penny arcade. Yet one of Jacovelli's friends said the greetings and free pens were all lovely, but she'd rather that person got behind the counter and moved the line along. Another customer complained there were too many greeters standing around. On one side: managers know their customers best. On the other: total laissez-faire is dangerous. Jacovelli's summing-up: Commerce is a bank and a brand, and it succeeds or fails on whether its service beats its competitors'. The question is what role Retailtainment plays in that mission. The four questions in front of Jacovelli: 1. Before Retailtainment, how well did this service delivery system mesh with the competitive strategy it supported? Which design choices mattered most? 2. What problem is Retailtainment trying to solve? Has it succeeded? If it should change, what should change? 3. How should competitors have responded to Commerce's entry? 4. Which lessons from the rise of online banking still apply in the age of AI? My Thinking The operating model and the strategy have to bite on the same screw Commerce is not a better bank. It's a retailer that happens to take deposits. The strategy is one sentence: win on service and convenience, not on rates. That 62% versus 3%. Every design choice grows towards that sentence — 7:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., weekends, midnight drive-throughs, the 10-minute rule; four kinds of checking, not a dozen; deposits and loans both credited to the store; no deposits, no loans; 14,000 shops a year, raises tied to scores; never pushing people away from the counter. Hill said that even if not a single person came in to do business on a Sunday, opening on Sunday would still make sense, because it says: I'm always here. The fit shows up in the income statement. An efficiency ratio of about 70% against the industry's 60% — they were more expensive, just as promised. Cost of interest-bearing deposits of roughly 2.4% against 5.4%. Return on equity was still higher, 15% against 12%. Net income doubled in four years while the industry grew by a fifth. Deposits grew 37.5% in 2001, against 5.1% for the industry. This operating system isn't decoration on the bank. It is the strategy, running. The 45% versus 87% loan-to-deposit ratio is the same screw. The spread they earned wasn't enough to buy credit risk. Falese said some of our best loans are the ones we didn't make. Securities made up 40% of assets, against less than 20% for the industry. They were a deposit-gatherer that made a few loans, not a lender with branches. Take away the hours, the short menu, the store getting credit, the "we won't push you out," and the 62% story starts to leak. Retailtainment isn't on that list. My own reading is that when Frances Frei calls this class Service Excellence by Design, "design" isn't about aesthetics. It's what trade-offs look like once they've been written into process. Excellence isn't doing a few more good things. It's a set of things you refuse to do. The WOW that's really worth something is replicable design The Penny Arcade and the hot dog cart are two completely different kinds of innovation. The coin machine solves a job competitors refuse to do. Other banks started saying no to large quantities of coins, or charging for them. Hill put down US$10 million: pour them in, get a receipt, swap it for notes, free for customers and non-customers alike. In 2001, 750,000 transactions, US$71.7 million. Falese said: once they're in, keep doing it. The umbrellas, the 10-minute rule, the phone beside the ATM, the cheque images you can see the next day — same category. Designed once, copied in every store, checkable by mystery shoppers, solving real problems: rain, opening hours, coins, whether a cheque has cleared. The hot dog cart solves "make it look like something's happening." So does the guitarist. So does the letter-C costume on roller skates. They can't be replicated as the same screw, and they can't be measured by 14,000 shops. Some stores will become something fans talk about; some will make the news. Commerce spent thirty years turning white brick and black roofs into an identity customers recognise with zero learning cost, and the first thing Retailtainment loosens is exactly that. My own leaning: if WOW can't be written into a script, it isn't operations yet — it's just personality. Personality is charming in one store and a risk across 185. Pauls said the hardest thing about becoming a big bank is not becoming a big bank. Identical stores, Traditions, killing stupid rules — that's an attempt to turn personality into a system. Friday improvisation hands the system back to personality. Retailtainment solved the wrong problem What it was trying to solve wasn't the queue. It was anxiety — competitors had started copying the easy layer: evening and weekend hours, warm-and-fuzzy ads, cafés, televisions in front of the line. Pauls wanted the next penny arcade. That's understandable. The bank deliberately pays less interest; once the service gap is closed, those 50 basis points become a reason to leave. But the case offers no numbers for success. No lift in deposits, no drop in perceived waiting time, no mystery shop scores. What it does have are idle greeters, a friend who wishes the line would move, and a fire. With 40,000 to 100,000 visits a month, the bottleneck is tellers, not atmosphere. Juggling while the line stands still is strategy and operations contradicting each other. My own choice: shut down Retailtainment as Friday variety hour. Keep the search for "the next coin machine," and do it the way they already know how to open stores — one idea, scripted jointly by marketing and operations, piloted in a few stores, with safety checks and a rule for killing it. The hot dog cart had been approved by marketing, and it still caught fire. Approval without a script is not control. One line for Jacovelli: send the greeters back to the counter first, then talk about guitars. Competitors shouldn't copy the lobby They copied the lobby. Washington Mutual's kids' corners, ING's espresso, Bank of America's TVs. What they copied was the layer Commerce could swap out next Friday. Money-centre banks shouldn't play on this field. Hill said this delivery model can only be built from scratch; mergers, at bottom, are about cutting costs. He said "every big bank merger in this country has failed" — that's his sentence, not history's verdict. The direction is clear, though: you can't retrofit a service cult into an institution that has just finished merging. By 8:15 in the morning, Robbins had already walked across the street from Citibank to Commerce. Her former employer didn't lose her for want of a coffee machine. If you insist on competing for the 62%, what you should copy is the trade-offs: the hours, the short menu, crediting deposits to the store, your own university, fourteen thousand shops a year of your own, paying less interest and framing it as the price of the experience, accepting a higher expense ratio, and not closing branches to save costs in cities where Commerce is opening stores. Commerce gave employees US$5,000 when competitors closed branches. That's the clue. Your exit is their marketing. The response that looks fierce but is actually weak: open on Sundays too, install another coffee machine. The response that looks passive but is actually hard: pick a different axis of excellence, and stop pretending you're competing on service while the economics still require pushing people into a phone tree. My own reading is that most boards would reject a five-year rebuild. That rejection is itself a response — cede the service segment and harvest the 3% who want rates. Pretending to respond does more damage to the brand than not responding at all. Don't push people where they don't want to go The story of online banking in this case isn't that digital won. It's that banks used a new technology to push customers where the bank wanted them to go, while Commerce used the same technology to follow customers to where they already were — and ended up with higher digital usage, not lower. The industry advertised ATMs and websites and occasionally charged US$3 to visit a teller. Commerce said every channel should be good. Online usage of 34%, higher than Wells Fargo, alongside tens of thousands of store visits a month. An expensive channel that's loved brings the cheap channel along as a complement; an expensive channel treated as a dumping ground takes both down with it. That's the most underrated number in the whole case. AI will rhyme with this. Self-service, chatbots and all-digital relationship managers will look free at the margin, just like websites in 2002. If you push people there to save on staff, that's the US$3 teller fee all over again. The phone Commerce installed next to the ATM is the right posture — new technology that makes it easier to reach a person, not harder. So are cheque images that appear the next day. High Tech in service of High Touch, not a replacement for it. The gimmicks will still arrive first. Retailtainment is 2002's "we should have an AI demo on Fridays." The Penny Arcade is 2002's real workflow. You still can't be excellent at everything. Commerce was excellent at convenience and ordinary-to-weak at rates and credit. AI can't lift trade-offs away. Use it to be cheapest, warmest and most comprehensive all at once, and you'll get a bot that can apologise in the jargon of four product lines. My own reading: write the script first, then let the machine copy it. Consistency is what scales. Treating personality as the exception is Friday juggling at software speed. Killing stupid rules is still human work. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading about this bank that calls its branches stores, what comes to mind isn't whether we should be warmer, but whether our operating system bites on the same screw as our strategy. First, don't push people where they don't want to go. The online banking lesson still holds for AI. Technology should thicken the meeting — memory before it, a second pair of eyes during it, the record after it — not turn the meeting into a turnstile you have to pass through first. Digital channels that people follow you into are the ones that stick. Second, keep the menu short so the front line can be warm without getting things wrong. Commerce had only four kinds of checking. The industry had a dozen or more, and after mergers forced customers to switch products. Once the breadth of service exceeds what the delivery system can hold up, warmth turns into errors. Before adding one more "we can do that too," ask first: is it still the same screw? Third, the real wow is replicable design, not an improvised show. Umbrellas, coin machines, the 10-minute rule solve jobs competitors can't be bothered with. Guitars solve "make it look like something's happening." Family services have both kinds too. The former deserves to be scripted, the same in every "store." The latter makes the news. Fourth, incentives have to face the same way as the strategy. Deposits are credited to the store; raises depend on shop scores. If credit goes to the product and the relationship is left to the front line, the front line will hate the product — Fleet already acted that out in the case. Whoever serves, books it. The write-up after every real delivery is our mystery shop. Fifth, copying the theatre is not a response. Competitors copied the lobby. What they should copy is the trade-offs, or openly switch to competing on another axis. For an institution whose product is trust, the most expensive pretence is this: the script already sounds like Nordstrom, while the scorecard still counts visits. In Closing Before class, the line I agree with most is: "Don't push people where they don't want to go."

Unit 3, Professor Martin Sinozich, Finance, Spyder Active Sports—2004. The previous piece, Nantucket Nectars, was about the seller — a company is worth the most in the year someone else needs you. This one is about the seller too, but the question flips over: the same company, with a different shareholder, isn't worth the same number. Not because the model changed, but because the people showing up to work next Monday changed. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Spring 2004, Boulder. David Jacobs is seventy, his office walls covered with ski photos and memorabilia. He can still ski the mountains near Denver, and still ski Europe. Outside the window is the company he started from his kitchen in 1978. Seven years ago, the Denver private equity firm CHB Capital Partners came in; over those seven years, sales grew from about $10 million to $61.4 million. Now CHB wants out, and it's time for him to turn his own stake into cash. What he has to think about is: what is this company worth in the public market, and — once it's sold to someone, will it still be the same company? The story starts with the two times he fell. Jacobs was a Canadian downhill champion and national team coach. In the 1960s he and Bob Lange made racing ski boots; the company went public, then recalled 25,000 pairs over a liner material, and was eventually sold. He walked away with $80,000. In 1972 he started Jacobs Corp., making children's ski wear and adult cycling gear; he first sold 45% to venture capitalists, then sold the rest to García — which went bankrupt in 1978. The Hong Kong buyer asked him to stay on as vice president; he refused. He started two more companies of his own, one of them called Spyder: high-end racing sweaters, sold by mail order, made in Hong Kong, with a logo that had to be "powerful, a little menacing." For the first two years it ran out of the family kitchen, with his two teenage sons, Bill and Jake, helping mail catalogs. To grow, he sold stock to Hanson in exchange for $75,000 and a warehouse; in 1982 Hanson itself went under first, and he either had to pay $50,000 to buy the company back or lose it. He had no money, so he brought in his Osaka manufacturer, Tsunehisa Shimokubo. The contract included a line he would go on to use again and again: once sales reached $2.5 million, Shimokubo's stake would be topped up to 50%. They hit the target in 1986 and became 50/50 partners. In his words: The market isn't big, but I knew that if I could hold that small slice at the very top, there wouldn't be many people fighting me for it. Fabrics came from Japan and Switzerland, insulation from 3M, snaps from Italy. In 1988 he landed the U.S. Ski Team, and Picabo Street and Tommy Moe appeared at World Cups and Olympics in spiderweb-patterned race suits. Sales went from $3.4 million in 1987 to $7.9 million in 1990, and the channel shifted from mail order to specialty ski shops. Jake went to the University of Colorado, to Los Angeles to study design, to factories in Japan, to Hong Kong to manage production, and was then poached by Nike to Singapore. In 1995 his father called him back as vice president of design and manufacturing. By 1995, the company was stuck between $10 million and $15 million. Jacobs was nearly 65, and his money had always stayed in the company. Tommy Hilfiger, Nautica, Prada and Armani began making ski fashion, and Hilfiger ran a two-page ski ad in Men's Health . He said: this is my turf. His advisers' conclusion came down to two sentences — either sell the whole company or find a minority partner; selling 51% is the same as selling all of it. In February 1997, Robertson Stephens took the materials to market. Nike was rumored at one point to want a majority stake, but went off into skateboarding and hockey instead. CHB caught his attention: its name was Closely Held Businesses — closely held. Tad Kelly said equity capital had become as commoditized as debt, "we have to offer more than money." They were willing to put in about $5 million and accept a minority stake, but required a minimum 30% return. After due diligence they felt the projections were too high, and proposed a stake that would slide with cumulative EBITDA from 1998 to 2002: if it fell short of $10.5 million, CHB would go up to 60%. Jacobs rejected the sliding scale and insisted on a fixed percentage. On September 25, 1997, CHB invested an initial $2.5 million for 22%. By the end of 1998 at the latest it could invest another $2 million, bringing it to 37.9% fully diluted after both tranches. Jacobs and Shimokubo each kept 25.4%, with employee options at 11.3%. Kelly and Flanigan joined the board, and Blake Morris watched day-to-day operations. Board meetings went from "whenever I'm in Japan we meet and toss a page into the minutes" to formal quarterly meetings. They pushed the company to spend about $1 million on a J.D. Edwards ERP system — "if you want to build a $100 million brand, don't install a $10 million system, install a $400 million one." In May 1998 they brought in 31-year-old John Walbrecht from outside the industry, Dr. Martens' head of global sales and marketing. Marshall Field's in Chicago took a 1,500-square-foot concept shop. At the end of 1998 CHB put in the second tranche; Jacobs and Shimokubo chose not to take out that $1 million in cash. The growth came with losses first, profits later. Walbrecht took the sales meeting, which under Jacobs had never cost more than $25,000, and turned it into a $150,000 launch in Vail, flying in 75 dealers from Germany and Australia. Kelly said it was a signal: Spyder was willing to spend money ahead of revenue and stake out its position in the market first. Walbrecht himself traveled 250 days a year, working out for retailers how to display the merchandise, what music customers should hear and what prices to charge. Morris boiled the industry statistics down to a one-page chart: third in insulated jackets, crushed by The North Face in shells — and only then did they act. Jake moved his father out of the design seat and expanded the product line and buying team the Nike way. Products expanded from the core $300–$1,000 line into kids' wear, snowboarding and a lower-priced line, and distribution reached Sports Authority, Dick's and Macy's. Europe switched from multiple distributors to direct sales. In 2000 the books showed a loss of $972,000, and the bank got nervous; they stripped out the one-time investments, and the bank accepted two sets of numbers, "before investment / after investment." By 2004, the report card had turned a page. Net sales went from $27.3 million in 2001 to $61.4 million, jumping 52% in a single year; EBITDA went from $1.3 million to $9.6 million, with margin rising from 4.9% to 15.6%; net income went from $83,000 to $5.1 million.
