The Canadian and Austrian national teams were added. Retailers valued the high margins and high sell-through; Spyder's rule was always to sell one fewer — one fewer than the market wanted. Bill was also called back to run Northern California. CHB had tried to exit in 2002, but the market wasn't there; by the end of 2003 this was the only unrealized investment left in one of its funds, held for seven years, beyond the expected 3 to 5. Jacobs said there was a huge amount of cash out there with nowhere to go, and smart money was looking for brands. An IPO was ruled out: the company was relatively small, could sell $22 million in June alone and almost nothing in January, and its working-capital borrowings swung from 0 to $23.4 million. They hired two investment banks to split the fees and responsibilities — Financo knew retail, Wachovia knew consumer products, and the banker in charge was someone they knew from the 1997 round. The last page of the case leaves three deals on the table: sell to another apparel company; sell a large block of equity to another PE firm; or he keeps control himself, and CHB can only sell its 37.9%. The three questions in front of Jacobs: 1. Does this company's value depend on who owns it? Beyond ownership, what else determines the price? 2. By DCF, by trading multiples, by acquisition multiples, what is it worth? Do these numbers capture what really matters in a sale? 3. Of the three deals, which would he choose for himself? Which would CHB choose? Who else gets rewritten? My Thinking A company has no price independent of its owner In the Nantucket piece, the same juice company was worth $47 million going it alone and $144 million inside a strategic buyer. The difference was the buyer's problem. In Spyder, the difference is whether the next shareholder will rewrite the company itself. Strategic buyers — Columbia, VF, Nike, Adidas-Salomon — could plug Spyder into their own sourcing and their own stores. That's EBITDA that doesn't exist in the standalone model. Financial buyers don't have that. What they buy is the company as it is today, plus the governance they'll add, minus the extra leverage and a 3-to-5-year exit clock. CHB's own 37.9%, if sold on its own, is yet a third number: a residual stake that can't direct anything, can't go public and can't easily be resold, and buyers will pay less for it. The harder part is the people. Blake Morris has one line that could carry an entire valuation: Jake and Walbrecht are "the creative engine of the company." The path in the selling memorandum — from $61 million to $166 million in four years, EBITDA from $9.6 million to $27.9 million — is a model in which they're still there. A strategic buyer that folds Spyder into its portfolio and pushes them out shouldn't pay for that path. A PE firm that lets them roll over their equity and keeps Jacobs on as coach can. My own understanding is that ownership isn't a footnote to the DCF. It's an input that rewrites the cash flows. The wrong shareholder doesn't buy Spyder — they buy the brand that used to be Spyder. Hilfiger in Men's Health in 1995 was the first warning. The Snappleization in the last piece, Nantucket, was the same movie on a different shelf. $100 million is a number you can say out loud; the DCF is a story hung on the wall First, what can be defended. Seven comparable companies, enterprise value over EBITDA: median 10.4x, mean 10.7x. Columbia at 10.3x, Quiksilver at 10.4x. Applied to the year Spyder just finished — EBITDA of $9.58 million — that's about $100 million. On sales, the median is only 1.13x, about $69 million — which still treats it as the 5%-margin company it was three years ago. It no longer is. Gross margin went from 39% to 49.5%, EBITDA margin from 4.9% to 15.6%. Europe moved to direct sales, scale arrived, the structure changed. The sales multiple misses this inflection point; the EBITDA multiple catches it. Acquisition multiples write ownership back into the table. Strategic buyers, excluding the loss-making The North Face, have a median of 10.3x, about $99 million; financial buyers a median of 9.1x, about $87 million. The gap isn't large, but the direction is clear: control plus synergies is worth one tier; sponsor-style ownership is worth another. The DCF is a different face. Using management's projections, a 35% tax rate, a 12% to 14% discount rate and an 8x to 10x exit multiple, enterprise value lands between $169 million and $204 million. That still requires 28% annualized sales growth for four years — after a year that already jumped 52%. This is the selling memorandum talking. FY2004 is still unaudited. One warm winter could change the tail years. CHB had them install an ERP fit for a $400 million brand; the DCF is that ERP talking. Buyers won't pay for the ERP's ambitions. My own inclination: walk into the financial buyers' room with $90 million to $110 million, and into the strategic buyers' room with $100 million to $130 million. $100 million is a number you can say with a straight face. The DCF hangs on the wall to keep the auction honest, not for anyone to write a check against. What's not in the tables is what you actually underwrite at closing The multiples know the margins just appeared, and know 2004 is a better year to sell than 2002. What they don't know is whether Jake will sign. A $186 million DCF that loses the engine is fiction. A $100 million check that keeps them and rolls the 11.3% of options in could be the better deal. Once channels cross, Christy's $600 jacket gets marked down to $300 at Gart — the board already spends half its time guarding against exactly this. A strategic buyer that pays 11x and then pushes into department stores, versus a PE firm that pays 9x and then writes channel protection into the covenants: this is where price and value part ways. A 70-year-old Jacobs, CHB's overdue fund, two sons inside the company, the Japan line in Shimokubo's hands — none of these are in the discount rate. They're all in the term sheet: rollover equity, puts and calls, employment, non-competes, who can fire the conductor. My own understanding is that the most important consideration in a sale isn't finding an even more refined multiple. It's getting clear on: next Monday, who's running this company. He should pick the deal that keeps the engine If I were Jacobs, I'd sell a large block to a new financial buyer. Take most of my own 25.4% out in cash, and let Jake and Walbrecht roll in. Keep a small slice only if the exit formula is written down in black and white. Not a sale to an apparel company. That check is thicker, about 10 to 11x. It also hands both sons' careers over to an integration committee. He has walked this road twice: Lange sold into a bigger company, Jacobs Corp. sold into García, which later went bankrupt. He knows how this movie ends. And not keeping control himself while CHB sells only its 37.9%. That was him in 1995 — "never below 50%." That man was 62 and still drawing the designs himself. The man today has already stepped back, and has said in his own words that being fairly cashed out matters more than controlling the direction again. Keeping control would give him something he just said he doesn't value as much, deny him the liquidity he says he wants, and leave his partner of seven years stuck with a residual stake. The costs, stated plainly: he's no longer the boss. The new PE firm will want its own 3 to 5 years. Jake's second bite of the apple depends on someone he doesn't know yet. All of this has to be written down, not just sealed with a handshake. CHB should keep the strategic buyers in the room to push up the price If I were CHB, I'd want an auction aimed at a 100% strategic sale — while keeping two or three financial buyers in the process. CHB's job isn't to protect the Jacobs family story. Its job is to pay back its first fund. Seven years, the last deal, a 30% target. At $100 million of equity, the 37.9% is about 8.4x, roughly 36% annualized; at a strategic $120 million, more; as a minority residual stake, it could fall back to around 30%, with its people still sitting on the deal. In 1997 Kelly said what they competed on wasn't money but expertise. In 2004 that line turns around: they don't have control, so they can't force the highest price. What they can do is run the process — two banks, one clock, more than one kind of buyer. A strategic sale is the ask. A financial buyer taking out everyone is an acceptable close. Selling only the 37.9% is the failure case. If Jacobs refuses to sell his own stake, CHB shouldn't die on the hill of the highest price. A forced minority sale is worse than a slightly cheaper full exit. What really gets rewritten is the next generation and that engine Jake has been at it for 16 years, from the warehouse to the Japanese factory to Nike and back. In a strategic sale, he becomes an employee of a bigger company, or he leaves and the projections leave with him. In a financial recapitalization, he can become the public face. If his father keeps control, he's still the founder's son, waiting for a succession that hasn't been called yet. Walbrecht isn't family. He's the man who turned a sleepy little company into a "player." A sale to an apparel group is where he runs into a corporate boss; a sale to a new PE firm is where he gets bought as an asset. Shimokubo wants cash, and also holds Japan. Specialty ski shops buy Spyder because it's "the real thing," and because it won't turn up discounted at chain stores. The sponsorships of the U.S., Canadian and Austrian teams are a halo that a cost-cutting shareholder could pull in year one. The employees in Boulder are the reason Walbrecht could spend $150,000 on a sales meeting and have it work. A deal's price is written in the multiple. A deal's consequences are written at these people's desks on Monday. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading this case, what came to mind wasn't ski wear, but a table we sit at almost every week: the first generation is past 60, the children are in the business, outside capital is on the shareholder register, someone wants liquidity, someone wants control, someone wants the next stretch of growth. First, a family business has no price independent of its owner. The same factory is one number to a strategic buyer who would shut down lines, another to children who would keep the people, and a third to a PE firm that would add leverage and a time limit. The seller's job is to get the latter two numbers into the room, rather than accepting the first one as "the market." Second, a minority stake isn't financing, it's control design. When Jacobs rejected the sliding scale in 1997, he was writing 50% into the contract at the front door. A friendly minority shareholder turns into an overdue seller. The clock should be announced on day one, not discovered in year seven. Third, liquidity and succession are one decision, often sold as two. A strategic sale solves for cash and gambles with the next generation. A recap can do both, at a headline number one notch lower. The number to care about is the one that keeps the engine. Fourth, key people aren't in the discount rate — they're in the term sheet. Who stays, how you pay them to stay, whether the channel can be crossed and discounted — if these aren't written clearly, the projections are just wishes. Fifth, the 1995 line "never sell 51%" isn't the 2004 self. A founder's utility function changes. The record should date that change, rather than using a sentence from ten years ago to argue with the person of today. Final Words Before class, the line I agree with most is "ownership isn't a footnote to the DCF — it's an input that rewrites the cash flows."
Should everyone adopt the new way of working?

Unit 3, Professor Das Narayandas, Market-Facing Functions, New WOW at Equitable (A): A New Way of Working. The previous piece, Belden, was about switching sales from parts to solutions in the very year the financials looked best. This one is the same course, but it asks about a layer further in: you can dream up the solution, but can the organisation's metabolism keep up? A life insurer founded in 1859 has just moved out of its French parent's house, and the CEO says he wants to build a home he actually wants to live in — only to discover that the old habits, closing the books twice a year with a US$200 million error threshold, can't move into the New York Stock Exchange. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary Early 2025. Equitable Holdings CEO Mark Pearson and COO Jeff Hurd are looking at a report card. The new way of working — they call it NWOW — has been rolling out across the company for about 36 months, and roughly 80% of people have embraced it. The board chair has just spoken about its power at an industry forum. Management layers have shrunk from 26 to 5; psychological safety is up 25%; click-through on group retirement's online customer service is up 400%, and the extra 13,000 outbound calls translated into US$70 million in additional sales; by the end of 2024, total shareholder return since the 2018 IPO stood at 175.5%, against 86.1% for core peers. Pearson is still uneasy. The sense of urgency he had hoped to ignite never reached the intensity it should have. Wealth management is in the middle of its rollout, and the preference for the status quo there is very high. He asks Hurd: is 80% enough? Can some divisions make a few adjustments? Can we declare victory? Rewind seven years. In 2018, France's AXA spun off this US subsidiary in an IPO that raised US$2.8 billion. The new company kept Athena on its blue shield. Pearson became CEO. Born and raised in Zimbabwe during its war of independence, he couldn't afford university, went abroad into insurance at 17, built growth in Hong Kong and Japan, and parachuted into New York in 2011 to take on the post-financial-crisis job of rebuilding the balance sheet. He describes himself as someone with the patience to get things done — not the type who tears everything down and then leaves. The IPO gave him his first chance to design the brand, principles, structure and goals from scratch. He said he wanted to move out of mother AXA's house and build the one he wanted to live in. But the habits still lived in the old house. In the words of CFO Robin Raju, after going from a mutual to the subsidiary of a large overseas conglomerate, "the culture was relaxed and comfortable, but there was very little accountability." Accounting was done twice a year, with a 50-day turnaround and a US$200 million error threshold. Group insurance relied on 1,500 policy enrollers. The rejection rate on enrollment forms was 61% — 61% of forms had to be sent back and filled in again. The internal refrain was: these ways have always worked, so why change? The board approved targets that had to be delivered publicly by 2020, and then asked one question: do you have the culture to achieve these results? Pearson read John Doerr on OKRs, sat in on a design-thinking seminar at Stanford's d.school, and visited Spark, ING and USAA. That 61% became a signal — ordinary improvement asks how to bring the rate down; design thinking asks how to get to zero rejections. In 2019 he launched NWOW, and at year-end handed the Innovation and Design Office to his former chief of staff, Hillary Menard, with five pillars pushed together: OKRs, adaptive leadership, design thinking, enterprise agile, and dynamic enablers who contribute by skill rather than by title. The new organisational units were called tribes, squads, centres of excellence and self-managed teams. Squads were capped at 10 people. Raju said that beyond 10, you can't move fast. He insisted on staffing the IDO with insiders, bringing in McKinsey only as an accelerator. Menard designed a five-day bootcamp covering all five pillars at once. "If we ask people to keep coming back to learn more, we'll lose them." Once the bootcamp ended, teams had to run on NWOW. In early 2020 he took the top 30 leaders to an off-site in New York, with Empowered as pre-reading. Steve Scanlon, head of group retirement, walked in thinking it was just another meeting about making everyone a better manager. When it broke up, most people were still in wait-and-see mode. Pearson pulled him aside: you will be the first to put this approach into practice in a business line. The squads were picked within a day. Then the world stopped. The original assumption was that everyone would be in the same room. Raju asked whether they should pause. Hurd decided to do the opposite and accelerate — agile and design thinking were exactly the capabilities needed in uncertain times. At the same time, Pearson ended the engagement with McKinsey: "The moment the people driving the culture change are no longer Equitable's own, this thing dies." Wholesalers used to visiting clients and playing golf were forced home, and sales fell 20% to 40%. Group retirement had 1,200 enrollers and no technology at all for handling enrollment by phone or online. Scanlon gave Bernadette Mitchell's squad a month to produce a transformation roadmap; they delivered in two weeks. They launched a minimum viable product with some features still in development, and revised it as advisers' feedback came in. Scanlon said: we would never have launched an unfinished product before. Now this was the squad's mission — not something people were pulled off other work to do on the side. Resistance grew at the same time. Wholesalers' calendars were already full, and they refused daily stand-ups. In operations, a single payment collection involved more than 130 touchpoints, and people with 25 years on the job asked: if you change this, how do I know it'll definitely work? When Christy Chandler joined in 2023, her operations team's employee Net Promoter Score was just 0.7. Hurd himself sat for an hour next to a junior employee, watching her do something obviously inefficient and refuse to give it up, before conceding: in this situation, NWOW isn't the most efficient way. Some people with 30 years in and only a few years to retirement chose to leave early. They adjusted, too. Chandler listened first, ran a 90-day comparison, and had IT extend the timeouts for when seven systems were open at once, so the team stopped losing what they'd already entered. Fafian's turning point came when new business was growing exponentially and adding people wasn't enough — the NWOW people showed up as people who'd come to help. Scanlon told managers: two meetings to explain why; at the third, I tell you this is how it's done. He said he didn't care what page 35 of Empowered said; he cared about output. The B case is the 70-page playbook actually handed to employees in February 2021. It opens with a letter from Pearson: about 10,000 people turn 65 every day, and the retirement gap is heading from US$28 trillion to US$137 trillion. The playbook states that it is not a how-to but a set of building blocks to be hand-picked according to mission — and that it is itself an MVP. Then it spends over thirty pages on daily stand-ups, sprint planning, backlog refinement, reviews, retrospectives, PO Sync and Big Room Planning. The archetype best suited to call centres and branches — the delivery unit — had not yet been mobilised even once. The case stops at three questions: 1. With 80% already on board, should they keep pushing to 100%? 2. The divisions that resist — leave them be, or pull them in with metrics and oversight? 3. Going forward, should they only hire leaders who will fully embrace NWOW? My Thinking This isn't a pilot — but that doesn't mean copying every page Pearson said the words he couldn't take back very early on: this will change the way we work. This is a cultural change. This is not a test, and it is not a pilot. He was right. A scoreboard that has already been announced publicly, run on an operating system that still closes the books twice a year, just means more frequent disappointment. The board wasn't asking whether the targets were credible; it was asking whether the culture could keep up. NWOW is the answer to that question, not another HR programme. And 80% isn't enough to declare victory, either. The remaining 20% isn't a random tail. It sits in distribution, operations and wealth — the layer that faces customers, and the layer that's regulated. Wealth management's preference for the status quo is very high. The retirement business generates US$1 billion of cash flow a year, and that market peaks around 2030. A divided company will leak the next decade through the half that never converted. Scanlon says that if you can't get to 100%, it degenerates into a philosophy, then becomes voluntary, then fails. That's how social physics works. But what the 100% applies to has to be spelled out. What's 100% is the mission, OKRs, end-to-end ownership, and the customer's voice in the room. Not every meeting on the 2021 calendar. The playbook itself says on page 4: hand-pick the building blocks for the mission in front of you. Hurd saw with his own eyes that, for some processes, it isn't the most efficient way. Wholesalers can give you upstream demand signals; they won't give you 15 minutes every morning. Forcing the calendar on everyone is how you turn a good operating system into box-ticking. My own reading is that what truly can't be compromised in Pearson's statement is the operating system, not Tuesday's agenda. Bundle the two into one thing, and the last 20%, in the name of doing it right, will turn the first 80% into theatre as well. What really moved the numbers was that this is now your full-time mission Mitchell's squad turned in a one-month assignment in two weeks. Scanlon's remark is almost the entire theory: in the past, we had to pull people off other work and have them do it on the side; now this is the squad's mission, and they're highly focused. The impressive numbers that followed — click-through up 400%, 13,000 outbound calls, US$70 million — weren't trained into existence by stand-ups. They came from the work no longer being part-time. Individual retirement put product, IT and pricing into the same squad, handoffs were killed, and new products moved faster. The 10-person cap is a constraint: the right people have to be in the room, and the wrong meetings have to go. Shrinking from 26 layers to 5 is the same thing at company scale. Moonshot OKRs do something else: they make "grow 3%" sound like you've picked the wrong sport. The playbook says hitting 70% of a moonshot counts as success, while commitments like regulatory requirements and dividends must be hit at 100%. Without the first rule, people hold something back; without the second, stretch reaches the point where it can shut the company down. The question design thinking asked of the 61% rejection rate — how do we get to zero returns — is the same muscle. MVP here isn't a software trick; it's a cultural licence. They shipped an app with one section still in development, took in advisers' feedback, and revised it. Scanlon says they would never have done that before. Covid made that licence urgent; the method made it legitimate. Rituals are the accountability layer, and they come second. Stand-ups make it hard to hide — that's true. But Chandler took operations' employee NPS from 0.7 to 29.5 by listening for a few months first, running a 90-day comparison, and fixing the timeouts across seven systems. The way NWOW earned its keep there was by granting a licence to fix the work, not by adding another meeting. Shareholder return since the IPO is double that of peers. Raju says that if cultural change doesn't ultimately show up in this number, it means nothing. I agree with that as the final test. I don't agree with crediting the number to stand-ups. Operating speed, calls, layers, whether employees would recommend the place — that's NWOW. The valuation also contains interest rates, AllianceBernstein, and that book of index-linked annuities. Both things are true at once, and in class we don't need to pretend there's only one. The playbook's backbone is buried under a calendar The B case isn't an analysis; it's the actual thing the company sent to employees in February 2021. That makes the classroom unusually honest — what we're reading isn't best practice summarised after the fact, but the operating-system manual everyone had in hand at the time. Its backbone is good. The CEO personally wrote 10,000 people turning 65 every day into the opening letter. US life insurers' earnings were growing at 2.7%, against 5.5% for the S&P 500; NPS was 4.5, versus 77 for USAA; by 2025 millennials would make up half the workforce, yet only 4% were willing to join this industry. Why to change is written before how to change. Squads and self-managed teams, tribes and centres of excellence are separated out — the structure acknowledges that a call centre isn't a functional team. The role cards list "what I don't do": no micromanaging, no playing the boss, no going missing, no assuming I must have all the answers. That column is more useful than all the Spotify terminology. Then it spends over thirty pages issuing a timetable. Daily stand-ups, sprint planning, backlog refinement, reviews, retros, a sync every sprint, a review every month, a day of Big Room Planning every quarter. The delivery unit — the best fit for branches, advisers and call centres — had not been mobilised even once at the time, and that empty archetype is precisely where resistance later grew. Mindset is drawn as the underwater part of an iceberg, said to matter more than the tools, yet gets only two pages. New hires would learn the calendar first, before learning to switch from "analyse until perfect" to "act, then iterate." My own inclination: keep the first 20 pages and the "what I don't do" on the role cards. Turn the rituals into a menu. Before using this thing to push the last 20%, write the two missing chapters: regulated operations, and frontline distribution. A clickable PowerPoint frozen in 2021 is not a system still alive in 2025. Thirty-six months of scars — 130 touchpoints, seven-system timeouts, wholesalers willing to give signals but not sit through stand-ups — should already be written in. That they aren't is itself a kind of answer. Without Covid, it could still have moved — just not like this The ideas came before the virus. Public quarterly targets, a board asking about culture, a five-day bootcamp, Scanlon already handpicked — none of that needed a pandemic. Nor did Covid create the 61% rejection rate or the 1,500 enrollers. A man who had rebuilt a balance sheet after 2008 would have kept pushing. But the NWOW in this case — 80% in 36 months, an unfinished app already in the market, a COO sitting next to a clerk for an hour — needed a deadline that made refusal very expensive. Only when sales were down 20% to 40% did an MVP become legitimate. Only with offices closed was the method something other than "new meetings in the same room," hard to fake and hard to simply wait out. They fired McKinsey because they couldn't afford to wait. Pearson put it bluntly: once the consultants leave, the thing dies, so our own people have to take the lead as fast as possible. The irony of 2025 is the proof. Now people are asking: why bother? The pandemic is over, there's no fire to put out, and we're doing fine. If this method needed a crisis to get to 80%, the last 20% won't move forward on nostalgia. A set of habits that only works in wartime isn't an operating system yet. What Pearson has to prove now is that when people can go back to playing golf, mission plus squads is still worth something. Classify the resistance first, then prescribe Don't leave it be. And don't pull people in with nothing but a maturity score. There are at least three kinds of resistance in the case. The first is where the playbook doesn't fit the work. Operations, wholesalers, the delivery unit that stayed empty. The cure is to redesign the last mile together with them. Fafian's turning point wasn't a kanban board; it was new business outpacing capacity, adding people not being enough, and the other side being people who came to listen to ideas. Put the metrics they already believe on the wall: cycle time, errors, employee NPS, first-year premium. There should be oversight. But HQ's scorecard can't be the only lever. The second is leaders who don't buy in. Hurd asked: if they won't embrace it, are you willing to replace them? For this kind, yes. A sceptic among 26 layers can be outlasted; a sceptic among 5 layers runs a fifth of the company. Scanlon's two meetings plus a third "this is how it's done" fits perfectly here. Beyond that, it's a matter of selection, not change management. The third is people with two or three years to retirement whose rational strategy is to outlast you. Let them go. Save the coaching inventory for pipelines like TAP — of its 24 participants, 54% have already been promoted, and the employee NPS among diverse employees is 33, above the company's 27. A single company-wide adoption rate treats the first and second kinds as the same disease. It will be gamed, and it will poison the teams that genuinely need to change their processes. What can be done in 90 days: publish a menu of rituals by archetype; for the first kind, kill one bottleneck and pick one metric of their own; for the second kind, decide this quarter whether they stay or go. Don't announce 100%. Announce that by the end of the quarter, no team can be without a mission and OKRs. That's the floor no one opts out of. Leaders must be inside the operating system; experts needn't love stand-ups For future hiring, the bar for leaders should be hard, and the bar for talent can't be written as the same sentence. For Tribe Leads, product owners and coaches, the job description is the operating system. The role cards already spell out what they don't do. A candidate who can't sign up to that is applying for a job the company is about to delete. The interview can include a live problem: 130 touchpoints, a wholesaler who refuses stand-ups — what do you keep, what do you cut, what do you measure? Anyone who says the whole playbook, no exceptions, fails. Anyone who says my team, my rules, also fails. Anyone who can separate principles from rituals passes. Experts and revenue generators are a different matter. Dynamic enablers were always meant to be skill-first. Someone with 25 years who knows which of the 130 touchpoints will break things for the customer is exactly who Chandler's 90-day comparison needs. Frontline wholesalers, even if they hate the rituals, are, in Hurd's words, the voice of the customer. By 2025 only 4% of millennials want to join this industry. Adding a "please love the agile terminology" requirement on top of craft that's already scarce is a shortage you can't afford. A rainmaker who refuses to let go of decisions — you can do without. An expert who hates daily stand-ups but still delivers on time — keep. Treat those two as the same culture problem, and the company will be fighting on the right battlefield against the wrong people. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading this case, what came to mind wasn't life insurance but any company that starts writing its own operating system. We're doing exactly that. The only difference: Pearson's licence came from an IPO; ours was written on the day the company was founded. First, public goals without a new operating system just mean more frequent disappointment. The board's question — "can the culture keep up?" — is worth asking of every team that writes a beautiful plan. If the scoreboard changes but the metabolism doesn't, all that's changed is the reporting frequency. Second, the operating system has to be run by your own people, and consultants should be burned off when their time is up. Pearson paid the price of going slow and still wouldn't give up this step. Once the people driving the new way are no longer the people living by it, it turns into a slide deck. Building the team internally is slower. Slowness is its insurance policy for survival. Third, the unit of change is a squad with a mission and no second job. You can't deliver a minimum viable product on borrowed evenings. One module, one family, one delivery unit of no more than ten people — that's closer to Mitchell's two weeks than company-wide training. Fourth, write the missing page of the playbook now: which meetings, and which kinds of people, don't attend. Equitable only discovered its wholesalers and claims later. If the cadence for the frontline and the external expert network isn't split out, resistance will show up in the form of "I'm already very busy" — and they'll be telling the truth. Principles at full strength, rituals as a menu by archetype — that way "we made adjustments" doesn't become a euphemism for "we didn't execute." Fifth, leaders must be inside the system; experts are chosen for craft. Someone who won't put their files into the shared source of truth is a dis-enabler. Someone who doesn't love stand-ups but still delivers their expert memos on time is an expert. The interview question can be lifted straight from that 130-touchpoint live problem. Sixth, the burning ambition has to be about people, not tools. Pearson was still using 10,000 people turning 65 every day in 2025, because the playbook's "why" could no longer move the last 20%. Tools are building blocks. Ambition is the backbone. If a company can only talk about which methodology it bought and never gets to the people outside the methodology, the last 20% won't move. Final Thoughts Before class, what I agree with most is "this is not a test, and it is not a pilot" — I agree with it as a statement about the operating system. I don't agree with it being heard as: every meeting in the 2021 playbook must be held at 100%. Innovation: Now Is the Time for Courage
Courage is a skill you can practice

Unit 3, Professor Ranjay Gulati, Innovation: Now Is the Time for Courage: Five strategies to drive bold action amid uncertainty. This is the third reading in Professor Gulati's unit. The previous one, Roaring Out of Recession, was about "what" progressive companies do in a downturn — save on processes, invest in customers. This one steps back and asks a more fundamental question: plenty of people know what they should do, so why do so few dare to do it? His answer is that courage isn't a personality trait; it's a skill you can break down and practice. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary The article begins with a finding the author himself didn't see coming. During the 2008 financial crisis, Gulati and his colleagues studied how 4,700 public companies had navigated the three previous recessions. They found that about 9% of companies came out of each recession stronger than they went in — not just because they cut costs cleverly, but because at the same time they took calculated risks to invest in growth. As he puts it, they had "inadvertently documented the enormous difference that courage makes in business." For the next decade and more, he turned to a different question: faced with the same hard situation, why do some leaders dare to move while others don't? He starts by defining courage : the willingness to take bold, risky action in pursuit of a purpose you believe is worthwhile, in the face of persistent fear. Then he quotes Mandela — courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it. From Socrates and Aristotle to Mencius, philosophers have long argued over whether bravery is an innate virtue or something that can be taught; modern research in psychology, neuroscience and medicine supports the latter: many people who never thought of themselves as brave have shown bravery when the situation demanded it. But almost no one has systematically studied "how a person can become braver." So, drawing on the literature, archives and more than 200 in-depth interviews, he put together a playbook. He draws a line. Many experts say the way to overcome the anxiety that uncertainty brings is risk management — treating bold action as a "smart bet" built on careful weighing of the odds. Running a cost-benefit analysis does indeed lower the odds of a bad outcome. But the economist Frank Knight long ago distinguished between two things: what you can assign probabilities to is risk; what you can neither enumerate nor estimate is uncertainty. In the face of the latter, most people feel a loss of control, which triggers fear, and then they either freeze or retreat. What sets brave leaders apart is that they can take back the initiative and choose a third response. At the time of writing, 76% of S&P 500 companies had mentioned "uncertainty" on their earnings calls, up from 37% three months earlier. Then come five strategies, each with three practices. First, build a positive narrative. Start by "hunting for risks" — not driving risk to zero, but identifying the unknowns one by one so the world looks more orderly. BlackRock's Larry Fink built his entire career on this: his first employee was tasked with developing a comprehensive risk-assessment platform, which came to be called Aladdin and became the industry standard in finance. In his 2025 annual letter, he pointed out that US$25 trillion was sitting idle in US banks and money market funds, while the world would need about US$68 trillion in infrastructure over the next 25 years — numbers that gave management the confidence to make three big acquisitions in a row at the end of 2024. Next, "find a moral purpose." In 2014, CVS's Helena Foulkes and her team decided to stop selling tobacco, giving up US$2 billion in sales: "We debated it for a long time, and not everyone agreed... It was scary to walk away from such a big piece of the business. But we had 25,000 pharmacists at the time. For them, and for all of us, working at a company that made such a bold decision really created a sense of pride." Finally, "draw on faith." Research shows that entrepreneurs spend more time praying than the average person, and that people who believe they'll have good luck have a stronger sense of agency. Former PepsiCo CEO Indra Nooyi kept a statue of Ganesha in her office: when the pressure became unbearable, she would close her eyes and picture a temple, and "suddenly I felt I could take on the world." Second, cultivate confidence. Confidence comes from what the psychologist Bandura called self-efficacy — "your belief in what you can accomplish across a range of situations with the skills you have." Practice one is deliberate training. Sully Sullenberger's pilot training had no lesson on "ditching in the Hudson after a dual engine failure," but as he said: "I had been preparing for that moment my entire life." GE's Larry Culp drew on the lean skills he'd honed over 25 years at Danaher to complete GE's turnaround. Staff at the Taj Mahal Palace hotel in Mumbai held their posts during the days of the 2008 terrorist siege — every one of them had been through an 18-month onboarding program that taught not just the job but the "guest first" culture. Practice two is building a big toolkit: NASA astronauts say boot camps that teach mental endurance are as useful as technical training; Foulkes's team's tool was transparent debate, "letting people say what they were excited about and what they were nervous about." Practice three is focusing on what you can control. In sports this is called "process over outcome"; football coach Nick Saban told his players: "We don't talk about what we're going to achieve; we talk about how we're going to do it." Aloke Bajpai, founder of the Indian online travel agency Ixigo, ran out of money at least four times; each time the founders put their own money back in and took subsistence salaries, and employees took pay cuts — "and most importantly, we kept shipping products." Third, take small steps. Many people equate boldness with big moves, but the leaders the author studied probed with small steps before they leaped — what the organizational psychologist Karl Weick calls sensemaking. When the 2011 tsunami hit Fukushima, Naohiro Masuda, the head of the Daini nuclear plant, faced 55-foot waves crashing into a plant designed for just 17 feet. He and his team gathered around a whiteboard, wrote down the data they had, and analyzed what might go wrong. After the main control panels failed, he sent people out at personal risk to inspect the equipment on the ground, and on that basis hypothesized that the cooling systems had lost power. They first tried to draw power from the only building on site that still had electricity; that proved technically too difficult, so they switched to the only generator still working; after judging that another reactor was in greater danger, they shifted their work there. Small steps, observe, learn, iterate — and in the end they averted disaster, which the Daiichi plant a few kilometers away did not. Amazon calls decisions like these, which you can walk through and back out of, "two-way doors." Fourth, find connection. Contrary to popular belief, lone heroes are rare. Chanel CEO Leena Nair says that when people questioned her abilities as a woman and as a leader with an HR background, she would think of the women in her family whose own ambitions had been suppressed but who had great faith in her — "they would say, let Leena have that chance." Her mentor Nooyi told her not to think about her limitations but about what she could bring. Bajpai had bridge funding from investors; Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen had two support organizations behind her. And you can't surround yourself only with cheerleaders — one of former LEGO CEO Knudstorp's mottos was "listen to the complainers," and Culp is known for walking the shop floor to hear directly from frontline workers. Fifth, stay calm. Sleep, nutrition, hydration — "you can't think clearly when you're running on empty." As Nair puts it: "Put on your own oxygen mask first." Rituals: every morning Steve Jobs looked in the mirror and asked whether, if today were the last day of his life, he'd be happy with what he was about to do; Bernanke kept Greenspan's habit of always facing the clock in Fed meetings. And reframing — imagining the situation in three versions: pessimistic, realistic and optimistic. Fink wrote in his annual letter: "We've been through moments like this before. Somehow, over the long run, we've always figured things out." It ends with a judgment. This is not to say leaders should take excessive risks, "but most of us tend to be too timid rather than too reckless." Bravery is a skill every businessperson must learn — and teach to others. The professor's three questions for this session: 1. What does courage mean to you? 2. Can courage be learned? If so, how? 3. How can organizations become braver? What can leaders do? My Thinking Courage begins where the spreadsheet runs out Knight's line is the first thing in the whole article I want to make clear. Risk and uncertainty are not the same thing. Risk is when the probabilities can be calculated — a new product's failure rate, whether an acquisition's synergies will materialize, whether a client will renew. What these call for isn't courage but good analysis. Do the analysis thoroughly, then decide: that's prudence, and prudence is a skill, not cowardice. Uncertainty is something else: the outcome itself is unknown, and you can't even list everything you should be afraid of. At this point analysis stops, because it can't give you an answer. Most people's reaction here is instinctive — freeze, or retreat. Courage doesn't replace analysis; it takes the baton once analysis has run its course. Fink's story demonstrates this sequence very cleanly. Aladdin calculated everything that could be calculated; the US$25 trillion and US$68 trillion in the annual letter were calculated figures. The three big acquisitions were the step that came after the calculations ran out. Only once you've calculated everything you can does courage earn its place on stage — reverse the order and it becomes recklessness. My own take is that this line matters especially for those of us with "good training." Business school teaches you to turn everything into something that can be analyzed, which is great, but it can also lead you to believe the analysis can go on forever. It can't. There's always a moment when the last row of the spreadsheet is blank and the decision still has to be made. Recognizing that moment is the first step of courage. The fear stays put; the test is whether you moved In Gulati's definition of courage, I'd underline two phrases: "risky" and "persistent fear." Risky means the cost is real. CVS gave up US$2 billion in sales to stop selling tobacco; Haugen gave up a well-paid job. If you aren't putting anything on the line, that's not courage, just an opinion. It's also why I don't really trust "bold statements" that cost the speaker nothing — what separates them from courage is the bill. Persistent fear means the fear doesn't go away. Foulkes said walking away from such a big piece of the business "was scary," and then they did it anyway. The article is careful here: the goal isn't to stop being afraid, but to act while the fear is still in the room. So courage isn't a feeling; it's an observable behavior: did this person move, or not? Defining courage as a behavior rather than a feeling has a very practical benefit — it becomes something you can practice. You can't practice a feeling, but you can practice a behavior. You don't need to become someone who isn't afraid first; you just need to do the thing while you're afraid. Do it once, and the second time is different. Sully's training didn't have that lesson, but he'd been flying his whole life; the Taj staff weren't hired for heroism — they went through 18 months of onboarding and then, in those few days, "fell back on their training." What looks like character from the outside is built through repetition. Bold doesn't mean big; bold means early, and reversible Of the five strategies, the third is the most counterintuitive. We tend to picture bravery as a single leap — quitting, going all in, betting everything. That's not what the leaders Gulati studied did. They probed with small steps first, kept a way back, and corrected course as they went. Masuda's days at the Fukushima Daini plant are the most complete story in the article, and there isn't a single heroic big decision in it. What there is: a whiteboard, a few sets of numbers written down, a risky on-the-ground inspection, a hypothesis, and two changes of direction. The first plan — drawing power from the building that still had electricity — failed, so they switched to the generator; they judged another reactor to be in greater danger, so they moved people there. Every step was small enough to be corrected by the next. The Daiichi plant a few kilometers away faced the same tsunami. Weick says sensemaking "is not about truth and getting it right; it is about continually rewriting an emerging story so that it becomes more comprehensive, incorporates more of the data, and is more resilient in the face of criticism." In my last piece I wrote about his old map — when you're lost, any map will do, because it gets people moving. This piece is the flip side of the same idea: once you're moving, each step should be small enough to walk back. Amazon calls it a two-way door. Bold doesn't mean big. Bold means early — taking a step while others are still waiting for clarity; and reversible — if this step is wrong, you can come back. People who understand courage as big moves keep waiting for the moment "worth betting everything on," and that moment usually never comes; people who understand courage as small steps can start today. My own take is that this also explains why so many smart people seem timid. It's not that they don't dare; it's that they treat every decision as a one-way door, applying one-way-door caution to two-way-door matters. And most decisions are, in fact, two-way doors. There are no lone heroes; courage is a team sport In our cultural narratives, courage is an individual quality — one person steps up, one person carries the weight. After interviewing hundreds of people, Gulati says that behind almost every brave leader stands a group of less visible supporters and a set of constructive critics. The passage about Nair is beautifully written. When she was doubted, what she thought of wasn't her own résumé but the women in her family whose ambitions had been suppressed yet who had great faith in her — "Let Leena have that chance; she's smart, she's talented." She was borrowing other people's confidence in her. What her mentor Nooyi gave her wasn't encouragement either, but a specific reorientation: don't think about your limitations; think about what you can bring. Then there are resources. Bajpai ran out of money four times, and each time there was bridge funding from investors; before Haugen released the documents, she had two organizations behind her. Money and people are a safety net — only when people have a way back can they afford the cost of moving forward. That's not weakness; it's physics. Finally, the critics. You can't have only cheerleaders around you. The point of Knudstorp's "listen to the complainers" and Culp's shop-floor walks isn't humility — it's that a judgment others have tested and picked holes in is one you can act on with more conviction. Of the fifteen practices, I think accepting feedback is the hardest, because it means letting others judge a decision you're already afraid of. But what it buys you is exactly the confidence that decision needs. This has big implications for organizations: if courage is a team sport, then an organization's courage can be designed, rather than depending solely on hiring brave people. Organizational courage: the leader says it first and pays first, then lowers the cost for everyone else My answer to the professor's third question: organizations become braver the same way individuals do — through the same five strategies — except that in an organization each strategy can become a system; and there's one thing the leader does that no one else can. First, the systems. Risk hunting can be a risk map everyone can see, not a register only the legal team reads. Building confidence can be Taj-style 18-month onboarding — long enough that "guest first" becomes the default, not the exception. Taking small steps can be a decision taxonomy: which are two-way doors — fast, delegated, reversible; which are one-way doors — slow, senior, deliberate. Connection can be institutionalized dissent — transparent debate, going to the front line, listening to the complainers. Calm can mean treating rest as an operational necessity rather than a weakness. These are all things you can write into how an organization works. Then, the leader. In the previous article, Gulati said that the cultural barrier of loss aversion can only be overcome by "explicitly cultivating courage as a cultural value, with leaders going first." Here, Foulkes's story spells out what "going first" means: the team debated for a long time, not everyone agreed, and the decision became a source of pride only after it had cost US$2 billion. A leader who asks others to be brave while taking no risk themselves is really asking for obedience. And there's one more thing I think matters even more than "leading by example": lowering the cost of bravery for everyone. What most people in an organization fear isn't the market — it's the boss. Two-way doors, blameless post-mortems and visible safety nets make bold action cheap enough that ordinary people are willing to take it. Masuda didn't tell his team to "stay calm"; he gave them data they could write down. This is also how the unit's three cases fit together. Cynthia Carroll is the entire playbook embodied in one person — a moral purpose, a visible cost, allies and critics; Roaring Out of Recession is about what progressive companies do; this piece is about how the people inside those companies find the nerve. Most of us are too timid, not too reckless In Book III of the Nicomachean Ethics , Aristotle places courage between two vices: cowardice at one end, recklessness at the other, with courage as the mean. More than two thousand years later, after hundreds of interviews, Gulati adds an empirical judgment: the mean is the mean, but most people lean toward the cowardly side. That sentence is worth reading aloud to yourself. Well-trained people are especially prone to treating caution as the whole of virtue — one more set of data, one more quarter of waiting, one more round of opinions. Each step on its own is right. Put together, they make a person who never moves. And the article is blunt: this is not to say leaders should take excessive risks, "but most of us tend to be too timid rather than too reckless." So for people like us, "be a bit more careful" is most likely not the right correction. Back to the professor's first question — what does courage mean to me? In my own early writing, three words kept coming up: brave, caring, earnest. Having read this, I'd change the order. Caring comes first — it determines what is worth paying a price for; bravery is what you do for the things you care about. My one-sentence answer: courage is paying a real price, while you're still afraid, for something you've decided is worthwhile. As for how to practice it, I reordered the fifteen practices from easiest to start with to hardest: first look after your body, then list what you're afraid of, then state your purpose, then work on your craft, then focus on what you can control, then take small steps through two-way doors, and finally build a team with allies, resources and critics. The easiest is the first — and it's also the one most leaders skip. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading this, I thought of what we do every day — accompanying a family through its uncertain decisions — and of how we make decisions ourselves as a young company. First, hunting for risks on a family's behalf is one of our core deliverables, and we should describe it that way. When a family hesitates over succession, structure or allocation, it's often not because the risk is large but because they don't know what they're afraid of. Turn "not knowing what you're afraid of" into a list you can work through item by item, and the fear shrinks by half — which is exactly what Aladdin did for Fink. Our diagnostics and profiles are essentially this. Second, calculate everything you can before talking about courage. Knight's line applies to a family just as it does to a company. Things with calculable probabilities are solved with analysis; only once the analysis runs out does the part that needs courage begin. You can't cut corners on either side: using "courage" to skip analysis you should have done is reckless; using "one more round of analysis" to delay a decision you should make is timid. Third, sort decisions into two-way and one-way doors, and handle them at different speeds. That goes for families and for us. A new tool, a new content column, a one-off partnership — these are two-way doors: move fast, retreat fast if wrong. Licenses, equity structure, key partners — these are one-way doors: slow and deliberate. Most decisions are actually two-way doors, yet we often make them at one-way-door speed. Fourth, keep a critic around who won't go easy on you. Allies and resources are relatively easy to find; "complainers worth listening to" are the hardest to find and the most useful. A judgment that's had holes picked in it is one you can act on with more conviction. It's worth regularly inviting one or two people whose job is to pick holes in our strategy and narrative. Fifth, the founder's pace is the company's pace. Nair's "put on your own oxygen mask first" is addressed to every founder. A small company's tank is the founder's tank; when it runs dry, the organization freezes by default. This one belongs at the front of the five strategies, not the back. Sixth, courage has to be voiced by the founder first, and paid for with a concrete decision. "We can be brave" only goes from slogan to precedent once it's been backed, in the tightest quarter, by money invested anyway and a client turned down anyway. Only then has it earned the right to be asked of others. In Closing Before class, the line I agreed with most was: "most of us tend to be too timid rather than too reckless."
