In the middle of a transformation, choose the acquisition target that fits you

Unit 3, Professor Juan Alcacer, Strategy: Axel Springer: Reinventing a Legacy through Global Acquisitions (A). The last piece, Nantucket Nectars, was about the seller — a company is worth the most in the year someone else is missing exactly what you have. This one moves to the other side of the table: a buyer who has just been told, at the airport, that a deal a year in the making has fallen through, who is still holding a billion-dollar budget, and who now has two alternative targets in front of him. It's a story about "what do you buy after you lose," and also the story of how an old German newspaper group sold itself off piece by piece and then bought itself back piece by piece. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary July 23, 2015, Tegel Airport, Berlin. Mathias Döpfner is sitting at the gate waiting for a phone call. He is the CEO of Axel Springer, about to fly to London to sign the agreement to buy the Financial Times from Pearson — a deal worth more than a billion dollars and the centerpiece of the group's strategy of "entering the English-speaking world." Everyone wants to board. He says no: we wait for final confirmation from Pearson's board. The call comes. During the board meeting another offer arrived, and the board had to accept it. The Financial Times has been sold to Nikkei. Döpfner later said: "We negotiated for a year. At the last minute Nikkei showed up with 'the same piece of paper' — meaning, let the Germans negotiate for a year, then we take their contract, add 10%, take it or leave it." Deputy CEO Jan Bayer remembers the two of them talking about it all summer, deeply frustrated. Then they met in Berlin and said: going international was still the right direction. We're going to America. Rewind seventy years. Axel Springer was founded in Hamburg in 1946 by the journalist of the same name. Hamburger Abendblatt in 1948, Bild in 1952, the purchase of Die Welt in 1953, the Ullstein publishing house in 1959. By the 1960s it was Germany's most important news publisher. It put its headquarters right next to the Berlin Wall at Checkpoint Charlie, and in 1967 laid down five "Essentials" still in use today: freedom and democracy, Israel's right to exist, the transatlantic alliance between the US and Europe, the free market, and opposition to extremism. In the 1960s this made it a target of left-wing protest — and, interestingly, the street leading to the headquarters today is named after the protest leader of that era, Rudi Dutschke. Bild is the newspaper with the largest readership in Europe, and it was still running photos of topless women as late as 2012. Gerhard Schröder once said all you need to govern Germany is three things: Bild , Bild am Sonntag and television. Welt has a much smaller circulation and is the group's intellectual flagship. In 1985 Axel Springer listed 49% of the company and died the same year, leaving control to his widow, Friede Springer. From then on, day-to-day management passed to professional CEOs and an executive board of three to five people, with Friede sitting behind them as a supervisory board member and major shareholder. In 2002, Döpfner took over. He was 39, had studied musicology, and had spent 16 years in journalism, the last four as editor-in-chief of Welt . Friede admits everyone doubted him at the time: "They said he was too young, a music critic with no business experience... I said, I want him. And I have the majority." His plan was just three phrases: strengthen the core business, digitize, internationalize. He said that the first time he read a news website he understood it would replace newspapers. The company was losing €200 million a year, its governance was unstable, and its culture needed to change. In his words: "The good news was that we were in really bad shape — there was little to lose and a lot to win. That gave me the freedom to think outside the box." He cut 40% of jobs, a restructuring that by German standards was "brutal, radical, fast," and sold or shut down unprofitable assets. Within a year the company went from losing €200 million to making €200 million. Almost everyone was against him: "This young man is destroying our business." 2004 to 2005: the first wall. They tried to acquire ProSiebenSat.1, Germany's largest private TV group — a company bigger than Axel Springer was at the time. The team designed a multi-step deal of "tender for the preferred shares, raise capital, then merge." The structure worked; Germany's antitrust authority blocked it. Bayer says this was the turning point: Döpfner concluded that they had to dramatically accelerate digitization and internationalization, and use the print business to fund it while it was still profitable. Over the next decade, three lines moved forward at once. Digitizing the news went slowly — Bild only launched its paywall in 2013, offering Bundesliga highlights, sweepstakes and slot-machine games along with the news, and reached 680,000 digital subscribers by 2016. That same year, they sold a group of regional papers and magazines — including the ones the founder himself had started in 1948 — to Funke for €920 million. In 2012 those assets had revenue of €512 million and EBITDA of €95 million, so the price was about 10x EBITDA. Bayer says this was probably "the last possible exit" from the regional print business; Friede "immediately understood the opportunity and agreed decisively — she always looks forward, never back." The second line was classifieds. Döpfner saw early on that the real estate, job and car ads in newspapers were being replaced by the Craigslists and Zillows of the world. So he went shopping globally: StepStone, Immonet, aufeminin, Seloger, Totaljobs, Immoweb, consolidating them into horizontal groups by jobs, real estate and autos, with disclosed deal values above US$1.4 billion. Analysts called Axel Springer "one of the most aggressive buyers of classifieds in Europe." The third line was the result: by 2014, more than half the group's revenue came from digital businesses. How they bought companies became a philosophy in itself. Döpfner doesn't do deep integration. He named his approach after the film company Charlie Chaplin and others founded in 1919 to protect creative independence — the "United Artists model": "I respect entrepreneurs. I want Axel Springer to be their home — to give them room to run independently and go their own way, as long as they deliver a plan and results." Bayer's metaphor is a jazz band: improvising within a clear framework, with no preset direction. "We don't believe in top-down synergies. We always tell the companies we acquire: you can treat Axel Springer like a buffet — knowledge, technology, product, legal, M&A — but you don't have to." The deal structure followed from this: the founders keep a substantial stake and later exit through a put/call — overdeliver and you get 12x EBITDA; miss the targets and it's 8x. Andreas Noth, deputy head of M&A, says: "If a founder wants to sell 100% in one go and walk away, we're generally suspicious — he may not believe in his own company's potential." America in 2015 was hot. NBCUniversal had invested a combined US$400 million in Buzzfeed and Vox; Buzzfeed was valued at US$1.5 billion, about 13x revenue. Hearst and Disney bought 10% of Vice at a US$2.5 billion valuation, about 5x revenue. By estimates, none of them was profitable. The year before, Forbes had sold to a Hong Kong investor group for US$475 million, about 3x revenue and 22x EBITDA. Axel Springer narrowed it down to two targets. Business Insider , founded in 2007 by former DoubleClick CEO Kevin Ryan and Henry Blodget — Blodget, as a Wall Street analyst, had been investigated by the SEC, banned from the industry and fined US$4 million, but Ryan still believed in him. Purely digital business and tech news, known for its high output, SEO and social distribution, and also criticized for "clickbait headlines, more ads than content, and slideshows built to farm clicks" — Blodget himself said the criticism stung, and also made them better step by step. About 75% of revenue came from advertising, plus a small B2B subscription research product, BI Intelligence. Venture-backed, with shareholders including Bezos and Andreessen. In 2013 AOL offered around US$100–150 million; the board refused, asking for about US$250 million. In January 2015 Axel Springer led its Series G: US$20 million for 9% and a board seat. Noth calls this "a foot in the door" — put in a small amount first, get to know the management, the founders, the culture. By mid-2015 BI had nearly 90 million monthly unique visitors and revenue close to US$50 million. The Huffington Post , founded in 2005 by Arianna Huffington, Kenneth Lerer, Jonah Peretti and Andrew Breitbart, a liberal news and opinion site that grew into a general-interest giant on the back of aggregation, original content and thousands of unpaid bloggers. By 2015 it had 13 international editions and had just launched an Arabic one. AOL bought it in 2011 for US$315 million, when its annual revenue was about US$30 million. Its business model relied entirely on advertising, with no paid product. Revenue in 2014 was estimated at US$146 million, still loss-making; 2015 was expected to bring US$168 million in revenue and EBITDA of just over US$10 million. In 2015 Verizon bought AOL for US$4.4 billion, and was rumored to be spinning off HuffPost for about US$1 billion — roughly 6 to 7x revenue. The case stops here. Döpfner, recovering from the Financial Times setback, has to answer: 1. Buy Business Insider or HuffPost? The former has about US$50 million in revenue, is doubling every year, and at the market multiples of the time would be valued at a little over US$400 million in total; the latter has US$168 million in revenue, is growing 15%, and is asking about US$1 billion. 2. This time, how do you make sure the deal doesn't fall apart at the last minute? My Thinking The boldest step in the transformation wasn't buying something new — it was selling the newspapers the founder started himself Reading this case, what sticks most easily is the buying — a dozen-plus acquisitions, US$1.4 billion of classifieds, a billion-dollar Financial Times . But the transaction that truly holds the whole story up is a sale. 2013, €920 million, a group of regional newspapers, including the Hamburger Abendblatt the founder himself launched in 1948. At 10x EBITDA, that was a very good price for the moment; Bayer called it "the last possible exit" — meaning that a year or two later, that price would have been gone. What makes this hard? Not the valuation, but emotion and power. These were the founder's newspapers, and the founder's widow was the major shareholder, sitting on the supervisory board. Any professional manager knows the risk of making that proposal. And Friede's reaction was to "immediately understand and agree decisively." A major shareholder who "always looks forward, never back" is the precondition for this company being able to transform — more important than any CEO. My own take is that the most expensive money in a transformation is often not how much the new business needs, but when the old business gets sold. Sell too early and the cash cow is still giving milk; sell too late and nobody wants it. Axel Springer sold in the year when "someone was still willing to pay 10x." It's the same logic as Nantucket Nectars in the last piece, just seen from the seller's seat: sell something valuable while others still need it, not when you yourself no longer do. The real money for the transformation wasn't in news — it was in classifieds The case title is "reinventing a legacy through global acquisitions," so the reader's attention naturally lands on the news brands — FT, Business Insider, HuffPost. But the acquisition list in Exhibit 2 tells a different story: StepStone, Seloger, Immoweb, Totaljobs, Immonet — all classifieds platforms for jobs, real estate and cars, with disclosed amounts alone exceeding US$1.4 billion. This is the thing Döpfner understood earliest: a newspaper's profits never came only from the news, but from those few pages of small-print ads next to it. What the internet took first wasn't readers, it was those pages. Craigslist and Zillow don't write news, but they hollowed out newspapers' income statements. So half of Axel Springer's digitization wasn't "moving the newspaper online" at all — it was "buying back, in platform form, the ad pages that used to sit in the newspaper." When digital passed half of revenue in 2014, most of that came from these platforms, not from BildPlus's 680,000 subscribers. That shapes how you look at the 2015 question. Spending a billion on a news brand — are you paying for returns, or paying for identity? News is this company's mission and its voice — every one of the Essentials is about which side the news should stand on, and none mentions classifieds. But the mission costs money; classifieds make money. An honest CEO has to admit that first, and then decide how much a news brand is worth spending. Buying a company isn't buying an asset — it's giving an entrepreneur a home, then writing the exit as a formula The United Artists model is the thing I most want to take away from this case. On the surface it's a management philosophy — no integration, no faith in top-down synergies, acquired companies can treat the parent as a buffet. That sounds like respect for entrepreneurs, and it is. But underneath is a very hard-nosed deal structure: the founders keep a substantial stake; a few years later they exit through a put/call; overdeliver and it's 12x EBITDA; miss and it's 8x. This structure does three things. First, it lets founders, after selling their company, still run it as if it were their own — because the value of that slice of equity depends on their results over the next few years. Second, it saves the parent the most expensive things: the management cost of integration and the risk of integration failing. Third, and the easiest to overlook, it's a filter — Noth's line, "we're suspicious of founders who want to sell everything at once and walk away," amounts to saying: if there's no founder willing to bet on the company, we don't buy it. Run both candidates through this filter. Business Insider has founders: Ryan is chairman, Blodget is CEO, the VC shareholders are willing to exit, and management has equity they can roll over. HuffPost has been a division of AOL since 2011; its founders either left or became executives in someone else's company; Arianna is the face of the brand, but she's an employee, not an owner; and the seller is a telecom company that just spent US$4.4 billion buying AOL and wants to spin this off. My own take is that this company's M&A philosophy and its M&A targets define each other. United Artists isn't just "how to manage it after you buy it" — before you buy, it has already crossed off half the targets for you. Being shut out twice actually nailed the direction down Döpfner says the two biggest setbacks of his tenure were ProSiebenSat.1 and the Financial Times — "and both, looking back, were healthy, because they made our shift more radical and faster." That sentence is worth unpacking. ProSieben being blocked on antitrust grounds taught that in Germany, the road to growing through traditional media had been sealed off by regulators, so the only ways left were digital and abroad. FT being snatched away by Nikkei taught that spending a year negotiating a contract without exclusivity means doing someone else's due diligence for them — the other side only has to take the same piece of paper and add 10%. Each setback carried a different message. One was about direction, one about process. Döpfner's approach was to treat them as information, not as losses that needed to be made up for. The difference between these two reactions decides what you buy next. People who treat setbacks as information ask: what has this just told us? People who treat setbacks as losses ask: so what do we buy instead? The first group arrives at "the direction is right, go to America, but this time move fast, lock in the people first, and leave a buffer for a counterbid"; the second can very easily arrive at — find something about as big and as expensive as FT, and spend that billion. The airport scene matters because it's the most emotionally charged moment in the whole case. A year of negotiation, a plane waiting to take off, a CEO who won't let everyone board. The next decision is made on top of that emotion. Three times the revenue, two and a half times the price, a fifth of the growth — HuffPost's three ledgers don't add up The professor's second question asks us to work out the strategic, financial and cultural ledgers separately. Done separately, the conclusion actually gets clearer. The strategic ledger. HuffPost's selling points are scale and international reach: US$168 million in revenue, 3.4 times BI's; 13 international editions plus the Arabic one, so the "internationalize" box seems ticked right away. But most of those 13 editions are partnerships with local media — you're managing relationships, not ownership. And its business model is 100% advertising with no paid product, competing with Buzzfeed and Vox for the same pool of programmatic ad budgets. BI is small, but it has a seed of paid revenue — BI Intelligence, subscription research that corporate clients pay a few thousand dollars a year for — which is exactly the logic BildPlus proved in Germany: business readers will pay for content; general-news readers rarely do. And BI is still small enough for Axel Springer to be the platform that takes it to Europe, which is something it would do. The financial ledger. On revenue multiples the two are close: HuffPost at about 6 to 7x, a controlling deal for BI at roughly 7 to 9x. But on growth, the gap is huge: BI went from US$20 million to over US$40 million in a year, doubling; HuffPost went from US$146 million to US$168 million, 15%. On profit, HuffPost's billion is roughly 100x its expected 2015 EBITDA — paying a growth-stock price for a company whose growth has already slowed. Then look at the budget: FT was a little over a billion; HuffPost would use up exactly that money, and spend it on a pure-advertising asset; BI would take about 40% of it, leaving the rest for classifieds — where the real money is. The cultural ledger. Axel Springer's Essentials are conservative, pro-Israel and free-market, and Döpfner calls himself a "non-Jewish Zionist"; HuffPost is the emblem of American liberal media. Editorial independence can be written into a contract, but the headline "German conservatives buy American liberal outlet" will write itself — in both newsrooms, every day. BI's territory is business and tech, which doesn't collide with any of the five Essentials; and the third one, the "transatlantic alliance," is itself a reason to go to America. BI brings a different kind of cost: Blodget's SEC history and its clickbait reputation. But Axel Springer owns Bild — it knows better than anyone how to live with a tabloid reputation, and how to turn it into money. Add up the three ledgers and HuffPost wins on only one thing: being big right now. And "big right now" is exactly what a buyer who has just lost a big deal wants most. My choice: buy Business Insider, and sign it in weeks, not a year If I had to pick a side in class, I'd pick Business Insider — buy the remaining roughly 91% at a total valuation of US$400–450 million, about 7 to 9x its US$50 million in revenue. Let the billion-dollar HuffPost go. The reasons are all written above; boiled down to one sentence: BI is the only target that matches all three verbs and the United Artists filter at the same time. Digitize: it has a seed of paid revenue. Internationalize: it's English-language, American, and still small enough to be taken to Europe. Strengthen the core: business and tech sit right next to Welt 's readers, and Bild understands its traffic DNA. The founders are there, equity can roll over, the put/call can be used. And Axel Springer has already been sitting on its board for half a year — the "foot in the door" was prepared for exactly this moment. As for how to make sure it gets signed, the answer is all in the FT lesson. This time, don't run a year-long process; do a short, bilateral negotiation: first line up Ryan, Blodget and the VC funds — their alternative is another venture round at four or five times revenue, so a strategic exit at seven to nine times with rollover equity is a better deal for them than for anyone. Lock in the founders' retained stake and management terms before the price goes public. Trade speed and certainty — no financing condition, almost no regulatory risk — for an exclusivity period and a break fee. Most important of all: before the first meeting, write down the ceiling, with that 10% "Nikkei buffer" already built into the number, and then don't move it. A wounded buyer is the one most likely to overpay, so the discipline has to be set before you fall for the deal. I accept the costs, too. US$50 million in revenue is tiny for a €3 billion group; BI has to be a platform, not an endpoint, followed by European and Asian editions. Blodget's history and the "clickbait" criticism will show up in every German news story, and have to be owned head-on. It's still loss-making or barely profitable, dependent on advertising, with Google and Facebook holding its traffic. And there's one cost nobody will put in a model: FT is a trophy; BI isn't. After losing the glamorous one, you still have to be willing to buy the less glamorous one. Why not wait? Because the print cash flow propping all this up is shrinking, and Bayer already called 2013 the "last window" for the regional papers. The American window is open now; valuations are high but affordable. Two years from now, BI will either be bigger and more expensive, or already someone else's. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading this case, what came to mind wasn't newspapers, but the kind of transformation we ourselves are going through — the old business feeding the new one, with only a limited window. First, the bill for a transformation is often paid by selling something you're emotionally attached to. Axel Springer's digital future was paid for by the newspapers the founder started in 1948, and they were sold in the year when someone would still pay 10x. Every company in transformation has its own "regional newspapers" — businesses with history, with emotional weight, still making money, but with no future. The question isn't "should we sell," but "which year is the last window when someone will still pay a good price." Second, a cash cow buys you time, but not unlimited time. The print business fed the digital business for a decade, yet Bild didn't put up a paywall until 2013 — too slow. Profits from the old business can trick you into thinking you can take it slowly. Set a year by which "new-business revenue overtakes the old business," then work backward from that year; it's more useful than any strategy slogan. Third, partnerships and acquisitions buy people, not assets; write the exit as a formula. The core of United Artists is: retained equity, autonomy, and an exit multiple determined by performance. It's both respect for entrepreneurs and a filter — people who want to take the money all at once and leave, no thanks. For any organization that delivers through partners and networks, this is worth copying outright: buffet-style enablement, plus an exit written as a formula. Fourth, before a big decision, get "a foot in the door" first. US$20 million for 9% and a board seat bought half a year of inside view before betting US$400 million. Information asymmetry is the most expensive part of any partnership; a small partnership with real delivery is the cheapest way to eliminate it — with clients, and with partners alike. Fifth, after losing a big deal, beware of healing the wound with a more expensive one. HuffPost happened to cost exactly what FT did, and Döpfner happened to be "wounded." The ninety days after losing a big deal are the ninety days when you are most likely to sign the wrong contract. Give yourself a rule: for the next deal after a lost one, run it through your three verbs and your filter first, then talk price. Sixth, values are a filter, not decoration. The Essentials didn't pick anything for Axel Springer, but they ruled some things out, however tempting the scale. If a company's principles have never made it walk away from a single good deal, they probably aren't principles yet. Final Thoughts Before class, the line I agree with most is this one: "People who treat setbacks as information ask: what has this just told us? People who treat setbacks as losses ask: so what do we buy instead?" Innovation Case: Roaring Out of Recession
In a recession, the fastest to cut jobs lose the most; save on process and spend on customers to expand against the wind

Unit 3 of Professor Ranjay Gulati's Innovation — Strategic Thinking for Turbulent Markets: Roaring Out of Recession and Investing in Growth Through Uncertainty. This session has no single case company. Instead, it's two articles by the same author, written thirteen years apart. The first is a study of 4,700 companies that answers the question "what do companies that come out of a recession stronger actually do during it?"; the second circles back to a harder question — "why, even knowing what to do, do most people still not dare to do it?" Belden began its transformation in its most profitable year; these two articles are about how to spend money in your least profitable one. Opposite directions, same principle. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary December 2008 : the Great Recession is in full swing. Three scholars launch a year-long project to answer a question that everyone talks about but almost no one has studied empirically: what strategy should you use during a recession in order to win after it? There's plenty of folk wisdom — Procter & Gamble, Chevrolet and Camel cigarettes survived the Great Depression by advertising heavily, stories we've all read many times — but very little data. They took 4,700 public companies from S&P's Compustat database and ran them through the last three recessions: 1980–82, 1990–91 and 2000–02. For each one they looked at three periods: the three years before the recession, the recession itself, and the three years after. They used six balance-sheet items to measure where companies shifted their resources during the recession — headcount, cost of goods sold as a share of sales, R&D spending, SG&A, capital expenditure, and the stock of fixed assets. Only changes in the top or bottom third relative to the industry average counted as "significant." The results are glaring. 17% of the companies didn't survive the recession — they went bankrupt, were acquired, or went private. Of those that survived, 80% had not regained their pre-recession growth rates three years after the recession ended; 40% hadn't even returned to their absolute pre-recession levels of sales and profits. Of the growth leaders before the recession, 85% were knocked out of that position during it. Only about 9% of companies did better after the recession than before it, outperforming their peers by at least 10% in both sales and profit growth. The winners were neither of the two types people would expect. Drawing on the theory of Columbia University psychologist Tory Higgins — that people have two modes of self-regulation, "promotion focus" and "prevention focus," one seeking gains and the other avoiding losses — the authors sorted companies into four groups. Prevention-focused : cut almost everything, and invested more than rivals in nothing. Promotion-focused : invested more than rivals in at least one area, and cut more than rivals in none. Pragmatic : both cut (laying off staff or reducing cost of goods sold) and invested (in at least one of sales, R&D, capex or fixed assets). Progressive : reduced cost of goods sold but didn't lay off more people than peers, while investing more than rivals both on the market side — sales and R&D — and on the asset side — capex and fixed assets. The probability of each group "breaking away" after the recession — leading peers by more than 10% in both sales and profit growth — was 21%, 26%, 29% and 37% respectively. In the three years after the recession, the average annual growth of prevention-focused companies was 6% in sales and 4% in profits; promotion-focused, 8% and 6%; progressive, 13% and 12%. After the 2000 recession, the 200 largest companies averaged US$12 billion more in sales than before the recession. The prevention-focused ones added only US$5 billion, with profits up US$600 million; the progressive ones added US$28 billion, with profits up US$6.6 billion — eleven times as much. Then comes a set of contrasting stories. Sony and HP: two directions in the same recession. In the two years after 2000, Sony cut its workforce by 11%, R&D by 12% and capital expenditure by 23%. Its profit margin rose from 8% in 1999 to 12% in 2002, but sales growth fell from an average of 11% a year before the recession to 1% afterwards. It went on to lose e-readers to Amazon, game consoles to Microsoft and Nintendo, and OLED TVs to Samsung. In December 2008 it announced yet again that it would cut US$2.6 billion in costs, lay off 16,000 people and postpone a badly needed LCD TV plant in Slovakia. HP went the other way. As then-CEO Carly Fiorina put it: "In blackjack, when the odds are improving, you double down. We're going to double down." So it bought Compaq for US$25 billion — the largest acquisition in the company's history — raised R&D by 9%, spent US$200 million on brand advertising and US$1 billion on rolling out information technology in developing countries. These moves stretched the organization and spread management's attention thin. When the recession ended, HP found it couldn't catch up with the profitability of IBM and Dell: in 2004 HP's EBITDA margin was 8.4%, IBM's 16.8% and Dell's 9.3%. Office Depot and Staples are the cleanest pair. Office Depot laid off 6% of its staff, but its operating costs didn't really come down; it launched a sales incentive program, yet sales growth still fell from 19% before the recession to 8% afterwards, five percentage points below Staples. Staples closed a batch of underperforming stores but grew its headcount by 10% — to support the new premium categories and services it was launching — while keeping operating costs under control. Its sales doubled from US$7.1 billion in 1997 to US$14.6 billion in 2003; Office Depot's went from US$8.7 billion to US$13.4 billion, up by half. In the three years after the recession, Staples' profit margin was about 30% higher than its old rival's. Target and TJX both expanded during the recession, with opposite outcomes. In the 2000 recession, Target raised its marketing and sales spending by 20% and its capital expenditure by 50%, growing from 947 stores to 1,107, and from 30 SuperTargets to 118. Rather than build its own e-commerce, it partnered with Amazon to sell its goods; it collaborated with designers like Michael Graves, Philippe Starck and Todd Oldham, cementing its "cheap chic" image; it was also one of the 12 retailers that founded the WorldWide Retail Exchange, using a B2B electronic marketplace to drive down purchasing costs; and it folded its Dayton's and Hudson's department-store brands into the better-known Marshall Field's. During the recession its sales grew 40%, its profits 50%, and its profit margin went from 9% to 10%. TJX — parent company of T.J. Maxx and Marshalls — added 300 stores to its 1,350 between 2000 and 2002, increasing floor space by 25% and nearly doubling capital expenditure. Rivals were contracting, and real estate was cheap. Sales did beat peers by four percentage points, but three years later its profit growth was 9% below its peers', whereas before the recession it had been on par. There was only one reason: it simply scaled up its old model without changing it. The article ends with a nine-box grid. Three defensive moves (cutting staff, operational efficiency, both) and three offensive moves (market development, asset investment, both). The best box is "operational efficiency × investing in both markets and assets": sales growth of 13.0%, profit growth of 12.2%. The worst box isn't "cut only" but "cutting staff × investing in both markets and assets": sales growth of 3.3%, profit growth of minus 5.2%. Thirteen years later, the same author comes back to talk about mindset. The 2023 article opens with Alaska Airlines. In early 2020, US airline passenger traffic plunged 96% year on year. It did everything its peers did: froze hiring, cut executive pay, renegotiated supplier payments, suspended buybacks and dividends, slashed capex. But that December, as rivals were cancelling aircraft orders, it ordered 68 Boeings plus options for 52 more — the only major US airline to place a big order that year — and used the opportunity to consolidate its mixed Airbus-and-Boeing fleet into an all-Boeing one. In the words of CEO Ben Minicucci: "We knew supply chain issues would slow aircraft deliveries, but this deal put us first in line. After all, in this business, you can't grow without airplanes." In 2021–22 it exercised those 52 options, locked in another 105 aircraft through 2030, and in 2022 concluded five labor agreements, including one with the pilots' union. In 2022 its pretax margin was among the highest in the industry. Gulati says the 2010 study only answered "what to do." It didn't answer what kind of mindset allows a handful of leaders to dare to retrench and invest at the same time. He offers three: sensemaking (getting moving even in the fog), a bootstrap ethic (start-up-style frugality), and stakeholder balance (spreading the pain across everyone). Then come the stories of Edward Jones, Firefly, Panera and Levi Strauss — which I'll save for the next section. The article closes on a question, borrowing a popular line from writer Vivian Greene: would you rather crouch down and wait for the storm to pass, or learn to dance in the rain? The professor's three questions for this session: 1. What are the foundations of building competitive advantage in turbulent markets? 2. How do companies in different industries use creative strategies to grow both revenue and profits in tough markets? 3. How exactly did these companies put change into practice? My Thinking Both of the fastest roads lead to mediocrity: cutting costs across the board, and flooring the accelerator Start with the prevention-focused. Their logic is airtight: the recession is here, survive first, cash is king, stop everything that can be stopped. The article says these companies have a 21% chance of breaking away after the recession — the lowest of the four groups. Why the lowest? The authors list four things. An organization that only looks at losses sets its goals low, so innovation and cost-saving both become a matter of squeezing out the last drops; it doesn't learn to run more efficiently, it just "does the same with fewer people," so quality drops first and customer satisfaction follows; cost-cutting decisions get centralized in the finance department and applied across the board, and no one can tell which expenses are the seeds of post-recession growth; pessimism spreads, with centralization, tight control and the constant threat of another round of cuts — everyone is thinking about how to survive personally. And the fastest cut turns out to be the most expensive. Only 23% of progressive companies cut staff, versus 56% of prevention-focused ones. Companies that relied on layoffs alone had an 11% chance of breaking away. Layoffs lower this quarter's costs; what you pay back is the next cycle's hiring costs, morale, and the window for expansion you missed. Office Depot cut 6% and its operating costs didn't fall; Staples added 10% more people and kept operating costs under control — because what it closed was stores, what it changed was the model, and what it added was people. Now the promotion-focused. Fiorina's "double down" sounds like courage; the data gives it a 26% probability. Optimistic organizations attract optimistic people and develop a kind of positive groupthink, in which dissenting voices get sidelined and early signals like shrinking customer budgets get ignored. Worse still: prevention-focused companies can push costs as a share of sales down by three percentage points, while promotion-focused ones can't push them down by even one. When they finally have to cut, every department believes it's vital to the company, everyone blames everyone else, no trade-offs get made, and decisions freeze. My own reading is that Sony and HP made two sides of the same mistake. One treated cost as the goal; the other treated optimism as a strategy. Both forgot to look at what customers, in this recession, had stopped buying — and what they still needed. Reefing the sails isn't abandoning the voyage: the money you save in process should go where customers will come back What the progressive companies do can be put in one sentence: their defense is selective; their offense is comprehensive. They cut cost of goods sold by rethinking supply chains, organization and processes, not by cutting people; and when they invest, they invest on both the market side and the asset side at once — R&D, marketing, and plants and equipment bought while they're cheap. One number in the nine-box grid deserves a second look. The worst box isn't "cut without investing" but "lay people off, then invest across the board" — profit growth of minus 5.2%. Why? Because the people who would carry out the investment are gone. You've bought the equipment, opened up new markets, increased the R&D budget, but the people who could turn all that into products and sales are the ones you showed the door three months ago. Defense and offense aren't two ends of one line, a compromise between "cut a bit more" and "invest a bit more"; they're two dimensions, and they come in a sequence. The contrast between Target and TJX says something else: cheap assets are not an advantage in themselves. Both bought stores after 2000, and TJX bought even more. The difference is that Target simultaneously changed how it purchased (the B2B exchange), its brand (designer collaborations, merging its department stores) and its channels (partnering with Amazon rather than building its own), while TJX simply doubled down on centralized buying and flexible distribution. Three years after the recession, one had a margin going from 9% to 10%; the other's profit growth trailed its peers by 9%. Alaska Airlines demonstrates the sequence most clearly. It first completed every defensive move — froze hiring, cut pay, stopped dividends, renegotiated payments — made sure its balance sheet was strong enough, and only then placed that order for 68 planes. Offense is earned by defense; it isn't a substitute for it. And the order was itself a defensive move: consolidating a mixed fleet into all-Boeing permanently lowered its operating costs. So where do you invest? The two articles offer only one filter: the customer. The 2010 article writes that progressive companies "stay closely connected to customer needs — the most powerful filter for investment decisions." In 2008 Target saw same-store sales slipping as Walmart's "everyday low prices" hit home with consumers. Instead of discounting across the board, it noticed something more subtle: consumers were cutting their "wants," not their "needs." So it doubled the size of its food sections, expanded its private labels Market Pantry and Archer Farms, and shifted the emphasis of its slogan "Expect more, pay less" to the second half. By 2008, food had become a US$1.8 billion business for Target. You reef the sails so the ship can keep moving forward — not so it can sit still and wait for the wind to pass. When you're lost, even an old map can save your life — get moving first, then correct course The organizational psychologist Karl Weick tells a story that he himself admits may be apocryphal. A unit of soldiers was lost for days in snowstorm-swept mountains. Someone found a map in his pocket, morale soared, and they used it to find their way back to base. Only later did they discover that the map was of a different mountain range. Weick's conclusion: when you're lost, any old map will do. The map saved them not because it showed the right way, but because it got them moving. Once you move, the terrain under your feet starts giving you feedback, and the route can be corrected. This is what Gulati calls sensemaking. Difficult situations paralyze people, but we don't need to have everything figured out before taking the first step. Resilient leaders fix the ultimate goal, take a deliberate first step, and adjust as they go. In fact, the 2010 article ends with a similar line: few progressive leaders enter a recession with a master plan; instead, they encourage their organizations to discover what works and then combine those discoveries into a portfolio of initiatives. Edward Jones is the best example of this mindset — and it happens to be a wealth management firm. In the mid-2010s it saw that its clients were aging and that its traditional model — advisers selling products to long-term investors — was under threat from cheaper, more convenient digital competitors; industry surveys showed consumers were broadly dissatisfied with the financial advice they got, most of it narrow product advice rather than holistic wealth management. In 2019 it launched a multi-year transformation called "human-centered holistic wealth management": advisers would understand clients' needs beyond money, and the firm would invest in systems, processes, talent and training. Just as the transformation got under way, the pandemic hit. It didn't stop; it let investment grow faster than revenue. In late 2022 and early 2023, as the economic outlook darkened again and peers were all cutting costs and laying people off, some people inside once again asked whether to pause. CEO Penny Pennington's answer: not investing is the more dangerous option. But the approach changed. It postponed hiring 1,000 employees; it strengthened its financial planning and analysis capability so that every new investment needed a business case and success metrics; it prioritized by value — upgrading the IT systems for its fixed-income business first, then those for equities. The destination didn't move; the steps got smaller, and each one came with a measuring stick. In her own words: "We invest in good years, and we invest in bad years." My own reading is that Weick's old map and Edward Jones's FP&A don't contradict each other at all. One says "don't wait for a perfect map before setting off"; the other says "once you've set off, every step has to be measurable." Put together: the destination stays fixed, the steps can change, and every step can be measured. The most common stupidity is forgetting what you set out to do Nietzsche said that the most common form of human stupidity is forgetting what one is trying to do. Gulati uses this line to introduce the second mindset. Panicked executives, in pursuit of lower costs, often cut away the company's future along with them — some call it the "efficiency trap," others the "death spiral." Drucker's old saying gets put to use again here: efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things. When cutting costs, the question isn't "how much more can we save?" but "after we save it, can we still deliver the products, services and processes that will get us to our destination?" Gulati calls this mindset the bootstrap ethic: living like an early-stage start-up. Obsessive about customer value, and stingy about everything else. The filter is still the same one: does this project, this team, this product line make us better at serving our target customers? If yes, keep it and invest more; if no, cut it. Firefly is a company that puts advertising screens on top of taxis and ride-hailing cars. When stay-at-home orders hit in 2020, nobody was looking at outdoor ads and revenue went almost to zero. CEO Kaan Gunay cut staff in sales, marketing and sales support, cut everyone's pay by 20%, renegotiated contracts with fleets and drivers, and moved operations and engineering to Turkey, where engineers are cheap but first-rate. Then, with the money saved, he hired a seasoned chief revenue officer and kept investing in engineering and product, because what customers wanted in 2021 and 2022 was better ad optimization, forecasting and planning tools; and, taking advantage of market pessimism and low valuations, he acquired a US peer in 2021 and a UK peer in 2022. Panera is an example from the other end: a big company. In recent years the restaurant industry has faced slowing sales, labor shortages and rising costs all at once. The bottleneck CEO Niren Chaudhary saw was general-manager turnover — when a store manager leaves, the customer experience goes with them. So he doubled down on people, against the grain: substantially raising base pay, giving managers more training, and tying more of their compensation to store performance, so that the best managers could earn six figures. Where did the money come from? Menu prices rose faster than inflation, while new products (flatbread pizza) and promotions for price-sensitive customers (the US$10.99-a-month Sip Club unlimited drinks subscription) kept traffic up. The result: revenue growth that outpaced the industry, rising market share, and employee turnover down 10%. The real crux of this session is in a passage in the middle of Gulati's article: there are three obstacles to playing offense and defense at the same time. Organizationally, adding and cutting happen simultaneously, and reallocating budgets triggers infighting — the fix is to use customer focus as the basis. Strategically, short-term efficiency and long-term investment are hard to tell as one coherent story — the fix is an overarching purpose. And culturally, there's loss aversion: people are wired to fear losing, and a crisis magnifies that fear. His fix is a single sentence: explicitly cultivate courage as a cultural value, make courageous behavior the norm, and have leaders go first. Minicucci said "we wanted to be aggressive"; Pennington said "not investing is the more dangerous option" — in both cases the CEO said it out loud first, and only then did the organization dare to follow. A chef who can make sweet and sour lets every party hurt a little less, instead of making one party bear it all Gulati's late colleague Sumantra Ghoshal — a professor at London Business School and the founding dean of the Indian School of Business — had a metaphor: the best leaders are like Chinese chefs, because they can make sweet and sour. They know how to look after stakeholders whose demands are completely different, all at the same time. This is hard enough in good years, and harder in a crisis. Once the fear of scarcity takes hold, groups inside and outside the company become tribal, cling to their own interests and resist change — which makes both cutting costs and investing harder. Left unchecked, decisions become timid, unimaginative and short-sighted. What resilient leaders do, Gulati calls practical idealism: ask certain groups for short-term concessions, but limit their pain, while attending to longer-term needs. Here's what Levi Strauss did in 2020: suspended dividends, cut 15% of its workforce, saved US$100 million — that was defense; but it extended health insurance for departing employees, added benefits for those who stayed, gave suppliers nearly US$2 million in grants and helped them find financing, and didn't stop a single sustainability program. CFO Harmit Singh said you can't "do it today and then forget about it tomorrow because a recession is coming." It could have saved more. It chose to keep the people and suppliers it would need in the recovery. I love what Singh said next: "There's no right answer, there's no formula, and I'm sure someone could find fault with what we did. But if I can sleep at night, I think we're in the right place." At Edward Jones, Pennington talks about "financial balance" among three Cs: clients, colleagues, community. In 2023, even as she tightened spending, she kept investing in new tools for clients, kept paying advisers bonuses (smaller ones), and kept putting tens of millions of dollars into "financial fitness" programs for high school students. This is the one genuinely new dimension the 2023 article adds to the 2010 one. The 2010 study looked at six balance-sheet items, and stakeholders weren't among them. Thirteen years later the author added this one, and my understanding is that it's because he had seen that relationships cut in a recession can't be bought back in the recovery. In thirteen years the method hasn't changed; what's changed is whether you dare Reading the two articles together, the most interesting thing isn't what they say but the distance between them. The 2010 conclusion was a nine-box grid, a set of probabilities, a playbook of "what to do": save through efficiency, invest across the board, filter by customer. Thirteen years later the same person came back, didn't revise a single number — 9% is still 9% — but wrote at a different level: sensemaking, bootstrap, stakeholder balance. He admits himself that the earlier research "was largely confined to the strategic and tactical level and didn't explore the mindset that enables leaders to embrace protective and forward-looking strategies at the same time." My own reading is that this distance is itself the answer. The method has been public since 2010: HBR published it, consulting firms followed up with several rounds of research, every CEO could read it. Yet only 9% of companies pulled it off — the bottleneck was never the method, but whether people get bent out of shape by fear. BlackRock's Mark Wiedman said in 2023 that crises send executives into "panic mode — they don't really want to lead, they don't want to lean into anything new." In Book Five of the Meditations , Marcus Aurelius wrote: the impediment to action advances action; what stands in the way becomes the way. Gulati also cites the Stoics at the end of his article: adversity isn't just a threat to be contained, but a unique opportunity for personal and organizational growth. Put those two lines side by side and they say the same thing as the nine-box grid. If I were asked in class which type my company is today, and what I'd cut first and protect first in the next recession — my answer would be: cut first everything that amounts to "doing the same with fewer resources" — repetitive manual work, meetings that don't produce decisions, tools that don't change what the client gets; push all of that into systems, which lowers costs permanently. Protect two things first: the people sitting across from clients, and the system that remembers what clients have said. They're Minicucci's "airplanes" — you can't grow without them, and if you let them go in a recession, you can't buy them back at the original price when demand returns. The price of this choice is a thinner buffer and a slower road to fatter margins. I accept that. Staples' numbers tell me the asymmetry runs in this direction. Belden began its transformation in its most profitable year; these two articles are about continuing to invest in your least profitable one. Put the two ends together and they amount to the same sentence: the best time to transform and invest is never when it feels safest. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading these two articles, what came to mind wasn't families — it was us. Gulati writes about CEOs in a recession, but a start-up has no "non-turbulent period" — resources are always fewer than the things you want to do, and every quarter you're deciding what to cut and what to invest in. So for us, that nine-box grid isn't a contingency plan; it's daily life. I want to treat the points below as Arcus42's own basic principles for allocating resources in any period — not just advice for a recession, and not just advice for families. First, cutting and investing are two lists, not one dial. The easiest mistake is to think of resource allocation as a single line — "let's be a bit more conservative this quarter" or "a bit more aggressive." What progressive companies do is keep two lists open at once: the defensive one written very narrowly, the offensive one written very broadly. For us, every quarter should answer two questions at once: which expense can be brought down permanently? Which investment should be bigger than everyone else's? Answer only one and you're prevention-focused or promotion-focused, with odds below 30% either way. Second, save on process, not on the people facing clients — and don't get the order backwards. A start-up's biggest cost item is people, and the quickest way to save is also people. But in a business built on trust, the people facing clients are the product. The costs that can truly be brought down permanently lie in repetitive analysis, drafting, organizing and meeting notes — the part systems should take over. First let systems take over the repetition, then look at headcount. The worst box in the nine-box grid is exactly the one that gets the order backwards: send the people away first, then invest. Third, every expense has to pass just one test: does this help us understand this family better? Gulati's filter is "customer needs." For us the question is more specific: does this tool, this process, this partner, this new service line make our understanding of this family deeper and our response faster? If yes, keep it and invest more; if no, cut it. It has another benefit — it turns budget arguments into a question everyone can answer. When we do asset allocation for families, we advise them to use the same question to screen out "wants" and protect "needs"; when spending on ourselves, there's no reason to switch questions. Fourth, something cheap only counts as an investment if it changes the model; otherwise it's just scaling up. TJX and Target both bought stores when they were cheap; one saw profits fall, the other saw them rise, and the difference was whether they also changed how they made money. For us, tools, licenses and talent will all have their "cheap" moments; the test isn't price, but whether it changes our marginal cost of serving a family. If it doesn't, we're scaling up an old model — revenue can go up, profit won't. Fifth, the destination stays fixed, the steps can change, and every step can be measured. Uncertainty most easily produces two kinds of paralysis: waiting until things are clear before moving, or moving without looking. Edward Jones took the middle road:
A company is worth the most in the year someone else needs you; don't wait for the year you need cash to sell

Unit 3, Professor Martin Sinozich's Finance course, Nantucket Nectars: The Exit. The last few pieces were all about how to build a company — Olay took its brand apart and put it back together, Belden transformed while profits were still rising, Bajaj guarded the gap between two purchases. This one runs the other way: the company has been built, and two founders in their early thirties have to decide whether to sell, to whom, and how. It's a story about "what it's worth," and the answer isn't in their own books. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary In the fall of 1997 , Tom Scott and Tom First were sitting in a room they had never been in before. Five companies had expressed interest in buying part of Nantucket Nectars — Tropicana (owned by Seagram), Ocean Spray, Triarc, Pepsi, and one unnamed. What set it off is the interesting part: in July, Brandweek magazine ran a story saying Triarc was in acquisition talks with them. It was wrong — at that point they hadn't even formally met anyone from Triarc. But Ocean Spray and Tropicana read it, and within a few weeks Triarc and Pepsi came knocking too. Every meeting was held away from the office, so that no employee would worry. The most memorable day had been a few days earlier: the two Toms ran so long with Ocean Spray that they were late for their second meeting with Pepsi. So they split up — Firsty stayed with Ocean Spray, Scott went to see Pepsi. Ocean Spray never knew there was a Pepsi meeting that afternoon. Tom Scott said they had learned everything on the job, under fire, but this was something entirely new. The road here starts at Brown University. The two Toms met as freshmen and painted houses together on Cape Cod. Tom Scott later recalled that of the six guys, everyone wanted to be the boss except him and Tom First, who never fought over it — "we liked the whole more than our individual roles." After graduating they went back to Nantucket and started a "floating convenience store" called Allserve, delivering ice, beer and newspapers to yachts in the harbor, pumping out sewage, delivering groceries, doing laundry. Back then they didn't even sell juice. In the winter of 1990, Tom First recreated a peach juice he'd had in Spain. That spring they blended it up, poured it into milk cartons and wine bottles — "whatever we could find" — and sold it from the boat. The first year they sold 8,000 cases, the second year 20,000. The two of them put in all their savings, US$17,000 in total. For the next two years they got by on a small bank loan. By early 1993, several employees hadn't been paid in a year, and the two founders hadn't paid themselves in three and a half years, getting through the winters on odd jobs. They could see the juice taking off; they just had no money. Then came Mike Egan. Founder of Alamo Rent-a-Car, holding 93% of Alamo's stock. The two Toms had met him in their early days servicing his boat in the harbor. Egan put in US$600,000 for 50% of the company. They worried about handing control to an outsider, but they had no other choice. In Egan's own words: "I made this investment because it makes me wake up in the morning feeling like I'm twenty-five again, starting a company from scratch." Egan served as an adviser and stayed out of day-to-day operations. The money changed their distribution and inventory: they found better independent bottlers; rented their own warehouse, bought used trucks, went out and sold themselves, delivered themselves, stocked the shelves themselves — and while they were at it, moved their bottles in front of the Snapple. To speed things up, they took on exclusive distribution rights for Arizona Iced Tea in Massachusetts; within three months the distribution team grew from 7 to 100 people, and monthly volume went from 2,000 cases to 30,000. By the end of 1994 revenue had passed US$8 million. But distribution is a business that needs a "big brand" to spread its costs. After losing US$2 million in 1994, in 1995 they sold the distribution business and focused on "selling juice": their own sales force plus outside distributors, with salespeople going door to door to small stores, making sure the product sat at "eye-to-thigh" height, and checking along the way whether distributors were slacking. Tom Scott said they didn't want to build a house of cards; they wanted solid long-term growth. On product, they didn't count margins. Pure cane sugar, not high-fructose corn syrup; four times the juice content of the big brands; a proprietary 17.5-ounce bottle against the market's standard 16 ounces. In three years they went from 3 flavors to 27. Under each cap was a printed saying, and their radio ads told stories like the time employee Ned crashed the truck on his first delivery to Boston and destroyed all the juice, or how Larry dropped the first payment into the harbor. Customers loved the story. The report card looked great, and it was thin. Revenue went from US$233,000 in 1991 to US$29.49 million in 1996, up 92% year over year last year. They turned their first profit in 1995; in 1996 EBITDA was US$969,000 and net income US$369,000. But gross margin was only 30.5%, among the lowest in the whole category: four times the juice, pure cane sugar, plus no futures contracts — growth was too fast to forecast, so they couldn't sign forward purchases. In 1995 the cranberry crop failed, Ocean Spray locked up the supply, and they didn't get a single cranberry. The weather was changing, too. New Age beverages were the hot spot in 1992–95: ready-to-drink tea grew 24% a year on average, water 34%, juice 32%. But in Exhibit 4, alternative juice drinks, growing about 38% a year in 1991–95, were projected to grow only about 9% a year in 1995–2000. More than a hundred companies crowded in; Coca-Cola, Pepsi and Seagram all wanted to be "total beverage companies," and one of the big players' competitive tactics was squeezing small brands off the shelf. Supermarkets sold 55% of the category's volume but accounted for only 1% of Nantucket Nectars' sales; 93% of their business was in "other" small outlets outside convenience stores. The Midwest and the West were only 9% each. Then there was Snapple. In November 1994, Quaker Oats bought Snapple for US$1.7 billion; in 1997 it sold it to Triarc for US$300 million, and the CEO was fired. US$1.4 billion evaporated in three years. The industry put it down to two things: Quaker replaced the Howard Stern and "Snapple Lady" ads with corporate-sounding slogans; and, far worse, it tried to take the most profitable distribution business away from the old distributors and hand it to its own Gatorade channel. The distributors put Snapple in the deep freeze, and sales fell off a cliff. From then on the industry had a new word — Snappleization : when a brand is acquired by a big company, the distribution network that helped it win its market is the first thing thrown away. So these were the questions in front of the two Toms: 1. Sell or not? The company was in better shape than they had ever imagined. Exhibit 7 says that going it alone, it was worth US$34–58 million; inside a strategic buyer, US$106–176 million. 2. If they sold a majority stake, who would they be afterwards? Both wanted to keep running it. Take cash, or take the acquirer's stock to share in the upside? They didn't want to hold another company's stock. 3. Sell to whom? Ocean Spray had a similar culture, was private, had good cash flow, and would lose Pepsi's distribution in May 1998 — about US$200 million of single-serve sales at risk, on a base of US$1.05 billion. Pepsi had the deepest pockets but a history of "downgrading" products to buy volume. Triarc was the best platform for growing the business over the next two years, but it already had Snapple and Mistic, and distributors would get cut. 4. What about the 100 employees — 57 in sales, 20 in marketing, 15 in finance? Would that culture of "no suits, anyone can walk in and find the two Toms" survive? 5. Tom First asked the hardest question of all: "The hard part is figuring out what Nantucket Nectars is worth to someone else, not just to us." My Thinking A company doesn't have one price, only a price to someone Exhibit 7 is the whole case. Same company, two tables. Going it alone: 20–25% growth in 1999–2002, gross margin flat at 34.3%, a 14% discount rate, exit at 10x EBITDA — enterprise value of about US$47 million. Inside a strategic buyer: growth becomes 25–30% (supermarkets open up), gross margin rises to 37.3% (purchasing scale cuts costs by 10–20%), operating margin reaches 13%, same discount rate and multiple — about US$144 million. A difference of US$97 million. Three times. That US$97 million isn't a difference in valuation methods; it is the buyer's problem converted into money. Ocean Spray needs to fill a US$200 million hole, and to it Nantucket Nectars' 57 salespeople and that small-store network are worth one number; to Pepsi, it's an entry ticket into juice, worth another; to Triarc, part of the value would be cannibalized by its own Snapple — yet another number. Value isn't a property of the company; it's a function of who needs it on the day the deal is signed. Snapple demonstrated this most brutally: almost the same brand, US$1.7 billion in 1994, US$300 million in 1997. No financial crisis happened in between. What happened was that the buyer changed, and the buyer's problem changed. My own read is that the two sides of the negotiating table are looking at two different tables. The buyer's offer will always be anchored to the one on the left — "on your own, this is all you're worth; I'll give you a bit more." The seller's entire job is to get the table on the right into the room. And the way to do that isn't to argue; it's to have another buyer sitting outside the door. The window is opened by others, so move in the year they need you In 1993 the two Toms needed money and sold half the company for US$600,000. In 1997 Ocean Spray needed them, and half the company might be worth US$50 million. Four years apart, same company; the only difference was which side was more desperate. This time, the window didn't cost them a cent. A story that got it wrong, plus Pepsi breaking up with Ocean Spray in May 1998. Neither was something they could have manufactured, and neither would last forever. Once Ocean Spray patched its own distribution, once Pepsi bought someone else, once Coca-Cola got onto the shelf too, these five companies would drift away from the door. And on their own side, time was not on their side. Category growth was dropping from 38% to 9%; the 30.5% gross margin was the price of pure cane sugar and four times the juice, and without scale it couldn't be changed; supermarkets wanted multi-packs, shelf power and slotting fees, and 57 people couldn't buy that ticket; one bad cranberry harvest and the supply belonged to someone else. The standalone model assumed 20–25% growth; in a 9% category, that means taking share — from Coca-Cola and Pepsi. The best time to sell is when the other side's need is at its peak, not when your readiness is. Founders rarely sell when they're "ready," because that day never comes; the company is always one channel, one flavor, one more year of results short. But the other side's gap has a deadline. My own inclination is to treat that window as one of the hardest numbers in the case: May 1998. It will determine the price more than any discount rate in Exhibit 7. What's really valuable is the few things big companies can't build The two Toms made their own list of what underpinned the company's value: a better story than any juice company; a cost structure that was stabilizing; access to 18-to-34-year-olds; the last decent single-serve channel in New Age beverages; and the best vehicle for a juice company to get into juice cocktails without risking its own brand. The list splits into two halves. One half is what big companies can't build : the story that started on a boat, the sayings under the caps, the employee who dropped the first payment into the harbor, the office with no suits, young people, the affection of small-store owners who watched the two founders stock the shelves themselves. Ocean Spray has 5 bottling plants and can't build that; Pepsi has shelves nationwide and can't build it either. The other half is what big companies can fix : gross margin, purchasing, bottling costs, supermarket shelves. Ocean Spray is the world's largest buyer of non-orange juice; in its hands the cranberry problem doesn't exist; 10–20% saved on COGS is exactly where those three points of gross margin in Exhibit 7 come from. That determines how to negotiate. It's easy for the two Toms to apologize for the second half — "yes, our margins are low," "yes, we're not in supermarkets." They shouldn't. The margin gap isn't a weakness; it's synergy — a reason for the buyer to pay, not a reason to push the price down. What really needs protecting is the first half, because it vanishes the moment it's integrated. After selling a majority, whether you're a shareholder or an employee is decided by the contract The professor's second question reads most like a question about life: if they sell a majority but not all of it, what are the two Toms' roles afterwards? On paper, they'd still be "running the company." In reality, the big decisions would move up: capital, distribution, pricing, recipes, the hiring budget, where this brand ranks in someone else's portfolio. Their daily job would become protecting the story and those 57 people inside someone else's organization. They would be minority shareholders and employees at the same time. Whether that's a good position depends on three things, and all three are written in the contract, not in a handshake. First, why the buyer is buying. If it wants the story and the young people, the founders are an asset; if it wants to fill a gap and cut duplication, the founders are a transition cost. The first thing Quaker did after buying Snapple was change the ads; the second was change the distributors. Second, whether the retained stake has an exit. A minority stake is only an asset if it comes with a formula-priced put/call — say, at a fixed EBITDA multiple in years three to five. Otherwise it's just a piece of paper you can't sell, and what you're holding is still a company you no longer control. The two Toms said they didn't want someone else's stock; translated, that means: take most of it in cash, keep a slice for a second bite of the apple, but write the exit first. Third, autonomy has to be spelled out. Control over the brand and recipes — no switching to corn syrup; keeping the Nantucket office and the no-suits rule; no involuntary changes of distributors for 24 to 36 months; a committed growth budget; a retention pool for the 100 employees, especially the 57 in sales. They had in fact already lived with a 50% outside shareholder for four years, and it worked because Egan stayed out of it. The first time, you rely on character; the second time, you rely on the charter. The ideal form of a majority sale is "Egan 2.0 plus a distribution network"; the worst form is Quaker. My own read is that the real answer to this question isn't in the contract; it's in whether the two Toms are willing to say the honest thing out loud: they will be very rich, and they will no longer be the boss. Once that's said, the put is a choice, not a trap. Five buyers aren't luck; they have to be lined up What they were doing now was improvising. Seeing two companies separately on the same afternoon, holding meetings out of sight of employees, Ocean Spray not knowing Pepsi existed. In the short run that makes a great story; over three months it's a leak waiting to happen — if employees, distributors or retailers caught wind of it, Snappleization would happen before the deal was even signed. What they should do is replace improvisation with choreography: a short information memorandum, a data room, NDAs signed first; a timeline — four weeks for indicative bids, three or four buyers into management presentations, final bids accompanied by a markup of the draft contract; make buyers bid on structure, not just price: cash or stock, how much they're buying, the founders' roles, employee retention, commitments to distributors. Set the clock to May 1998. Do they need an investment bank? Yes. Not because the two Toms aren't smart, but because a US$100 million deal with four or five buyers is a process, and they are running a company growing 90% a year at the same time. A bank also lets them stay the "good guys" — staying friends with their future bosses and leaving the hard talk about price to someone else. A success fee of one or two points on a US$100 million deal is one or two million; if competition pushes the price up by just a tenth, that's ten million. But buyers are buying the two Toms' story, so they should handle the relationship conversation themselves and hand off the price conversation. There's one more thing to finish before seeing anyone: get aligned with Egan. A partner holding 50% who may want to cash out, and two founders who want to stay and keep building, are two different kinds of seller. Shareholders falling out of step at the last minute will kill a deal. My choice: sell a majority to Ocean Spray, keeping a slice of equity and a ticket out If I were asked to pick a side in class, I would choose: sell now, sell a majority, sell to Ocean Spray, through a short, competitive process, keeping a slice of equity and a put written into the contract. All three reasons for Ocean Spray are structural. It is the most desperate — a US$200 million hole and a May deadline are the best thing a seller can run into. It complements Nantucket Nectars rather than overlapping — it's strong in supermarkets and the Northeast, while Nantucket Nectars is 93% small stores and only 1% supermarkets; less overlap means fewer distributors fired and fewer people laid off. It's private with a similar culture — the two Toms really might be able to stay. Triarc is the best growth platform with the worst integration risk; Pepsi has the deepest pockets and the worst cultural fit. Let those two supply the pressure, and let Ocean Spray win on fit. Price target: over US$100 million for 100% of the equity — that is, capturing more than half of that US$97 million in synergies. Structure: Egan's 50% and most of the founders' stake for cash, the two Toms rolling over 20–25% between them, a put/call in years three to five, no public-company stock. I accept the cost. They give up the small chance of "two guys building a US$200 million brand on their own and keeping all of it," and accept a slower, more corporate second half. Some of the culture will be lost; the contract can only slow that down. Why not stay independent? Because independence means taking a 30% gross margin into a slowing category to fight Coca-Cola and Pepsi for supermarket shelves, and the growth capital they'd raise would dilute them anyway. Snapple already showed what big players do to the category leader. Why not sell everything and walk away? Because that leaves the second bite of the apple and the fate of 100 people on the table — unless the winner is Pepsi, in which case sell it all and leave with the story intact. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading this case, what came to mind wasn't juice; it was a moment we see in families all the time: a business that has been running for twenty or thirty years, and someone comes knocking. First, before answering "what is it worth," answer "to whom." The same business is three different numbers to an industry buyer, a financial investor, and a foreign company wanting into the market. When preparing a family for a sale, the first sheet of paper isn't a valuation table; it's a list of "who needs us right now." The synergy lives inside the buyer, not in your own books; a seller who only calculates "what we're worth" leaves that part on the table. Second, the window is external; the preparation is internal. The buyer's gap has a deadline, while the seller's preparation — the books, the equity structure, key people, contracts — never gets finished without one. So preparation has to happen when no buyer is knocking. Wait until the knock comes to get organized, and you either miss the window or get squeezed on price inside it. Third, "who am I" after the sale has to be written down before signing. A founder's role after a majority sale isn't decided by feelings; it's decided by the charter and the exit: how much to roll over, when you can get out, at what formula, which things others can't touch. This question is harder than price, and fewer people ask it in advance. What we can do for families is ask it before anyone has made an offer. Fourth, the relationship network is the first asset to be integrated away in a deal. The word Snappleization is worth remembering. Often the hardest thing to replicate in a business isn't the product; it's the distributors, suppliers and longtime customers built up over twenty years — and they are exactly what the acquirer "optimizes" first. Protection periods, retention pools, rules on replacement — all of it has to be written into the deal documents, not left to trust. Fifth, don't be both the seller and the negotiator. The two Toms should tell the story themselves, but they shouldn't negotiate the price themselves. Families are the same: the head of the family is the story itself and shouldn't stand on the opposite side of the price. Professionals manage the process, manage the competition, and say the unpleasant things; the family side needs someone at the table to help them read the contract's structure, align the shareholders, and, before the money lands, map out where the money will go. Final Words Before class, the line I agree with most is: "A company doesn't have one price, only a price to someone."
