The promise can change; condescension can't stay

Unit 3, Professor Das Narayandas, Market-Facing Functions: Facelift at Olay (A). Before class, I cast my vote for "fewer and clearer." Don't sell the brand. Don't chase 19-year-olds' acne. Cut the overlapping claims on the shelf and tell the red jar's story clearly. Swap "anti-aging" for a line that doesn't frighten anyone. After class, that vote still stands. It's been shifted one place over, though, and underneath it a layer showed up that I hadn't written about beforehand. Here goes — enjoy: Fewer, the red jar, science: these three are still standing In class, Olay's problems first landed in three places. Too many SKUs; customers are confused, so cut, and keep the red jar. Innovation needs science underneath it. And one more line: be where your people are. Don't stand under the streetlight. Before class, I'd written about the budget. In the case, about 80% of advertising spend was still on TV, with digital channels under 5%. The light is on TV because it's bright there, and because the organisation knows how to spend money there. Customers are no longer standing under that light. If your positioning is a fog, you can still win the war. It just costs a lot more. On the product line, the number given in class was a cut from about 150 to 80. The red jar is still the hero that gets kept. Nobody said the science was outdated. Fewer, and clearer, didn't get moved in class. Between the two groups, what you need is a bridge Before class I wrote a hard line: a brand can't say "I understand you best" to a 19-year-old's acne and a 55-year-old's wrinkles at the same time. The money is in the over-35s. The US$8 million spent on Fresh Effects was a failed attempt to court the young. Acne treatment for 19-year-olds still isn't this door. What the professor wanted was something else. Build a bridge between the existing customers and the new ones; find common ground. The promise can change. The people you already have can't be dropped. The existing customers are older women, and the old promise was called anti-aging. Once daughters no longer wanted to do what their mothers did, that story stopped. The world changed before our eyes. New customers understand skincare far more deeply. The internet drove the cost of information right down, and brands lost control over customers. What I wrote down, sitting there, was: our generation grew up inside control, our brains like hardware soldered onto a control mechanism. The new generation didn't grow up that way. Korean brands came in through that loosening gap. The woman in the research was called MI30 in class — a millennial around thirty. She wants to be treated as special. She still buys in mass channels. So the way you segment customers has to change. The thing they share about their skin keeps both of them inside the same sentence. You change the promise so that the people you have can still hear it, and the new ones can walk in. My own reading: giving up on 19-year-olds holds up. Push 30-year-olds out as well, and the bridge breaks. The way in is the year she first takes a serious look at her own skin. Under "anti-aging" lies a kind of condescension Before class I wrote: the science isn't outdated, the language is. The replacement line I'd prepared was, "skin that looks young, so it won't give away your age." In class, when the language was peeled back, what lay underneath was a relationship. The word "anti-aging" makes people feel they are getting old. What it evokes is fear. An even older tone is: I know better than you, but I care about you, so I have to help you. The master and the one being looked after. The professor called it patronizing — a kindness delivered from above. People who grew up in the digital world want equality. Brands used to own consumers. Customers no longer recognise that ownership. The approach discussed in class was to drop the word "anti-aging." The subtext of that phrase is: I'm getting old, something is wrong with me. Marketing, product and packaging have to speak in the same tone. And knowing your customer isn't checking a dataset. Checking looks at numbers. Knowing means getting into her emotions and mindset. The moment a customer senses the slightest condescension, it's over. My notes also mention implicit bias. Men and women both have it — the kind that, in the past, didn't take women's words seriously. I gave myself homework: take Mahzarin Banaji's test, and also look at myself — am I actually listening? Condescension often starts with not listening. If the relationship is still condescending, then even with a new slogan, the one speaking is still the master. Function on the left, loyalty on the right In class we used Kevin Lane Keller's brand pyramid and its four questions. Who are you? This layer is salience: being remembered. What are you? There are two ways to answer. Performance, the way BMW answers "how do I drive?" Imagery, which answers "who am I with?" What about you? Performance leads to judgements; imagery leads to feelings. What about you and me? At the top is resonance. Whether the relationship is still there, whether loyalty is still there — it all lives at this layer. The left side is functional and rational; mass markets lean this way. The right side is emotional; premium brands lean that way. You have to get to both in the end. The left is easier: if you really are better than the alternatives and stand up functionally, the road is open. The right is harder, and holds on to people better. That loyalty is reassurance, being able to sleep at night. The people buying it are often buying for their children, for their grandchildren. Someone asked whether business customers, at least, are functional. The professor's answer was short: that's emotional too. What they want is safety, calm. My own reading goes half a step further: function gets someone to buy the first time. Reassurance is what makes them stay, and want to hand it on to the next generation. The jar, search and the counter say the same thing Before class, my piece stopped at a multiple-choice question. What class added was how a promise becomes something you can touch. She's searching for retinol. Competitors all use it. The way to stand out is Retinol 24: working around the clock, twenty-four hours. Those words on the jar should be printed as big as OLAY. Find out what she's looking for first, then decide what to print. Texture is a promise too. The cream is whipped, not greasy. People in the organisation were brought face to face with customers. Department stores used to have beauty advisers. Once they were gone, Olay Skin Advisor took over: one photo, one questionnaire, an answer to "what's right for me." It's a web page, not an app you have to download first. Meet her when she's ready. Take search back into your own hands. Have direct contact with customers. The digital moves didn't sprawl. What the professor wanted was a common language inside the organisation. Transparency is today's rule. What could once be hidden can't be hidden now. One thing. Make the promise, then keep it. Fewer means the jar, the search results and the counter all saying the same thing. A brand is the one sentence you promise your customer The professor asked us to tell the person next to us: what's your brand promise? My neighbour, Sam Vu, said: Make sure you win. Employees win, partners win, you win financially, and you win emotionally too. What I asked myself were two closer questions. What does Arcus42 promise? What do I promise? Earlier I'd used a phrase to describe my relationship with clients: Reflective Ally, an ally side by side. The brand had also been placed somewhere very high. This class separated those two things. High can mean the resonance on the right side of Keller's pyramid. High can also mean "I know better than you." Clients can tell the difference. Marketing, delivery and the tone in the meeting have to be the same relationship. The moment a client senses the slightest condescension, even the loftiest brand line is void. In Closing "Fewer and clearer" — that vote still stands. What got moved was slicing people up by age alone. What I newly saw was the relationship. Brands no longer own customers. The promise can change. Condescension can't stay.

Unit 3, still Professor Das Narayandas's Market-Facing Functions. This time the reading is Bajaj Finance: Building an Omnipresent Financial Services Firm. Olay was a brand taking itself apart. Belden was reassembling parts into solutions while profits were still rising. Bajaj Finance has already done the assembling — more than fifty products, more than fifty million customers; the case calls it India's largest consumer finance company. In August 2021, it has to decide what comes next: dig deeper into its existing customers' wallets, or race Amazon to open shop in India's smaller towns. I wrote this before class. I'm putting my judgement down here first, and I'll come back to check it against the discussion afterwards. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary August 2021 , Pune, a stormy day. Sanjiv Bajaj (HBS MBA 1997) and managing director Rajeev Jain are sitting in a conference room. Bajaj Finance — BFL from here on — has US$21.2 billion in assets under management and 50.5 million customers. They want to turn a company that sells loans through stores into one that is "omnipresent": loans, services, and the consumer durables, insurance and investments embedded in them, with online and offline forming a single journey. There are two camps in the room. One wants to go deeper with existing customers. The processes and people are already in place, and the capital expenditure is modest. The other wants to go to smaller towns. Bajaj's worry is this: the middle class there is growing, and neither brands nor consumer finance have arrived yet. If they move a step too slowly, Amazon will leapfrog them with a financial services platform and catch those hundreds of millions of people. Amazon has already invested US$6.5 billion in India, has 140 million users, and plans to add another 100 million from small towns. It calls itself "Earth's most customer-centric company." The story begins in 1987. Back then it was called Bajaj Auto Finance, a subsidiary of Bajaj Auto. The Bajaj Group's flagship makes two-wheelers; its founder, Jamnalal Bajaj, was Gandhi's adopted son. At first it only lent to people buying Bajaj vehicles. After India opened its economy in 1991, global goods poured in. The new middle class wanted to buy them, but inflation meant they couldn't afford them all. There was no credit bureau, and banks only lent to people who could show proof of income. Salaried workers had it; the huge number of people in informal employment did not. Companies like GE Countrywide filled the gap: a small interest-free loan of about US$350 to buy a fridge, a TV, an air conditioner. On the day, you paid a small processing fee and a token down payment, and cleared the rest over 8 to 12 months. Retailers got their money within one to two weeks. Manufacturers were willing to pay a subvention of 5% to 6% of the loan amount, reckoning it was cheaper than discounting all year round. BAF followed suit and spread to more than 500 towns. Every branch ran its own system and sent its data back to headquarters on CDs once a month, with the paper files couriered separately for data entry. Later, competitors started sharing the subvention with retailers; BAF's margins were squeezed thin, and it had no choice but to share too. In 2007, the business was spun off , with Sanjiv Bajaj in charge, and in 2010 it was formally named BFL. He had little finance experience. Beside him was his uncle Nanoo Pamnani, who had just stepped down as chairman of Citibank Asia, and they brought in Jain, who had done consumer finance at GE, Amex and AIG. Their first bet was consumer durables loans. As Devang Mody later put it, this was the only category where you could acquire millions of customers without spending a single dollar — riding on footfall that retailers and manufacturers were already paying for. But at the time the business was losing money. Competitors approved loans the same day; BFL took 3 to 5 days. The loans were small and short-term, customer acquisition costs were high, and the subvention still had to be shared with retailers. The company had no unified software; information sat in silos, and credit risk was impossible to keep an eye on. Non-performing assets reached 15%, three times the industry level. Nobody in the group wanted to do this thin-margin business. Lending against Bajaj vehicles was far easier. They did it anyway, with a project called WOW that brought approval time down to 3 hours. In Bajaj's own words: If parents can tell their children that the TV they bought today will be installed the same day, we create enormous delight, and word of mouth will carry itself forward. Change the experience, and you change the boundaries of the game. Field credit officers reviewed documents in the store and approved on the spot. Alternatively, store staff phoned a call centre and a rules engine decided yes or no. By March 2008 they were doing 621,000 consumer durables loans a year through 19,000 dealers. Then the financial crisis hit. Net NPAs rose to 7% of assets. They had neither the technology nor the people for collections. Peers exited in droves. Bajaj, Jain and Pamnani did not. They shut 330 locations, dropped 14,500 dealers, laid off several hundred people, stopped sharing the subvention with retailers, and ended personal computer loans — some people took the computer, sold it on the black market, and vanished. Mody remembers Pamnani saying that if things didn't improve, the business would be shut down. Only once the books were clean did they start building a different kind of company. They were just getting started; they couldn't afford a price war, and they couldn't win on scale either. As Bajaj put it, no insurance policy or loan contract can be so beautiful that people will pay 10% more for it. Non-banks can't take current-account deposits, so their funding is expensive. So they took a different road: draw on the trust built up by Bajaj scooters and motorcycles, offer the middle class a full suite from loans to protection to investment, and lead with technology. First use data to establish a person's credit, then sell them the next thing that suits them, building a 360-degree relationship. Very few non-banks were doing this. Tata's finance company was happy to lend to its own suppliers; Chola was content with truck financing. BFL was the smallest horse in the group stable, so whatever it did didn't much matter, and with Pamnani there, the board was at ease. There were two rules. One: build a Mercedes, not a Ferrari, and not a Ford — every new line of business had to be big enough to be worth doing properly. The other was Pamnani's: try anything, but don't develop hobbies. The first new businesses were unsecured personal loans and small business loans. Without a banking licence they couldn't issue credit cards, so this was the substitute. Later came the EMI card: a pre-approved limit for existing customers that turned into a loan with one swipe at thousands of outlets, starting from about 5,000 rupees. The product range gradually grew to more than 50. Jain said they would take care of retail and SME customers' needs from birth to death, except current accounts and car loans. They were expanding geographically too. Branches in the big cities, franchises in small places; franchisees shared sales, marketing and service costs on a variable basis, so pushing into ever smaller locations wouldn't immediately wreck breakeven. For big retailers stocking up for festivals, they offered trade advances that could be offset. And there was a famous early scheme: cutting the down payment from the usual 33% of the product price to 1 rupee. At one large retailer in South India, 2,000 people showed up on the first weekend. Manufacturers such as LG put BFL's name in their own advertising. People who came in for a 32-inch TV walked out with a 43-inch; people who came to look at a single-door fridge left with a double-door. The customer strategy was clear. About 30% of each year's new customers were getting credit for the first time, mostly in smaller, newer markets — places where nobody else was yet. Buying a phone or an appliance in a store, you could get a zero-interest loan within minutes on basic documents. The case notes that even people who could afford to pay in full didn't mind taking the zero-interest loan. Alongside the loan came an extended warranty, which Panchal likened to jam on bread. Once customers were in, data drove the cross-selling. In Jain's words: Cross-selling is the holy grail. The dumbest thing an ROE-focused company can do is pay twice for the same customer. For most people, the second product was the EMI card. For those who had only ever been able to borrow from informal moneylenders, it was often their only card. Only technology could carry the complexity. Partners supplied the software and hardware — what Bajaj called the arms and legs; the processes and approval rules were written in-house — what he called the brain. A cloud-based loan origination system adapted from a CRM had the rules built in. Retailers were initially reluctant to provide their own computers and internet connections, but once they found that waiting times were shorter and customers less likely to change their minds, more than 3,000 signed up within a year. On Diwali itself, 300,000 applications would come in; if the point-of-sale system went down for 5 minutes, the internal portal lit up red. In 2015, Jain required that data from every system and business be pulled into a single enterprise data warehouse. Handing over customer data was seen by some as handing over the crown jewels. The resistance wasn't loud — management was either new or already knew the old way didn't work. Those who said "our market is different" were invited to go work for a competitor; Mody says nobody left. Data was aggregated daily rather than monthly, structured data into the warehouse, unstructured into a data lake, stitched together into a 360-degree view of each customer. Sharing didn't run on slogans. A business unit using another unit's customer data had to pay the source an internal transfer fee. Consumer durables and mobile financing contributed 90% of the customers, and 35% of their own profit came from these fees. Organisationally, each product was a business unit run by a mini-CEO, accountable for profit, sales, risk and people; only technology and operations had to be shared. New businesses had to double every year. Mature businesses had to grow at least 20%; if they couldn't, they were fixed, and if that failed, shut down. Infrastructure lending was shut down, because whether customers could repay depended on when the government released funds — nothing to do with the core capability of "financing an individual's discretionary consumption." Field and call-centre life insurance sales were stopped too. Operations were turned into a science. Panchal says they had 10,000 metrics in all. Every Tuesday at 8 a.m., Pamnani would arrive in Pune from Mumbai, and anyone walking in at 8:01 would run into his temper. Risk was separated from day-to-day approvals, and collections were also held accountable for losses. Customers with a home loan defaulted at roughly a quarter of the rate of everyone else. A retailer's approval rate adjusted automatically according to how its past customers had defaulted, and it was made public — so dealers, wanting bigger and faster approvals, would bring better customers to the counter on their own. When a cheque bounced, they got in touch immediately, while the customer still felt a little embarrassed. Processes were being trimmed, too. Processing a 10 million rupee SME loan secured against property once cost 45,000 rupees, about US$610. Jain asked for it to be halved; the team cut it to 8,000 rupees, about US$110. On the consumer loan side, the cost came down from 1,200 rupees to 800. By 2019, the report card looked great, and the weather was changing. In rupee terms, over fourteen years AUM grew at a compound rate of 37%, profit after tax at 51%, and operating expenses at 29%; expenses as a share of net interest income fell from 58% to around 31%. Net NPAs were brought down to 0.12% in FY2012; the overdue threshold for classification was later tightened from 6 months to 3, and in FY2021 the figure was still 0.75%. In Exhibit 8, the net interest margin is 13.9%, against roughly 4% for banks. Market capitalisation was US$42.4 billion, with loans outstanding of about US$15.8 billion. The competition had changed. Banks, with their low-cost funds, were offering instant loans and zero-interest instalments on e-commerce platforms. More than two thousand fintechs had raised venture capital. Paytm had spread from payments into other financial services. Amazon was India's second-largest e-commerce player, with a 36% share, 140 million monthly active users, and 2 million Pay Later customers. The buy-now-pay-later market was expected to reach US$40 billion by 2026. Small towns were getting richer. Between 2016 and 2025, the number of affluent households with annual income above US$15,400 in emerging cities of under a million people was projected to grow 2.5 times, versus 2 times in the metros. 40% of phone purchases were unplanned. By 2023, 63% of consumer durables sales were expected to be digitally influenced. When buying these things online, 90% of people preferred aggregator platforms. Panchal said the new generation will only buy online, so we have to be online in order to survive. There was also an internal worry: revenue and expenses were both growing in a straight line, and if this continued, expenses would overtake revenue. Historically, expenses had in fact grown more slowly than revenue. What they feared was the next chapter — that the physical-network route was about to lose the operating leverage it had had in the past. In November 2019, they wrote down the "omnipresent" framework. A few months later, the pandemic arrived. Jain called in the top 100 leaders and said: after the pandemic the economy will shrink, and we will get smaller too, but we are not organised for that smaller size. Imagine you have US$1 billion of capital, and tell me how you would rebuild your department. He later recalled that everyone knew the answer was to accelerate digitisation and become a consumer-centric company. BFL handled 30% of India's electronics and 15% of its smartphones. Going online could give its own merchants a path that didn't depend entirely on Amazon, while building up data for lending. They mapped every offline process, deleted the steps that added no value, and then put them into the app. The people designing the interface sat inside the businesses, because ideas grow out of the business. A customer who left halfway through in any channel could pick up where they left off in the same channel or a different one. The marketplace had more than a million products, zero-interest loans and 24-hour delivery. Shopping, bill payments, travel and cashback were there to make people open the app again and again. Which brings us back to the question in the conference room. 1. The 50.5 million existing customers hold 45% of India's outstanding mortgages, 65% of its credit cards, and US$100 billion in personal loans. BFL captures only about 10% of their wallet. Going deeper requires almost no new capex. 2. They still need to add 6 to 7 million new customers a year. Appliances are replaced slowly, and cross-selling can't make up that growth. Without new geographies, competitors will catch up. 3. Distribution covers only 62% of Indian households; the other 38% have never been touched. The app could become a partner for small-town retailers facing e-commerce. But there is little credit history there, more reliance on franchisees, service will be uneven, and customers unfamiliar with formal repayment may bring higher defaults. Bajaj says they have a history of reinventing themselves in the face of adversity. This time, the opponent is Amazon. My Thinking You can compete with Amazon — as long as you don't try to become a second Amazon Yes, it can compete. But the layer it competes on is the credit decision and repayment, not the shelf. In 2020, e-commerce was only 5.8% of Indian retail, and Amazon held 36% of that e-commerce layer. Multiply them and you get about 2% of all retail. BFL stands at the other end: the store, the approval, the collection. It handles 30% of electronics and 15% of smartphones, with 50.5 million customers; Amazon Pay Later had 2 million at the time. A net interest margin of 13.9%, against around 4% for banks. That's the moat — and also the target everyone is aiming at. Non-banks can't get current-account deposits. Amazon can use its e-commerce profits to subsidise buy-now-pay-later. Fighting a price war with a 13.9% margin would mean blowing yourself apart. So my choice is to take both roads, with the order fixed in stone, and to explicitly not take a third. First, guard the moment of purchase. An application half-filled in a store must be continuable in the app. Someone already standing at the counter shouldn't end up finishing their next purchase on somebody else's phone. Then treat the 10% wallet share as profit, not as a substitute for growth. Cross-sellable customers grew only from 24.1 million to 27.4 million in two years, while new customers come in at 6 to 7 million a year. Nobody buys a fridge every quarter. Panchal says using cross-selling to replace new customers is "easier said than done," and I agree. The 38% of uncovered households have to be reached. But go there carrying the approval rules already proven in the cities, not the enthusiasm of franchisees. In June 2021, about 70% of rural locations were franchises. In 2008 they shut 330 locations and dropped 14,500 dealers to bring net NPAs from 7% down to 0.12%. There's no need to pay that tuition again. Until defaults on franchisee-originated loans line up with those of company-owned branches, their limits should be capped. Shopping, bill payments and travel should serve only as reasons to open the app. Of people buying appliances online, 52% are after a lower price and 46% after convenience. The case also says that 90% of consumers prefer aggregator platforms over a brand's own app. A price war will be lost. What can win is "zero interest, next-day delivery, a warranty" — and only on the purchase that needs financing. The moment the marketplace becomes another Amazon, BFL is competing for business with its own 114,000 retail partners. Amazon is buying the next time you open the app. What BFL has to protect is that the door is still there the next time you want to borrow. I accept the cost of this choice: some towns will be reached a year later. In FY2021, provisions rose from US$519 million the year before to US$816 million, and return on equity fell from 20.2% to 12.8%. In FY2019 it had still been 22.5%. What blew a hole in that year was credit cost, not expenses. Slow is better than paying for this lesson a second time. My own inclination: if I'm forced into an either-or in class, I'll pick "wallet first, then small towns," not "only dig into existing customers." Halting the 6 million new customers a year is handing the next town to whoever shows up first on people's phones. The year digitisation really began was 2015, when the data came back to the company The app is the final chapter. Before it come seven decisions, and next to each one is a pit. Clean up the books first, then talk about scale. Expanding with net NPAs at 7% means diluting bad debt with growth. They did the reverse, cutting urban consumer durables stores from 19,000 to 2,000, then rebuilding bit by bit to 26,900. That cut was strategy, not a clean-up. Change the game to same-day delight, not lower prices. Three to five days brought down to 3 hours. The pit next to speed is having no rules — bad debt was at one point three times the industry level. The rules were later put into software; change one, and it takes effect across every location. Only do what's big enough to be worth doing, and shut the rest. Fifty products sounds like Olay. The difference is that things get shut down: infrastructure lending exited, life insurance sales that couldn't take off were stopped, new businesses double, mature ones grow at least 20%. Pamnani's "don't develop hobbies" is product strategy, not a description of personality. In 2015, customer data was defined as belonging to the company, not as a department's crown jewels. An order alone wasn't enough. Business units using others' customers had to pay a transfer fee, and the source — consumer durables and mobile financing, which brought in 90% of the customers — got 35% of its profit from it. Sharing became revenue, and people were willing to hand things over. The arms and legs can be outsourced; the brain stays in-house. Approval rules and process design don't go into a vendor's black box — nor do they build every system themselves. Approval, risk and collections are split into three jobs, with the latter two jointly bearing losses. Retailers can see their own approval rates. When the rate drops, they bring in better customers on their own. Control doesn't have to sit at headquarters. Only last comes 2019. During the pandemic, those 100 people were asked to rethink their departments for "a smaller economy and US$1 billion of capital." The head of technology admitted they had always been B2B and had hardly built a consumer-facing layer at all. The processes were mapped first, the steps that added no value deleted, and only then did it all go into the app. The people building the interface sat inside the business. What they avoided weren't technology pits, but incentive pits. Handing over data earned you money, bad debt couldn't be hidden, and businesses that didn't work couldn't survive. There were also three kinds of grown-ups in the room: an owner, a person who had spent a lifetime lending, and an operator. And a scar. A company that has seen 15% bad debt doesn't put risk in an appendix. My own reading is that many companies understand "digitisation" as a launch date. If BFL could only remember one date, it should be the year the data came back to the company, not the year customers could download the app. Without that earlier step, the app just moves the silos online. This is a company that deeply understands the moment of purchase — but not yet a customer-centric company At the moment of purchase, they are serious. Parents want the TV on the wall the same day. People who aren't in a hurry for cash want good service, so salaried loans can keep the algorithm in the back office while the front desk still approves. One rupee brings people through the door, and it's the customers themselves who push up the basket size. The organisation, though, runs on a different logic. Each product has a mini-CEO. Cross-selling is pushed by a separate, heavily incentivised team, with risk pre-approved. An existing customer can't walk up to this team on their own and ask for another loan. The company decides when a customer is allowed to buy more. After the pandemic, Jain said the answer was to accelerate digitisation and "become" a consumer-centric company. If you're becoming one, you weren't one when you set out. The head of technology said it more bluntly: they did B2B for many years and never seriously built the consumer-facing layer. That line, "don't pay twice for the same customer," is a sentence about acquisition cost. Here, the customer is an asset. And the asset is very well managed. My own view is that customer-centricity isn't about making the experience smooth. Smooth they've already achieved. Customer-centricity is when the customer can walk into the next product on their own, rather than waiting for a team they can't reach to push it to them. Amazon describes itself as "most customer-centric." BFL describes its ambition as "omnipresent" and manages itself by ROE. Both statements are true. They are not the same statement. Loyalty stops at zero interest and that card The EMI card does bring real repeat purchases. For people who can't get a bank card, it's the only door. People come back to a door that doesn't exist anywhere else. That's loyalty through access. Zero interest is another matter. People who can afford to pay in full take it anyway. While the terms are there, the people are there. When another counter writes the same zero-interest offer, people no longer need to be. The wallet tells the rest of the story. These customers hold 45% of India's mortgages, 65% of its credit cards and US$100 billion in personal loans, and BFL accounts for only about 10%. Home finance is just 12% of its own loan book. That 45% of mortgages wasn't lent by BFL. Where customers truly have a choice, nine rupees out of ten go elsewhere. Then look at the pace. Six to seven million new customers a year, yet the cross-sell pool grew by only about 3.3 million in two years. About 30% of new customers are first-time credit users. This is a superb customer acquisition machine. A business compounding on loyalty wouldn't need this many strangers to keep growing. People repeat something that's convenient and unavailable elsewhere. Once the convenience is available elsewhere, the repeating stops. The TV goes up on the wall the same day, and the delight is real. After the delight settles, it will be a long time before this company is needed again. Bill payments and travel are there to fill that gap. Fill it clumsily and it becomes a hobby; don't fill it, and the next time the customer wants to buy something, they open somebody else's app. Get one ledger in order close to home before talking about being everywhere If I could take only one thing away from this case, it would be the sequence. Close to home: first consolidate each customer into a single ledger, and make sure the people who hand over that ledger get credit for it. BFL had the warehouse and the transfer fees first, and the app afterwards. Do it in reverse, and digitisation just asks the same questions again, faster. In the middle: map the process first, delete the steps that don't change any decision, then write the system. Split speed and standards into two jobs, and make both accountable for losses. Before starting anything new, write down the criteria for shutting it down, and give it a date. A rule without a date never happens. Further out: being everywhere isn't an app with more goods hanging on it. It's still being there the next time someone truly needs you. For a consumer durables finance company, the next time might be years away. The same goes for any business with a long natural cycle: if frequency isn't designed, the relationship will go dormant on its own. When competing with a platform, hold on to the judgement it can't yet make. BFL's judgement is: if this person borrows, will they pay it back? The shelf, logistics, whose price is lower — that's a battlefield someone else already holds. My own inclination is to treat "customer numbers are rising" as a figure that needs correcting by wallet share. The 50.5 million is real. So is the 10%. A company that reports only the first number will think it already owns these customers. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading Bajaj, what came to mind wasn't lending in India, but something more ordinary: we too are very good at bringing someone through the door, and then assuming they'll stay. First, the interface is the last step; the file is the first. If the facts about a client are still scattered across different people, different spreadsheets, different conversations, building a new entry point just moves the scattering online. First consolidate it into one file, assign an owner, and make it possible for a second person to explain this family clearly without gathering everything again. If we can't do that, the "omnipresence" that follows has nothing at its core. Second, whoever hands over a client must get credit for it. BFL didn't tear down departmental walls with speeches. Departments using others' customer data had to pay, so the source was willing to keep acquiring customers. Inside a company, whoever builds the trust should still be visible when the next piece of work is done by someone else. Otherwise everyone will keep a ledger that belongs only to them. Third, move fast, but don't let standards loosen along with the pace. Three-hour approvals didn't slide back to 15% bad debt because the rules were in a different group's hands, and losses were shared. The relationship can move quickly. The threshold for judgement doesn't drop because the other side is in a hurry, or because we want to close. The threshold is best made public, so people further up the line can screen themselves, rather than being turned down at the very end. Fourth, the time between meetings has to be designed; you can't count on the transaction itself to keep people. Zero interest brings people through the door. Behind the door is a long gap. A family office's natural cycle is even longer: an inheritance, a liquidity event, the next generation coming in. If we only show up at those moments, we are that zero-interest loan: there when the terms are good, gone when the terms aren't the only thing that matters. Frequency should come from the work itself — reviews, governance, the next generation in the room — not from bolting on more features unrelated to the core business. Fifth, don't copy the platform's shelf in order to compete with the platform. The moment BFL turns its marketplace into another Amazon, it loses both its margin and its retail partners. Our reason for people to stay should be that the judgement, the records and the trust are here, that the product serves a family's own allocation — not that we happen to offer every item on somebody else's menu as well. A longer menu is not presence. Final Thoughts The pre-class me most agrees with this line: "What you win is the moment of the sale; what lies empty is the space between two sales." After
Leadership Case: Cynthia Carroll at Anglo American
When everything has been said, only a decision that costs you something is believed, even shutting down your own mine

The third case of Unit 3 moves over to Professor Jeff Polzer's Leadership course, and the reading is Cynthia Carroll at Anglo American (A). Olay was the story of a brand taking itself apart; Belden was a company rebuilding itself just when its numbers looked best. Carroll's story is harder-edged — a CEO four months into the job, sitting in a helicopter, hears that a 29th person that year has died in her mines, and then has to decide whether to do something no one in the industry has ever done. I wrote this before class. I'm putting my judgement down here first, and I'll come back to check it against the discussion afterwards. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary On June 27, 2007 , Cynthia Carroll flew back to Johannesburg from the platinum mines at Rustenburg, South Africa. When she landed, Ralph Havenstein, CEO of Anglo American Platinum, pulled her aside: "I have some bad news. Another person has died." It was the 29th that year. From 2002 to 2006, an average of 46 Anglo American miners a year were killed in accidents. In the previous few weeks, five people had died in three accidents at Rustenburg alone — three buried by an inrush of mud, one thrown from a conveyor belt, one struck by a blasting barricade. And the case goes out of its way to add one line: Anglo's South African mines were no worse than those of other South African mining companies, and their safety had been improving noticeably in recent years. Where Anglo American came from : founded in South Africa in 1917 by Ernest Oppenheimer, with J.P. Morgan among its backers, it got its start in gold, diamonds and platinum. Economic sanctions and exchange controls during apartheid forced it to buy up a pile of unrelated businesses at home — steel, timber, consumer goods — and by the 1990s it controlled roughly a quarter of the market value of the South African stock exchange. In 1999 it moved its headquarters and primary listing to London. By the end of 2006 it was the world's fourth-largest mining company by market value, with revenue of nearly US$25 billion and 162,000 employees, two-thirds of them in South Africa. Forty percent of the world's platinum came from here. Who Carroll is : a geologist by training, she worked as a petroleum geologist at Amoco, then joined Alcan after graduating from Harvard Business School in 1989. The case goes into her three stints at Alcan in detail: She took over a foil plant with US$29 million in annual revenue. A major customer responsible for a third of its profit wanted to cut its four suppliers down to one, and it was closer to another supplier. Her team said, "Nothing we can do — let's find other business." She said "No way" — and within two years she had quadrupled output and won the exclusive contract. Four years later the plant's revenue was US$79 million, and a year after that US$105 million. When she ran an alumina refinery in Ireland, new EU and Irish environmental tax rules threatened the plant's survival, and the company's lawyers said a public fight like that could not be won. Eight months pregnant, she was on the front pages of the newspapers every day — "People threatened me; everyone said all we could do was go along with it" — and in the end she turned the whole thing around. From 2002 she ran Alcan's primary metal group, which made up 75% of the company's operating income; it posted the highest profits in the company's history, and lost-time injuries improved by more than 80%. She once summed herself up this way: "You do what you believe in. You can be influenced in all sorts of ways, but if you think it's right — even if you're the only one who sees it that way — in the end, you do it." How she came to Anglo : at Davos in 2006, she saw a silver-haired man eating breakfast alone and asked whether she could join him. He was Mark Moody-Stuart, chairman of Anglo American. They talked about geology, Oman, South Africa and AIDS. Later, when Anglo went looking for a CEO, her name appeared on the shortlist. After meeting her, board member Mamphela Ramphele said: "Before I met her, I worried she wouldn't be tough enough to handle our environment. She is tough enough." In March 2007 she became the first non–South African and the first woman to be CEO of the 90-year-old company. What she inherited : a federation. Each business unit ran its own show. In Australia she asked the heads of the mining businesses how often they met, and was told: "We don't meet." One executive described it like this: "The heads of the businesses are like tribal chiefs. Ask them to do something on safety or talent and they'll tell you to get lost." In a commodity bull market, the share price had lagged BHP and the sector. Citigroup estimated the company could cut US$560 million to US$1.1 billion in costs. The board gave her one more assignment: repair a strained relationship with the South African government. As for safety, the board's exact words were: "It has already improved, but you might want to pay attention to it." The South African context : apartheid was legislated in 1948 and ended only in 1994. Mining had always meant white men managing and Black men going underground. Over more than a century, the mines evolved a language called Fanagalo — simplified Zulu and Xhosa mixed with English, Dutch and Portuguese, about 2,000 words, most of them commands. A Black South African told Moody-Stuart: "Mark, you have to understand, this language is fundamentally in the imperative. The conversation goes one way — from supervisor to worker." Someone at the union Solidarity described Anglo Platinum's management style as "strongly hierarchical, autocratic. Employees cannot question management's decisions. When a general manager comes back from the mine, all he talks about are financial and production targets. The human factor is almost never mentioned." On safety : Moody-Stuart said that great progress had already been made in reducing risk through technology; what remained were "low-tech accidents" — and the prevailing attitude in South Africa at the time was: "The people who got hurt took shortcuts and broke the rules; they were stupid. That's just how it is." On her first tour after taking over, Carroll talked to one executive about "zero harm," and he replied: "Cynthia, that won't happen in our lifetime." Another executive said the industry saw mining as "a man's undertaking, like going to war." The numbers: between 1900 and 1993, 69,000 miners died in South African mining accidents. In 1996, 463 died, and the government passed the Mine Health and Safety Act, whose Section 54 gave inspectors the power to shut mines down. In 2003 the industry held a summit and pledged to cut deaths by 20% a year — by 2007 it was 20% to 25% behind that target. When Carroll took office, a miner in South Africa died in a workplace accident every 44 hours. Rustenburg : the highest-risk of Anglo Platinum's seven mines. Nine shafts, up to 1.5 kilometres deep, extending another three to four kilometres horizontally — workers at the rock face could be as far as 5.5 kilometres from the surface. The ore reef was only a metre thick, so workers spent their days in a space a metre high. One tonne of ore yields 3 grams of platinum; a single platinum ring takes 280 tonnes of rock. 30,000 workers, with an illiteracy rate of about 70%. It generated around US$8 million in revenue a day and 35% of Anglo Platinum's steady-state profit — and Anglo Platinum in turn made up 23% of the group's operating profit. In the first seven months of 2007, 16 of Anglo's 29 deaths happened here. The exhibits contain an even more uncomfortable number: Rustenburg's lost-time injury rate rose from 1.84 in 2006 to 2.28 in 2007. Senior management was already "on board"; the resistance was in the middle. "The people most resistant to change are our front-line supervisors." There is one more technical detail, and it is the strongest argument against shutting the mine: once a deep shaft sits idle, it can actually become more dangerous — the rock keeps shifting even when no one is watching it. Carroll's reaction : "This organisation is out of control. I will not support operations that are killing people." She was even considering shutting the mine — something no company in the industry had ever done. The case stops there. The professor gave us two questions: 1. What should she do about the safety problem at Rustenburg? 2. To achieve "zero harm" across all 160,000 people at Anglo American, taking every stakeholder into account, what should she do? My Thinking The most dangerous kind of "normal" is the kind no one has tested in ninety years The most unsettling thing in the case isn't the number 29. It's the line "Anglo was no worse than other South African mining companies." That line is true. It is also the whole problem. When something happens every day and goes on for ninety years — 69,000 people — it stops looking like a decision and starts looking like geology. No one "decided" to let miners die; everyone simply accepted a baseline and then worked hard to improve on it. The 2003 summit was exactly that kind of effort: cut deaths 20% a year. It sounds ambitious, but its premise is that the people who died this year are the starting point. To accept the baseline is to accept the deaths that come with it. And the counter-evidence was always just outside the room. Mines in Australia, Canada and the United States have far lower death rates. Same mining, same rock, same gravity. The executive who said "not in our lifetime" wasn't lying; he had just never been asked to test that judgement — and for ninety years no one had asked. My own reading is that a leader's first move often isn't to set a new target, but to take something that has been treated as "geology" and turn it back into a "decision." That is exactly what Carroll did: she refused to accept "no worse than our peers" as the starting point. When everything has been said, only a decision that costs you something is believed My answer to the first question: stop. Shut all nine shafts, now — and shut them herself. The reasoning isn't complicated. Every gentle approach had already been tried. The processes were in place, the board said; the attitude wasn't, the board also said. The industry had made a pledge and missed it. At the shareholders' meeting in April she had already said "these deaths and injuries are unacceptable," and two months later several more people had died. A CEO four months into the job giving one more speech would just be adding one more sentence in a language that only speaks downward. Shutting the mine is different. Rustenburg brings in US$8 million a day, its fixed costs are high, and the losses from stopping "fall straight to the bottom line." Roughly US$56 million a week, about US$240 million a month — given that Rustenburg is 35% of Platinum's profit and Platinum is 23% of the group's, a one-month shutdown works out to roughly 2.4% of the group's annual operating profit. It hurts, but it won't kill you. Only a decision that costs money gets believed — it turns "unacceptable" from an adjective into a number everyone understands. There is also a very practical reason: if she doesn't stop it, the government can. That is exactly what Section 54 of the Mine Health and Safety Act is for. A CEO who shuts her own mine holds the narrative; a CEO whose mine is shut by an inspector is just like every other South African mining company. A shutdown isn't the end of a decision; it's the start of a test But if shutting the mine is only a shutdown, it is just an expensive silence. The case lays out the arguments against it honestly, and I think every one of them has to be taken seriously. An idle deep shaft can be more dangerous. So the shutdown has to be short and planned, with core crews kept on for ventilation, drainage and support inspections, and production restarted one shaft at a time, each one signed off against a written standard. 30,000 workers, 70% illiterate, many of them migrant workers paid by the shift. A shutdown without wages is a strike you've called on yourself. The answer on pay has to be ready before the announcement. Havenstein runs a company that is controlled by the group but separately listed. Overruling him four months into the job carries a governance cost. So the sequence should be: tell him first, insist on the outcome, let him carry it out — but the public words must be hers. Then comes the most important point: what the shutdown time is used for. Everyone gets retrained, supervisors first — because the supervisors are both the resistance and the bottleneck. And write down in advance what "the shutdown worked" looks like: months of zero deaths after restart, the lost-time injury rate back below 2006 levels, supervisor turnover, whether conversations have become two-way. Let the numbers say whether this was the right call, not loyalty. My own inclination is that, in the same breath as announcing the shutdown, she should spell out all the costs herself first: output, shareholders, Havenstein's authority, the supervisors who might wait for the storm to blow over. A leader who names the costs before her critics do is much harder to argue with. A shock changes attention; it doesn't change the language If I had to pick one detail from the whole case, it would be Fanagalo. 2,000 words, most of them commands, "fundamentally in the imperative." For a hundred years, South Africa's mines ran on this language. It is very efficient — which is precisely the problem. A language that can only carry commands can't carry a question. When a worker sees a crack in the hanging wall, how does he say in Fanagalo, "I don't think it's safe here — can we stop for a moment?" Moody-Stuart said something I think is the key to the whole case: "Build trust among all the parties, and safety will take care of itself." Technology can solve the high-tech deaths — support, ventilation, monitoring. Behind each of the low-tech deaths that remain — the mud inrush, the conveyor belt, the blasting barricade — is a judgement that was never spoken, or was spoken and no one listened. So the real work after the shutdown is to turn the language around. Give every worker the right to refuse unsafe work, protected from retaliation, and require supervisors to report how many times that right was used — if the number is zero, the right doesn't exist. Train people in their own language: two-thirds of Rustenburg speaks Setswana, not Fanagalo. Add leading indicators to supervisors' evaluations: how many near-misses were reported, whether stop-work calls were respected. The case even contains ready-made proof that this workforce can trust the company: Anglo was the first major employer in Africa to provide free antiretroviral treatment to its employees, and 110,000 people volunteered to be tested. When the company acts first, and visibly, workers believe it. Safety can borrow that trust — and should borrow the method. Zero harm isn't a forecast; it's a stance "Cynthia, that won't happen in our lifetime." I read that line several times. The person who said it was most likely sincere, and on the data he may well have been right. But another executive in the case added something more worth remembering: "You cannot publicly say that any target less than zero harm is acceptable — whether or not it can be achieved." The point of zero isn't whether it can be reached; it's that the moment you accept any non-zero number, you have said how many deaths are OK. That is the difference between a target and a stance. A target can be negotiated, phased in, "cut 20% this year." A stance can't. Carroll's approach — "everyone has the same right to finish a day's work and go home to their family" — is a stance, not a KPI. With one sentence, she is tearing down the ceiling. My own reading is that much of a leader's job is precisely to hold an "impossible" zero. Not out of naivety, but because the moment you give ground on zero, every layer of the organisation gives a little more ground below you. Turn the people who can stop you into people watching the same number as you On the second question — how to reach zero harm across 160,000 people in 40 countries — my answer is a sequence. Structure first, mobilisation second. Anglo is a federation, and the "tribal chiefs" don't meet. There can be no zero harm in a federation. So step one: one safety standard for the whole group, with "fatal risk standards" set for the handful of things that actually kill people — local rules can be stricter, never looser; get the business-unit CEOs into a room every quarter, each reporting their own numbers to their peers — public comparison does what memos can't; and tie her own pay and every business-unit CEO's pay to safety outcomes, not as a small modifier but as a gate. Then replace the first person who doesn't comply and shrugs it off. One visible departure beats ten speeches. Next come her two hardest groups: the unions and the government. They are the ones who can stop her — strikes, and Section 54. And the reason the 2003 summit fell short was that it was a pledge from companies to companies, with no third party keeping watch. Bring the unions and the Department of Minerals in to write the standard together — one target, one scoreboard, published together — and the people who can stop you become people who own the same number as you. Incidentally, the government's own pension fund, the PIC, is also an Anglo shareholder. Finally, the shareholders. Three kinds of them — long-standing South African shareholders who want dividends, London institutions holding it because it's in the FTSE 100, and international investors seeking emerging-market exposure — and not one of them will applaud lost output. Her argument has to be made in the same sentence every time: "Performance follows safety." Then prove it: every death means a stoppage, an investigation, a Section 54 risk, a supervisor lost in a hot labour market, and a question about the licence to operate in a country that already distrusts the industry. Put safety and financials on the same sheet and report them together every quarter. She also has something no one else has: first non–South African, first woman, four months in — she has no history to defend. That lets everyone say "she doesn't understand mining," and it also lets her say things this industry has never said to itself. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading Carroll, what came to mind wasn't mining but the word "normal." First, every industry has its own "no worse than our peers." In mining, it's dozens of deaths a year; in wealth management, it's advice driven by product commissions, accounts that don't know about each other, fees layered on fees. These things have gone on so long they look like geology rather than decisions. The biggest temptation for a new firm is to "improve" on this baseline — a bit more transparent than the peers, a bit cheaper. Carroll's reminder: to accept the baseline is to accept everything that comes with it. Second, a stance needs a visible cost, or it's just a slogan. Shutting the mine at US$8 million a day turned "unacceptable" into a number. For any firm that says it is "on the client's side," the same question applies: what have you given up for that stance, can you put a figure on it, and do you dare tell the client? A promise with no price attached is taken seriously by no one — including the person who made it. Third, zero is a stance; the exception is the ceiling. The value of "zero harm" lies not in whether it can be achieved but in the fact that it leaves no room to give ground. Conflicts of interest work the same way: make one exception for one deal, and every layer of the organisation gives a little more ground below. The zeros worth holding must be held as non-negotiable. Fourth, look at the layer with the most resistance. At Anglo, senior management was already on board and the workers at the rock face had no voice; where the culture actually lived was among front-line supervisors. Whenever an organisation needs to change, first ask: who least wants to change, and holds day-to-day power? The answer is usually neither in the boardroom nor at the very bottom. Fifth, the test of a culture is whether conversation has become two-way. The problem with Fanagalo isn't that it's crude; it's that it can only speak downward. Is the way a service firm talks to families — plans, recommendations, "you should" — also in the imperative? The real test is simple: have our clients ever taught us something back, and did we write it down? Sixth, bring the people who can veto you to the same scoreboard. Carroll had to face the unions and the government; a family office has to face the other members of the family, the family's lawyers and accountants, the incumbent banks. They can block you. Rather than wait for them to block you, let them look at the same numbers you do — the same asset map, the same risk list. The lesson of the 2003 summit: a promise you make to yourself, with no one watching, will fall through. Final Thoughts Before class, the line I agree with most is "Build trust among all the parties, and safety will take care of itself." After class, I'll see which of these got overturned, and by what.
Make the risky leap from selling parts to selling solutions while profits are still rising

The second case of Unit 3, again in Professor Das Narayandas's Market-Facing Functions: Belden and Digital Transformation: From Product Sales to Solutions Sales. Olay was the story of a brand taking itself apart. Belden is the opposite — a company that has sold cable for 120 years and wants, at the very moment business is best, to put itself back together: to stop selling parts and start selling outcomes. In Capital , Marx called the conversion of a commodity into money a "salto mortale," a perilous leap. What makes Belden's leap perilous is that, at take-off, the ice under its feet is still solid. I wrote this one before class too. I'm putting my judgements down here and will come back to check them after the session. Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary November 2022. Ashish Chand, head of Belden's Industrial Automation business, is sitting on a pile of good news: the division's revenue and EBITDA have both beaten budget, and the five-year plan is ahead of schedule. But three things are weighing on him — a dispute with a French distributor, a procurement deadlock with an American metro customer, and US$26 million in budget that has to go either to sales or to R&D. Where Belden comes from : founded in Chicago in 1902, it makes wire, cable, connectors and switches. By 2019 it had 10,000 employees, factories in 13 countries, US$2.1 billion in annual revenue, and a customer list that included BMW, Disney, ExxonMobil, General Motors, Goldman Sachs and Hilton. Its way of growing was textbook: since 2007 it had acquired 16 companies and accumulated 15 brands. The acquired sales teams kept selling their original brands — the Hirschmann people were still selling Hirschmann; the acquired distributors kept their original distribution rights — some could sell only one brand, some several. The 15 brands had never been assembled into "one Belden." How much IA matters : nearly half of Belden's revenue and 54% of its EBITDA. 3,735 people, 281 of them in sales. Inside were 9 product-based business units, each with its own P&L, setting its own prices, its own margins and its own strategy. The old way of selling , in one sentence: you take a product list to meet someone holding a purchase list. The buyers were plant maintenance supervisors, purchasing managers and project managers. They had an equipment list and a target price, and they decided based on immediate technical needs and budget. The sales process had five steps and a deal could close in a week. Pricing was cost-plus. Bonuses were based only on revenue, booked at shipment; profit wasn't part of the evaluation. Meanwhile, IT vendors like Cisco and IBM were meeting the CIO, CTO and CEO at the same customers, talking about "what your data can do." In Chand's own words: "IT vendors are talking to our customers' CIOs and CTOs about the possibilities of data, while we are being relegated to component suppliers." The melting iceberg. The phrase comes from John Kotter's fable Our Iceberg Is Melting — a colony of penguins discovers that the iceberg they have lived on for generations is melting from below. Chand used it to describe IA's situation: OT hardware was commoditising and margins were falling; IT and OT were converging into "Industry 4.0," a market expected to grow from US$102 billion in 2020 to US$337 billion in 2028; value was shifting from "the wire" to "the data"; and Belden's growth in recent years had come mainly from buying companies, not from growing on its own. In 2019 he launched the transformation, renamed the division Industrial Automation Solutions (IAS), and called the first step ESD — Enhanced Solutions Delivery. What ESD changed : It picked 7 sub-industries and sized the addressable and serviceable market for each. Rail transit was the largest, with a serviceable market of US$504 million; consumer packaged goods (CPG) was piloted first. The 9 P&Ls were merged into 2, and in July 2022 into 1. The direct sales force was reorganised from regions and products to industries. Pricing authority moved from the product groups to sales. Account managers were upgraded to "solutions account managers" (SAMs), and two new roles were created: digital automation consultants (mostly former plant managers, US$230,000 a year in cost) and solutions consultants (Industry 4.0 technology experts, US$190,000). In the first phase they hired 7 of the former and 51 of the latter. The sales process went from 5 steps to 8, with each item checked against a MEDDICC scorecard: metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, identified pain, champion, competition. A deal took at least 6 months, whereas a product sale took a week. Pricing switched to value-based. A tool called the Value Calculator took in a customer's downtime, changeover time, cleaning time and scrap rate, and calculated how much OEE improvement — and how much money — the solution would deliver. In one sample beverage plant, OEE went from 68% to 81%–88%. The average solution sold for US$200,000–250,000; the same scenario sold as products was US$150,000. Network audits were charged up front: US$10,000 for a single plant, US$80,000–120,000 for multiple sites. If the customer signed the full deal, the audit fee was credited; if not, they paid anyway. Compensation changed to 70% revenue and 30% ESD orders, credited at signing rather than at invoicing six months later. Two Customer Innovation Centers (CICs) were built, in Stuttgart and Santa Clara, where customers could see solution prototypes and put on VR headsets to watch how data flowed through their own plants. Chicago, Shanghai and Bangalore were in the queue. The report card and the bill : IAS revenue grew from US$1 billion in 2019 to US$1.4 billion in 2022, with EBITDA US$84 million over budget. ESD itself: 69 customers, US$7.7 million in revenue, US$16.3 million in orders — less than 1% of the division's revenue, against a goal of half by 2026. The transformation had so far funded itself, thanks to a pandemic-era surge in small projects, maintenance and replacement orders. But the R&D bill for edge-to-cloud software was on its way, and Google Cloud had announced a manufacturing solutions unit in May 2022. The three questions in front of Chand : 1. French distributor NTE had found a lead at an autonomous logistics company, but NTE couldn't do network audits, and it was demanding to take part and get 20% of the service fee — US$28,000. The customer wanted to deal only with Belden directly, and required delivery within 5 days of ordering. 2. A city transit authority in the US Midwest, with 8 metro lines and more than 160 stations, was willing to buy a passenger information system solution. But the solution spanned several Belden brands, and its usual distributor, Magenta, didn't have distribution rights for some of them. Making an exception for Magenta would upset other distributors; making Magenta buy through someone else would squeeze its margin. The third option was to spend US$300,000 and 6 months building a dedicated "ESD partner category." 3. US$26 million in additional budget. A salesperson costs US$250,000 a year and brings in US$2.7 million of EBITDA over 5 years; the same money in R&D brings US$2.15 million over 5 years, but US$1 million in year five alone — and the sales figure didn't account for attrition, while the R&D figure didn't account for the channel, which makes up 70% of Belden's revenue. My Thinking The hardest transformation starts in the year the numbers look best When an iceberg melts, the people standing on it can't feel it — the ice under their feet is still solid. That is exactly Belden's situation: IA contributes more than half the company's profit, revenue grew 40% in three years, and EBITDA beat budget. Not a single number is crying for help. Every danger Chand sees lies outside the financial statements: the direction of margins, who the customer's C-suite is talking to, whether growth is bought or grown. That also dictates how he can transform. He can't "burn the boats," because that pot is cooking the whole group's profits. So ESD is a case of the old business feeding the new one: cash flow from product sales pays the new consultants' salaries; the windfall from pandemic-era replacement orders pays the CIC bills. The speed limit of a transformation is the speed the cash cow allows. My own read is that this is actually the more genuine kind of transformation. Most companies only move once the numbers turn ugly, and by then there's no cash cow left to feed a new business. Belden's problem is a luxurious one: when the numbers look great, how do you convince everyone that "we must change"? Chand's answer was to explain the why first — the case notes that team attrition since the transformation began has been under 7%, and he says: "Good people leave when you don't have a strategy. Once they understand why we're doing ESD, they want to stay." Selling solutions changes not your pitch, but who you meet The biggest change in ESD isn't "from comparing specs to asking about pain points" — that's just the pitch. The real change is that the person sitting across the table on the customer's side is someone else. When selling products, Belden met the maintenance supervisor. He had a list, a target price, and this quarter's budget. When selling solutions, Belden has to meet the CFO, the COO, the VP of supply chain, sometimes the CEO. They don't have a list; they have KPIs — throughput, downtime, scrap rate. The budget is different too: solutions come out of capital expenditure, not the operating budget. Fernández, who leads the solutions consultants, puts it precisely: "We don't go to customers with a predetermined solution. So what we need are people who can ask the right questions of the right people." There's one detail in the case I think is most worth remembering: the SAMs who close fastest are the ones who move slowest at the start. The fast-moving SAMs often discover halfway through that there's an economic buyer they've never met, and have to tear it all down and start over. The slow SAMs meet every person who has a say, and the second half goes smoothly instead. At its core, the MEDDICC scorecard forces salespeople, before they start selling, to write down "who decides, what they care about, who will help me, who will block me." It's a discipline, not a technique. The paid audit is where pricing power begins Belden did something many companies "in transformation" don't dare to do: it charged for consulting up front. Network audits cost US$10,000 to US$120,000, credited if the full deal is signed, payable regardless if not. On the surface it's a small revenue line, but in practice it does three things: it filters out customers who aren't serious; it makes the customer acknowledge "this is worth money" before they commit; and it means Belden's consultants' time is no longer free pre-sales. The Value Calculator is the other side of the same logic. It translates the value of a solution into language the customer's CFO understands — how much OEE improves, how much is saved each year — and then pegs the price of the solution to that number rather than to the cost of the parts. In the words of sales VP Mehrotra: "When we can understand and articulate the value of a solution, we earn the right to price on value." US$200,000–250,000 versus US$150,000: the premium doesn't come from the products getting more expensive. It comes from the conversation shifting from "how much does this cable cost" to "how much does your line lose every year to downtime." The half that didn't change is becoming the new bottleneck ESD changed a lot, but a few things were deliberately left alone: channel managers' responsibilities didn't change; distributors' brand-by-brand distribution rights didn't change; product KPIs didn't change; 70% of compensation still depends on revenue, and profit still isn't part of the evaluation. The case is very honest about why. The channel accounts for 70% of revenue and handles things Belden can't do itself, like 5-day delivery: "We don't have the resources, the infrastructure, or the desire to replace our channel partners." Switch compensation to 50/50 overnight, and salespeople's income would plunge during the 6-month ramp-up, and people would leave. Piloting in CPG first and building new rules once there's enough volume is a reasonable pace, too. But the cost has already appeared. Management noticed that SAMs generally hit their product quota first and only then work on ESD — because products count for more in their bonus. People follow the compensation plan, not the strategy speech. And not one of the three questions in front of Chand is a new problem; all of them are fruit borne by "the half that didn't change": channel conflict, brand distribution rights, revenue-driven evaluation. It's something I also wrote about in the Olay piece, seen again from a different angle: at Olay, the strategy changed three times but the metrics didn't, so the strategy never landed; at Belden, the strategy is set but the metrics have only half changed, so the strategy has only half landed. The three questions are really one: turning exceptions into rules NTE, Magenta, the US$26 million — they look like three separate matters, but underneath is the same problem: how a channel system designed for selling parts can accommodate selling solutions. On the NTE deal, I'd go with a hybrid: Belden delivers the audit and services itself, since the customer only wants to deal with Belden anyway; all products ship through NTE, which can do 5-day delivery; and NTE gets a lead referral fee, say 5%–10% of the service value, rather than 20%. Don't use the German partner — that would be telling every distributor "bring us a lead and we'll cut you out." The US$28,000 is small; the signal it sends to a channel that makes up 70% of revenue is big. Then turn this into a lead registration policy, rather than negotiating deal by deal. On the Magenta deal, I'd do both: first make an exception for this deal, clearly labelled "verified ESD projects only" — rail transit is IAS's largest serviceable market, and you can't make a flagship customer buy piecemeal from three distributors; and at the same time immediately launch that US$300,000 ESD partner category. Solutions naturally span brands, so this kind of conflict will keep recurring. US$300,000 is roughly the size of one ESD deal, and what it buys is turning an "exception" into a "rule" every distributor can see. Sales pays back fast, R&D pays back big, so it isn't either/or On the US$26 million question, the table from finance is interesting: one salesperson yields US$2.7 million of EBITDA over 5 years, with US$300,000 in year one; R&D yields US$2.15 million over 5 years, almost nothing in the first two years, and US$1 million in year five alone. But Fernández adds two footnotes that matter more than the table itself: the sales figures don't account for staff turnover; the R&D figures don't account for the channel — 70% of Belden's revenue is sold through the channel, so a new product gets amplified by that 70% channel, and a new salesperson doesn't. Stretch it to 10 years and R&D usually wins. There are also diminishing returns: not every salesperson can build a US$5 million pipeline, and once a region or an industry is saturated, each further sale gets harder. My own inclination is a 60/40 split: 60% on the market-facing side, 40% on R&D. The market-facing money shouldn't simply hire 100 SAMs — US$26 million divided by US$250,000 is about 104 people, while the entire sales force today is only 281, ramp-up takes a year, and talent is scarce. A large share should go to consultants, who are the real bottleneck, and they should be placed in regions where there's a CIC and existing SAMs to work with. On the R&D side, invest only in edge-to-cloud software tied to use cases already validated in the CICs — the window is closing, and Google is already in. Growth and profit will fight, and an organisation that measures only revenue can't see the fight. Solutions carry higher deal sizes, but also higher cost to serve: consultants, 6-month cycles, CICs. If you look only at revenue, you may well end up with a pile of unprofitable growth. What really needs calculating is the profit on each solution, including the additional product sales it pulls through. One more point, not among the three questions, but which I think matters more than all three: set a date for switching compensation to 50/50. Otherwise the extra salespeople you hire will still go off and sell cable. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading Belden is more uncomfortable than reading Olay — because most of us recognise Belden's problems. First, we have our own "cable" too. Every service firm has that kind of thing with a short sales cycle, that customers understand instantly, with good cash flow — an insurance policy, a structure, a single service. It's the cash cow, feeding the things that take 6 months to build: the family's asset map, the IPS, the governance structure. Belden's reminder comes in two sentences: the cash cow sets the speed limit of the transformation; but if the team's bonuses stay tied to "cable," they'll always sell cable first. Second, charging for diagnosis is where pricing power begins. Belden's audits cost US$10,000 to US$120,000, credited against the full deal. A family office's first step — pulling together into one picture the assets, structures and risks a family has scattered across various institutions — is work of the same nature. Do it for free, and it's pre-sales; charge for it, and only then is it delivery. And for a family, what corresponds to Belden's Value Calculator is a different arithmetic: how much the same family leaks every year through duplicated risks, layer upon layer of fees, and accounts that don't know about each other. Only once you've calculated that number do you have the confidence to charge on value. Third, families have MEDDICC too. The person who decides is never just the patriarch or matriarch. The spouse, the next generation, the CFO of the family business, the current private bank and lawyers — some are champions, some are blockers. Belden's best SAMs are the slowest at the start, meeting every single person. That's even more true for a family office: miss one person early on, and you'll have to tear it down and start over later. Fourth, the way out of craftsmanship is a solutions factory. High-end family services today are still essentially a high-priced craft — one plan per family, each plan starting from scratch. Belden's CICs offer a very concrete answer: first turn the problems that recur within an industry into standard use cases, validate them, then customise per client. For a family office, it's about which modules — cross-border residency, trusts, insurance, governance — can be made into "standard components" first and then adjusted for each family. That is where being AI-native really ought to land. Fifth, the best use cases come from customer conversations, not from the lab. On the US$26 million question, Belden's sales side has one very solid argument: most of the use cases in the CICs grew out of conversations between salespeople and customers, not out of R&D working behind closed doors. For a family office betting on AI, that's a reminder — however powerful the system, the founder and senior advisors must stay in front of the families. Every real conversation should flow back into the system; otherwise what the system learns is only the family as we imagine it. Final Thoughts Before class, the line I agree with most is "the SAMs who close fastest are the ones who move slowest at the start." After class, I'll see which of these gets overturned, and by what.
How did a US$2 billion brand get cut in half?

Unit 3 has begun, with Professor Das Narayandas's Market-Facing Functions, and the first case is Olay: Facelift at Olay (A). This is not a story of "an old brand beaten by new brands." It is the story of a brand that took itself apart. I wrote this before class. I'm putting my judgement down here first, and I'll come back to compare after class.
