Here goes — enjoy: Case Summary On October 4, 2017 , Chris Heiert, general manager of P&G's North America skin care, received an email from senior leadership: Olay's July–September sales were down 12% year on year — a big miss even against already low expectations. Does the full-year growth you promised still stand? Where Olay came from : born in South Africa in 1952 as a bottle of pink "beauty fluid." It came into P&G with Richardson-Vicks in 1985, when it had just 5 SKUs and annual sales of US$165 million. The golden decade (2000–2009) : In 2000 it dropped "Oil of" and became Olay; it launched Total Effects at US$19.99, "fighting the seven signs of aging," positioned as "the efficacy of Lancôme and Estée Lauder at half the price." In 2003 it launched Regenerist, with pentapeptides, "without surgery." After a dermatologist endorsed it on morning TV, shelves were cleared out. In 2007 it launched the "red jar," Regenerist Micro-Sculpting Cream. P&G called this playbook masstige (mass + prestige): department-store efficacy, sold at Walmart. In 2008 Olay held 16.7% of US facial care, and in 2009 its global retail sales passed US$2 billion. The decline (2010–2017) : Five sub-brands sat on the shelf at once, up to 140 SKUs at Walmart alone, with overlapping efficacy claims. Consumers saw an ad, came into the store, couldn't remember which jar it was, and walked out empty-handed. 30–40 new products launched every year. In one retailer's words: "Olay hasn't delivered on its promises; we no longer count on it to drive category growth." In 2013, to win over college students, it launched the Fresh Effects acne line. First-year sales: US$8 million. Between 2008 and 2015 it went through three general managers, each with their own strategy. Millennials called it "Oil of Old Lady." In fiscal 2017, retail sales fell back to just over US$1 billion. Cut in half. The world outside : the market itself was growing — US skin care was worth US$17.7 billion, growing 6.7% a year; China, US$26.9 billion, growing 8.7%. The growth went to others: Glossier through Instagram and "unboxing"; Rodan + Fields through dermatologists plus social-media direct selling, passing US$1 billion in sales in 2017 and overtaking Olay; K-beauty got into Walmart with sheet masks, serums and the "10-step routine." Meanwhile, 80% of Olay's advertising budget was still on TV, and less than 5% on digital. What was still in hand : 90% awareness among US adults. The red jar was the category's best-seller; Good Housekeeping testing showed it beating creams costing four times as much, and it was rated 4.5–4.7 stars online. Skin-care gross margins were healthy. But the red jar's household penetration was just 2%. Heiert's three choices : 1. Sell or not? In 2015 P&G had just sold 43 beauty brands to Coty. 2. Focus on 35-plus, or chase 21–35? 3. Expand the product line, even go all in on DTC — or cut SKUs? My Thinking Don't sell — selling cures headquarters' impatience, not the brand's problem Selling means dumping a still-living asset at its lowest point. 90% awareness, the category's best-seller, reviews of 4.5 stars and up, healthy margins, a category that is still growing — this is not a brand to be liquidated. What P&G sold in 2015 was CoverGirl and Clairol; what it kept was Pantene, Head & Shoulders, Olay and SK-II. Olay sits in the pillar tier. Selling cures headquarters' impatience, not the brand's problem. The money is over 35; "young people drive growth" is the retailers' anxiety Let the data speak first. US skin-care sales in 2017: 55-plus accounted for 40%, 45–54 for 24%, 35–44 for 20%, and under-35s only 16% — and those shares barely moved in three years. "Young people drive growth" describes the growth rates of new brands and the anxiety of retailers, not where the sales are. The tier Olay once won was US$17–25, which is 35% of the category. The price band wasn't wrong; what was wrong was that the products within it were impossible to tell apart. And Olay has already run the "win over young people" experiment once — Fresh Effects, US$8 million, which also muddied "what Olay actually is" even further. Young women's entry product is makeup-removing wipes, which is Neutrogena's turf; natural ingredients belong to Aveeno; conversational feel belongs to Glossier. One brand cannot say "I understand you best" to a 19-year-old's acne and a 55-year-old's wrinkles at the same time. 140 SKUs are both the result and the cause of decline 140 SKUs and 5 sub-brands are both the result and the cause of Olay's decline. With 30–40 new products a year, retailers had already stopped believing. Adding yet another line now, or charging into e-commerce precisely because "we have no DTC experience," would spread already thin resources even thinner. The red jar's household penetration is only 2%. There is far more room in selling this one jar clearly than in building yet another sub-brand. Olay wins by becoming clear, not by becoming young Look back at Olay in 2000–2009 and the formula was actually simple: one promise (visibly younger), one price logic (premium within mass channels), and a few hero products with real science behind them. The decline was Olay dismantling that formula itself. Five sub-brands fighting over the same line, "innovation" reduced to launch speed, three general managers with three strategies. The brand's meaning shrank to the two lines from internal interviews: "Olay is a warm wool scarf. You need it, but it isn't fashionable." "If Olay were in a high school and the popular girls ranked 1 through 8, she'd be number 9. Close to popular, but not in that circle." The word "anti-aging" went out of date before the products did In 2016 Olay surveyed 6,800 women in 11 countries: two-thirds felt that age no longer mattered as much as it had for their mothers' generation, and 80% believed it would matter even less in future. Olay's science isn't outdated; Olay's language is. So the answer isn't "go back to the 2009 slogan," but to go back to the structure that actually worked back then — few products, clear, proven efficacy, numbers that add up for retailers — and then say it differently: move from "fighting aging" to the line the team had already hit upon, "skin that looks young, so it doesn't give away your age." Olay didn't lack strategy; it had too many strategies in seven years The course description has this line: "No good strategy can succeed without excellent execution." Olay's problem was precisely not a lack of strategy, but too many strategies over seven years. The four hardest things in execution: Retailers won't give you shelf space back just because you promise to simplify. If you cut SKUs yourself, they'll give the freed-up space to Neutrogena, K-beauty, Drunk Elephant. So this isn't pleading — it's a trade: voluntarily give up dead stock, on condition that the hero products' facings are written into the next planogram. Walmart accounts for US$10 billion of P&G's sales; this negotiation is the strategy itself. In the quarter you cut items, the numbers will look worse first. Be honest in replying to that email — this quarter's growth won't be won back by launching more products. Swap the growth promise for a path with dates on it. Lost customers are hard to win back. As Heiert herself said: the brand gave her a reason to leave, she left, and she discovered another brand. The awareness is still there; the habit isn't. The incentive system works against the strategy. If the front line is still measured on "how many SKUs we launched," they'll read "cut the product line" as "give up on growth." Strategy and metrics have to change together — stop the launch quotas and look at only four numbers: red-jar sell-through, repeat purchase, retailer gross margin per foot, and household penetration. One more thing: from headquarters, first get one commitment — no change of strategy and no change of general manager for 24 months. The failure pattern of the past seven years was a change every year. Takeaways for Arcus42 Reading about Olay, I kept thinking about us. The easiest mistake for a multi-family office is exactly Olay's: wanting to do everything, saying "we have that too" to everything, so that clients stand in front of the "shelf" unable to tell what you actually are — and leave empty-handed. First, answer "who are we for" before answering "what do we do." 35-plus or 21–35 is not a market-segmentation question; it's a question of "whom are we willing to give up." A family office is no different — being willing to serve everyone means serving no one. Second, there can be only one hero product. What the red jar is to Olay is our one core deliverable that "shows visible results and adds up financially." Everything else is a bridge. Bridges can stay, but budget, people and attention go first to the end that has already been proven to work. Third, the entropy of trust starts with 30–40 "new products" a year. When retailers said "you haven't delivered on your promises," Olay still thought it was innovating. Every promise you can't keep quietly lowers the odds of being believed next time. With family clients, this is a debt we can even less afford to run up. Fourth, language goes out of date before products do. Olay's science was fine; the word "anti-aging" was what went stale. Of the words we say to families — "succession," "structure," "allocation" — which are still being heard, and which have already become background noise? I don't have an answer to this, but it's worth asking once a year. Fifth, strategy and metrics have to change together, or strategy is just a PowerPoint deck. All three general managers had strategies. What never changed was the metric "new launches = growth." An organisation does what it is measured on, not what it is told. Final Words Before class, I cast my vote for "few and clear." After class, I'll look at which of these got overturned, and by what.

Unit 3, Scott Snook's leadership course. Assigned reading: Daniel Goleman, What Makes a Leader? The article opens with a story everyone in business has heard. An executive, extremely intelligent and highly skilled, is promoted into a leadership position — and fails. Another, solidly intelligent but not dazzling, steps into a similar role — and soars. We're far too used to explaining leadership with smarts. Goleman's verdict is blunt: IQ and technical skills are the entry ticket — they decide whether you get in the door. Once you're inside, what sets people apart is emotional intelligence. Here goes — enjoy: The higher you go, the less the gap is about technique, and the more it's about people Goleman analyzed competency models from 188 companies, most of them large multinationals, Lucent, British Airways and Credit Suisse among them. He sorted capabilities into three groups: technical (accounting, business planning), cognitive (analysis, big-picture thinking, long-term vision), and emotional intelligence (working with others, leading change). When he ran the numbers, emotional intelligence carried roughly twice the weight of technical skills and IQ in outstanding performance — at every level. At the top, the technical differences are already small. Nearly 90% of the gap between stars and average performers can be attributed to emotional intelligence. In 1996, David McClelland saw a more concrete picture at a global food and beverage company: when senior managers had a critical mass of emotional intelligence, their divisions beat yearly earnings targets by about 20%; without that critical mass, they underperformed by almost the same amount. Divisions in the US, Asia and Europe all pointed the same way. These are his samples, not laws. But I buy the direction. As you move up, the work changes — you rely less and less on getting a problem right yourself, and more and more on other people being willing to get it right. Emotional intelligence lives in the other half of the brain, which is why classrooms can't teach it Are leaders born or made? Goleman's answer is both: part genetics, part experience, and the proportions can never be pinned down. What is certain is that it grows with age. The old word for it is maturity. People who aren't mature enough need training. Unfortunately, too many leadership programs put their effort into the wrong part. Emotions, impulses and drive sit mainly in the brain's limbic system. It learns through three things: motivation to change, sustained practice, and feedback from others. Concepts and logic live in the neocortex. The neocortex learns by reading, attending lectures, mastering frameworks — how to run a regression, how to make a sales call: reading a book is enough. Learning empathy the way you'd learn regression isn't just slow. Goleman and his colleagues found that such programs sometimes actually made job performance worse. He tells the story of a Wall Street executive. This executive wanted to improve his empathy — his ability to read other people's reactions and see their perspectives. Up to then, his subordinates had been afraid to work with him, and bad news never reached him. When he confronted these facts for the first time, he was shocked. He went home and told his family, and they only confirmed what his colleagues had said: when their views differed from his, they were afraid of him too. He hired a coach. The first step was a vacation in a country where he didn't speak the language. There, he paid attention to how he reacted to the unfamiliar, and to how closed off he was to people different from himself. A week abroad taught him humility. Back home, he had the coach shadow him several times a week, critiquing how he handled differing opinions. He treated his interactions at work as practice — deliberately listening to views that contradicted his own. Finally, he had his meetings recorded and asked his subordinates and colleagues to critique them: had he really listened? Months went by, and his emotional intelligence did improve, and his overall performance changed along with it. Not a single step of this process could have been done by reading a book. Emerson is quoted here: nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm. Short courses aren't enough; manuals aren't enough. A person first has to genuinely want to change. My own take goes half a step further: AI is making the neocortex side of the work fast and cheap — analyzing, drafting, building frameworks, writing a well-judged letter. The entry ticket has gotten cheaper. What's behind the door hasn't. Five capabilities: three for managing yourself, two for managing others Self-awareness: daring to name your weaknesses isn't weakness — it's the precondition for seeing your organization clearly Self-awareness means having a deep understanding of your own emotions, strengths, weaknesses, needs and drives — and knowing how they land on other people. Goleman describes a department store manager. The company was about to launch a personal shopping service, and she had reservations. No one asked her, but she took it upon herself to explain to her team and her boss: "It's hard for me to get fully behind this project, because I really wanted to run it and I wasn't chosen. Bear with me while I deal with that." A week later, she was all in. The way to spot it is quite concrete, too. In an interview, ask the candidate to describe a time they got carried away by their feelings and later regretted it. Self-aware people admit it frankly, often with a touch of self-deprecation. In performance reviews, such people actively ask for constructive criticism; people with weak self-awareness hear "you need to improve" as a threat. In many rooms, candor is treated as "not tough enough." Goleman argues just the opposite. Only people who can assess themselves honestly can assess the organizations they run — do we have the management capability to acquire a competitor? Can we launch this product in six months? Self-regulation: when the impulse comes, don't let it sign on your behalf Biological impulses can't be switched off. What you can do is carry on an ongoing inner conversation. Goleman offers a scene: an executive has just watched his team botch a presentation to the board. In the gloom that follows, he might feel like pounding the table or kicking a chair, might yell at the team, or might glower and storm out. Someone good at self-regulation takes a different path. He chooses his words carefully, acknowledges the team's poor performance, but doesn't rush to judgment. He steps back to think: was it a lack of effort? Were there mitigating factors? What role did he himself play in this debacle? Once he has thought it through, he calls the team together, lays out the consequences, says candidly how he feels, and offers his analysis and a proposed solution. Trust slowly grows up around such people. There's less office politics, and good people want to stay. And it flows downward — if the boss is known for staying calm, a hot temper starts to look out of place. It also has to do with integrity. Inflating profits, padding expense reports, abusing power for personal gain — these are rarely planned. Most of the time an opportunity comes along, and someone with weak impulse control says yes. An executive at a food company would openly explain his cost structure when negotiating with distributors. That meant he didn't always get the best deal. He occasionally felt the urge to conceal his costs and make a bit more — but he held it in check. What he got in return was strong, lasting distributor relationships, far better than any short-term gain. A fiery temper is often seen as a sign of decisiveness and charisma. In Goleman's research, extreme displays of negative emotion have never once emerged as a driver of good leadership. Motivation: people who work for the sake of achievement bring their standards to the whole organization There's a kind of passion that isn't about salary, or title, or the company's name. These people want to get things done because getting this thing done is the point. A manager at a cosmetics company couldn't stand waiting two weeks to see sales results from the field. He found an automated phone system that called every salesperson at five o'clock each afternoon and had them enter that day's calls and closed deals. The feedback time shrank from weeks to hours. Such people keep raising the bar, and they like keeping score. Goleman knew a fund manager who, at the start and end of every working day, checked his fund's performance against four industry benchmarks. When the score looks bad, they stay optimistic. Another portfolio manager, after several successful years, saw her fund fall for three quarters in a row, and three large institutional clients took their business elsewhere. Some people would blame the circumstances; others would take it as proof of personal failure. She saw it as an opportunity — to prove she could lead a turnaround. Two years later she was promoted to a very senior position in the firm, and looking back she called it "the best thing that ever happened to me." The last piece of evidence is loyalty. Because they love the work itself, they feel loyal to the place that makes the work possible — when a headhunter puts money on the table, these are the people more likely to stay. Standards are contagious. If you've set a high bar for yourself, then when you have power in your hands, you'll set a high bar for the organization too. Empathy: not pleasing everyone, but factoring other people's feelings into decisions Empathy isn't much respected in business; the word sounds too soft. It isn't taking on other people's emotions as your own and trying to please everyone. That way, decisions grind to a halt. It's something else: when making a hard decision, counting other people's feelings as one of the variables. Two large brokerage firms merged, creating redundancies in every division. One division manager called his people together and gave a gloomy speech emphasizing how many would soon be let go. Another manager also gathered his people, but he spoke candidly about his own worries and confusion, promised to keep everyone informed, and to treat everyone fairly. The first manager watched his division's morale collapse as his best people left one after another. In the second manager's division, the best people stayed, and remained productive. The only difference was empathy. Goleman gives three reasons empathy matters more today: teams need consensus, and four or five people will split into factions; across cultures, a long silence isn't necessarily a rejection; and when people leave, they take the company's knowledge with them. For the second, he describes a scene. An American consultant and his team had just finished a pitch to a Japanese client. With Americans, a pitch is usually followed by a barrage of questions; this time they were met with a long silence. The team took the silence as a no and started packing up. The lead consultant signaled them to stop. He wasn't especially familiar with Japanese culture, but what he read in the client's faces and postures wasn't rejection — it was interest, even careful deliberation. He was right: when the client spoke, they gave the team the job. Social skill: leaders get things done through other people's hands, and this is that hand The first three are about managing yourself. Empathy and social skill are about what happens between people. Social skill is friendliness with a purpose — moving people in the direction you need, whether that's agreement on a new strategy or getting a group genuinely excited about a new product. It's the outlet for all the others. Empathy that can't be expressed might as well not exist; passion that can't be transmitted to the organization leaves motivation empty. An executive in the strategy group of a global computer manufacturer became convinced in 1993 that the company's future lay in the internet. Over the following year, he sought out like-minded people and, across levels, departments and national borders, wove together a virtual community. With this de facto team he built the company's website — one of the first among big companies. Then, with no budget and no formal standing, he signed the company up for an annual internet conference, persuaded multiple divisions to chip in, and rallied more than fifty people from a dozen-plus divisions to attend. Less than a year after the conference, this group became the foundation of the company's first internet division, and he was formally put in charge of it. So chatting in the hallway often isn't idle chat. Socially skilled people don't arbitrarily limit the range of their relationships — they know that someone they've only just met today may be exactly the person they'll need next. Final Thoughts: what you hand over in a succession is a person, not intelligence Three points. Smarts and craft are the threshold. Only past the threshold does the gap begin. The higher the position, the more that gap is about people and the less it's about technique. This ability can be learned — but the method is the opposite of learning technique: not through understanding it once, but through being seen, being corrected, and doing it again, over and over. In family businesses, this is especially unforgiving. The first generation often builds a company from nothing through craft and decisiveness. When it's passed to the next generation, people are still looking for the same kind of smarts. Goleman's research points somewhere else: the higher you go, the more smarts are merely the entry ticket. What a succession has to hand over is a person who can see themselves clearly, keep a situation under control, and make others want to stay. I haven't scored myself on the five yet. The self-awareness section is the most grueling — in many rooms, naming your own weaknesses still feels like showing weakness. That's where I'll start looking at myself. That's where these notes end. These are reading notes. The research findings in this piece are paraphrased from Daniel Goleman's What Makes a Leader? ( Harvard Business Review , January 2004). The figures describe the samples he analyzed; they are not an assessment of any individual or company, and do not constitute management or investment advice.

My first two notes both ended on the same question: supplements. This is the third, covering the last part of the book. In the first one I mentioned that I've taken NMN regularly for years. When I read the line "supplements probably can't help you live longer," I paused. In this part, Topol unpacks that line. The question is simple: with medical science this advanced, surely there must be some drug that helps with longevity? Could it be hiding among all those assorted supplements on the market? Here goes — enjoy: 1. Fish Oil: 25,000 People, Five Years, No Effect Let's start with the oldest name in the game — fish oil. In 2019, a huge clinical trial called VITAL published its results. 25,871 healthy adults were followed for more than five years. The researchers wanted to know just one thing: does a standard daily dose of one gram of omega-3 fish oil — the kind you can buy in any supermarket, with a mix of EPA and DHA — really keep heart disease and cancer at bay, as the legend goes? The result: no effect. Whether for cardiovascular events overall or for cancer incidence, there was no significant difference between people taking fish oil and people taking a placebo. Topol's analogy is not exactly gentle: you think that daily gram of fish oil is giving your blood vessels a deep clean, but in reality it's more like your house is on fire and you're throwing a mouthful of water at it from a shot glass. Worse still, taking too much DHA over the long term can also weaken immune function and affect platelet aggregation. A piece of common sense people have lived by for decades, quietly set down by data from 25,000 people. 2. Blood Swapping: Youth at US$10,000 a Litre Fish oil is an old-school supplement. So what about Silicon Valley's more sci-fi-sounding "black tech"? Take blood-swapping therapy. You may have heard the story of Silicon Valley multimillionaire Bryan Johnson — he once swapped blood with his young son, hoping that an infusion of young blood would reverse ageing. Later, Johnson himself admitted it hadn't worked as hoped. Topol says there are indeed companies offering young plasma infusions and plasma exchange, at prices as high as US$10,000 a litre. But there's very little human research on blood swapping, and the few studies that exist found essentially no benefit — for example, a small randomised trial in 9 Alzheimer's patients treated with plasma donated by young people showed no effect. He stresses one point in particular: besides being expensive and lacking evidence, plasma infusion and exchange carry a serious risk of disease transmission. Paying for a hope with no evidence behind it, while accepting a risk that definitely exists. That's less like medicine and more like a ritual. 3. NAD+: The Part Where I Paused And then we get to my part. NAD+ is a metabolite produced by mitochondria that plays a central role in energy metabolism — promoting gene repair and slowing cellular ageing. As we age, NAD+ levels in the body decline. So many companies started selling products claiming to restore NAD+, most commonly NR and NMN. One is a form of vitamin B3, the other a small organic molecule; both are converted to NAD+ once in the body — a high-tech version of "you are what you eat." Topol's verdict: these products were never validated by human clinical trials before being sold widely. For NAD+ to work in the body, it depends on the cooperation of many other substances the body produces itself. Simply taking synthetic analogues from outside may well be futile. More worrying still, some research institutions and biopharma companies have deliberately downplayed its possible side effects — such as an increased risk of cancer. For someone who's taken NMN for years, this section wasn't comfortable to read. But discomfort is often the moment a book is doing its work. I'm not going to jump to a conclusion. I've just moved it from "routine" back to "to be verified" — until there are large human randomised controlled trials, it shouldn't hold a settled place. Much of what we do to our bodies is, at heart, paying for a story that hasn't been proven yet. 4. So, Is There Anything? Topol sums up "biohacking" methods in a single sentence: they either lack evidence of clinical benefit from large human randomised controlled trials, or come with huge risks. So is there anything that actually works? He gives an answer, and one many people wouldn't expect: GLP-1 drugs — semaglutide and tirzepatide. These drugs were originally used to treat diabetes and obesity. How could drugs for diabetes and obesity have anything to do with longevity? To answer that, you first need to accept one of the most subversive ideas in Topol's book. 5. All Diseases Share One Root Heart disease, cancer, dementia — three life-shortening diseases that seem to have nothing to do with one another share a common underlying mechanism: chronic inflammation and immune system dysfunction. Start with heart disease. The conventional view is that atherosclerosis is simply blood vessels "clogged" with fat, like limescale in a water pipe. But at its core it is inflammation of the vessel wall — and all inflammation, ultimately, is triggered by the immune system. Topol cites a piece of evidence. In a large clinical trial called CANTOS, scientists injected heart patients with a powerful targeted anti-inflammatory drug (canakinumab) designed specifically to suppress immune-driven vascular inflammation. The result: patients' heart attack rates fell significantly. Unexpectedly, the incidence of fatal lung cancer also dropped sharply. Two birds with one stone. Cardiovascular disease and cancer share the same inflammatory switch. Next, cancer. Cancer itself usually isn't fatal; what kills is metastasis. For cancer cells to roam the body and seed themselves, they first have to evolve extremely good camouflage to escape the immune system's pursuit — and an ageing immune system is precisely the easiest to fool. Topol says that as long as the immune system stays strong, in the vast majority of cases cancer cells will stay locked in where they started. Finally, neurodegenerative disease. Medicine long believed that the brain, protected by the blood-brain barrier, was an island largely untouched by the immune system. Now we know the brain is home to macrophages called "microglia" — the brain's sentinels, and its rubbish collectors too. As we age, these sentinels become exhausted and fall into a state of "end-stage inflammation": instead of clearing metabolic waste, they start releasing pro-inflammatory factors, damaging synapses and causing brain cells to die. Topol says it plainly: without this "inflammatory riot" inside the brain, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's would struggle to truly destroy the brain. Three diseases, one source. 6. A Twenty-Year Window If all these diseases share a root — traceable to an immune system out of control and chronic inflammation — then there's a way to break through. Topol says these three big chronic killers usually take twenty years or more to lie dormant and develop. That gives us an extremely wide "early interception window." GLP-1 drugs are currently the best-evidenced tool within that window. A large randomised trial of 17,600 obese patients with a history of heart disease showed that after three years on semaglutide, the treatment group's risk of heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death fell by 20%. What's more interesting is the order in which things happened. In these patients, inflammation levels and cardiovascular risk fell first — and only then did weight. What does that tell us? That the underlying logic by which GLP-1 saves lives isn't just "losing weight makes you healthier." It first, and independently, lowers chronic inflammation throughout the body, thereby lowering cardiovascular risk. Weight is the result we can see. Inflammation is the cause we've never been able to see. 7. The Key Is Hidden in the Gut GLP-1 drugs have also shown surprising potential in neurodegenerative disease. In a clinical trial of patients with early Parkinson's, GLP-1 drugs successfully stopped motor symptoms from getting worse — and this protective effect persisted even after the drug was stopped. Biologically, this is a mystery. Many large-molecule GLP-1 drugs simply can't cross the blood-brain barrier directly in any significant amount. Scientists speculate that these "gut hormones" use a kind of "remote control" mechanism: via the "gut-brain axis," they send signals directly to the cerebral cortex and hypothalamus, shutting down the inflammatory riot that drives neurodegeneration inside the brain without breaching the physical barrier. In other words — the key to treating the brain's incurable diseases may be hidden in the gut. In the second note we said that what determines your blood sugar response isn't the food, it's your gut microbiome. In this one, the gut shows up in the answer once again. The body isn't a collection of organs each going its own way; it's a web we still haven't fully learned to read. I should be clear: GLP-1s are prescription drugs, with their own indications and side effects. What Topol writes about is the possibility they open up in medicine, not a shopping list. The same goes for me. Final Words And with that, my three notes are done. At the end of the book Topol keeps returning to one idea: what our generation can do — and the only thing we should do — is not try to reverse the underlying biology of ageing, but use existing technology to precisely intercept the specific chronic diseases quietly brewing inside us. Looking back, these three notes are really one sentence unfolded three times: 1. Longevity doesn't mainly depend on genes — genes explain only 25–30%; the rest is in our hands; 2. There's no universal perfect diet, no universal exercise prescription, no universal screening age — only the set that's right for you; 3. Nor is there a universal longevity pill — fish oil, blood swapping, NAD+ are mostly hopes without evidence; what actually has evidence comes, of all things, from a drug originally meant for diabetes, and the insight behind it that "all diseases share one root." Topol says the truth about longevity is actually simple: it isn't a war against ageing, but a revolution of choices. Choosing the diet and way of eating that suits you better, choosing more personalised testing and medicine, choosing more exercise, choosing closer social connections, and a more meaningful purpose in life. In On the Shortness of Life , Seneca wrote: it is not that we have too little time, but that we waste a great deal of it. Two thousand years later, a cardiologist used a whole book's worth of clinical data to say much the same thing — The question has never been the length of life, but how long the healthy part lasts. True longevity isn't living longer but living better: a body full of vitality, a clear mind, a rich emotional life, a life with meaning. The book is finished. The practice has only just begun.

At the end of my last post, I said I'd report back once I'd finished the sections on health check-ups and supplements. This is the second set of notes. Last time we established one thing: longevity is mostly not a genetic lottery — genes explain only 25–30%, while lifestyle and environment account for 70–75%. Which raises the question: what kind of lifestyle actually extends healthy lifespan? In this part of the book, Topol re-examines three things one by one: eating, moving, and screening. Some of the conclusions are very different from what we assume. Here goes — enjoy: 1. There is no universal perfect diet Let's start with eating. Van Tulleken's experiment proved the harm of an unhealthy diet. So, flipping it around, if you eat by a "healthy menu," will you live longer? Topol cites a paper in the top journal Cell . Scientists at Israel's Weizmann Institute of Science recruited 800 ordinary people without diabetes and fitted each of them with a continuous glucose monitor, recording their blood sugar fluctuations around the clock as they went about their daily lives. They logged every one of the more than 52,000 meals these 800 people ate. They drew blood, measured waists and hips, and even collected stool samples to sequence the genes of every microbe in each person's gut. Then came the conclusion. When these 800 people ate exactly the same food — the same slice of whole-wheat bread, the same banana — their blood sugar responses were worlds apart. For some, that "healthy" slice of whole-wheat bread sent their blood sugar soaring; others ate ice cream, supposedly off-limits, and their glucose curve stayed perfectly calm. If it isn't the food itself that determines the blood sugar response, then what is? The scientists put more than a hundred variables into an algorithmic model, and the factor that came out on top, with absolute dominance, was — the gut microbiome. The trillions of invisible bacteria in your belly. Topol's metaphor is a lovely one: the gut isn't a simple digestive funnel; it's more like a complex trading market. The food you eat is just raw material. How much nutrition and how much sugar ultimately reach your bloodstream depends on the "traders" inside you — the makeup, metabolism and responses of your gut flora at that moment. This is the emerging field of "personalised nutrition": there is no universal perfect diet, only the perfect match for you. 2. Not even genes can give a standard answer As soon as this conclusion came out, people objected: what if it's genetics? What if I was just born with a better metabolism? It really isn't. In 2020, King's College London led a cohort study called PREDICT 1, with more than a thousand people — and crucially, a large number of them were identical twins. Identical twins are the perfect control group for studying genetic influence: bodies cast from the same mould, exactly the same hardware. If genes truly determined how we respond to food, then when twins ate the same plate of pasta, their glucose curves should overlap perfectly. The result: even with 100% identical DNA, the two people's blood sugar trajectories were still wildly different. Beyond the gut microbiome, PREDICT 1 found another key factor — how you eat. The time of the meal, the order in which you eat things, the state you're in before and after. Vegetables first, then meat, then rice last; versus a bowl of rice on an empty stomach first, then everything else — you think it's more or less the same, but to your metabolic system, these are two completely different scripts. Meal timing and order, layered on top of your one-of-a-kind microbiome, have an overwhelming effect on metabolism. We are always searching for a universal formula, a plan that works for all of humanity. But the body — or life itself — is precisely the thing that most refuses to be standardised. Topol's advice is practical: under the guidance of a health professional, wear a continuous glucose monitor and test how each food, and each way of eating it, affects you. The answer isn't in a recipe book; it's in you. 3. When it comes to exercise, we may all have it wrong After eating, moving. When we think of exercise, we think of jogging, swimming, cardio — and that's always the standard script doctors give their patients. And strength training? Many people think that's something young people do in the gym while taking selfies in the mirror. Topol admits he thought so too at first, until a set of numbers changed his mind: Human muscle mass and strength begin to decline at around age fifty. Between sixty and ninety, men quietly lose about 33% of their muscle mass, and women about 26%. What does muscle loss mean? It means stooping and hunching; it means back pain and arthritis come knocking; it means that even stepping down a single stair, you might lose your balance and fall and break something. After seeing these numbers, this towering figure in cardiology, in his seventies, dutifully started doing resistance and strength training four to five times a week, twenty to thirty minutes each time. In his own words: "If I'm destined to get old, I'd rather be a strong old man." 4. Strength training doesn't need a gym When many people hear "resistance training," they picture intimidating barbells. It really isn't that. It doesn't even require spending a penny on a gym membership. All you need is to learn to work with gravity using your own body: push-ups, pull-ups, sit-ups, squats, lunges; or a resistance band that costs a few dozen yuan, a pair of small dumbbells at home. As long as it works the muscles in your arms, chest, abs, legs, glutes and back, that's enough. There are two numbers in the book worth copying down: First, the wall sit. Back against the wall, thighs parallel to the floor, three times a week, eight minutes each time — its effect on lowering blood pressure is comparable to aerobic exercise, even high-intensity interval training. Eight minutes is probably the cheapest blood-pressure medicine in the world, and it has no side effects. Second, sixty minutes of resistance training a week in total — about the time it takes to binge a few episodes of a short drama — lowers all-cause mortality by about 25%. Clinically, that's a very big number. 5. Started at seventy, a champion at ninety-three You might be thinking: at my age, is it too late to start? There's a man in the book called Richard Morgan. For the first seventy years of his life, he had almost nothing to do with "exercise." In his seventies, for the first time in his life, he sat down at a rowing machine in an old shed in his backyard. After that, he rowed an average of forty minutes a day, paired with a high-protein diet and strength training twice a week without fail — dumbbells, lunges, curls. At ninety-three, he won four world championships in indoor rowing. The total distance he has rowed over the years is the equivalent of ten times around the Earth. Morgan's granddaughter happened to be a researcher in the physiology lab at the University of Limerick in Ireland. The scientists invited the old man into the lab and gave him a thorough full-body examination: of the mass on his body, 80% was muscle and 15% fat; his maximal oxygen uptake was on par with a young person's; his peak heart rate during exercise was 153 beats per minute — equivalent to a healthy fifty-year-old. A man who only started exercising at seventy had rowed his body back forty years. It's never too late to start. 6. The truth about check-ups: screening is stuck in the 1960s Now for check-ups — the question left over from last time. Regular check-ups, early detection, early treatment — surely that can't be wrong? Topol's verdict is blunt: our current cancer screening strategy is "still stuck in the 1960s." For a long time, for the five major cancers — breast, colorectal, lung, cervical and prostate — the medical establishment's only screening criterion has been age: for example, start colonoscopies or mammograms at 50. This crude strategy has three consequences: First, it's extremely ineffective. In the United States, mass screening detects only 14% of cancers, yet costs more than US$40 billion a year. Second, false positives and overtreatment. Take mammograms for breast cancer: over a ten-year screening cycle, about half of women will get a "false positive" — even though 88% of them will never develop breast cancer in their lifetime. Worse, one in seven women aged 50 to 74 has been "overdiagnosed": tiny lesions that would never have threatened their lives are found and treated, putting healthy people through surgery and chemotherapy they didn't need. Third, it misses young people. In recent years, the incidence of colon cancer and other malignancies among people in their twenties and thirties has surged, and one-size-fits-all screening built on a 50-year threshold doesn't reach them at all — by the time they're diagnosed, it's often already late-stage. So what do we do? Topol says future screening must abandon "age determinism" and turn to technologies such as AI and genetic assessment to pinpoint each person's disease risk. A study of a Finnish genetic database covering 450,000 people showed that, using polygenic risk scores, those in the top 1% of risk should begin colorectal cancer screening at 49, while the lowest-risk 20% could safely wait until 67. There's nothing wrong with check-ups themselves. What's wrong is measuring everyone with the same ruler. 7. Further out: reprogramming cells, and AI that can hear ageing At the end of this part, Topol looks further ahead. The first is cellular reprogramming. Shinya Yamanaka, winner of the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, discovered that activating four specific transcription factors can turn adult cells back to a younger state, erasing the marks of ageing that the years leave behind. The technique has already been validated in primates — after precise cellular editing in crab-eating macaques, the biological age of some tissues fell by 5 to 7 years. But Topol also offers a warning: the technology is far from mature, and the slightest misstep in reprogramming cells could trigger cancer. How to find the precise balance point between "turning back the clock" and "cells running out of control" remains the core unsolved problem in the field. The second is AI. Topol says there is a decades-long "silent window" between us and disease — heart disease, cancer and Alzheimer's often take more than 20 years of slow accumulation before they strike. All that time, the body is quietly sending out signals; we just haven't had tools sensitive enough to catch them. AI is the first technology truly capable of hearing those signals. For example, a trained AI model can analyse the features of a person's voice — not what they say, but how they say it: whether their speech has slowed, whether the rhythm of their pauses is unusual, whether subtle slips have crept into their word choice. These changes are imperceptible to the naked eye. But AI can raise a warning six years before the symptoms of Alzheimer's actually appear. The body has always been talking; we just couldn't hear it before. 8. Lifestyle+: be social, not lonely Still, Topol doesn't land on these new technologies. He says that rather than pinning our hopes on technology that isn't mature yet, we'd do better to look to ourselves — and improve our healthy lifespan in lower-barrier ways. He calls this "Lifestyle+." So what's the "+"? Popular health advice has always been about diet, exercise and sleep. Topol says that isn't enough — social factors have to be added. Be social, not lonely. A long-term health tracking study of 2.2 million people showed that loneliness raises the risk of premature death from all causes by 32%, cardiovascular death by 34%, and cancer death by 24%. And "social isolation" — a lack of social contact — raises the risk of premature death almost as much as smoking, obesity and physical inactivity, and increases the risk of dementia by 50%. These numbers line up, quietly, with what the Wellderly project found in my last post: those 1,400 super-healthy older people were almost all optimistic and sociable — bridge, dancing, volunteering, still needed by life in their nineties. So it wasn't that they were lively because they were healthy. Quite possibly, they were healthy because they were lively. Final Thoughts These notes boil down to four lines: 1. Eat: there is no universal perfect diet. The answer isn't in a recipe; it's in your microbiome, how you eat, and how your body responds; 2. Move: beyond cardio, take strength seriously. Sixty minutes of resistance training a week lowers all-cause mortality by about 25% — and starting at seventy is not too late; 3. Screen: more check-ups aren't necessarily better. One-size-fits-all screening by age is outdated; the future belongs to precise screening tailored to individual risk; 4. Connect: the harm of loneliness is on par with smoking. Good friends rival the very best longevity drug. Having written all this, I realise that what this book really wants to say may come down to one sentence: Longevity isn't a secret waiting to be discovered; it's a daily practice. As for the truth about supplements, that's further on in the book. I'll report back once I've finished it. To be continued.

Over the years, I've read quite a few books about longevity. Most of them, once finished, just reconfirmed common knowledge I already had. But with Super Agers , which came out in Chinese only in March 2026, I stopped halfway through. Because it quietly dismantles two "truths" we've been taught since childhood: First, longevity comes down to genes — if your parents lived long, chances are you will too; Second, master a healthy lifestyle — eat well, exercise regularly, get regular check-ups, take a few supplements — and you'll live longer. This book says: longevity has little to do with your genes. And a large part of the so-called healthy lifestyle, such as check-ups and supplements, may not help you live longer either. As someone who has taken NMN regularly for years, I paused when I read this. First, the author. Eric Topol is a leading American cardiologist, a professor of molecular medicine, and one of the ten most-cited researchers in medicine worldwide. Not a wellness blogger — a frontline scientist. To write this book, he spent six years following 1,400 people over the age of 80 with no chronic disease. Below are my notes on the first part, along with some personal reflections — enjoy: 1. Three billion base pairs sequenced, and no "longevity gene" found In 2008, Topol launched a project called the "Wellderly," dedicated to finding people who were at least 80, had never been seriously ill, and had no chronic diseases. How strict was that standard? It took them nearly six years to find 1,400 people. They then sequenced all 3 billion base pairs of these people's genomes, hoping to find the "longevity code" hidden in their DNA. The result: they found nothing. There was no magic "longevity gene" in these super-healthy elders' genes. Their genetic risk markers for Alzheimer's and heart disease were almost no different from those of ordinary people. 2. Their genes had nothing in common — but their way of living did The real finding lay outside the genes. These people, with an average age of 84, had a few things in common: They were noticeably leaner — on average about 13 kilograms lighter than their peers. "Being lean in old age is worth more than gold," as the old Chinese saying goes; the ancients did not deceive us; They exercised more; They were better educated; They were very optimistic and deeply engaged socially — bridge clubs, dancing, circles of friends, and many were community volunteers. There's a detail in the book I love: Some of them were still so busy in their nineties that the researchers had a hard time booking them in to take part in the study. In your nineties, and still needed by life — That's probably the best picture of growing old I've ever read. Notice: lean, active, optimistic, sociable. Not one of these four things is written in your genes. All of them can be cultivated. 3. Three parts fate, seven parts effort So do genes not matter at all? Not quite. The figures Topol gives are: genes account for roughly 25-30% of the influence on lifespan; lifestyle and environmental factors account for 70-75%. "Three parts fate, seven parts effort" — it turns out the old saying has literature to back it up. Even if we didn't draw a "longevity gene," we can still significantly extend our healthspan through lifestyle. 4. Healthspan ≠ Lifespan This is the most important distinction in the whole book. Topol is talking about "healthspan," not "lifespan." Lifespan is how many years you live; Healthspan is the number of years you live in optimal health — free of disease or disability. Ten more years in a hospital bed and ten more years in your study, in the mountains, and beside your family are two completely different things. What we should really be tending was never the total number, but the stretch within it when we're clear-headed, free, and strong enough to love. 5. Topol himself is the evidence Topol is frank that he "inherited bad genes": His father went blind from diabetes at 49; His mother died of cancer in her early fifties. But he didn't bow to his genes. He is 72 this year and still doing frontline research, and in 2025 he was named one of 25 people in the US who have made major contributions in fields such as business, education and public health. Many people write about longevity. Few have made their own lives the evidence. 6. An experiment on himself: ultra-processed food What shook me most in the first part was a cautionary example — from Topol's friend, the British researcher Chris van Tulleken. He wanted to test one question: just how much damage does an unhealthy lifestyle do to your health? The "unhealthy lifestyle" he chose had only one element: eating more ultra-processed food day to day. What is ultra-processed food? Take the potato as an example: A potato dug out of the ground — unprocessed food; Shredded in the kitchen, with salt, vinegar, soy sauce and chilli added, and stir-fried into a plate of hot-and-sour potato strips — processed food; Mashed in a factory, rapidly dehydrated, mixed with emulsifiers, fried in hydrogenated oil, flavoured with artificial flavourings, and made into vacuum-packed crisps — ultra-processed food. In a nutshell: industrially produced, the original ingredients barely recognisable, with industrial ingredients and additives you'd never use in a home kitchen. Van Tulleken pushed the share of ultra-processed food in his daily diet straight up to 80%. After one month, unsurprisingly, he had gained 14 jin (7 kg). But gaining weight was the least noteworthy side effect of the experiment. What was truly frightening was the data from the in-depth medical tests that followed. His brain had been rewired. An MRI scan showed that between the area at the back of the cerebellum responsible for "unconscious habits" and the area of the limbic system responsible for "addiction," an extremely active high-speed connection had been forcibly built. This meant that when he reached for crisps, it had long since stopped being because he was hungry — It had become a compulsive, mechanical action, like not being able to stop scrolling your phone in the middle of the night. The precise formulations of industrial food had directly hijacked his neural circuits. His body, too, had gone into systemic abnormality. Hunger-related hormones soared, and C-reactive protein, a marker of whole-body inflammation, doubled outright. In effect, he had made himself spend an entire month hungry, craving, and inflamed all over. 7. Identical twins: the same genes, outcomes 40 jin apart The experiment had a second half. Van Tulleken brought in his identical twin brother to take part as well. In theory, with identical genes and both eating 80% ultra-processed food, they should have gained roughly the same amount of weight. In the end, his brother gained 54 jin in a month — a full 40 jin (20 kg) more than van Tulleken himself. The reason was that the brother had layered other bad habits on top. The same genes, a different way of living, one month — a 40-jin difference. Genes aren't everything; lifestyle matters more — It's hard to find a cleaner proof than that. Final Thoughts Marcus Aurelius wrote in Meditations : you have only a limited time, and if you do not use it to clear the clouds from your soul, it will pass, and you will pass, never to return. After finishing this part, I thought: genes are probably the share that fate allots us — But how we live always remains within our own power. Be a little leaner, get moving, stay optimistic, stay connected to people. None of these four things is expensive, but all of them need to start today, to be built up slowly. As for the truth about check-ups and supplements, that's in the later chapters of the book. When I've finished reading, I'll report back. To be continued.
Language, the Oldest Brain-Computer Interface: Seven Thoughts on the AI Native Family Office

Founder's Notes Lately, as I build my company, I've been feeling more and more strongly that AI's impact on family offices won't just show up in who's better at asset allocation or who writes better research reports. It will show up at a more fundamental level: rebuilding understanding, and redefining delivery. A few scattered thoughts — writing them down, writing them down. Thought One Feeding AI your past articles, diaries, meeting transcripts and talks is an early, rough kind of "brain-computer interface." By "brain-computer interface" I don't mean the narrow sense of implanting a device in the brain, but something broader: how the outside world gets into a person's cognition, and how that cognition is in turn read and rewritten from outside. Language is exactly this kind of ancient interface. Its influence on people is often underestimated precisely because it's so commonplace. Of course, language can't capture the whole of a person. A person's experience, intuition, bodily sense, shame, fear, need for control and sense of responsibility mostly can never be fully put into words. Text has never equalled the person, and records have never equalled the full picture of consciousness. Even so, language is still today's most widespread, lowest-cost and highest-leverage cognitive interface. Because it is constantly "reading and writing" our brains: words of encouragement can rewrite a person's judgement of risk; a new name can change how a group understands something; a good question can compress vague anxiety into something that can be discussed and decided. Neuroplasticity means the nervous system changes its structure, function and connections in response to internal and external stimuli. In other words, language is not just a tool of expression — it is also a tool for shaping cognition. People speak at about 150 words a minute; the bandwidth isn't high, but the penetration runs very deep. A person's full consciousness can't be exhausted by language, yet language remains humanity's most widespread, lowest-cost and most powerful brain-computer interface. Thought Two The family office has never been an industry that simply handles wealth. On the surface it manages assets; underneath, it is dealing with "people problems." The hardest things in a family usually aren't in the financial statements or the legal clauses. They're in a "let's wait and see" at a meeting, in a silence, a change of subject, a complaint tossed off lightly. What a family office really manages is, on the surface, money — and underneath, always, cognition organised by language: how to define "safety" how to define "fairness" how to define "is the next generation ready" how to define "conservative" and even, how to define "why do we still want to hold on to this wealth" None of these are purely financial questions. They are first people questions, then structural questions, and only last product questions. And because of this, the traditional family office is, at heart, a high-priced handicraft. Thought Three The three great dilemmas of the family office: 1. Over-reliance on a handful of "decagon partners" who understand law, tax, investment and human nature all at once; knowledge sinks into individual heads and never into the system; 2. Sell-side commissions seep in like poison, quietly rewriting advice; 3. The family's most crucial unspoken needs are steadily worn away through round after round of meetings, note-taking, retelling and delivery. I call this "the entropy of trust." Advisers take commissions, institutions have KPIs, lawyers want to wall off risk, tax advisers only calculate tax, investment managers only watch returns — no one stands in the family's shoes and looks down on the whole picture. Every expert works faithfully on their own island, but put together, what the family gets is a plan that's neither fish nor fowl. Worse: every few years a core adviser leaves, someone new arrives, and the family has to explain itself all over again. A decade's worth of accumulated understanding of the family — the founder's worries, the second generation's pressures, the wife's unspoken anxiety about risk — all reset to zero. What the family really wanted to protect often ends up reduced to a set of clauses that are rigorous in form and very low-resolution in substance. Thought Four AI will rewrite this industry's most fundamental mode of production. What large language models truly unlock is not the ability to answer questions, but, for the first time, the chance for machines to process humanity's most important unstructured data at scale — language. AI absolutely should not be just "a smarter investment adviser." It can continuously record, compare, abstract and review; it can spot contradictions between earlier and later statements; it can identify topics that keep getting sidestepped; it can gradually distil "what's left unsaid" into a structured cognitive map of the family. For the family office industry, this means that for the first time we have a chance to turn long-term understanding of a family from individual experience into an organisational asset and a system asset. What we should build isn't a "family office ChatGPT," but a complete cognitive system for family succession: it recognises the family's consciousness and expands the family's cognitive bandwidth; it doesn't make decisions for the family, but preserves — over the long term, continuously and traceably — the family's true ranking of values, its language of risk, its relational tensions and its decision-making style. Thought Five Commercially, this is a market with enormous potential. First, there's the tide of the times. According to Deloitte, the number of single family offices worldwide grew from about 6,130 in 2019 to 8,030 in 2024, and may reach 10,720 by 2030; their AUM is projected to grow from US$3.1 trillion to US$5.4 trillion. McKinsey notes that from 2023 to 2030, about US$5.8 trillion in intergenerational wealth transfer is expected among HNW/UHNW households in Asia-Pacific, while the number of single family offices in Hong Kong and Singapore has grown to about 4,000 since 2020. Second, the real big opportunity isn't in existing family offices, but in pushing the capability downmarket. McKinsey's analysis shows that only about 5% of UHNW households in Asia-Pacific have a single family office, compared with over 15% in Europe and the US; in Asia-Pacific, a single family office with AUM above US$100 million typically has operating costs of 1–3%, and below that size the operating cost ratio can even reach 4–6%. At the same time, staff costs are often the largest expense, accounting for 45–65% of operating expenses. This means that once AI can replace most junior, repetitive, standardisable labour, what it changes isn't a single process but the economics of the entire industry: capabilities that could once only be supplied by extremely high-cost organisations can, for the first time, potentially be productised, platformised and made continuous. One of McKinsey's views on the future of wealth management: as AI, data integration and platform automation advance, the integrated capabilities once available only to UHNW family offices will gradually extend to broader HNW and even affluent client segments — "when every client is a family office." Services will also move from single-point investment advice towards integrating family governance, tax and estate structuring, trust administration, insurance, philanthropy, medical concierge and lifestyle services. Another McKinsey view is also worth chewing on: in wealth management, task-based efficiency tools can already save advisers 20–30% of their time; and as AI moves further towards intelligent orchestration and team-level complex workflow applications, what changes isn't just a few minutes saved, but the very logic of growth and delivery. What's really worth building isn't a note-taker, but a system that links understanding, execution and review into a closed loop. Thought Six An AI Native family office isn't about "removing the human." Quite the opposite — it raises the bar for the "human" even higher. AI first eats up a large amount of junior, repetitive, standardisable labour. What gets freed up isn't the "human" as such, but people's time, judgement and empathy. It lets people deliver, at lower marginal cost, service that is more stable, more private and more continuous than the traditional model. But language can never exhaust a person, so I don't believe a system can "copy a person" either. And that's precisely not bad news. Because the most promising thing about AI has never been replacing a person's full consciousness, but becoming a high-quality, sustainable, correctable interface for cognitive interaction: it helps the family express itself more accurately, understand one another more clearly, build up judgement over the longer term, and, in decision after critical decision, ask the right questions. A truly high-calibre system shouldn't pretend it fully understands a family: it should know that language conceals, know that it can only reach the expressible layer, know that silence is also information, and know where it must probe further, where it must not overstep, and where only a human can judge and bear the consequences. AI handles the process, humans handle the key points. AI handles memory, alignment, retrieval and scenario modelling, humans handle judgement, ethics, boundaries and taste. To truly achieve — High Tech, High Touch. Not a bunch of programs serving a family, but a group of people who can own the results, using an AI brain to deliver high-density service that was impossible before. Thought Seven Open up the "black box of trust." Values are the soul of an organisation. In large traditional institutions, people are both the process and the nerve endings; values often lose out to KPIs, and people's actions always get distorted. But in an AI Native organisation, values have, for the first time, a chance to be written into processes, permissions, blocking mechanisms and review standards — becoming something executable, auditable, even testable. A buy-side stance no longer has to be merely a professional virtue; it can gradually become a system constraint. For the family office industry, this will be a very deep restructuring. In a sense, it's closer to the platform I want to build. Our Technical Path We're working to build two things: Single Source of Truth In plain terms: a tamper-proof master ledger of the family's will Within a family, the preferences and decisions shown by different people, in different settings and with different needs, aren't just different — they can contradict each other: over dinner with the lawyer, the lawyer, for compliance's sake, notes down only: "set up a trust in the Cayman Islands." On the golf course with the private banker, the banker, wanting to sell wealth products, notes down only: "the family needs 8% annual cash-flow dividends." During a fight with his son, he shouts: "If you carry on like this, forget about ever getting on the board!" The son remembers that line. This is what you call "multiple sources of truth." The family's true intentions are torn into fragments, scattered across three different people's heads. Once conflict breaks out, the documents and testimony these three produce all contradict one another, and the family is instantly plunged into an inheritance fight that tears it apart from within. Arcus42's Single Source of Truth (SSOT): we use AI to take in all these fragments, reconcile and clean them, and form a single, complete, tamper-proof "family digital master ledger." This ledger contains not only trust clauses and cash-flow requirements, but also "the boundaries of people's power." The point of a "Single Source of Truth" is this: whether 50 or 100 years have passed, however many rounds of lawyers and bankers have come and gone, when the family faces a major decision, Arcus42's system holds one single "panoramic map of true intent," undistorted by interested parties. That is irreplaceable trust. "Super Control Tower" In plain terms: an "air traffic control centre" hovering above the entire family Buying services for family succession today is like building a plane with no control tower. The tax adviser says: "To avoid tax, let's move all the assets to Singapore." The lawyer says: "No — under Singapore's marriage law, your son could risk walking away with nothing." The investment manager says: "All the money is stuck in the structure — I can't invest in that fantastic unicorn I saw yesterday!" Everyone gives the "optimal solution" from inside their own deep professional well, but added together, the whole family's operations end up in a mid-air collision. Super Control Tower: the control tower is originally a concept from aviation and global supply chains. The airport tower doesn't fly the planes (it doesn't directly sell wealth products or draft legal documents), but it can see every plane's flight path and is responsible for coordinating and dispatching them to prevent collisions. Answers will eventually go out of date. A system that can remember, reflect, evolve — and knows its boundaries — will become the most important new infrastructure for family succession in the age of AI. I'll put this out there for now, and I'd love to hear from anyone who shares this view or is interested — come and talk it through with me!

One Mother, Nine Children: A Century of Kennedy Family Glory

A Message for Women's Day May you wear gentleness as your armor, resilient and full of love, blooming through the years and enduring through what you pass on. Today I want to share my guiding light with you — Rose Fitzgerald Kennedy, daughter of a Boston mayor, wife of the US ambassador to Britain, mother of President JFK; a woman of the century who raised nine children and held up America's foremost political dynasty, forging love, discipline and mission into a family cornerstone that has lasted a hundred years. She is one of the women who has influenced me most, and The Nine of Us , the book written by her daughter Jean, US ambassador to Ireland, completely changed how I understand women's strength. Rose The work is from the Women of Kennedy series supported by the Kennedy family, created by the renowned artist Vincent Xeus, and is in the collection of Arcus42's founding family. In many people's minds, the Kennedys are one of America's most legendary political families. One president, several senators, and many activists and philanthropists. For over a century, this family has kept shaping America in politics, business and public service. But if we turn the clock back, we discover — the Kennedy family wasn't born into glory; it began with a mother. Her name was Rose Fitzgerald Kennedy. Over her lifetime she raised nine children. Nine children, each a pillar Upbringing is a family's real strength. Rose regarded raising children as "the most noble profession in the world," and with a replicable set of family education principles, she led each child toward excellence: Eldest son Joseph Jr.: the family's benchmark, a World War II hero, a role model of courage and responsibility Second son John: the 35th President of the United States, who embodied the ideals and style of an era; Third son Robert: US Attorney General, a steadfast champion of civil rights and fairness; Youngest son Edward: the "Lion of the Senate," one of the most influential senators in American history, serving 47 years; Daughter Eunice: founded the Special Olympics, rewriting the fate of people with disabilities through love and inclusion; Daughter Jean: US Ambassador to Ireland, carrying on the family's mission of public service; The other daughters also worked deeply in charity, society and public causes, becoming extensions of the family spirit. Rose never saw herself as "the mother of a political family." In her view, her real job was something more long-term: building a family with responsibility, conviction and discipline. With an exceptional sense of order, firm faith and a quiet, unshowy strength, she became the Kennedy family's anchor. The starting point: coming from a Boston political family Rose was born into a family already steeped in public spirit. Her father, John F. Fitzgerald, had been mayor of Boston and was a prominent early Irish-American politician. From childhood, she lived in an environment where politics wasn't power, but a public responsibility. Later, she married Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. — an extremely ambitious businessman and political figure. But many historians believe: the Kennedy family's spirit and character came not from the father, but from the mother. Joseph Kennedy was in charge of building wealth; Rose Kennedy was in charge of building order. A family of nine children: discipline matters more than talent Rose's expectations of her children were very clear. She believed: success comes from habits, not talent. At home, there were a few clear rules: Read every day Write letters every day Pay attention to current affairs Take part in family discussions In The Nine of Us , Jean also mentions something very interesting: Rose kept a record card for each child, listing: Grades Interests Health Friends Strengths In a family of nine children, this was almost a household management system. Someone later remarked: Rose was really running something like a small organization. She once said: "Life is not a matter of milestones, but of moments." Life isn't defined by achievements; it's made up of experiences. The "family parliament" at the dinner table There are so many wonderful details from inside the Kennedy household, and one of the most famous traditions was the discussion at the dinner table. Every day Rose would set out freshly ironed newspapers for the children, and their father would pose questions at the table, such as: "If you were president, how would you handle the war in Europe?" "If the country faced an economic crisis, what would you do?" "Why would a certain politician make a decision like that?" Every child had to express their own view. In Jean's memory, family dinners were almost like a small forum. Many years later, Robert Kennedy recalled: our dinner table was our first university. From a family governance perspective, this was actually a very advanced way of educating children. What it produced wasn't "obedient children," but members with judgment. When disaster strikes a family, who is its anchor? Rose's life wasn't only glory. She went through many family tragedies: 1941: her daughter Rosemary Kennedy was left permanently disabled by surgery 1944: her eldest son Joseph Kennedy Jr. was killed in World War II 1948: her second daughter Kathleen Kennedy died in a plane crash 1963: her second son, President John F. Kennedy, was assassinated 1968: her third son Robert F. Kennedy was assassinated 1969: her husband Joseph died A mother lost four children. Fate tested her in the harshest possible way, yet through daily Mass, a strict routine and unceasing charity work, she pieced what was broken back into a whole, and turned pain into legacy. She wasn't crushed; instead, she showed astonishing resilience. At 69 she learned to drive a car; at 80 she learned to ski like a young person. Her optimism and composure in the face of upheaval became the spiritual pillar that carried the whole extended family through one adversity after another. She once said something very famous: "Birds sing after a storm. Why shouldn't people?" After a storm the birds still sing — so why can't people? Many historians believe it was precisely this spirit that let the Kennedy family keep its enormous public influence after tragedy upon tragedy. This is exactly the core of the "family governance" that we at Arcus42 value — people are a family's core asset; only people can play the crucial role in major decisions and crises, helping a family make it through cycles and change. A legacy beyond wealth Rose died in 1995 at the age of 104. Her long life itself made her a living bearer of the family's memory and values; she witnessed the upheavals of the 20th century and passed the family's stories and spirit on to her grandchildren and even great-grandchildren. In 1951, in recognition of her "exemplary motherhood and charitable works," the Vatican gave Rose the title of "Papal Countess" (Countess of the Holy See); she was the sixth American woman to receive this honor. It was not just a religious honor, but recognition of the social value she had created as a mother and philanthropist. Looking back on the lives of Rose and her children — through John F. Kennedy's Peace Corps, the Special Olympics founded by Eunice Kennedy, Robert Kennedy's justice reforms and social advocacy, and the whole family's sustained commitment to public service — the Kennedy family's influence long ago went beyond political power and the accumulation of the family's own wealth, becoming a symbol of the pursuit of social progress. Every member of the Kennedy family has a remarkable story, and I hope to have the chance to write about them at length; they show what "passing on goodness" looks like in concrete form. These brilliant stars of human history are precisely the source of Arcus42's values — passing on the family's spirit and sense of responsibility to future generations, so that family wealth resonates with human well-being. We believe "passing on goodness" isn't only charitable giving; it's also actively sharing professional expertise, practical experience and systems thinking, so that every family deserves a better legacy: values, judgment, and an understanding of the future. Rose's life is the most vivid illustration of "passing on goodness." At the end of The Nine of Us , Rose's youngest daughter Jean wrote: "We were lucky children indeed." We were truly lucky children. And that luck wasn't only because of wealth.
