Learn to Rest, and Rest for Real.

Spring Festival greetings First of all, to my friends, partners and family! Happy Spring Festival! Wishing you a lucky Year of the Horse! ㊗️ Wishing you, and those who love you and those you love, that everyone you hold dear stays by your side, and every wish in your heart comes true. Amid all the rushing about, may you keep your composure; amid lofty ambitions, may you never forget gentleness. The world is vast, and the heart roams free. Me, off the grid I'm so sorry that I didn't reply in time to the many greetings friends sent me this Spring Festival. I've been trying to focus on resting (though I haven't done it all that well). This is a really important thing: since I started my company in 2025 my rhythm has been a bit out of whack, so I tried to use the Spring Festival to tune myself back in. Today I'm getting ready to go back to work, and before I head off, I want to write a little about "rest". "Leisure" makes us civilised Real spiritual growth in human beings happens precisely in the time that isn't driven by utility. As Russell said: leisure makes us civilised. A civilised society must give people leisure. Without leisure, there is no real thought or creation. —— In Praise of Idleness , Bertrand Russell In an age of information overload, we have holidays, but we aren't necessarily resting. Because passive rest isn't necessarily recovery. Lying around scrolling on your phone, eating and drinking to excess, sleeping until you wake up naturally — none of these are necessarily good ways to rest. In those moments our nervous system hasn't switched modes; it is still in a state of high-frequency information input, rapid decision-making, emotional swings and external evaluation. On this, the Harvard Business Review has put forward a concept —— Leisure Planning. Design your own recovery system What is "leisure planning"? Leisure planning emphasises three things: Setting personal goals Building social connections Learning and growth The point isn't "efficiency", but resting intentionally and a sense of engagement. Eleven field studies of more than 2,400 working professionals showed that, compared with passive forms of leisure, people who do leisure planning have more energy, more stable moods, greater happiness, a stronger sense of autonomy and competence, and higher work engagement and creativity. The good part is that planning doesn't take more time — it only takes changing how you do it. My Spring Festival "recovery system" 1️⃣ Nervous system recovery At least 1 hour of screen-free time every day Getting some sun Deep breathing Low stimulation, to reset the sympathetic nervous system. 2️⃣ Metabolic system recovery Setting aside one "light-eating day" A 15-minute walk after meals Drinking fresh homemade yoghurt Letting the body recover, for steadier moods. 3️⃣ Cognitive system recovery Making fewer decisions Less pointless socialising Removing one long-standing source of drain Saving cognitive energy 4️⃣ Emotional system recovery: doing housework, decluttering; journalling, sorting through my emotions; cuddling cats and hugging dogs; feeling and taking care of my own emotions 5️⃣ Meaning system recovery: giving gifts to friends Reading the cards friends gave me for my birthday, and feeling loved. Coming back to my original intentions Besides sleeping, exercise is rest too Stretching Gentle yoga And allowing myself to do nothing at all Simply zoning out, completely emptying my mind; binge-watching the TV dramas Yongzheng Empire and Zhu Yuanzhang with Grandma. After all, balance matters more than perfection.
A Love Letter Four Years Late

January 10, 2026, the Hong Kong Palace Museum, Gaoshan's tenth anniversary. As one of the alumni, I gave a TED-style talk. Because of time, I didn't get through my whole script, which left me with a few regrets. So here is the original text — This is a love letter four years late, from someone who found her spiritual homeland, turning back to speak to her fellow travelers. To show my sincerity, this script was written entirely by hand — no AI. Gaoshan: the end of the road for business schools I'm an investor, and I love learning of all kinds. I've studied at Peking University, Oxford, Harvard and other institutions, so when friends ask me what kind of place Gaoshan Academy is, I tell them, a little mysteriously: Gaoshan is where business school ends. If I had to describe my Gaoshan experience in a single word, it would be: life changing. And it's not just me — whenever I talk with classmates, everyone feels the same. I enrolled in February 2022. In March, at the opening ceremony, our self-introductions were like a stand-up comedy show — we laughed until we doubled over, and at the same time I was filled with admiration. Everyone had something in them I wanted to become, and it rekindled my thinking about how many ways there are to live a life. In April, Shanghai went into lockdown, and Gaoshan quickly set up mutual-aid groups. In circumstances that hard, classmates were arranging supplies, connecting people with medical care, and picking up and delivering things every single day. That was when I felt I hadn't just signed up for a program — it was more like I'd joined some secret society, a brotherhood. In August came our first in-person module, in Inner Mongolia. Together we watched a red moon rise over the grassland and meteors streak above the bonfire. By day, we learned from Professor Zhang Shuangnan about the evolution of the universe, wormholes, black holes, white holes and the multiverse; by night, under the Perseid meteor shower, we listened to a concert of suona, violin, guzheng and piano playing together. It still feels magical to me. Live a GASA Life After that, there were courses and activities big and small every month. You could say that if you wanted to, you could truly live a GASA life. The US Releases Its National Security Strategy

What is the National Security Strategy? Late at night on December 4, 2025, the White House released a 33-page National Security Strategy. As the Trump administration's first overarching global strategy since returning to the White House, it is one of the highest-level guiding documents in US national security. The National Security Strategy is a national security policy guidance document that, under the Goldwater–Nichols Department of Defense Reorganization Act of 1986, is signed and issued by the President and submitted to Congress. Since the Reagan administration first issued one in 1987, each administration has used it to set out America's national security goals for a given period, its reading of the international situation, and its strategy for using national power in diplomacy, economics, the military and other areas￼￼￼. At its core, the version released by the Trump administration this time pulls back the global strategic front lines and focuses on core interests, proposing to abandon the idea of global hegemony and shift the strategic centre of gravity to the homeland and the Western Hemisphere. It not only serves as the core guide to how the US government will govern, but also profoundly affects global geopolitics, US–China relations and how America works with its allies. I've copied out the report's outline and content below — savour it yourselves 😂 I. What Is America's Strategy? 1. How America's "Strategy" Went Astray 2. President Trump's Necessary and Welcome Correction II. What Should America Pursue? 1. What Do We Actually Want? 2. What Do We Want from the World? III. What Means Does America Have to Achieve These Aims? IV. Strategy 1. Principles 2. Priorities 3. Regions A. Western Hemisphere B. Asia C. Europe D. Middle East E. Howard Marks: Is AI in a Bubble?

On December 9, Howard Marks published a memo at Oaktree Capital titled "Is It a Bubble?" It lays out, clearly and systematically, that the real risk of an AI bubble lies not in the technology failing, but in this: we are betting on an "incalculable future." Good technology does not equal a good investment. This is a great, great, great piece, and I strongly recommend reading the whole thing. That said, I've quickly summarised the five insights I took away from it. As for whether there really is a bubble… that's for each of you to judge. Highlight 1. The biggest risk of AI is not "the bubble bursting" but "the bubble being impossible to price." This is not 1999, and it is not 2007. So far, when it comes to AI, we… don't know its final form (tool / platform / infrastructure / general intelligence) don't know where the profits will go (model companies / cloud providers / chipmakers / the application layer) don't know the competitive structure (oligopoly / commoditisation / open-source disruption) don't know the time horizon (5 years? 10 years? or an exponential leap?) What this means: the market isn't "mispricing" so much as forcibly modelling something that cannot be modelled. That makes it different from traditional bubbles. 2. "Inflection bubbles" are dangerous precisely because they make wrong decisions look like right ones. Railways, electricity, the internet, AI… are essential to civilisation, but not necessarily to investors. What history shows again and again is this: the more real the technological progress, the easier it is for investors to justify "the wrong price, the wrong company, the wrong structure." In the AI context, it sounds like: "The direction is right, never mind whether it's worth it; this is infrastructure, you can't judge it by traditional ROI; as long as you back the winner, nothing else matters"… The most dangerous thing about inflection bubbles: they systematically dull investors' sensitivity to mistakes. 3. This may be the first technological revolution with deep debt involvement. This is the most underrated — and most lethal — insight in the whole piece. Past technological revolutions — railways, electricity, the internet… — were mostly trial-and-errored with equity capital. This time, though, we have… 30-year bonds off-balance-sheet SPV structures data centres as collateral long-term fixed interest We are moving at scale into a highly uncertain technology race. Debt only works when "the outcome is uncertain but can be assessed." When "the outcome is pure guesswork," debt is dangerous. In the past, technological failure ≠ financial failure; this time, technological failure will mean stress on the financial system. The question isn't "will the bubble burst?" but "if something goes wrong, will the financial structure amplify it into a systemic event?" 4. The AI industry is already showing a "perpetual-motion-machine"-style financial illusion. This is a very contemporary, very concrete risk. It doesn't say OpenAI or Nvidia have a problem; it points to a structural illusion — A gives B money B uses that money to buy A's services Both sides get to "talk growth, talk investment, talk future" This genuinely happened in the 1990s telecom bubble, and ultimately produced a boom that "looked profitable, while the system created no real external demand." When most of an industry's demand comes from "players buying from one another," the market overestimates how mature real societal demand is. This badly misleads: the pace of capital allocation the scale of capacity build-out judgements about debt sustainability 5. AI may, for the first time, simultaneously destroy the "work–income–meaning" trinity. This isn't an emotional postscript; it's the ethical foundation of the whole piece. If what AI replaces is entry-level jobs + cognitive work + apprenticeship paths, then how does society go on producing "experienced people"? This isn't Luddite (anti-technology) anxiety but a structural paradox — AI raises productivity → fewer jobs Fewer jobs → lower purchasing power Experience-building jobs disappear → professional pipelines break Loss of meaning → less social stability This means AI's risk isn't just an economic cycle but a reshaping of the social structure. These conclusions deserve real vigilance and serious attention, and even more precious is Howard's brilliant line of reasoning. Here goes — enjoy: Is It a Bubble? We are living through an extraordinary moment in world history. A transformative technology is emerging, and its backers claim it will change the world forever. To build it, companies must invest sums far beyond anything in living memory. News coverage is full of widespread worry that America's largest companies are propping up a bubble that is about to burst. When I visited clients in Asia and the Middle East last month, I was often asked: is there a bubble around artificial intelligence? Those discussions are what prompted this memo. As usual, I'll start with some disclaimers: I don't take part in the stock market; I simply regard it as the best barometer of investor psychology. Nor am I a technology expert — I know no more about AI than most generalist investors. But I'll do my best. The most interesting thing about bubbles is their "regularity" — not regularity in timing, but consistency in how they unfold. Something new and seemingly revolutionary appears and quietly works its way into people's minds. It fires the imagination, and the excitement quickly gets out of hand. Early participants reap enormous gains; onlookers are filled with intense envy and regret, and, driven by the fear of continuing to miss out, they rush in. They don't know what the future holds, nor do they care whether the price they're paying can deliver a reasonable return at an acceptable level of risk. The result, almost always, is pain for investors in the short to medium term, even if, given a long enough time, they may eventually come out ahead. I've lived through several bubbles and read many accounts of others, and every one of them fits this description. You might think the losses from past bubbles bursting would be enough to prevent the next one from forming. But they aren't, and I'm convinced they never will be. Memories are short, and prudence and natural risk aversion are no match for the dream of getting rich on a revolutionary technology that "everyone knows" will change the world. The passage I quoted at the start comes from Derek Thompson's November 4 newsletter, "AI Could Be the Railroad of the 21st Century. Brace Yourself," which explores the parallels between today's AI build-out and the railroad boom of the 1860s. The fact that the passage applies word for word to both illustrates the saying often attributed to Mark Twain: "History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme." Understanding Bubbles Before getting into whether there's an AI bubble — I've read a great deal for this — I'd like to clarify a concept. People keep asking, "Is there an AI bubble?" But the question itself is ambiguous. I think we should distinguish between two different but related bubble possibilities: one in the behaviour of companies within the industry, and one in the behaviour of investors toward the industry. I'm in no position to judge whether AI companies' current aggressive expansion is justified, so I'll focus mainly on the question of a bubble in financial markets around AI. The main job of investment analysts — especially those of us from the "value investing" school — is to: (a) study companies and other assets and assess their intrinsic value and prospects; (b) make investment decisions based on that value. Most of the change analysts encounter in the short to medium term shows up in asset prices and their relationship to intrinsic value. And that relationship is, at bottom, the product of investor psychology. Market bubbles aren't caused directly by technological or financial developments, but by excessive optimism about those developments. As I wrote in my January memo "On Bubble Watch," bubbles are temporary manias in which the developments in question become the object of what former Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan called "irrational exuberance." Bubbles usually form around new financial developments (for example, the South Sea Company in the early 18th century, or subprime residential mortgage-backed securities in 2005–06) or technological advances (fibre optics in the late 1990s, the internet in 1998–2000). "Newness" plays a huge role. Without historical constraints, imagination can run wild, and the future of the new thing seems to have no ceiling. And when the future is believed to be limitless, people justify valuations far beyond historical norms, causing asset prices to become detached from their predictable earning power. My favourite description of the role of "newness" comes from a book that influenced me enormously — John Kenneth Galbraith's A Short History of Financial Euphoria . Galbraith talks about what he calls "the extreme brevity of the financial memory," and notes that in financial markets, "past experience, to the extent that it is part of memory at all, is dismissed as the primitive refuge of those who do not have the insight to appreciate the incredible wonders of the present." In other words, history can limit our awe at the present and our imagination about the future; in its absence, anything is possible. The key point: new things naturally inspire great enthusiasm, and bubbles are what happens when that enthusiasm swells to irrational levels. Who can draw the line between rational and irrational? Who can say when an optimistic market has turned into a bubble? In the end, it's simply a matter of judgement. It occurred to me last month that my two most successful "calls" came in 2000 — when I warned about the market for tech and internet stocks — and in 2005–07, when I pointed to the dearth of risk aversion and the prevalence of crazy deals ahead of the Global Financial Crisis. First, in neither case did I have any expertise in the subject of the bubble itself: the internet, or subprime mortgage-backed securities. All I did was observe the behaviour going on around me. Second, the value of my calls lay mainly in describing the foolishness of that behaviour, not in insisting on labelling it a "bubble." Getting hung up on whether to use the word "bubble" often lands people in trouble and gets in the way of sound judgement; in fact, simply by assessing what's going on around us and working out the appropriate behaviour, we can accomplish a lot. The "Benefits" of Bubbles Before going on to whether AI is in a bubble, I'd like to spend a moment on a topic that may seem rather academic for investors: the positive role of bubbles. You may feel I devote too much space to it, but I do so because I find it highly illuminating. The November 5 Stratechery newsletter was titled "The Benefits of Bubbles." In it, Ben Thompson (no relation to Derek) cites a book called Boom: Bubbles and the End of Stagnation . Its authors, Byrne Hobart and Tobias Huber, propose two kinds of bubbles: "Inflection bubbles" — the good kind, as opposed to the more destructive "mean-reversion bubbles," such as the subprime bubble of the 2000s. I think this is a very useful distinction. The financial manias I've read about or lived through — the South Sea Company, portfolio insurance, subprime mortgage-backed securities — all fired the imagination with fantasies of "high returns without risk," but no one thought they would advance humanity as a whole. No one expected the subprime movement to revolutionise housing, for example; people just thought they could make money backing new buyers. Hobart and Huber call these "mean-reversion bubbles" because they aren't expected to move the world forward. The fad simply rises and recedes. By contrast, bubbles based on technological progress — like railroads and the internet — are what they call "inflection bubbles." After such a bubble, the world doesn't go back to where it was. In these bubbles, "investors decide that the future will be meaningfully different from the past and trade accordingly." As Thompson puts it, the definitive work on bubbles has long been Carlota Perez's Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital . When Perez wrote the book in 2002, bubbles were seen as negative, something to be avoided; the world was then in the downturn following the bursting of the dot-com bubble. Perez didn't deny the pain bubbles cause. In fact, she pointed out that similar crashes marked every previous revolution, including the Industrial Revolution, railways, electricity and the automobile. In each case, the bubble was not a regret but a necessity: the speculative mania enabled what she calls the "installation period," during which large amounts of necessary but not necessarily wise investment laid the groundwork for the "deployment period" that followed. The bursting of the bubble marks the transition to the deployment period — and what underpins that period are precisely the investments that lost money. This distinction matters a great deal to Hobart and Huber, and I agree. They note: "Not all bubbles destroy wealth and value. Some can be understood as important catalysts for technological progress." But I'd restate it this way: "mean-reversion bubbles" — in which markets soar on some new financial miracle and then collapse — destroy wealth; whereas "inflection bubbles" based on revolutionary technologies accelerate technological progress and lay the foundation for a more prosperous future, while also destroying wealth. The key is not to be the investor whose wealth is destroyed in the process of driving progress. Hobart and Huber go on to describe how bubbles finance the infrastructure new technologies need, thereby accelerating their adoption: Most new technologies don't appear out of nowhere, fully formed. They build on earlier failures, trial and error, iteration and historical path dependence. Bubbles create opportunities for the capital needed for deployment, making large-scale, parallel experimentation possible and thereby speeding up potentially disruptive technologies and breakthroughs. By creating a positive "enthusiasm–investment" feedback loop, bubbles can produce net benefits. Optimism can become a self-fulfilling prophecy. Speculation provides the enormous funding high-risk exploratory projects need; enthusiasm that looks excessive in the short run, or investments that look bad, end up being the necessary starting point for social and technological innovation… A bubble may be a collective delusion, but it can also be the expression of a collective vision. That vision becomes a platform for coordinating people and capital, allowing innovation to proceed in parallel. Progress doesn't happen linearly but in bursts, simultaneously across many fields. As enthusiasm runs high, risk tolerance increases and network effects become ever more pronounced. FOMO draws in more participants, entrepreneurs and speculators, further reinforcing the positive feedback loop. Like bubbles, FOMO has a bad reputation, but sometimes it's a healthy instinct. After all, no one wants to miss a once-in-a-lifetime chance to "build the future." In other words, bubbles based on technological progress are "beneficial" because they inspire investors to pour in vast sums — a good share of which will be wasted — "carpet-bombing" a new area of opportunity and thereby kick-starting its development. The key point: if people always remained patient, cautious and rational, and stuck to value principles, building out a new technology might take many years, even decades; the frenzy of a bubble compresses that process into a very short time — a few winners earn life-changing investment returns, while vast sums are incinerated. Bubbles have both a technological and a financial dimension, but the passages above are written largely from the standpoint of those eager for technological progress, who are perfectly willing to have investors lose money for it. "We," on the other hand, want technological progress but don't want to burn money for nothing in the course of driving it. Ben Thompson ends his discussion: "This is why I'm excited about new technologies whose prospects are unknown." I love that line — it expresses both excitement about future possibilities and an acknowledgement that the shape of the future is unknowable (in our world, we'd say: the risk is extremely high). Assessing the Current Landscape Now let's get back to "seeking truth from facts." What do we know? First, I've never met anyone who doesn't believe AI has the potential to be one of the most important technologies in history. It could reshape daily life and the global economy. We also know that, in recent years, the economy and markets have come to depend more and more on AI: AI accounts for a very large share of corporate capital expenditure; capex on building AI capacity has been a major source of US GDP growth; AI stocks have contributed the great majority of the S&P 500's gains. Fortune ran this headline on October 7: 75% of gains, 80% of profits, 90% of capex — AI's grip on the S&P is total, and Morgan Stanley's top analyst is "very concerned" Beyond that, I think it's important to note that while AI-related stocks account for a disproportionate share of the gains across all stocks, the excitement AI has injected into the market has surely pushed up the prices of non-AI stocks as well. The performance of AI stocks has been astronomical, led by the AI chip leader Nvidia. Founded in 1993, the company was valued at about US$626 million when it went public in 1999, and later briefly became the world's first company with a US$5 trillion market cap. That's an increase of roughly 8,000 times, equivalent to a compound annual return of about 40% for more than 26 years. No wonder imaginations have been set on fire. Where Are the Uncertainties? It's fair to say that while we know AI will bring enormous change, almost none of us know what exactly it will be able to do, how it will be commercialised, or on what timetable. Who will the winners be? What will they be worth? When a technology is believed to be world-changing, people also tend to assume the leading companies that own it must be enormously valuable. But how accurate is that assumption? Warren Buffett observed in 1999: "The automobile was perhaps the most important invention of the first half of the 20th century… If you had foreseen in the days of the first cars how the car would shape this country, you would have said, 'This is where I must be.' But of the roughly 2,000 car companies, only three survived a few years later. So the car had an enormous impact on America, but the opposite effect on investors." — Time , January 23, 2012 In AI there are currently some extremely powerful leaders, including some of the richest and most dominant companies in the world. But new technologies have always been highly disruptive: will today's leaders win, or be displaced by latecomers? How costly will the arms race be? Who will win? What are shares in start-ups worth? Compared with leaders worth trillions of dollars, some potential challengers have enterprise values of just a few billion — or even a few million — dollars. CNBC reported on June 25, 2024: A team founded by college dropouts has raised US$120 million from investors led by Primary Venture Partners, with plans to build a new AI chip to take on Nvidia. Etched CEO Gavin Uberti said the company is betting that, as AI develops, most of the most energy-intensive computing needs will be met by customised, hard-wired ASIC chips. "If transformers go away, we're dead," Uberti told CNBC. "But if they stick around, we're the biggest company of all time." Even if Etched doesn't become "the biggest company of all time," suppose success would bring it a valuation of one-fifth of Nvidia's peak — US$1 trillion. What probability of success would you need to justify a US$120 million investment? For simplicity, assume that investment buys 100% of the equity; then as long as you believe there's a 0.1% chance of reaching a trillion-dollar valuation, the expected return is more than 8x. Who can say Etched doesn't have that chance? And if so, who wouldn't take part? This is what I call "lottery-ticket thinking": the fantasy of a huge payoff is enough — indeed, bound — to drive people into a venture with a very high probability of failure. There's nothing wrong with this way of calculating expected value in itself; top venture capitalists use it every day. But the premise is that the assumptions about the potential payoff and the probability of success must be reasonable. Once you're thinking about "trillion-dollar payoffs," any calculation can easily be overwhelmed by that fantasy and lose its reasonableness. Will AI produce profits? Who will they go to? We know almost nothing about two things: How much profit will AI bring its providers? What will its impact be on non-AI companies (the companies that use AI)? Will AI become a monopoly or duopoly, letting one or two leading companies charge high prices for its capabilities? Or will it turn into a fiercely competitive free-for-all in which many companies wage price wars for users' AI spending, turning it into a commodity? Or, more likely, will the industry take a hybrid "giants + specialists" form, with some companies competing on price and others on proprietary advantages? Some say the services that answer AI queries today (such as ChatGPT and Gemini) lose money on every query (of course, "loss leaders" are not unusual in new industries). Will the leading tech companies — used to winning in winner-take-all markets — be willing to lose money on AI for years in exchange for share? Hundreds of billions of dollars are being poured into the race for AI leadership. Who will win? What will the outcome be? Likewise, how will AI affect the companies that use it? Clearly AI is a powerful tool for raising users' productivity, including by replacing employees with labour and intelligence supplied by computers. But will this ability to cut costs lift users' profit margins? Or will it set off price wars among those companies as they fight for customers? If the latter, the cost savings may be passed on to customers rather than kept by the companies as profit. In other words: is it possible that AI raises corporate efficiency without raising corporate profitability? Should we worry about so-called "circular deals"? In the telecom boom of the late 1990s, fibre was overbuilt, and the companies that owned it traded with one another so that they could report profits. If two companies each owned fibre, it was just an asset on their books; but if each bought capacity from the other, both could report profits… so that's what they did. In other cases, equipment makers lent money to network operators to buy their equipment, when the operators didn't yet even have the customers to justify the build-out. All of this led to illusory profits. Today, some deals have come to light that give the impression of money "going round in a circle" among AI players. Those who believe there's an AI bubble can easily view these deals with suspicion: are they aimed at achieving genuine business objectives, or at exaggerating progress? Adding to the concern, critics argue that some of the deals OpenAI has struck with chipmakers, cloud computing companies and others form a strange loop: OpenAI receives billions of dollars from tech companies, then pays billions back to those same companies for computing power and other services… Nvidia, too, has done deals that raise the question of whether the company is paying itself. It announced it would invest US$100 billion in OpenAI. The start-up receives this money and, at the same time, uses it to buy or lease Nvidia's chips… Goldman Sachs estimates that 15% of Nvidia's sales next year will come from what critics likewise call "circular deals." ( The New York Times , November 20) Notably, even though OpenAI isn't yet profitable, it has made investment commitments to industry partners totalling US$1.4 trillion. The company has said explicitly that these investments will come from revenue paid to OpenAI by those same partners, and that OpenAI also has ways out of these commitments. But all of this raises the question: has the AI industry developed a "perpetual motion machine"? On this subject, I've always enjoyed articles questioning whether humans can really grasp the word "trillion." I think the idea is spot on: a million dollars is US$1 a second for 11.6 days; a billion dollars is US$1 a second for 31.7 years. We can grasp that. But a trillion dollars is US$1 a second for 31,700 years. Who can really fit the meaning of 31,700 years into their head? How long will AI assets last? We can't help wondering whether the question of "depreciation/obsolescence" is being handled correctly in the AI world. How long will AI chips last? In estimating P/E ratios for AI-related stocks, how many years of earnings growth should be assumed? Will chips and other AI infrastructure last long enough to repay the debt taken on to buy them? Will "artificial general intelligence" (a machine that can do anything the human brain can) be achieved? If it is, does that mark the end of progress, or will there be further revolutions? Which companies will win? Will businesses reach a stage where the technology stabilises and they can extract economic value from it? Or will new technologies keep threatening to replace old ones as the new path to success? On this point, two items mentioned in a Financial Times newsletter hint at how fluid the competitive landscape is: A study by MIT and the open-source AI start-up Hugging Face found that newly released Chinese open-source models rose to 17% of downloads over the past year. That exceeds the 15.8% share of US developers such as Google, Meta and OpenAI — the first time Chinese teams have overtaken their American counterparts… Nvidia's shares fell sharply yesterday on fears about Google's progress in AI, wiping US$115 billion off its market value. (FirstFT Americas, November 26) Dynamic change creates opportunities for breakthrough technologies, but the same dynamics can also threaten the dominance of leading companies. Amid all this uncertainty, investors must ask: are the assumptions of "continued success" implicit in the prices they pay fully tenable? Is the frenzy leading to speculative behaviour? To take an extreme example: in venture capital there's a trend toward US$1 billion "seed rounds" for start-ups. Here's a little anecdote: Thinking Machines, the AI start-up led by former OpenAI executive Mira Murati, just completed the largest seed round in history: US$2 billion at a US$10 billion valuation. The company hasn't released any product and declined to tell investors what exactly it plans to do. "It was the most absurd pitch meeting I've ever seen," said one investor who met with Murati. "She was basically saying, 'We're going to build an AI company with the best AI talent, but we can't answer any questions.'" ("How the AI Bubble Will Pop," Derek Thompson's Substack, October 2) But that's already "ancient history"… a mere two months ago. Here's the latest: Thinking Machines Lab, the artificial intelligence start-up founded by former OpenAI executive Mira Murati, is in early talks on a new funding round at a valuation of about US$50 billion, Bloomberg reported on Thursday. The company was valued at US$12 billion when it raised about US$2 billion in July. (Reuters, November 13) And Thinking Machines Lab isn't alone: In one of the boldest bets of the AI arms race, the stealth start-up Safe Superintelligence (SSI), founded by former OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, has raised US$2 billion at a US$32 billion valuation — even though it hasn't publicly released any product or service. (CTech by Calcalist, April 13) Where will it all end up? One problem with AI is the unusual nature of its "newness." It isn't like a traditional business, which designs and sells a product and makes money as long as the price exceeds the cost. It's more like a group of companies "building the plane while flying it": only when the plane is built will they know what it can actually do, and whether anyone will pay for its services. Many companies justify their spending because they aren't building a product but creating something world-changing: artificial general intelligence (AGI)… The problem is that none of them really knows how to get there. Still, University of Virginia economist Anton Korinek says that if Silicon Valley achieves its goal, all of this spending will be justified. He's optimistic that it can. "This is a bet on A.G.I. or bust," Korinek said. ( The New York Times , November 20) This quality of "an industry being built whose nature hasn't been determined" is best captured by a paraphrase of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman: "We'll first build a system that is generally intelligent, and then have it figure out how to generate an investment return for us." For investors who have always invested in businesses whose "models are fully understandable," this ought to be a warning. A technology equal to or surpassing the human brain should obviously be worth a great deal — but is it worth so much that it's beyond any calculation? But now companies are making commitments that require debt financing, and for some of them, the investment and leverage are fairly described as aggressive. The AI data centre boom can't be financed with cash alone. The projects are too big to pay for out of pocket.
