What Makes Us Precious as Humans Comes Precisely from Our Limits

Today's almanac: "Auspicious for abstaining from AI" In 2023, not long after ChatGPT came out, I added "use AI at least once a day" to my list of daily check-in habits. Yet today we're already asking — beyond immersing ourselves in AI's convenience and grandeur, how do we find the value that truly belongs to "humans"? — So now I require myself to have "non-AI writing time." This shift both frighteningly shows AI's influence on humanity's collective mind, and reflects the precious pursuit of, and struggle for, meaning and self-worth by our tiny species. Now, to bring myself back to "me," I'm letting go of the wave I've been working so hard to keep up with and returning to a more primal path of practice. Writing by myself is a choice. What characterises humans, what makes us unique, comes precisely from the narrowness of our brains' abilities. In the age of AI, the place of humans may also come precisely from our "limits." Realising that I am both everything and nothing. A couple of days ago I came across this passage: "Each of us is both everything and nothing — a huge paradox. From our own point of view, we are everything. For instance, when our life ends, the whole world disappears for us... That is why, for most people (and other species), losing one's life is the worst thing there is, and living the best life possible is immensely important. But if we look down on ourselves from nature's perspective, we clearly carry no weight at all. The reality is that each of us is just one of roughly 7 billion humans, and humans are just one of roughly 10 million species on Earth. Earth is just one of roughly 100 billion planets in the Milky Way, and the whole universe has roughly 2 trillion galaxies. 🪐 A human lifespan is only about 1/3,000 of human history, and human history is only 1/20,000 of Earth's history. In other words, we are unimaginably small and fleeting, and whatever we achieve, its impact is negligible." We instinctively want our lives to mean something. How can we seem to matter? Do we matter to others? But from the big-picture view, they don't matter any more than we do. Or do we matter in some larger, more mysterious sense we can never truly understand? Or is the question of whether we matter not even important? Questions like these are both profound and funny to think about. Where does human value come from? A couple of days ago at Tsinghua University, I sat in on an undergraduate psychology class. Before the class, a group of undergrads presented on a really interesting topic: Once emotional value and caregiving value are replaced by AI and machines — what is special about long-term, stable, exclusive intimate relationships between humans? Their 15-minute presentation was fascinating in both content and delivery, full of philosophical reflection — they laid out the differences between the two from six angles, for example: Human interaction is in-the-moment and spontaneous, while technology is a preset framework; The experiences human lovers create through unspoken understanding are private and limited, while technology is the "big Other," the sum of all information; Human lovers have subjectivity, and love is spontaneous, while technology carries a strong purpose — it is service-oriented; technology has no room to choose, so we can't feel chosen. They were brilliant! Better still, at the end they even critiqued "the method of critique" itself: So far, all human experiences of intimacy have been based on "human-to-human experience." When we criticise machines, we can't use our existing, habitual human yardstick to compare what humans can do and machines can't. Because that yardstick of critique is unfair to technology. So why do we choose to love that one "particular person, THE ONE"? Is each person unique? When we place ourselves in the wider world, no one is unique. Abstract far enough, and everyone is a patchwork. Experiences, memories and personalities share a great deal of similarity. Memory is a construction — what I remember remembering isn't necessarily what I actually remember. But a human life lasts only a few short decades, and the chance of meeting "a person like this" is vanishingly small — so to me they are unique, and so am I to them. Memory too — my time flows in only one direction, I have only one youth; it may be like everyone else's, but it carries my label. We don't have to, and shouldn't, always place ourselves in the boundless expanse of time and space. Intimacy is something I bestow; it carries my projection, and to myself, I am unprecedented and unrepeatable. What am I actually trying to say? What I want to say is: In the garden of forking paths, we have countless choices. In countless parallel universes, the me of this moment has countless things to say to you, countless things to do, books to read, people to love — countless "unfinished selves." And yet, because of my brain's limitations, my finite time and my life's one-way direction, in every present moment my personality, my understanding and my expression can only be one of those choices. That choice isn't necessarily the most perfect answer, precisely calculated by AI; it is in-the-moment, full of chance, and irreversible. It is exactly these limits that make up "me." In the past, we pursued rich understanding and complete unfolding; now, human value may come precisely from this — I can only be this way, and I choose to be this way.
Kosmos: The Next-Generation Autonomous Research AI Scientist

AI for Science is easily one of the most astonishing areas of progress, and the era of AI-accelerated research is not only here, it is steadily unfolding. I read every single one of my friend Renee's AI observations, and with her permission, I'm sharing this one with you too. Here goes — enjoy: FutureHouse is an organization focused on AI + scientific research, co-founded by researchers with deep backgrounds in AI, biology, neuroscience, materials science and other fields. It positions itself as "an AI research lab for scientists + a research tools platform." FutureHouse first caught the research community's attention with Robin (an AI Scientist prototype). Kosmos is Robin's next-generation upgrade, released by Edison Scientific, a new company spun out of FutureHouse, with the paper published at the same time: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.02824. Compared with the previous-generation Robin, Kosmos is a major leap in both capability and scale. A new paradigm for AI scientists Earlier AI Scientists (including Robin) were mainly constrained by the limited context length of language models → they tended to "run out of steam" when reading and integrating large amounts of information. As a result, the depth of reasoning and the complexity of research they could handle were limited too. Kosmos's core innovation: Structured World Models, which can efficiently integrate information across hundreds of agent trajectories and maintain a coherent research goal at the scale of tens of millions of tokens. A typical full Kosmos run includes: reading 1,500 scientific papers; executing 42,000 lines of data-analysis code That scale far exceeds any agent system known to date. One day of Kosmos, half a year for humans Compared with Robin, Kosmos can carry out more complex and fine-grained analysis. Beta users estimate: one day of Kosmos work ≈ 6 months for a human researcher. Its conclusions are 79.4% accurate. Kosmos has already made seven scientific discoveries spanning neuroscience, materials science, metabolomics, statistical genetics and other fields, several of them validated by outside scholars. The era of AI-accelerated research is truly arriving. User feedback: a single Kosmos run ≈ 6 months of PhD/postdoc research time. And a rare inference-time scaling law for depth of scientific reasoning has emerged. This estimate comes from a survey of 7 Beta users. A Kosmos run at a depth of 20 steps yielded an average of 6.14 months of human-equivalent research time. More objective metrics back this up too: for three studies that had previously taken humans 4 months, Kosmos reproduced the core findings in a single run each. Another independent estimate: reading 1,500 papers (15 minutes each); executing a number of analysis trajectories (2 hours each); totals roughly 4.1 months of human work. Auditable and reproducible Kosmos is designed to follow scientific norms — every conclusion can be traced back to: the specific code used; the specific passage in the scientific literature Research must be auditable and reproducible, and Kosmos guarantees this at the system level. In addition, researchers used Kosmos to: reproduce unpublished results; produce genuinely new discoveries All of which are included in the technical report. The technical report presents seven of Kosmos's discoveries. Three of them independently reproduced earlier findings by human researchers: 1. Metabolomics: the brains of hypothermic mice Using metabolomic data, Kosmos reproduced a study that had not yet been published at the time: nucleotide metabolism is the most significantly altered pathway in the mouse brain under hypothermia. The original study's preprint was uploaded to BioRxiv only after the Kosmos run. 2. Materials science: perovskite solar cells Kosmos reproduced another preprint (published after the model's training-data cutoff), which showed that absolute humidity during thermal annealing determines cell efficiency, and identified the critical threshold (above roughly 60 g/m³, devices fail). 3. Neuroscience: cross-species rules of neural connectivity Kosmos identified the mathematical law of cross-species neuronal connectivity reported by Piazza et al. Although that preprint was not accessed during the run, it predated the model's training-data cutoff. Four new contributions In the other four studies, Kosmos produced entirely new contributions: 4. Myocardial fibrosis: the causal role of SOD2 Using public GWAS and pQTL data, Kosmos provided evidence that high levels of SOD2 may causally lower myocardial T1 times and the risk of myocardial fibrosis. This mechanism had previously been validated mainly in mice. 5. Type 2 diabetes: a new molecular mechanism Combining multi-omics and statistical-genetics data, Kosmos proposed a potential molecular pathway by which a specific SNP lowers T2D risk. 6. Alzheimer's disease: the mechanism of tau accumulation Kosmos developed a new analytical method to reconstruct, from AD patients' proteomic data, the sequence of molecular events by which tau accumulates in neurons. 7. Neurodegeneration and aging: a new mechanism (clinically relevant) Task: understand neuronal vulnerability in aging. Kosmos ran a large-scale unbiased analysis of single-nucleus transcriptomes from young and old subjects and found: In entorhinal cortex neurons, flippase gene expression declines with age → increased external exposure of the PS "eat-me" signal on the membrane → triggering phagocytosis by microglia. The researchers validated this in an independent human AD dataset: in entorhinal cortex neurons at Braak stage II, flippase expression does indeed decline, coinciding with the onset of tau pathology. These findings are now being further validated in wet labs. Using it Kosmos is live, but it is completely different from an ordinary chatbot; it is closer to a "Deep Research Tool." https://platform.edisonscientific.com/ You need to learn some prompting techniques; pricing is $200 per run (200 credits); academic users get a certain free allowance Kosmos is more like a high-value research reagent kit than a chat model. Significance and future directions This suggests that the way METR and other organizations currently evaluate AI by "human-equivalent task duration" may be too simplistic: the "sustainable reasoning time" varies enormously across task types. For example: PaperQA2 can write high-quality Wikipedia articles (far beyond 4–15 minutes); a single math proof generated by GPT-5 also clearly exceeds 4 hours of human-equivalent time So the real-world capacity of AI to accelerate research is far more complex. Moreover, the deeper a Kosmos run goes, the more likely it is to veer off course (for example, chasing spurious correlations). Depth does not deliver unlimited positive gains. Stronger models will still be needed to solve this problem.
The FST Family Succession Triangle Model (Opening Piece)

I have to write this down — The question of "taking over" or "succession" has been with me for more than 25 years — from a seven- or eight-year-old child wanting to make her parents proud, to an adolescent existential crisis, to my early adulthood's mix of dependence on and rejection of the resources and platform my family gave me, and then to learning how to "fly on the wind." You could say that, for me, understanding myself and understanding succession are intertwined and inseparable. You could say I'm writing this piece for myself. Before I begin The FST Family Succession Triangle Model is an original theory and model I've distilled from decades of thinking about and studying "family succession." At first glance it's a simple triangle, but each element connects downward to its own sub-models. Writing this theory down has long been a wish of mine. But I wanted so badly to write it well that for years I couldn't bring myself to start. Because I know it isn't comprehensive enough; it can't perfectly cover every aspect of family succession. Succession involves social change, organizational innovation, scientific progress, the stretching of human nature, even our resistance to death — family succession is the most delicate patchwork of business, law, technology, the humanities, art, devotion and love, persistence and letting others flourish. Still, I dare to hope to finish this work. It may cause some misunderstandings or expose my foolishness, but it might be of some use to families and friends who are thinking about succession. Because they always hope to think about family succession systematically: in time, looking beyond a single generation to see what this generation can contribute on a hundred-year scale; in space, looking across at how people in other cultures and regions of the world realize the vision of succession. I hope FST can be a usable "walking stick," like the theories we lean on to understand history. That it can spark some thinking and some longing, so that beyond pursuing one generation's achievements, we can also grow creative aspirations on a longer time horizon and with a wider reach of influence. If readers have any further corrections to this theory, please do let me know, so I have the chance to improve it. What is "family succession" When I began thinking seriously about "succession," I found a very simple fact that is easily misunderstood — Succession isn't a rich people's thing; it's a human thing. It isn't that "complicated thing" that happens in billionaire families, multinational companies and trust structures, but an "instinct" embedded deep in our genes from the moment we humans first had surplus food and tools. Back then there were no companies, no asset allocation, no lawyers. But one thing had already quietly appeared: "I hope what I worked hard to gain can go on nourishing the people I love." In a sense, this is civilization's earliest spark. What is a family? Not wealth, not headcount I'm often asked: "How many assets make a family?" "How many generations make a family?" "Do you need US$1 billion before you need succession planning?" Let's take a different case: A rural family where two brothers completely fell out over a tile-roofed house worth 50,000 yuan. That is also a succession case. What they're fighting over isn't a tile-roofed house, but: who is entitled to inherit who is seen by the family whose contribution is recognized who has the right to decide the family's future Family isn't a concept of "scale"; it's a concept of "relationships." As long as a group of people share a destiny, stories and responsibilities, they form a family. The FST Family Succession Triangle Model In this model, I move the focus away from specific tools and "techniques" like "structure design," "tax planning" and "business succession," and back into a framework at the level of "the Way" — defining the three elements of family succession: Family – Enterprise – Capital, and the dynamic energy system the three of them form. Element one: the family's members — the source, the spark, and the ultimate meaning. A family's true foundation isn't the assets on the books or the size of the business, but the values, knowledge, judgment, resilience of character and mutual trust accumulated in its members. These human assets can cross borders, cultures and systems, flowing, migrating and rebuilding with the family. Just like those peoples throughout the long river of history who lost everything again and again and rebuilt their future each time: as long as the spark of "people" stays lit, a family always has the ability to start over. Element two: the family's enterprise — an amplifier, and a training ground for people. The enterprise isn't only the family's achievement; it is also the amplifier of the family's spirit. It carries culture and mission, and through organization, products and platforms, it spreads the energy of "people" into stable and lasting creativity. Driven by the right mission, the enterprise can keep iterating, transforming and expanding, becoming the most important platform for the family's dialogue with its era. Element three: the family's wealth — a reservoir, a store of energy and a converter between forms. Capital is a buffer against risk, fuel for innovation, and the family's instrument for keeping its commitments to society. It can convert freely between the tangible (assets, equity, cash flow) and the intangible (reputation, knowledge, philanthropy, social trust): in prosperity it settles into assets, in turbulence it evaporates into the intangible, and in recovery it condenses back into new opportunities and resources. Only capital that flows, converts and has direction is truly living capital. The "energy channels" circulating among the three 1. People ⇄ Enterprise People create enterprise; enterprise tempers people. When people's values and abilities are poured into an enterprise, it gains resilience and the vitality to ride through cycles. An enterprise is born of people and changes because of people. From a higher vantage point, the enterprise is also shaping people. It isn't a burden on family members but their place of practice: in the enterprise, the younger generation faces real markets and competition, and so develops judgment; in the enterprise, values aren't written on the wall but tested through decision after decision; in the enterprise, people of different generations work together, and culture is passed on and also iterated; in the enterprise, human capital isn't "carried on your back" but "put on the field." For people, the enterprise is a mirror, a school, a laboratory. A person's value is honed ever clearer in the enterprise. 2. Enterprise ⇄ Wealth The enterprise generates cash flow and builds brands; these are the sources of wealth. Wealth, in turn, can reshape the enterprise's horizons: longer R&D cycles (no short-term profit pressure) better teams (attracting outside experts) more strategic room (no anxiety about the next funding round) stronger resilience to risk (riding out cycles on cash reserves) Wealth with a sense of direction is an amplifier for the enterprise. 3. Wealth ⇄ People Wealth nourishes people, and people also decide the future form of wealth. The benefits of wealth to people are obvious: it provides educational resources, room for trial and error, an international outlook and a cushion against risk; it lets the family's descendants not have to suppress their curiosity for the sake of survival, and gives young people the courage to try, to fail and to start again. But in turn, people also decide the form wealth takes. Whether wealth is resented or respected depends entirely on how people use it: people with strong values turn capital into philanthropy and reputation; wise people steer capital into the right industries and assets; responsible people make capital a virtuous cycle for society rather than a source of strife within the family. Wealth gives people more possibilities; people decide whether wealth is good or evil. The strong make wealth a blessing; the weak make wealth a curse. My ideal of family succession A truly mature family doesn't cling to any gain or loss of a particular time and place, and doesn't use "family succession" to constrain people — instead it completes the perfect cycle of the FST model: 1. Converting forms When it's time to turn the spark into an enterprise, don't hesitate; when it's time to turn the enterprise into wealth, decide calmly; when it's time to turn wealth into education, philanthropy and reputation, spare no investment. Energy never solidifies and never disappears; it only changes form. 2. Adjusting the rhythm In different economic cycles, life stages and historical contexts, the weights of people, enterprise and wealth can shift dynamically; the center of gravity can move, but the cycle must not stop. 3. Continuing across generations When the next generation understands the systemic logic of succession, rather than inheriting static assets, the family gains true sustainability. What is passed on isn't a pile of assets, but a system that keeps renewing and repairing itself. Let's come back to the human scale Is succession necessary? First there has to be consensus — one generation has to be willing to "pass it on," and the next has to be ready to "take it up" Succession isn't a one-way action; it's a joint project between two generations. The older generation has to be willing to let go, willing to express themselves, willing to embrace uncertainty The younger generation has to be willing to take responsibility, willing to grow, willing to find their own place What matters most in between isn't how much wealth there is, but one word: consensus. Consensus matters more than structure, understanding matters more than plans, relationships matter more than assets. However the tools change, whether a family can endure ultimately depends on: whether its people are growing whether they have a sense of their place whether they keep believing in each other whether they are willing to create together whether they are willing to take on greater responsibility Finally, I hope that through "thinking about succession" we can see ourselves: where you come from, where you're going, and what you're willing to hold on to. The future of this series Going forward I will discuss further: 1. Why people are a family's most essential asset 2. Defining family members 3. Family governance: the secret to a family's longevity. 4. The four quadrants of the family–business relationship. 5. Succession on different time scales: 10 years, 50 years, 100 years... 6. Cultural differences in family succession: comparing succession in Japan, the UK and China 7. A family's tangible and intangible assets 8. Asset management of family wealth: strategy and practice. 9. The next step for wealth: from rich to noble. 10. Exploring your own succession strategy: the attributes of different families. and so on Anyway, here's the first piece — out it goes! Yeah~

A rather special letter "The Quiet Buffett" On November 10, 2025, 95-year-old Warren Buffett released this special letter from Omaha. It is unlike his usual annual letters to shareholders — it reads more like a farewell, a thank-you note, a letter written to time and to life itself. He announced that he would no longer write Berkshire Hathaway's annual report or hold forth at the annual meeting, and, with a touch of British humour, said: "I'm 'going quiet' — sort of." In the letter, Buffett looks back on his ninety-five years: from the 1938 appendicitis that nearly killed him to his sixty-four-year friendship with Charlie Munger; from childhood stories in small-town Omaha to his ultimate reflections on wealth, family, fate and kindness. This is a centenarian-to-be's last long conversation with all of his "shareholders." But what he talks about is not just money — it is how a life gets allocated: the redistribution of time, love and luck. He talks about luck, fate, ageing, inheritance, kindness, and the courage to choose your heroes. The letter is both a century-long investor looking back and the farewell of an era. In what looks like a private letter, we see not only Buffett's life but also the art of reconciling capital with human nature. Arcus42 has chosen to publish the letter in full — not to pay tribute to wealth, but to pay tribute to the kind of wisdom that stays clear-headed, restrained and humorous over a very long stretch of time. Below is our translation of the original. Here goes — enjoy: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. News Release For Immediate Release November 10, 2025 Omaha, Nebraska (BRK.A; BRK.B) Today, Warren E. Buffett converted 1,800 Class A shares into 2,700,000 Class B shares in order to give those B shares to four family foundations: 1,500,000 shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation; 400,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and the NoVo Foundation. These gifts were delivered today. Mr. Buffett's letter to shareholders: To my fellow shareholders: Starting this year, I will no longer write Berkshire's annual report or talk endlessly at the annual meeting. As the British would say, I'm "going quiet." — Well, "sort of" quiet. At the end of this year, Greg Abel will take over at the helm. He is an outstanding manager, a tireless worker and an honest communicator. Please wish him a long tenure. I will still talk about Berkshire with you and with my children through my annual Thanksgiving letter. Berkshire's individual shareholders are a very special group who generously share their gains with others. I enjoy the chance to stay in touch. Allow me this year to reminisce a little first, then to discuss my plans for distributing my shares, and finally to share a few thoughts on business and life. I. Memories As Thanksgiving approaches, I am surprised and grateful to still be alive at 95. When I was young, that would not have looked like a winning bet. In fact, I nearly died early. It was 1938, and Omaha's hospitals were naturally divided into "Catholic" and "Protestant" ones — a classification locals took entirely for granted. Our family doctor, Harley Hotz, was a friendly Catholic who made house calls carrying a black bag. He called me "Skipper" and never charged much. That year I came down with a bad stomachache. Dr. Hotz came over, examined me and said, "You'll be fine by morning." Then he went home, had dinner and played a little bridge. But something kept nagging at him, and in the middle of the night he decided to send me to St. Catherine's Hospital for an emergency appendectomy. For the next three weeks I lived in a ward surrounded by nuns. I adapted quickly and rather enjoyed being "the one at the little podium." I liked to talk — yes, even back then — and the nuns were happy to listen. Even more thrilling, my third-grade teacher, Miss Madsen, had each of the thirty kids in my class write me a letter. I probably threw away the boys' letters, but I read the girls' over and over. Being in hospital had its rewards. During my recovery — the first week was actually quite dangerous — what delighted me most was a present from my Aunt Edie: a professional fingerprinting kit. I promptly fingerprinted every nun who looked after me. (I was probably the first Protestant child they had ever seen, and they didn't know what to expect.) I had an absurd theory at the time: one day some nun would go astray, and the FBI would discover that it had never fingerprinted nuns. Americans in the 1930s idolised the FBI and its director, J. Edgar Hoover, and I fantasised that he would personally come to Omaha to inspect my "precious files," and that together we would crack the case and become famous nationwide. Of course, the fantasy never came true. Ironically, years later it turned out that the person I should have fingerprinted was Hoover himself — he ended up disgraced for abusing his power. That was Omaha in the 1930s. Back then, the treasures my friends and I dreamed of were sleds, bicycles, baseball gloves and electric trains. Now let's look at a few people of that generation who grew up in Omaha — people I didn't know at the time but who later shaped me profoundly. I'll start with Charlie Munger — my dear friend of sixty-four years. In the 1930s, Charlie lived just one block from the house I bought in 1958 and still live in today. We very nearly became friends early on — very nearly. In the summer of 1940, Charlie worked at my grandfather's grocery store, earning $2 for a 10-hour day (thrift is a Buffett family tradition). A year later I did similar work there, but we didn't meet until 1959 — he was 35 and I was 28. After serving in World War II, Charlie graduated from Harvard Law School and settled in California. But he always said his early years in Omaha were the most formative. For more than sixty years he influenced me profoundly; he was the best of mentors and older brothers. We had disagreements but never an argument. "I told you so" was not in his vocabulary. In 1958 I bought my first and only house. Naturally it was in Omaha — about two miles from where I grew up, less than two blocks from my in-laws, six blocks from the Buffett grocery store, and only a six- or seven-minute drive from the office where I have worked for 64 years. Now another Omahan — Stan Lipsey. In 1968 he sold the Omaha Sun to Berkshire. Ten years later, at my invitation, he moved to Buffalo. At the time, Berkshire's Buffalo Evening News was fighting a morning paper — and losing ground steadily. Stan eventually built our new Sunday paper, and for several early years it helped the once loss-making paper earn more than 100% a year (pre-tax) — a hugely important stream of money for Berkshire back then. Stan's home was only five blocks from mine. One of his neighbours was Walter Scott Jr. You may remember that he brought MidAmerican Energy into Berkshire in 1999 and served as a director until his death in 2021. He was a philanthropic leader in Nebraska, and he left his mark on Omaha and the whole state. Walter attended Benson High School, where I would have gone too — until my father unexpectedly defeated a four-term incumbent congressman in 1942. Life back then was full of surprises. There's more. In 1959, Don Keough's family lived across the street from me, barely a hundred metres from where the Mungers' old house had been. He was a coffee salesman then, but he was destined to become president of Coca-Cola and a loyal Berkshire director. When we first met, he earned $12,000 a year; he and his wife Mickie had five children, all of them in pricey Catholic schools. Our two families became good friends. Don grew up on a farm in northwest Iowa and graduated from Creighton University in Omaha. He married an Omaha girl, Mickie, early on. After joining Coca-Cola, he became a legend worldwide. In 1985, Coca-Cola launched the ill-fated "New Coke." Don gave a famous speech apologising to the public and bringing back "Coca-Cola Classic." He explained at the time that letters addressed to the "Supreme Idiot" were delivered straight to his desk. His "retraction speech" is a classic and can be found on YouTube. Don admitted frankly: "Coca-Cola really belongs to the public, not to the company." Sales soared afterwards. You can watch his wonderful interview on CharlieRose.com (the episodes with Tom Murphy and Kay Graham are excellent too). Like Charlie, Don always remained an enthusiastic, friendly, unpretentious Midwestern boy. Finally, there are Ajit Jain and Greg Abel — one from India, one from Canada — both of whom lived in Omaha for a few years in the late 20th century. In fact, in the 1990s Greg lived on Farnam Street, not far from my house, though we hadn't yet met. Could there really be something magical in Omaha's water? I lived in Washington, D.C. as a teenager (my father was serving in Congress then), and in 1954 I found what looked like a permanent job in Manhattan, New York. There I received careful mentoring from Ben Graham and Jerry Newman and made friends for life. New York has a charm all its own — it still does. Yet only a year and a half later, in 1956, I returned to Omaha and never wandered again. My three children, and some of my grandchildren, all grew up in Omaha. My children all went to public schools — the same school attended by my father (class of 1921), my first wife Susie (class of 1950), Charlie, Stan Lipsey, the Blumkin brothers (who built up Nebraska Furniture Mart) and Jack Ringwalt (class of 1923), founder of National Indemnity. National Indemnity was sold to Berkshire in 1967 and became the cornerstone of our huge insurance business. America has many great companies, schools and hospitals, each with its own particular strengths and talent. But I was lucky: I made lifelong friends, met both of my wives, got a sound foundation in public education, came to know many kind Omahans when I was young, and made wide-ranging friendships in the Nebraska National Guard. In short, Nebraska is my home. Looking back on my life, I believe Berkshire's success and mine are inseparable from our roots in Omaha. The geographic centre of America is a wonderful place to be born, to raise a family, to build a business. By pure luck, I drew a "ridiculously long straw" at birth. II. On Age Now let's talk about my advanced age. My genes haven't been much help — before me, the longest-lived member of the family made it to 92 (and the further back you go in the family tree, the hazier such records get). But I've been lucky: from Dr. Hotz to this day, I have been cared for by smart, kind, dedicated Omaha doctors. They have saved my life at least three times, and their practices have all been within a few miles of my home. (I did give up fingerprinting nurses long ago, though. At 95 you can keep a few quirks, but there are limits.) Living to an old age takes an enormous amount of luck: every day you have to dodge banana peels, natural disasters, drunk or distracted drivers, lightning — you name it. But Lady Luck is fickle — no description fits better than "capricious and unfair." Many leaders and rich people receive far more than their share of good luck, and they are often unwilling to admit it. Heirs born into wealth gain lifelong financial independence at birth, while others struggle in hellish circumstances, or are robbed by physical or mental illness of everything I took for granted. Had I been born in many of the world's other populous places, my life would very likely have been miserable, and my sisters' fates would have been even worse. I was born in 1930, healthy, smart, a white male, and in America. Wow! Thank you, Lady Luck. My two sisters were just as bright and had better personalities, but the opportunities they faced were entirely different. Lady Luck visited me often throughout my life, but by my nineties she ought to be busy elsewhere — luck has its limits. Father Time, on the other hand, has become increasingly interested in me. And he has never lost — on his scoreboard, everyone is eventually marked down as a "win." When your balance, eyesight, hearing and memory all start to steadily decline, you know he's nearby. I became "old" fairly late — ageing arrives at different times for different people — but once it arrives, there's no denying it. What surprises me is that I feel fine overall. Although I move slowly and reading is hard, I still work in the office five days a week with a terrific team. Occasionally I still come up with a useful idea, or encounter an opportunity that wouldn't otherwise have come along. Given Berkshire's size and market conditions, such ideas are getting rarer — but they're still not zero. III. Distributing Wealth and Family Succession My unusual longevity has inevitable and important consequences — both for my family and for achieving my philanthropic goals. Let's talk about them. Next Steps My three children are all past normal retirement age — they are now 72, 70 and 67. It would be a mistake to count on all of them slowing their ageing the way I have. To raise the odds that they finish distributing my estate before successor trustees take over, I need to speed up my lifetime gifts and put more Berkshire shares into each of their foundations. They are now at their peak in experience and wisdom, but not yet truly old. This "honeymoon period" won't last forever. Fortunately, this "course correction" is easy to carry out. But there is one more thing to consider: I want to keep a significant number of A shares until Berkshire's shareholders develop the same sort of trust in Greg that they had in Charlie and me. That day won't be long in coming. My children and Berkshire's directors are 100% behind Greg. My children now have the maturity, wisdom, energy and instincts to handle enormous wealth. They will outlive me and, if necessary, can respond flexibly to future changes in tax law or philanthropic policy. The world keeps changing, and they must adapt too. "Ruling from the grave" has never worked well, and I have never wanted to try it. Fortunately, all three children inherited their dominant genes from their mother. Over the years I've also become a better role model for them — though I'll never match their mother. As a precaution, I have named three alternate trustees who can step in should a child die early or become incapacitated. The alternates are not ranked, and none is tied to a particular child. They are all excellent, worldly people with no conflicts of interest. I've assured my children that they don't need to work miracles, nor fear failure or disappointment. These are part of life, and I've made plenty of mistakes myself. They need only do a bit better than the average government programme or conventional philanthropy — after all, neither of those ways of redistributing wealth is perfect either. In my early years I dreamed up all kinds of grand philanthropic plans. None of them were realistic. Over the years I've also watched plenty of failed attempts by political opportunists, family heirs and eccentric philanthropists. If my children can do a "pretty good" job, their mother and I will be pleased. Their judgement is sound, and for years they have practised allocating money in gradual increments — from small sums at first to more than US$500 million a year today. They all love working long hours to help others — each in their own way. IV. On Berkshire and Management Speeding up my gifts does not mean my view of Berkshire's prospects has changed in any way. Greg Abel has fully met the high expectations I had of him as my successor CEO. His understanding of the company's businesses and people far exceeds what I can now grasp, he learns extremely fast, and he often spots issues that an ordinary CEO would never even notice. I can't think of a CEO, management consultant, academic or government official better suited to manage your savings and mine. For example, he understands the potential and the risks of Berkshire's property and casualty insurance business more deeply than most veteran insurance executives. I hope he enjoys good health and a long life. If our luck holds, Berkshire will need only five or six CEOs over the next hundred years. We should particularly avoid choosing CEOs who are bent on retiring at 65, flaunting their wealth or building a family dynasty. In reality, painful situations also arise: a loyal, excellent CEO — whether of the parent company or a subsidiary — may develop dementia, Alzheimer's or some other long-term illness. Charlie and I both ran into this and failed to act in time. That can be a major mistake. The board must stay vigilant, and the CEO must stay vigilant about the subsidiaries. Easier said than done, but my advice is: stay alert and be willing to speak up. In the past, regulators tried to shame executives by requiring disclosure of the "ratio of CEO pay to average employee pay." As a result, proxy statements ballooned from 20 pages to more than 100. But good intentions didn't produce good results — they backfired. What I've mostly observed is this: the CEO of Company A looks at the pay of the CEO of rival Company B and hints that he himself should be worth more. Along the way he raises directors' pay too, and hand-picks the members of the compensation committee. The new rules brought not restraint but one-upmanship. The wealth spiral feeds itself. What really bothers wealthy CEOs — they are human, after all — is not that they earn too little, but that others earn more. Envy and greed always walk hand in hand. I have never seen a consultant recommend a sharp cut in CEO or director pay. Overall, Berkshire's mix of businesses is a little better than average, supported by a number of unrelated and extremely valuable "gems." Still, ten or twenty years from now there will certainly be many companies outperforming Berkshire — the price of size is unavoidable. Berkshire is about the least likely company I know of to suffer a catastrophic crisis. Its management and board are also more shareholder-minded than nearly any company I know. Moreover, Berkshire will always be run in a way that makes it an asset to the United States, never a dependant. Over time our managers will become wealthy — they shoulder major responsibilities — but they have no wish to build dynasties or show off their wealth. Our share price will keep fluctuating — during my sixty years in charge it has fallen by roughly 50% three times. Don't despair — America always recovers, and Berkshire's stock will recover along with it. V. Final Thoughts Allow me a slightly self-indulgent remark: I feel better about the second half of my life than the first. My advice: don't beat yourself up over past mistakes — learn something from them and move on. It's never too late to become better. Find the right role models and copy them. You could start with Tom Murphy — he was the best. Think of Alfred Nobel. As the story goes, when his brother died, a newspaper mistakenly printed Nobel's own obituary. Reading what the world thought of him shook him deeply, and he changed his life. Don't wait for a newspaper mix-up to wake you up — think about what you'd like your obituary to say, and then live a life worthy of it. Greatness does not come from wealth, fame or power. When you help others in thousands of ways, you make the world better. Kindness is priceless, yet it costs nothing. Whether or not you are religious, the Golden Rule (do not do to others what you would not want done to you) remains the best guide to behaviour. I write these words knowing that I have been thoughtless and made mistakes countless times — but fortunately I have learned from many wonderful friends how to be a better person (though I'm still far from perfect). Always remember: the cleaning lady and the chairman are equally human. I wish everyone reading this letter a happy Thanksgiving. Yes, even the "jerks"; it's never too late to change. Please thank America — it has maximised our opportunities. But remember too that its rewards are often handed out haphazardly, even unfairly. Choose your role models carefully and strive to emulate them. You can never be perfect, but you can always be better. AI leaders are pulling ahead A report worth reading carefully Every year, Bain & Company publishes its Technology Report . This year's (2025) title is: "AI leaders are extending their edge." The report was written by the team of David Crawford, chairman of Bain's global TMT practice, based on two years of tracking the AI wave and on empirical company data. Unlike the "trend sketches" of years past, this time Bain seems to be opening a file on a brand-new world order: AI is becoming the central variable that determines wealth and the competitive landscape between nations. For us — whether investors, entrepreneurs or managers of family offices — this is not just a technology report but a map of where capital will flow over the next decade. The AI leaders' flywheel: winners in an age of compounding Bain points out that 2025 has become the inflection point of AI divergence. Among the world's twenty most valuable tech companies, the top five (Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Nvidia) account for more than 70% of total market value. Nvidia's market cap alone has grown more than 800% since 2023. These giants are forming a "self-compounding" closed loop — they no longer just do AI; they use AI to reshape the three-layer ecosystem of infrastructure, models and applications. Meanwhile, a crop of nimble challengers is breaking through at every layer: Foundation layer: start-ups such as CoreWeave, Mistral and Anthropic are tearing open entry points in GPU cloud and model innovation; Application layer: Anysphere's AI code editor Cursor and Perplexity's AI browser are redefining the boundaries of "human-machine collaboration". AI is no longer a product but a systemic self-evolution. Sovereign tech and a fragmented world Bain defines this era as "Sovereign Tech, Fragmented World". It is a global realignment around "who controls the lifelines of technology". The US leads in chips and large models, reshaping supply chains through export controls and tariffs; China is accelerating semiconductor self-sufficiency, already holds about 20% of global wafer capacity, and is breaking through in models and robotics; Europe has launched the €200 billion InvestAI plan to build homegrown AI gigafactories; New players in the Middle East, such as Saudi Arabia's Humain, are building 500-megawatt-class AI data centres and developing Arabic multimodal large models. The "sovereignisation" of AI is pushing the world towards multipolarity: AI systems will increasingly resemble national products, reflecting their own political and cultural contexts. This means tomorrow's global companies will need to understand not only market logic but also "algorithmic geopolitics" — finding ways to stay compatible and survive across different sovereign AI systems. Capital logic reshaped: the end of software's "easy growth" era The report notes that tech M&A accounted for 22% of all deals in the first half of 2025, but "the era of easy growth in software is over". Over the past decade, software investing generated returns through scale and multiple expansion; over the next decade, value will come more from operational efficiency and AI-enabled innovation. Bain's data reveals: since 2010, 53% of investment returns have come from revenue growth, while the contribution of multiple expansion is declining; investors will have to rely on more refined forms of growth — AI-driven product iteration, data monetisation, cross-regional expansion. This is also an era that shifts from "riding the wave" to "sculpting growth". Agentic AI: the next paradigm after SaaS In Bain's view, the next act of AI is called Agentic AI. It means software begins to have "the power to execute" — to reason, plan and complete tasks on its own initiative. SaaS moved software into the cloud; Agentic AI gives software a brain. This transformation is upending three core logics of the software industry: Pricing logic: from charging per seat to charging per outcome; Ecosystem logic: companies must control the right to define the semantic layer of their data, or platforms will siphon off their value; Standards logic: competition such as that between the MCP and A2A protocols is deciding who becomes the "grammar gatekeeper" of the AI world. Disruption is mandatory. Obsolescence is optional. Disruption is inevitable; becoming obsolete is a choice. Compute, energy and machines: AI's "physical bottleneck" AI's ambitions are putting pressure on the planet's power systems. Bain estimates that by 2030, US demand for AI compute will reach 100 gigawatts — the equivalent of adding an "AI continent" to the national grid. Building these data centres will require US$500 billion of investment a year. Even if companies reinvested all their IT savings and AI gains, there would still be an US$800 billion gap. Meanwhile, humanoid robots and quantum computing are becoming AI's "extended limbs": Humanoid robots: capital is enthusiastic, but limited by battery density and operational complexity, near-term deployment will remain in factories and warehouses; Quantum computing: a potential market of US$250 billion, but still more than a decade away from reliably replacing conventional computing. AI is not just an algorithmic revolution but a restructuring of energy and physical infrastructure. From pilots to systems: the real watershed of AI transformation Bain's final conclusion is worth reflecting on for every company and every family: Leaders have already lifted EBITDA by 10%–25% through AI, while companies still "piloting" are falling dangerously behind. This means AI competition long ago stopped being about "whether you've deployed it"; it's about whether you've completed the reshaping of organisational structure, data, architecture and talent. From top-level decision logic to bottom-level data governance, everything needs an "AI-native" redesign. What the winners have in common: they use AI to transform processes, not to decorate them; they treat AI as a factor of production, not an outsourced tool; they see speed of innovation as a threshold for survival, not a metric for awards. The operating system of a new civilisation AI competition has shifted from single-point innovation to system-versus-system rivalry; it tests not only compute and capital, but even more the speed of cognition and the resilience of organisations. For family capital, this means: the core of intergenerational succession is no longer the continuation of wealth, but the ability to understand the new structure. Whoever first understands the structural forces of AI and positions for them will keep their voice in the new era. The future won’t wait for you to be ready. The future will not wait until you are prepared.
In Southern Fujian, Seeing the Power of the Clan

The Xiamen docks in early autumn, under a blazing sun, the air thick with salt and sweat. This is a place close to the sea, and "The Waves of Gulangyu" is its romantic tune. On the other side of the old docks, Guanyin Mountain faces Little Kinmen, where a solid, fierce wind blows. What this wind carries is not idle leisure, but a fierce drive to get things done. Most of the listed companies and family offices from southern Fujian have their headquarters here; the HQ towers of Anta, Xtep, Septwolves, ERKE and others stand side by side... The windy spot is where Quanzhou people believe wealth gathers. Over the Mid-Autumn Festival, I came here with the Arcus team and close friends to visit local listed companies and family offices. More than their market value, strategy or business success... what struck me most was the family and succession culture behind them. After a few days of visits, we came away with a new understanding of the word "family." Understanding Minnan Culture To outsiders, southern Fujian families look complicated in structure and heavy on personal ties; but to them, this is exactly the most stable kind of order — the rules are not written on paper, but written into relationships. Unity: the clan is the strongest trust network Southern Fujian families may not use a word like "governance," but the clan is their most natural governance system. Here, family members both compete and cooperate with one another. The headquarters of the most famous listed footwear and apparel companies sit right next to each other; they compete on the same track, yet also co-invest in projects together. This sense of being "a community of shared destiny" may well be the true underlying character of southern Fujian families. Their unity doesn't rest on slogans, but on long experience of working together and winning together. Tempering: the founders are still learning, and the second generation takes over on its own terms They are not shy about a "horse-race mechanism" — let the second generation run on their own, and whoever comes out ahead naturally takes over. The elders don't deliberately hold on to control; instead they are willing to let go, and let the young ones go out, venture forth and make mistakes. One entrepreneur said with a smile: Family members can't all be equally smart, but you have to trust that time will weed people out, and sort them too. On the question of second-generation succession, they are also more decisive than outsiders imagine. Many of the younger generation join the group early on to rotate through roles, and some even set up their own investment funds and make decisions independently. The founders have not "retreated behind the scenes"; instead, they stand alongside as "learners," observing and guiding. This state of "learning together" lets the family's knowledge and power be passed down while staying in motion. Mechanisms: the evolutionary logic of southern Fujian family offices Southern Fujian always has someone willing to be the first to try the crab, and they are willing to spend the time to take those methods apart, absorb them and put them back together. On this trip to Xiamen, the development path of southern Fujian family offices was also striking; every one of them bears the deep imprint of the business and the entrepreneur behind it. Standing on the shoulders of cognitive giants, they copy more cleverly. The keyword is — iteration What I admire most about southern Fujian founders is not their hard work, but their willingness to keep learning. Southern Fujian families rarely tear down an old system; instead, they use time to iterate on it. They believe good governance is not a charter written on paper, but a tacit understanding hidden within relationships. Southern Fujian family offices are quietly upgrading too As the companies iterate, so do the family offices, from the initial stage of "pooling personal investments" all the way to today's professional systems: Stage 1.0: consolidating the founder's scattered personal investments; Stage 2.0: setting up dedicated investment companies and hiring outside teams; Stage 3.0: professionalising, with focused resources and a focused direction. Gradually they build their own decision-making systems — the boss, the investment committee, the team, outside advisers — constantly iterating and learning. This way of thinking is the key to how they ride through cycles. They don't seek "perfect decisions," only "effective consensus." This is the flexible wisdom of southern Fujian families: neither stubborn nor blindly following. Trust is another unique asset of southern Fujian family offices. Many family office teams are made up of veteran group employees who have moved over, having worked alongside the founder for more than a decade. They understand both the boss and finance, striking a rare balance between trust and professionalism. By contrast, this is exactly the biggest challenge for many family offices elsewhere — either too much trust and not enough expertise, or too much expertise and trust collapses. Philosophy: whatever exists has its reasons Every family's situation is different, but whatever exists has its reasons. This line came up again and again in every conversation. What we saw clearly was not fatalism, but a kind of maturity: they know every family develops at its own pace, and there is no need to copy someone else's. From Reason to Love I often wonder: why have southern Fujian families been able to rise, wave after wave, over several decades? Perhaps the answer isn't on the balance sheet, but in their collective temperament. It is a patience with time, a trust in family, a love of learning. They don't talk about "generational anxiety," nor are they in a hurry for an "international transformation." What they care about more is — "whether the next generation has grown into people who can be trusted." This trip to southern Fujian helped me understand the meaning of "succession" anew: succession is not the handover of power, but the continuation of the ability to learn. Here, I saw a Chinese civilisation that is deeply rational yet full of warmth: the "company" is an extension of the family, and the "family" is the real company.

Processes are driven by people, with AI assisting execution / Processes are driven by AI, with humans calibrating and deciding. It may be a little irreverent, but I can't resist a joke — the biggest winner of this year's Nobel Prizes turns out to be Gaoshan Academy! 🤣 Among the 2025 Nobel laureates, three have taught us in the past three years — Professor Shimon Sakaguchi won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and Professors Susumu Kitagawa and Omar Yaghi shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. What a magical organization this is. Getting to meet these professors "before the prize" is a stroke of luck we owe to Gaoshan's academic eye and its ability to connect. Here, listening to lectures by Nobel laureates has happened many times. Every one of these professors can explain the most cutting-edge science in a way that is deep yet accessible, letting us see how science truly changes the world. Every time, I'm struck by it: masters really are different — how do they make such complex science clear enough even for me to understand? But honestly — taking the class first and seeing the prize come later feels far better than simply attending a Nobel laureate's lecture! Because it means we witnessed, with our own eyes, "greatness in the making." Even better, right after his lecture this April, I was certain: Professor Omar Yaghi would definitely win a Nobel Prize. I just didn't expect this "prophecy" to come true so quickly. Out of heartfelt pride, I'd like to try to capture the scientific spirit of Professor Yaghi's class for everyone who loves science. Professor Yaghi's story: a love of molecules at first sight, for a lifetime "When I was ten, I happened to open a book in the library with drawings of molecular structures — one glance, and it was forever. From then on, my life was devoted to molecules." Background and original motivation: a Jordanian/Palestinian family, short of water since childhood; went to the U.S. alone at 15. Pioneering a field: Reticular Chemistry — using strong bonds to stitch "molecular building blocks" into crystalline, programmable 2D/3D materials, with MOFs (containing metal nodes) and COFs (all-organic frameworks) as the classic examples. The shock of MOF-5: a coin-sized sample, thanks to its enormous internal channels, can have a surface area on the scale of "a football field"; the pores act like "parking lots," allowing CO₂, H₂O, H₂ and so on to be adsorbed and released in an orderly way. Harvesting water from air: materials represented by MOF-303 absorb water at night and release it during the day; according to data shared in class, 200 g of MOF can produce ~5 L of ultrapure water a day and can be cycled for 6–7 years; engineering designs from 2 kg/120 L per day up to 1 tonne/60,000 L per day have all had their concepts validated. Carbon capture and scale-up: COFs/MOFs adsorb CO₂ with high selectivity through "channels like parking spaces," and have the potential for cyclic regeneration and scale-up. The periodic table of materials, "reinvented": the "combinatorial universe" of different metal nodes and organic linkers is like a "periodic table of reticular chemistry," and every cell is worth a lifetime of exploration. Molecular weaving: building "the toughness of cloth" into materials In class, Yaghi used a brilliant analogy of "weaving cloth": when molecules "interlace like warp and weft" in angle and topology, the material becomes as tough as cloth, and can even be made into 3D interlocking structures that remain stable under stress. This is the power of "ordered networks" — once a structure is precisely designed, its properties can be precisely tuned. AI × materials: from 2–3 years to 1 month Integrating data and experiments: using literature mining + reaction image recognition + robotic synthesis + Bayesian optimization to digitize the traditional bottleneck of "crystallization conditions." Doubling the discovery rate: on a dataset of 8,000+ ZIF reactions, AI raised the success rate by ~30%; across 2,688 experiments it achieved a discovery rate about 2x that of random exploration and faster topology classification. The intelligent research group: 7 agents dividing up the work (planning, retrieval, modeling, robotics, 3D printing, safety, data analysis), compressing "a 35-year road" into "1 month." "Two years ago I didn't believe it myself, until a student from Beijing said to me: why don't we try using AI? Now I believe it — AI will absolutely change our research." My requirement: if you want to join us, you must know how to use AI. Why people are slow to adopt AI: Lack of understanding: many people don't fully understand how artificial intelligence works or how it can benefit them, which leads to hesitation. Fear of job loss: AI is often associated with automation and replacing human jobs, which creates anxiety and resistance. High costs: implementing AI can require substantial investment in technology, infrastructure and technical staff — a barrier especially for small businesses. Data privacy concerns: AI systems rely heavily on data, and people are increasingly worried about how data is collected, used and protected. Ethics and bias concerns: people worry about AI making biased or unfair decisions, especially in sensitive areas such as hiring, healthcare or law enforcement. Regulatory uncertainty: with no clear rules or standards, some organizations wait before investing heavily in AI. Change management: adopting AI often means rethinking workflows and company culture, which can be difficult and time-consuming. Medicine and sensing: from low-invasiveness detection of proteins such as PSA to early warning of hazardous gases.
