Before He Won the Nobel, We Were Already Listening to the Future

The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to the Japanese immunologist Professor Shimon Sakaguchi. Two years ago, he taught a class for us at Gaoshan Academy. After that class, I came to understand "the true wisdom of immunity" in a whole new way. This piece is both a set of study notes and a thank-you to Gaoshan Academy. How Immunity Works Many people know that immunity is about "fighting off foreign invaders," but few realise that immunity also has to learn how to "hit the brakes." Professor Sakaguchi discovered and named regulatory T cells (Treg), showing that they can suppress excessive immune responses and maintain self-tolerance. This line of research went on to become one of the three major themes in immunology, and it is closely tied to many diseases. Milestones 1995: CD25 is pinned down as a surface marker of Treg; 2000: "Regulatory T cells" are formally named in Cell ; 2003: The master control gene Foxp3 is discovered; Foxp3 mutations cause the fatal IPEX syndrome, pointing to Treg as the hub of immune homeostasis. Professor Sakaguchi often stresses that the goal of the immune system is not to be "permanently fired up," but to reach a kind of "powerful balance" — able to respond to challenges without harming itself. Its applications span allergies, autoimmunity, organ transplantation, cancer and more. From the perspective of the history of science, this is a paradigm shift: immunology is not just the science of attack, but the science of regulation. 1. Why immunity must "throw punches and also hit the brakes" Memory and specificity: vaccines work because the first exposure builds antigen-specific memory; when the same antigen shows up again, the secondary response is faster and stronger. The two-axis dilemma (in plain terms): Overreaction × self → autoimmunity / allergy Underreaction × non-self → infection / tumours The solution is to let Treg act like "police," keeping the "hot-headed effector T cells (Teff)" in check. 2. The "chain of evidence" for Treg Removing CD25⁺CD4 T cells (the classic Treg population) in mice leads to multi-organ autoimmunity; putting them back eases the inflammation — animal evidence that "the brake exists and works." IPEX syndrome and Foxp3: infants suffer a body-wide immune "overshoot" and rarely survive; once the cause was identified as a Foxp3 mutation, the Treg–disease–gene chain was complete. 3. Why are "autoimmune diseases" more common in modern society? The hygiene/affluence correlation": infectious diseases are declining while autoimmune diseases are rising; regions with higher GNP and "cleaner" environments have higher incidence — less stimulation, less training, and a system more prone to imbalance. 4. Attack and defence in cancer immunology: when to "ease off the brake" Treg are often more abundant in the tumour microenvironment, where they suppress Teff; so approaches such as Anti-CTLA-4, Anti-GITR and Anti-CCR4 are used to "cut back Treg and boost Teff." The class was also candid: overall efficacy is still limited, "working in about 30% of cases," but within a 20-year horizon, combination strategies and new technologies could significantly widen the range of treatable conditions. TCR-T vs. CAR-T: CAR-T is mature for blood cancers but limited in solid tumours; TCR-T holds more promise for solid tumours (more precise targeting). 5. Organ transplantation: from "heavy immune suppression" to "engineered tolerance" Traditional systemic immunosuppression brings risks such as infection and tumours; the class laid out four more precise paths: Suppress only Teff; Expand Treg outside the body and infuse them back (already being explored for type 1 diabetes in children); Use drugs to turn Teff → Treg; Take Teff out of the body, convert them into Treg, then infuse them back. Mouse models show that Treg infusion can improve transplant tolerance, with FOXP3 markers rising in the tissue. This is an engineered path that "protects both the organ and the immune system." 6. Translation and entrepreneurship: from "generic Treg" to "specific Treg" The key tension in bringing this to the clinic: functional stability versus accessible delivery. The class introduced RegCell's approach: take lymphocytes from a patient's blood, culture "antigen-specific Treg" in a targeted way, cryopreserve them, and move toward human trials; the long-term goal is to scale up batches and bring down costs. 7. Q&A Is it possible to clear only "the Treg inside tumours"? — By finding tumour-specific molecules/receptors; clinical attempts are under way. NK cell therapy: logical as a first line of defence, but its durability and real-world benefit still need stronger evidence. Allergies and COVID-19: lots of papers, but no consistent conclusion yet; reasoning from the mechanism, moderately boosting Treg might ease an immune "overshoot." Take Away Understanding immunity: stronger is not better — what matters is knowing how to fight and how to stop; The space to watch: making Treg specific, localised and part of combination therapies will be one of the main threads of the next decade (tumours / autoimmunity / transplantation / pregnancy, etc.); For industry, two things decide success: differentiated targets + accessibility (convenient delivery, controllable costs, the ability to organise trials); On a personal level: Moderate eating, regular exercise, good sleep and stress management, a healthy gut microbiome = "everyday immune engineering." "Too much is as bad as too little" — balance wins! Thank You, Gaoshan Academy Before he won the prize... they had already brought this future Nobel laureate into our classroom. That day, he spoke about "the balance of immunity," and about "when holding back is actually the smarter move." In that moment I thought: what Gaoshan truly values are new directions that are "not yet widely proven, but coherent and profound." That takes "academic intuition and patience." Getting to learn from the professor in the same room before he won the prize was an honour, and also a reminder: true vision means seeing the value of something while it is "still unproven." Thank you, Gaoshan, for bringing "the future" into our classroom ahead of time; and thank you to the scientists willing to walk in silence. May we always keep, between knowledge and common sense, an "unpaved little path" for ourselves.

If you just follow along with what others are doing, then when they get stuck, you'll be stuck there too. — Professor Yitang Zhang Over the years, having met so many great scholars and been through the ups and downs of starting a company, I've slowly come to a realization — Not knowing too much about others' successes and failures is actually a kind of luck. Because knowing too many "settled conclusions" can sometimes box you in. As Professor Yitang Zhang put it: "You have to be able to think of what others can't think of. That's very hard. ...But if you don't pursue original ideas, it's hard to produce new results." During the days that were, by worldly standards, hard times, precisely because no one paid attention to him, he kept his own perspective. In the years when Yitang Zhang was thinking intensively about the twin prime problem, the mathematical community held an authoritative workshop that reached a pessimistic conclusion. But Zhang only learned of the workshop two years later. Through years when no one cared, he kept working on twin primes; he missed the workshop where "the mathematical world had already passed a death sentence," and so he was free to go on believing in his own path. In science, this may be a universal truth. Independent thinking takes hard-won courage, and it is also the freedom of not being boxed in. Starting a company is the same.
Family Business Succession Case: Sam Steinberg (Part 2)
Why do family businesses always lose just when they're winning?

The rest of the story: from glory to oblivion After Sam died, Steinberg’s problems surfaced fast. There was no succession plan, union contracts were neglected, and costs shot up; without its leader, the company lost its way. A non-family CEO briefly improved results in 1984, but the power struggle among the four daughters only grew fiercer. The shares were split equally but had to be voted together; the result was that nobody could really make the call. Mitzi took firm control, alienated the others, and in the end even resigned. By the late 1980s, squeezed by infighting, costs and competition, the company was forced into an auction. In 1992 it went bankrupt and the brand disappeared. All that lived on for a while were the real-estate company Ivanhoe (later folded into Quebec's pension fund, CDPQ) and the Pik-Nik restaurant chain. The Steinberg family is still wealthy, but the business is gone. Here's the timeline in detail: Sam first appointed his son-in-law Mel as company president, though he knew himself it wouldn't work. Mel wasn't the most qualified person; really, the job should have gone to a professional manager. But Sam loved the feeling of "family building it together, running it together," and didn't want to deprive the family of "the chance to run the company." Four years later, Sam put his eldest daughter Mitzi in charge of the discount department store Miracle Mart, despite strong objections from senior non-family managers. The business kept losing money. In 1978, Sam died. The trouble began immediately: there was no succession plan. Union contracts were poorly managed, driving up costs. With no leader, the company lost direction. In 1984, a non-family CEO took over. Voting rights were split equally, but had to be voted as a bloc. Nobody could really "have the final say." Mitzi began taking control of more and more, but alienated many people. In 1985 she resigned. She wanted to sell the company, but her sisters blocked her, and it ended up in court. Some improvements were made, and the share price rose. But by then a power struggle had broken out among the four daughters. By the late 1980s — family infighting, power grabs, rising costs, fiercer competition — the company was forced into an auction, valued at US$1.5 billion. Loblaw’s tried to buy it but was blocked on antitrust grounds. In 1989 it was sold for US$1.3 billion to a shipping company and the Quebec pension fund (financed largely with debt). Operations improved for a while, but to service the debt they started selling assets, selling the Ontario stores to Loblaws. Because rent now had to be paid, profitability declined. Bankruptcy in 1992 Recession, heavy debt, suppliers losing confidence, rising wages. Loblaws tried to buy it again, but the Quebec government vetoed the deal and arranged a sale to a local competitor. In June 1992, Steinberg's supermarkets and department stores vanished entirely. (Only 14 years later.) Aftermath: Its real-estate company Ivanhoe still exists today, but now belongs to the Quebec pension fund CDPQ. The restaurant chain Pik-Nik held on until the mid-2010s. The Steinberg family remains wealthy. To be fair, Sam's succession arrangements did at least keep the family wealthy, in three ways: 1. Wealth and tax planning He set up four parallel trusts: after the IPO in the 1950s, he established a separate trust for each of his four daughters. Each of the four trusts held 25% of Rockview, which in turn held 40% of Steinberg’s voting shares; add the 12% Sam held personally, and the family controlled 52% in total. Voting trust: even with the shares dispersed, while Sam was alive he could still exercise the votes collectively, preventing his power from being diluted. This helped the family avoid a huge hit from estate taxes, and ensured the family stayed wealthy after Sam's death. 2. Passing on culture and values During the war he insisted on low prices and honest dealing, refusing to go "black market," and stamped "customer first" deep into the company's DNA. That customer-centric thinking left the family a brand reputation and a cultural legacy. 3. A sense of family involvement Sam placed his brothers, sons-in-law and nephews in the company. There were problems in execution, but at least it ensured that "family members were present." This kept the family feeling like "owners" of the business, rather than just indifferent shareholders. Still, it's a real pity to see such a glorious business disappear. For a family business to carry on, it always has to face one question: how do you turn "one person's certainty" into "an organization's certainty"? Many family businesses don't lose because they can't make money. They lose at the moment of shifting gears. The day "the successor is announced" is like someone yanking out the router. Why? Class notes I. What’s at stake: what exactly is being passed on? Four dimensions 1) Interests (Wealth & Tax) What's passed on isn't "money." It's the structure of the money: Equity layer: voting rights (who gets to vote). Dividend layer: cash flow (who gets the returns). Tax layer: trusts, multiple jurisdictions (how to minimize leakage). Liquidity layer: buybacks, exits, buy-sell clauses (who can get in and out). Tool Card A Ownership map Draw four layers: voting / dividends / tax / liquidity. For each layer fill in: current state → target state → how to close the gap. 2) Power (Power & Governance) What's passed on is verifiable power. Not "I'm the one who decides." But who decides what, within which boundaries, and how. It has to be visible, traceable, and clear enough to question. Tool Card B Decision-rights matrix Left column: list of major matters (M&A, share issues, key appointments, budgets, red lines). Top row: shareholders' meeting / board (nomination and compensation) / CEO / EXCO. In the cells: right to recommend / right to decide / right to veto (tick). 3) Values (Values & Culture) What's passed on is "who we are." Values aren't slogans on the wall. They have to be built into processes, metrics, rewards and penalties. Tool Card C Values implementation checklist Value → which process → which metric → how rewards and penalties are triggered. Example: integrity → supplier onboarding → pass rate of two-person review → any violation is an automatic veto. 4) Identity (Identity & Legacy) What's passed on is the identity narrative. How the founder steps down with dignity. How the next generation steps up with dignity. Giving up a position is easy; giving up an identity is the hardest thing of all. How long does a first-generation founder actually need for a handover? The answer I heard at Harvard: succession plans of 10 years or more, every time. Maybe you could start with these three questions: 1) When do I stop managing day-to-day operations? 2) Which boundaries do I keep (strategy only / culture only)? 3) When there's a disagreement, whose "final word" do I accept? II. Why so hard: why is this so difficult? (Four factors) 1) Emotion and mortality Talking about succession = talking about death, about losing control. So everyone naturally avoids it. "The company is my child" — you can't bear to let go. (Sam's famous moment: the board voted "7 for, 2 against," and he laughed, "The opposition wins." A strongman culture makes systems useless.) 2) Complexity rises exponentially Scale × geography × business lines × regulation × relatives = an explosion of complexity. The era of phone calls plus gut feeling is over. You need a new order of process + rhythm + data. 3) Legitimacy shift Before, employees believed in the person. After the handover, they have to be made to believe in this system + this team. Renewing trust is the essence of family business succession. 4) Role confusion and the in-law variable Family vs. professional managers Siblings vs. spouses Shareholders vs. operators Multiple identities inevitably create friction. (Sam staked positions on his son-in-law and nephews, professional managers were sidelined, and the conflict spilled over into the company.) Every person's role here comes with unclear, or mutually contradictory, interests, rights and responsibilities. And once the family starts fighting, management won't be in much better shape. Family members aren't necessarily shareholders, but they work in the family business; Shareholders aren't necessarily family members, but their interests are aligned with the company; Operators aren't necessarily family members, nor necessarily shareholders — so how do you motivate them? How should each of these three identities — family member, shareholder and operator — conduct itself? Has this question been thought through? Tool Card D Seven questions on family participation 1 What's the bar for joining? 2 What are the qualifications for each role? 3 What are the recusal rules? 4 What are the reporting lines? 5 What are the limits on promotion? 6 What's the exit mechanism? 7 How is pay benchmarked against the market? III. Five common kinds of "failure" (counterexamples are the most instructive) Collapse once the patriarch leaves: everything is tied to one person. Fix: separate the layers — ownership, management and culture, running in three parallel lines. All-or-nothing roles: the founder goes from "all-powerful king" to "invisible emperor" or "completely out of touch." Fix: put the Chair/CEO boundary in writing; an annual "power check-up." The ghost that won't leave: a shadow CEO pulling the strings. (Sam left the chairman's seat but still had the most say.) Fix: a list of major matters; a reverse-delegation process; "three vetoes and it goes to the board." The chosen one: bloodline over competence. Fix: separate positions from dividends; succession follows a "competence path" (rotations + P&L + mentors). Everyone for themselves: the board, the family council and management at war. Fix: a majority of independent directors; nomination/compensation committees lead appointments and succession; the family council handles family matters only. Tool Card E Failure-path self-check Go through the five ways to lose and tick each one that applies. For each, write one "stop-the-bleeding action you can take today." IV. Spelling out "fairness": Merit × Inherit, a mixed order of competence and kinship Fairness has to be broken apart: Pay = contribution in the role (Merit): benchmarked to the market, not tied to bloodline. Dividends = returns on equity (Inherit): by shareholding, regardless of performance. Governance = qualification to govern: determined by experience/competence/recusal rules, and you can move up or down. Hard rules (3) 1) Pay for a role uses market bands; dividends follow ownership percentages. 2) A family employment policy: hiring bar, recusal rules, performance-based exit. 3) Scoring for governance seats: competence is assessed when terms expire, and violations trigger exit. Tool Card F Three-way split table Three columns: pay / dividends / governance. In each column write: who participates, how it's calculated, when it's adjusted, exit conditions. V. From "event" to "process": the timetable is what really matters Succession isn't "the day it's announced." It's a project you work backward on over 10 years. When the moment arrives, it's always too late — fix the roof while the sun is shining. Frankly, the late Zong Qinghou started passing on the business early, but the passing on of his wealth seems to have been settled only very late. That's a big problem too. Four milestones: 1) Target state: org chart + boundaries of authority and responsibility + values implementation table. 2) Candidate pipeline: rotations, P&L, mentors, a shadow board, succession drill days. 3) Board upgrade: a majority of independent directors; nomination/compensation committees; annual stress tests. 4) Emergency plan: a one-page succession checklist (who takes over, for how long, who supports, how it's evaluated). To be fair, what old Sam did well: If Sam could do it all over again... "Never put your life in the hands of a developer." → Don't put your life in the hands of luck and connections; put it in the hands of process and structure. "The opposition wins." → Let the system constrain the strongest person, not the other way round. "Ten years from now I must never look like that dim little shop." → Ten years from now, the organization can't be running on a single phone call. We've talked about plenty of failures; in the final part we'll look at what success looks like. As the saying goes... All happy families are alike; every failed family fails in its own way. Coming up in the final part: The ARC blueprint — turning "interests / power / values / identity" into a systemic capability of Assets × Roles × Capabilities. The family business episodes and lessons in this article are all inspired by the case of Sam Steinberg (HBS Case, condensed version), and abstracted from the course materials and practical experience.
Family Business Succession Case: Sam Steinberg (Part 1)
From business pioneer to succession impasse

Because family succession is the thing I care about most, I'm going to review this case in as much detail as I can. If possible, I'd even like to read it again word by word and squeeze every last drop of experience, knowledge and insight out of it. It's split into three parts: one, two and three. Part 1: the story → Sam Steinberg's retail legend and his succession impasse Part 2: distilling the universal succession problems, failure paths and methodology Part 3: the ARC model of succession — a blueprint and practical guide for passing things on Note this!! What a coincidence! 👇 The ARC succession model == our ARC! Here goes — enjoy: It all starts with a story Sam Steinberg: the "strong horse" that got the whip 1) Opening: a tale of two horses Montreal, 1911, a cramped upstairs flat in the immigrant quarter. A tiny grocery shop, piled with cardboard boxes, wooden planks and grease stains. Fourteen-year-old Sam stands behind the counter, celery leaves still stuck to his hands. He asks his mother: why is it always me working in the shop, while my brothers get to go out and play? His mother, Ida, looks up and says just one thing: "When two horses pull a cart, you whip the stronger one." From that day on, Sam understood: his fate and this shop were tied together. 2) The rise: self-service supermarkets, switching lanes in one go In the 1930s, Sam went to Toronto to study Loblaw's new playbook — customers pick up the goods themselves and pay together at the end (self-service). He came back and did three things: renamed the store outright to "Wholesale Groceteria," cut every price tag by 15%–20% overnight on a weekend, and handed out flyers to draw in crowds of first-time "supermarket shoppers." The result — "so busy you couldn't squeeze in." By 1935 he had converted every store to self-service; in 1943 he made the meat counter self-service too, reportedly the first in North America to do so. Sam's one-liner was blunt: "I saw a little shop that had been open for 10 years and was still so drab, and I thought — ten years from now, I can never be like that." He also brought shopping carts and transparent fresh-food packaging into Canadian supermarkets, turning the experience of "pick fast, pay fast, see the freshness" into a set of processes and store flows. 3) Customer first: data and human warmth side by side During the war years, many goods were rationed and scarce, and plenty of people turned to the "black market." Sam stuck doggedly to low prices and legitimate channels, and that cemented his reputation. Every morning he would make more than twenty calls in a row to store managers, asking personally about displays, restocking and customer complaints; he set up 20 stores as test stores, with another 10 as a control group; he assembled a panel of 650 women shoppers specifically to test new products, helping "male buyers" see things from a woman's perspective. This one-two punch of "frontline sensing + in-store experiments" had already taken shape in the 1940s–1950s. 4) Capital acceleration: a store every 47 days, and being your own shopping-centre landlord After the war, suburbanisation began and shopping centres took off. What Sam focused on wasn't "will others give me a spot," but — "don't hand your fate to the developers." So he went into shopping centres himself, and at the same time opened the financing floodgates: in 1952 he issued C$5 million in corporate bonds, in 1955, C$5 million in preferred shares, and in 1957 an IPO raised C$8.5 million; With this ammunition, from 1953 to 1960 he managed to "open a store every 47 days on average." By 1969, Steinberg's had 170+ stores and 17,500 employees, with annual sales of nearly C$500 million and net profit of C$6 million+. 5) Crack 1: milking the "strongman dividend" to the limit Sam was a retail genius, and an out-and-out "patriarch." Legend has it 250 people reported directly to him; at board meetings, even with "7 votes for and 2 against," if he was on the side against, he would say, half-joking and half-serious: "The minority is right." This speed advantage of "the minority vetoing the majority" worked when there was a single region and a single format; but once the organisation grew, the institutional support couldn't keep up. 6) Crack 2: the "asymmetry" of diversification In 1959 he bought 39 Grand Union stores in Ontario in one go, only to fall into the trap of "poor locations + strong rivals + price wars"; in the 1960s he moved into discount department stores (Miracle Mart), restaurants, petrol stations, stores in France, sugar/flour and more. Apart from some synergies in baking/sugar and the supply chain, most of these dragged down the core business. In 1968, the company's net profit fell by about C$1.5 million from the year before — the signs of weakening were already written in the financial statements. 7) Family and business: when "succession" is mistaken for "seating by closeness of kin" Sam and his wife Helen had four daughters. He longed for a son to take over, and even lost his temper when his youngest daughter was born, saying: "Another girl." So he pinned his hopes on his sons-in-law and nephew: his eldest son-in-law, Mel Dobrin, started in accounting and later ran retail + Miracle Mart; his second son-in-law, Leo Goldfarb, was in charge of real estate expansion and was seen by many as "the successor most like Sam." Unfortunately, the conflict between Mel and Leo grew ever fiercer. In 1968, Leo left the company and also divorced Sam's second daughter. Most crucially: Sam never really did any "consensus-building through communication"; he relied on "I appoint." When he tried to "make Leo the successor," he had Leo himself go and "inform" Mel... Need I say more — the conflict went off the charts right there. 8) 1969: lights out and handing over the baton At 64, the board and senior management together "invited" him onto the succession agenda. Sam decided to move up to chairman and held a three-day closed-door meeting to pick a president. The candidates were: his younger brother Nathan (very experienced, but more of an executor), his nephew Arnold (Harvard MBA, but junior), his son-in-law Mel (had the position, lacked the stature), and veteran Jack Levine (strong on regions and stores, but short on political capital). Three days later, the answer was still unclear. Because the real question wasn't "who is most like Sam," but "who can keep the institution running?" 9) Wealth succession vs. power succession To be fair: at the level of wealth and tax, Sam's planning was early and very smart — he set up parallel trusts for each of his four daughters; each of the four trusts held 25% of Rockview, and Rockview in turn held 40% of the company's voting shares; add Sam's personal 12%, and the family controlled 52% in total; there was also a voting trust that concentrated voting rights with Sam while he was alive, and estate tax was managed by "placing assets into trusts in advance." But at the level of power and leadership, he prepared too late, communicated too little, and found it too hard to let go. And he was far too lacking in imagination. He had only daughters, yet never once considered having a daughter succeed him. That's also why, even with 170 stores, tens of thousands of people and C$500 million in sales, on the day of handover the organisation could still drop offline in an instant. Sam's life took "the strong horse that gets the whip" to its extreme. With hard work and intuition, innovation and speed, he pulled an entire era forward; and through over-concentration, nepotism and discomfort with institutionalisation, he left the company wobbling at the turning point of succession. His story is like a mirror: wealth can be designed to be passed on, power has to be painstakingly practised, and values must be lived out day after day. Next, we'll take the "intuition" and the "method" in this mirror apart, and break down "family business succession" again from a more universal perspective.

Case Summary C&S Wholesale Grocers is a 70-year-old grocery wholesaler. In 1988 it landed a big contract with A&P supermarkets, and sales jumped from US$450 million to US$650 million. But with it came congested warehouses, more accidents and severe staff attrition (annual turnover among warehouse workers was close to 90%), and both productivity and quality fell. CEO Rick Cohen found that the traditional warehouse model of "division of labour + layer upon layer of supervision" was inefficient, blurred responsibility and was costly. He tried "self-managed teams": small teams responsible for an entire order (picking, loading, checking, signing off), choosing their own members, supervising themselves, and accountable for performance as a team. The experiment showed higher productivity, better quality, and workers who felt a greater sense of achievement. But Cohen faced a decision: roll it out across the board? How should it be implemented? Was now the right time? Timeline: 1918: Israel Cohen founds C&S. 1958: wins the Big D supermarket chain account and begins to grow sharply. 1975: a union strike nearly bankrupts the company → it moves to Brattleboro, Vermont, and becomes non-union. 1981: a new warehouse opens; annual sales are US$98 million, the target is US$300 million, and it ultimately reaches US$400 million in 1986. 1987: Cohen becomes CEO. 1988: signs A&P; sales jump to US$650 million, but the warehouse is overloaded and accidents and turnover are high. Summer 1988: Cohen tests "self-managed teams," with positive results. Autumn 1988: Cohen weighs whether to roll out teams at scale. Class Notes 1. Make sure there is accountability! No AccountabilityLow motivationNo link to role 2. The owner must be willing to relinquish control. 3. You have to choose the right people — team leader has to be a certain type of people. 5. They went from 4 hours of work at the start down to 2 hoursKPIs - incentivesClear Goals - own pallets - start to finish 7. Planning top-down vs Execution bottom-up 8. That is the people who they are？OR...What they act, is part of the production of the organization — MotivationBecause there is NO ROOM to doing so.There are room to get WAY MORE than you get from your employeesChange it and the employees are so better off.There are so many dissatisfied employees in the world 11. Get the influencer, getting them on boardWhen you try to do the organization change, get those people on board.Get the people with Right Amount of Ego! They need drive, but they can't be people who want to hog the credit 13. Teams will do training internally, because training new people also affects the team's output. 14. The feedback loop has to be very fast: everyone knows every day how many cases each person handled. Measurable output is crucial 15. How to do real [Self management team] instead of just saying it? How do you get people to truly drive themselves? Don't step in too much 16. Get the people early on, Listen to them！they can improve a lot40% fewer people - 30% is quality controlPeople do their job , it is their world To sum it up: on the surface this looks like a problem with the warehouse picking process, but underneath it touches on the leader's mindset, employees' motivation and the organisation's culture. 1. Accountability: someone has to own the responsibility The biggest keyword is Accountability. In the traditional model, an order is split among different workers, and when something goes wrong, nobody is responsible. The logic of a self-managed team is: one team owns it from start to finish — they earn money together and take the blame together when things go wrong. But there's a precondition: the leader must be willing to let go. If the boss watches every detail like a hawk, employees will always be mere "executors" and never "owners." 2. High Commitment Practices: getting employees to think like owners In class we heard an example: Walmart gives store managers company stock, so that they care about both their store's results and the company's overall performance. This is what High Commitment Practices are: turning "my job" into "my enterprise." In the warehouse, when workers know: how many cases I picked today → I can work out my pay the same day; if something goes wrong → the team bears it together; their sense of identity changes. Pride in ownership is the strongest motivator there is. 3. The original problems: low efficiency, high turnover, no accountability Before C&S introduced the reform, the warehouse was riddled with problems: Employees were overloaded and exhausted, and accidents were frequent. Picking aisles were blocked, pallets were left everywhere, and stress was high. Turnover was extremely high — most of the workforce was replaced within a year. No one owned responsibility → low motivation, work felt like going through the motions. This is very much like the pain points of many companies: busy, chaotic, error-prone, and in the end nobody is happy. 4. Self-managed teams: benefits and risks Benefits: Employees have a sense of ownership and are more willing to improve the process. KPIs are tied to incentives and goals are clear (e.g. 9,000 cases per shift). Owning an order "from start to finish" → quality improves markedly. Fast feedback → every day you know how much you earned. A little story from class: In 1992, in a small American town, three 17-year-old boys were the most efficient loaders in town. A job that originally took them 4 hours took only 2 once the father designed an incentive of "US$14 per person to load a truck of watermelons." Incentives and accountability really can squeeze out people's potential. Risks: Not everyone is suited to team self-management. It's easy to start and hard to sustain; leadership has to keep cheering people on. The team needs the right people: driven, but not the kind who fight for credit and glory. Training new people also has to be counted in the team's costs, or it will affect output. 5. Key points for organisational change The top sets the direction; execution is left to the front line: Planning top-down, Execution bottom-up. Fast feedback: daily numbers so employees can feel cause and effect. Culture + compensation, two wheels driving together: without culture to support it, even the best incentives get distorted. Attract the right people: find people with the right amount of ego — who want to win, but don't just want the credit. Bring the key opinion leaders (Influencers) along: organisational change has to win these people over first. Everyone longs to be proud: if they can't find that pride with you, they'll look for it somewhere else. 6. My Reflections The professor reminded us to be careful about our assumptions about "human nature." How employees perform is not entirely "human nature"; it's shaped by the organisational environment. A lot of the time, employees aren't "unmotivated" because they're lazy, but because the organisation hasn't given them room. Design the right mechanisms, and people's potential goes far beyond what we imagine. This class reminded me of a line: "Everyone wants to be proud of something. If the company doesn't give them the chance, they'll find it elsewhere." At its core, the self-managed team isn't just an experiment in a warehouse; it's a management philosophy: Give employees room Build accountability Drive with feedback Push forward on the two wheels of culture and incentives This doesn't just apply to warehouse pickers — it applies to our startup teams too.
Finance Case: What First Aid Beauty Teaches Us About the Delicate Balance Between Investors and Control

Case Summary Background: Lilli Gordon is the founder and CEO of First Aid Beauty (FAB for short). She was previously an executive at the skincare company Fresh and sold that company to LVMH. Her own skin is sensitive, so she decided to create "a skincare brand that provides first aid for sensitive skin," positioned as "affordable but effective premium skincare." Growth: After FAB was founded in 2009, it quickly got into Sephora (the US premium cosmetics chain) and QVC (a TV shopping channel). First-year revenue was US$2.7 million; by 2014 it had reached US$16.3 million, with US$24.8 million projected for 2015 Funding: At the start it relied on US$1 million put in by herself and friends; later came several small funding rounds and a bank credit line (US$2 million in 2015) Challenge: In 2012 growth slowed, and Sephora warned that the brand had to grow faster or be pulled from shelves. She sold her house, self-funded and poured money into advertising, and in 2014 sales doubled. Now: By 2015 FAB was profitable, but cash flow was tight and it had to raise its bank credit line every year. She held 47% of the shares, and at this point two PE (private equity) firms offered term sheets: Firm A: US$85 million valuation, investing US$25.5 million (buying 30% of the shares, common stock). The money would mainly be used to buy out existing shareholders. Pros: strong expertise and a good team fit; cons: a lower valuation and more equity given up. Firm B: US$100 million valuation, investing US$20 million (buying 20% of the shares, preferred stock). Pros: higher valuation and looser terms; cons: preferred-stock provisions and an overbearing operating partner. Class Notes When a company needs outside money, how do you choose between "money" and "control"? 1. Where the story starts: growth eats cash FAB was founded in 2008, positioned as "a first-aid kit for sensitive skin." With the combination of Sephora (the anchor retail channel) + QVC (the TV conversion channel), the brand leapt within just a few years from annual sales of a few million to a projected US$24.8 million in 2015. But rapid growth comes with an iron law: accounts receivable and inventory pile up fast, and every year you have to go to the bank to raise your revolving Line of Credit — by 2015 it had already climbed to US$2 million. Growth is, at heart, a black hole for cash. Growth eats cash! This is a lesson for Arcus42 too: we have to treat cash flow and working capital as core management metrics. Keep a constant eye on cash flow. 2. Enter the investors: Firm A vs Firm B By 2015, founder Lilli Gordon was facing two term sheets: Firm A Valuation: $85M Investment: $25.5M (30% common stock) Cash-out: the founder could take $14.8M Control: consent-rights threshold ≥15%, shares are common stock Firm B Valuation: $100M Investment: $20M (20% preferred stock, 1x liquidation preference) Cash-out: the founder could take $12M Control: holding any shares at all carries consent rights; any sale/IPO/restructuring within five years requires both parties' agreement B looks better (higher valuation, less dilution), but its terms are stricter. Core Tensions: A → more dilution, but looser terms; B → less dilution, but tighter restrictions. 3. The subtle clauses of control Compare the two firms' Investor Consent Rights: Firm A original text: "Any material change in the Company's Core Business … (Core Business = skincare, haircare, beauty products)" → Core business is defined narrowly, and consent rights only kick in with a stake of ≥15%. Firm B original text: "Any material change … (Core Business = skincare, haircare, beauty products including beauty supplements)" → Core business is defined more broadly, any stake at all carries consent rights, and even an IPO/restructuring within five years needs both parties' agreement. What this shows: control isn't your percentage of the equity — it's the contract terms. Is FAB short of money? It isn't short of day-to-day profit, but it relies on the bank raising its credit every year, and its cash flow is a roller coaster. 4. My takeaways Growth is a cash black hole: you have to work out ΔNWC (the increase in net working capital) ahead of time, so growth doesn't eat up all your cash. Debt for turnover, equity as insurance: day-to-day working capital should come from bank lines or supply-chain finance; equity financing is more about gaining "long-term partners + a safety cushion for the founder." Look at control along two dimensions: don't just look at your shareholding percentage — also look at the threshold clauses, the definition of core business, and restrictions on a sale. Agree on governance with investors: independent directors, consent-rights thresholds and the triggers for converting preferred into common should all be written into the agreement up front. Founder insurance matters: the founder's family cash flow can't be stretched too thin, or it will undermine a long-term mindset. Equity financing isn't simply "trading shares for money"; it's an art of "governance by contract." Valuation, dilution and terms intertwine to decide who really has their hands on the company's steering wheel. Control ≠ equity percentage; control = equity + terms. That's all — I hope it offers some inspiration as you think about "bringing in capital versus keeping control."

Case Summary In 2015, Google split itself into its core businesses (Search, Ads, YouTube, Android) and a bunch of exploratory subsidiaries (self-driving cars, smart home, a longevity lab, smart cities...), all gathered under the name Alphabet. What we discussed in this class was: why do this? What benefits and headaches does a structure like this bring? Why: Google's founders believed that to stay innovative, they should be like Berkshire Hathaway, using a holding company structure to house different subsidiaries and keep big-company bureaucracy from slowing down venture-style exploration. Financials: In 2015 Alphabet's total revenue was $74.9 billion, of which Google contributed $74.5 billion (about 99%); Other Bets brought in only $448 million (0.6%) but lost $3.6 billion. Typical examples: Nest (smart home) grew only modestly after being acquired — 2015 revenue was $340 million, far below expectations — and went through turmoil over management problems. Boston Dynamics was sold because it was too far from profitability. The relative successes were Android, YouTube and DoubleClick. Culture: Google was once famous for 20% time and for rewarding failure, but as it grew it became bureaucratic and lost talent; many employees preferred to go start their own companies. Investor reaction: In the early days of the restructuring the share price rose 6.2%. Investors felt transparency had improved and that Ruth Porat (CFO) brought financial discipline. The Q4 2016 results showed strong growth in the Google segment, while Other Bets kept burning cash. The tension: Should Alphabet keep backing the "Other Bets", or concentrate on the core advertising business? Can the holding structure really make innovation succeed, or will it lead to fragmentation and inefficiency? Questions for the future: How can Other Bets actually produce profitable businesses? In the wave of generative AI (Gen AI), should Alphabet change its structure to gain a competitive edge? Class Notes 1. The logic of diversification: why "do many things at once"? When a company diversifies, it has to answer two questions: 1. Better-off test: if the two businesses sit inside one company, do they create more value than they would independently? Example: Disney owns films, theme parks and TV networks, so one IP can be monetised again and again across different platforms — that is "supply-side logic". Google/Alphabet's logic is different: it has billions of users around the world, and this "demand pool" can be developed over and over, driving more new businesses — that is "demand-side logic". 2. Ownership test: does it have to be owned outright? Or can it be achieved through investment or partnership? Some businesses you have to do yourself, such as the core search algorithm; others can be done through investment or partnership, such as a venture fund investing in AI start-ups. 2. Explore vs. Exploit Once a company matures, it runs into a dilemma: Exploit: push the existing core business as far as it can go (Google's ads and search are the "cash cow"). Explore: go after new opportunities that may bring in no revenue for ten years (such as self-driving Waymo or health tech Verily). The problem is that these two kinds of business need completely different ways of being managed: Exploit emphasises efficiency, profit and stability; Explore emphasises trial and error, risk-taking and tolerance of failure. So Alphabet's approach is to manage the core business and the exploratory businesses separately, giving each the soil that suits it. Explore vs. Exploit Recognising the differences here is really important! 👇 Dimension Explore (innovation) Exploit (extraction) Strategic intent: innovation, growth cost, profit Critical tasks: new products, breakthrough innovation efficiency, incremental innovation Structure: adaptive, loose, team-based, often independent formal, hierarchical, specialised Processes: focused on generating, selecting and developing ideas; looser financial and operational controls focused on strategic/operational planning and capital allocation Rewards: milestones, growth margins, productivity Culture: risk-taking, flexible, experimental efficiency, quality, customer satisfaction 3. What are the benefits and headaches of this structure? Benefits: A clear separation of where the money comes from and where it goes (investors feel more reassured). New businesses get room to experiment quickly like start-ups, without being slowed down by big-company bureaucracy. The founders hoped Alphabet would become "the next Berkshire Hathaway", holding all kinds of companies for the long term. Headaches: Money burns fast. In 2015 Other Bets made up less than 1% of revenue but lost US$3.6 billion. Independent subsidiaries sometimes clash with the parent company's culture (Nest is the classic case: management conflict, and in the end the founder left). Independence also means knowledge-sharing is hard, and new technology doesn't necessarily flow smoothly into the core business. 4. Lessons for Arcus42 1. A company has to learn to "walk on two legs": squeeze every bit of value out of the core business while continually placing bets on the future. 2. But seeds can't burn cash forever — set milestones and be ready to cut them at any time. 3. Should exploration sit inside the company? If it sits outside (say, only through investing), you may lose the long-term vision and the capacity to absorb the technology; but if it sits inside, you have to accept the cash burn and the failures. 4. Not every exploration needs to be owned. Sometimes a market transaction is cheaper; the key is to work out the costs and the strategic value clearly. 5. Most important of all: a mature company only avoids being left behind when the next technology wave arrives if it keeps its ability to "explore" (Nokia is the cautionary tale).
Operations Management Case: Zara's Supply Chain

Case SummaryZara belongs to Spain's Inditex group and is the group's oldest, largest and most successful brand. In 2018 Zara accounted for 69% of group sales (about €18 billion). Its core is a responsive supply chain that can design, produce and put new items on shelves within three weeks. Customers come back often because there are always new styles in store. In 2010 Zara launched Zara.com. By 2018 online sales were 12% of group sales, reaching 14% in countries with e-commerce operations. But online orders brought high return rates and complex reverse logistics. Zara's response: - Launched "store optimization": closing small stores and concentrating resources on large flagships. Example: four small stores in Bilbao merged into one flagship, with more space and higher sales. - Rolled out RFID (radio-frequency identification tags) across the board, lifting inventory accuracy from below 70% to above 98%. - Began trying to ship from store inventory instead of relying entirely on distribution centres (DCs). - Launched Click & Collect (order online, pick up in store), which caused in-store congestion; Zara experimented with a robotic sorting system to ease it. - Invested heavily (€1.8 billion in 2017, €1.4 billion in 2018) to become "fully integrated, fully digital, fully sustainable." Core questions: with e-commerce growing fast, what is the future role of the store? How should inventory be integrated? Should Zara replicate its UK "integrated store + DC" model in other markets? Class Notes 1. Low-Hanging Fruit: the basics, improved In the early stages of a supply chain, improvements tend to focus on links that are easy to see and easy to measure: Better inventory accuracy (Zara used RFID to raise the industry's 70% accuracy to 98%). More efficient transport and warehousing (for example, integrating DCs and stores to cut duplicate inventory). Store optimization: merging small stores into big flagships, reducing redundant inventory and improving the experience. These are the "low-hanging fruit" — the first step in raising efficiency. 2. The real challenge: managing uncertainty On the slides, the professor particularly stressed: We have to learn to manage uncertainty. In fashion, uncertainty shows up as: Large demand-forecast errors: forecast error for functional products is around 10%, but for innovative fashion items it can reach 40%–100% (see the table on slide 13). Short life cycles: 3 months to 1 year for new fast-fashion items, far shorter than the two years for functional products. High return rates: the average online return rate is 30%, three times that of offline. Zara's approach is delayed commitment: test with small batches first, then go to large-scale production once market signals are clearer. Shein pushes this logic to the extreme, making 100–200 pieces of each style first before deciding whether to scale up. 3. Responsiveness is harder to copy than efficiency Zara's core isn't "better equipment than everyone else," but an organization that can respond fast. As a former general manager of Inditex put it: "We don't understand why others don't do this. Everyone has the equipment, and anyone can copy the processes." Behind that line lie the barriers of organizational habits, process coordination and culture. Rapid response is very hard to copy wholesale. Lessons for Arcus42Where is our "supply chain"? As a multi-family platform, our "goods" aren't clothes, but time, knowledge, vendors and experience. For Arcus42: Knowledge = inventory: it needs unique IDs, visibility and reuse (like Zara's RFID). Vendors = partner factories: they need profiles, a matching engine and a feedback system. Experience = test orders: pilot at small scale first, then replicate to more family clients. Client managers = frontline stores: they need to travel light, with the middle office backing them all the way. In other words, our middle office is Arcus42's "Zara warehouse + system." AI's new opportunity: from "fast fashion" to "real-time intelligence" The slides ended with a question: could there one day be a model even faster than "ultra-fast fashion"? The answer may be AI-driven real-time feedback. For Arcus42: AI can do "case search" and "solution recommendation" — the equivalent of real-time restocking. Client behaviour data (questions, needs, document edits) are trend signals. Through AI routing, the middle office can quickly dispatch work to the best-suited expert or vendor. This is our own "real-time supply chain." I always remind myself that doing things well takes enough time, patience and persistence. Operations is work that grinds down your temperament, but I believe there may also be people who are simply born loving these daily routines. Find people like that, and treat them with great enthusiasm and recognition. Tell them they are important.
Leadership Case: Designing the Future of Work (Distributed Work)

This case got me thinking a lot — I absolutely loved it. Everyone understands the principles in it; the hard part is execution. It's like losing weight: "eat less, move more." There's no secret martial-arts manual; the skill is built day by day. What I most need to improve next is execution — actually making things land. A good operating system empowers a team and helps it "win" better. Making the team succeed is every leader's ultimate dream. Case Overview Atlassian turned "distributed work" (employees collaborating without being in the same location) into a company-wide system: policies + tools + metrics + space. The data is striking: faster hiring, higher satisfaction, more controllable costs, stronger connection. 2019–2024: a product portfolio (Jira/Confluence/Trello/Bitbucket), annual revenue reaching $4.17B, 250k+ customers, covering 85% of the Fortune 500. The distributed policy became part of company strategy. 2020: the two co-founders made a "one-way door" decision: employees can work from anywhere in the 13 countries where the company has legal entities, with no mandatory return to the office. 2022–2024: they set up the Team Anywhere Lab (a ways-of-working lab) to run experiments around a system of work built on "information → goals → execution": page-led meetings, async-first, regular in-person gatherings (ITGs), and more. Space and data: they invented Cost Per Visit and Tidal Flows, and used them to close floors, redesign spaces and open new sites, matching real usage of "few people on site permanently + teams gathering periodically." Results: job applications doubled, offer acceptance rate +20%, 92% say distributed work lets them do their best work, 91% say it's an important reason they stay; one "swap meetings for Loom" experiment saved 5,000 hours in two weeks. Class Notes 01 Using a "leave experiment" to reveal organisational fragility Put key people on a mandatory one-week leave. See which processes stall and which knowledge exists only in someone's head. Two kinds of fragility get exposed: System fragility: handoffs with no documentation, meetings that depend on one person, approvals done over private chats. Financial fragility: revenue concentrated in one client, tight cash flow, heavy fixed costs for physical offices. A truly resilient organisation can "keep running fine with one person missing" at any time. 02 Remote Work: Benefits vs. Challenges. Benefits Services/support cover more time zones. Better hiring: a larger talent pool and more favourable demographics. Challenges Need a system: without standard operating procedures and documentation, remote only gets messier. Misplaced effort ("don't work hard"): it's not that people don't try, but that the effort goes into low-leverage synchronous meetings. Disengaged teams: trust decays over time. Meeting addiction: Zoom hogs the whole day, and deep work gets fragmented. 03 Key plays. Product and rhythm An intangible product (software) means output must be amplified through processes and accumulated knowledge. Flexible hours: guarantee at least 4 hours of time-zone overlap each day, and move everything else forward asynchronously. "Replicate interaction": even online, you need the weak ties of "chatting while walking" — use short videos, walking 1:1s and open collaboration hours to stand in for the office kitchen. Culture & Norms Write habits down as "explicit norms": how to set up a meeting, how to do documents first and discussion second, how to decline unnecessary meetings. Explicit/Transparent: information is public by default, lowering the cost of "asking around." Documentation-first Documents are "AI's raw material": write down goals, decisions, dependencies and next steps clearly, and only then can AI search, summarise and remind. Move beyond the "remote vs. in-person" debate: as long as documentation + async are in place, in-person time is just a periodic "amplifier." Emphasize differences Remote amplifies individual differences: those who are self-driven, write clearly and collaborate asynchronously will stand out markedly. Management should put "output and contribution," not "hours online," into performance reviews. Communication Digital meetings come with "5 minutes of silent reading together before the meeting." Ask: "Does being together actually bring a net gain?" If the answer is unclear, let async go first. AI assistant (AI recommend you what to do?) Make AI the "recommendation engine for your schedule and tasks": read your documents and meeting notes → remind you of next steps → generate to-dos and assignments. Offer suggestions and templates for "replacing meetings with video/documents." Formalizing good practices Lock in policies & procedures: Every meeting invitation must include "goals and expected outputs." Recording and filing of notes by default. A purposeful in-person gathering every quarter (3–5 days) to fully recharge the "connection battery." 04 Two iron rules under the remote assumption Transparent process: you can see who's pushing things forward, where they're stuck, and when they'll deliver. AI better: only if things are "well written and structured" can AI truly act as an assistant. 05 The pitfalls of hybrid (disadvantages of location) Geographic bias: people near headquarters are more "visible," while remote people are left passive. Split cultures: the office forms cliques, and remote staff feel like outsourcers. Efficiency loss: the same team stratified by location, and decisions slow down. Govern hybrid with "remote-first" processes. All important information is completed in documents first, then confirmed synchronously. What are the assumptions about people and work behind remote work? Assumptions: frontline employees are able and willing to manage themselves; pushing information down improves quality and speed; a sense of belonging drives performance. Agree: provided goals are clear, incentives are aligned and training is in place, self-management improves responsiveness and reduces hierarchical friction. Risks: unclear goals lead to loss of control; seniors mentoring newcomers is uneven; when external volatility is high, a stronger central coordinator is needed. Pros and cons of self-managing teams? Pros: faster decisions on the ground; stronger engagement; problems surface earlier. Cons: inconsistent standards; short-term performance swings; leadership development has to keep up. How do you make it land? Three steps: 1. Clearly define the boundaries (list the red lines on safety/quality/finance). 2. Training + shadowing: rotate team leads, dual sign-off on key decisions. 3. Rolling reviews: retrospectives every 4–6 weeks, keeping a rollback switch and a "library of experience templates." Overall, I think remote work is more conducive to becoming AI-native — using AI to amplify reuse, and rhythm to sustain connection. If you're also running a remote/hybrid team, I'd love to hear from you in the comments: What's your most painful remote scenario? What are the 3 little things you'd most like AI to automate for you? —— End ——

Intern Projects That Outlived the Internship

A blog post by my Harvard classmate Dan inspired me: Internships can be really cool! They can be hugely productive, especially in the areas interns are good at! I need young people — young people with passion who want to build some cool stuff! Lessons Learnt: Intern = project-based contributor Short-term focus, fast results Interns don't need to take on complex long-term strategic tasks; as long as they solve one clearly defined functional problem within 2–3 months, they can leave behind real results. Both of the author's projects (the podcast workflow and the Slack exporter) worked this way: focused function → pain point solved → immediate impact. Driven by a sense of achievement Interns often lack organisational influence, but if their project can be "used by the whole company," they get a huge sense of psychological satisfaction and belonging. That experience does far more to retain talent than "doing research and writing memos," and can even turn interns into long-term advocates. A win-win model For the company: a neglected but time- and energy-draining pain point gets solved at very low cost. For the intern: they see real, deployed results in a short time, which they can even put on their CV or blog — value that compounds over the long run. What we can put into practice at Arcus42: - Design the internship as "solving one functional problem": for example, Arcus42 could have an intern own a "client file auto-organiser" or a "family office knowledge Q&A mini-tool." - Keep the scope small but deployable: the goal isn't a "grand strategic plan," but a project with a clear deliverable. Give them a stage and visibility: once it's done, have the team use it and give recognition, so the intern gets a sense of achievement and a positive cycle forms. A potential talent-screening mechanism: interns who can deliver a valuable tool in a short time are more likely to become core team members in the future. My next post will be recruiting interns! Below is the original blog post: Intern projects, Machine learning, Working at Trail of Bits Most of the time, when your summer internship ends, your project gets abandoned. I've had that experience before. But Trail of Bits is different. As a business operations intern under Dan Guido and Sam Sharps this summer, I used Claude (Anthropic's AI model) to build two automation tools: a podcast workflow that saves 1,250 hours a year, and a Slack Exporter that lets employees find key company knowledge with a single query. Both tools will continue to be used company-wide after my internship ends. Podcast workflow Trail of Bits has expert teams across multiple fields, many with PhDs, covering AppSec (application security), AI/ML, blockchain and cryptography. They wanted to take part in more relevant podcasts to share with the outside world how we're pushing the boundaries of cybersecurity (and to encourage others to do the same). To contribute to the community, they focus on filling extremely niche knowledge gaps that almost only they can answer. But screening these keyword-relevant podcasts one by one by hand would take hundreds of hours of listening and research every week. To make sure we could find the "needle" in a sea of information, and do it at scale, we needed an automated workflow. Here's how it works: Users can run it manually, or schedule it to run automatically on a given day and time. The system detects whether an episode contains the right keywords, and Claude then generates all kinds of key information: a summary of the episode, the guest's views, timestamped quotes, draft outreach emails and more. All outputs are displayed through a Replit front end. While building it, I found that Claude had some limitations. For example, it would invent employees who didn't exist to match a podcast guest. To solve this, users can upload an Excel file to the Replit front end that maps Trail of Bits employees to the keywords they specialise in. Claude also couldn't find hosts' contact details directly. But it could extract the host's name and website, and then retrieve the contact details through an external API. Below are examples of insights generated by Claude and other supporting tools (such as the Excel file). This tool can monitor more than 50 podcasts a week — that's 2,500 episodes a year! Even with a conservative estimate of 30 minutes per episode, this workflow saves 1,250 hours of listening time a year. Not to mention the additional time saved finding hosts' contact details, matching the right employees and writing outreach emails. Slack exporter Trail of Bits' Slack has hundreds of channels, each potentially containing hundreds or even thousands of messages, so searching and analysing historical information is very time-consuming. To address this, the company had previously built a terminal-based Slack export tool that could export channels as JSON or Markdown files, which could then be uploaded to Claude for summaries and insights. However, this approach had two major limitations: Every employee needed to use the Slack exporter, but because it only ran in the terminal, only engineers could use it. Users had to know in advance which Slack channel contained the information they needed, because Claude could only understand the content of the exported channels. To solve the first problem, I released an Electron desktop app for the Slack exporter. Users just launch the app to export channels — no terminal commands needed, usable by everyone. The UI is also more efficient: users can search for channels, and even select all channels at once: Once one or more channels are selected, users see a range of export options (JSON, Markdown and so on). To solve the second problem, I used Claude's MCP (Model Context Protocol) to expose our Slack workspace directly to Claude. That way, through Claude's desktop app or code interface, users can search across all public channels and the private channels they've joined, with no need to export anything. Want to know the progress of every project in the company? Just one query. Need to onboard a new hire, but everyone on the team is too busy? Again, one query. With this tool widely adopted, our team can focus its energy on pushing the frontier of cybersecurity instead of digging through Slack channels for information. Generating excitement Everyone's talking about AI applications, but simply copying and pasting into a chatbot is just the tip of the iceberg. These projects show how far AI applications can go. To build applications like these, you have to understand users' problems and keep them involved throughout. My testing process went roughly like this: find a bug → urgent on-the-spot fix → receive a new feature request → test the new feature the same day. Unlike most intern projects, which "die" as soon as the internship ends, my tools survived because, through testing, employees applied them to their own challenges, experienced real efficiency gains, and then built them into their daily work. Just as importantly, they shared that excitement with other employees, which turned these tools into company-wide infrastructure. Through these projects, Dan, Sam and I hope to show everyone that AI doesn't replace employees — it augments their abilities. Every team has AI use cases waiting to be discovered. At Trail of Bits, we're working hard to find and implement them, and everyone can contribute — even interns. Another fun detail: to give this party some proper intellectual heft, I had AI write a business case on Pop Mart and attached it when I invited the professors. I'm rather fond of the title, <How to Industrialize Surpirse — "Hope you enjoy the case your students wrote for you" =D Taking the art of stirring things up to the max hhh Here's the case: Pop Mart: How to Industrialize "Surprise" — From a Small Beijing Shop to the Global Labubu Phenomenon Opening Hook: An Underrated Beginning In 2010, in a corner of the Europlaza Mall in Beijing's Zhongguancun, a small stationery and knick-knack shop of barely twenty or thirty square meters opened its doors. The owner was 23-year-old Wang Ning, a young man from Henan who had just graduated in advertising from Sias International College of Zhengzhou University. He had neither the halo of an Ivy League school nor any connections in venture capital. His four years at university were ordinary; like most of his classmates, his initial goal was simply to find a stable job. But after graduating, unwilling to settle into a life of following the script, he resolutely turned down an offer from an advertising agency and set out on the entrepreneurial path with RMB 100,000 in savings scraped together by himself and his family. In the shop's first few months, he guarded the shelves every day, watching monthly revenue in the ledger come in at less than US$4,300 (about US$4,100), and often fell deep into thought. The only goal he could come up with was: "Keep the shop alive first." No one could have imagined that fifteen years later, this little stationery shop would grow into a designer-toy giant with a market capitalization of about US$49 billion, surpassing countless well-known internet companies on the capital markets. Chapter 1: Three Rounds of Trial and Error — From Selling Goods to Searching for a Soul First Attempt: Trendy Stationery Wang Ning initially positioned the shop as a "trendy stationery store," with shelves full of imported Korean stationery. He even went to Hong Kong himself to bring back brands not available on the mainland, hoping to attract students and white-collar workers. But the stationery business was fiercely competitive with razor-thin margins. He often worked late into the night sorting inventory, only to open the ledger the next day and find that after selling a whole pile of stationery, the profit wasn't even enough to cover utilities and rent. Second Attempt: Imported Toy Collection Store In 2013, he decisively pivoted, turning the shop into a "trendy toy collection store" selling Japanese capsule toys, American figurines and little designer dolls from Hong Kong. For a while, the shop really was buzzing, with customers lining up to drop coins into the capsule machines. But the good times didn't last: these products depended on imports, with long supply cycles and high costs. He often stayed up late running to the airport to pick up shipments, hauling back boxes of toys only to find competitors immediately selling the same items at lower prices. His business was stuck in a loop of "sell a batch, run out, go find more stock." His margins were squeezed almost to nothing. Detail of failure: At his lowest point, he had to cut prices to clear stock, hanging a "buy two, get one free" banner in the shop, yet customers kept dwindling. During that period he nearly gave up, and even considered going back to find a job. Third Attempt: Searching for "Emotional Resonance" Amid the failures, Wang Ning gradually realized: what customers really wanted wasn't a functional "notebook" or "doll," but something that could spark emotional resonance. In 2015, at the Hong Kong International Toys Fair, he came across Kenny Wong's "Molly." That little girl with lake-blue hair and a haughty look made him instantly understand that "emotion is value." In 2016, Pop Mart launched its "blind box + IP" model. The randomness of the blind box created "surprise," while Molly's expression satisfied young people's craving for "buying things to make yourself happy." Pop Mart finally moved from "selling goods" into a new stage of "managing emotions." Chapter 2: Blind Boxes and Emotion — The Secret of the Model Blind Boxes: Probability as Design Every box hides an unknown design, and "secret editions" and "limited editions" set users' hearts racing. Blind boxes aren't gambling, but "probability-based experience design." Core users' annual repurchase rate exceeds 80%, with each buying an average of 12 blind boxes a year. Emotion: Products as Social Currency Unboxing blind boxes gradually became a social talking point. Consumers weren't just buying a doll, but "the feeling of being understood" — a social identity. Chapter 3: Labubu's Breakout — The Second Growth Curve In 2019, Pop Mart partnered with Belgian illustrator Kasing Lung to bring the picture-book character Labubu to market. With its sharp teeth, at once goofy-cute and rebellious, it struck many people as "weird" at first. Yet the younger generation saw themselves projected in its weirdness. Labubu quickly broke into the mainstream, becoming a vehicle for the "loneliness economy" and "self-expression." Business takeoff: In the first half of 2025, Pop Mart's total revenue was about US$1.94 billion; The Monsters (including Labubu) contributed about US$670 million, up 668% year on year. The plush versions sold US$860 million in six months, 44.2% of total revenue. Gross margin reached a whopping 70.3%. Cultural moments: In Los Angeles, fans spontaneously held a "Labubu Rave," treating it as an emotional symbol of the club scene. At the US Open in New York, Naomi Osaka took to the court with a custom Labubu, setting global social media alight. At Beijing's Yongle Auction, a 131cm Labubu sold for about US$150,000, officially entering the realm of fine art. Labubu became the "second curve" after Molly, powering Pop Mart's new growth engine. Chapter 4: The Smart Moves Behind It Testing the Waters with RoboShop Vending Machines Before opening a store, Pop Mart often deploys RoboShops first as market tests. Three days to install, real-time data collection, and only once a trade area's potential is confirmed does it invest heavily. In the first half of 2025, RoboShop revenue doubled year on year, and "home delivery" was added. Omnichannel Touchpoint Density In 2024, Pop Mart had 401 stores and 2,300 RoboShops in China; and 120 stores and 172 RoboShops overseas. Overseas TikTok revenue grew +5,779.8% year on year. In 2025, stores in the Americas increased to 41, with online revenue up +1,977% year on year. Compliance as Experience China requires a ban on sales to children under 8 and mandatory disclosure of odds and value. Wang Ning didn't dodge this, but built the rules into the product: semi-blind/open boxes, guaranteed pulls for members. Compliance became part of the user experience too. High Share of Proprietary IP In the first half of 2025, about 99% of revenue came from proprietary IP. Wearable IP Labubu was turned into bag charms and accessories, becoming a "social symbol" carried everywhere. Chapter 5: Capital Markets and Uncertainty. Record market cap: In August 2025, Pop Mart's market capitalization was about US$49 billion. Hang Seng inclusion and share price dip: On September 8 it was added to the Hang Seng Index, but its shares fell 7–9% that same day as investors worried about dependence on a single IP. At a board meeting, Wang Ning said: "Write the heat into the moat." His strategy: a multi-IP portfolio, global expansion, and compliance innovation. Lessons and Discussion A Non-Elite Entrepreneur's Breakthrough From an ordinary university, with no resources, he still succeeded. The key lay in a keen insight into "emotional needs." The Power of Model Innovation Pop Mart has no technological moat, yet it restructured the industry's value chain through "IP + blind box + social." Sticking with Long-Termism In an era where traffic is king, Wang Ning refused low-price promotions and stuck to the long-term experience. In the end, he won the trust of the world. Conclusion The Labubu story is a case of how an ordinary university graduate turned "surprise" into an organizational capability. From a little shop with monthly revenue of less than US$4,300 to a global IP contributing US$670 million in six months. Pop Mart proves that in the age of consumption, precisely capturing users' emotional gaps, combined with relentless execution, can let an ordinary entrepreneur build a business empire of his own.
