He transformed the store into a “trend toy collection shop,” importing Japanese capsule toys and American figurines. For a while, it drew curious young customers; lines even formed around new gachapon machines. But it wasn’t sustainable. Supply was unstable, margins were crushed. He would personally haul boxes from the airport, only to discover competitors selling the same toys at lower prices the next week. Failure detail: At one point, he resorted to “buy two, get one free” clearance banners to move inventory. Sales still fell, and customers stopped coming. He nearly gave up and considered finding a salaried job.Third Attempt: Discovering Emotional Resonance Repeated setbacks led to reflection. Why were customers willing to buy certain toys again and again? Wang realized the answer wasn’t functionality—it was emotion. At the Hong Kong Toy Fair in 2015, he encountered artist Kenny Wong’s Molly. With her turquoise hair and sulky expression, Molly had no backstory, but she radiated emotional character. Wang instantly saw its potential. In 2016, Pop Mart launched the “Blind Box + IP” model. Blind boxes provided surprise; IP characters provided emotional resonance. It marked Pop Mart’s transformation from selling products to managing emotions. Chapter 2: Blind Boxes and Emotion—The Secret of the Model Blind Boxes: Probability as Design Each purchase was a moment of suspense—would you get the common figure or the secret rare? Scarcity and exclusivity fueled repeat buying. This was not gambling, but probability-based experience design. Core users showed over 80% annual repurchase rates, averaging 12 blind boxes per year. Emotion: Toys as Social Currency Opening blind boxes became a social ritual. People collected, traded, and posted their finds. They weren’t just buying figurines; they were buying the feeling of being understood and belonging to a community. Chapter 3: Labubu’s Breakout—The Second Growth Curve In 2019, Pop Mart partnered with Belgian-born illustrator Kasing Lung to commercialize Labubu, a mischievous monster with spiky ears and sharp teeth. Initially “too weird” for some, Labubu soon resonated with younger consumers seeking self-expression and a quirky antidote to loneliness.Business Impact: By the first half of 2025, Pop Mart’s revenue reached $1.94 billion. The Monsters series (including Labubu) contributed $670 million, up +668% YoY. Plush Labubu alone added $860 million, 44.2% of total sales. Gross margin soared to 70.3%.Cultural Moments:In Los Angeles, fans organized a “Labubu Rave,” dancing with plush Labubus like emotional totems.In New York, Naomi Osaka brought custom Labubus courtside at the US Open, igniting global media buzz.In Beijing, a 131-cm Labubu sold for $150,000 at Yongle Auction, cementing its place in art collecting. Labubu became Pop Mart’s “second curve,” following Molly, and proved the model’s scalability. Chapter 4: Smart Moves Behind the Success RoboShop Market Testing Before opening costly stores, Pop Mart tested demand by installing vending-machine-style RoboShops. Installation took three days, and sales data guided location strategy. In 1H 2025, RoboShop revenue doubled, and “home delivery” was added. Omnichannel Density By 2024: 401 stores and 2,300 RoboShops in China; 120 stores and 172 RoboShops overseas. Overseas TikTok revenue jumped +5,779.8%. By 2025, the Americas had 41 stores, with online revenue up +1,977%. Compliance as Experience Regulators required bans on under-8 sales and transparent odds disclosure. Pop Mart embedded compliance into design—semi-blind boxes, guaranteed pulls for members—turning rules into part of the delight. Proprietary IP Share In 1H 2025, about 99% of revenue came from proprietary IP, ensuring bargaining power and margins. Wearable IP Labubu charms and accessories made the IP visible on the street, magnifying organic reach and social sharing. Chapter 5: Capital Markets and UncertaintyMarket Cap High: By August 2025, Pop Mart’s market cap was about $49 billion.Hang Seng Inclusion & Stock Dip: On September 8, Pop Mart joined the Hang Seng Index. Shares promptly fell 7–9% as investors worried about over-reliance on Labubu’s hype. At a board meeting, Wang Ning remarked: “We must turn heat into a moat.” His strategy: diversify IPs, globalize distribution, and innovate compliance-based design. Lessons and Discussion The Underdog Entrepreneur From an ordinary provincial university, with no elite resources, Wang proved success comes from sharp cultural insight. Power of Model Innovation Pop Mart didn’t rely on cutting-edge tech, but reinvented the toy industry with IP + blind box + social sharing. Long-Term Discipline While livestreaming and discount wars boomed, Wang resisted short-term temptations. He focused on experience, earning trust and long-term growth. Conclusion Labubu’s story is the story of Wang Ning’s hero’s journey. From a struggling shop making less than $4,100 a month, to a single IP contributing $670 million in half a year, Pop Mart shows how industrialized surprise—when combined with emotional insight and operational discipline—can transform an ordinary entrepreneur into the builder of a global empire. The "social contract," as seen from Singapore

Case Overview. Starting point: when Singapore became independent in 1965, its GDP per capita was just US$516; it had no resources and a divided society. Yet under the governance of Lee Kuan Yew, GDP per capita reached US$82,808 by 2022. Institutional foundations: public housing (HDB), the Central Provident Fund (CPF), a highly efficient civil service, and the Economic Development Board (EDB) as the "visible hand." It attracted foreign investment (MNCs) on a large scale and drove export-oriented industrialization. State capital: it founded state-owned enterprises (GLCs) such as Singapore Airlines, DBS and the port company, and later set up Temasek and the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation (GIC) to manage its wealth. Economic path: first labor-intensive, then high-skill, then tech innovation. Industry moved from electronics assembly to high-tech manufacturing, biomedicine (Biopolis), aerospace and chips. In services, Singapore became a financial center and a shipping and logistics hub. Social governance: a strong emphasis on multiracial harmony, but a heavy political hand (the PAP has governed for decades), with limits on the press and on assembly. Its social policies earned it the label "Nanny State" — banning chewing gum, restricting smoking in public, and so on. Crisis management: from the 1997 Asian financial crisis to the 2020 COVID pandemic, the government responded quickly. During the pandemic, migrant workers exposed problems of inequality. Current challenges: slowing growth (2023 GDP forecast at 3.5%). An aging population and low fertility (total fertility rate ~1). Reliance on foreign workers vs. local sentiment about jobs. The need to shift from efficiency-driven to innovation-driven growth. The risk of global deglobalization. A moment of handover: Lee Hsien Loong is preparing to pass the baton to Lawrence Wong. Wong has proposed to "refresh the social compact" — keeping growth going while becoming more equal, inclusive and green. Class Notes Throughout history, there have always been "empires" dominating the world order. The question is: by 2038, will we see an alliance of small countries, or a set of concentric spheres around big empires? 👉 If we turn the world upside down — suppose the big powers are no longer the protagonists — can small countries become "safe harbors" of stability and innovation? Singapore's Situation and Choices Back Then When Singapore became independent in 1965, it was practically "an island with no resources and no hinterland, caught in the middle of the Cold War." It had to solve three fundamental problems: 1. Politics: Lee Kuan Yew (LKY)'s top priorities were security and order. The social contract: the people gave up some freedoms (such as the press and assembly) in exchange for guaranteed housing, jobs and public safety. A strong bureaucracy (a central bank, a clean and well-paid civil service, continuity of the rule of law) kept the machinery of state running efficiently. 2. Economy: "Free market vs. socialism"? The answer was a hybrid. State-led government-linked companies (GLCs), plus direct investment attracted from multinationals (MNCs). Streamlined administration and slashed red tape meant foreign firms like Texas Instruments could start production within 50 days. Guaranteed monetary and institutional credibility attracted long-term capital. 3. Strategic positioning: It positioned itself as a "safe harbor" and a "neutral intermediary." Using its geographic location and trade networks, it turned a small country into a key node in global supply chains. The Singapore Model's "Social Contract" The old model: the state trains you to become efficient, technically skilled talent; you hand over part of your freedom in exchange for social security and stability. The result: decades of high growth that took Singapore "from Third World to First." But today, that contract is wavering. The Challenges It Faces Now 1. The innovation dilemma Singapore's economic model is built around "efficiency," but efficiency is not the same as innovation. Creativity, risk-taking and critical thinking are exactly what the old system suppressed. The experiences of Taiwan and China also remind us: strong execution ≠ strong innovation. 2. Social tension Of a population of 5.9 million, about one-third are foreigners. The number of foreigners has risen since the pandemic, sparking debate about jobs and social fairness. Young people feel the "social contract has broken down," and their sense of loyalty is declining. 3. Cost of living Rising home prices and living costs leave young people feeling that "hard work doesn't necessarily pay off." The social contract — "as long as you work hard → you'll have a home and security" — is no longer as solid. 4. The ebb of globalization The Singapore model depends heavily on globalization: free trade, cross-border capital, foreign talent. As globalization slows or even reverses, the "efficiency-driven" model starts to hit its ceiling. Why Transformation Is Inevitable Singapore has to think about: From efficiency to innovation: not just "skilled workers," but cultivating entrepreneurs and risk-takers. From content to context: not just mastering knowledge (content), but having soft skills too (EQ, contextual thinking). From "growth above all" to "a balanced social contract": fairness, inclusion and green become the new keywords. If this is no longer the age of globalization, the old model may not work. Singapore's success rested on "social contract + efficiency + globalization." But when the environment changes, the contract has to be renewed, or it will lose loyalty and trust. "In the past, the state fed the family (EAT your FAMILY); in the future, it must rely on the innovative power of families and individuals to give back to the state." 🤔 So... If the future really is a world of "clusters of small countries," can the Singapore model be replicated? What clauses should "Social Contract 2.0" contain to still hold up in a post-globalization era?

Pinkerton: Entrepreneurship and Doing the Math

The ending of this case is really interesting. It made me think, and it also helped me understand myself better — once you've taken care of your family, you should aim for something bigger. The Story. Background: In 1987, Tom Wathen was the founder and sole shareholder of California Plant Protection (CPP). He wanted to acquire Pinkerton’s, one of the largest security companies in America. Industry: The security industry splits into in-house "proprietary" security and outsourced "contract" security. It was a US$10 billion industry growing 6% a year, but fiercely competitive with thin margins. The trend was big companies absorbing small ones. Pinkerton’s: Founded in 1850, once a legendary brand. Acquired by American Brands in 1982 for US$162 million. 1987 revenue was US$408 million, but net profit was close to zero. CPP: In 1963 it had just 18 employees and US$160,000 in revenue. By 1987 it had grown to US$250 million in revenue, 20,000 employees and 38 states. Steady profitability, with 1987 net profit of US$4 million. Motive for the acquisition: Wathen wanted to be "the biggest in the industry," and believed Pinkerton’s brand value could lift pricing, that operations could be integrated and costs cut, and that working capital could be improved. The bid and the dilemma: CPP bid US$85 million but was turned down. The investment bank demanded at least US$100 million. CPP's board had only reluctantly accepted US$85 million and would find it hard to agree to more. Financing options: Mixed plan: US$75 million of debt (11.5% interest, 7-year term, principal repaid at maturity), plus US$25 million of equity financing, giving up 45% of the equity. All-debt plan: a US$100 million loan (13.5% interest), with principal repaid in instalments of US$5 million a year and a single US$70 million payment at the end of year 7. Core tension: CPP lacked financial capacity and cash flow was tight. Both the board and the banks doubted CPP's management capability and the financing risk. The ending: In 1998 Wathen cashed out $120m (for his 31% stake); discounted at 14% back to 1988, that's ≈ $32m — about the same as CPP's own valuation back then. Over the same period the stock market rose fourfold → the financial return lagged the broader market. Class notes 1. How do you think about the brand price? - How could CPP turn Pinkerton from loss to profit? Will I have the synergy? 2. Is a 14% discount rate credible? Is this number really credible? Everything depends heavily on the 14% assumption. What if it were 12%? 18%? 3. Non-financial Factors: Apetit For Risk. “I want it.” Competition. Risk of doing NOTHING?? — If you don't do it, the consequence is being continually squeezed in a fiercely competitive market. People are good at measuring the first risk - the risk of doing something - but terrible at measuring the second one, which is doing nothing. 4. Doing the valuation? — Find the most professional people! This is work for very, very specialised people. 5. Make the best choice based on: Maximizing Value Creation; Limiting the risk These two contradict each other! This is art instead of science 6. Lessons on the value logic of M&A Scale and standing M&A is the fastest way to make a "strategic leap." CPP went straight from regional second tier ($251m revenue) to national leader ($650m+ combined). Relying on organic growth alone, it might never have made the first tier. Synergies must be specific and quantifiable Cost synergies: cutting headquarters and redundant offices brings the expense ratio down from 6% to 5.8%. Working-capital optimisation: NWC falls from 9.5% to 6.2%, releasing cash. Brand premium: gross margin rises from 8.5% to 10.25%, while CPP's own profit gains an extra US$1.2–3.0 million a year. The case's reminder: synergies must be broken down into specific metrics (gross margin bps, expense ratio bps, NWC as a share of revenue) to support a bid. Brand and pricing power The Pinkerton name was the biggest source of value. Although American Brands had dragged it down-market into low prices, at heart it was a "premium heritage brand." The core of the acquisition was restoring the brand's positioning: trading a premium for higher margins, rather than fighting for volume on low prices. Lesson: brand value and pricing strategy can become mismatched; a good acquisition realigns them. 7. Lessons on financing and risk management Trade-offs in financing structure All-debt financing ($100m, 13.5%) → it can hold up in the short term, but after 7 years $70m of principal falls due and cash flow is bound to collapse. Mixed financing ($75m debt + $25m equity) → sacrifices 45% of the equity but sharply reduces risk. Lesson: better to be diluted than to let interest eat up your cash-flow freedom. Cash-flow coverage vs. accounting profit Goodwill amortisation of $5m a year makes the income statement look ugly but doesn't affect cash flow. So the success or failure of an acquisition should be judged on Free Cash Flow, not book net profit. Refinancing risk A large principal repayment at maturity (bullet payment) is essentially "a bet that you'll be able to refinance in the future." Lesson: structural design must take refinancing capacity into account, or the "1994 collapse point" is inevitable. 8. Lessons on organisation and integration The importance of management depth The board criticised CPP: no COO, no CFO, no head of marketing — it lacked the capability to run a national giant. Lesson: an acquisition isn't "buying assets," it's "buying complexity." Without enough organisational depth, synergies can't be delivered. Customer tiers and the logic of price increases Raising prices doesn't mean every customer will pay more; it means screening out low-price customers and keeping those willing to pay a premium. Lesson: post-acquisition pricing strategy has to dare to "let go," rather than fantasise that every customer will accept it Fit between culture and strategy CPP's path was "high quality + training," and Pinkerton had a "premium brand." The two pointed in the same direction; Pinkerton had simply been mismanaged. Lesson: cultural/strategic fit matters more than the financial model alone. 9. Lessons on strategy and opportunity cost The scarcity of the window of opportunity American Brands was determined to sell and the other buyers' financing had fallen through — only then did CPP get its chance. Lesson: M&A windows are driven by timing; "waiting for a better opportunity" often means the opportunity disappears The cost of not acting If CPP hadn't bought, Pinkerton would have fallen into a competitor's hands and CPP would have remained a regional second-tier player forever. Nor would it have had the chance in 1998 to be acquired by Securitas for $384m. Lesson: not acting has a cost too — it isn't merely "conservative," it may mean losing the chance of a future cash-out Strategic success vs. financial mediocrity But! The 32–33m is a "theoretical valuation," not "an amount you can actually cash." In that industry and market environment, acquiring Pinkerton turned CPP into a "national leader + heritage brand," and that is what created the "ticket" for the later high-priced cash-out when Securitas bought it. 10. Analogies and broader lessons The snake swallowing the elephant CPP acquiring Pinkerton is a classic "snake swallows elephant": the buyer was smaller (1:1.6). Similar historical cases: Tata–Jaguar Land Rover (1:1.6), Lenovo–IBM PC (1:3.3), AOL–Time Warner (1:3). It's hard, but the size gap isn't decisive; what matters is whether the brand/strategic logic holds and whether integration capability is strong enough. How entrepreneurs choose differently Wathen chose to take the risk → and fulfilled his dream of "being the biggest." A more conservative person might have chosen not to buy, keeping the finances sound but missing the exit opportunity. The final decision is often not about calculating IRR but a reflection of the entrepreneur's character and ambitions. M&A is not financial arithmetic but a strategic bet. It tests whether pricing power can be restored, whether synergies can be delivered, whether the organisation can digest the deal, and whether the entrepreneur is willing to bear enormous financial and managerial pressure for a "strategic leap."
Nokia: The Risky Leap at the Tail End of a Company's Life

Case SummaryNokia began in 1865 as a Finnish timber company and later moved into telecommunications. In the 1980s it started making car phones and military communications equipment, and helped push for Europe's unified GSM standard. In the 1990s, CEO Jorma Ollila boldly divested the chemicals and consumer electronics businesses to focus on mobile phones and telecom networks. Thanks to patents, design, rapid iteration and global production, Nokia overtook Motorola in 1998 to become the world's number one, with a 23% market share. In the 2000s, Nokia was hugely successful in Asia and emerging markets, with annual revenue of more than €50 billion and thousands of patents. However, after the iPhone launched in 2007, the industry shifted from "hardware manufacturing" to "software ecosystems." Consumer demand moved from "hardware features" to "app experience." Nokia stuck with its own Symbian system; it was slow to react, the operating system was clunky, and developers didn't want to write apps for it. Its rivals' iOS and Android ecosystems grew fast: by 2008 the App Store already had 300,000 apps, while Nokia's Ovi had only 30,000. By 2011, Nokia's smartphone market share had fallen to 25% (from nearly 50% in 2007). CEO Elop issued the "burning platform" memo, announcing that Nokia would abandon Symbian and switch to Microsoft's Windows Phone. But the transition dragged on too long, sales collapsed, and in 2013 the business was finally sold to Microsoft for US$7.2 billion. Class Notes 1. We should present that irony too: it could have been so expensive, so inconvenient, but look how different we can make it! 6. Change structurally in the industryOperators changed, shifting from phone calls to Data users: young people prefer texting to calling; many features that lived inside apps were later turned into built-in features by the iPhone — this is also a source of continuous innovation. 7. Although Apple has matured, the app ecosystem has kept it innovativeEntrepreneurship does NOT have to be only youBut also someone around you 8. Internal barriers to respondAlready Invested in SymbianLate — MicrosoftWhy did Nokia still stick with SymbianIf you go into Android, it made itself a commodity 9. Don't drink until you're tipsy. 2. Silence. Don't say things that harm others or yourself. Avoid idle gossip. 3. Order. Put everything back in its place; do each task at its proper time. 4. Resolution. Resolve to do what you ought to do, and once you do it, see it through to the end. 5. Frugality. Don't spend idle money that does no good to yourself or others; eliminate waste. 6. Industry. Treasure your time. Always keep your hands busy with something useful. Cut out everything pointless. 7. Sincerity. Don't harm others; don't deceive. Temperance Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation. 2. Silence Speak not but what may benefit others or yourself; avoid trifling conversation. 3. Order Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time. 4. Resolution Resolve to perform what you ought; perform without fail what you resolve. 5. Frugality Make no expense but to do good to others or yourself; i.e., waste nothing. 6. Industry Lose no time; be always employed in something useful; cut off all unnecessary actions. 7. Sincerity Use no hurtful deceit; think innocently and justly, and, if you speak, speak accordingly. 8. Justice Wrong none by doing injuries, or omitting the benefits that are your duty. 9. Danaher: How to Squeeze the Value Out of a Mature Business

Another company I could never learn to copy, but through it I saw the rules and inevitabilities of how businesses develop and how the business world works. From 1986 to 2010, over 24 years, Danaher grew revenue from US$296 million to US$13.2 billion, an annualized growth rate of nearly 30%, with annualized shareholder returns of 25%, beating GE and Berkshire. It's a bit like a PE firm, yet in many ways it goes further than PE firms ever do. The most important point: just as every person must eventually die, you have to think about the company's entire life cycle! Corperate Stategy is about when you enter? when you expand and when you exit. Case Summary Origins and growth: Danaher was founded by the Rales brothers in the 1980s, initially building itself by acquiring low-profile industrial companies. By the mid-1980s it had already entered the Fortune 500, emphasizing a "No. 1 or No. 2" market position. Culture and methodology: from 1988 it learned from Toyota's lean production, gradually forming the Danaher Business System (DBS), whose core is "continuous improvement (kaizen)." Leadership and transformation: under George Sherman from 1990 to 2001, the company shifted from tires and tools toward higher-value-added areas such as environmental testing and electronic instruments; in 2001 Larry Culp took over as CEO and kept strengthening the platform strategy. Strategic growth platforms: the company is organized around 5 major segments: Environmental, Test & Measurement, Dental, Life Sciences & Diagnostics, and Industrial Technologies. Each platform expands through a model of "large platform acquisitions + small bolt-on deals." DBS in detail: built around four Ps — People, Plan, Process, Performance — with emphasis on a 100-day strategic plan, kaizen events, and Policy Deployment (something like a "lighthouse for strategy execution"). After an acquisition, it rapidly introduces DBS culture and tools. Example: Radiometer, a blood-gas analyzer company acquired in 2005: after the acquisition, DBS cut the production cycle from 18 days to 2, shortened the R&D cycle by 33%, and raised operating margin by 4%, while R&D investment increased at the same time. Results: from 1986 to 2010 revenue grew from US$296 million to US$13.2 billion, an annualized growth rate of nearly 30%; annualized shareholder returns of 25%, beating GE and Berkshire. Challenges: 1. Can growth be sustained when acquisitions slow? 2. Competition from private equity funds (Blackstone and others) is driving up acquisition prices; 3. Can the culture of continuous improvement be maintained over the long term? 4. Is DBS suited to moving into high-tech fields? Class Notes 1. After an acquisition, how do you get the team "pulling in the same direction"? I can force my children to do things, or by embrace them. If you can't even force your own children, how can you get a team to buy in willingly? How do you help them understand? Asking Questions: co-creating the strategy Within 100 days of a deal, Danaher works with the target company's management to draw up a "strategic blueprint." Not by handing them a thick PPT deck and telling them to follow it, but by putting the problems found during due diligence on the table and asking: "Where do you think the gaps are? How do we close them?" Radiometer's CEO once said: "Danaher didn't tell us what to do; it kept asking: are you really capturing every growth opportunity?" Through "co-creation," the original management feels it has a voice, and the culture is not steamrolled but activated. 2. Visible victories (Quick Wins) Soon after a deal, they run a value-stream mapping + kaizen exercise. For example, Radiometer's plastic-parts process: 18 days → 2 days. This kind of "see it, touch it" improvement instantly wins over the skeptics: "Oh, so this method really can help me." Danaher calls this "action learning" (learning by doing). 👉 Culture isn't built by shouting slogans, but by building confidence one small win at a time. 3. To acquire or not? — The Best Ownership Test Disney is the best for Pixar; Pixar is the best for Disney 4. The different stages of a business: Danaher shows up at a company's mature stage. The mature stage is when you should raise efficiency, and DPS happens to raise efficiency — so it isn't like PE, which merely buys; it buys companies in order to "squeeze out the profits." 5. What do you do when a business has already entered decline? Sell; Change, jump to another technology/industry; Concentrate: like Lego, they jump to provide for the adults instead of children

Ron Johnson: A Career in Retail

Case SummaryBackgroundRon Johnson (HBS Class of 1984) created successful retail innovations at Target and Apple and was seen as "the Steve Jobs of retail". In 2011, at the urging of Bill Ackman (an investor holding 18% of J.C. Penney), he became CEO of J.C. Penney with the goal of a complete transformation. J.C. Penney's predicamentAn old-line department store whose customers were middle-class, price-sensitive suburban mothers. From the 2000s it was squeezed from three sides — discount superstores (Walmart, Target), upscale department stores (Macy’s) and fast fashion (H&M, ZARA) — plus e-commerce (Amazon), and its market share and profitability kept sliding. Johnson's transformation measuresPricing: scrapped 600 annual promotions and introduced "Fair and Square Pricing", with no more discounts or coupons.Placement: proposed a "Store within a store" concept, like a small town's main street plus square, to create an experience.Product: brought in designer brands and exclusive products and reinvented the private labels.People (culture): eliminated sales commissions and adopted Apple "Genius Bar"-style advisory service.Promotion: a new logo, a new spokesperson (Ellen DeGeneres), and slogans in the colours of the American flag. ResultsImplemented too fast and without testing; loyal customers were disappointed (they were used to coupons), and new customers never became loyal. In 2012 the company posted heavy full-year losses, the share price fell from US$24 to US$16, sales dropped 20%–27%, and thousands were laid off. OutcomeIn April 2013, Johnson was forced out and former CEO Ullman returned. The board felt that while the direction of the transformation was visionary, its execution was far too aggressive and bordered on disaster. Negotiation Process Case Summary The opening and the stakes In 2009, Fairstar (a Dutch heavy marine transport company) bid for Australia's Gorgon natural gas project (total investment US$42 billion). If it won, the transport contract would be worth US$80–100 million and would significantly lift the company's standing. After 8 months of waiting and three announcement dates that "slipped," CEO Philip Adkins was finally asked the clincher: "What's your best price?" (Asking for the "best price" is a common buyer probe to push prices down.) The industry and the company Heavy marine transportation uses open-stern semisubmersible vessels to carry giant modules directly on deck (faster and more stable than wet or dry towing). For complex projects, front-end engineering can run to 25,000 hours. Day rates for top vessels can reach US$100,000/day, far above operating costs (see Exhibit 2). Fairstar was founded in 2005; its shipbuilding and refits overran by two years, and it lost US$7.53 million in 2007–08; by 2009 it had revenue of US$50.67 million and net profit of US$12.36 million, with an industry-leading EBITDA margin. It shifted its strategy to high-end module transport, targeting 80% utilization × US$80,000/day. Its two vessels, Fjord and Fjell, are open-stern, which gives it more bargaining power. The rival and the opportunity Industry leader Dockwise had 15 vessels and a significant market share. Gorgon needed roughly 250,000 tonnes of LNG modules shipped from fabrication yards in Singapore, Korea and China to Barrow Island in Australia (a Class A nature reserve with very strict environmental standards). Fairstar's asbestos-free vessels, shallow draft, and Fjord's 45m beam were an excellent fit for loading the largest modules. A "no-contact" bidding process The KJVG, led by KBR/Chevron, required that the whole process be anonymous, with no contact and a single online Q&A, where questions and answers were visible to all bidders; it also provided a "non-binding" sample transport agreement. Fairstar quoted US$95k/day for Fjord and US$75k/day for Fjell, with no discount, betting on "winning with quality." Both "announcement dates," in October and December, slipped. A new variable appears On February 25, 2010, Dockwise withdrew (presumably because its vessels contained asbestos and didn't meet environmental requirements), and Fairstar instantly became the favorite; but on February 28 the third announcement slipped again. Meanwhile, Fairstar had made a verbal commitment to Guangzhou Shipyard for two new vessels (US$101 million each), with payment due in June — but only on the premise of winning Gorgon. The financial and reputational pressure soared. The buyer "changes the contract" In April 2010, KJVG sent a new version of the contract: the terms were more one-sided, including a 10% performance payment it could withhold at will, and the right to replace crew members at will. Fairstar struck out every new clause in the electronic system and sent it back, gambling that it would "be called in to meet." Sure enough, the next day it got a call, and a face-to-face negotiation was set up in London. Into the negotiating room At the first meeting on May 11, it was 7 against 1 (Chevron/KBR lawyers + project managers vs. Adkins). The two sides went through the terms one by one: KJVG accepted some of the changes; Fairstar also conceded on "replacing crew" — the other side explained this was a uniform management clause needed because of another bidder, a Korean company new to the industry. Contract scope: Fjord for at least 1 year from 2012, with Chevron/KJVG able to extend by another 4 months; Fjell was excluded because the modules had grown larger. When they met again the following week, the only thing left unsettled was price. The final kick The board had discussed a "token reduction of US$5,000/day" (≈ US$1.5 million/year in concessions), but also worried about undermining its positioning and shareholder returns. In the meeting room, the other side's single line, "What's your best price?", pushed Adkins to a decision: hold the price? Concede a little? Or offer a structured price? Class notes 1. Could have been better?Have the meeting soonerChange offer when it came to 2 to 1 ？ 2. Should he go ALONE or TAKE SOMEONE The upside: CLOSE THE DEAL, Confident. Case Summary Disney's long-term success rests on a "synergy flywheel" (Synergy: businesses driving one another) that runs from content (IP) → distribution → parks and consumer products (Parks & Merch) → and back to content. Michael Eisner took over in 1984 and revived the company with strong management and the "20-20" targets (20% annual growth in ROE and profit); but in his later years, over-diversification, micromanagement and misallocated resources led to slowing momentum and governance controversies. After that, Bob Iger extended the company's run by "buying big IP, cutting non-core businesses and betting on streaming (DTC)," but making streaming profitable became the new problem. Case Discussion Now: linear TV is declining, streaming is hard to make profitable, and parks CAPEX is high, forcing the company to rebalance. Main tensions: the long-term synergy flywheel vs. over-diversification and organizational governance; content scale vs. streaming cash flow. Some important facts about strategy 1. Performance varies enormously — it's not "everyone's about the same." The average return on invested capital of US companies in 2013–2022 follows a "fat middle + long tail" distribution, with the top and bottom pulled far apart; most companies' ROIC sits around 10%. 2. Returns really do differ a lot across industries: cross-sectional differences in ROIC are significant — choose your industry carefully! 3. Industry ≠ destiny Within the same industry, different strategies lead to equally "sharp divergence" in performance; which industry you enter matters, but what matters more is "how you play within the industry"; advantage isn't static — it's also about "how fast you respond to change." 4. The main factors that affect company performance Firm effect 40% = the company's own choices and activity system, including: whom you serve, what you sell, how you price, how you go to market, how you run your processes, what incentives you use, and where you put your money. Dynamic effect 36% = external/internal dynamics that change over time: technology curves, user preferences, competitors' plays, distribution rules, regulation and the macro environment change the game over time. Industry effect 14% = the average level of the industry structure: different industries have different "ceilings/floors" (different Five Forces and profit-pool positions) — "industry matters, but it isn't destiny." Corporate effect 10% = the effect at the group/parent level: in multi-business groups, capital allocation, sharing of talent/brand/data, governance and incentives can boost or drag down each business unit. What is strategy? A set of mutually reinforcing choices that lets a company find its niche in its industry and earn long-term returns. Strategy is responsible for three things: 1. Look at the whole picture from the outside. Size up the environment of an organization in its entirety. 2. Configure the company's internal choices into an "interlocking" system. Configure all of a firm's internal choices to attain a competitive advantage and create value within an external environment 3. Develop sustainable competitive advantage amid internal and external change. Sustain a company's advantage over time in the face of internal and external dynamics See the whole picture outside → configure all choices inside into a system → keep the advantage "alive" through change. Strategy isn't writing down a goal at the start of the year — it's a closed loop of "external–internal–sustainability." The first thing: see the whole picture What to look at? Find the profit pools: see clearly in which link, which segment and which region the money is really being made. Identify the "gates": who controls the distribution shelf, standards, data and payments — these determine your bargaining power. Anticipate shifts: technology S-curves, regulation, macro funding conditions, changes in user habits — the factors that rewrite the rules of the game. Set clear boundaries: tell the team what not to do; make your trade-offs dense. How to look? Customer needs/scenarios (Jobs-to-be-done): in what situations is it "you or nothing" for the customer? Direct rivals & substitutes: who is attacking you today; who might cross over and attack you tomorrow? Distribution/channel shelf: platform take rates, traffic rules, conversion costs. Supply and bargaining power: upstream concentration, key scarce resources (talent, compute, IP, licences). Rules/regulation/tax: market access, compliance costs, cross-border restrictions. Technology curve: which stage you're in (emerging/accelerating/mature/being replaced) and its impact on cost and experience. Capital and macro: interest rates, exchange rates, risk appetite — who's paying. Complementors: who can make your product more valuable (ecosystem partners, content/IP, hardware). Answer three questions: Whom do you serve? How will you win? What won't you do? Common mistakes: looking only at the industry "average" and ignoring divergence among peers and differences between segments. Treating rivals as the environment and forgetting that platforms/distribution/regulation are the bigger chessboard. Looking at the static picture, not the dynamics (review key metrics and triggers quarterly). Information too scattered, never landing in decisions (enter/exit, raise prices/cut costs, M&A/partnerships). Too much detail, missing the first-principles questions: where's the money, where's the power, where's the change? The second thing Configure the company's internal choices into an "interlocking" system (to win in the external environment) Internal choices include 8 levers 1. Customers and value proposition (who, and what wins them over) 2. Product/service mix and pricing (what to sell, how to bundle, how to charge) 3. Channels/distribution (direct sales? agents? platforms? who controls the shelf) 4. Operating processes (delivery, SOPs, quality standards, SLAs) 5. Core capabilities and assets (technology, data, brand, IP, supply chain) 6. Organization and talent (reporting lines, roles, hiring standards) 7. Incentives and KPIs (where the money points, what counts as winning) 8. Capital allocation (what to invest in, what not to; the split between R&D/capacity/M&A) How to "configure it into a system" One chain: "acquire customers → close the deal → deliver → repeat purchase/referral" as a single chain At each link, keep only the actions that make the next link stronger! Set reverse constraints: pair every choice with a not-to-do list For example: no ultra-customised work, no loss-making customer acquisition, no low-margin channels Clean up conflicts: wherever KPIs and incentives run counter to the strategic direction, fix the incentives first For instance, if you want "high repeat purchases," don't just pay "new-customer commissions" 3 signs of a good system A clear customer profile, and fast team decisions A new hire can run 80% of the processes within 2 weeks Optimising a single point amplifies along the whole chain rather than being cancelled out The third thing: build "sustainable competitive advantage" amid internal and external change No single trick in strategy works forever — you change shoes as you run: sensing change (external + internal), running small experiments, and reallocating resources all at once, so the advantage carries through cycles. Where does change come from? External: technology curves, customer preferences, platform/distribution rules, regulation, interest rates/funding conditions, competitors' plays. Internal: the organization slowing down, bloated processes, incentives drifting off course, generational turnover in talent, ageing products. 4 mechanisms for staying alive (S→S→R→N) 1. Sense: set up a quarterly strategy hour Customers/rivals/technology/regulation/channels, etc. 2. Seize: place small bets (pilots) Set stop-loss lines and success thresholds, using time, cost, retention, etc. 3. Reconfigure: set a hard rule of reallocating 20–30% of the budget each year Move money and people from old projects to new directions that have proven effective). 4. Nurture: write successful practices into SOPs and build them into the shared platform Data, tools, templates, etc., so that onboarding new people gets cheaper and cheaper. 6 "sources of sustainability" — pick 2–3 and take them to the extreme 1. Scale cost advantage (the more you do, the cheaper it gets) 2. Network effects (the more users, the better it works) 3. Data/model advantage (others can't copy it) 4. Brand and mindshare (first-choice position, courage to charge) 5. Switching costs (painful migration, contractual lock-in, ecosystem lock-in) 6. Scarce assets (exclusive content/IP, licences, channel positions, rare talent) Common mistakes (every single one hits home for me...) Only adding projects, never cutting them, leading to an "overloaded stack" (a habit I often fall into❗️) All metrics are "lagging indicators" (revenue), with no "leading indicators" (retention, repeat purchases, TTM) A culture that only talks about "trial and error" but sets no stop-losses ends up as a "collector of unfinished projects" The "moat" stays a slogan, with no concrete practices or quantified targets When should you change strategy? 1. Your core customers' needs/usage scenarios have changed 2. Distribution rules have changed (platform take rates, traffic entry points) 3. Unit economics start deteriorating and haven't been fixed for 2 consecutive quarters

My biggest takeaway from this class: have plenty of specialists on board as suppliers, and have a plan ready in advance. Case Summary On June 27, 2017, the destructive worm (a self-propagating virus) NotPetya wiped out almost the entire digital system of TNT Express, which FedEx had just acquired. FedEx immediately activated its crisis playbook (BCDR), "cutting off + protecting itself" on one hand and "relaying by hand + rebuilding step by step" on the other — a live exercise in turning a "technical disaster" into "operational resilience." That morning, the Americas headquarters received an alert from Europe. TNT's computers and servers went down like dominoes: "black screen + ransom screen." At first it looked like ransomware, but it was soon confirmed to be wiper malware, whose aim was "destruction," not "money." It spread extremely fast: within minutes "a whole site was down," within tens of minutes "clients worldwide were down." About 40,000 of TNT's computers + 10,000 servers were written off. FedEx quickly set up a Cyber Incident Response Team (CIRT) and cut the connection between TNT and FedEx ("hit the big red button") to protect the "mothership." That night it decided to report a material event to the SEC (8-K) and briefly halted trading to explain. The share price stayed basically steady. The next day it issued a press release: other businesses were operating normally, TNT was affected, and the financial impact "could be material." On the technical side, a war room was set up in Atherstone, UK. All TNT had left were scattered paper network diagrams and files on a few laptops that hadn't been networked. The phone system was down, so they communicated via WhatsApp. The team first rebuilt accounts/directory services (Active Directory) and "the five things needed to stay alive" (communications, payables/receivables, etc.). On the operations side, they didn't shut down. Using the primary-secondary-tertiary (P-S-T) model: whatever could be switched to FedEx systems was switched; whatever couldn't went "fully manual." Trucks kept running, with routing done by "muscle memory." Meanwhile "FedEx Bank" injected working capital to make sure TNT stayed alive first. The backup system was the pain point. TNT mainly used cold backups on tape, which couldn't be restored quickly in parallel. FedEx made an emergency purchase of hard drives, copied the tapes onto disks for parallel recovery, and created "three copies" of new backups — cloud, disk and offline; privileged accounts were cut from "thousands of people with access" to "just 8 people, like FedEx." At the same time, 900 applications were shed. On the customer side, the CIO's team reassured 40 major customers "one-on-one." There were still week-long delays, the media reported "parcels piled to the ceiling" in warehouses, and competitors seized the chance to poach customers. FedEx had no cyber insurance at the time, and the losses were mainly lost business. Tracing it back confirmed it was a supply-chain attack, infiltrating through the legitimate update channel of a Ukrainian accounting software package. Many global giants were hit, with total losses estimated at ≥ US$10 billion. The share price did not take much of a hit. Class Notes 1. When a crisis hits, are you in Plan mode or Responding mode? 2. A crisis management company can first become a supplier and run crisis rehearsals for the company. Let the risk management side run "phishing stings" to check who is the weak point; anyone caught has to take an extra two-day weekend training. 3. Take Blame and Failure out of the discussion — Focus on MissionCEO NOT emotional is really important 4. Before bring a new company to your car, you need to understand the materials of this new company. 5. What is the last time you ask your people to put the company above them. 6. Are your people BURN OUT? All My Crisis Response Advice Stabilise the situation first Confirm the real scope and impact of the crisis; avoid both excessive panic and overreaction. Immediately set up a temporary crisis team to centralise communication and decisions. Protect the core First secure cash flow, key customers, core employees and brand reputation. If it's a PR crisis, quickly align on one message to avoid confusion. Communicate transparently Internally: let employees know what's going on, to head off rumours and panic. Externally: stay reasonably transparent with customers, partners and the media — acknowledge the problem and communicate the solution. Draw up a short-term action plan Set clear priorities within 72 hours (e.g. stopping the losses, stabilising relationships, compliance response). Break the problem into a few actionable small steps and carry them out one by one. Long-term repair and prevention After the crisis, do a post-mortem: why did it happen, and which internal mechanisms failed? Build an "early-warning system" and drill routines, turning the crisis into an opportunity to upgrade the organisation.
Operational Leadership: From Founder → Scaling → Professional Managers

My biggest takeaway from this round of classes is Start with Charisma, Scale with Process. Without process, there's no optimization. If you want to scale, you first have to build up your inner strength. Professionalizing management is a process of organizational change. A large company may need a 20-year handover. Case Summary The 2024 decision: three brothers gather in a backyard in Dubai to celebrate CEO J. Joseph completing nine years in the role. He'll step down at the end of this year, and for the first time a non-family CEO will take over. The strategy for the next five years: double down on Saudi Arabia + double down on modular construction. But the organization is going through the biggest centralization and digitization overhaul in its history — is it safe to "raise the bet" now? Background: the market and the window. Saudi Vision 2030 has brought a wave of giga-projects (estimated at about $1.25T in total). In 2023, new contracts signed in the GCC hit $205B, a record high, mainly in Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Modular grew from $2.9B to $3.5B in 2020–2023, with demand strengthening. But by 2024 the Saudi sovereign fund's cash was only about a quarter of its 2020 level; fiscal shortfalls are visible, and the window is limited. Decentralized expansion (1993–2002): founder Chebel set up AMANA in the UAE in 1993. It entered a new country every year, with country managers given broad authority plus profit-sharing, like "little kingdoms." The result: low efficiency, high risk, and a loss-making headquarters. At this point Riad was brought in, on the condition that a corporate headquarters be built, operating manuals written, and key powers such as approval of large contracts pulled up to headquarters. In 2005 the group returned to profit. From then on it held for years to retaining ≥50% of net profit each year as a buffer, did only short-cycle industrial contracting, and kept an 80/20 client mix dominated by private and quasi-government clients to sustain cash flow (he compared the portfolio to "plywood" — if one layer cracks, the others hold it up). "Chase profit, not revenue" (2008–2013): after the financial crisis, to protect jobs, a majority of the leadership team voted to enter oil and gas EPC. Five projects quickly exposed underestimated complexity and labor costs, and by 2012 they had lost several million dollars. The lesson: chase profit, not revenue. In the end the company developed its "three risk questions": what have we done / where / for whom — if two of the three are "never done," be cautious; and it added a bidding gate scored on 25 indicators. At the same time it merged several entities into one legal entity, filled the CFO role, and spent five years gradually improving back-office accounting and processes. Disrupting itself, betting on modular (2010–2016): Chebel insisted on disrupting himself first. He judged that Middle Eastern clients prefer "solid walls," so he chose concrete boxes over light steel and light walls — technically harder, but in line with the local preference for a "sense of permanence." In 2010 the company built 150 prototype rooms at one of its own remote sites; in 2015 its first external client project was delivered two months early. In 2016 the modular team was branded DuBox and delivered 250+ Gardenia townhouses in Dubai in one go, validating the technology and the business case. The pain of independence and the merger back (2016–2017): DuBox's early projects were sparse; the factory and workers were often idle, and running independently made it hard to move people across projects, so it burned cash. In 2016 DuBox was merged back into the group: staff went into a shared pool, procurement gained economies of scale, and incentives were consolidated; the same year Riad became vice chairman and J. Joseph became CEO. In 2017 the industry turned down; AMANA went from 14 BUs → 4, centralized banking/cash/procurement at headquarters, gave departing managers "golden parachutes" and gave those who stayed raises/bonuses, completing the re-centralization quickly and quietly — and it moved into data centers as an adjacent track, opening a new pipeline. The big breakthrough in the Saudi window (2019–2021): the Saudi government was actively looking for innovation. In 2019 AMANA won Turtle Bay and delivered it on schedule in 22 months during the pandemic; it then won the Red Sea project. The advantages were very clear: less environmental disruption, material waste cut by about two-thirds, only a tenth of the on-site labor, and — more importantly — materials in an urban factory are significantly cheaper than at a remote site. The company realized from this that in remote settings, modular has structural cost and speed advantages. Productizing the "room" — DuPod (from 2020): DuPod was incubated in the Red Sea project: high-end "bathroom/kitchen" pods whose plumbing and electrics plug in like a "washing machine connection." A standard catalog was tried first and didn't work — clients preferred customization — so they switched to BIM (3D collaboration), letting clients settle the details in the digital model in one go, with physical mock-ups when needed. The goal is to productize: in the future you'd pick a "ready-made office" the way you browse IKEA, installed in six months; skipping the design phase can shorten the total schedule by 20–30%. But the price is a mandatory "design freeze" + Day-1 procurement; once a concrete box is the wrong size, it can only be torn down and redone. This forced the company to rewrite its processes: the project manager is fully accountable for schedule/budget, and even "who handles paint touch-ups on site" is written into the responsibility matrix. The 2024 picture and the "changing of the guard": by 2024, AMANA had nearly 6,000 people and 1,500+ projects in total (including Amazon and IKEA), 18 consecutive years of profit and zero debt; about 50% of revenue in Saudi Arabia and 40% in the UAE; industrial contracting is 85%, modular about 10% but growing fastest, with 186,000 square meters signed since 2020 and about 35% completed. Shared services continue to roll out; profit-sharing remains, but bonuses are concentrated on Top Performers. A non-family CEO (Abboud) takes the baton; the new CFO/CHRO, after coming on board, pointed out areas for improvement: not enough KPIs, headquarters costs on the high side, an ERP is needed, geographic concentration is too high, HR needs to be institutionalized, and so on. The open question: can you "raise the bet" in the middle of change and be both fast and steady? Opportunity: the Saudi window is big, client culture in the short term favors the "permanence" of concrete, and AMANA is both a general contractor and a modular supplier, delivering faster and more efficiently. Risks: rising concentration in Saudi Arabia; Vision 2030's funding pace is tied to oil prices; modular is still ramping up and depends heavily on front-end design freezes; organizational digitization/governance is still in progress. The core question: can it find a balance between "discipline (centralization, process, cash retention) + agility (BIM co-creation, productization)," and, once the founding family steps back to the board, "institutionalize" the culture and operating discipline? Case SummaryThe Protagonist and the Starting PointThe protagonist is former hedge fund manager Demond Martin, who founded WellWithAll: a consumer brand that turns "business profit + health equity" into a single flywheel. From day one, the company wrote into its commitments that 20% of profits would be reinvested in community health, and designed measurable "impact accounting" (such as the HEAL Academy model). The competition is formidable (Monster, Red Bull, PepsiCo and others); to break through, it has to turn "values-based leadership" into a replicable operating system. Mission and PositioningThe brand's core audience is communities long neglected by health disparities (especially Black and brown communities). The company has built "purpose—principles—practices" into its institutions and requires continuous delivery in corporate governance and external partnerships: each year it takes stock of the 20% profit commitment and the inputs and outputs across three major health themes, and publishes an "impact annual report." Products and ChannelsTwo product lines: nutritional supplements (as a series) and health-oriented energy drinks. Formulas and claims follow an "evidence chain" approach, with standardized documents and processes (PRDs, a health-claims compliance checklist, etc.); the energy drinks' technical specs are clear (e.g. "natural, zero sugar, vitamin-fortified"), making it easy to align with suppliers and retail category teams. Channel Partners and Reach (How to Amplify)The company doesn't "go it alone"; it leans on large partners for complementary capabilities: for example, Campbell's provides manufacturing and distribution, Target and Thrive provide shelf space and foot traffic, and Advocate Health and UNC Charlotte provide health-system and community reach. All partnerships sit within a "JBP + QBR (joint business plan + quarterly business review)" governance framework: sales and community metrics are written into the targets first; brand guardrails and pre-review of health claims ensure "authenticity"; data sharing is written into contracts, especially data from major events (e.g. Essence Festival validated demand and reached about 500,000 people). If a partnership dilutes the brand or drags down the pace, a simple exit clause can take effect at any time. Hidden Risks of Growth (the Cost of Speed)Rapid expansion brings organizational and pacing risks. The front line uses the metaphor of "50 fish biting at once, with a small crew rushing rod to rod" to describe opportunity overload; the team says the CEO pushes ahead at "light speed" and it's hard for everyone to keep up; when external shocks hit (such as insurance changes), there's a "flood of urgent tasks," which easily pulls the team into firefighting mode. After a "mismatched hire" left, the team felt a sense of "relief," which also pointed to an earlier culture/role mismatch; mentors also warned that if people can't safely push back on the CEO and the pace of growth isn't controlled, the organization may be consumed by "growing too fast." The Leader's Challenge (Purpose → System)This isn't a company that "runs on passion"; it anchors its mission in systems: People and culture: write a culture handbook, use RACI to define responsibilities, convert to full-time after a probation period, and set up a fixed "Challenge-the-CEO" mechanism to make sure people "dare to speak up." TPS needs to be Reinforced ConstantlyInterview with Katsuaki Watanabe, President of Toyota in HBR (July-August 2007)."I realize that our systems may be overstretched....We must make that issue visible.""If a time comes at Toyota when I need to put my foot on the brake pedal rather than on the accelerator, I won't hesitate to do so.""It's my job to pull the Andon cord." Andon Cord — managers should say thank you to whoever pulls it!! The “Andon cord” is one of the core tools of the Toyota Production System (TPS) and a key practice of its “Just-in-Time (JIT)” and “Jidoka (autonomation)” principles. Its core purpose is to let anyone on the production line who spots a problem quickly pause production, expose the problem and drive its resolution, thereby preventing defects from moving downstream and improving productivity and product quality. 1. Core definition and originsEssence: a physical pull cord (or button, or electronic trigger), usually laid out along the production line (e.g., beside each machine or above each workstation). Any employee on the line (regardless of rank) has the right to pull it upon finding any of the following: a quality defect in the product (e.g., a part installed incorrectly, a cosmetic flaw); an equipment abnormality (e.g., a breakdown, a precision deviation); a material shortage (e.g., parts not delivered on time); a safety hazard (e.g., an operational risk, an environmental abnormality); a process hold-up (e.g., poor handoffs between steps, disrupted takt time).Origins: Toyota's car plants in the 1950s. Toyota founder Kiichiro Toyoda and engineer Taiichi Ohno designed it to solve the problem of “defects hidden in mass production.” In traditional production, employees often concealed problems for fear that “stopping work would hurt efficiency,” leading defective products to pile up; the Andon cord, by “allowing work to stop and encouraging problems to be exposed,” reduces waste at the root (“defects,” one of the “seven wastes” in TPS). 2. How it works: a closed loop from “pull” to “resolve” The Andon cord follows a strict process to ensure problems aren't shelved, forming a closed loop of “detect – respond – resolve – review”: Pull: when an employee spots a problem, they pull the Andon cord at their workstation (or press the button); Alert: once the cord is pulled, the line's “Andon Board” (usually an electronic screen or signal lights) lights up the indicator for that workstation (e.g., red = emergency stop, yellow = assistance needed), possibly accompanied by a buzzer; Respond: the team leader, technician or support staff (e.g., maintenance, materials handlers) must arrive at the workstation within a set time (e.g., within 30 seconds); if the problem can't be solved quickly (e.g., within 2 minutes), the team leader escalates the response and may even stop the entire line; Resolve: the team analyzes the root cause on the spot (e.g., using the “5 Whys”) and fixes it quickly (e.g., replacing parts, adjusting equipment, replenishing materials); Reset & Review: once the problem is solved, authorized personnel reset the Andon system and production resumes; afterward, the cause and solution are recorded and fed into training or process improvement so the same problem doesn't recur.6. Core value: more than a “stop-work tool” The significance of the Andon cord goes far beyond “pausing production”; its core value reflects the underlying logic of the Toyota Production System: Empowering employees and breaking down hierarchical barriersNew or veteran, every employee has the right to “stop” production, embodying a management philosophy of “respect for people” — employees are closest to the shop floor and most likely to spot problems, and empowering them sparks initiative and a sense of responsibility.Exposing problems immediately to avoid “hidden waste”In traditional production, “producing with defects” leads to rework in later steps, wasted materials and customer complaints; the Andon cord, through “immediate stoppage,” nips problems in the bud and lowers downstream costs.Driving “continuous improvement (Kaizen)”Every pull is a “problem signal,” and data from many pulls can be aggregated and analyzed (e.g., a workstation that frequently triggers due to equipment failure), becoming the basis for process optimization, equipment upgrades and employee training, driving continuous iteration of the production system.Safeguarding quality and safetyIt stops defects from flowing downstream at the source while quickly eliminating safety hazards, in line with the production principle of “quality first, safety foremost.”7. Applications: from manufacturing to other industriesCore applicationsAutomotive manufacturing (e.g., final assembly and stamping lines at Toyota, BMW, Volkswagen and other carmakers), electronics manufacturing (e.g., phone and home-appliance production lines), machining and other discrete manufacturing — these industries have many process steps and densely packed workstations where problems easily travel downstream, so the Andon cord's “immediate response” value is significant.Extended applicationsServices: some restaurant chains (e.g., for kitchen order hold-ups) and logistics warehouses (e.g., for picking errors) have introduced similar mechanisms, using “call buttons” to respond quickly to problems; Healthcare: some hospital operating rooms and wards use “emergency call cords” (though focused on emergency care, the logic is similar: “immediate trigger – rapid response”). I've found that sharing everything I've learned after every single class is almost impossible. New knowledge keeps rushing at me, and new things keep piling up one after another. So writing down a few important takeaways and inspirations in good time is already pretty good. "Done" matters more than "perfect." The Dr. John's Case Case SummarySerial entrepreneur John Osher's team created a low-priced electric toothbrush, the SpinBrush (retail price <$6), powered by two AA batteries, with a "Try me" button on the packaging so shoppers could feel the power without opening the box. From 1999 it was tested on a small scale in channels such as Meijer, selling up to 7 units per store per day, far above the norm of "one a week" for an ordinary toothbrush; by early 2000 it was selling more than 6,000 units a day, had entered big-box chains such as Wal-Mart and Target, and was starting to show up in the IRI rankings. But the giants (P&G/Crest, Gillette/Oral-B, Colgate, J&J/Reach, etc.) could follow at any moment, and the team faced a choice: keep expanding independently? License the brand? Or sell the whole company? Why the company could break through the market1. It came in at the "<$6" price band, solving the pain point that "electric toothbrushes are too expensive"; 2. A hybrid brush head (fixed + moving bristles) kept the feel of a manual brush while cleaning more efficiently; 3. Try-me packaging dramatically lowered the barrier to a first try; 4. It leveraged high-quality Chinese contract manufacturing and 30-day payment terms to drive down cash needs and costs; 5. A lean 9-person team dealing directly with big retailers, with an ultra-small span of management Industry and key dataIn 1999 the US toothbrush market was about $800 million in retail sales, of which manual toothbrushes were about $545 million (1999 retail sales 544.8m) and electric/accessories about $231 million (1999 retail sales 230.8m); penetration of electric toothbrush bases in US households was only about 15%, leaving plenty of room for growth. Osher's "Sixteen Mistakes Entrepreneurs Do Not Have To Make" is very good, so I've put it here in both Chinese and English. John Osher's List of the Sixteen Mistakes Entrepreneurs Do Not Have To Make: Wrong Expectation Mistakes 1. Miscalculate size of market, timing and ease of entry, as well as potential market share. Overestimating/misjudging: getting the market size, the timing and difficulty of entry, and potential market share wrong. 2. Underestimate financial requirements and timing. Run out of money. Underestimating how much money you need and when it arrives: underestimating the amount and timing of funding, leading to a cash crunch. 3. Over-project sales volume and timing. Fall short of sales projections. Overly optimistic sales forecasts: estimating volume and pace too high, and ending up missing the sales forecast. 4. Cost projections too low. Key points explained • Few-Shot Learning: the input contains only a few examples (usually 10 to 100); from these examples and the task description, the model can understand and complete the task without any additional gradient updates or fine-tuning. • One-Shot Learning: the model sees just one example and can still complete the task. • Zero-Shot Learning: the model has no examples at all and completes the task from the task description alone.This reduced the reliance on large amounts of task-specific training data and fine-tuning, opening new directions for research and application in natural language processingIt used to be that "pre-training" mattered; now we realise "post-training" matters tooWe used to be shaped by search enginesNow: getting the task done well matters; it doesn't need to respond in secondsThe new consensus: the Scaling Law splits into three: pre-training, post-training, test timeTest-time scaling"reasoning": thinking is needed when the user asks a questionSFT and RLHF in ChatGPTSFT: Supervised Fine-TuningRLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback🤖SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) and RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) in ChatGPT are two key training stages used to improve the model's performance and its alignment with human preferences. SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) • SFT is the first step in training ChatGPT, fine-tuning a pre-trained large language model (such as text-davinci-003 from the GPT-3.5 series). • Training uses a high-quality demonstration dataset carefully written by human annotators, showing how the model should answer questions "correctly". • The goal is for the model to imitate these demonstration answers and learn to generate the expected output; the training is still based on the "next-word prediction" language-modelling objective, only with more supervised data. • Because the demonstration data is limited, the SFT model improves basic abilities but may still fall short in understanding user intent and in alignment. RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) • RLHF is the second stage of training after SFT, aimed at further optimising the model to better match human preferences. • Concretely, human annotators rank several answers generated by the SFT model, marking which best meets human expectations, which is used to build a "reward model". • Using the reward model, a reinforcement learning algorithm (such as Proximal Policy Optimization, PPO) optimises the SFT model so that its answers keep improving in quality and in fit with human preferences. • This training lets ChatGPT not only generate reasonable text but also better understand user intent and avoid inappropriate or useless answers. In summary, SFT is supervised fine-tuning of a pre-trained model on human demonstration data, establishing basic answering ability; RLHF then further fine-tunes the model through human feedback and reinforcement learning so its output better fits human expectations and preferences, improving ChatGPT's usefulness and safety.ChatGPT used only 100,000 pairs for trainingThis is also related to "emergent abilities" and the "few-shot learner" — very uncanny (Long) Chain-of-Thought (CoT) + RLAIFChain-of-Thought: CoTRLAIF: Reinforcement Learning from AI FeedbackThese are two key technologies driving the performance and alignment of large language models (LLMs); combined, they offer a new paradigm for model training. The core role of Chain-of-Thought (CoT)Chain-of-thought is a technique that improves a model's ability to handle complex tasks by explicitly showing the reasoning process. Its core features include:Step-by-step reasoning: the model breaks a problem into intermediate steps (such as working through a maths problem step by step), imitating the human logical thinking process.In-context learning: prompts guide the model to generate answers with a reasoning path (for example: "Let's think step by step...").Performance gains: experiments show that CoT significantly improves model performance on tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense reasoning, with especially notable effects on large-scale models (such as GPT-3).Example:Input: "Xiaoming has 5 apples, eats 2, then buys 3 more. How many does he have now?"CoT output: 1. Initial apples: 5 2. Remaining after eating: 5 - 2 = 3 3. Total after buying: 3 + 3 = 6 Answer: 6 2. The RLAIF technical processRLAIF replaces human annotation with AI-generated feedback to optimise the reinforcement learning training process. The main steps include:Generating comparison samples: generating multiple candidate answers to the same question (such as versions differing in helpfulness/safety)[6][8].Generating AI feedback: using a teacher model (such as GPT-4) to assess answer quality and produce preference rankings or reward scores[2][5].Training the reward model: training a Reward Model on the AI feedback to quantify how good each answer is[3][10].Optimising the policy model: iteratively updating the model with reinforcement learning algorithms such as PPO to maximise reward[4][8].Key innovations:Lower labour costs: AI feedback can process massive amounts of data automatically, avoiding RLHF's reliance on human annotation[2][4].CoT improves feedback quality: when generating feedback, the teacher model is asked to provide its reasoning (such as "Why is answer A better than B?"), improving the accuracy and interpretability of the assessment[6][8]. 3. The synergy between CoT and RLAIFCombining the two creates gains at the following stages:Feedback generation: CoT prompts make the teacher model show detailed analysis when assessing answers (for example: "Answer A is safer because it avoids sensitive word X, while answer B may cause misunderstanding Y..."), helping the reward model capture subtle differences[6][8].Policy optimisation: through the reasoning paths generated by CoT, the model can more precisely understand the logic behind the reward signal (such as "reduce subjective statements" or "add fact-checking"), speeding up policy iteration[6][9].Experimental results:In harmless dialogue generation, the RLAIF+CoT model's harmlessness rate (88%) exceeded RLHF (76%) and the baseline model (64%)[5][10].In text summarisation, there was no significant difference in human preference win rates between RLAIF and RLHF (71% vs. 73%)[5][10]. 4.
