Van Gogh: There Is a Fire in Everyone's Heart, but Passersby See Only Smoke

Boston Van Gogh Exhibition: The Roulin Family Portraits There is a fire in everyone's heart, but passersby see only the smoke. Yet there is always someone, always that one person, who can see the fire, and comes over to keep me company. In the crowd, I saw his fire, and hurried over, afraid that if I were any slower he would be buried in the dust of the years. I carried my passion, my coldness, my fury, my gentleness, and my baseless faith in love, and walked until I was out of breath. Stammering, I said to him: What is your name? It started with "What is your name," and then, there was everything. — Van Gogh, Dear Theo On April 7, a drizzly, rainy afternoon, we hurried over to the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. The exhibition brought together 23 works by Van Gogh, including 14 portraits of members of the family of the postman Joseph Roulin. Van Gogh painted these portraits in Arles, France, between 1888 and 1889. The exhibition also included early works influenced by classical Dutch portraiture, as well as the artistic inspiration he drew from Japanese ukiyo-e prints, helping visitors fully understand Van Gogh's artistic vision and the context of his work. Van Gogh's life and work at the time: from 1888 to 1889, Van Gogh spent the golden period of his artistic career in Arles, producing nearly 300 works; his style became more mature and distinctive, his colors intense and full of life. A man like me, tormented by so much suffering, could not go on living without something greater than myself — my life, and the power to create. If we can no longer create physically, let us try to create ideas instead of children. That way, we are still part of humanity. Ah, the portrait — the kind of portrait that captures the thoughts and soul of the model — it seems to me that it is bound to come. — Van Gogh to Theo van Gogh, September 3, 1888 The sunshine in Arles was bright and the light intense, kindling Van Gogh's passion for color; he hoped to capture that unique play of light and shadow in his work. The Roulin family and Van Gogh: Van Gogh's life was rather lonely then, and he had little contact with the locals. The Roulins were Van Gogh's neighbors in Arles. The postman Joseph Roulin, his wife Augustine and their three children became important subjects of his portraits, and in the Roulin family he also found emotional comfort and a family-like warmth. The family not only gave Van Gogh moral support, but also became a source of inspiration for his exploration of the modern portrait. In October 1888, the painter Paul Gauguin came to Arles, bringing a brief period of artistic collaboration and hope, but the two men's personalities and artistic ideas were too different, and the partnership did not last. The place of this series in Van Gogh's art The Roulin family portraits embody Van Gogh's passion for the "modern portrait" and represent an important breakthrough for him in portraiture. With their vivid colors, forceful brushstrokes and deep expression of the sitters' inner worlds, these works are among the signature pieces of Van Gogh's late art. Among Van Gogh's roughly 2,100 works, this series of portraits not only broadened his subject matter but also deepened his portrayal of people's emotions and personalities; it is an indispensable part of understanding his artistic career. I want to make drawings that touch people. What I want to express, in figures or in landscapes, is not sentimental melancholy but serious sorrow. — Van Gogh, Dear Theo Van Gogh is the first painter who ever made me cry; seeing his brushstrokes chokes me up. It was only when I read the book Dear Theo that I understood why — because he had a pure, unalloyed soul. When I paint the sun, I want to make people feel it revolving at a terrifying speed, giving off waves of light and heat of tremendous power. When I paint a wheat field, I want people to feel the atoms in the grain growing and bursting. When I paint an apple, I want people to feel the juice of the apple splashing onto their skin, and the seeds in its core pushing outward toward blossom and fruit! When I paint a man, I want to paint the whole torrent of his life. Lust for Life

Yesterday I decided to spend some time alone with myself: go to the Zen center where Steve Jobs used to meditate, and read and sit. Early in the morning I finished my work, packed a picnic, hopped into my good friend's beloved car that I'd borrowed, and off I went! Destination: Jikoji Zen Center in Los Gatos Picnic menu: two boiled eggs, two bottles of drinking water, a banana, an apple, two segments of red grapefruit, 25g of nuts. Jikoji Zen Center It was founded by the Japanese Soto Zen monk Kobun Chino Otogawa. Jobs embraced Zen Buddhism at 20, and Kobun Chino Otogawa was his spiritual mentor and friend; on March 18, 1991, he officiated at the wedding of Jobs and his wife, Laurene Powell. Address: 12100 Skyline Blvd Los Gatos, CA 95033 United States Without navigation, it's easy to miss on a road where cars are speeding past, and on top of that, the entrance is marked private property. In American movies, walk into a place like this and you're liable to end up staring down the barrel of a shotgun... After a lot of hesitation, I drove on down anyway. The whole temple has a beautiful atmosphere, tucked deep in the mountains amid wonderful natural surroundings. Along the way, a few deer bounded from one side of the road onto the hillside on the other, then turned their heads to stare at me, their gentle big eyes without the slightest fear of humans. Following the mountain road downhill for 5 minutes, I reached a parking lot. Two buildings full of Japanese Zen feeling, the Zendo, sit among the mountains, with wisps of smoke curling up from a chimney that made it feel even more tranquil. The sun was lovely. By the entrance stood two whiteboards with the Zen center's opening hours and a hand-drawn map of the layout, plus the rules and etiquette to observe once inside, such as keeping quiet, and stillness during meditation. Walking down the steps should take you to where guests are received, and following the forest path deeper into the woods brings you to the Zendo for meditation. Every blade of grass and every tree seemed especially lovely, full of Zen. I stood at the entrance for a while. It was hushed and there was no one around. It turned out you needed to "ring the doorbell," which is this bell with a real sense of age~ Beside it, a mallet hung from a nylon cord, and when you strike the bell it rings out clear and crisp. A white practitioner greeted me. It turned out that on ordinary days you need a reservation to meditate and sit on your own. Every Sunday at 9:30 a.m. it's open to the public, with beginner meditation and stretching classes, followed by lunch together. 20 spots, first come, first served. Here's the official website, you're welcome~ www.jikoji.org Mindful Hiking Meditation was off the table, but I still wanted to walk around a bit. The weather was just too good, and besides, I'd come all this way. With the Zen practitioner's permission, I left my car in their parking lot and followed the little path beside it toward the forest. The afternoon sun filtered through the yellow autumn leaves onto the forest path, still wet from the recent rain. I came to a lake, its water reflecting the trees and the sunlight, full of vitality. Past this fence, the standard hiking trail begins. Keep walking and you reach a fork in the path; I chose the Peters Creek Trail. This was my first solo hiking From here, I began my "mindful walking." What is mindfulness? It's focusing on everything happening in the present moment; it's a process of seeing, accepting, and letting go. In the end, just three things matter: How well we have lived. How well we have loved. How well we have learned to let go. — mindfulness teacher Jack Kornfield The first ray of light that meets your eyes when you wake up in the early morning; The stabbing pain in your mouth from an ulcer; The sweet, fresh taste bursting out as sea urchin is crushed in your mouth; The seaside wind, cold enough to cut to the bone; A meeting so drawn-out it puts you to sleep; The restless anger inside when you argue with family or friends; And, Walking along the path, the rustling murmur of the woods and the crisp sound of the stream. Everything is noticed just as it is, and met with love. The very first time I practiced mindful walking, I fell in love with this activity that sits somewhere between exercise and meditation: the practice lifts you out of overthinking and lets you notice your body as it walks. Feel, as you walk, the space you're in, the air, the sounds, the feeling of walking on the ground, how balance is broken and rebuilt, how your center of gravity shifts, letting the body become the focus of your attention in that moment. Feel, as you walk, the instant your soles touch the ground: every step down is an embrace of the earth, and at the same time you are embraced by it. Feel, as you walk, the thoughts and emotions when it's flowing, when it's slow, when it's fast, when it's interrupted. Without noticing, I arrived at a spot with an open view, where there was a semicircular bench built of stone, facing the distant mountains, the wide-open sky, and a valley filled with green. Someone must have really loved the view here to have built a bench like this on purpose, just so others could sit in this spot and enjoy the beautiful scenery from exactly this angle. This is the view you see when you sit down. Because the scenery was so beautiful, I started to stray from my planned route: instead of going back the way I came, I continued down a trail with the same name. And sure enough, after walking for a while, a rustle in the grass on the hillside startled me, and I started to feel scared. I glanced at my phone: no signal at all. A string of questions instantly flooded my brain: What if an animal attacks me and I'm bleeding, what do I do? What if it gets dark and I still haven't made it out, what do I do? If I get lost, which direction should I go? Looking up, the road ahead was unknown, and the road back was distant and long... So much like life at certain moments. Right then, I made it clear to myself that "I have to acquire some wilderness survival skills." But that was a matter for the future. How did I solve the problem in the moment? Luckily, offline maps still work... When I finally saw a familiar trail sign, I let out a long sigh of relief. At last I was in the mood to pick up a few pretty branches to take home. In the end, it took 2 hours to complete a little mindful hike + solo hiking. Art is sometimes an accident. My lens got smudged, and it somehow captured a dreamlike forest. A little adventure.
A Collection of Views on US–China Relations

During my time at Yale, whoever was talking, the conversation always seemed to come back to US–China relations. Some of the views were well-worn; others gave me real food for thought. As I organized my notes, I've laid out the views of a former US Secretary of State, a Yale economics professor, a Yale law professor and others. Because politics is a sensitive subject, and my paraphrasing may not be correct or precise, I'll state this up front: this piece follows the Chatham House Rule — participants are free to use the information received during a meeting, but may not reveal the identity of the speakers or the institutions they're affiliated with. This piece is simply a collection of views I heard secondhand. It does not represent any position or opinion of my own, and where the views contradict or conflict with one another, I present them as they were. Here goes: America has never faced such a broad-ranging competitor. America's competition with China is very different from its competition with the former Soviet Union. The Soviet Union didn't have China's technological capabilities, America had no comparable investment in the Soviet Union, and back then there was no competition beyond military weapons. The competition between China and America is far broader, and keeping such competition under control is far harder. Americans know very little about China. Partly because of the media, the American public now has a great many misconceptions about China. Americans don't understand China's 5,000 years of cultural background, so much of what is happening in China today is baffling to them. The Chinese and American political systems have always been different. Twenty or thirty years ago, many people believed that once China joined the WTO, US–China relations would keep improving and China would become more democratic — but China won't change; it is still China. After Deng Xiaoping's Southern Tour, he invited many world leaders, including Americans, and said something along these lines: I read your news, I know what you're thinking — yes, of all the changes I'm making now, the biggest is that I can open China up: American students can come to China, Chinese students can study abroad, and China will develop and prosper. But don't make the mistake of thinking that because we use your economic skills and experience, China's political system will change — those are two different things. When you talk to your media, they assume that a change in China's economy will change its political system. Deng was very clear: we have our system, a system that has endured for centuries, with a much longer history than yours. Don't expect us to change. Economic issues are also political and national security issues. The line between economic policy and national security policy is getting blurrier and blurrier. It's increasingly evident in Washington: the nation's economic policy and international economic policy can't be separated from foreign policy and national security. The two are tightly bound together. In the past, at meetings, economics was economics and diplomacy was diplomacy; now officials from every department need to be involved. The two are closely intertwined. American isolationism. America has had isolationism in its history, and it's growing now, much like the mood during the Korean War. There was strong isolationism in Roosevelt's time; he worked very hard to prepare the country to fight World War II, but he wasn't sure he'd have the public's support, and he used many policies to win it. Had it not been for Pearl Harbor, America might not have entered World War II; America was forced into the war, and at that point it hadn't even declared war on Germany. America has negotiated a great many free trade agreements, but the people around Trump are deeply hostile to free trade, and didn't want to renew NAFTA either. Democrats, or those on the far left, don't want America to play an international role either — let alone the Republicans who support Trump. These people have influence at home; they focus more on domestic issues and distance themselves from international influence. When the country wants to play a bigger international role, it doesn't get support at home. It isn't complete isolationism, nor complete decoupling, but it is a tendency, a shift, a change. What do people want? Do they want the country to play a more important international role? When the economy recovers, people become more willing to let the government play an international role. US–China decoupling will hurt students and scholarship. At Johns Hopkins, every doctor will tell you that to solve problems, we need the smartest people in the room. With US–China decoupling — the medical field used to have many Chinese people in research; 15 years ago the best papers were co-authored by Chinese and American authors, two or three Americans and two or three Chinese. Their papers were published in the world's top academic journals. But because of the loss of trust, each country feels the other will exploit its knowledge. Trust is scarce and precious. Who will suffer? All of humanity — everyone will suffer. Sullivan's view: "small yard, high fence." I once talked with Sullivan. I said: the yard keeps getting bigger, expanding every year, as more and more products have potential military uses. If you're going to use this metaphor, you also need to clearly define what counts as "military-related" technology. Every technology related to quantum, AI, rare earths, 5G and 6G is both commercial and military — that's true for both China and America. Trade is complicated. It isn't only about the economy and jobs, or domestic worries about job losses and people needing training for new work. Trade now brings people in Washington together in meetings: trade meetings used to have no military representatives, but now they do, because they're highly vigilant and very worried that some trade deals could affect the military. For companies, if you want to sell high-tech products, a major challenge is that your product may be deemed to have military implications. Because technology is changing by the day and people today don't understand its impact, many products and industries end up being placed under controls. 🙏 May we all have the wisdom to make the world a little better.
An Adventure at a Polling Station on US Election Day

My first week at Yale happened to coincide with US Election Day on November 4. Thanks to an idea from our ever-curious Professor Jiang Changjian, we decided to slip away from campus and go see a polling station up close. Looking back, it was super, super interesting — easily a highlight of the Yale trip. It was a bright, sunny day. During the lunch break, six of us drove across New Haven's enormous city green towards City Hall. When we rounded to a narrow, ordinary street behind that elegant, stately building, we knew without any navigation that we'd probably found the right place: the road was clearly much more crowded, with cars parked all along both sides. After illegally parking in a lot clearly marked "Government Employees Only," we crossed the street towards an unremarkable back door. By the roadside outside the door stood a makeshift table and chair, with a banner bearing Harris's name hanging in front. A woman sat there, presumably doing some last-minute canvassing. Following her directions, we entered City Hall; the polling station was one floor down, in the basement. There were no signs at all, either outside the building or inside City Hall. Without a local to lead the way, I doubt we'd ever have found it. We took an ancient elevator down to B1, then walked along a perfectly ordinary long, narrow corridor, and at an inconspicuous dead end, we finally found the polling station. Polling stations, it turns out, are assigned by the first letter of your street name — this one was for streets starting with A through N. (It reminded me of China's neighbourhood committees 😂) We stayed about 15 minutes in all, and roughly every minute someone came in to vote. We even saw an elderly lady with a walker making her way to the polling station with great effort, at an extremely slow pace of about three metres a minute. At first we just poked our heads in at the door, but the Black gentleman guarding it was very friendly and actually let us in to observe and take photos. The polling station was a sunken hall, looking a bit smaller than a basketball court. Inside sat volunteers from the various streets — men and women, white and Black, none of them looking particularly young. Their main job was to help log the number of votes. From that day on, I began to feel the "gentleness" of the people of New Haven. Not warm hospitality exactly, but "gentleness" — I can't find a more fitting word for that generosity of always obliging whatever you ask. A big group of us with Chinese faces walked into the voting hall and drew only a few curious glances; we felt no rejection or scrutiny whatsoever, so we started "pushing our luck." From watching at a distance at first, to slowly edging closer and chatting with people, to boldly asking to take photos, and finally going right around behind the table to watch one person cast their vote from start to finish. In the end, even residents who had come to vote had to stand and wait a while before they could vote, because we were having such a good time chatting with the staff. Thinking about it now, it's really funny — and I suddenly find myself missing the people of New Haven. At one point the Black gentleman told us they had to sit there from 7 in the morning until 7 in the evening. It was hard work, but the pay was decent. Having had our fill of fun, we followed the corridor out of City Hall. At the door, a pretty young woman came up to us. It turned out she was a reporter doing an investigative piece on the vote; she thought we were voters and came over to interview us. She said that, of the people she had interviewed by the time she ran into us, most had voted for Trump. That result surprised us a lot. After all, Connecticut is traditional Democratic territory, and a clear Trump lead turning up here — even with a tiny sample — was still unexpected. Anyway, I've written a rambling log, just to keep a record. Perhaps ten years from now, looking back, this will have been a day that changed American history, maybe even world history.

My two weeks of study and life at Yale are over, so I'm writing this to keep a record. My earliest memory of Yale is a book by a Chinese girl about her studies in America, something like Harvard Girl Liu Yiting . I don't even remember whether she ended up getting into Yale, but her journey — from naivety about society, to curiosity about the world, to growing into a soul bold enough to explore — inspired the clueless me just as much. The girl in the book first encountered philosophy in high school, at a summer camp at Yale. There they pondered eye-opening questions, such as: How do people become aware of their own existence? Does a person's sense of freedom come from being looked at by others? If a human were alone on a desert island with only monkeys around, could they realise what a self is, and what makes them different? Does "the circle" really exist? Or are there only round objects in the world, and no "circle"? Before that, I had never thought about questions like these; after that, they never left me. So when the chance came to study at Yale, the answer could only be Yes. One autumn, I came to Yale. On the first day I copied this passage into my diary, to push myself to make the most of every minute there: ...from Pericles, Bismarck and Disraeli all the way to Jefferson, Madison, Lincoln, Wilson, Roosevelt, Churchill and Mandela. Their careers are an education in reality, teaching us how to negotiate all manner of affairs in moments of crisis. Once you have read these books, and only after you have read them, can you say you have fulfilled the highest duty of a Yale student — the words carved on the Memorial Gate of Branford College: "For God, for Country, and for Yale." Impressions of Yale A Young Cambridge Like Cambridge, the whole city is made up of Yale's various colleges, and every street feels like part of the campus. Especially the Graduate Hotel in New Haven where we stayed — it really felt like living in an old student dorm. The hotel kindly opens its doors to students studying, so reading in the lobby at night felt very much like my student days. Step outside and there are bookshops and libraries; walk one more block and you reach the undergraduate residential colleges. A Friendly, Gentle Community The people in the area where we spent our time were very, very, very friendly. On morning runs, people always smiled and said good morning. When we were carrying a drunk friend back to the hotel, people kept coming over to help. The professors were also very friendly and did their best to meet any request we had, almost to the point of granting every wish. It doesn't have Harvard's sharpness and efficiency, but over time it gives you a different kind of calm and gentleness. A Simple Life The food here is as unpretentious as the people — to the point that only one Chinese restaurant has private rooms, and the bustling life of New York and Boston is almost nonexistent. The Courses This programme covered listening, US-China relations, technological change, a brief history of creativity, stem cell research, artificial intelligence, the impact of industrial revival policy on companies and nations, the leadership mind, acting, how the human brain learns, geology, social network interventions, understanding the American presidency, the systematic study of creativity, and more. Getting to meet Professor Amy Chua, JD Vance's mentor, was another big highlight. Life Outside Class The Peabody Museum is right across from the School of Management where we had class, so at lunch or during breaks we'd dash over to look around. Listening to President Ma Weihua tell his stories was practically a history of China's banking industry. With the Yale instructors and Xu Zheng, we experienced the flow of emotion that acting brings. Getting up past 6 a.m. to run — finishing a 10K was sore and exhilarating at once~ At the museum, I saw great works of art up close with no glass cases, including my beloved Van Gogh. Enjoying peaceful reading time in the city library As for my reading notes, I hope I'll find time to sort them all out this time. Special thanks: many of the photos in this article are by my Yale classmate, Brother Gu.

Yale's quiet, gentle scholarly atmosphere stirred up a real passion for reading and learning. So outside of class, we got in touch with a dozen or so Yale PhDs and talked with them every day over dinner and after dinner, with no limits on field — spanning quantum computing, AI, philosophy, Latin American literature, political science, theology, mysticism, behavioral economics, macroeconomics and more. For several nights in a row, we talked and debated in classrooms, in the hotel, in restaurants… from six until past ten, four hours of nonstop input and output, and yet it still felt like we had only scratched the surface and wanted more. We want to keep this reading group going, and we gave it a wonderful name — the Junto reading group. The word comes from "juntar" in Spanish and Latin, meaning "to join" or "to gather." It's a tribute to Benjamin Franklin. In 1727, he founded a small reading and discussion group in Philadelphia whose official name was the Junto. Through regular meetings, exchanges of ideas and social activities, the group explored all kinds of questions about life, business, politics and morality. Its purpose was to help members cultivate themselves, deepen their friendships, and together come up with ideas for the development of their community. Junto members came from different professional backgrounds — craftsmen, merchants, doctors, lawyers and so on. Its ideas had a wide influence among American intellectual circles, and it is considered one of the prototypes of the "homegrown academic club." On different nights, we discussed the philosophical questions of AI, the impact of the Great Famine on the rejuvenation of companies, subsidy policies for electric vehicles, theology in Southeast Asia, quantum computing and cryptography, Buddhism, tarot, the multiverse and Borges… Looking back now, what fun those evenings were.
Lessons from the Case Method and a Lost Debate

One of the playbooks of business school case teaching While reviewing Harvard cases, I suddenly noticed a certain playbook the professors use. One of them goes in three steps: Step one: before class, have each group discuss a few questions thoroughly. In the Dr. John case, for example: how should the company be valued — using P/E? Using EBITA? Step two: in class, spend some time letting everyone voice their views fully, weighing the pros and cons of the two valuation approaches through discussion, so classmates learn from each other. Step three: change tack and reveal an outcome that stuns everyone. In the Dr. John case, the price at which the company was acquired was 10 times what everyone expected. The professors use that moment to deliver an especially important model or idea — in the Dr. John case, if the acquirer didn't buy Dr. John, the cost would be ceding market share to fiercely competitive rivals... The main conclusion: when thinking through a problem, you can't consider only internal factors; you have to consider external ones too. This ties in with a class I took at Gaoshan a while ago, where we lost a debate 7:1. It was just a friendly debate, but while many past wins left no deep impression, this loss taught me a great deal in the post-mortem. For example: Don't focus only on the local battle; focus on the whole war. When you have victory locked up on logic, you often lose some of your emotional expression. A good debate isn't one where every sentence is airtight, but one that leaves the audience feeling they've gained something.

Right now, through a mess of tears and a runny nose, I've just finished Steve Jobs , Walter Isaacson's biography, and I want to let the feeling linger a little longer, to burn into memory this moment and the jolt Jobs has given me. This book has permanently changed a part of me. At the very least, in my Yale classes it has made me even less able to tolerate the ordinary and the mediocre; when I'm arranging music or writing scripts, it has made me trust my own instincts and taste more; and when I'm driving things forward, it has made me more direct and more honest. I want to share two passages I love. The first is the copy Jobs helped craft for the "Think Different" ad when he returned to Apple in 1997. It was also played at his funeral, in his own voice. As it drifted over the crowd, it felt both heartbreaking and piercing. "To those who are a little mad. They go their own way. They refuse to be tamed. They stir up trouble. They never quite fit in. They look at things through different eyes. They have no taste for convention, and no wish to settle for how things are. You can side with them or against them, sing their praises or tear them down — the one thing you cannot do is ignore them. They push humanity forward. Others may see them as madmen, but to us they are geniuses. Because it is only those mad enough to believe they can change the world who actually end up changing it." The second is something I just want to read again and again and again — his own words, from the many times he talked about the legacy he hoped to leave behind: My passion has been to build a company that lasts, where people are driven to make great products. Everything else comes second. Sure, making money is great, because that's what lets you make great products. But the motivation comes from the products, not the profits. Sculley got it backwards and made money the goal. It's a subtle difference, but it shapes everything: who you hire, who you promote, what gets talked about in meetings. Some people say, "Give customers whatever they want." That's not how I work. Our job is to figure out, one step ahead, what they're going to want. I remember Henry Ford saying something like, "If I'd asked customers what they wanted, they'd have told me: 'A faster horse!'" People don't know what they want until you put it in front of them. That's why I never rely on market research. Our task is to read what isn't on the page yet. Edwin Land of Polaroid used to talk about the intersection of the humanities and science. I love that intersection. There's a kind of magic there. Plenty of people are innovating, but innovation isn't the main thing that sets my work apart. The reason Apple resonates with people is that there's a deep humanity buried inside our innovation. I think great artists and great engineers are alike: they both have a hunger to express themselves. In fact, some of the best people who worked on the original Mac were also poets and musicians. In the 1970s, computers became a way for people to express their creativity. Some great artists, like Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, were also masters of science. Michelangelo knew a great deal about quarrying stone; he didn't just know how to sculpt. People pay us to integrate things for them, because they can't think about all this stuff 24/7. If you have a huge passion for making great products, it pushes you toward integration — toward tying together your hardware, your software and your content management. If you want to break new ground, you have to do it yourself. If you want your products open to other hardware or software, you have to give up some of your vision. In the past, different companies at different times have been the model for Silicon Valley. For a long time it was HP. Then, in the semiconductor era, it was Fairchild and Intel. I think for a while it was Apple, and then that faded. And today I think it's Apple and Google — a bit more Apple. I think Apple has stood the test of time. It's had its ups and downs, but it's still out in front. It's easy to point out Microsoft's shortcomings. They've clearly lost their dominance and have become basically irrelevant. But I appreciate what they did, and I know how hard it was. They were very good at the business side. They never had the ambition about products that they should have had. Bill likes to describe himself as a product guy, but he really isn't. He's a businessman. Winning the business mattered more than making great products. He ended up the richest man around, and if that was his goal, he achieved it. But that was never my goal, and I doubt, in the end, that it was his. I admire him and the company he built — it's impressive — and I liked working with him. He's smart, and actually quite funny. But Microsoft never had the humanities and the artistic sensibility in its DNA. Even after they saw the Mac, they couldn't copy it well. They completely missed what it was about. I have my own theory about why companies like IBM or Microsoft decline. A company like that does well, it innovates, it becomes a monopoly or close to one in some field, and then the quality of the product starts to matter less. The company starts valuing the great salespeople, because they're the ones moving the sales and changing the revenue numbers — not the product engineers and designers — so the salespeople end up running the company. John Akers at IBM was a smart, articulate, terrific salesman, but he knew nothing about product. The same thing happened at Xerox. When the sales people run the company, the product people stop mattering as much, and many of them lose their creative passion. That's what happened at Apple after Sculley came in, which was my mistake, and it's what happened when Ballmer took over Microsoft. Apple was lucky enough to come back, but I don't think Microsoft will get anywhere as long as Ballmer is at the helm. I hate a certain kind of person: people who call themselves "entrepreneurs" when what they really want is to start a company and then sell it or take it public, so they can cash out and walk away. They're not willing to put in the effort to build a real company, which is the hardest work in business. That's the only way you truly contribute and add to the legacy left by those who came before. You build a company that will still be standing a generation or two from now. That's what Walt Disney did, what Hewlett and Packard did, and the people who built Intel. They created companies that last, not just money. That's what I want for Apple. I don't think I'm harsh with people, but if someone screws something up, I'll tell them to their face. It's my job to be honest. I know what I'm talking about, and it usually turns out I'm right. That's the culture I've tried to build. We're brutally honest with one another — anyone can tell me they think I'm full of shit, and I can say the same to them. We've had some ferocious arguments, yelling at each other, and those were some of the best times of my life. I don't feel bad saying, in front of other people, "Ron, that store looks like crap." Or saying, "God, we really fucked up this process," right in front of the person responsible. That's the rule here: you have to be super honest. Maybe there's a better way, like a gentlemen's club where everyone wears a tie and speaks in refined, polite language full of elegant euphemisms, but I'm not very good at that, because I'm a middle-class kid from California. Sometimes I've been tough on people, maybe tougher than I needed to be. I remember when Reed was six, he came home on a day I had just fired someone, and I was thinking about how a person tells his family and his little kid that he's lost his job. It was hard. But someone has to do it. I've always felt it was my responsibility to make sure the team was excellent, and if I didn't do it, no one would. You have to keep pushing to innovate. Dylan could have kept singing protest songs forever and probably made a lot of money, but he didn't. He had to move on, and when he brought electric sounds into folk in 1965, he alienated a lot of people. His 1966 European tour was his peak. He would come out first and play acoustic guitar, and the audience loved it. Then he'd bring out The Band, all on electric instruments, and sometimes the crowd would boo. Once, just as he was about to play "Like a Rolling Stone," someone in the audience shouted "Judas!", and Dylan said, "Crank it up, loud as hell!" And they did. The Beatles were the same. They kept evolving, moving, refining their art. That's what I've always tried to do — keep moving. Otherwise, as Dylan put it, if you're not busy trying to live, you're busy dying. What drives me? I think most people who create things want to express gratitude for being able to build on what came before us. I didn't invent the language or the math I use. I make hardly any of my own food, and not a single item of my own clothing. Everything I do depends on the rest of humanity, on their contributions and achievements. Many of us want to give something back to society, to add one more stroke to the long river of history. We can only express it in the way that most of us know how — because we can't write Bob Dylan songs or Tom Stoppard plays. We try to use whatever talent we have to express our deepest feelings, to express our gratitude for everything those before us contributed, and to add a little something to the stream of history. That's what drives me.

A Glance at Natural History & Museology

A few museums in the Netherlands left a deep impression on me. Back in China, the packed crowds at the Sanxingdui Museum and the ceramics museum in Jingdezhen were also a huge shock. The Depot in Rotterdam, the Netherlands In recent years more and more people seem to be visiting museums and galleries — I'm one of them — and I've gradually come to feel how different conceptions, different systems and different ways of running a museum lead to "a different final presentation." A good museum and good curation are never simply a matter of sorting things out and introducing them, let alone piling up categories. They are an immersive experience with a sense of flow, letting you see history, see the threads that connect things, see the past — and see the present too. Same as above So I got curious about putting different museums side by side, poking my head a little way into this field and taking a hurried glance: How did natural history begin? What is the relationship between natural history and science? And what is museology? Let me start with the Rijksmuseum Boerhaave in Leiden, which gave me a very different kind of visiting and learning experience. Leiden, the Netherlands Rijksmuseum Boerhaave The museum isn't large. Its entrance is on a very narrow street and so inconspicuous that you could easily walk right past it. On the outside wall, Einstein's field equations are written on a big blackboard. But inside is a superb collection and presentation of the history of science, which truly let me see how natural history and experimental science drove the scientisation and professionalisation of modern science. Our visit began with a "historical relic": an old anatomical table, moved here from a church. This is exactly how students once stood here learning "human anatomy" — yes, real human dissection. The skeletons around it are all genuine bone specimens used for teaching at the time. At first there's a simple human model in the middle, an old building, an ordinary ceiling and walls. Then projectors shine onto it, and the process of an anatomy lesson of the past slowly unfolds. From the whole human body to the skeleton, to the blood... Next, the walls and ceiling are also used as screens, conjuring up the shock that scientific progress brought to the human mind in different historical periods — now the unveiling of the body's secrets, now the evolution of the microscope, now the exploration of the starry sky. Standing there, I thought of the solemn Hippocratic Oath, of generation after generation of astronomers on their lonely quests, and of how valuable the mistakes in the history of science have been. You don't need grand architecture or lavish, wasteful materials. What you need is a deep grounding in the philosophy of science and the ability to communicate it to the public. Natural history and science Natural history is an ancient branch of learning about how humans deal with nature: macro-level observation, description and classification of animals, plants, minerals, ecosystems and so on. In fact, natural history encompassed much of what today we call astronomy, geology, geography, biology, meteorology, anthropology, ecology, nature writing, ethology, conservation biology and other disciplines. The Chinese term 博物学 corresponds to the English "natural history." In ancient times, "history" meant roughly research or inquiry, so the phrase literally means inquiry into nature. This indeed matches what Professor Cohan called "natural knowledge" before the Scientific Revolution in the history of science. In the world of natural history, Aristotle of ancient Greece is impossible to avoid. He described more than 500 kinds of plants and is hailed as the first naturalist of antiquity. Aristotle again — he wasn't only a philosopher; or rather, philosophers in those days also took in exploring and thinking about the world. The natural history tradition of the ancient European world went on to drive the development of science in the modern era... The rise of modern natural history The road of science really was carved out by many forces pushing together. What drove natural history wasn't only pure curiosity, but also social fashion, and even vanity. Imagine: in seventeenth-century Paris, the capital of culture, an elegant lady at a salon takes out a letter and, as she opens it, "casually" shakes out some grains of sand tucked between the pages — it's a letter from a naturalist/explorer she sponsors, sent back from the other side of the world. That was the fashion of the day, a flex on a par with "bringing out an award-winning red from your own Bordeaux château," or "a 30-year-old Macallan, independently bottled with a label you designed yourself." The Age of Discovery and the formation of Europe's overseas expansion networks created favourable conditions for the rapid development of natural history from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries onwards. Besides seizing colonies and conducting trade, European countries' overseas expeditions were accompanied by a great deal of scientific exploration, including collecting, observing and analysing all kinds of animals, plants, geology and rock formations, in an attempt to build new classification systems for natural history that could take in the whole of the natural world and construct universal scientific knowledge. Understanding nature also had religious significance. Religious figures were always an important force behind natural history; they pursued it as a delight, firmly believing that through it they could discover and glorify God. Later, the development of scientific instruments pushed science a big step further. The famous neuroscientist Sdyney Brenner has a well-known saying that I wholeheartedly agree with: progress in science depends on new techniques, new discoveries and new ideas, probably in that order. Progress in science depends on new techniques, new discoveries and new ideas, probably in that order Museology Once there was natural history, it took a little added love — the wish to pass things down and to share knowledge with the public — for the museums that followed to come about. As I said at the start, simply piling things up does not make a museum. Hence museology. Is museology an independent discipline? This question has been widely debated for a long time. As long as the definition of "museum" hasn't been fully settled, the museum as the object of a discipline can't be pinned down either. Our understanding and building of museums is a process of continual change. Early understanding of museums: collection-oriented institutions The National Museum of Antiquities (Rijksmuseum van Oudheden) in Leiden is one of the oldest museums in the Netherlands. Looking back, it held a number of early archaeological collections. In 1818, as a national institution, the National Museum of Antiquities hoped both to guide the public and a new generation of artists, and to let the Netherlands hold its own against other modern nations intellectually and in national pride. The National Museum of Antiquities, on the Rapenburg in Leiden (the Netherlands), founded in 1818 In the same period, the young Kingdom of the Netherlands built a system of national museums on the basis of collecting and research. Besides the Museum of Antiquities, there was a natural history museum, a national history museum and an art history museum. A little later, the National Museum of Ethnology joined as an independent institution. The National Museum of Antiquities' holdings fall into five parts: the Egyptian collection (one of the ten largest in the world), the ancient Near East, Greek and Roman antiquities, and the large Dutch archaeological collection, divided into prehistoric, Roman and medieval periods. Egyptian galleries: the Egyptian galleries of the National Museum of Antiquities, Leiden (the Netherlands) Dutch archaeology galleries: the Low Countries archaeology galleries in the National Museum of Antiquities, Leiden (the Netherlands) For its foreign collections, the National Museum of Antiquities served merely as a collecting institution, while for its Dutch collections it could fully be called a local museum. Once the whole country became a "site" telling the complete story of the nation's archaeology, the museum hoped to become that site's "visitor centre." In the 1990s, the people running and founding museums began to ask these questions: Is the museum an archaeological institution, or a museum that happens to have archaeological collections? Is the museum only about objects, or is it a distinctive medium? Content or container? Academically, does the museum belong to archaeology or to some other field? Should it work with cultural heritage management authorities? Whom should it invite to the opening? What professional backgrounds should its staff have? At the Dutch national museum of the time, the museum learning model favoured by most curators/researchers and educators tended to treat visitors as little archaeologists, a tendency especially popular among curators of European prehistory. This may not count as a theoretical issue, but in all kinds of practice it made a lot of things different. The spread of new museology: function-oriented museum structures. Beneath the seemingly superficial tension over whether a museum's subject is its identity or its means, another issue lies hidden. Broadly speaking, in the 1970s and afterwards, most Western museums disappeared because of the second museum revolution. After the student movements of the 1960s, in response to major social shifts, museums began to re-examine their values and to engage with society and visitors in different ways. The long-standing way of organising museums hierarchically by specialist field also began to shift towards community-oriented service. France was a pioneer of this movement, and although with marked local or regional characteristics, new museology (nouvelle muséologie) began to spread rapidly around the world. By this period, the overall principle for structuring museums was based on function, rather than on collections and the disciplines supporting them. The "second museum revolution" of the 1970s (after van Mensch, 2004) Communication activities by museum staff, formerly under the direct control of the director, were now placed alongside the curatorial function. These activities were also called public service and presentations, including education, exhibition planning and visitor services (guides, docents). In this organisational structure, the noun "curator" also came to be used as a verb (collecting, communicating). Today, the curator's main job appears to be research; many of their earlier roles were those of specialised collection keepers, archivists and registrars. Although curators still play an important part in making exhibitions, they are no longer in the lead. Most importantly, the museum's exhibitions and activities for visitors no longer directly reflect the museum's behind-the-scenes work. Interdisciplinary story themes and narratives determine which objects are displayed. The collection departments (such as paintings, works on paper, textiles, applied arts) do not have their own galleries. Museology: the study of the processes of musealisation and heritagisation At this point, the museum's core functions had been successfully interlinked, while also achieving a sustainable balance. At the Reinwardt Academy in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, museology is the official name of a postgraduate programme, and it is the study of the processes of musealisation and heritagisation. Museums and other organisational entities are its objects of study. From this perspective, the museum is a meaningful and important form of social expression, a field in which cultural heritage is produced. It requires combining different kinds of knowledge and disciplines, including history, ethics, ethnology, social anthropology, sociology, conservation, collection management, meaning-making and communication, and cultural leadership. If these are arranged and summarised within a logical framework, museum functions can be rewritten as heritage competences. Redefining museum functions as cultural heritage competences Today, museums are increasingly seen as collaborators in meaning-making. Museums are influential in social engagement; in the UK, museums have even changed lives. To remain effective, the cultural heritage workflow should be set up as a circle, not a line. The purpose of communication by museums and heritage institutions is to get feedback, so that meaning can be constructed together. If a museum is genuinely interested in visitors' responses, its impact on visitors, users and co-owners will show in later stages. This requires the museum to participate in, respond to, adopt and adapt to the whole process; even in collecting, choosing to add or to remove can become a response within the process of co-constructing meaning. More and more people believe that this is what museums today should be doing. Most of the museology content in this article is adapted from "Content or Container? Museology as a Discipline," originally published in Museum magazine, 2017, Issue 3. Author: Riemer R. Knoop, Reinwardt Academy, Amsterdam University of the Arts. Translator: Xu Jie, School of Humanities, Zhejiang University Time is too limited, otherwise I should also talk properly about the Depot in Rotterdam, an art storehouse that's a wonderful, very special place well worth visiting again and again. Let me just put up some photos for now. All in all, Museology has gradually shifted from institutions that held the fruits of natural history and archaeological collecting into an interdisciplinary field that helps people understand the underlying processes of heritagisation. It keeps starting from practice, and it has always maintained a critical, reflective stance towards society and its own discipline. Its transformation is precisely the transformation of how people relate to history, to cultural relics, and to their own "self-narrative."

Why Did Modern Science Emerge in Europe?

The first lesson of my Netherlands trip began with a class on the "history of science." More precisely, it began with what "science" is. "I will avoid using the word 'science' for any period before the Scientific Revolution. 'Science' did not yet exist then; we can call it 'natural knowledge.'" — Professor Cohan This kind of "natural knowledge" existed in ancient China, and in ancient Greece too. (Most of what follows is excerpted from my notes on the professor's lecture.) The ancient Chinese tradition of "natural knowledge" Zhang Heng of the Han dynasty discovered a link between the tides and the phases of the moon. The rise and fall of the Yangtze's tides gave him his data — but what led Zhang Heng to connect two things that seemed to have nothing to do with each other? After taking office in the Northern Song, the erudite Shen Kuo discovered a spring containing a substance that, when added to an iron pot, turned the iron into copper — this was alum. What led Shen Kuo to such a discovery? How did they come by such keen observations? — Through the theory of the Five Phases (wuxing). The "Five Phases" were ancient China's worldview of nature. Metal, wood, water, fire and earth stand both for kinds of substance and for stages in how things unfold; seen one way they generate one another, seen the other way they overcome one another. And they cycle round again and again. (Wow, how sophisticated!) The Five Phases theory was one of the ways ancient Chinese scholars explained the world; another was "yin and yang." It offered a flexible language that was ideal for talking about "balance" — not quantitative balance but dynamic balance: more complex sequences of growth, decay, mutual generation and mutual overcoming. So the Chinese view of the cosmos was ever-changing and organic, always shifting with the spontaneous changes of its components. Understanding the world meant understanding not only substances but the relationships between them. Of course, China was not the only civilisation to produce a complete worldview — another was Greek civilisation, but it differed from ancient China in many ways. The ancient Greek tradition of "natural knowledge" Ancient Greek "natural knowledge" developed into different schools: the schools of the four Greek natural philosophers, and the Alexandrian school. But this late-5th-century poem best captures pre-Socratic philosophy; it is seen as a major source of Western thought, and also as the point where Western and Chinese thought parted ways. "Being, how could it perish? How could it come to be? For if it came to be, it is not, nor is it if it is ever going to be. Thus coming-to-be is extinguished, and perishing unheard of." The ancient Greeks of this period held that change is an illusion and that such an intermediate category cannot exist; by the time Athens became the centre of thought, the "phenomenon of change" (non-phenomenon) had become the focus of attention. The four natural philosophers of the Greek city-state: 1. The school founded by Plato: change is confined to everyday appearances, and these appearances are hopelessly imperfect 2. Aristotle: "change" is the actualisation of what is potential 3. The Stoics Change is a permanent state of tension 4. The Atomists Change is the motion of tiny, unobservable particles What do these four schools have to do with our real lives? — Not much, but all four are first-principles thinking. Each school's structure of knowledge is comprehensive and derived from general knowledge, yet fragmentary when it meets reality; examples serve almost no purpose beyond illustrating the a priori foundations. Another mode of natural knowledge: Alexandria, the House of the Muses, became the city of learning for ancient Greece and Rome Euclid's Elements brought together the achievements of generations of Greek mathematicians; its flaws were not discovered until the 19th century This was demonstrable mathematics: even the most self-evident theorems received the most rigorous proofs Music, light, the equilibrium of solids and liquids, planetary orbits — all were highly specialised fields of study, and their practitioners were not only the greatest mathematicians of ancient Greece; there was also Archimedes' fundamental theorem on equilibrium As Ptolemy said: the link between the real world and mathematics is very weak; Alexandrian mathematics had almost nothing to do with reality The aim of the Athenian disciplines was to "explain phenomena," to give phenomena underlying principles so they could be understood Every philosopher would pick the examples from reality that best suited him Qualitative rather than quantitative explanation — that was the natural philosophers' goal Alexandria's goal was different Ancient Greece: first principles are the core of everything vs. Alexandria: utterly indifferent to first principles, they didn't want to explain, only to determine and analyse — not as illustration but as the starting point for mathematical analysis; this kind of research ran in one direction only. It sought no connections, let alone a place within a whole Any educated person could discuss philosophy, but mathematical discussion required training. Looking at the big picture: the ancient Chinese way emphasised observation and practice, grounded in observable phenomena and understood through the Five Phases and yin and yang; the ancient Greek way argued in the most anti-empirical way people could conceive of. Both the Greek and the Alexandrian modes carried an epistemological flavour and involved a process of abstraction. Here is the interesting part: why was it not ancient China's empirical method but the ancient Greek schools — whose modes of knowledge were far removed from practical use — that evolved into modern science? And a science capable of changing the world in unimaginable ways, too. "Think back to the first time you met your future spouse and it becomes very clear: many things in life have their own 'inner logic,' while others are simply 'how chance would have it.' World history is shaped by a mixture of this 'inner logic' and 'happy coincidence.'" — Professor Cohan How "natural science" turned into "modern science" It happened in the 15th century... 1. The key word is "transformation," especially "transformation of thought." Large systems of thought lose their freshness after a very short initial period. Once the founding phase is over, followers keep repeating the founders' ideas, seek variation through competition with one another, and pass the founders' ideas on to the young in the most convenient way. Was there any chance of renewal? Could China's organic change and Athens' worldview look at long-settled old questions in new ways? In the West: exchange through hand-copied texts and with rival schools of thought — but how much vitality can there be in endless "protective" defence? In the East: Han-dynasty China valued observation highly — but the chance of starting afresh and transforming was minuscule. In short, once a discipline's golden age is over, it closes in on itself and grows stale. 2. A ruler's mood swings or change of interests could alter a scientist's fate. Especially in imperial states, the ruler's attitude was key. Whether natural philosophers were valued was closely tied to "medicine" and "astronomical observation"; beyond the court, nobody cared. Philosophy had no such problem, because every aspect of life called for philosophers. 3. In the pre-modern world, the understanding of natural science was unstable. The peculiarities of Greek natural philosophy include: Athens was a priori, while Alexandria was computational. The two did not blend. So where did the difference lie? Neither in China nor in the Roman world could a new character emerge. If renewal can't come from within, it may come from without. Clashes between civilisations have been where novelty and innovation cluster in history: when foreign ideas, peoples and civilisations pour in, new opportunities arise. Because of military, political and historical upheavals, Greece kept meeting new experiences. By comparison, ancient China saw no such transformation. Because outsiders were rapidly sinicised as soon as they came in. After Christianity reached China in the late 16th century, the pursuit of natural knowledge, though it spread to Korea and Japan, did not develop well. Precisely because Chinese culture and institutions matured and solidified too early, its brilliant civilisation radiated out to its neighbours, but lacked opportunities for renewal within. The "organic worldview" that permeated the Chinese natural system held many "opportunities," yet in the end it was Greece that gave birth to science. Athens and Rome were taken up elsewhere three times in succession, each time because of war. The first time: at the end of the 7th century AD, natural philosophy was translated into other languages, and was not only adopted but given new meaning (for example, the role of light). The second time: the Christian rulers of northern Spain reconquered the Muslim principalities, and the Toledo route in 1085 provided the opening — wandering scholars translated Greek texts from Arabic into Latin. These texts had circulated widely in Arab civilisation, and Aristotle's thought spread across Europe. The end result: the Aristotelian school achieved a monopoly. This was a period when it fitted Christian doctrine. The Aristotelian school began to innovate in the 13th–14th centuries. The third time: Western Europe received the transmission of Greek texts, which happened when the Ottoman Empire conquered Byzantium. We still have the legacy of Greek texts preserved today: texts that Byzantium had kept for more than 1,000 years were carried to Italy. Plato's dialogues and Stoic writings reached Europe, and the Aristotelian school lost its monopoly; some had passed into medieval Europe and the Arab world, and mathematical texts were also translated into Latin, straight from the Greek originals, and together with the natural-philosophy texts reached the Catholic world — the European Renaissance, where Platonism and Stoicism got their chance. The use and enrichment of ancient Greek thought resembled what happened in the Middle Ages (the mathematical astronomer Copernicus refined "heliocentrism"). This was an outstanding example of describing the "empirical world" less on the basis of epistemology and more through accurate description and a more empirical approach. By the early 16th century, the three modes of natural knowledge (Alexandrian, European empiricist, Platonic), through other procedures of testing, bound science more tightly to the real world. Empirical description and measurement turned into experiment. These three parts formed the beginning of the "Scientific Revolution." Then came the "Scientific Revolution"... It was Christiaan Huygens (1629–1695) tackling natural phenomena with mathematics and experiment; it was the arrival of Galileo (1630s); it was Descartes' revolutionary transformation of the Athenian school; it was Huygens (1629–1695) and his earth-shattering words: no scientific conclusion is beyond doubt. In the past, China's unified philosophy, Athenian philosophy and Islamic theory — so many of these theories were considered settled "once and for all," with room for innovation only in very local corners. But science's understanding of nature is a never-ending exploration. Every scientist must spare no effort in testing whether their conclusions are right; most of the time this includes finding the weak links in their own conclusions and designing ingenious experiments to see whether the conclusions hold. Gradually, scientists who were good with their hands came on the scene too, and Huygens was one of them: he designed and improved telescopes and microscopes, improved Galileo's pendulum... In short, I love his scientific style — "this is very interesting, but I can do better." Why did science emerge in Europe? As Professor Cohan said: "That science developed in Europe may have been accidental, a stroke of luck; it was not bound to happen." This class pulled me out of science itself to look at the relationships between civilisations and between sciences. Through military, political and historical upheavals, Chinese civilisation survived as one continuous, unbroken civilisation, successfully withstanding the Mongols — very different from Greek and Roman civilisation, whose world ended with barbarian invasions. A civilisation is also fragile and must embrace innovation and revolution, which are indispensable to modern science. But if a civilisation is strong, stable and sustainable, it finds it hard to embrace revolution and innovation, and so it misses certain opportunities. We should try our best to understand the "inner logic" of things, but also accept the surprises — and the helplessness — of "chance encounters." BTW, the Q&A session left a deep impression on me. First of all, it was not exciting at all. Whatever the students asked, the professor either answered a different question, spoke in a very uncertain tone, or simply said he didn't know. This was very different from the lively Q&As I'd seen before. But it was precisely these answers that showed me the rigour of real scholarship: every step of reasoning has to be tight; you can't answer just for the sake of answering. There was a kind of German-style rigour, awkwardness and endearing charm about it. About the lecturer, Professor Hendrik Floris Cohen Born in 1946, he studied history at Leiden University, served as director of the Museum Boerhaave in Leiden from 1975 to 1982, and since December 2006 has been Professor of Comparative History of Science at Utrecht University. He loves the pipe organ and sport, and is passionate about popular science. His books include The Revolution in Physics , How Modern Science Came Into the World , Quantifying Music: The Science of Music at the First Stage of the Scientific Revolution and The Scientific Revolution: A Historiographical Inquiry . In 2008, his The Re-creation of the World: How Modern Science Came About (translated into Chinese by Zhang Butian) won the Dutch Eureka Prize. Two or three hours of lecturing and the professor never paused once — it turned out he had written out a word-for-word script. Again, that German-style rigour, awkwardness and endearing charm. Even more fun: three years ago, three Dutch sinologists translated Dream of the Red Chamber , and Professor Cohan actually took time off to read the whole of this Chinese classic — and a year later he read it all over again. When I was little, my mother used to say, "Girls shouldn't read Red Chamber ," afraid it would make me too sentimental... As a result I've never finished it even once! And this Dutch grandpa has read it twice! How embarrassing...
The Netherlands, a Country to Be Proud Of.

Friends who have studied or built careers in the Netherlands have all, one after another, mentioned their time in this small European country with real pride in their voices, and back then I didn't pay it much attention. In my teens I travelled through the Netherlands — 7 days, 5 countries, a whirlwind of sightseeing. If anything truly left a mark, it was probably only The Diary of Anne Frank , which shaped the mindset and openness with which I've kept a diary ever since. For all these years, the Netherlands, as a not-very-conspicuous European country, brought to mind only tulip mania, windmills, Delftware, ASML and the red-light district... But now, when the Netherlands comes up, what springs to mind is: governing water as you govern a nation, freedom, cooperation, innovation, and this famous, proud Dutch saying: "God created the world, but the Dutch created the Netherlands." I wouldn't say I was "blown away" — only that "you have to hand it to them." This small country, surviving in the cracks between three European powers — Britain, Germany and France — with a land area just 2.5 times that of Beijing, this tiny patch of land that has lived under the threat of floods year after year, showed me the courage, determination and humanitarian spirit human beings are capable of... Looking back now, I understand where my friends' pride comes from — people who have been steeped in the culture here and trained in its abilities really have received a rare experience and gift. Netherlands First Impressions "Nether" is written "Nieder" in Germanic and means low-lying land, so "Netherland" means "the low country, the lowlands." A quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, another quarter is less than 1 metre above it, and the lowest point, near Rotterdam, is nearly 7 metres below sea level. Surrounded by sea on several sides and harassed and threatened by floods year after year, it is the lowest-lying country in the world, yet also the one best able to defend against floods. The Netherlands had the world's first stock exchange, and was once an "empire on which the sun never set," dominating the globe for more than a hundred years; The Netherlands was the first country in the world to pass a same-sex marriage law, and also the first to legalise euthanasia; Its brain bank is famous for its complete system of case records, and has supported a great deal of brain research around the world. The Netherlands has enviable lithography technology and has given birth to world-shaping companies like Philips and ASML; With 2.5 times the land area of Beijing, it has become the world's second-largest agricultural exporter; The Dutch invented the microscope, and invented Wi-Fi... Not to mention great artists like Van Gogh and Rembrandt; It has nurtured the pragmatic, innovative and deeply cooperative Dutch people; and it gave rise to the Polder Model, a form of social organisation full of human communal wisdom. Starting with how the Dutch manage water... In 2008, the Netherlands held a national debate: with sea-level rise now a certainty, the country faced 3 choices: (1) Relocate, as Tuvalu has, with some people emigrating to Germany; (2) Retreat back from the current coastline; (3) Be stubborn: reclaim land from the sea, build dams, fight the water and live with the water. — The Netherlands chose the third. This wasn't the first time they'd made that choice. Since the 4th century AD, the Netherlands has been building dikes continuously. Having held back the external threat with the world's longest flood defences, the Netherlands then found itself troubled by an internal one: how to drain floodwater from its inland waterways. They discovered that building canals not only helped drainage and kept residential areas safe from flooding, but also opened up water and land transport and developed irrigation and drainage for farmland, so they threw themselves wholeheartedly into the great enterprise of digging canals. By the 17th century, the Netherlands had made canal-building into something it did better than anyone in the world. Today, the Dutch are already considering raising their water-management works from once-in-a-thousand-years and once-in-ten-thousand-years standards to the once-in-ten-thousand-years level. Short on time, so I'm just throwing my notes on water management up here. To sum up how I feel: the scientific understanding, technical capability, engineering capability, grasp of the environment and ecology, and modes of social governance that water management demands are highly complex and systemic, requiring a country that is highly developed in every respect to coordinate all sectors of society, and even negotiate with other countries, to get it done together. This is not only a practical problem but also a philosophical one worth thinking about. A society that holds the individual in the highest regard accomplished all of this through collective strength. The reason goes back to the documentary about the great flood of 1953, and the two words the Dutch said after suffering such painful losses: Never Again.
You Walked With Me as I Grew Up; Now I'll Walk With You as You Grow

In 1998, Mum sent me to Professor Kang's home to learn English. To keep me company, she became the oldest student in the class; In 2022, I joined Gaoshan Academy. Science reawakened my curiosity, and with it came a rethinking of every aspect of life; In 2024, after much persuading on my part, Mum became my Gaoshan "junior schoolmate" — and once again she was the oldest student in the class. And so we set off on a journey to explore the world through the eyes of science. People always say the parent-child relationship is "you walk with me as I grow up, and I walk with you as you grow old" — I profoundly disagree. At one end of time lies the past. It was you who fed your youth to me, who shielded me with your experience and your arms, so that fragile little me could form a safe connection with the world; At the other end of time lies the future. When the time is right, I will take your hand and extend the arc of your growth; let you see, standing on your shoulders, the view I have seen; and become the bridge between you and the future. Life is a journey through changing scenery, and its destination is a richer self at life's end. It's true that our perceptions, preferences and tastes are largely set in our youth, and in old age we are all, more or less, trapped in times gone by. But the difference between lives lies precisely in that "more or less." Fast or slow, as long as the direction is right, just keep walking. Ageing begins with refusing new things. Admittedly, when someone's strength and memory visibly decline, finding a sense of meaning and reward in "the present" becomes hard, and "the past" inevitably becomes the safe zone they retreat into. But children can become their parents' "second-stage rocket." When the engine between parent and child switches over — from "parents leading the child" to "the child taking the parents along" — where exactly should we take our parents?
