Reading across time and space has a lovely quality. Some passages, when interpreted — even if the reading strays from what the author meant — can still bring insight and a jolt of awakening. Meditations is one example. On the other hand, I've come to feel more and more that a person's thought and views have to be read against the backdrop of their era before you can truly grasp their weight. Hayek's thought was born in a very particular period: around the First World War. It was the bygone age described in Zweig's The World of Yesterday — a peaceful, art-filled, intoxicating Vienna; the end of the Austro-Hungarian Empire; the collapse of the system of states; countries attacking one another, people of the same country attacking one another too; many intellectuals swept along by the times, shouting fanatically... Thinking clearly in an age like that is incredibly hard — like pulling a single rope out of a tangled mess. As the introduction to this biography says: From this Hayek: A Biography we learn that when he began to think seriously about social problems, it was around the time of the First World War. Europe at that point had two basic features. One was the major change in the social and political environment, symbolised by events including the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917, the abdication of Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1918, and, in the same year, the end of the Habsburgs' 700-year rule over Austria-Hungary. And Hayek's own hometown, Vienna, once a supremely flourishing cosmopolitan city, was about to become a city that was free but soon to decline. Linked to these political events was the gradual spread of universal suffrage across Western European countries, and the challenge that the resulting rise of mass parties posed to traditional parliamentary systems. This led traditionalists on the Continent to deeply doubt whether the elite liberalism of the nineteenth century could survive. According to Hayek, intellectuals at the time widely believed that "socialism was the next stage of social development, both ethically and empirically." Spurred on by the October Revolution in the Soviet Union, this current of thought gradually moved beyond the study and the newspaper debate and began to enter the political processes of some countries; for example, after the First World War the governments of Germany and Austria passed nationalisation acts one after another. It is fair to say that in the first thirty years of the twentieth century, three great events — the First World War, the Russian Revolution and the Great Depression that followed — had sent the traditional liberalism of the first half of the nineteenth century into complete shock. The theory of the capitalist market, built on freedom of contract, was increasingly being replaced by rhetoric emphasising state intervention, and its most active champions were, of course, Europe's left-wing socialists. That's why I really enjoyed reading these two books together. Getting to know Hayek's life while starting on The Constitution of Liberty . Every time I read Hayek it's an intellectual challenge, but finishing it feels fantastic. 1. The historical backdrop and the state of people's minds at the time. Defeating ideas with ideas. Anyone whose intellectual growth took place in the twentieth century must have a deep sense of socialism's unrivalled capacity for mobilising intellectuals. In leading people to care about broad social questions and inspiring them to display the strength of their moral courage, probably no other doctrine could come close. Moreover, because the newly emerging institutions of mass democracy made large-scale political mobilisation possible, countless intellectuals, faced with a capitalist world they regarded as sordid and disorderly, resolutely took the path of left-wing political activism. — Translator's foreword (in lieu of a preface), Hayek: A Biography 2. The early Hayek was a "mild socialist," but the debates of his society let a young man, right from the start, explore back and forth between two completely different roads. Like many young people of the time, Hayek was influenced by the spirit of the age. As a sensitive mind, he keenly felt the severe challenges facing the existing order amid the turmoil. Like many young people seeking a way forward for European civilisation, he became a "mild socialist." During the First World War, he used his spare time on the Italian front to read some "economics works of a mildly socialist character," and after the war, at university, he even immersed himself in socialist pamphlets during theology classes. Just as Hayek was being drawn to socialism, Mises launched the great debate over the problem of economic calculation in planned economies. His attention to this debate, and his acquaintance with Mises soon after, became the first occasion that prompted him to reflect on the mainstream socialist thought of the day. In thinking seriously about the planned economy, he had to face a question that anyone who takes scientific research seriously would ask: could these so captivating socialist plans actually be realised? This line of thought launched Hayek's research into market information, so one could say that without this question, there would have been no later Hayekian economics built on a foundation of the theory of knowledge. — Translator's foreword (in lieu of a preface), Hayek: A Biography 3. Liberalism is an important theoretical cornerstone of the market economy. At a time when our country's specific economic institutions are all "converging" with those of developed countries, it is unthinkable not to study liberalism seriously as an important theoretical cornerstone of the economic institutions of developed countries. Some of liberalism's tenets are indeed at odds with our country's ideological system, but it must be admitted that, as an important theoretical foundation of the free market economy, liberal theory reflects and sums up the general laws of how a market economy operates. Our current economic reforms seek to establish a system of active market players, a unified and open market system, and a complete system of market economy laws and regulations; in fact, these goals are consistent with what liberalism advocates. Furthermore, demonstrating how our socialist market economy differs from Western market economies also requires us to study Western liberal theory systematically. — Translator's preface, The Constitution of Liberty 4. Interesting — perhaps our fuzziness about liberalism and democracy is just like the West's inability to tell apart the teachings of Confucius and Mencius. "Liberalism is a doctrine about what the law ought to be, democracy a doctrine about the manner of determining what will be the law." There are some misconceptions in our understanding of liberalism. First, we have often treated Western liberal-democratic thought as an undifferentiated whole, and many people even think liberal thought and democratic thought are one and the same. In fact, modern Western liberal thought and democratic thought are two independent theoretical traditions: in terms of origins, liberal thought arose in England, while democratic thought arose in France. During the period of the European bourgeois revolutions, the two traditions showed a tendency to merge, and some French thinkers (such as Montesquieu and Tocqueville) preferred the English tradition, while some English thinkers (such as Hobbes) held the French tradition in the highest esteem. Nevertheless, the basic theoretical orientations of the two are entirely different, and the reason for this difference is that "the empiricist worldview once dominated in England, while the rationalist worldview once dominated in France." — Translator's preface, The Constitution of Liberty 5. To sing against the tune of an entire era, and to lift that tune from academic economics up to the level of sociology and even philosophy — what a fighting spirit that person's heart must have had. In an age when collectivism prevailed, a serious attitude towards the problem of knowledge within economics alone, without any sense of historical mission, would probably not have been enough to make a person resolve to devote a lifetime to building a comprehensive social philosophy. We see that, in fact, from the time Hayek entered economic research until the end of the 1930s, although he had moments in the limelight — his debate with Keynes in professional economics journals, for instance, won him wide renown and for a time meant that at the London School of Economics (LSE) almost "everyone became a Hayekian" — this fame remained confined to economics. The second occasion that prompted Hayek's transformation from a professional economist into a social philosopher came at the end of the 1930s. By then, the economic crisis the capitalist world had just come through had long since made people stop caring about Hayek's theories of money, prices and business cycles. In Keynes's words, his economic theory was nothing but a "muddled hodgepodge of gibberish" and "rubbish." This plunged Hayek back into silence in academic circles. Hayek did not abandon his convictions because his academic standing had been marginalised. He remained unwaveringly sceptical of those who believed the prescription of state intervention could save the West from its crisis. This was first of all because he believed his theory of the division of knowledge had a solid scientific foundation. His isolation only made him more tenacious, and he began to think deeply about a phenomenon that went beyond pure economics. The purely epistemological question he had raised — whether the socialist planned economy could reach the ideal goals it had set for itself — began to evolve into a question of much broader scope: why, when thinking about how to improve their social condition, are human beings so commonly governed by mistaken ideas?

Why Israel relies on assassination This has to do with the dire situation on the eve of and in the early days of Israel's founding in 1948: surrounded by powerful enemies, with limited strength of its own, international aid and support still uncertain, and on top of that the psychological trauma of the Nazi Holocaust in the Second World War. So, to survive, the newborn Israel had to use every means available to guarantee its security and eliminate its enemies. 2. In politics, there really are no permanent enemies and no permanent friends. Britain "supported or abandoned" Israel according to whether it was "useful or useless." During the First World War, the Palestine region was under the control of the Ottoman Empire, which sided with the Central Powers of Germany and Austria in the war. So Britain needed an ally in the Middle East to keep its colonies from falling into enemy hands, especially the hub of global trade and transport — the Suez Canal. Britain therefore decided to support the Jews' return to their ancestral land of Palestine to found a state. Yet after the First World War, the pragmatic British government decided that the Jewish presence in Palestine looked weak, and so, to protect its own political and economic interests in the Middle East, it ought instead to court the powerful Arab tribes that had been established there for many years. And so, in May 1939, British Colonial Secretary MacDonald put forward a brand-new outline of Middle East foreign policy, which was adopted: this was the MacDonald White Paper. The same goes for the United States. With the Israeli intelligence services' string of successes and victory in the Second Arab-Israeli War in 1956, Israel rose rapidly: this small country once thought to be living on borrowed time quickly became a military power and an intelligence powerhouse. It gave me a new understanding of Shimon Peres's "using creativity to forge peace." And also: only with strength is negotiation possible. Beginning in 1962, Israeli intelligence learned that Egypt had recruited a group of German scientists from the Second World War era to develop ballistic missiles, and had already carried out test launches. Egyptian President Nasser publicly declared that these missiles could strike anywhere on Israeli territory. So secretly sabotaging Egypt's missile program became the Mossad's top priority. The head of the Mossad believed the most direct and effective approach was to carry out targeted killings of these German scientists, or to frighten them into leaving Egypt. In August 1962, Mossad agents tracked down Krug, a German scientist on the core team of Egypt's missile development program. He was at home in Munich, in southern Germany. Mossad agents posed as envoys from Egyptian military intelligence, went straight to his door and abducted him, then drove across the German-French border and took him to Marseille. In Marseille, Krug was injected with a heavy dose of sedatives. The Israeli agents forged a false identity for him, claiming he was a gravely ill Jewish immigrant, and put him on an Israeli passenger plane prepared in advance, flying straight to Israel. Under interrogation, Krug revealed everything he knew about Egypt's missile development program, but in the end he was still secretly executed. The Mossad went on to plan several other assassinations of German missile scientists on German soil, but because of various unforeseen circumstances, these operations did not succeed. The failed assassination attempts caused an uproar in Germany and across Europe, instantly plunging the Israeli government into a diplomatic predicament. In fact, Israeli intelligence agents and special forces of the Israel Defense Forces would go on to carry out many more covert operations that violated international law and infringed on other countries' sovereignty, sometimes killing and injuring many innocent civilians, leaving Israel persistently isolated and condemned. In the end, the Mossad had to change course and strike a deal with a former mortal enemy: they sought out the notorious Nazi war criminal Skorzeny, commander of the SS special forces. Skorzeny, nicknamed "the most dangerous man in Europe," had led many special operations during the Second World War, including Operation Oak in 1943, which rescued the Italian fascist leader Mussolini, and he was deeply trusted by Hitler. As a result, Skorzeny knew many of Nazi Germany's top secrets inside out. Although he had regained his freedom after the war, Skorzeny still lived in terror, afraid that the elusive and ruthless Israeli agents would come knocking. So the Mossad and Skorzeny reached an agreement: Israeli intelligence would let bygones be bygones regarding his past crimes, but Skorzeny had to use his connections to provide a detailed list of all the missile experts, and persuade these scientists not to go to Egypt anymore. To save his own skin, Skorzeny completed the task quickly and efficiently. At the same time, an Israeli government delegation including Deputy Defense Minister Peres visited West Germany and used the intelligence provided by Skorzeny and the Mossad to pressure the West German government. In the end, the West German government agreed to have West German aerospace companies lure all the German scientists back with high salaries; with that, Egypt's missile development program collapsed. Wisdom comes not only from reading widely and learning from the wise, but also from turning inward and seeking inner calm, so that the truth can surface. It's Chinese New Year's Eve tonight. Outside the window, firecrackers go off without end; inside, the songs of the Spring Festival Gala. Everything is so peaceful and quiet that it feels lonely. The mood is right for saying what's in my heart. I'm a little ashamed to say it, but sometimes I feel my life right now couldn't be any better — so good that I'm almost afraid to break anything. I have family and friends who look after me, like-minded partners, a stable team, a carefree life; I get to see immortal cities, immortal paintings and the most beautiful scenery on earth; I'm free, not tied down by any institution or career, my work is my joy, and, more importantly, it feels meaningful. If I felt no gratitude at all and took all this as the most ordinary life, that would truly be a sin. And yet, always moving forward, always staying curious, always being a creator, always living up to the spirit of striving — that is the promise I've made to myself. I'm still eager to "set off". I don't know what's waiting ahead, but either life won't always be this cloudless, or I'm bound to take all this good fortune and give back to society and to heaven. Either way, something is driving me, and I can't stop. Even though I can't yet see clearly what it is. I long to be like I was when I first started my company — jumping onto a fast train and growing wildly at full speed. But looking around at the dangers on every side, I've lost the reckless courage of the newborn calf that doesn't fear the tiger. Sometimes a wave of panic rises out of nowhere — have I wasted my time? Do I no longer dream big? The only cure for the panic is to carefully hone myself and prepare myself. My 2024 Flags🚩 come down to three words: habits, getting things done, focus. 1. Habits "Habits" are a person's foundation. Reading, journaling, planning and exercise are the daily habits I've wanted to build for years. But they're like an "impossible quadrilateral" — I can never keep all four going at once. Reading has gone best: thanks to the likes and positive feedback I get every day, my "WeChat Moments check-ins" have given me growth I wouldn't have dared imagine, three years in a row. A positive feedback loop really is a powerful tool for building good habits! Speaking of which, I have to thank my friends once again. In 2024 I'll keep leaning on your strength! Read on more than 300 days Journal on more than 300 days Plan on more than 300 days, defined as: being clear on the three things I must get done that day Hit my exercise target on more than 200 days, defined as: walking 10,000 steps or getting my heart rate to 130 For building habits, routine is extremely important. I plan to read and plan from 7:30-8:30AM every morning when I wake up, read and journal from 10:30-11:30PM before bed, and keep half of every Sunday for myself. I hope these become habits nothing can shake — friends around me, please keep these times free for me, and hold me to them. 2. Get Things Done If you're doing the right thing, there's always a way. Choose what I "should do" rather than what I "can do", and watch out for sliding into "easy mode". Do what I say and finish what I start, especially promises to myself; a planner and follow-ups matter a lot. Finish on time, finish early Hold an asset meeting every Monday, without fail 3. Focus Do fewer things, do them better, and truly own myself. Declutter further: cut clothes, bags, shoes and ornaments by a third. Take on fewer things. Build a new habit: don't say yes to people straight away; first ask myself three questions: How much time will this take? Looking back a year from now, will it have been worth doing? Looking back ten years from now, will it have been worth doing? Regularly clear out my weekly, monthly, quarterly and yearly to-do lists That's all — please hold me to it. Life has many truths, and none of them are wrong; in life there is no right or wrong to begin with. It is our "choices" that make us who we are.

New knowledge: Bed rest has serious side effects; after a fracture, simply lying still is not the best approach. First, bed rest is practically a second injury after a fracture. 1. Bed rest causes severe muscle wasting, and it happens fast! A week in bed and your leg muscles can shrink by 10%; a month in bed is enough to leave you unable to stand and walk normally. The standard muscle mass for women is 25–27%; I used to be close to 30%, dropped to 23.3% after 10 days in bed, with a low of 21.5%. 2. Bed rest causes bone loss, and to a surprising degree. The body's "use it or lose it" really is no joke. No wonder so many astronauts have to be carried when they return to Earth: the lack of gravity in space makes bones lose calcium, lowering bone density and wasting muscle. It gets so bad that, back on Earth, a spacesuit weighing a few dozen jin can fracture a bone. What's the mechanism? Bone is an active tissue, constantly remodelling and maintaining itself. The process involves bone resorption (bone cells absorbing old bone) and bone formation (bone cells producing new bone). Gravity is very important to bones: it provides the mechanical stimulus and load they need. When we stand, walk, bear weight or do other physical activity, our bones are loaded, which triggers bone-cell activity. These loads and mechanical stimuli help keep bones healthy and prompt bone formation. When bones no longer bear weight, they lose that mechanical stimulus, and bone cells receive fewer signals to make new bone, while resorption of old bone carries on; resorption outpaces formation, and that is bone loss. Looked at another way, standing and walking at the right time and in the right amount actually helps bones repair and grow. 3. Prolonged bed rest can increase the risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). DVT is when blood clots in a deep vein; the clot may break loose and cause serious complications such as pulmonary embolism. 4. Prolonged bed rest may reduce lung capacity and function. Of course, by the look of it I won't be in bed for very long, but the damage from just a week or two is already this great — truly beyond what I'd imagined. Our blind spots are everywhere, and knowledge matters so much. Fortunately, exercise rehab can make a big difference. A quick word of thanks: once again, I'm proud to thank my treasure of classmates at Gaoshan Academy. They showed they cared right away, patiently answered all my questions, and in the end even put me in touch with a UC Berkeley-certified rehab therapist who works with the national team. I really am incredibly lucky. Talking with the therapist shifted my thinking from static rest and waiting to a dynamic understanding of the relationship between muscles, soft tissue and bone — seeking a balance between "keeping the bone stable" and "the right amount of stimulus." Starting rehab training promptly can help me get back to normal life sooner, recover better, and better guard against the risk that this injury leads to bone spurs, lumbar muscle strain and the lower back pain that comes with them. Muscles, especially the deep muscles, are crucial. There are many muscles around the lumbar spine — the superficial muscles handle most movement, like steak or tenderloin; the deep muscles grip the spine, like the meat on lamb spine bones. The deep muscles hold the lumbar vertebrae in place and make the body more stable. This fracture will have a negative effect on my body's mechanical structure, and I have to accept that objectively. But the body has redundancy: by adjusting spinal mechanics and muscle stability, you can absolutely tap into that margin and get your body into better shape. Over the long term, a bad thing might well become a good one. Much of the body's ageing and pain is caused by "long-term improper use." Lots of small faults and errors in movement patterns, underuse or overuse, pile up over the length of a life and turn into serious wear and strain. No habit is a small matter. Effort is non-negotiable. Taking my bones seriously this time, along with rehab training and learning, may change my old bad habits for a long time to come. As the saying goes: never waste a crisis. Only by starting rehab training promptly can I best help my bones grow and get my life back. I've started changing my daily schedule to make enough time for rehab. My rehab plan 1. Overall approach: progress from bodyweight to small equipment, then to machine training. Move from a low level of everyday activity gradually back to my original abilities. 2. Belly breathing: use belly breathing to stimulate the deep muscles and stabilise the lumbar spine. When breathing out, draw the abdomen in tight against the spine, as in a plank. 3. Exercises lying down: lying flat puts no load on the lumbar spine. When there's no risk, you can feel the muscle stimulus of each movement without worrying. 4. Using a physiotherapy device: on the doctor's recommendation, I've started using a Compex 8.0, a Swiss brand founded in 1988. It works on the thighs, glutes and lower back — rotate between areas! But passive stimulation gets you only half the result for double the effort; you still have to feel and direct the movement through your brain and nerves. 5. Exercise plan Ankle pumps: 6 seconds each, whenever you have a spare moment Clamshells: 15 reps × 3 sets Dynamic dead bugs: 8–12 reps × 3 sets Single-leg glute bridge (knee extended): 8–12 reps × 3 sets Rest 1 minute between sets for all of the above; once or twice a day. Finally, beyond exercise, I have to stress diet: 1. Your diet must include enough protein, calcium, and micronutrients such as vitamin D. Be careful not to take calcium alone! Calcium needs vitamin D and other micronutrients to be absorbed; excess calcium that isn't absorbed ends up in the blood as blood calcium and raises blood pressure. 2. Bear in mind that your basal metabolism has already dropped, so don't overdo the supplements. Especially all the traditional bone broths, which can easily lead to weight gain, higher blood pressure, metabolic problems and so on. My records show that after I fell and was confined to bed on January 7, my metabolism dropped noticeably. You do need to build yourself up, but pay attention to what with. And last of all, a few more points: 1. Know your limits, progress step by step, and speed up recovery only while staying safe. 2. Wear a back brace to prevent slipping, which could damage the nerves. I hope I recover soon, and that a bad thing becomes a good one, and I hope that from here on, we all use these machines of ours more "correctly."
