My Birthday: A Whole Day of Small Joys.

‍ Today is my birthday. I have been in this world for exactly 13,140 days — ten times 1314, the number that sounds like "one life, one lifetime" in Chinese. Lying in bed, I had no time to be sad about getting hurt, nor to feel lucky for surviving a close call. I just tried my best to throw myself into the right frame of mind — live each day well, soak up the love around me, review my mistakes while they're still fresh, carry out my recovery plan, get to know myself through the present, understand the people around me from the perspective of someone being cared for... so many things to do. Past, present and future: I've never cared much about the past — I'm still young, with no time for wistfulness. People always say "live in the moment", but "the moment" is mostly fleeting emotion, not reliable enough. And yet, without a past and a present, what would there be to look forward to in the future? Is it possible for a person to transcend time, to live in the past, present and future all at once? Perhaps, seen from another dimension, the present is eternity, and every moment of life is a slice that runs through the whole of it. Like today. Today, everyone I love checked in on me and sent their wishes; my family, after being frightened half out of their wits, pulled themselves together, made me three meals a day and were endlessly patient with me; my partners stayed by my side, took care of me in every way, and even put thought into preparing a surprise; a group of friends in my life whom I admire, even look up to, gave me boundless joy and care; thinking of you all, my heart feels full and my soul feels rich. Thinking back on the people I once loved, the friends I once thought would be friends for life, the people who disappeared, the greetings that stopped coming — I gently said goodbye to them again in my heart. I loved them, and I must have hurt them too. I hope they have forgiven me. Today didn't go according to plan. I video-chatted with friends and sang together over the mic 🎤 all day long, the day passing in small fragments, drifting with the current. I happily replied to every birthday message, and then did nothing at all. And yet, I was very happy. I casually filmed snippets of daily life. This is life too: no camera moves, no close-ups, nothing grand or sweeping, no mysteries, no epiphanies — just a whole day of small joys. Just as the background music in the video sings: If people didn't believe that their dream life can sometimes be very bitter Comforted by a kiss, made steadfast by a vow, sorrow would soon be soothed Lastly, let me share my birthday present and cake today — an intangible cultural heritage from Shanxi — a gorgeous big flower basket of huamo, decorative steamed buns, where even the basket itself is made of steamed bun! The peonies symbolise "glory and wealth", the lucky bags "blessings in abundance", the apples "peace and safety", the gourds "fortune and prosperity", plus "rising step by step", "five blessings at the door" and all sorts of other surprises and lovely auspicious meanings... I spent the whole day immersed in the joy of carbs.
To the Friends Who Care About Me

Dear friends, It's been a week since my injury, and I've received so, so, so, so much love and concern. I can't reply to everyone in time, so here is one big (virtual) bow of thanks to you all. A friend once told me that when your family is worried about you, you should share how you're doing before they ask. Tell them more than they ask, answer the questions they haven't thought of yet, give more detail, more layers, deeper reflection. I couldn't agree more. So let me report back to you all, one by one: the doctors' advice, my recovery plan, my daily schedule and my learning goals. I hope this puts your minds at ease — and suggestions for improvement are very welcome. About the injury The combined opinion of several hospitals A compression fracture of the L3 vertebra. The vast majority of doctors recommend conservative treatment. Conservative treatment: lie flat, avoid standing or sitting as much as possible, and occasionally lie on my side. In another 2 weeks, I'll go back to the hospital for a new CT scan plus a fat-suppressed MRI. Does it hurt? Honestly, it doesn't. Medication: none About recovery Lying flat — lying flat is the whole game. Diet Mostly light food in the early stage A daily multivitamin, plus an extra 1000 IU of vitamin D 300 ml of milk a day In the first week I had no appetite and took in 800–1000 kcal a day, but I didn't force myself; I just listened to my body. From the second week my appetite opened up a bit, so I'm gradually increasing my protein intake and trying to eat a little more fruit. No special supplements needed — food is the best natural nutrition Sleep 8–9 hours a day (sleep maxed out) A 20-minute nap at noon No sleeping during the day unless I'm tired, to keep my circadian rhythm as steady as possible Exercise Every day I stretch whatever can move — head and neck, back, arms, ankles; Every day I consciously tense local muscles to slow muscle atrophy as much as I can. Meditation: 10 minutes in the morning, and a few times during the day. Daily schedule"In the old days the sun moved slowly / carts, horses and mail were all slow / a lifetime was only long enough to love one person" 7:00 - 8:3010 minutes of meditation and stretching + muscle training, reading check-in Listening to "Dedao"8:30-9:30 Breakfast9:30-12:00 Work During the day I try to get some sun on my arms and legs ☀️. The calcium that bones need to grow has to be absorbed with the help of vitamin D, and sunlight is the body's main way of producing vitamin D. Strictly speaking, it's hard to get the light you need through glass, but it's better than nothing — and a bit of sunshine feels nice anyway.12:00-13:30 Lunch13:30-14:30 Nap + odds and ends14:30-16:00Work 16:00-18:00 Study18:00-19:30Dinner 19:30-21:30Reading, journaling, writing 21:30-22:30Wash up, sleep "Study" means content with some intellectual challenge; "Reading" means purely relaxing reading; I reply to WeChat in the breaks between every 25 or 50 minutes of work, study or reading, so my replies will be slow and patchy — please forgive me; Work is mainly carrying on with what I was already doing, still to a high standard; new work is limited to chatting, offering ideas, and doing the talking. In two weeks, once the backlog is cleared, I hope to give my afternoons over to study. Learning goal: large, unbroken stretches of time are so rare in life — so, so rare. I want to systematically learn AI and how to use AI tools, and hope to claim a small seat in this wave. I'm pitifully green here and my fundamentals are far from solid, so I don't mind starting from the basics, the key definitions and the key logic. Please share any good courses, books, videos and study materials with me. Send me the best things you've seen about AI — this is the moment I need your support. Since the injury, life has slowed down. Every glass of water, every meal, every time I brush my teeth or wash my face has become a delicate operation. It can't be rushed, and there's no point rushing it. My range of movement and control is tiny, limited to the reach of my own arms, and I need my family's help very often. Getting used to this process with the people around me takes a bit of a sense of humour from everyone. I'm learning to adjust my expectations for everything, and to use the gaps to breathe deeply. While waiting for my family to respond, I always feel a flicker of impatience, but if I turn that time into my own deep-breathing time, I feel much calmer. My daily fun also comes from improving the bed-rest experience bit by bit. Today I take stock of my mood, tomorrow I add a box of floss to the bedside, the day after I buy a Bluetooth keyboard... I help order groceries online and talk with my family about what to have for each meal. I have to say, I'm truly lucky. Not only because, after such a dangerous fall, I wasn't hurt as badly as expected. But also because there are so many people around me who love me. So many. So many. My tireless family, the friends who rushed to my side straight away, the friends and teachers who found doctors at major hospitals to look at my scans, the brainy crowd who were still discussing my condition at their get-together, the seniors who generously offered me resources at major hospitals, the fun, boredom-busting gifts and flowers from all over the country, the friends and colleagues running around on my behalf, the friends planning to fly in from other cities to visit me, and on WeChat, all that restrained yet heartfelt care and all those greetings... All this care will become my motivation to "lie flat" properly, so don't worry, everyone~ ❤️ hugs

Never let a good crisis go to waste. — Winston Churchill On my first day of bed rest, I gave myself a small task: to really feel what it's like to be a bedridden patient, so that if I ever need to care for a family member in future, I can be more empathetic. It's only been a short while, so I'll start by slowly noting down a few things: What a bedridden patient needs is to be "supported," not "managed." "Care" is a subtle word. To what extent should the carer decide what the patient can eat? What they can't eat? Whether they can get up to use the toilet? — This is an art. There's no right or wrong, but it calls for communication. When you're bedridden, it's important to keep as much ability to look after yourself as possible. However devoted a carer is, they can never be as instant and timely as you are when doing it yourself, so for anything you can do on your own, make it as easy as possible. Details include: A small table by the bed with tissues, wet wipes, a cup with a straw, a power bank, lip balm, hand cream and other everyday items, within reach; At home, the room's lights can be swapped for smart lights so you can adjust the lighting yourself. This is when smart home tech really shows its importance — open the curtains when you wake up, close them when the sun is too strong, set the lights to the brightness and colour temperature you find comfortable... and so on The environment within your line of sight affects your mood, so keep it as tidy and orderly as possible. After all, you're in this space 24 hours a day; the slightest untidiness gets noticed, and looking at it while being powerless to do anything feels bad. Conversely, if everything you see is a neat, elegant layout, your mood is much better. Besides the ceiling light, the room should have other light sources — ideally a desk lamp or floor lamp. Because a bedridden person lies flat, facing the ceiling light directly is very glaring. Dim the ceiling light and add soft light from the side, and it's much more comfortable. One or two smart bulbs greatly boost your happiness. Keep a regular routine even in bed. Try to keep breakfast, lunch and dinner at fixed times, and agree on when to switch the lights on and off morning and night. This avoids bodily changes caused by a disrupted body clock. Since you're already bedridden, the rest of your bodily functions need looking after all the more. About Me It really doesn't hurt much — hugs to everyone who's been hugging me. This is my "lying flat" pose. Hahaha, some people are curious how I type when I'm bedridden — look, this is how I type. My attitude and mood have stayed firmly on point. On the day of the injury, in the emergency room, while they disinfected my palms full of wounds, it hurt so much that I loudly recited texts from my middle-school Chinese lessons to distract myself... From "When Heaven is about to confer a great task upon a person, it first tries their mind with suffering, toils their sinews and bones, and leaves them in want" to "A mountain need not be high; it is renowned if an immortal dwells there" to "The waters of the Yellow River come down from the sky, rushing to the sea, never to return" and on to "I have a dream" — a whole medley of poetry, and the entire emergency room was filled with laughter... Seeing me like this, you can all rest assured 😁. But for all my friends' care and support during this time, a simple "thank you" can't express the solemn gratitude in my heart... Life has given me so many gifts, and this time it let me escape disaster once again. At the same time, heaven has given me time to lie down properly, not to be busy, but to take a good look at the people around me who love me — you. Every message and every bit of support from you makes me feel like a lucky one wrapped in love. You make me feel that this world is so worth it. I'll rest and recover well, and be up and bouncing around again soon!

At 8:10 PM on 7 January 2024, just before the climbing gym closed, determined to climb the route I'd been working on all day from start to finish, I fell off the wall because of my own stupid mistake. Later the gym manager said someone had once ruptured their internal organs this way, and a friend said a friend of theirs had hit their head and simply died... Thinking about it like that, it's truly frightening in hindsight. Out of countless possibilities, I only fractured my L3 vertebra — I was really lucky. I could choose not to have surgery and just rest in bed for a few months. Along the way I've had a few reflections and lessons. While the fright is still fresh, I'm writing them down as a reminder to the people around me: Climbing is a dangerous sport. Never get careless just because you're familiar with it; always keep a sense of respect for it. When you love a sport and do it often, the odds of a low-probability event happening go up dramatically. Staying alert all the time is extremely hard. Safety needs systems to protect it, and those systems must be followed. At the time, I wasn't careless or cocky; my whole body and mind were on the technical moves, and I completely forgot the safety rules. When climbing, you must have a spotter beside you, or an experienced partner. After an injury, do not move yourself! Do not move yourself! Do not move yourself! Call an ambulance (120) immediately. After an injury, don't eat anything, and don't drink water either, because you don't know whether your internal organs are damaged. Stay calm and look after yourself. While waiting for the ambulance, I asked people to help me change out of my climbing shoes, cover me with my down jacket, put on a heat pack, and I put on a mask. These all turned out to be very useful: in the ER you have to wait, and it's very cold if you're not wearing enough; the friend who took me to the hospital didn't wear a mask and caught a cold instead. If your head is clear, think ahead about where you're injured and what needs to be checked. The ER is chaotic — the doctor even forgot to disinfect the wound on my hand. You have to ask for these things yourself. There's one more thing... and it's what I've reflected on most deeply this time: Tell the people who love you right away. When it happened, I didn't tell my family. My mum only found out the next day. It hurt her a lot. Why didn't I tell her? First, I was afraid she'd worry; the diagnosis wasn't out yet, and I didn't want her to be frightened. Second, I thought I could handle it myself — her rushing back from out of town wouldn't change how it was handled or how it turned out, so why put her through that at night. Third, I was also really afraid of getting told off. But looking back, what if my situation had been more critical and I'd lost the ability to make my own decisions? Who would have told her then? Given my condition, I really should have been kept in hospital for observation in case of internal bleeding overnight. But the ER doctor didn't support that, so I went home that same day. If my family had been there, maybe they could have pushed for a better plan for admission. Why do I want to stress this point in particular as a lesson? Looking back, my brain no longer had the capacity to think through these possibilities; I made the decision on instinct, because instinctively I didn't want her to worry. On reflection, that was bad for her and for me. Hurting each other because of love is the most melodramatic thing in the world. So next time, telling my family right away should be the default. Trust the people you love — and besides, facing things together is the whole point of being a family. Shutting them out at the very start is also a kind of emotional hurt. Of course, I hope there won't be a next time.

Looking back through my diaries and notes, the painful moments of this year gave me the most. 1. Routine is sooo important. It helps not only with building habits but also with an inner sense of order. With order inside, it becomes easier to let go of some things in order to gain others. If you travel for work a lot, keep yourself steady in terms of time. Find a few anchors — when you go to sleep and wake up, time for reading and journaling, blank time for yourself, and so on. 2. First solve the right problem; only then solve the problem right. There are too many problems; grabbing the main ones, the priority ones, is the key to not getting life's big direction wrong. 3. "Compromise" is a great way to solve problems. 4. Shape your era instead of being shaped by it; don't be just a fleck of spray on the wave of the times. 5. You progress fast only when you have a goal. Whatever the goal, give yourself one that's hard to reach. Even writing a BP helps you absorb a book more efficiently and more deeply. 6. "A man who lives more seriously inside will also begin to live more simply outside." — True Nobility , Hemingway 7. Buffett and Munger lived very regular lives, but that didn't stop them from having brilliant, rich lives. 8. On negotiation - What makes a negotiation succeed may not be technique but strength — sheer power beats a hundred tricks. - Prepare thoroughly; having some lines of thinking and templates ready always helps. - I'm a negotiator who softens easily; I need to think clearly about my walk-away price. 9. On public speaking - Don't speak unprepared - For specific occasions, prepare some speech templates or frameworks - Find your own style - Always try humour 10. Everyone's life is a narrative of their own. If the "facts" others see differ from yours, don't be surprised, and don't force it. 11. The gap between knowing and doing really is that vast. 12. On communication - It's not about making the other person think I'm great, but about making them feel great about themselves. - When discussing a complex issue with someone, it's best to begin by reaching consensus on what the words mean. Take the definition of "taking care of the family" — the differences in it are enough to make us approach all communication with awe. 13. I really love this passage, for no particular reason; it feels like a portrait of the state of my life: In the best times of my life, I always want to clear some space in my heart, and then clear some more. There I would shovel away the snow, I would lift the sagging sky a little higher, and there is an overflowing sea there too, and I would let the seawater spill over — the fish would come to rescue me — the seawater floods the dense forest, and deep in the forest I would hunt a troop of new monkeys. Everything is so vivid, only the space is never big enough, yet I have never asked: what is this space for. I have no answer to: why; I can only keep, keep doing this, until I am utterly exhausted. Only by doing this does my life have value. — The Human Province , Canetti, 1942 p8 14. A person needs a bit of a "rebellious spirit"; throw off "should" thinking and you can be freer. Step outside the box and you'll find the world outside has far fewer obstacles. 15. "My problem is that I am not rational and I am extremely prone to drowning in randomness and suffering emotional torture as a result. I am aware of my need to ruminate on park benches and in cafés away from information, but I can only do so if it is taken away from me. My sole advantage in life is that I know some of my weaknesses, mainly that I am unable to tame my emotions about news and keep a clear head. Silence is much better." — Fooled by Randomness That's right: the longer I live, the more I understand that I'm as ordinary as a person can be, forever unable to overcome my irrationality and flaws. 16. Stay away from toxic people, no matter how attractive they seem. 17. "Scarcity" really does make people dumber. No time, no money, no room to manoeuvre — all of these are "scarcity." Try not to let yourself fall into scarcity; that's how you have more chances. 18. Always have something useful in hand. When Professor Zhang Shoucheng was a child and an ad break came on while he was watching TV, he would pick up a book and read for a bit. 19. On choosing hotels: in every case, choose the one that saves the most time — give yourself the most rest; among equally close options, choose the cheapest chain hotel. 20. On getting around: within 20 minutes, if you can bike or walk, don't take a car; if you can take a taxi, don't drive. 21. The top leader of a company must have a "founder's spirit," and one of a founder's most important qualities is "unwavering resolve."

This picture has always been in my heart; I give it to all my friends. Reading isn't only mental training, isn't only endless fun, isn't only a way to connect the hidden links between different things... Reading is like a journey lingering through the world: it lets the mind expand without limit. One interest gives birth to countless interests, one question leads to countless questions, ceaselessly, endlessly. Reading is also a good remedy for keeping inner calm. It's like a gentle lover: if you don't seek him out, there's no pressure; if you do, there's a rich inner world to explore. We are born into civilisation, and civilisation makes us a promise: A better, saner, kinder self is waiting for me further along in life, and I will surely find a way to reach her. "Reading" is the cheapest, most accessible and richest of those paths. There are too many books I could recommend, and these are all far too wonderful — yet this list doesn't capture even one per cent of how brilliant they are. The problem is mine: most of what I've "eaten" gets used up fending off the trivia of daily life. The rest is too bloated and badly digested; it just piles up in my stomach and won't come out, so I always seem to fall flat. All I can do is keep reminding myself that "perfect is the enemy of done" — writing it is better than not writing it. 1. The Road to Serfdom Friedrich August von Hayek (UK). This book is so good there's nothing more to say. Obscurantism tries to make us believe that everything we have done was either wise or unavoidable. We shall not grow wiser before we learn that much that we have done was very foolish. Working through this book is both a challenge and a pleasure for the intellect. Starting with this book, I fell in love with brain-burning doorstoppers. 2. Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much Sendhil Mullainathan & Eldar Shafir (US) Defining "scarcity" as a psychological problem rather than a resource problem is a wonderful and profound perspective. Scarcity captures a person's mind, making them so focused on what is scarce that they lose their normal judgement, which makes the scarcity worse still. So what's truly frightening isn't the scarcity of resources, but the scarcity mindset that captures our minds. That conclusion is a warning that will serve you for life. 3. The 13+1 System: Building a Continuously Healthy Organisation Huang Xu (China). This is a very easy-to-use practical handbook that makes it fairly easy to get started on "mission, vision, values, strategy, three-year plan..." all the way through to implementation. Following along page by page is a great way to read it. Once you've survived, you can afford the luxury of thinking about these questions. 4. Meditations Marcus Aurelius (Ancient Rome) "Every moment think steadily as a Roman and a man to do what thou hast in hand with perfect and simple dignity, and feeling of affection, and freedom, and justice." I first read this book at university. Rereading it this year, I was still deeply shaken. Read it at any time, read any passage, and it always gives you strength. 5. Bygone Days in Nehe Huang Rong (China). If you want to wash your soul clean with tears, read this book! Justice and love are the eternal heroism. 6. Excellent Advice for Living Kevin Kelly (US) Flip through it anytime, anywhere, and your life benefits immediately. It truly lives up to "opening a book always brings some benefit." 7. Chip War Chris Miller (US). Reading this book, you see how the tides of an era shaped the coastline. There's so much detail: even though we're all familiar with the story of chips, only by going back to the scene of history can you understand the undercurrents surging through it and history's true face. 8. The World of Yesterday Stefan Zweig (Austria). Beyond the understanding of history, Zweig's prose is a pure sensory pleasure. Through his pen, I came to know Europeans anew, and to know a group's will to live. 9. Fooled by Randomness Nassim Nicholas Taleb (US). The way the world works at random is sometimes called "fate." Only when life's randomness is laid out before us do we understand how easily we are fooled, and only then can we understand what "better to prepare than to predict" means. In this era, that is especially important. Remember this deeply: no matter how sophisticated our choices, how good we are at dominating the odds, randomness will have the last word. All we have left is our dignity. When bad luck strikes, emphasise the elegance of your personal conduct; we should show that, whatever the circumstances, we know "how to survive." 10. Traditional Government in Imperial China Qian Mu (China). Institutions must be matched by people. This book shows us how people and institutions intertwine, shape each other, and drive history forward. As for institutions, there must be a corresponding moral will and devotion of loyalty poured into them.

First, the overall picture How the Flags 🚩 I planted at the start of 2023 turned out 1. Get up early and read on 300+ days ✅ 311 days 2. Hit my exercise target on 300+ days (10,000 steps / heart rate up to 170 / 300+ calories burned in one session) ⭕️ Not tracked Around 100 times 3. Keep a diary on 300+ days ⭕️ 191 times 4. Plan on 300+ days ⭕️ 58 times 5. Sleep a full 7.5 hours on 300+ days ⭕️ 85 times 6. Write 52+ high-quality WeChat posts ⭕️ 27 posts 7. Read 50+ books ✅ 51 books 8. Listen to Dedao for 144+ minutes a day (details below) ⭕️ Daily average 70 minutes (at 1.75–2x speed) 9. In 2023 I completed one "off-the-books" task: levelled up my climbing 🧗 — I can now touch V4. Diary: roughly 130,000 characters My Dedao stats By comparison, the completion rate on the Dedao study list I drew up for myself is too painful to look at. Ha, how pitiful — I finished hardly any of it. When it comes to learning, I follow my whims more and more, and I don't know whether to be happy that my "curiosity has finally gone through the roof," or worried about my "stress-free slackness." Compared with 2022, I set quite a few fewer flags in 2023, but the sense of reward didn't drop. First, because the intensity of individual items like reading went up by 30%; second, as HBS teaches — too many metrics on a balanced scorecard blur the strategy; most of the time, LESS is MORE. Honestly, I like my 2023 flags better: more focused, and with higher leverage. Reflecting on what I did and didn't complete, a few thoughts: Routine is very, very important. The only two targets I hit were both tied to my "early-morning check-in"; a fixed time and a fixed action are absolutely key to building habits and getting things done. One post a week is easier to manage than 52 posts a year. Every bit of progress needs to be internalised and embedded into every day, every hour and every week of life. Remember the motto I love: what counts is persistence — why rise at the third watch and sleep at the fifth? Nothing is less useful than one day in the sun and ten in the cold. Optimising time management takes method. In my diary on January 7, 2023, I wrote: "Two big ways to save time: subtract, and combine." Subtract: cut entertainment, cut pointless socialising, cut the photography hobby, cut binge-watching, cut shopping, cut the beauty salon too... Try imagining the last day of your life and you'll see what you can't let go of and what doesn't matter. Then decisively cut the "second-tier" things. Combine: listen to Dedao while washing up and walking; exercise together when meeting friends; put on a face mask before writing; read while stretching... and so on. With work, exercise, and time with family and friends on top, how could there ever be enough time? It has to be combined with other time — so I've basically stopped driving and listen to books on the road; driving is distracting and not very safe anyway. This year I put both of these into practice, and they helped a lot. When it comes to learning, I follow my whims more and more. I don't know whether to be happy that my "curiosity has finally gone through the roof," or worried about my "stress-free slackness." Sleep always gets sacrificed and needs special attention. It takes a herculean effort not to sacrifice the most important things in life, like sleep, like family. Setting targets for them keeps us from going off track. Review your goals regularly. If I'd reviewed my Dedao list earlier, I'd have done much better. Every year more of my flags fall than stay standing, but that's all right. It reminds me of a line a French winery wrote in a bad-weather year: The weather made the grapes sour; let this glass toast the imperfections of the year.

What affects a negotiation — - A sense of urgency - A friendly relationship between the two sides - In an unclear negotiation, neither side knows what a good deal looks like - Gender differences - Differences in status and rank … 1. Preparing for the negotiation BATNA: the best alternative Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement — the best alternative is what else is possible if the negotiation falls through. Your BATNA doesn't depend on what counts as fair, what you've paid for something, or what you think you can get out of the negotiation; it is simply your fallback if there's "no deal". Consider every alternative and pick the best one — that is your BATNA. Identify your "no deal" alternative in advance. Always have a BATNA. RV: Reservation Value This is the worst deal you're willing to accept. A seller's RV should be above their BATNA; for a buyer it's the reverse. This is my "walk-away price". Guard against information asymmetry Listen — pay very close attention to listening. Negotiation is about exchanging information; sometimes the other side is happy to share, sometimes not. Ask directly. The more direct you are, the harder it is for the other side to hide; direct questions are hard not to answer. Pay close attention when they don't answer, and have a plan ready for when they don't. Adapt. Adjust on the fly as information is revealed, changing your plan and expectations. If… then… Form expectations about your negotiating partner's BATNA and RV Calculate the ZOPA, the Zone of Possible Agreement The zone of possible agreement is the set of deals every party is willing to accept, lying between the buyer's and the seller's RVs. 2. Improving: strategies for managing information The more information you have, the stronger your position, so you need a clear strategy for managing it. Listen — the more you talk, the harder it is to listen. Ask questions: reasonable questions, sharp questions, questions nobody can dodge. Respond to new information and put forward new proposals. What if the other side asks something I don't want to answer? Prepare in advance: what questions might they ask? How will I respond? Thinking through your answers ahead of time helps you hold your "moral bottom line" and not lie. 3. Improving: setting the frame of the negotiation 1. Set a goal: without a goal, it's too easy to give in as soon as the price beats your BATNA. 2. Frame the negotiation's boundaries for others The famous story from Roosevelt's campaign The anchoring effect: when we name a price, the other side will adjust, but not stray too far from the anchor. Anchoring information is extremely powerful — for example, fair market value or the first offer you hear. Statistics show that the higher the opening offer, the higher the final price. 3. When should you make the first offer? When you have an information advantage. If the other side is a big industry player, you may not have that advantage, and it's best to wait a little. If prices are moving against me, make the first offer; if they're moving in my favour, wait. 4. Justify your offer — give a reason 5. Consider goodwill — after all, many negotiations aren't one-off deals. 4. Reacting to the first offer If you're surprised by the first offer and find it too aggressive or too generous… you can ask further questions, or haggle hard and watch their reaction to probe their real price. 5. Two different negotiation strategies Value-claiming strategy Guard information strictly Make firm demands Value-creating strategy Communicate clearly Be creative and flexible Whichever kind of negotiator you are, that's the strategy to choose. Being well prepared makes it easier to become who you want to be.

To make it easier to think, I've jotted down the key points in short phrases rather than long paragraphs. There are a few questions here that deserve careful thought: 1. Who is your real customer? Allocate resources to the customer — this is the supreme principle. McDonald's first customers were property developers; later they were consumers. Visa's customers were regional banks; Mastercard's were global banks. Harvard Business School's customers are not the students but faculty and staff around the world. Does every one of your partners understand what the real customer values? For example, P&G executives go shopping with customers. 2. Five ways to organise to create the most value for customers Low-price strategy Walmart: the vast majority of resources go to purchasing, marketing and merchandising — lowest price, lowest cost — while store managers have very few resources and can't adjust the shelves, lighting or air conditioning. Local value creation Push resources down to the regional level so they can create value for local customers. Restaurant chains are an example: different regions want different desserts and spices. Global excellence standards GE / L'Oréal: organised by business unit, so wherever they are, customers get the best core product. Dedicated service relationships IBM, Sibal and other technology companies have many different types of customers across different markets. Specialist expertise: Google, hospitals, university R&D departments: R&D gets the most resources, and at Google R&D and the market-facing side are kept separate. Can you pursue two strategies at once? It depends on the industry. If yours is a low-price industry and you spread your strategy thin, someone will come in, focus purely on low prices and steal your customers. Ask yourself: have you minimised the resources going to people who don't serve the main customer? Investor relations, HR, community affairs… here, "just enough" is fine. Frugality frees up resources for customers. Seen this way, my company scores pretty low… 3. Setting KPIs If you measure everything, you end up with an endless list of metrics. You have to find the metrics for the most critical outcomes. How do you find them? How do you set them? Step 1 From a "competitive strategy" perspective, you need to look ahead. How? Imagine failure: five years from now your strategy has failed, your best people have left and your customers are gone — on which dimensions did you fail? For different companies, it might be… - not staying at the technological frontier, not keeping up with digitalisation; - land costs too high, over-expansion, too much debt, political turmoil - losing distributors, too little R&D, no successors for frontline staff … Step 2 Build metrics and performance accountability: who executes and follows up? Is it tied to rewards? What are the consequences? Scoring myself, I still come out very low. 4. Controlling strategic risk Risk usually comes from people, and people are prone to mistakes when facing "pressure + opportunity". To avoid people rationalising "mistakes", set clear boundaries that remove the ability to rationalise, like the Ten Commandments in the Bible. Ask yourself: does everyone in the company know which behaviours are forbidden? - Use a code of business conduct to constrain ethical behaviour; - Protect goodwill by prohibiting certain actions Stay tight on strategic priorities by being clear about which opportunities to avoid. Say no to 100 good ideas that fall outside your strategic priorities. Have this kind of strategic discipline — we will not pursue an opportunity unless it meets these conditions: - Top 1 or 2 in market ranking - 15% average annual growth - Revenue greater than… - Able to command a price premium and competitive advantage - Standardised product - A clear exit strategy … 5. Getting the team to think like winners Set internal and external benchmarks Revenue growth Improved margins / profits Cost savings Improved cash flow Customer acquisition Customer satisfaction Cross-selling Individual rankings Department rankings Encourage cross-departmental innovation Make "span of accountability" "span of control". Make people responsible for things beyond what they control — more responsibility with fewer resources — and encourage an entrepreneurial spirit in your partners. An entrepreneur is: an individual who pursues opportunity regardless of the resources they currently control. Allocate costs. Get teams to pay attention to the costs other departments generate. Build cross-functional teams Matrix accountability That said, there's one thing we need to remember: Doing all of the above is like going to a restaurant and ordering every dish on the menu! What matters is asking the right questions, and avoiding lists of: - too many customers - too many metrics - too many values … Force yourself to make hard choices. I really didn't know how to make strategy before. Now I've caught a tiny glimpse of how it's done — the rest is practice.
Assessing an Organization's Capabilities: Resources, Processes, Priorities

The most crucial thing in innovation is trial and error. You need enough resources to experiment cheaply, and keep at it until something works. Let's keep looking at "disruptive innovation" from an organizational angle. The case here is Nypro. The background: Nypro wanted to adopt an innovative molding technology. It made mold changes in the production process much easier and gave far more capacity for flexible manufacturing — short cycles, small batches — though it certainly wasn't as precise as the old technology. At this point Nypro faced three options: 1. Build a factory that uses only the new technology, overseen personally by the CEO; 2. Install 2–3 of the new machines in each of its 21 existing factories around the world; 3. Put it into one of the factories, focus on making it succeed there, then replicate it in the others. On the organizational question of innovation: Many companies' innovations fail not because of some fatal technical flaw, nor because no market exists yet. They fail because the innovative business wasn't entrusted to a fitting organization. The very DNA that made an organization successful may be exactly what blocks its path to innovation. I really like the RPP model. It helps you understand what an organization is, what it can do and what it can't — and, more importantly, when a new technology or new business comes in, it lets us re-examine where in the organization the "existing capabilities" and the "disabilities" lie. When we talk about "capabilities," we can break them down into three elements: Resources Processes Priorities That's the RPP model. Resources: the most tangible — people, equipment, technology, product designs, brands, information, cash, even relationships with suppliers, distributors and customers. Resources are visible and flexible; they can usually be measured, hired, bought, sold and transferred across organizations. Processes: an organization creates value by transforming inputs of resources into products and services of greater worth. The patterns of interaction, coordination, communication and decision-making it goes through along the way are its processes — including how it develops and manufactures, and the methods it uses for procurement, market research, developing employees, allocating resources and so on. Some processes are "formal": clearly defined, codified and documented. Others are "informal": routines or ways of working that have formed over time, some of which have even become part of the organization's culture. Processes emerge in response to specific recurring tasks. They are set up to help employees perform recurring tasks consistently and well, time after time, without intensive managerial oversight. In organizations whose targets shift, this tends to work well. But in a flexible, fast-changing business, a process that is effective for one task can become an obstacle to another. When analysing whether a process is a capability or a disability, what matters most is not the obvious value-adding processes in logistics, development, manufacturing and service, but the underlying processes that support investment decisions: the habitual ways market research is done, how analysis is translated into financial projections, how plans and budgets are negotiated, how that data is delivered, the types of goals management is held accountable for, KPIs and so on. An organization's most serious disabilities in building disruptive growth businesses are most likely to come from these processes. Whether a process is a capability or a disability for a new business is hard to judge. But one question you can ask is: has this organization faced a similar task before? If it has handled this kind of business repeatedly, it has very likely formed a particular process. That's when you need to take care to build a more suitable process, or managers will instinctively follow the old one. Priorities: team members at every level have a ranking of priorities. Management decides how to allocate funds to new products, services and processes; salespeople decide which customers to call, which products to push and which to de-emphasise; engineers choosing design options and production schedulers sequencing orders all work from an order of priorities. Let members at every level make priority decisions autonomously, in line with the company's business and profit model. Every member must prioritise "the things that help the company make money the way it should and ensure it survives and thrives." Resources and processes tend to define what a company "can do," while priorities define what an organization "cannot do." For example, if a company's overhead structure requires it to achieve 40% gross margins, then its decision rule is that no decision below a 40% gross margin can be proposed or approved — vs. another company whose business model has a different cost structure, which might pursue that same decision urgently and as a priority. A successful company's priorities can shift along two dimensions: Rising gross margins. As companies upgrade their products and services to compete in higher-end markets, they tend to add overhead, so margins that once looked attractive may no longer appeal. What a company can put at the top of its priorities may change as it moves upmarket. Declining appeal of small opportunities. As successful companies grow larger, they need bigger absolute revenue gains to sustain the same high growth rate. So they cannot deploy resources against markets that are very small today but will be very large tomorrow — their already-changed priorities don't allow it. This is also why mergers and acquisitions are so hard. After two already-huge companies merge, they think they've saved costs and strengthened their resources, but what the resulting company should treat as its priorities requires enormous care. Their organizations are so vast that they often have no appetite for small opportunities. Unless it keeps dividing itself into smaller units, sheer size becomes a very real disability. Startups should pay attention to RPP too In the early stage, a company relies mainly on resources: a few key people joining or leaving, the success of a patented technology and so on. Over time, organizational capability migrates towards processes and priorities. As people successfully tackle recurring tasks together, processes get defined; as the business model succeeds, it becomes clear which businesses should be given the highest importance. Many startup teams lose their shine after their initial success, and one very important reason is that the original resource — the founding team — failed to establish the processes and priorities that would keep the company's growth momentum going. If the centre of gravity of the original innovative capability successfully shifts from R to PP, then who is assigned to which project starts to matter less. The classic example is McKinsey: roughly as many people join each year as leave, yet that doesn't stop them delivering high-quality work. That is a textbook case of not depending on resources. The initial Ps are validated by being right time after time. Once members of an organization adopt certain PPs as a matter of course, without needing rational judgement, those PPs become the company's culture. As a company grows from a handful of employees to hundreds and thousands, culture lets members act autonomously while staying aligned on goals. When the most powerful factor defining an organization's capabilities has moved from resources to processes and priorities, and finally into corporate culture, it also becomes extremely hard to change. The best innovation is creating new businesses while the company's mainstream business is still healthy, but that requires different processes and models. So while forming new processes and priorities, management also has to maintain the existing processes and priorities that make the core business succeed. This kind of ambidexterity is quite subtle and hard to master. An innovative business must have matching organizational processes. We can divide teams into four types: Functional teams: organizational boundaries are drawn around departments — finance, marketing, manufacturing, engineering and so on — divided by professional skill. Different functional departments work independently; once one department finishes its task, the work moves on to another. Lightweight teams: when one department might hinder or affect the timing, manner or process by which another department gets its work done, you need a lightweight team, because the people/departments involved in the project have predictable interdependencies. So you need a coordinating, lightweight project manager who shuttles across departments to make sure the work fits together in time and space. But the main work and responsibility stay within the departments. At meetings, each department can send a representative to make sure each department's independent work is on schedule and links up correctly. Many amoeba and matrix organizations are lightweight. Heavyweight teams: when a product's and process's architecture needs to change, unpredictable interdependencies arise — you can't clearly foresee and specify who needs to interact with whom — and resolving these problems often means sacrificing one department's interests in exchange for another's. That's when you need a heavyweight team. For example, optimizing the product architecture may require developing a new component and swapping out others. Every department with key influence on the project must send someone to join this team, and each member must not keep thinking about "representing" their department's interests; instead, everyone's goal is to jointly work out a better way to coordinate and optimize product performance, quality, cost, customer convenience and so on. All members must work in the same location and be led by a manager with significant clout — someone with a big-picture view who is able to make decisions beyond their own professional expertise. A heavyweight team is a tool for creating new processes and new ways of collaborating; lightweight and functional teams are tools for exploiting existing processes. However, once a product's and process's framework has been defined and the departments have been set up, keeping a heavyweight team creates a lot of unnecessary overhead. So heavyweight and lightweight teams may be temporary mechanisms, while autonomous teams may be a more lasting organizational form. Autonomous teams: when facing disruptive innovation, and the company's existing processes cannot rank it ahead of other investments, this is the type of team you need. What does autonomy mean? Not geographical location, nor ownership structure — a disruptive venture can be wholly owned by the parent company. The key to autonomy lies in processes and priorities: the freedom to create new processes and a new cost structure, so that it can be profitable even when making and selling its first products, and to be allowed to compete with sister divisions — even to cannibalise the existing market. No organizational unit can effectively accommodate two completely different cost structures or business models at the same time. When managers forcibly merge two units in the name of "saving costs," one or even both will be destroyed. When facing disruptive innovation, an organization needs to create a new organization with a new cost structure in order to develop "the capability to put innovation at the top of its priorities." In any case, we should remember: An organization cannot disrupt itself. Judging at which level of the organizational structure each project should be embedded is a question the CEO must think through when developing new businesses and new processes. Creating new capabilities? — Build or buy. On acquisitions Build-or-buy is usually about "resources": develop a component or buy it, develop a technology or license it, and so on. But "processes" can also be built or bought — take Toyota. Toyota regularly compiles manuals based on design problems it has solved. Every time it develops a new platform through a heavyweight team, it puts huge effort into codifying the knowledge of the architecture and interfaces, so that it doesn't need to set up heavyweight teams for subsequent product designs. A great deal of interaction information is recorded in "lessons learned" books, so that Toyota's approach turns one-off experience into processes. Some teams are always gaining experience but never build processes from it. Codifying experience into processes lets you earn compound interest on time. When acquiring, the question to ask is: What is the acquired company's core value? Resources or processes? If it's "resources," then integrating it into the parent makes a lot of sense: plug the acquired people, products, technology and customers into the parent's processes to leverage the parent's existing capabilities. If it's "processes," then the last thing it should do is fully integrate it into the parent. If processes and the profit model are the key, it's best to keep it independent and have the parent inject resources. On building When facing innovation and change, first determine whether you have the "resources" you need, and then you must think through the following questions independently: Are the work processes people in the organization are used to suited to solving the new problem? Will the organization's business model allow the innovation to be given priority? It's fine if the answer is "no" — understanding a problem is the most crucial step in solving it. In addition, When attempting innovation, the choice of customers is one of the key points of leverage. Strategy can be top-down and "deliberate," or bottom-up and "emergent"; an organization can formulate strategy through its resource allocation process.
The Innovator's Dilemma: U.S. Steel's Choice

For a company or industry in crisis, innovation is a bit like the difference between waiting to die and courting death. That's why you fix the roof while the sun is shining. "Prepare for danger in times of peace" is ancient wisdom — the kind of thing that can only be proven over a long span of time. Not long after we finished discussing the U.S. Steel case, the company announced it was being acquired, ending its life as a century-old steelmaker. Because business schools hold the copyright on their cases, I'm not sure how much information is appropriate to share. You can search "U.S. Steel" for more background and detail; roughly, here's the story: In December 2023, U.S. Steel (USS), once a giant of American steel manufacturing, was finally "sold off cheap" to a Japanese company for US$14.9 billion after a four-month bidding contest. This steelmaker was once a pillar of the American economy, with a 122-year history, and was once the largest and most valuable company in the world. At the start of the last century, the steel it produced helped the United States become a global economic superpower. It witnessed the rise of one American building after another, supplying steel for skyscrapers, dams and bridges, as well as for the cars and appliances American consumers dreamed of. Its competitive power was so great that it helped prompt the creation of American antitrust law, and it was the first company in the world whose market value passed US$1 billion. In 1943 the company had 340,000 employees in total; by last year, only 22,500 remained. And the valuation in this sale is less than 0.5% of Apple's. The company's decline is just a microcosm of the fall of American steel. In fact, the entire American steel industry today is little more than an empty shell, and not a single company makes it into the world's top ten steel producers. As for the reasons why, First, a lack of technological innovation. The company kept using technology from the 1940s. The American steel industry long relied on the traditional blast furnace–converter method of producing steel, neglecting the development of new technologies such as electric arc furnace steel and continuous casting and rolling, which led to high production costs, low quality and serious environmental pollution. Second, changes in market demand. The American steel industry depended mainly on demand from industries such as autos, construction and machinery, and in the late 20th century these industries all declined or transformed, reducing demand for steel. Third, intensifying international competition. The American steel industry faced fierce competition from Japan, Europe, China and other countries, whose steelmakers used more advanced technology, lower costs, higher quality and more flexible strategies, seizing market share from American steel. Finally, unfavourable policies and institutions. The American steel industry was affected by excessive government intervention, excessive union protection, excessively restrictive environmental regulation and other factors, leaving steelmakers with low operating efficiency, weak innovation capacity and poor adaptability. The Innovator's Dilemma identifies two different categories based on the environment of innovation: "sustaining innovation" and "disruptive innovation." In a "sustaining innovation" environment — when the competition is about making better products that can be sold at higher prices to attractive customers — we find that incumbents win almost every time. In a "disruptive innovation" environment — when the challenge is to commercialise a simple, convenient product and sell it at a lower price to new or unattractive customer segments — the upstarts often win. This is the phenomenon we so often see of successful companies being toppled. Of course, it also implies that for upstarts, the best way to beat the well-known players in an industry is to use a disruptive strategy. Just like U.S. Steel (USS), which gave up its market share bit by bit, steadily and gradually attacked from the thin-margin bottom by the mini-mills. Were they all just too stupid? No. When we dig into the case from back then, we can clearly see that traditional "sustaining innovators," when facing choices about innovation, "each had their own difficulties," and each had good reasons — it was rational choices that led them, step by step, to be disrupted. Imagine: when facing new technologies like "electric arc furnace steel and continuous casting and rolling," who would be in the room at a USS leadership meeting? The union, customers, sales reps, the finance team, shareholders. Would each of these roles want the new technology or the old one? The union: the old technology, because it keeps their jobs. Customers: the old technology, because they want good, stable products. Sales: the old technology, because they need to keep customers happy. Finance: the old technology, because the numbers look better on the statements — new technology has to be amortised, and profits take time. Shareholders: also the old technology, because they care more about the statements. Does the CEO want the new technology? Maybe yes. But who, at the negotiating table, will take on the risk of choosing to invest in new technology? This isn't an event; it's a process. Many big players look down on the meagre profits that new technology brings at first, ignore disruptive innovation, and choose to put their effort into sustaining innovation. If the decision-makers don't have to answer for the company's "hundred-year plan," then decline seems the most likely outcome. — Here, family businesses actually have something of an advantage. Sometimes strategy is about seeing how the battlefield is shifting. As one entrepreneur said during the discussion: "I can go without making money, but this technology must be invested in — that's how you lock the small competitors into the low end of the market." That kind of boldness got my heart racing a little. Anyway, let me jump to a conclusion: We should pursue "innovation" beyond what "rationality" alone would dictate. Rationality calculates and judges based on the "known," while innovation is full of unknowns — innovation is being vaguely right. Other truths that are just as right: "To love" is always better than "indifference" "To forgive" is always better than "holding a grudge" "To learn" is always better than "standing still" "Openness" is always better than "closedness"

This is a tool for how founders manage their companies, and the core takeaway is about how to "budget" your management energy. There are three things that need to be balanced: 1. Top-down direction vs. bottom-up creativity The side effect of order is less innovation. In management, how do you encourage innovation while running efficiently? 2. Unlimited opportunities vs. limited energy We have so many opportunities, and it seems we could achieve a lot. But there are only 50–60 hours in a week, and every hour has to be productive enough. 3. Self-interest vs. employees who contribute Everyone reacts differently in different situations. If an employee isn't performing well, look for problems in management first. How do people know their work contributes to the company's vision? They need clear goals, boundaries, wins, room for innovation and creativity, and to be competent at their jobs. What tools can help the team achieve these? — The four management systems Boundary systems: avoiding risk Belief systems: letting values drive growth Diagnostic control systems: using critical performance variables Interactive control systems: dealing with strategic uncertainty 1. Boundary systems Grey lists, codes of business conduct, codes of professional ethics and so on all exist to let the team know where the boundaries are. The most famous boundary system is the Ten Commandments in the Bible: The first commandment: You shall have no other gods. The second: You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor bow down to such images. The third: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. The fourth: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, and do no work. The fifth: Honor your father and your mother. The sixth: You shall not murder. The seventh: You shall not commit adultery. The eighth: You shall not steal. The ninth: You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. The tenth: You shall not covet your neighbor's house; nor your neighbor's wife, nor his servants, nor his ox or donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor's. This actually helps innovation, because if people get their knuckles rapped every time they try something new, they'll stop trying. If people know where the boundaries are, they can experiment with innovation within them. It's a kind of "guardrail." 2. Belief systems Core values — mission, credo, statements of purpose. A great example is "Johnson & Johnson's Credo." The J&J Credo was written in 1943, and looking back, it was remarkably forward-looking — it even covers ESG. Their values are alive, used every day. — To become a J&J supplier, you have to learn the J&J Credo; every rotating manager has to study the Credo together with their suppliers, to make sure the suppliers understand it. They often say the "Credo" is the foundation of everything they do. In an organization whose hierarchy is highly decentralized, this lets employees do the right thing on their own. "Reality isn't as good as we imagine, but we spend a lot of time on the Credo. Our actions have to reflect our values, our beliefs. We invest a lot in this, and we firmly believe that if employees understand the Credo, they will do the right thing." 3. Diagnostic control systems: critical performance variables, KPIs This system can help us… communicate business strategy and support clear goals, and keep senior management focused — with a target to aim at ‍ The "Balanced Scorecard" may be a fairly useful tool, but… There are many dimensions here, with lagging indicators and leading indicators, and we have to look at things from different perspectives, including but not limited to: The financial perspective: revenue, profit margin, gross margin… The internal business perspective: the ground we must take, the areas where we must achieve excellence. The customer perspective: how do customers see us? The innovation and learning perspective: can we keep innovating and creating value, and how? What matters is putting "strategy" at the very center; every metric serves the strategy. Some companies have only KPIs and no strategy. If you want to improve, you can follow this process: (1) communicate the business strategy with every department (2) set and support clear goals (3) make good use of managers' attention: it's an extremely scarce resource, so make good use of every day and every hour. If we get it right and connect "strategy" and "performance goals" very efficiently, we get the payoff — the company will run on autopilot and head in the direction we want. Otherwise, you'll find management effectiveness drops sharply. 4. Interactive control systems "Those below follow the example of those above" is a trait of human nature, and a very neutral phrase. The positive side is "the power of example"; the negative side is "what you say doesn't matter, only what you do." Everything about a company's boss, from their code of conduct to how they treat people, even their taste in clothes, invisibly influences the people below. Plant a seed, and the company's strategy takes shape. Every manager should pay enough attention to themselves and check whether their own behavior is consistent with their strategy. As for how to hear feedback from the front line, what matters is to keep asking the people at the very bottom: what needs adjusting? And to keep up with technological developments. Below is J&J's powerful profit-planning process. As the professor said in class, very few companies discuss their profit plans this frequently: Finally, all these tools look great, but does every company need to use all of them? I don't think so. Different strategic positions call for focusing on different metrics. At the end of class, the professor said, "It's just like raising kids." The boundary system is punishing them when they do something wrong; the belief system is telling them what the right way to do things is; the diagnostic system is their grades and achievements; the interactive system is the conversations you have when you chat together on weekends. He said, all in all… "We don't need McKinsey to tell us how to do it."

My biggest takeaway from this trip came from a classmate — a senior figure in business — who said that everything needs a model. So, while reviewing what I'd learned, I tried to use models wherever possible, and it really did help me understand the problems better. What Is a Model I still can't fully grasp the precise definition of a "model," but I've summed up a few of its characteristics: It can define certain elements in a business; It can precisely describe how those elements interact with each other; It helps people abstract business problems more effectively, so they can think more completely and better grasp the core problem and the key elements. The "Value Based Strategy" Model Willing To Pay (WTP): the highest price a customer is willing to pay; above this price, the customer walks away. WIlling To Sell (WTS): the lowest price a supplier is willing to accept; below this price, the supplier walks away. Price (P): the selling price Cost (C): the cost WTP-P = customer value C-WTS= supplier value Looks like a no-brainer, right? Let's look at two Harvard cases: Apple and Uber Case: Apple — Willingness to Pay (WTP) Apple, as the earliest personal computer to appear, very quickly became the most popular computer. When IBM came along, even though it was cheaper than Apple, was it bound to seize the market? Not necessarily — because at this point Value A = Value B: the customer value customers got from Apple was the same as what they got from IBM. Implication here is... being more expensive than others doesn't mean I don't offer higher "customer value." What really changed things was the rise of software. Apple's closed system was excellent, but a huge amount of software couldn't run on it. At this point "network effects" kicked in: the more people used IBM machines, the more popular they became ➡️ the more popular IBM became, the more software was developed for it. IBM's WTP kept rising, while on the other side Apple's WTP kept falling in the competition. Until one day, having lost its market share, Apple's revenue would no longer be enough to cover its operating costs. What brings you down can also lift you up — the later success of the iPod owed precisely to Jobs being forced to accept making iTunes work on Windows. Here's what he said... (it's really hilarious) "Over my dead body will Windows users get to use the iPod." Thankfully, the rest of Apple's senior team forced him to change his mind, and he finally gave in. iTunes and the iPod are very important "complementary products" — when one product's usage goes up, it greatly expands the use cases for the other. Think razors and blades, or cinemas and snack bars. So, with the iPhone's market share now falling steadily, will Apple be in trouble? The problem is how big the market share needs to be, it will be really hard to be small, and also, don't miss the next disruptive scenario and product. Case: Uber — Willingness to Sell (WTS) In this case, let's hold back and not consider the decisive role technology played. We'll focus on just two variables: WTP and WTS What did Uber bring passengers? Availability: hailing a cab used to be hard; now it's easier. Control: you know the exact time Convenience: getting a ride is more convenient Safety: before, I wouldn't dare let my kid get into a stranger's car Easier payment More transparent prices and room to choose: a clean car, a luxury car, a cheap car But Uber isn't always cheaper than a taxi ➡️ WTP went up. What did Uber bring drivers? A lower barrier to entry Flexible hours You can do it part-time Drivers' safety is better assured It added a social element There's a heat map, so drivers have more productive time and the power to choose passengers But Uber drivers earn less than taxi drivers ➡️ WTS went down. Implication here is... it isn't only "good product, high cost" — we can equally make "good product, low cost." The questions to ask yourself are: Do I do sth. to make a product better? Higher the WTP. Do I do sth. to make a job a better job? Lower the WTS. There's also a "Selection Effect" (two-way selection) here. If I lower WTS, the people who come have been reverse-selected — we see that many Uber drivers are highly educated people and women. A more extreme and famous example is Harvard Business School itself, where faculty and staff earn US$20,000–30,000 less than the market average. This makes it easier to attract people whose values align — at HBS, people who don't love teaching don't stay. Strategy comes in two steps: Step one, create value; Step two, ask why I can do what others can't. Ask whether you've created a new WTP or a new WTS. Pursue creating a value axis different from everyone else's. For example, ZARA and Raksul.

Sorting Out My Travel Packing List

I've just wrapped up a two-month trip in the US, and discovered that at least 1/3 of the things in my suitcase went almost entirely unused — I honestly can't remember why I packed them in the first place. On past trips, I kept carrying lots of unnecessary things with me, and never once reflected on it. I'm always finding that I need this, need that. Could I think about it the other way round? Which items do I not need at all? I'll aim to pick out one thing I no longer need to bring after every trip. The illustrations were made by AI, in a Matisse style hahahaha. "Cut Wherever Possible" [Clothing] Formal wear Half of the formal wear I brought was never worn at all. From now on I'll only bring one piece dresses: no need to coordinate, they don't take much space, and three at most. Socks Every time there are some I never wore, because I wash them as I go. 3 pairs each of long and short is plenty. Silk scarves and shawls Every dress has its own matching shawl, and whenever there's spare room I fill it with these. I should bring just one that goes with everything. Shoes Onitsuka Tiger white sneakers go with almost every dress but aren't for exercise; this time I found On's white sneakers can do both. For short trips wear just one pair; for long trips bring one spare. Activewear of the same type Activewear is practically my everyday clothing, but no more than two pieces of the same type. [Toiletries] Face masks At home I never do face masks, so where did the confidence come from to pack enough for a mask every day of the trip? One jar of mask a month is plenty. Too much sunscreen Same as the masks: I normally don't wear it, so I have no idea why I needed to carry three bottles of sunscreen to the US. Too many skincare products Skip the serum and toner; a face cream is enough. [Electronics] The most ridiculous item: this time I brought along a humidifier fan! 😂 Solar charging panel Last time I even brought a satellite phone for driving Highway 1. How little faith I had in the survival conditions in America The little speaker is one I'm a bit torn on. A good speaker really is a lot of enjoyment and great for driving, but do I really care that much about enjoyment? I can leave it behind. Things I absolutely must not buy again T-shirts, especially all kinds of souvenir T-shirts. Hats, especially all kinds of souvenir hats. All kinds of souvenirs - the best souvenirs are photos, videos, travel writing, and the new friends I've made. Little sources of happiness I can't skimp on Swimsuit, climbing shoes. Sun-protection face masks: essential and easy to lose, so bring at least 3. Hats: one baseball cap and one sun hat. All-in-one power bank: no need to bring plugs + backup cables. Massage gun: can bring, but leave the case behind. Water bottle: a collapsible one. I don't need it in China but do when abroad, so it can have this space quota. Supplements: in small bottles, packed for the number of days planned, no big jars. Dietary fiber: my newest favorite is Whole Psyllium Husks, much less sugar than All Bran, and much smaller than bringing cereal; microwave miracle gadget: Potato Express, for freshly steamed sweet potatoes anytime Burning Man Prep List Based on my experience at Burning Man this time, here's a very "personalized" list, not necessarily right for everyone. Gifts that are truly my own, from the heart: the Burning Man spirit of gifting A hands-free umbrella: the king of physical sun protection, worn on the body; otherwise I didn't dare go out biking during the day. Sun and wind goggles, have several ready for different weather and times of day: Daytime goggles: fully sealed, consider ski goggles, to protect your eyes; Daytime sunglasses: for when there's no wind, max comfort; Nighttime goggles: clear, maybe ones that light up. Tight-fitting fancy clothes: fits the Burning Man style, protects from the sun, and keeps you warm at night. Wigs: you truly don't need to wash your hair, and they keep out wind and sand. Good-looking nighttime decorations A blanket to carry around, or even clothes you can wrap up and sleep in: biking around the Playa is a wonderful thing, and falling asleep wherever you are when you're tired is a free thing, but it's cold at 3 a.m., so you need something thick to wear. A basket on the bike: for holding the blanket and clothes. A small backpack: I hope to keep using this year's backpack next year; Food: bring less! Don't overdo it! Water: big bottles, at least 3L a day, for cooking as well as drinking. Wet wipes: bring plenty, for wiping cookware, dishes and everything else, and not the kind with detergent. Have two cups on you: a sealed one to carry water (in the desert you must drink plenty of water!), and a collapsible one for handy "alms-gathering." A collapsible bowl: carry it for handy "alms-gathering." Several times I came across ramen, miso soup and all sorts of tasty things, and asking people to give you a disposable bowl is awkward. Face masks, a light body lotion. Get your nails done: my nails really did get too dirty, and a manicure to cover them up makes you feel much better.
