🎼 First, a quick plug for our orchestra: we're calling on friends to come learn music with us and form a band. Location: Shanghai. Requirements: an interesting soul. Time: able to attend class weekly or every other week, for 2 months. Tuition: not expensive. Content: Professor Zhou Haihong will personally teach the key sessions, a whole series on music appreciation, from reading staff notation to conducting. The rest of the time, under a teacher's guidance, everyone will learn to play a mystery instrument. Feel free to DM me if you're interested~ On June 17, Professor Haihong taught us "Lesson 05: Conducting Along with the Music and Appreciating Music Through the Score." To enjoy music under the guidance of a music appreciation expert this witty, funny and passionate about education is a once-in-a-lifetime experience. The best part was the nonstop stream of brilliant lines. I never expected a music appreciation class would have me taking notes at lightning speed~ Here's what I'd like to share with you: Why we should enjoy music: Life should be built up from layer upon layer of all kinds of experiences. After a night of cards and drinking, people are listless; people who have just enjoyed art have eyes that shine and lives full of vitality. If you have the means to live this way, don't miss out. Why people should listen to the classics The classics never go out of date, because the classics are the ceiling of human wisdom. The difference between gentle and harsh in music: A fast attack sounds harsh, e.g.: "Can I take the day off?" — "No." A slow attack sounds gentle, e.g.: "Can I take the day off?" — "Why's that? Ah, maybe let's not?" Rhythmic pulse: an even beat with a cycle of strong and weak. Music without a strong-weak pulse is rigid music! Even-numbered meters: a swinging motion Odd-numbered meters: a circling motion. Pitch and crescendo Rising with a crescendo means positivity and passion Rising with a diminuendo means parting Don't inflict "educational harm" on children Learn a technique, end up hating an art. Punish hard so they never make the mistake again, and you destroy their entire motivation to learn. I don't yet know what education can give a child, but at the very least it shouldn't do harm. People have an innate, fundamental capacity for experience Look forward to, and listen for, children's expressive ability in music "Music: what is the number one foundation of talent? It's 'relaxation.' So much of our education makes children tense. A great many Chinese kids can't take off, precisely because they're tense; there's a whole range of technique that could have developed, but it can't because of the tension." So having children practice piano by holding an imaginary egg in their hand is wrong. I started with the egg too. That path is wrong. Even though I did learn the piano, that doesn't mean it's the path you have to take. 1353 piano practice: the experiential order of knowledge and the psychological order in which knowledge is built don't line up. What exactly is the point of children learning an instrument? The purpose of learning an instrument is to come to love music through the instrument, to love art through music, and to love life through art. Should children take grading exams? Today children are taught instruments by the professional standards of professional musicians: the hand position must be exactly right, and so on. But in sports like swimming, tennis or ping-pong, who demands that their own form be textbook perfect? If your form isn't standard, does that mean you can't play, can't enjoy it? A performing musician needs to be someone with an almost religious reverence for every single note. People who play the piano face one kind of despair: the despair of attention. Giving every note feeling and attention takes enormous willpower. Expressing love Focused gaze: look at them intently, for more than 8 seconds Closeness (physical proximity): cats and dogs both know that if you come close, it means you like them Speaking softly and gently: a slow attack Teasing and play: when repairing a relationship, just talk about play. Physical touch: loving strokes and hugs These five steps are what Professor Haihong promotes and practices as the "Five-Step Gradual Method for Repairing Parent-Child Relationships," and the order can't be reversed. Reportedly, when he teaches it to students for finding a partner, it works every time! 😂 Six things to match when finding a partner: Shared values; Emotional preferences; Intellectual level: this determines the cost of communication and the speed of thinking; Energy state; Being considerate of the other person's feelings; A willingness to adjust Values: the six needs of life: The need for survival; The need for affiliation; The need to excel; The need for achievement; The need for beauty; The need for freedom Everyone has all of these needs, in different strengths. A music teacher has two abilities: music and teaching. The younger the child, the more teaching ability matters compared with musical ability. You need to meet the child's six needs; the practice pieces you give children should sound good; if a child isn't making obvious progress on a piece, move on quickly; let them feel they're improving, that they're winning. It also has to sound good, and they must be able to feel "obvious" progress. Games have so many designs built around human needs like dopamine, so why don't we design children's education the way software companies do? That's what matters most. Comparing Chinese and Western art The sounds humans make naturally don't have a very precise rhythm, and the pitch isn't all that standard either. Yunwei, that lingering charm: it comes from time, rhythm and pitch being not quite so precise. Listening to Chinese music feels very relaxed and free. But it has one drawback: it's hard to play as an ensemble. To keep everyone aligned, European music gave up a sense of freedom. It gained the great civilization of the symphony, and at the same time lost that lingering charm. Different kinds of music each have their strengths and weaknesses; different peoples have different cultures. Chinese painting is the same: landscape painting isn't precise, but it has charm Ink wash is light and delicate; you couldn't paint Father in ink wash. And if you use oil to paint a Chinese painting, no matter how you do it, it's never translucent enough. Watercolor is very light, but compared with ink wash it still doesn't work. The ambiguity in Chinese culture: when you're on the rise, you're a Confucian; when you're down, you're a Taoist. "When successful, serve the whole world; when in hardship, cultivate yourself alone." A bit Confucian one moment, a bit Taoist the next, so it's not so easy to get depressed. Chinese culture leaves people a way out. Each appreciates its own beauty, and appreciates the beauty of others; when beauty is shared, the world is in harmony. Does Chinese music lack anything earth-shattering and soul-stirring? Ancient China wasn't like that: in the Warring States period, orchestras often had more than a thousand musicians. Did China have no bass instruments? In the Warring States period the "se" zither could be as long as 2 meters, The Warring States period had the "eight sounds" system for classifying instruments, and orchestras of three thousand; the musical forms couldn't possibly have been simple. China's ancient music wasn't preserved. With every change of dynasty, nothing was handed down, and everything started over from scratch. The forms got smaller and smaller, which is a real pity. Folk songs They have lots of filler syllables: "yi" and "ya" are yang, bright and placed forward; "wu," "ye" and "o" are yin, dark and placed back. That's yin and yang. Humans have an innate, fundamental pursuit of balance between yin and yang. Yue Yunchuan: collecting folk music in the field, protecting a whole province's intangible cultural heritage and keeping it safe. That's all. My biggest takeaway from the day was feeling that real education is "one person lighting up another," and also feeling how sad "educational harm" is. I hope that when I have little ones of my own, I'll still remember these lessons. Let me also share this video, one I shot myself and inexplicably love. After Professor Haihong's music class, I rode through a pouring rainstorm back to Shili Fangfei in Hangzhou. At one in the morning, I boarded a boat at the ferry landing and drifted all the way to Xunmei Islet. Sailing on water far from any lights, the lake was quiet and serene, reflecting the cool moonlight, and in my ears was the "swish~ swish~" of the water as the oars cut through it. In that moment, every thought and every emotion went still. Just like that: a simple love for something, no need for it to be profound.
On Public Speaking, On CAS Cohort 27

Years ago I heard that we should shift from being "T-shaped talent" to "Π-shaped talent." Roughly speaking, T-shaped talent needs both breadth and depth, while Π-shaped talent needs not just breadth and depth but several depths (and comb-shaped talent is even more impressive! But life is finite.) — Of all the general-purpose skills, public speaking is one of the most rewarding. Whether you're a technologist, a thinker, a craftsperson or a manager, speaking is an amplifier and a lever: it lets large numbers of people recognize your abilities in the shortest possible time, which brings more opportunities. And besides, standing on a stage is enjoyable in itself. So I went to CAS to learn public speaking, and came away with lots of friendship and kindness, plus guidance from several teachers. I'm grateful to everyone I met there. Below are some of the things I took away from the course — many are the teachers' golden lines plus my own reflections. For the record: The Way of speaking Every speech is a gift. Think about what you want to give your audience. A blessing? An insight? A principle? Going in with the mindset of "giving a gift," it's harder to get caught up in ego. Once you understand how important the "field" is for anyone who communicates and expresses, you'll feel deep reverence for everything and every detail of a speech. The "field" is the environment (lighting, space, music, backdrop), and also the situation (the audience's emotions, the atmosphere in the room) The "field" can be open/closed, cold/hot, output/inspiration — collectively, the more abstract yin and yang. A good speech stirs emotions and drives action. The techniques of speaking You can open with a question to grab the audience's attention and make them feel involved. Ask about something everyone cares about. How many friends here are from Beijing? How many of you have children? Guess what the world's average wealth per person is? Old people, children and so on are things everyone cares about.2. Check-in activity: have everyone describe how they felt yesterday and how they feel right now, then demonstrate a gesture and have everyone do it together. - Feeling examples: I slept really well yesterday / this morning I saw two squirrels fighting Gesture examples: a stretch / cheering yourself on3. Leave an impression through stories — telling a story means opening up, breaking down, and moving people. People naturally resist having things forced on them; a master speaker is always a master storyteller. Why tell stories They're visual They're more vivid They hold attention better What kind of story leaves an impression? One that's visual Fake stories: you think you've told a story, but actually you've stated an opinion. Opinion: my network is amazing Story: taking 5 tycoons out for lamb skewers The winners are usually the stories that grip your soul. The teller makes it look effortless; the listener is blown away. 4. Show it through performance: in front of the audience, act out the stark contrast between "telling a story and stating an opinion directly." 5. Use reversals well: first set up a point; even if everyone knows a twist is coming, as long as the lines are fun, it's great!6. Stories principles: if you can tell a story, don't lecture. No child at bedtime has ever said, "Mommy, I'm going to sleep, but I want to hear one more principle." 😂 7. Everyone's heart is built for gossip "Principal, let me talk to you about public speaking technique" — "Teacher Chang, Lai Xing lately..." Sometimes a product launch is just a giant gossip session 8. Always pack a formal outfit when you travel: never miss a chance to host or speak. 9. Life of Pi debate opponents - Once you've heard someone's story, it's easier to forgive them. Because knowing their story means knowing what they've been through - If you don't know another's pain, don't urge them to be kind. When people hear opinions, someone always wants to rebut them; stating opinions is training up debate opponents 10. The all-purpose story structure Most of the time you can follow this structure Men tend to linger too long on "a calm, sunny day" — spending ages setting up the background - Women tend to linger too long on "a bolt from the blue" — like Xianglin's Wife We should linger longest on "primordial power" - A good speech illuminates; it doesn't show off. Every speech is a gift, and the gift is hidden in the "primordial power." 11. The advanced method: "benchmarking," commonly known as "copy and surpass" — learn from good role models. 12. Learn to laugh at yourself13. Everyone should have their own "golden story" and "all-purpose story" Once dug out, these stories can be told a hundred times In your past experiences and in your values, there are stories worth digging out and telling 14. When describing the people in a story, give each one a code name; it's easier to describe them, otherwise the audience gets confused. 15. Don't use verbal tics like "and then" — this takes training, day after day. My review1. Be clear about the core idea - For every speech, think clearly about what the core idea is, what gift you're giving, and to whom. Make the core point clear; with a normal order and structure, it won't turn out too badly 2. The speaker's role: lead or supporting? If you're supporting, don't steal the scene. If you're the lead, prepare thoroughly in advance. 3. Structure Montage can be used, but use it sparingly! (I blew it this time~) If you open with a montage, presenting a single scene is enough. 4. No spoilers — don't give a spoiler speech! If you're telling a story, keep the audience from guessing the ending at the start If the story you tell has nothing to do with the theme, the audience will be preoccupied by the emotion or opinion the story delivers, which works against the message the speaker wants to convey Save the story's climax for later Plant foreshadowing early on The story should have ups and downs: set up reversals and contrasts 5. The most important thing: be sincere - A way to come across as sincere: even when telling someone else's story, put yourself into it. Otherwise it sounds a lot like documentary narration. - Make the story relate to yourself, or to the audience.6. On stage presence - Hold the microphone a bit away; don't block your face. - Use open, expansive body language; hold a good gesture for 2 seconds (so the photographer can catch it!) Finally, I don't think "the Way" and "technique" rank above or below each other. Many people chase "the Way" first, always trying to grasp the mysterious "Way" before anything else. As if after enlightenment you could soar to the sky in one leap. But oh, there's no secret martial arts manual that can turn one day's work into ten years of skill. When I play golf, there are always hot streaks when every swing is beautiful, and there are always times when nothing goes right — it's almost mystical. Once, my dad asked: "Do you know why your game is so inconsistent?" "Why?" "Because you're not a professional." Yes — without consistent output on every swing, what's the point of talking about leveling up? Only by "keeping to the orthodox" can you "produce the extraordinary"; only solidity at the level of "technique" can bring insight and oneness at the level of "the Way." So my method is to pursue 1% progress each time and prepare myself fully. Not too much inner drama — let the insights and the feelings flow naturally. One last thing: charge ahead with abandon, enjoy the moment, and remember: Present is a present!
Mindful Walking on a Rainy Day at Shili Fangfei

This afternoon I hurried back to Shanghai from Shili Fangfei in Hangzhou for Professor Zhou Haihong's music appreciation class. On the little path from Xunmeizhu to the Shilizhou pier, a fine drizzle was falling, and the moss-covered flagstones were slippery. Afraid of falling, I didn't dare get careless, let alone look at my phone. So I simply started "mindful walking" — or rather, "mindful speed-walking". Before this, I had only dabbled in mindful walking through the Dedao app and a Bushiju course. Immersing myself in it again this afternoon was a truly wonderful experience. It was as if a seed I had casually scattered some time ago had been nourished by an occasional bit of sunshine and rain, and had put out a tender little sprout. The longer I live, the clearer it becomes how much "experience" matters to me. I stress "to me" because I've also gradually come to understand "the differences between individuals". Every life has its own path and way. Some people grasp a great deal without needing to experience it; some even prefer fewer experiences, so they can feel the purity of life. I'm probably clumsy, and greedy too, so I want lots of experiences — and I need lots of them. Experience is the way of growing that suits me best. Before I practised "mindfulness", for a very, very long time I didn't even know what "living in the present" meant. It's a principle I'd seen since childhood in books, on other people's walls and in calligraphy scrolls, and heard countless times, yet without experiencing it I could never have known — that walking can be just walking. Real education is "people lighting each other up"; it's the power of example. With many things, the question isn't whether you do them, but to what degree. The degree determines the result, which in turn determines whether the feedback is positive or negative. A good speech takes three months of preparation and 200 rounds of polishing. That simply wasn't part of my understanding before. Rehearsing 10 or 20 times was probably my limit, and I thought I was "well prepared". So without going through that kind of polishing and tempering, I would never have known how wonderful it is, once your craft is truly refined, to reach that state where emotion flows and you become one with what you're doing. In the same way, I once didn't know what "thinking carefully" was, what "resting properly" was, what "focus" was, what "listening patiently" was… For me, "unity of knowledge and action" has to begin as "unity of action and knowledge". You have to have loved to understand love; only after experiencing something once alongside a master do you know what the right degree is. So I want to collect lots and lots of beautiful "experiences", even if just for a moment. btw, Shili Fangfei really is a lovely place — recommended. This is a video I took on a sunny afternoon as my boat glided into Shili Fangfei. Very healing.
Today, I Sent a Hard Route — Injured

I've fallen in love with climbing lately. Since I only climb when I can steal a moment from a busy schedule, my timing is all over the place, so it's hard to book sessions with a coach, and my technique is far from textbook. My whole approach is basically brute force. It really is a slightly dangerous sport. But if you're just one move away from success, there's no way you won't try. Today I only had half an hour, and came back to grind away at this level-13 route. Last time I'd already cracked all the crux moves; I just didn't have the strength or the time to run the whole thing again. So this time I started climbing right after warming up, full of confidence that I'd get it done in one go! And then… I got hurt right off the bat… blood dripping all over the floor. But even injured, I still wanted to give it one more try! Standing in front of the wall, I closed my eyes and took 10 deep breaths, letting my nerves-raised heart rate settle, staying calm so my palms wouldn't keep sweating. Up I went, stopping to rest at every move along the way to keep my arms fighting fit; at the last rest point, I took big breaths and reset my mindset. To the last move: every time before, I'd jumped and couldn't reach it. Don't overthink it, focus on controlling my body — shift my weight, deep breath — jump! Got it!! Gave the bell🔔 a cheeky kick, and I'm happy for the whole day~~

If I had to say which day in 2022 nudged the course of my life just a little in some direction — a nudge that will keep compounding over the years to come until it makes a huge difference — then Gaoshan Academy's "Starry Sky Concert," that collective flow under the Perseid meteor shower, has to be the most wonderful of them all. It was guided in person by Gaoshan adviser Professor Zhou Haihong, former vice president of the Central Conservatory of Music, starting from "Why should music need to be understood?" and moving on to music's emotions, techniques, structure… The experience was beautiful beyond words. All I can say is: before and after that day, music has been a completely different presence in my life. The ripples of that emotion took a long time to settle. So, led by our Gaoshan classmates, we decided to act together and bring that beauty back — so that this emotion and what we gained don't stop with us. One of the stars this time is of course Professor Zhou Haihong once again. He is not only a music aesthetician but also a scholar of music psychology and education, with deep research in philosophy, aesthetics, and personality and motivation psychology, and he is deputy director of the Ministry of Education's National Steering Committee for Aesthetic Education in Primary and Secondary Schools. We are also fortunate to have invited a powerful lineup of musicians: Principal cellist of the Shanghai Philharmonic Orchestra — Wu Minzhe; Erhu virtuoso and professor at the Shanghai Conservatory of Music — Wang Lili; Pipa virtuoso — Xu He; Yangqin virtuoso and professor in the Department of Chinese Music — Yu Haiying; Prodigy pianist from the Middle School Attached to the Central Conservatory of Music — Du Peida; Prodigy violinist from the Shanghai Conservatory of Music — Bao Shennuo; Although one of them is only 14, mastery comes before age, so we call them all "maestro." And we've arranged a very~~ special venue 👇 The former Union Church (Xin Tian'an Church) This Gothic Revival building, a protected historic building at No. 4 on the Bund, was designed by William Dowdall. It sits in the Bund Origin area, the starting point of the "exhibition of world architecture" and the origin of modern Shanghai. When it was completed in 1886, it was the highest point on the south bank of Suzhou Creek, and it was the site of many important events in modern Chinese history. In 1920, the British philosopher Bertrand Russell gave a lecture here. (to be verified) In this century-old church, we will experience the wonder of music together. But believe me, this isn't just a concert — it's more like an education in aesthetics and an exercise in philosophical reflection. If you've ever been troubled by "not understanding music," it can set your mind free; "Music is the art of hearing; experiencing the beauty of pure sound is the most important value in appreciating the art of music. Just as fine art is the art of sight… fine food is the art of taste — no one asks what profound ideas and cultural depth lie in a plate of Dongpo pork knuckle." If you're a seasoned music lover, it lets you join professional connoisseurs in teasing out the delicacy and subtlety of music, strand by strand; "With Chinese folk instruments you can't just listen to the notes; you have to listen to the technique. With the guzheng, pay attention to the last third of each note." If you have children, please, please, please bring them along — opening the door to enjoying music early in life is an immense happiness. (Primary school age and up is fine~) "If a person's character is to approach completeness, they need not only the qualities to obtain the conditions for happiness, but also the qualities to experience the feeling of happiness." "The critical period for cultivating a person's sensibility is childhood; aesthetic preferences, habits and standards all take shape in childhood. … People raised amid the beauty of art will have a good sensibility, and even if they meet all kinds of negative influences later, they can dissolve them through a refined cultural and artistic life. This is the great significance of arts education in social life." AGAIN Time: April 1, 2023, 19:30–21:00 Venue: The former Union Church (also known as "Buzhi Space"), 103 South Suzhou Road, the Bund, Shanghai. In the future, we hope this kind of beauty keeps growing; that music inspires more people to appreciate the beauty of life; that the gift of musical awakening reaches more people, flowing on without end. Finally, one more quote from Canetti: "Music is the best healing, because music produces no words. The more people there are in the world, the more the forms of life resemble machines, and the more important music becomes. We are about to enter an age in which only music can slip through the dense net of function; the most important task of future scholars will be to guard music, the last stable, independent refuge of freedom in this world. Yesterday at the after party with my Gaoshan classmates, since my birthday began right after midnight, everyone gave me a few words each. It was a very touching moment. One friend described me as someone who "takes everything she does seriously." I was happy, and a little surprised. I didn't use to be like this. A handsome British actor whose name I don't know once said: I gave myself permission to care. There are a lot of people in this world who are afraid of caring or afraid of showing that they care, because it is uncool, it is uncool to have passion. It is so much easier to lose, when you've shown everyone how much you don't care if you win or lose. It is much harder to lose when you show that you care. But, you will never win, unless you also stand to lose. Do not afraid of your passion. Just give it free reign, and be honest and work hard, and it will all turn out just fine. I allow myself to care. Because there are many people in this world who are afraid to care, afraid to show that they care. Because it isn't cool enough; having passion makes you look less composed. This time I came to Silicon Valley with Gaoshan Academy for classes, and spent most of my time on the Stanford University campus. Guided by a wise, elegant, warm and resilient elder, we covered much of this 33-square-kilometre campus on foot. For a week we attended classes in lecture rooms, ate in the dining halls, and took our lunch breaks on the lawns playing frisbee… I've lost count of how many times I'd been here before, but this time I truly fell in love with the university and was won over by it. Not because of its fame and legends, but because of its atmosphere and institutions, so full of rebellion and openness, that spark creativity. Besides innovation and rebellion, there are stories like these: every year, graduates bury meaningful objects beneath the paving stones in front of Stanford Memorial Church; and when Chiang Kai-shek's diaries were donated, the director of the Stanford library felt they belonged to China, so rather than accepting the donation, the library agreed to keep them in custody instead. By the way, Stanford's campus is said to have more Rodin sculptures than anywhere outside France. Grandma Has COVID: What We Did and Our Contingency Plan (3)

Grandma today Blood pressure 130/80, heart rate 78, blood oxygen 96% (on oxygen), temperature 37.0, in much better spirits, able to get up and eat on her own, able to sleep lying flat — she's doing great! Honestly, I can breathe again; on the first day I was scared out of my wits. My personal feeling is that getting her on the antiviral promptly was a crucial step. Of course, close monitoring has to continue, but I hope this is the last post about how we're handling Grandma's COVID. Because that would mean no more surprises, no more scares — just good rest, calm, steady, uneventful days. This time I was in Beijing, taking part remotely in Grandma's medical care, medication and monitoring in Hong Kong, and I came away with two lessons. 1. A contingency plan is absolutely, absolutely, absolutely essential. 2. When caring for elderly relatives, communication, empathy and coordination among family members matter enormously. Perhaps this will be useful to some of you, so I'll go on at a bit more length; updates are shown in blue. Once again: this is specific to Grandma's situation — 86 years old, with twenty years of high blood pressure. It is not medical advice, just experience shared among friends. If you plan to use any of it, please be sure to consult a doctor and other professionals. Here goes: 0. Contingency Plan First, ideally, avoid infection altogether and help older people sit out this wave. Grandma caught it when she went out for her flu jab, so keep outings to a minimum. Make your plan before the elderly person gets infected. Once they're infected, there's no time to research, buy medicine, buy equipment and find a hospital, and you may miss the best window for treatment. Antigen tests lag behind. Be on alert at a sore throat or fever; at this point in the season, it's better not to count on luck. Things you can prepare in advance: - A home oxygen concentrator and portable oxygen cylinders (on the way to hospital on your own, a home concentrator is no use, but a portable cylinder is.) - A pulse oximeter and blood pressure monitor - A thermometer (a digital one is better — you can take a temperature without disturbing them while they sleep) - Fever-cooling patches and other physical cooling tools On medication, work out which drugs can be taken after infection and how - What their regular medications are, when they take them and at what dose - Whether their regular medications conflict with fever reducers and COVID antivirals - Which doses may need adjusting. For example, blood pressure may run low after infection, so measure it before taking blood pressure medication. On medical care, plan your routes and options Agree on what situations mean you call an ambulance without hesitation Where the nearest hospital is, how long it takes to get there, whether it has ventilators and ECMO. Get the family to agree on all of the above. 1. General Despise the enemy strategically, respect it tactically: monitor the elderly person's vital signs more closely than usual, but don't panic. Stay calm and give them a relaxed environment that reduces anxiety and tension; a calm state of mind helps recovery. Frail elderly people may not run a fever at all. Fever is the immune system responding, the body's own protective mechanism. When someone's health is very poor, even that alarm signal may be gone. That's why so many elderly people who passed away had similar readings: blood pressure not high, temperature normal, no fever. Be cautious about going to hospital: it's an ordeal, and it raises the elderly person's exposure to the virus, so if it isn't necessary, you needn't go; Encourage them — their state of mind, confidence and will to live all matter. Our agreed line was: Grandma's vital signs are very good and don't meet the threshold for admission, which is why the hospital didn't take her. (Rather than: she couldn't get a bed 😢.) Apparently the will to live has a big effect on physical condition. Being too anxious also hinders recovery. 2. Medication Paracetamol (compound acetaminophen): likely less of a conflict with blood pressure medication. Ibuprofen-type drugs: may affect high blood pressure. Use Lianhua Qingwen with caution: it has strong side effects; if it must be taken, halve the dose for the elderly and children. Use cough medicine with caution: some cough medicines raise blood pressure or can trigger angina, so read the leaflet carefully, and be careful with anything containing ephedrine-type ingredients. If phlegm is thick and hard to cough up, consider Mucosolvan (ambroxol). Doses for underlying conditions may need adjusting: during a fever, if they drink a lot and urinate a lot, blood pressure may drop, so blood pressure medication may need to be reduced appropriately to avoid harm from very low blood pressure, or a misdiagnosis. Can the COVID antiviral Paxlovid be used? A very important question — but to be honest, I don't know. What we know is: People over 60 can take it, but! There are many restrictions; Special groups, especially patients with kidney impairment, should use it with caution; It conflicts with many medications for underlying conditions — for example, Grandma's cholesterol-lowering drug. But if fighting the virus is the priority, you can stop that medication and take Paxlovid. This must be done under a doctor's guidance; we have no hands-on experience with it. Under a doctor's guidance, we used Merck's (MSD's) molnupiravir. Note: you must complete the full five-day course. Because it works by preventing the virus from replicating, sometimes the symptoms aren't obvious but the virus is still replicating, so finishing the course is the best choice. Reportedly, in clinical trials it was compared against a placebo and its toxicity was no greater than the placebo's. Click to view: the molnupiravir package insert and the Shanghai Pharmaceutical Association's introduction Found a very good tool: a CHECKER for whether COVID medications conflict with other medications, which you can use to check yourself before taking anything. Website: https://www.covid19-druginteractions.org/checker 3. Monitoring Monitor temperature, pulse, blood oxygen and blood pressure, and assess their overall condition together — do not, do not, do not look at just one indicator. The second day after testing positive is when it tends to be most serious, so monitor more intensively. Assess temperature, pulse, blood oxygen and blood pressure every 1–2 hours. A fingertip pulse oximeter can be worn continuously. Blood oxygen: a very important indicator; if it keeps falling to 93% or below, seek medical care. Heart rate: without fever, an elderly person's heart rate is around 80 beats/minute; for every 1 degree rise in temperature, pulse rises by 10 beats/minute; if there's no fever and the heart rate is above 90 beats/minute, consider a little diuretic. Temperature: an elderly person's normal temperature may be only 36 degrees, so 37 degrees already counts as raised. A heart rate of 88 beats/minute is within the acceptable range. A lung CT is an important indicator. When viral pneumonia first causes consolidation, a stethoscope sometimes picks up no positive signs; you only hear them once crackles appear, by which time it may be too late. So if the elderly person's condition and the available medical care allow, getting one can rule out a lot of uncertainty. Blood pressure: monitor continuously and compare with their normal readings. Track fluid in and out, i.e. urine output against fluid intake. Here's a piece of counter-intuitive new knowledge: elderly people shouldn't drink very large amounts of water. Drink moderately, and fairly warm — just enough to sweat. Drink too much without passing it promptly, and you add to the burden on the heart, increase blood volume in the lungs and add to the burden on the lungs. Watch the elderly person's mental state and how much they eat. It's not just the vital signs — if they're eating very little or stay drowsy and not fully alert, be on alert too! 4. Care Drinking: drink warm water, but little and often. Again, keep track of fluid in and out. Count the fluid intake from porridge, water and taking medicine; count the output from urine and sweat too. Eating: small, frequent meals; some nutrition, to give enough resistance, but beware of foods that increase phlegm; if they're sweating a lot, the food can be a touch saltier, because sweating loses salt — but only if they really are sweating, otherwise extra salt burdens the heart. On nutrition: steamed egg custard, egg soup, finely chopped leafy greens, fruit blended into juice (pear and orange are best), or you can cook the pears and oranges. Control the home oxygen concentrator's setting carefully. Blood oxygen should stay above 95%; too low and the oxygen flow isn't enough, too high and the elderly person will be uncomfortable. On the Vision Aire 5 we use, the second setting reaches a 27% concentration, but every machine is different, so use your own judgement. For concentrators with a humidifier bottle, change the distilled water often and keep it clean. If possible, keep the water at around 37 degrees; this little tip humidifies the oxygen so the airways don't dry out, which is more comfortable. 37 degrees is about the same as your hand. The elderly person's cooperation is important. Tell her that eating, drinking warm water, taking oxygen and taking medicine are four equally important parts of the treatment. Make good use of tools like a care log. First, you can see the trends; second, when family members take turns keeping watch, the handover goes smoothly. This is the format of Grandma's log, for your reference. My cousin is a nurse, so her records are remarkably detailed and professional. RA is Room Air; 1L/2L is the oxygen flow rate. 5. Symptoms That Mean Going to Hospital Chest pain, chest tightness, shortness of breath, angina Increased pulse Blood oxygen continuously falling to 93% or below Breathing rate above 30 breaths/minute Still above 38.5 degrees after fever reducers, for 2 days Temperature below 35 degrees Persistent pain or pressure in the chest Dizziness, unable to wake or stay awake Pale, grey or bluish skin, lips or nails Weakness or unsteadiness on their feet Seizures Persistent inability to eat or drink, or diarrhoea or vomiting for more than 2 days Marked worsening of existing underlying conditions 6. Seeking Medical Care Hong Kong's private hospitals do not admit positive patients. Current Hong Kong health policy is that all COVID-positive patients go to public hospitals; even a patient already admitted to a private hospital who unfortunately catches COVID gets taken by ambulance to a public hospital for admission. A few private hospitals' A&E departments will see positive patients, but won't admit them, and afterwards send them by ambulance to a public hospital. Going down the list of "Medical services provided by private hospitals for persons tested positive for COVID-19" published by Hong Kong's Department of Health, I called each one in turn. As of 25 December 2022, the hospitals that clearly confirmed they accept positive patients at A&E were: Union Hospital, Hong Kong +85226083388 Hong Kong Adventist Hospital – Tsuen Wan +85222756688 Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital was the only private hospital I could find that would admit positive patients, but beds were nearly impossible to get; we tried every channel and it simply wasn't possible. Some private hospitals won't do a lung CT for positive patients. Because she was positive, Hong Kong Sanatorium didn't give Grandma a lung CT, so unless it's an emergency, be sure to call and get clear answers before going to a private hospital. In an emergency, calling an ambulance is the most effective option, because ambulances carry equipment. So make sure you understand the process and plan clearly: what number to call, what to do, where the nearest public A&E is. 6. Communication The real work happens in ordinary times. When you discuss the "contingency plan" and "treatment plan," everyone's different knowledge and views on the virus, medical care and medication are bound to surface. Communicate more in normal times, communicate promptly, and share knowledge. Family members who aren't with the elderly person: don't panic too much, don't keep asking questions, and don't disturb the relatives who are on the spot handling things; Make good use of modern communication tools. You can post the latest updates formally to everyone in a WeChat group, using "sign-up chain" or "announcement" posts; you can also share the care log via Tencent Docs or Google Drive, to avoid repeated, overlapping questions and save everyone's mental energy; Take lots of videos and post them in the group. Sometimes seeing the elderly person's spirits, how they eat and how they sleep is more useful and more reassuring than any data. More information is attached below: LAST BUT NOT THE LEAST Special thanks to several of my friends 🙏🙏🙏 I've said thank you many times, and it still can't express it. I didn't ask your permission, so for privacy I won't mention names. The moment you saw my call for help, you messaged me, or even called me directly, and force-fed me the most crucial information; you got me up to speed fast on all kinds of medicines and why they mattered, and scoured the whole market, the whole market, to find medicines for me; you called on resources you don't even use for yourselves to help me find medical resources in Hong Kong; the frequency of your chats and pep talks even hit an all-time high since we've known each other... 😂 Words fail me; I'll keep all of it in my heart. I hope you're all well — let's get together after the pandemic! Portrait of Ah Ma Grandma in New York In front of the grand piano in the hall of the Harvard Club. Painted by Vincent Xeus. I went down the list "Medical services provided by private hospitals for persons tested positive for COVID-19" published by Hong Kong's Department of Health and phoned them one by one. As of December 25, 2022, the hospitals that clearly accept positive patients in their emergency departments are: Union Hospital, Hong Kong +85226083388 Hong Kong Adventist Hospital – Tsuen Wan +85222756688 "Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital" is the only private hospital I could find that admits positive patients, but a bed is nearly impossible to get — we tried every channel, and it just didn't work. Some private hospitals won't do lung CTs for positive patients. Because she was positive, Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital didn't give Grandma a lung CT, so if it's not an emergency, be sure to phone and ask clearly before going to a private hospital. In an emergency, calling an ambulance is the most effective option. How We Handled My Grandma Catching COVID

The human brain seems to have a strange mechanism: it assumes extreme events won't happen to us. My grandma has lived in Hong Kong for years, so her chances of being infected were high — yet I had no plan at all, and when I learned she had tested positive, I panicked for a moment. Besides starting to search for information, I also asked for help on WeChat Moments. Within minutes I received so many kind tips, offers of help, medicines rounded up for us, shared information and emotional support… Hundreds of messages in all helped me get past the panic and gradually learn the essentials of monitoring her and what to know about the medicines. My friends' kindness gave me enormous comfort and support — thank you all once again. To thank everyone, and to pass that kindness on, I've gathered and organised the information. It is all specific to my grandma's situation — she is 86 and has had high blood pressure for twenty years. It is not medical advice, just experience shared by friends. If you plan to use any of it, please be sure to consult a doctor and other professionals. Here it is: 1. General My grandma got infected when she went out for a flu shot, so the first priority is still to avoid infection and go out as little as possible. Despise the enemy strategically, respect it tactically: monitor the elderly person's vital signs more closely than usual, but don't panic. Stay calm and give them a relaxed environment that eases anxiety and tension — a peaceful state of mind helps recovery. Frail elderly people may not run a fever at all. Fever is the immune system responding — the body's own protective mechanism. When someone's health is extremely poor, even this alarm signal may be gone. That's why so many elderly people who passed away had very similar pictures: blood pressure not high, temperature normal, no fever. Think carefully before going to hospital: hospital visits are exhausting and also increase the elderly person's exposure to the virus, so you don't have to go unless it's necessary. Have a plan ready: if you do need to go to hospital, which one? Will you call an ambulance? How long will it take to arrive? Will they be seen right away? Do they have ventilators and ECMO? 2. Medication Paracetamol (compound acetaminophen): probably less likely to clash with blood pressure medication. Ibuprofen-type drugs: may affect high blood pressure. Be careful with Lianhua Qingwen: it has strong side effects; if you must take it, the elderly and children should halve the dose. Be careful with cough medicine: some raise blood pressure or can trigger angina. Read the leaflet carefully, and be cautious with anything containing ephedrine-type ingredients. If phlegm is thick and hard to cough up, consider Mucosolvan (ambroxol). Doses for existing conditions may need adjusting: during a fever, if they drink and urinate a lot, blood pressure may drop, so blood pressure medication may need to be reduced appropriately to avoid harm or misdiagnosis from blood pressure that's too low. Can the COVID drug Paxlovid be used? A very important question — but honestly, I don't know. What we know so far: People over 60 can use it, but! There are many restrictions. Special groups, especially patients with kidney damage, should be cautious. It conflicts with many drugs for underlying conditions — for example, my grandma's cholesterol-lowering medication. But if fighting the virus is the priority, you can pause that medication and take Paxlovid. This needs to be done under a doctor's guidance; we have no hands-on experience. We've booked a doctor's consultation for tomorrow and I'll update afterwards. I found a very good tool: a CHECKER for whether COVID medications conflict with other medications, so you can check for yourself before taking anything. Website: https://www.covid19-druginteractions.org/checker 3. Monitoring Monitor temperature, pulse, blood oxygen and blood pressure, and assess overall condition — do not, do not, do NOT look at just one number. Blood oxygen: a very important indicator. If it keeps falling to 93% or below, seek medical care. Heart rate: without a fever, an elderly person's heart rate is around 80 beats per minute; for every 1 degree rise in temperature, the pulse rises by 10 beats per minute. If there's no fever and the heart rate is over 90 beats per minute, consider a little diuretic. Blood pressure: monitor continuously and compare with normal readings. Watch fluid intake and output — that is, how much they urinate versus how much they drink. Here's a new, counter-intuitive piece of knowledge: elderly people should not drink very large amounts of water. Drink moderately, and drink it warm — enough to work up a sweat is fine. If they drink too much and don't pass it in time, it adds to the burden on the heart, increases blood volume in the lungs and strains the lungs. 4. Symptoms That Need a Trip to Hospital Chest pain, chest tightness, shortness of breath, angina Increased pulse Blood oxygen continuously falling to 93% or below Breathing rate over 30 breaths per minute Temperature still above 38.5°C after fever medication, for 2 days Temperature below 35°C Persistent pain or pressure in the chest Dizziness, unable to wake up or stay awake Pale, grey or bluish skin, lips or nails Weakness or unsteady on their feet Seizures Persistently unable to eat or drink, or diarrhoea or vomiting for more than 2 days Clear worsening of existing underlying conditions More information is attached below: Tomorrow, December 25, is Christmas — and it happens to be my grandma's birthday too. Once We Get Through the Pandemic, We All Have a Bright Future.

We know the "end" is finally coming; it's just that before the dawn, we still have a stretch of darkness to get through. What matters most right now is protecting ourselves and protecting our families. Once we get through the pandemic, we all have a bright future. I'm sharing an article from Dr. Zhang Wenhong's team, with the key points distilled for everyone. Here they are: 1. COVID symptoms are very similar to those of flu, colds and other viral respiratory illnesses — don't panic. 2. People with normal immune function can get through it with fever medicine, a good sleep, plenty of water and some vitamin C. 3. So far, the Omicron strain has not caused specific long-term damage to human organs (long-term sequelae); this is something humans can cope with and accept. 4. Based on overseas experience, the first wave of Omicron infections peaks with large numbers of cases, while later rebounds in a second and third wave will be significantly weaker than the first. 5. The rate of severe illness among children and adults under 60 has dropped significantly; older people (aged ≥60) are the high-risk group for COVID infection, and protecting the elderly is the top priority. Being over 80 combined with several high-risk factors — multiple underlying conditions, cancer, taking immunosuppressants and so on — further increases the rate of severe illness. 6. Vaccination is the best tool! Vaccination is the best tool! Vaccination is the best tool! Vaccination can reduce the rate of severe illness after COVID infection among the elderly by as much as 76–98%. Elderly people who have not yet been vaccinated should hurry and get vaccinated as soon as possible, before the first wave peaks. 7. For many people, their most recent vaccination was more than six months ago and their antibody levels have dropped; 3 doses are better than 2, and 2 are better than 1. 8. Delay infection among the elderly, and try to keep them from being infected during the first peak. If we can push back the overall infection curve for the elderly, even by just 1–2 months, society's vaccine immunity barrier will be stronger, and medical resources will be more ample and less stretched in getting through the first peak. 9. During the rise and peak of the outbreak, go out as little as possible, wear a mask, wash your hands often, ventilate often and keep indoor air circulating; get enough sleep and balanced nutrition to boost your resistance, and look after your mood. 10. Elderly people with chronic illnesses whose conditions are stable should avoid going to hospital unless necessary, and stock up on the medicines they take long-term for underlying conditions (such as blood pressure and diabetes medication). 11. Elderly people, especially those over 80, should be careful with fever and pain medicine; taking large amounts can easily damage liver function, and may also cause heavy sweating leading to low blood pressure and shock. 12. Family members should take it upon themselves to protect the elderly, cut down on unnecessary outings and gatherings, and, once infection is suspected, reduce contact with older relatives. Finally, Dr. Zhang Wenhong's team says: the novel coronavirus will gradually become one of our routine respiratory viruses, shifting from a pandemic to an endemic/seasonal disease. Perhaps one day we'll wake up and find that we have made it through the pandemic, hard as it was.
