Yunnan and the People of the Mountains

How do you fall in love, in three days, with a place you've been before? — Travel with someone who truly loves this land. I've been to Yunnan many times. In my mind, it was the Jade Dragon Snow Mountain at three thousand meters, Shangri-La's "Potala Palace," a string of somewhat over-commercialized old towns, the singing of Lijiang's Xiaoqian, the hot springs of Tengchong, and arty guesthouses beside Cangshan Mountain and Erhai Lake. The Yunnan of the past was beautiful, but it wasn't a spiritual home; it was more like a spiritual faraway. But the Yunnan of this past week was different. I saw and heard many stories here that made this border province in China's southwest corner — a foreign land home to nearly half of China's ethnic minorities — resonate with my soul. Here I went to the museum in Shiping to see the continuity of Chinese civilization; watched the dust thrown up by our car on dirt roads through steep mountains; heard stories of smuggling and drug trafficking on the border; listened to a man who came out of the mountains go from bloody fights and a hard-scrabble existence to becoming a tea fanatic; and saw the simple, sincere greetings of old people. It is still spring all year round here, but it's no longer only flowers; it also has those stories — poor, simple, bloody, romantic, savage, primal, long and lingering, light and quick. Shiping County Setting out from Kunming and driving south for two hours, you enter the Honghe Hani and Yi Autonomous Prefecture. A little over a hundred kilometers from the prefecture seat, Mengzi, is a county town called Shiping, our base before heading into the mountains to visit the elderly people living alone. It's a slightly magical county town: 95% of its 3,042 square kilometers is mountains, yet its buildings have a strong southern, Hui-style character. (This isn't a cultural heritage building; it's just a well-preserved building in the village) (The little town has a burly city gate tower, a sizeable Confucian temple and many old academies.) The Ming and Qing buildings here are preserved so densely and so completely that I was in a daze — how could this be a remote frontier town in southern Yunnan? Later I heard that during the Ming and Qing dynasties Shiping produced 638 juren , 77 jinshi , 15 Hanlin academicians and Yunnan's only zhuangyuan (top imperial scholar), Yuan Jiagu — hence the saying "three jinshi within five paces, two Hanlin academicians across the street." Even today Shiping's schools still rank near the top in the province, quite out of keeping with its location and economic standing. A local friend told me he was amazed that children elsewhere aren't tested on calligraphy when moving from primary to middle school. Here, every student has to practice brush calligraphy, a tradition that survives to this day. The old people in the mountains From Shiping County we drove more than 4 hours into endless mountains, and before we knew it the asphalt had disappeared. Dust flew wherever the wheels rolled; on either side were primeval rock faces and cliffs and mountains linked to mountains as far as the eye could see. The villages here have very few people left — as few as four or five households, at most a dozen or so. Going from one village to the next means going from one mountaintop to another; it feels as if you can see the cooking smoke curling up on the opposite side, but driving there takes four or five hours. One village has a lovely name: Mile Village (named after the Maitreya Buddha). Here lives an uncle surnamed Xu (after some thought, since the public account is a public space, I won't post anyone's photos). He lost both eyes at three, lost his only son in a mining accident in his forties, and then lost his partner... so now, at 78, he lives alone. Yet he has a radiant smile and a "superpower" — he can tell a banknote's denomination just by touching it; there's absolutely no way you could pass off a 50-yuan note as 100. He does his own laundry, cooking and housework, and keeps a pig behind the house. (When we arrived, a fire was going in the kitchen with a big pot of vegetables cooking — food Uncle Xu had prepared for the pig.) Uncle Xu even taught himself the erhu. He said that when he thinks of his wife and child he still feels low, and then he plays a sad tune to work through it... He also said: "You are good people; you've all studied Chairman Xi's thought." Another village is called Renshou Village (the village names here are all so stylish — Shazui Village, for instance, very Hong Kong). There lives an old man, Uncle Wang, who lost both legs as a child. He lives in a tent that looks like a rubbish heap, and in that rubbish heap there turned out to be some treasures. (Uncle Wang's painting 1) (Uncle Wang's painting 2) The relative who looks after him said that the old man usually does nothing, doesn't talk to anyone and has never left the village; he just paints on scraps of cardboard, and no one can understand what he's painting. To me, these paintings have a very Art Deco feel, with a touch of mystery. In the mountains I learned a local phrase, "bu xiao le, bu xiao le," which roughly means "no need, please don't trouble yourself." It's really useful, because every old person you meet here will warmly invite you to stay and eat, whether it's 8 in the morning or 3 in the afternoon 😂. One old man insisted on catching chickens for us to take away, even though his home was bare to the walls, he had lost most of his sight, he was himself receiving aid, and those few chickens might have been among the few assets he had. The amazing Brother Gao We didn't support the old people through a charity, but through a local friend — let's call him Brother Gao. Brother Gao is a Shiping local. Back then it was he who, through introductions from friends around him, helped us find, one by one, the old people who needed help, and twice a year he drives into the mountains to deliver money and daily supplies to them. Visiting all of them takes four or five days, leaving at 7 every morning and getting home at midnight. Brother Gao is a big, dark-skinned man, but he is also a tea fanatic who listens to the I Ching on long drives, and a philosopher who speaks in golden lines. During the days we visited the old people, "My Second Uncle cured my mental exhaustion" was going viral online. Seeing the optimism of Uncle Xu and so many other old people, I remarked that these were real-life "Third Uncles" — life had thrown these old people to rock bottom, yet they still lived optimistically. Brother Gao listened to me in silence and said softly, "It's the only way they can live." — That sentence filled me with deep shame, and in one stroke pierced my childish melancholy. Looking at Uncle Wang's paintings, he said: "There's no such thing as mad or not mad, only understood or not understood." Talking about the old people who had already passed away, Brother Gao said that each time he drives several hours to deliver money for the funeral. I said, why not just transfer it to someone else in the village, so you don't have to go to all that trouble. He said that besides making sure the money was used properly, he also wanted to go and kowtow a few times for those old people who had no children. He said: "When you've seen a lot of life and death, you treasure the people you meet more and respect life more." Along the way he talked about his maternal grandfather, who in his day had to carry 18 pairs of shoes for a single trip along the Ancient Tea Horse Road. He said that the lives of their descendants today were walked out by people like them, who opened up so many cities and mines for Honghe Prefecture. Through the stories he told, I understood what made him willing to spend time and energy helping us support the old people. He said that when he first went out into the world, his mother told him, "If you see a banana peel on the road, pick it up, because just because you won't slip doesn't mean others won't." He said that as a child he watched how the elders in his family did things — they lived at the foot of a mountain, on the path every villager had to take to go up and cut firewood, so many people would sit on the stone blocks at their door to rest, and his grandmother would tell his uncle to fill the water vat beside the stones so everyone could have a drink. He said he didn't want to let down the spirit of those who came before him. He said that after the pandemic he would definitely take his son, who's in third grade, to see more of the world. But when I asked which city he liked best, he still chose his hometown. Speaking of Pu'er, where he lives now, he said: "The people there have very dark skin but they're very clean, their smiles are healing, their hearts are simple, and there's no scheming. When you drink with them, no one pushes you to drink, but you just want to lose yourself in that moment." Looking at Brother Gao, with so much awareness of life and so much love and gratitude toward others, I find it hard to imagine that in primary school he hardly had shoes to wear, that he dropped out in the second year of middle school, and that he was once someone who, just to survive, ended up at the police station three or four times a week for fighting. Life must have left many scars on him, yet here and now he exists in such a peaceful, gentle way. People like Bill Gates and Rockefeller, who left immortal names in the history of human philanthropy, certainly deserve to be learned from and admired; but just as an ant can carry 5,000 times its own weight, meeting Brother Gao showed me those people in countless corners of the world who are not rich at all, yet are already giving, again and again. I've been back in the city for a week, and I still often think of the land south of the colorful clouds — its clear blue sky, those people, those stories. These stories flow like blood into the heart, building a mountain stronghold in some corner of my soul, carrying the romantic and primal spirit of Yunnan's mountains. They changed how I feel about that land and its people, and along the way changed my heart just a tiny bit.

Thank you to Miss JN for asking why I'd stopped updating my WeChat account — you nudged me back onto the road. There was no reason for stopping, other than laziness. And behind the laziness and procrastination was the fear that I wouldn't write well. I kept thinking I needed a solid block of time, a calm creative environment and frame of mind, as if after burning incense and taking a ritual bath. Little did I know that such a state almost never exists. What actually happens is this: once you start writing, you gradually slip into that state. Yes, perfectionism is sometimes a harmful form of self-suggestion. Today, let's talk about the benefits of becoming an “imperfectionist.” What's the flip side of perfectionism? First, a bit of science. In job interviews, we often come across people new to the workforce who, when asked about their weaknesses, offer “perfectionism” as filler. We all know it's another way of bragging; some sincere people genuinely believe it's a positive flaw, with a hint of pride in it. But in reality, perfectionism can lead to irrationality, negative emotions and limitations. Social anxiety, procrastination, low self-esteem and depression can all be partly blamed on perfectionism too. A six-year study of 450 older people found that those with perfectionist tendencies had a 51% higher death rate during that period than everyone else, and other research shows perfectionism is closely linked to higher rates of depression and suicide. Perfectionism and procrastination Perfectionism isn't necessarily an excuse for procrastination; it's actually a cause of it. There is a book called How to Be an Imperfectionist , whose author, Stephen Guise, also wrote a very well-known book called Mini Habits . As I see it, Mini Habits is about one thing: building habits through sheer willpower is an exhausting path — you can't lift yourself up by your own hair. But habits can be built by design, by working with how the human brain behaves, setting up small mechanisms that open a different, easier path to growth. Compared with “work out for an hour,” the psychological resistance to “do 3 burpees” is so small it's negligible. Chasing perfection does the exact opposite — it's designing obstacles for yourself. Perfectionism, involution and the local optimum trap My guess is that perfectionism and involution — that endless, zero-sum rat race — are also gifts from our genes: the Red Queen effect in evolution, where we have to keep running just to stay in place. Evolution never stops; both competition between species and competition within a species require us to keep racing forward. But once we hit the local optimum trap, perfectionism turns into involution: we put in huge effort just to be a tiny bit better than others, because in today's society of intense, homogeneous competition, you have to be a little more excellent, or a little more of a “slash” multi-hyphenate, to stand out. But chasing perfection takes a huge amount of energy and leaves us no slack to handle sudden risks. Under evolution, what happens to a species that climbs to the peak of a local optimum? — It goes extinct. Perfectionism and the pursuit of excellence People often say anti-perfectionist things like “done is better than perfect” and “the best is the enemy of the better.” Yet at the same time we prize the pursuit of excellence, high standards and strict demands. Where's the difference? From my own experience, pursuing excellence means aiming for the best overall in the long run, getting better across every dimension, and being strategic about focusing on what matters and letting the small stuff go; perfectionism, on the other hand, insists that every single detail be as good as it can possibly be. So where does the difference lie? To judge whether a mindset is good or bad, the key is how it affects our actions and how it makes us feel about what we do. What matters is that we consciously observe the difference between perfectionism and the pursuit of excellence. What perfectionism and the pursuit of excellence have in common is holding ourselves to a higher standard, and we often need to strike a balance between the two. My solution Deadlines and breaking tasks down. When you run into a specific problem in life, always look for humanity's leading answer to it — most problems have already been given excellent answers by extraordinarily clever people. The answer might come from cutting-edge theory, or from the practices of outstanding organisations or individuals. But as Chairman Mao said, “once you get specific, you go deep”: every excellent answer contains its own tree of knowledge, which often brings with it a pile of good new questions. So time planning and deadlines are important. Spending 20 minutes looking things up and then making a 10-minute phone call will certainly produce a better decision than going with your gut — but that's all the time you get, and there must be a result before the deadline. As soon as I notice myself tending to procrastinate out of perfectionism, I keep breaking things down into sub-goals and setting a deadline for each sub-task. Often, when I discover a knowledge gap, I grab a scrap of cloth from wherever I can and patch it first; if it really matters, I come back later and take a proper course to fill in the systematic knowledge. Other remedies for perfectionism Never use guilt as your motivation to move forward Focus on the process The timer method A results diary Imagine the worst outcome …… There's quite a lot more in the book How to Be an Imperfectionist . In short, remember: “imperfect” does not mean “failure.” So next time we tease ourselves, maybe we can say: “Ah, I really am such an imperfectionist.” 🤷‍♀️ One more little story: there was another trigger for today's writing. Today I suddenly realised that a few months ago, in a moment of panic, I made an extremely basic mistake that may have caused my team a huge loss. So I felt really low. The result of feeling low was that I lost the willpower for today's intermittent fast and instead walked into a Lawson by the road, bought a bag of crisps, and polished off the whole thing within 10 minutes. (The only saving grace: I chose the lowest-calorie bag of crisps on the shelf.) As I ate the crisps, I felt the urge to write. In that moment a flood of things I wanted to say and ideas came pouring out, and I realised a conflict was going on in my mind, good and bad thoughts locked in a tug-of-war. My good self was saying: It's nothing, just solve the problem. What you're feeling right now is only a chemical signal; negative emotions won't help you with anything. My bad self was howling in my head: How stupid! I can't do anything right! I'm just an idiot! Everything I've achieved was just luck. See? In the end, you're still the weakling. In that moment, it wasn't that I wanted to write; it was that my thoughts needed an outlet, and they rushed towards the outlet called “writing.” That kind of feeling doesn't last. This time, I didn't wait to get back to my computer; I picked up my phone and started typing. Because I knew: if I went with the flow and gave myself closure, the deep, thorough satisfaction of finishing this piece would make me even more eager to answer that call next time. It would be a wonderful start. On the other hand, if I let it slip away, the world is full of readily available placebos and anaesthetics that let you quickly shake off “the guilt and regret of missing a shining moment in your own life” and accept spending your time on nothing meaningful — just open your phone, scroll through a couple of videos, or even reply to a couple of messages in a work group chat, and the urge disappears. There are always callings in life, and they need to be answered. It's like a lamp: if you don't wipe it clean when it gathers dust, its light grows fainter and fainter until we can't see it at all. I'm glad that today, I answered the call. In fact, in that moment I only made a start; most of this was finished tonight. So, starting is success.
A Beginning: Renovating a House Turned Me Back into an Artsy Young Woman

Lately, because of the pandemic, I've been forced to work remotely and renovate a house at the same time. Yet another field I knew nothing about. From making an XMind map to interview designers, to feng shui (seriously), to circulation, lighting and style, to choosing an elevator — every step is a whole new discipline, and I've been learning it all with total infatuation. The house is in a residential compound in the old part of town, more than 20 years old. It's neither an old building with character nor a new luxury home. But somehow it makes us happy. Maybe it's because of how fiercely alive it is. From the start, the garden had a starfruit tree and a longan tree. None of us knew anything about farming and we hardly tended them, yet every year they gave everyone incredibly sweet fruit. These days, around August, my mom has to fly back, climb a tall ladder herself, and chop the longans down — branches, leaves and all — with big shears, to send to family and friends. Later, a papaya seed from who knows where took root and sprouted in our yard without asking permission; by the time we noticed, it was two stories tall and covered in fruit, which left us both exasperated and amused. Not to mention the bougainvillea outside the yard in the compound, which grows with total abandon — in summer, when you sit in the shade of its vines, the sunlight is blocked out completely. It's all so vibrantly alive that it's adorable. It truly deserves to be treated well, so recently I've switched into "immersive renovation" mode. For the sake of renovating the house, I've been visiting Xiamen's museums to learn the cultural history behind the house; touring old Western-style villas on the island and taking hundreds of photos of styles, colors and patterned tiles; and wandering into little streets and alleys to watch how people live. I want to know why this city, and its people along with it, have such a lovable temperament. And through getting to know this city, I also want to come closer to my mom and the childhood home in her memories. I want to know: in that early Northeastern city that didn't even have a McDonald's, what was she thinking when she taught me to use a knife and fork and to savor coffee? I want to know: in her memories of my grandparents secretly humming Teresa Teng songs at home during the Cultural Revolution, what kind of beautiful time was that? I want to know: when she was little and the three siblings had to take turns as a "human egg beater" for four hours, beating eggs until their arms nearly fell off just to eat a homemade cake — was it fragrant and sweet? I want to know: if we put our hearts into it, can a house, and the beautiful times with family, be like a gramophone — carrying a vintage melody that takes us back to a place of comfort for the soul? A few days ago, I was chatting with American friends, hearing artist and architect friends' suggestions for this renovation. The more we talked, the more excited we got — from Nanyang style to the history of overseas Chinese, from Matisse to the Mexican master architect Barragán. When I described what I'd been thinking and feeling during the renovation, they encouraged me to write the process down. That suggestion moved me instantly. It really is a warm, touching experience. So I plan to spend a bit more time writing about this inner journey — writing about how it's made me think about the relationships within a family; writing about the human care in renovation; writing about how, faced with so many breathtaking design styles, I went from "dazzled by choice" to "taking just one ladle from the river"; writing a log of my patterned-tile hunts; writing about what to watch out for in renovating for older people; maybe even writing about applying the "negotiation" I studied last year while buying the main materials? 🤔️ Unlike the renovation of the A Study, where we had a clear template — the Saint James hotel in Paris, the elegance and sophistication of French Art Deco, an unrivaled classic, where the closer we got to it the better — this time there's no concrete image at all. What keeps surfacing in my mind is that beautiful time, my warm and lovable family, the way a beam of afternoon sunlight falls from the yard into the dining room, a teapot full of tea stains and gloves caked with soil in the garden, a house that can breathe along with my mom. It won't stay the same forever, and it doesn't need to be meticulous. The cabinets will hold all the bowls and plates she loves, and the living room will have a KTV booth for her singing practice, a mahjong table for get-togethers, a drum kit and a piano. It doesn't need to be orderly; there's no need to force yourself for the sake of outward beauty. Because life is already beautiful enough. (Time's up for today, I need to go read. I'll stop here for now — once you've made a beginning, there's no turning back) On the floor of the hotel room: the patterned-tile samples I've been choosing lately.
So That's What My Recent State Is Called: an "Existential Crisis"

Lately my state has been this: everything is fine, yet I still doubt my life has any value. On the one hand I'm fired up every day — learning about Ray Dalio's cycles of great powers, researching how to renovate a house with a garden, being moved by the human history contained in a single patterned tile; on the other, I'm terrified of being "the one who takes half a step wrong and realises he's fallen a thousand li behind," lost about the values behind whether to lock down cities during the pandemic, anxious about the future of US–China relations, and wavering about the direction of my life's pursuits. But I can't stop either. Many questions can't be answered by thinking alone. And so much good fortune has come my way that it feels as if, unless I work with everything I've got, I'm letting down fate's gift; and if I don't grow, the times will discard me in no time. I know I'll certainly get through this life just fine, yet I'm afraid of idling my days away like an ant. But in this vast universe, who isn't an ant? While meditating today, the phrase "existential crisis" suddenly popped into my head. I looked it up, and my symptoms more or less match. Let's call it that for now — the term sounds very sophisticated, and it's at least much better than "midlife crisis." Tolstoy once fell into an existential crisis too; the classic symptom is constantly asking "why." Why should I care? Whatever I do in this life, whatever I accomplish, sooner or later it will be forgotten; sooner or later, I and the people I love will die, and "nothing will be left but stench and worms." Since everything vanishes and is in the end completely forgotten, what is the point of struggling? But then again, and moreover, why care? Why does being remembered forever matter? Does being remembered, or living forever, make something meaningful? Why do we need a meaning to existence at all? As the philosopher Epictetus said: "You must remind yourself that what you love is mortal, that nothing you love is your own; it is given to you for the present, not forever, nor inseparably, but like a fig or a bunch of grapes, at the appointed season of the year. If you long for it in winter, you are a fool. So if you long for your son or your friend when it is not given to you, know that you are longing for a fig in winter." It's about time I seriously read some philosophy. After graduating from university, I always wanted to do a master's in philosophy, because I know those questions that go beyond everyday life, the ones about life and death, have always troubled me. I believe the great philosophers have all thought about this question already. That said, though I've been lost about meaning lately, there's been plenty of joy — the joy of designing and renovating. I'm planning to talk about it in my next post.
4.5 Hours of Deep Sleep in One Night — What Did I Do Right?

There's no question about how important sleep is — Eileen Gu's secret weapon is sleep; sleep is one of the three measures for slowing brain ageing and preventing dementia, the other two being eating less and exercising. So what is deep sleep? During deep sleep, your brainwaves show a distinctive signature; your heart rate, blood pressure and body temperature all drop to their lowest levels of the day, you're very hard to wake, and rapid eye movement (REM) also appears along the way. This is the stage when the most immune substances are released, and also the stage when teenagers secrete the most growth hormone, so it has a big impact on health. It also matters a lot for consolidating memory, sparking creative thinking and improving the ability to learn. According to the China Sleep Index Report released on 19 March 2022, 28% of people get deep sleep (even 5 minutes counts). That's a very low number (I suspect it's a wristband problem — Apple Watch data generally comes out higher). Normally, deep sleep should make up 15–25% of each night's sleep. With 8 hours of sleep, normal deep sleep should be 1.2–2 hours, right? Enough talk — here's my chart. I actually got up at 7:20, after 6 hours 50 minutes of sleep, 60% of which was deep sleep. As a life hacker who has been tracking my sleep for nearly two years, comparing my body's data from every angle and combining it with all kinds of scientific research, I've put together the following sleep secrets that I've tested on myself and found to work. For my friends to consider: 0. Tracking Apple Watch, Xiaomi Mi Band, anything will do. Just like weighing yourself, tracking is where improvement begins. Comparing my deep sleep records a year apart, the difference is pretty clear. Here are the sleep methods I've personally tested and found effective: 1. Quit alcohol My deep sleep after drinking is zero. Zero. Zero. The probability of this happening to me is — 100%! Many people feel they sleep better after a drink, but that's not true. Alcohol excites the brain's nerves and makes it hard to get into deep sleep, and it also greatly suppresses how often REM sleep occurs. 2. Regularity, regularity, regularity Some people are early-to-bed, early-to-rise types, others are late-to-bed, late-to-rise types, and modern science says both are fine. The most important thing is to always get up at the same time, get out of bed as soon as you wake up — never lie in — and only go to bed at night when you're sleepy. If you're not sleepy, don't get into bed. Make sure you get up at the same time every morning, weekends included. A fixed sleep rhythm is very, very important, and very easy to break. Sticking to this rhythm as much as possible is the single most important thing for improving your sleep quality. 3. Find your own sleep cycle According to the R90 sleep programme, everyone has their own sleep cycle. Mine, for example, is 1.5 hours, so I need to sleep 1.5×N hours (N being a whole number). Usually I sleep 5 cycles, which is 7.5 hours, ideally leaving a 10-minute buffer on either side. If you insisted I sleep 8 hours, I'd most likely be jolted awake out of deep sleep and feel even more tired. Reference: Sleep (Nick Littlehales) 4. Get some sun My smart curtains open automatically at 7am to let the sunlight in. Sunlight passes through the optic nerve to the hypothalamus, which helps synthesise melatonin, and it also stimulates the secretion of serotonin. Serotonin and melatonin are both important drivers of sleep. (Friends who take melatonin supplements — here's some for free.) But sunlight is a major cause of ageing, so goddesses, don't overdo it. The research conclusion is to avoid the sun between 10am and 3pm as much as possible, when there's more UV. 5. Control the temperature, colour and smell of where you sleep Keep the bedroom as dark as possible, and especially avoid blue light, because blue light affects melatonin secretion. If you really must have a small light on, orange-yellow is best; The room should be cool, not hot and humid; the ideal temperature is 18–22°C. A drop in temperature lowers our core body temperature, which triggers the drive to sleep. When I started tracking my sleep, I discovered by chance, almost magically, that soaking my feet in the evening directly added 0.5–1.5 hours of deep sleep. The real reason is that your body temperature rises while you soak, and when you come out into the cooler surroundings, the drop in body temperature triggers the drive to sleep. 6. Exercise, especially aerobic exercise Exercise raises your body temperature and keeps it up for several hours; once the body cools down, the drop in temperature makes you sleepier. Exercise releases lots of hormones that dilate blood vessels and reduce anxiety; and during exercise your cells produce adenosine, one of whose main effects is to make the brain drowsy. 7. On coffee and tea Caffeine has a half-life of 4–6 hours, so give it enough time to be metabolised. Medically, the daily caffeine intake for one person is about 400 milligrams, roughly the equivalent of two Starbucks grande Americanos. 8. NMN I can't prove this one, but after my friends and I started taking it regularly, nights with 4 hours of deep sleep really did become more frequent. 9. Meditation It's a way to bring on relaxation and also a good way to relieve stress. Almost every time I listen to a bedtime meditation, I fall asleep within 5 minutes... Let me show off today's meditation record. It's from my new brain-computer-interface toy — the BrainCo meditation headband (thank you, Queen N!). I often fall asleep during meditation or sleep better afterwards... Highly recommended (this is not an ad!) Time for bed, time for bed — I'm already past my bedtime tonight 😴

Written after reading To Live Is to Shout at the Sky Those who write poetry in the midst of suffering are the brave, worthy of song They don't hide behind computers using fantasy novels or variety shows to escape their own lives reality left them nowhere to run long ago Their poems are inspiration wrung out of heavy pain, blood and tears They don't need self-discipline The very word self-discipline is a humblebrag You only need self-discipline when there is temptation Some lives have no temptation to speak of at all only disasters that cannot be avoided and choosing the lighter one as best they can They don't have to force themselves to work because without work there is no food They don't have to force themselves to log off and sleep early because their exhausted bodies passed out long ago They don't have to force themselves to exercise because they lost their healthy bodies long ago They don't have to schedule time to be with their parents because both parents passed away years ago They don't have to give up sugar because that's the holiday present saved for the children They don't have to go to great lengths to be on guard because apart from their own battered bodies they have nothing at all They don't have to, they don't have to They don't have to choose And yet, they still choose to let flowers bloom in the depths of their hearts The late poet Xu Lizhi wrote The paper before my eyes is faintly yellow / With a steel pen I chisel into it blacks of uneven depth / Filled with the vocabulary of migrant work / workshop, assembly line, machine, work permit, overtime, wages / They have trained me to be docile and obedient / I don't know how to shout, how to rebel / …… So many days, so many nights / I just like that, fall asleep standing. Wu Xia, a garment-factory ironing worker, wrote in Sling Dress The packing workshop is brightly lit / I hold the electric iron in my hand / gathering all the warmth of my hands / First I'll iron the straps flat / so they won't cut into your shoulders / …… I'll iron every pleat to the same width / so by your lake or on the lawn / waiting for the wind to blow / you can run too, but / be sure to let the hem fly up in an arc / like a flower / …… Unknown girl / I love you. In the mine, Chen Nianxi learned that his mother had late-stage oesophageal cancer. In pain and helpless, he finally chose to "split the mountain to save his mother," and wrote Chronicle of Explosion My tiny family / far away at the foot of Shangshan / they are ill / their bodies covered in dust / however much of my middle age I cut away / that much longer their old age can be / Inside my body are three tons of explosives / they are the fuse / Just last night / like rock / I burst apart all over the ground. Afterword Lately I haven't been very disciplined. The moment I hit a small problem, I feel defeated, anxious, can't sleep, and want nothing more than a good cry. Until today, when I listened to the book To Live Is to Shout at the Sky on the Dedao app, and then, holding my breath, read about the author Chen Nianxi's life and his poems, and felt a growing mix of shame and sorrowful courage in my heart. Writing the string of ramblings above can't express even a fraction of what I feel. In the end, I can only borrow the words of Jia Xingjia: "Before Chen Nianxi's book, I understood once again that I am worthy neither of my own good fortune nor of the suffering I have witnessed and felt."
Weekend Arts: Mao Jiake's Solo Exhibition

Yesterday I saw an interesting solo exhibition. The artist is the father of a friend of many years. He isn't a professional artist — he simply graduated in art when he was young, and most of his career has actually been spent first in government and then in business. Yet the upheavals and fierce competition of the worldly life did not wear away his love of art and his pursuit of it. The earliest painting I saw in the exhibition was completed in 2007, so the work spans more than 15 years. Most of the works were made in the artist's spare time from work — in hotels, on trains, in airports, museums, parks and even restaurants. I think only an almost addictive love could give a person such perseverance. Talking with the artist himself, I also found that he often approaches everything he does with a naive, romantic, youthful spirit, which makes his artistic pursuit feel unburdened and easy. I think it's this mindset that lets him find balance between work and art in an everyday, natural way. The Mirror Series "God has created nights well-armed with dreams, and mirrors, to make clear to man he is a reflection and a mere vanity. Therefore these alarms." — Jorge Luis Borges, Mirrors This series is influenced by Lacan's theory of the gaze and Borges's writings on "mirrors." Through presenting the "mirror image" as a special kind of existence, it tries to look back on and reflect upon the meaning and revelations of self, other, time and life. Mirror mirror-5 Lithograph/oil 29×31cm 2015 Mirror mirror-12 Etching/oil 29×31cm 2015 Mirror mirror-13 Etching/oil 29×31cm 2015 Mirror mirror-10 Etching/oil 29×41cm 2015 The Las Meninas Series According to the artist, the inspiration came from the portrait painting of the Spaniard Velázquez. The "maids of honour" are rendered in a sketchy, blurred way: a base is laid down, in parts or over the whole, by copperplate printing, and the image is then painted using oils, palette knives and so on. Homage to Velázquez – Las Meninas salute velasguizhi palacemnid-4 Oil 80×105cm 2021 Las Meninas palacemaid-2 Etching/oil 29×31cm 2017 The Manuscripts Series Flowers, plants, buildings and scenery are drawn in crayon and oil pastel on photocopies of Republic-of-China-era archive paper with a special significance. The interplay, and the rough brushwork, are very interesting. Manuscripts series Crayon/oil pastel 22×30cm 2021 Manuscripts series Crayon/oil pastel 22×30cm 2021 Manuscripts series Crayon/oil pastel 22×30cm 2021 Queen queen-4 Oil on paper 22×30cm 2019 The curator is Zhang Yuzhuo, a young post-90s talent, and the exhibition was arranged casually but with clever touches. Two international students from the Nanjing University of the Arts were invited to sing live at the venue; only later did I learn that one of them came from Zambia in Africa. The music was fun, too.

Spring always makes us delight in all kinds of possibilities. New life is the ripple stirring restlessly in the heart, the little leaps of joy you can't hold back, the urge to share a poem. Possibilities Wisława Szymborska (Poland) I prefer movies. I prefer dogs. I prefer the oaks along the Warta. I prefer Dickens to Dostoyevsky. I prefer liking people to loving mankind. I prefer keeping a needle and thread on hand, just in case. I prefer the color green. I prefer not to maintain that reason is to blame for everything. I prefer exceptions. I prefer to leave early. I prefer talking to doctors about something else. I prefer the old fine-lined illustrations. I prefer the absurdity of writing poems to the absurdity of not writing poems. When it comes to love, I prefer anniversaries that aren't round, so they can be celebrated every day. I prefer moralists who promise me nothing. I prefer cunning kindness to the over-trustful kind. I prefer the earth in civvies. I prefer conquered to conquering countries. I prefer having some reservations. I prefer the hell of chaos to the hell of order. I prefer Grimms' fairy tales to the newspapers' front pages. I prefer leaves without flowers to flowers without leaves. I prefer dogs with uncropped tails. I prefer light eyes, since mine are dark. I prefer desk drawers. I prefer many things that I haven't mentioned here to many things I've also left unsaid. I prefer zeros on the loose to those lined up behind a cipher. I prefer the time of insects to the time of stars. I prefer to knock on wood. I prefer not to ask how much longer and when. I prefer keeping in mind even the possibility that existence has its own reason for being.
Jiangsu Province’s Report on the Investigation into the “Fengxian Woman Who Gave Birth to Eight Children” (with Xiang Shuai’s Notes)

The moment I saw the title, my heart sank. It’s quite a title — “woman who gave birth to eight children.” I’ll let you savour that one yourselves. Ever since the day I started following this case, every time I read the facts and the reporting, it has made me physically ill — my stomach churning, my insides twisted into a knot. I know I’m worked up right now. But the internet is a public space: one must be civilised, decorous, harmonious, and mindful of the “Eight Honours and Eight Shames.” So many words have been churning inside me, circling round and round in my mouth. I can’t spit them out, and I can’t swallow them either. So once again I’ll borrow someone else’s words. Xiang Shuai has a public conscience, reason, wisdom and real substance. Here is what Xiang Shuai said: The Jiangsu provincial investigation has released its findings. A few points in them remain the focus of public attention: 1. Yang Mouxia and Xiaohuamei are the same person. 2. The most senior official punished is at division level (the county Party secretary), making Fengxian County the core of accountability. 3. On trafficking and abuse — issues that go beyond the limits of human ethics — the report still dodges the heavy questions, with its emphasis throughout on words like “drifted” and “mental disorder”… Overall, this is a by-the-book investigation report, and it’s not as though no effort was made — the public security authorities intervened directly in the DNA testing, and every procedure was more or less proper. But reading it, you still feel that a big matter is being shrunk into a small one. It lacks human warmth, and it lacks the empathy of “serving the people” that our Party has always stressed, as well as the deep self-awareness of “looking in the mirror” and “taking a bath” over one’s own problems. For example: why did no one ask about what happened to the “chained woman” for decades? What about the question of the local officials’ surnames? Why were all eight children she bore boys? And what about the large number of news stories compiled online about women in Xuzhou committing suicide? These questions are not just about Fengxian, or Xuzhou, and perhaps not even only about the Yellow River flood plain. Pressing further is painful, but necessary. Humanity is the nature that stands above every other “nature” — it is the starting point of our step from primates into “civilisation.” Without top-level changes at the level of law, “Fengxian” will be nothing more than one more bout of emotion fermenting on social media — Of course, many local governments may also be underestimating the power of emotion. Especially in capital markets, emotion is increasingly showing its devastating force — who would dare touch the urban investment bonds of Fengxian, or even Xuzhou? Won’t company valuations be affected? When a project is about to land, shouldn’t people think about the risks involved? These risks aren’t only about personal safety; they are the ESG (environmental, social and governance) risks that everyone now takes more and more seriously. Words like ESG look abstract, but behind them lies human society’s consensus on certain “boundaries”: environmental sustainability, the social responsibility of being human, fairness and openness inside and out, basic respect for people’s rights, and so on. Ordinarily these words may seem bloody useless, but breaching these shared bottom lines is itself a huge risk. Capital has legs, and it runs faster than anyone. When a wall starts to fall, everyone gives it a push — and walls are not always as solid as they look. As a self-media outlet on finance and economics, I rarely offer commentary on current affairs. If something is outside my professional field, not speaking about what I don’t understand is a basic principle. But as an ordinary person, I have my own basic values and ethical bottom line. As a woman and a mother, this time my bottom line wasn’t just touched — it was wounded to the extreme. I looked at that tormented face, in which you can still make out the fine, delicate features of her youth, and thought in a daze: one step away, and I would be her; one step away, and my child would be her (or him). What would become of my whole family, old and young, across generations? I don’t dare to think about it. Thinking about it leaves me cold all over. With the release of this report, in the spring of 2022, the Year of the Tiger, this surging tide — billions of reads, the basic conscience of hundreds of millions of ordinary people set alight — has, whether we like it or not, probably reached the tail end of its ebb. Tides rise and fall, swift and fleeting. That is the power of the social media age, and its sorrow too. There are too many tides; humanity’s limited attention is washed over again and again until it becomes a blank. I still couldn’t resist the urge: before everything turns blank, to write it down, to keep it on record, to remind our forgetful selves that we must remember. Remember this chain, this nameless woman referred to only as “Mou” — just as we remember Sun Zhigang, just as we remember Li Wenliang. Remember. After the “Fengxian woman who gave birth to eight children” incident occurred, the Jiangsu Provincial Party Committee and Provincial Government attached great importance to it, requiring and guiding Xuzhou City to quickly establish the facts, handle the matter seriously in accordance with the law, effectively safeguard the rights and interests of the public, and respond to public concerns in a timely manner, with relevant provincial departments taking part in the investigation. On February 17, 2022, the Provincial Party Committee and Provincial Government set up an investigation team to conduct a comprehensive and in-depth investigation and verification. Since the incident, in addition to investigating within our province, investigators also travelled to Yunnan, Henan and other relevant provinces for on-site investigations, visiting more than 4,600 members of the public and reviewing more than 1,000 archival documents. The findings and handling of the investigation are hereby reported as follows. I. On establishing the identity of the “Fengxian woman who gave birth to eight children” On January 27, 2022, videos about the “Fengxian woman who gave birth to eight children” circulated on social networking platforms. Upon verification, the woman in the videos is currently registered under the name Yang Mouxia; her husband is Dong Moumin, and they live in Dongji Village (later merged into Lizhuang Administrative Village), Huankou Town, Fengxian County, Jiangsu Province. Based on the marriage registration application materials for Dong Moumin and Yang Mouxia issued in June 2000 by Shao Mouzheng, accountant of the Dongji Village Committee, the public security authorities obtained a lead that Yang Mouxia came from “Yagu Village, Fugong County, Yunnan Province.” They immediately dispatched police to Yunnan, who, together with local police and focusing on Yagu Village in Fugong County, conducted door-to-door inquiries in the surrounding townships regarding Yang Mouxia’s identity, asking local residents to identify Yang Mouxia’s marriage registration photo and recent photos. According to He Moumou (a former village cadre of Yagu Village), Yang Mouxia might be Xiaohuamei of that village (whose parents are deceased). Following leads from further investigation, the public security authorities found Xiaohuamei’s half-sister by the same mother, Guang Mouying (formerly named Hua Mouying), in Xiangcheng City, Henan Province. On February 9, the Institute of Forensic Science of the Ministry of Public Security carried out DNA comparison of blood samples from Yang Mouxia and Guang Mouying against biological material extracted from the belongings of Pu Mouma (Xiaohuamei’s mother, who died in 2018). The results showed that Pu Mouma was consistent with a biological parent-child relationship with both Yang Mouxia and Guang Mouying. On February 13, the Institute of Forensic Science of the Ministry of Public Security also conducted DNA comparison of blood samples from Sang Mouluo (Xiaohuamei’s eldest maternal uncle), Li Mouyuan (her youngest maternal uncle), Sha Moufu (her eldest maternal aunt) and Li Moumei (her youngest maternal aunt), all of which were consistent with a kinship relationship with Yang Mouxia. On February 20, the Institute of Forensic Science of the Ministry of Public Security re-tested and compared the samples of the above subjects, and the results were consistent with the earlier ones. Based on the DNA comparisons, a review of Xiaohuamei’s household registration records in Yunnan and the field investigation, it was determined that Yang Mouxia is Xiaohuamei (registered name Xiaohuamei, born May 13, 1977, from Yagu Village, Fugong County, Yunnan Province). Regarding the question that “the woman in the photo on Dong Moumin and Yang Mouxia’s marriage certificate is not the same person as Yang Mouxia,” the public security authorities found that the recent photo of Yang Mouxia had been captured from a Douyin video and retouched before circulating online, and differed from her actual appearance. At the same time, owing to factors such as skin ageing, hair loss, the liquefaction of fatty tissue and missing teeth that come with age, Yang Mouxia’s appearance had also changed. On February 22, a facial identification by the Institute of Forensic Science of the Ministry of Public Security found that the facial features shown in the photo on Yang Mouxia and Dong Moumin’s marriage certificate, Yang Mouxia’s photo from her first marriage in Yunnan, screenshots of Yang Mouxia from the videos circulating online, Yang Mouxia’s ID card photo and recent photos of Yang Mouxia were the same, and determined them to be the same person. Regarding the question that “Yang Mouxia may be Li Ying, a missing woman from Sichuan,” the public security authorities carried out a special investigation. Jiangsu public security authorities, together with Sichuan public security authorities, conducted DNA comparison between Li Ying’s mother and Yang Mouxia, and the results ruled out a biological parent-child relationship. The Forensic Identification Institute of Nanjing Medical University subsequently conducted DNA comparison between Li Ying’s mother and Yang Mouxia, and the results again ruled out a biological parent-child relationship. On February 20, an identification by the Institute of Forensic Science of the Ministry of Public Security once again ruled out a biological parent-child relationship between Li Ying’s mother and Yang Mouxia. On this basis, it was determined that Yang Mouxia and Li Ying are not the same person. II. On how Xiaohuamei came from Fugong County, Yunnan Province, to Fengxian County, Jiangsu Province According to interviews, villagers of Yagu Village in Fugong County, Xiaohuamei’s maternal uncles, aunts and other relatives, and other informed residents reported that in 1980 Xiaohuamei followed her remarried mother from Puluo Village, Pihe Township, Fugong County, Yunnan Province, to live in Yagu Village, Zilijia Township; in 1995 she married into Baoshan City, Yunnan Province, and after divorcing in 1997 she returned to Yagu Village. Xiaohuamei’s relatives and fellow villagers reported that after returning to the village her speech and behaviour were abnormal. Residents interviewed during the investigation reported that in early 1998, Xiaohuamei was taken from Yagu Village to Donghai County, Jiangsu Province, by Sang Mouniu (female, born July 1974, from Fugong County, Yunnan Province). Investigation found that Sang Mouniu married Shi Mouzhong (born April 1955) of Donghai County in 1995, and in December 2000 the couple were sentenced to five and seven years’ imprisonment respectively for other crimes of trafficking women and children. On February 6, 2022, the public security authorities opened a criminal investigation into Sang Mouniu and Shi Mouzhong on suspicion of trafficking Xiaohuamei. According to the confessions of Sang Mouniu, Shi Mouzhong and Xu Moudong (male, born November 1965, from Donghai County, Jiangsu Province), at the end of 1997 Shi Mouzhong and Xu Moudong agreed that Sang Mouniu would help Xu Moudong find a wife, but that it would cost money, and Xu Moudong agreed. According to Sang Mouniu’s statement, in early 1998, under the pretext of introducing Xiaohuamei to a prospective husband and getting her medical treatment, she took Xiaohuamei to Donghai County and sold her to Xu Moudong, receiving 5,000 yuan in cash. According to Xu Moudong’s statement and his neighbours’ accounts, after living with Xiaohuamei for three or four months, one morning in early May 1998 Xu Moudong found that Xiaohuamei had gone missing; he and his neighbours and relatives searched for two or three days without success. Xu Moudong later demanded 2,000 yuan in “compensation” from Shi Mouzhong. On the question of how Xiaohuamei got from Donghai County to Fengxian County, the public security authorities conducted an in-depth investigation. Under further interrogation, Dong Moumin confessed that in June 1998, his father Dong Mougeng had bought Xiaohuamei for money through an introduction by Liu Mouzhu (of Huankou Town, Fengxian County). Under interrogation, Liu Mouzhu admitted the criminal facts. The public security authorities successively arrested Huo Mouqu and Huo Moude (both of Huankou Town, Fengxian County) and the couple Tan Mouqing and Li Mouling (of Xiayi County, Henan Province). According to the four, Tan Mouqing and Li Mouling found Xiaohuamei, who had drifted there, at the restaurant they ran in Luoji Township, Xiayi County; they took her in for a month and then sold her to Huo Mouqu and Huo Moude, who were working at a construction site near the restaurant. The two took Xiaohuamei back to Fengxian County and, through an introduction by Liu Mouzhu, resold her to Dong Mougeng. The relevant criminal facts are still under in-depth investigation. In June 2000, when Dong Moumin went to the village committee accountant Shao Mouzheng to obtain a certificate of marital status in order to apply for a marriage certificate, he changed the name Yang Mouying to Yang Mouxia on someone’s suggestion. Staff at the Huankou Town civil affairs office improperly processed the marriage registration based on the information Dong Moumin himself reported, registering the date of marriage as August 2, 1998, and Yang Mouxia’s date of birth (with “Yang” miswritten as a different character through a clerical error) as June 6, 1969. According to Dong Moumin’s statement, in March 2011, when Yang Mouxia gave birth to her second son at the Huankou Town health centre, the mother’s information was registered as “Yang Mouying”; the health centre required the newborn’s mother’s ID card, so his father Dong Mougeng had someone make a fake ID card for “Yang Mouying.” In November 2020, in order to apply for minimum living allowance, Dong Moumin applied to register a household registration for Yang Mouxia. In accordance with regulations, the public security authorities entered Yang Mouxia’s DNA information into the “National Public Security Information System for Finding Abducted/Missing Children” and the “National Public Security DNA Database” for comparison, with no match. On April 14, 2021, the Huankou police station, in accordance with the regulations for registering persons without household registration, issued her a collective household registration in the town and an ID card, registering her as Yang Mouxia, born June 6, 1969, according to the name and date of birth on the marriage certificate. Cadres and villagers of Dongji Village confirmed that the names Yang Mouying and Yang Mouxia were often used interchangeably and in fact referred to the same person. III. On the mental and physical condition of Yang Mouxia (Xiaohuamei) According to Dong Moumin’s statement and accounts from several villagers, when Yang Mouxia first arrived at the Dong family in June 1998, she was basically able to take care of herself and communicate with others, but sometimes showed signs such as giggling foolishly and a vacant stare. Dong Moumin said that Yang Mouxia had once told him her hometown was Yagu Village, Fugong County, Yunnan Province. According to Dong Mougang (Yang Mouxia’s eldest son), when he was little his mother sometimes took him to and from school. According to Dong Moumin’s relatives, after Yang Mouxia gave birth to her third son in 2012, her symptoms of mental disorder gradually worsened. On January 30, 2022, after a consultation by medical experts in Xuzhou, Yang Mouxia was diagnosed with schizophrenia. On February 19, a forensic assessment by the Forensic Identification Institute of Nanjing Brain Hospital concluded that Yang Mouxia suffers from schizophrenia and, affected by her current mental state, is unable to engage and communicate normally. On February 20, the Provincial Public Security Department commissioned the Institute of Evidence Law and Forensic Science of China University of Political Science and Law (Institute of Forensic Science and Technology) to conduct a review assessment, which reached the same conclusion. Yang Mouxia is currently receiving treatment in hospital. Examination results on admission showed that, apart from her mental illness and dental disease, no other illness was found. On February 4, Xuzhou dental experts conducted an oral examination of Yang Mouxia and read her CBCT scans, concluding that her oral hygiene had long been poor and that she suffered from untreated periodontal disease, with some teeth gradually falling out. On February 9, a further diagnosis by experts at Nanjing Stomatological Hospital found that Yang Mouxia suffers from severe chronic periodontitis, which they said can cause teeth to loosen and fall out.
