A Plea: Please Don't Stop Paying Attention to the Chained Woman of Fengxian

They think we have all fallen asleep, but in fact, every one of us is wide awake. They think we have all grown tired, but in fact, every one of us is holding on. They think we can be fobbed off, but in fact, not one of us has ever been fooled. Many people have advised me to keep my head down and stay safe! But I cannot calm myself. Some things, once you know them, leave you in tears, unable to eat or sleep, with no words for the anger and grief inside. How could anyone be unmoved by another's suffering, and simply look away/ For this woman in Fengxian, whose identity is still unclear, we must speak up. Others have already said it well enough, so let me borrow their words. Excerpted from the WeChat account Zhige 9774 (ID: gh edd5d78e8b82), from the articles it has published in fury since 1 February 2022. (1) Where did she come from? Who is she? What the people of Fengxian say is: she was picked up. What the Fengxian authorities say is: she was taken in. The wording differs, but both agree she was "not bought from traffickers." No one knows who she is, where she was born, what her original name was, or how old she really is. It is rumoured that Li Ying, the lost daughter of a martyr from Sichuan, looks very much like her, but there is no definite answer yet. (2) What did others do to her? Who put the iron chain around her neck? Who knocked out all her teeth? Who left her throat unable to speak? Who cut off part of her tongue? Who locked her up in a mud hut? Who forced her to bear 8 children? Who forced her to marry a man 20 years older? Who drove her out of her mind? Who left her stranded far from home? Human trafficking, unlawful imprisonment, forced childbearing, rape, abduction, bodily harm..... Every evil this world commits against women has fallen on this one mother. She has endured it for 24 years. (3) A folded society The standard of living in our big cities has already surpassed that of many developed countries. The standard of living in most of our countryside has only just risen out of poverty. This enormous contrast has long gone unseen. The rise of self-media has cruelly laid bare the ignorance and backwardness of the countryside to people living in the big cities. Their lives have always been folded away. Suddenly, they have been unfolded through the lens of self-media. How developed a society is is not measured by its tall buildings, but by what it gives to the weak. How civilised a society is is not measured by its economic wealth, but by its attitude towards the weak. (4) The banality of evil Fengxian is in the same country as us, and Yang Xia lives in the same era as us. Yang Xia is our sister. What happened to Yang Xia happens to every one of us. She herself no longer has any way of winning justice for herself. The people around her are all accomplices to the crime, and there is no justice to be found there. The local government, it seems, also wants to cover up this appalling crime. Everyone who cares about this should join forces with all their heart to win justice for her. Otherwise, we all commit the "banality of evil." The banality of evil, compared with the evil done to Yang Mouxia, is every bit as bad, if not worse. Because a particular crime harms its victim. But the collective banality of evil will destroy an entire society. The notice issued by the local Fengxian authorities is one we can no longer accept. The state has sent a higher-level investigation team to get to the bottom of the Yang Mouxia case. Voicing support is public opinion, and speaking out is the will of the people! (5) Justice will not be absent May Ms Yang Mouxia's 24 years of cruel suffering push forward the rule of law in our country. May no woman, from now on, ever again be trafficked, imprisoned or abused! The only complete sentence Yang Mouxia has ever been heard to say is: This world doesn't want me anymore. Then we also have something to tell her: This era will never abandon you. Here, I bow deeply to the netizens who brought this case to light. The attention of the public and of public opinion is the hope of Yang Mouxia, and of the women in Fengxian, in Xuzhou, and across the whole country who have been trafficked, imprisoned, raped, forced to bear children, physically harmed, and killed — their hope. This is the light of our civilisation; please don't let it go out.

This morning I wanted to write about Our Story ( Ping Ru Mei Tang ), and at the start of the book I read the preface by Chai Jing. I felt deeply that, if I wanted people to know this book, I could never write anything more moving or true. So I decided to simply share the preface in full. Here goes — enjoy: Bones, Clean and White Preface to Our Story By Chai Jing Every word I say is true, every story is true. As for the past, all those pictures are in my mind. Rao Pingru, photographed in 1945, aged 24 Rao Pingru, photographed in 1945, aged 24 01 The year he met Meitang, Rao Pingru was twenty-six. A graduate of the Whampoa Military Academy, he was in the 2nd Platoon of the mortar company of the 188th Regiment, 63rd Division, 100th Army, fighting on the outskirts of Xuefeng Mountain in western Hunan, and he nearly lost his life. A comrade beside him was shot in the belly; his intestines spilled out, and his screams were something Rao "couldn't forget for many years". Pinned down by gunfire, he lay flat on the hillside, gripping blades of grass, and looked up at the peak of the green mountain, where white clouds rolled across the deep blue sky. "So this is where I'll be buried. That's all right," he said. "Back then I was alone. I wasn't afraid — didn't know to be afraid. A boy's heart is coarse." When the war ended, in the summer of 1946, Rao Pingru's father sent him a letter, hoping he would use his leave to come home and get engaged. "Father took me straight to the home of Uncle Mao Sixiang at No. 3 Zhoujialing, Linchuan... our two families were old friends. As we walked through to the third hall, I suddenly saw that the window of the main room on the left was open, and a young woman of about twenty with a lovely face was looking at herself in a hand mirror, putting on lipstick — this was my first impression of Meitang." "Did you think she was beautiful?" I asked. "Back then I thought every woman was beautiful," the old man said honestly. The two of them barely spoke. His father went over and put the ring on the girl's finger, and just like that, the great matter of their lives was settled. Both young people found it funny; after the laughter, they went to sit in her room. Her little sisters played around the bed, Meitang rolled up a newspaper into a tube and sang, and she showed him her photo album. He thought she probably liked him, and took a few photos from the album with him. On the way back to camp, he stood at the bow of the boat in his uniform, watching the light glittering on the surging Yangtze, and felt that from now on he could not treat his life lightly, because there was now another person in it. When the civil war began, he didn't want to fight. He asked for leave and went home to get married. Meitang died at eighty. This year he is ninety, and he has painted more than a dozen albums, called Our Story . He had the black-and-white photo of her under the pomegranate tree reprinted, touched up her lips with a little red, and wrote beneath it: "This feeling might have become a memory to cherish, but even then I was lost in a daze." Stroke by stroke, he painted her from her childhood — how, as a little girl in the classroom, she envied the young maids playing on the swing outside; how she and her best friend, with permed hair and qipaos, went dancing at the dance hall... all painted just as she had told him back then. The photos of their wedding were burned in the Cultural Revolution. Relying on memory, he painted in the buildings, the scene and the people of that day. He had no particular intention as he painted; he simply felt that a panoramic view would let him paint everyone in, not missing a single one. Those who look at it can't help feeling that the angle is like a gaze, across the years, at the backs of the two of them. 02 After their marriage, times were turbulent. Rao Pingru took Meitang to Guizhou, where he worked as a clerk; to evade bandits, they hid her jewellery inside the wheels of a cart. Then they went into business in Nanchang. He painted the details of that era, writing: "The noodle shop did poor business, I went to night school to learn accounting, interviewed at the grain bureau, sent my CV to a survey team, sold dried chillies and couldn't figure out the scales — Meitang laughed that I wasn't a businessman at all, and I thought she was quite right. To this day I still don't understand how you're supposed to deduct the weight of the pan on a pan scale." Surprisingly, these were the happiest memories. He painted the young people with nothing to do, playing "suoha" — I had no idea what kind of card game this was; he explained it to me with great enthusiasm for ages, and I still didn't get it. I just saw that he had painted five people, with their seats clearly labelled, and like a child he had marked who each person was: "Old Wu", "Sister Ding"... and "Pingru" and "Meitang" sitting close together on a bench, smiling at each other. The house the couple lived in was just a pavilion with boards added on four sides to turn it into a room. "Back then it really didn't feel hard. It was fun. Why? Whenever it rained, the wind howled, the windows rattled and banged, there was thunder, the wind went whoosh — 'the wind fills the tower before the mountain rain arrives'. That poetry, that wild charm of the mountains, you can't experience in a concrete house." "The Chinese like to say that for a poor couple, everything is sorrow. Why did you find it poetic?" "I think it has to do with one's state of mind. No matter when, no matter where, no matter what life, a person with some poetry in them sees poetry in everything." 03 In 1949, Rao Pingru was supposed to go to Taiwan with everyone else, but then he thought: "My father-in-law married his daughter to me hoping she would always have someone to rely on. If I leave, I'm being irresponsible." So he stayed, believing there would always be a place for a humble family. In 1958, he was sent to re-education through labour. No one told him why, and there was no paperwork; he was taken straight from his workplace. His work unit went to his wife: "You need to draw a clear line between yourself and this man." At this critical moment, what Meitang said showed a crisp, sharp spirit: "If he were having an affair, I'd divorce him on the spot. But as I see it, first, he's not a traitor selling out his country; second, he's not corrupt; third, he hasn't stolen or extorted anything. I know what kind of person he is. How could I divorce him?" Rao Pingru went to a factory in Anhui for reform through labour, until 1979. He could come home only once a year — for twenty-two years, always the same. Over those twenty-odd years, none of the letters he wrote home were kept, but he kept most of the letters his wife wrote, and pasted them all into his albums. There are almost no words of affection in these letters; they are all about the hardships of life: how to get a bit of food, how he could bring back some eggs, how to get the children jobs, how to find them a match... He pasted them in order of date, and where the letters had become damaged over time, he filled in the gaps with a pen. The dozen-odd albums were heavy and large; laid on the table, they couldn't be spread out properly. So I lay on the bed to look at them, copying out phrases as I went, and in places I burst out laughing — Meitang had a fiery little temper. Sometimes she would write in a letter, "I'm so cross with you, I'm so angry, the more I write the angrier I get," then throw down her pen and write no more, and it would be a month or two before a new letter came. "How did you feel when you read that?" I asked Mr Rao. "I felt for her." I hadn't expected that: "Felt for her?" "She was usually very good to me. If she said something like that, she must have been under enormous strain." He often thought of a woman with several children, her wages not enough, carrying twenty-jin sacks of cement to earn a little money, saving sweets from the children's mouths to post half a bag to her husband. He wrapped them in a handkerchief and kept them under his pillow, and took half a month to finish them. Since she died, every time he passes the Shanghai Natural History Museum, he stops for a moment: "In these steps, I don't know which piece is the cement she carried, but I know that for the children, for our livelihood, she carried it on her back. Her back and her kidneys were damaged, and I'm afraid that's probably what caused it." 04 "You can't do anything!" — this was what Meitang said to him most often in her life. "Whatever I did, I'd be told 'you can't do anything' — like when my stir-fry wasn't good, when I didn't close a drawer, when I bought the wrong book for our granddaughter, and so on." He chuckled. Sometimes their children thought their mother a bit harsh, and the old man would quickly wave his hand, meaning: "She's teaching her own husband — what's it to do with you?" He said: "She was always grumbling at me, always laughing at me. But in that laughter there was no ridicule, no sarcasm. It was just as if it amused her: look at you, you can't even figure this out." "Some men might feel that's a bit too picky, and feel they'd lost face." "Not at all. What face? None of that." All these years, whenever his wife went grocery shopping he went with her, worried she'd have to carry heavy things. "I'd carry the basket and follow behind, getting some training. She'd teach me, like taking on an apprentice: 'How's this vegetable? How's that one?' I'd say, 'If you're not buying, why ask him?' She'd say, 'You silly thing. Ask at a few places, get a feel for it, and then when you buy you've got something to compare.' She thought I was too simple-minded. She'd pick and choose." "Most men would say, 'I'm not going, you go and shop,' wouldn't they?" "I never deceived her. I never told her any lies." 05 In 1992, Meitang's kidney disease grew worse. Rao Pingru was still working at the CPPCC at the time; he turned down all his work to devote himself entirely to caring for his wife. From then on, he got up at five every morning to comb her hair, wash her face, cook, and do her peritoneal dialysis, four times a day — disinfecting, mask on, connecting the tubes, draining the fluid — as well as giving insulin injections and keeping records. He didn't trust anyone else to help. "Were there times you felt irritable?" "No, no, not at all. This was my hope." In her pain she gradually stopped cooperating, and from time to time she would pull at the tubes in her body. Her hearing was poor and she could no longer see writing clearly, so he drew pictures to persuade her not to pull the tubes, but the pictures didn't work either. All he could do was stay up at night watching her the whole night through. But he was old, after all, and couldn't do that every day, so in the end he had to tie her hands. "She'd cry 'Don't tie me', and it hurt so much to hear it. What could I do... it was agony." Meitang's confusion grew worse and worse. One day she claimed her husband had hidden their granddaughter away and wouldn't let her see her. Whatever old Rao said, she wouldn't believe him. Already in his eighties, he sat on the floor and wailed. She watched him cry as if she couldn't see him. He said: "Ah, this is terrible, I'm afraid it's the end. It's like what Yang Jiang wrote: 'Our lives were full of hardship, and only in old age did we have a settled home, but old age and illness press upon us, and we have come to the end of our lives.'" Mr Rao's granddaughter said that after that, Grandma was rarely lucid: "When everyone else just treated what she said as nonsense, only Grandpa kept taking her words seriously. She had always been someone particular about quality. Whatever she asked for, Grandpa would still cycle a long way to buy cakes from a certain brand or cooked food from a certain shop. By the time he got back, she'd long forgotten what she'd said and wouldn't want to eat it any more. He wouldn't listen when we tried to talk him out of it. When Grandma asked where her black dress with red flowers had gone — a dress that never existed — Grandpa would absurdly say he'd go and find a tailor to make one." I asked Mr Rao: "The younger ones tried to persuade you, saying there was no point in any of this?" "If I didn't do it, my heart wouldn't be at peace, and I couldn't make it right with myself. It comes down to one phrase: knowing it can't be done, and doing it anyway. When I did it, I felt no guilt. If I didn't, it would be an eternal reproach. I'd never have a moment's peace for the rest of my life, asking myself: in this life, why didn't you do what you could have done?" When I heard this, something moved in me; my heart sank, and I almost lost the courage to keep asking. 06 "On the afternoon of 19 March 2008, she died, at 4:23. When I went in, I saw her from a distance lying on the bed. She was already... her life had no strength left, it was used up, but she still had a little awareness. She saw me and shed a tear — that was all the strength she had. She saw me, but she couldn't speak, she couldn't move. Her life was just that tiny bit." "Did you say anything then?" "I didn't say anything. She could no longer speak. I stroked her hand; it was still a little warm. Later I realised it had truly gone cold, so I took scissors and cut off a lock of her hair, tied it with red silk thread, and kept it at home... This is the only thing of her that remains, so it's a keepsake. A ring, a very small ring, the one she usually wore. I don't usually wear it. Today I wore it to come here." On his little finger was a thin band of gold. The ring his father had given the newlyweds back then had been sold when the family later fell into poverty; in her old age, he bought another and gave it to his wife. The interview light, covered with a layer of diffusion paper, fell on the old man's face. He wore a white shirt under a dark checked jacket. His white hair was fine as thread, the ring gave off a faint glint of gold, and all around was darkness. 07 There was a passage in the interview that didn't make it into the final cut, and I've always remembered it. Mr Rao said that one day last month he saw in the courtyard a black thing about twenty centimetres long. It was a bone someone had thrown away, with hundreds of ants swarming over it, gnawing. He said: "In the past I'd have swept it away and dumped it and been done with it. This time I thought: my strength is greater than theirs. If I want to sweep it, I sweep; if not, I don't. It's no bother to me, so why? I won't touch it. I went inside and left it alone." As I listened, I didn't know what he was getting at. "The next day, I went out to the courtyard again and the bone had turned white. The ants had eaten every last bit of the flesh off it, leaving only the bone, and the ants were gone too. That was something I never expected." I asked him: "What impression did that leave on you?" "They are life, and I am life. Why should I want them to die just because I have the power, the right? One step and they'd be dead, but why? They don't affect me. They are life too, and they also need to live." Several months have passed since that interview. I remembered these words but never thought about them closely, until one day I read Huang Yongyu saying in a book: "Beauty is better than prettiness, but goodness is better than beauty." When I read that, I thought of that bone, clean and white. This is goodness. 08 A while ago, our director Wang Jin (nicknamed "Ant") brought in a letter. The old man had painted a portrait for each of the camera operators and directors, with a note: "I painted eight holes in Xiao Wang's trousers, for the sake of fashion." The one he gave me was this painting: a man and a woman sitting by a window facing their books, with the words above: "When I push open the window, butterflies sometimes fly in." For this episode, everyone involved — Ant, Xiao Yu, Tianshu, Lao Fan, Li Lun, Zou Gentao, Shen Chao, Chen Xi... — treasured the albums. Ant transported the albums from Shanghai to Beijing and back again. I'm usually careless, but this time I was afraid of losing even a single scrap of paper. After reading each one, I stacked them neatly on the little tea table. At three in the morning there was a loud crash: half the little table had collapsed, but luckily no albums were damaged. We packed them in big cardboard boxes, sealed them and moved them downstairs, and Ant and Tianshu, laughing and joking, carried them away. This episode is nothing more than the ordinary sense and sentiment of everyday lanes and alleys, with nothing legendary about it — just the life of an ordinary man and woman across a century. We knew full well the ratings wouldn't be great, but we still had to make this episode. The old man's granddaughter Shushu wrote in a letter: "Times are different now. A line as heavy as the one on a page of his albums, 'Only in longing do I find the sea is not deep' — perhaps not everyone is fortunate enough, or brave enough, to apply it to themselves." Our producer Xiao Yu wrote back: "In my place, I would ask myself too whether I'd spare no effort, for a long time, doing something hopeless. But I think: because you love it, you're willing. Time can make one person unrecognisable, and make others ever clearer." I once asked Mr Rao: "You've written so much in these albums. What do you most hope future generations will remember?" "A person should be loyal and kind-hearted. Loyal, kind-hearted people always endure." He lived those two words all his life, like a fine rain soft as butter, falling without form or trace, and only from afar do you see the grass turning green, endless and boundless. After finishing the preface, I looked up Chai Jing's videos and Seeing to reread. I still welled up with tears, and I don't even know what I'm crying about. Perhaps it's what Seeing showed me: in the profession of journalism, the questioning of life, the insistence on justice, the compassion for others that runs through it all; perhaps it's nostalgia for the past — the reluctance and regret that has lingered faintly in my heart ever since I left my job as a journalist. May I often see my own ignorance, and always be moved to tears.
Our Joys and Sorrows Are Not the Times'

I promised myself one article a week, and here we are in week five, only just starting the second one. I honestly didn't know what to write. No editor chasing a deadline, no purpose, no sense of an audience — just picking a topic gives me a headache. I thought about writing on "carbon neutrality," a sector I've been watching for half a year, but I have no framework and don't know where to begin. Every day, one nerve in my brain frets about this. Unless I GTD it and clear it out, the pent-up pressure isn't good for my body. So I'll just write something casual and call it a warm-up! And now, to the point: Lu Xun said: "The joys and sorrows of human beings are not shared." Not only that — in my humble opinion, a person's joys and sorrows are not shared with their times, either. This sounds a bit counterintuitive. News today travels faster and further than ever before. Because everyone is so acutely sensitive to the big events and big trends of the age, we assume that individual fate is closely bound up with the times. That isn't wrong, but it isn't entirely right either. First, every era is a mix of good and bad. In 2021 the world saw inflation it hadn't seen in 30 years, a chip shortage swept the globe, the internet went through an unprecedented platform crackdown, and young people lived in a state of being "torn": on one side, pride in the rise of the nation; on the other, a personal view of the ceiling on survival and advancement — small cities in decline, sky-high housing prices in big cities, "involution" in education and credentials, fierce competition, and a road upward that seemed to grow ever longer and harder. That year was dubbed "the worst year of the past decade and the best year of the decade to come." And yet I've now seen that same verdict five years running. Let's pick a few other years from history at random. 1900 Waves of strikes swept across Europe; Famine in India left millions on the brink of death; During the Boxer Uprising, several hundred Boxers burned the church at Dazhai Village in Qinghe, Zhili, before returning to Shandong; The Qing government offered a bounty of 100,000 taels of silver for the capture of Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, and strictly forbade the public from buying or reading the newspapers they ran; In the Blagoveshchensk massacre, Tsarist Russia slaughtered the Qing subjects living in Blagoveshchensk; more than 5,000 people were killed. 1988 Chinese and Vietnamese forces fought a naval battle at Johnson South Reef in the Spratly Islands; The 7th National People's Congress confirmed its decision to accept Zhao Ziyang's request to resign as Premier of the State Council; The world's longest supertanker, the Knock Nevis (then the Seawise Giant), was hit and sunk by missiles from Iraqi warplanes; Iran Air Flight 655, flying an international air corridor over the Persian Gulf, was mistaken by a US Navy warship for an Iranian fighter jet and shot down by a missile; all 274 passengers and 16 crew on board were killed. In any year, there are people lamenting that "people aren't what they used to be" and that "the future is bleak." Some years bring more good things, some more bad. But even in the worst of years, the sweetness of life still has a chance to arrive. This realization came to me from the book Pingru and Meitang . Its author, Rao Pingru, was born in 1922 and lived through the War of Resistance against Japan and the Cultural Revolution — a life of hardship, uprooted again and again. Yet even amid war, the sweetness and bitterness of his life didn't rise and fall with affairs of state; they came from life itself. (I recommend the book — I may write about it later, which would conveniently give me another topic.) As the picture of life and history slowly unfolds with age and with more reading, I feel more and more clearly that individual joys and sorrows are not shared with the times — perhaps this year the flames of war are everywhere, yet someone happily finds their life partner; perhaps this year the economy is booming, yet someone suffers the loss of both parents. I believe: fate and happiness are related, but not equal. How to create my own meaning and small certain happinesses in an ever more uncertain era — I'm just as lost. But here are three sayings that can guide us: (1) Pessimists are right; optimists succeed; (2) The accumulation of wealth depends not on how many times you make the right call, but on how big a bet you dare to place when you're right; (3) The accumulation of happiness depends not on the intensity of any single happy moment, but on the frequency and number of joyful experiences. The third comes from Harvard's happiness course. Research shows that few experiences affect us for longer than 3 months; a person who has a dozen small joys every day is happier than one who has only a single great stroke of luck. So put on a comfortable pair of shoes, give the one you love a big kiss, treat yourself to a good meal. These things sound small, and they really are small things, but their effect is huge.

I spent "a whole week" carefully choosing my goals for 2022. I went back and forth many times, cutting a lot of them — and adding even more. The most unexpected discovery: after crunching the numbers again and again, I'm "convinced" I can get far more done in a year than I'd imagined. You have to dare to dream and dare to do. Here they are: Including my Dedao "core curriculum" (forgive the terrible layout) There you have it — the 🚩 is planted. Please hold me to it. I especially invite friends who work in the relevant fields to "volunteer" to keep an eye on specific goals. A few thoughts from the goal-setting process 1. What goals are really for None of these goals are, at heart, the Objective itself; they're the "Key Results" I designed in order to reach it. That is: OKR (Objectives and Key Results) Being able to tell an "objective" from a "key result" matters enormously. So what is my Objective? Steady, sustained growth for the company and the team, so that my partners get "growth and income" that match the company's development, while staying in a healthy, "sustainable" state. 2. A new 80/20 rule The Pareto principle: 80% of output comes from 20% of input So "five 20% inputs" should produce "400% output" Always remember: "efficiency is not the same as effectiveness" The outcome of your work depends not only on how fast or how well you do things, but even more on what you choose to do. For me, the five 20% portions point to five dimensions: "business, capability, health, relationships, and self." This year I want to make choosing a habit, and push "effectiveness first, clear goals, data-based measurement" a big step further. 3. Let the data speak At first I listed 20 core courses and thought that was already a lot. But the data showed the exact opposite — they'd only take 30 minutes a day (at 2x speed; in a quiet setting you can manage 3x), far below my current median listening time. That made me realize: over a whole year, if you stick with it, you can learn an enormous amount. So why not pursue my dream of becoming a "generalist"? Take every general-education course — law, mathematics, chemistry, ethics, astronomy, the lot. Even then, it would only come to 1.5 hours a day. And so came my current, utterly insane ambition: listen to "every single" business, economics and management course, plus all the general-education ones. (Sadly, to keep the hours in check, I cut Western Art and Chinese Art.) The Dedao core-curriculum plan now needs 2.5–3 hours a day, which fits comfortably into the time I spend washing up, commuting, exercising and eating. And that's assuming it only takes "185 days." That assumption leaves me plenty of time to learn about new things and new needs as they come up. Simple addition, subtraction, multiplication and division — letting the data speak — helps us make better decisions and plans. 4. Persistence, persistence, persistence People often "overestimate what they can achieve in the short term" and "underestimate what they can achieve in the long term." I dared to set these goals because my daily check-ins in 2021 let me taste the rewards of sticking with something. Break your goals down into daily actions, and over time, miracles happen. Don't burn yourself out, don't "work hard, play hard" — just make progress bit by bit. To borrow the couplet Chairman Mao wrote for himself as a student in Changsha, adapted from the Ming dynasty scholar Hu Juren: "If you value perseverance, why stay up till the third watch and rise at the fifth; nothing is more useless than one day in the sun followed by ten days in the cold." Finally, the New Year message I wrote for my team — I'm giving it to my 2022 self as well: We do not possess; we create. We do not chase; we explore. Though we will all vanish in an instant of this universe, we still honor the years — with song, with love, with hot tears, and with an everlasting, devoted dedication.

In 2021, I tried a few new things: The year I read more books than ever before in my life (86); wrote more than 70,000 words of diary; collected my first ever NFTs; took part in a national rowing competition for the first time; took on high training volumes for the first time: a 4,000-metre indoor rowing race, and 18 holes of golf four days in a row; moved from Beijing to Shanghai; decided to start living a low-carbon, eco-friendly life; raised my sleep from under 6 hours to an average of more than 7.5; officially announced I'd quit drinking; started learning to code (I didn't stick with it, but I'm restarting in 2022); got into the habit of getting up early, around 7; tried intermittent fasting, less red meat and a low-carb diet; let myself relax — skipped work to see the first snow of the new year at Ditan Park; did two big rounds of decluttering; studied interior design. Of course, I did even more silly things this year. For example, I bought a new computer to learn Python, and then didn't write a single line of code... I wanted to write about this year's growth and reflections, but when I picked up my pen, there were always a thousand threads. Then I read The Human Domain , and suddenly I was freed from the pressure that "writing needs structure and logic". In the form of notes, my wandering thoughts can simply appear as they are, raw and unpolished. I want to turn certain moments of thought from 2021 into a piece of amber, set it down in this moment, and then keep moving forward. What I share below has no logic; these are just thoughts from particular moments, and not mature ones. I'm posting them only to push myself to do better next year: A strong person needs to dissect even her own state of mind "ruthlessly", every cut to the bone, never deceiving herself in the slightest. To tolerate and accept her own foolishness, and then have the courage to change, to "try again". How difficult that is — but this is the life I want. Like "scraping the bone to heal the wound" or "cleansing the meridians and purifying the marrow" in xianxia novels, it all means going through pain, gritting your teeth to sort things out, and staying clear-headed. If you let yourself pass out, you wake up with nothing, nothing at all. Just as muscle is built up bit by bit, so is character: break down, rebuild, break down again, rebuild again. What's the point of squeezing yourself dry down to the last drop? It's nothing more than trying to relieve inner anxiety through physical exhaustion. It does nothing for body or mind; you still need balance between effort and rest. Repeating the other person's words is a powerful psychological cue — the human "convergent behaviour" signals that we are the same kind, that we can earn each other's trust, and that the relationship is moving towards harmony. Not only in words, but also in tone, body language, speech and eye contact — its core is imitation! On decluttering — although I didn't throw out heaps of stuff, every item was examined, and it gave me a real sense of control over my life. If the only standard is whether something can still be used, the bar is too low, and you end up surrounded by lots of things rather than mostly by things you love. After decluttering, you're surrounded by things you love, and your happiness rises enormously. Also, when you have too many things, you can't find what you want when you need it. If you can't find it you buy a new one, and it becomes a vicious cycle. Every anxious day is a wasted day. When you focus on solving your own problems, you can live this life well, because when you look inward, the world has so much knowledge and truth waiting to be drawn from. There is no road that leads to sincerity, because sincerity itself is the road. The best love is protecting the perfect/beautiful version of themselves that the other person holds in their heart. An "ego massage" has to find the right pressure point, and that point is the ideal self-image in the other person's eyes. Think Again : being both humble and confident means knowing your shortcomings while also knowing you can succeed if you put in the effort. Managing in the Gray taught me not to rely on myself, but to ask the people I hire to argue against me. Whatever the circumstances, never say "I don't have time" or "I don't have money" — never say there isn't enough time or enough money. — Yataro Matsuura. Because not having enough time or money is an objective law of the world. Pay attention to carrying out [the smallest action that can be taken immediately] and [a ladder of sustainable actions]. When a person loses control, they develop what psychologists call a "hostage mentality". Powerless in the confrontation, they become extremely defensive, or tend to lash out. What a useless and enormously destructive thing it is to lose your temper. A surge of gratitude rose in me, because this failure made me realise that a destructive temper and emotions are a huge thorn in my personality, and this incident will help me grind it down. I suddenly realised: the person I need to defeat is actually myself. I need to stay clear-headed through this process and keep my emotions under control. A good figure is the best fashion. "END THIS EGO TRIP. WE ARE TINY PARTS OF AN ENLESS UNIVERSE." DAVID ANEXANDER FLINN At every stage of your life, stay calm. If you can avoid getting angry, avoid flaring up — yes, slow your heartbeat down and let your mind focus on thinking about your most important goal — then you can be creative, and you can get things done. "We may use logic to reason our way close to a conclusion, but in the end it is our emotions that make the decision." Human animality, and the relationship between social development and human animality — we used to always debate whether human nature is good or evil, and Christianity also discusses humanity's original sin and its divine part. When I explain it through "animality", I understand it better. Whether jealousy, infidelity and lying, or sacrifice, tolerance and care, these don't come from two opposing sides of human nature, but from the "animality" carved into our genes over the course of our evolution across countless millennia. We need to survive as individuals and as groups, so we have competition and cruelty, and also altruism and devotion. In Zizhi Tongjian ( Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance ), Zhi Guo says to Zhi Yao: "When one person errs three times, resentment does not lie only in what is visible; one must plan against what is not yet seen." — If someone makes too many mistakes, don't wait until others' pent-up resentment explodes before thinking of a response; prevent trouble before it happens. "A gentleman who is diligent in small matters will have no great calamities." — If a ruler doesn't lose caution in the details, he won't bring great disaster upon himself. "Gnats, ants, bees and scorpions can all harm people, let alone a ruler or a minister." — Gnats, ants, bees and scorpions all refer to small insects; if even tiny insects can hurt people, how much more so the ruler and chief minister of a state? These three lines are so well said; even today they are the best words for urging people to be careful and thorough in how they act and conduct themselves. Just as a samurai's sword needs a whetstone, the mind needs books to sharpen it. One should follow the great Way, and the great Way is one's daily habits. Scheming how to gain a little advantage, how to hoodwink some people — these are the last things one should do. One should think about how to do a thing well, how to write an article well, how to spend this minute, this hour, this day well, how to listen to a song, appreciate a painting, understand a great person, or keep good company with the people you love, thinking about what matters to them; to sense other people's feelings and lives, to understand a period of history in depth, an ancient building or a new scientific discovery — all of this is the great Way, the right Way. Thinking about how bad some people are, dwelling on the weaknesses of human nature, may make me cunning and worldly, and at the same time will corrode one's heart. Better to be simple and plain than slick and worldly-wise. I'd rather be a bit clumsy, a bit foolishly plain, even a bit slow, but a bit more pure and kind. But not so blunt that it ruins things — best to be pure and kind but not stupid. I should live my life well: not lazy, not hasty, not slack, not anxious, with goals — very, very high goals, goals that go beyond my life, even beyond my lifetime. Don't rush. Don't rush to find something to do just because you want to find something to do. Keep learning, keep enriching yourself, keep searching, and keep testing as you search, until the thing falls into place naturally. Don't be afraid of being late, as long as you keep creating value along the way. A diary really is a wonderful thing; it makes you aware of your life. Aware of the good and bad things around you, rather than drifting through in a daze. Feng Tang said: "A good IQ and a good EQ are not as good as good habits." Having confirmed that I don't have a good IQ (and recently confirmed I don't have a good EQ either), this is what I must stick to. Good habits can help me overcome my shortcomings, or at least make up for them a little. "Act decisively; don't agonise over whether you already have the perfect plan, especially in fast-changing situations." Right now, this is very useful to me. Doing every single thing well — this is very important. "There's no such thing as perfection in the world, so design the best possible state within imperfection, and then stay there." The style I like has gone from chaotic, free-spirited bohemian, to Japanese-style organising, and then to the symmetry and lively richness of some traditional aesthetics. Quite a lot of change. I should take conscientious responsibility for every detail, because this is my life, and every minute and every second belongs to me. This is a live performance — no retakes, no starting over. Every second is my life, so since I'm doing it, why not do it as well as I can? I need to learn to recognise the weaknesses in my heart: what makes me easy to hook, what my weaknesses are, what can move me, or be used to manipulate me. Only by knowing these weaknesses clearly can I avoid them. Once there is a constraint, nothing else can get in. A person has to draw a circle on the ground for herself in order to have her own boundary; without a boundary there is no sense of domain. You can neither limit yourself, nor be without limits. Because before a person with a finite life, the infinite is "nothing". A person must set limits for herself — first set no limits, then choose a territory, a well, and dig until water comes out, until she grasps the next level of understanding. Otherwise "the infinite", for a finite life, is closer to "nothing". Because it can never be exhausted, and you can never see the end, so in the end there is nothing at all. (This passage should be read alongside "Cutting Clouds" in The Submarine at Night .) Why should a person aim high and hold the whole world in her heart? Because each of us has only 24 hours a day; however efficient we are, the variable can't become astonishingly large. But the difference in effectiveness between people can be astonishingly large, because the same time, used to do different things and to think about things in different dimensions, produces vastly different results. A person should have a heart as vast as the wide world, and the openness of having her feet on the ground; should look up at the stars, and also enjoy the present; should feel the urgency of a finite life, and also have the wisdom of seeing a world in a single flower. This is hard, and it requires a dynamic balance, but this is life's practice. If a person realises when young that ambition is not only what we can do for the world, but also a lighthouse we light in order to become better versions of ourselves. It will guide our growth, guide us through the boredom and emptiness of life, strengthen our bodies, firm up our willpower, and when we meet hardship and suffering, let us find joy and meaning in it. Ambition isn't something vulgar, clichéd or outdated. Ambition is where we come from, and also the road that takes us home. Finally, I'd like to give a poem by a Russian poet that I heard today to the coming year of 2022, and to my friends. A Lonely Ship Lermontov A ship sails alone upon the sea, it neither seeks happiness, nor flees from happiness, it simply sails onward, below it the calm, azure sea, and above it the golden sun. What it is about to face, and what has already passed, compared with what lies buried deep within it, are all mere specks of foam. Everyone, my wishes for the new year: may everything you meet bring you joy, and everything you gain be good and kind!

First, please accept my sincere bow of thanks — to every friend who liked and commented! Without you there would be no this article, and no better version of me today. Here are a few loose reflections On self-discipline In the history of my public goal-setting on WeChat Moments, I have publicly fallen flat twice: (1) learning the splits in 2020 (2) reading 100 books in 2021 Looking back, neither goal was easy to monitor or check progress on at any given moment, and both were the kind of thing where if you don't do it today, tomorrow is fine too. So I made the mistake every man and woman makes 🤷‍♀️. People really are short-term animals. For any long-term goal, breaking it into small goals and confirming you complete them step by step is crucial! Using my "circle" for my own ends worked remarkably well — it's a superb self-discipline tool. — The power of friends' encouragement, plus the vanity and pride of "not letting my persona collapse," make a remarkably strong driving force, and everyone should put it to good use. On goals The bolder you dare to be, the more the land will yield. — At the start of the year, I went too easy on myself. Afraid I wouldn't make it, I set 150 times. From experience, 200 or 250 would also have been (possibly) achievable. Being ahead of schedule halfway through actually made me slack off for a few months. In his book How to Avoid a Climate Disaster , Bill Gates shows us perfectly the "endgame thinking" that people who drive the world's development and change should have. On carbon neutrality, he says: "Setting a goal of merely reducing rather than eliminating greenhouse gas emissions is not enough. The only sensible goal is zero." I can't describe how stunned I felt when I read that. No matter how hard a goal looks, don't let the fear of failure tie our hands and feet. On reading Reading truly enriches the soul. — On the few days I didn't read, I clearly felt empty. How to read "useful books" — input alone isn't much use; I'm past the age of studying, and forgetting what you've read is normal. You need to read systematically in connection with what you're doing, thinking as you read and testing it as you work. Books like this are like a senior veteran in a field: if you want to understand an industry or a subject, first find the one you can most easily follow and let them walk you through it systematically; after that, even casual conversation will be rewarding, and when you have a specific question, just ask or look it up. How to read "useless books" — useless books are the most "useful" of all, for nourishing the soul, broadening your horizons and discovering your own ignorance. On the future A habit that took so much effort to form shouldn't be thrown away. I'll try to keep up my self-discipline and early rising offline, keep good records, and report back once a week. Also, I need to be tougher on myself — it can't just be input; it's time to pick writing back up too. So here are my goals for 2022: 250 times: up before 7:30 to read, pushing on in one go to lock in this habit. 52 articles, in theory one a week. Any topic, any length, as long as I'm not too embarrassed. I have to challenge myself. I plant this 🚩 as proof — please hold me to it. Finally, let me share a passage from my diary. I had just experienced a state of flow while reading and was still in a daze. But it was a genuine feeling after a year of reading. Suddenly an image appeared in my mind: I was like a naive child with no ability to protect myself, wandering lost across the land of the Trisolaran planet. The world was like a desert, and I was walking naked through it, with far, far too much that I didn't know. The only thing I had was a tiny tool, perhaps a spoon, a scrap of cloth to cover myself, or a walking stick as thin as a matchstick, almost useless. It symbolised the education I had received since childhood, that pitiful little bit of critical thinking. But it was all I had, and I could only rely on it as I pressed forward, directionless, through this chaotic and dangerous world. Barely picking myself up after each fall, occasionally with its help climbing a not-very-high peak, or scooping a mouthful of water from a spring by the road, barely moving on. Wherever I went, the territory of my thought expanded, but in the end I could take nothing with me and leave nothing behind. Even if I spent my whole life, I could never expand the map of my thought far enough to see clearly the continent I am standing on. This is both a sad and a happy thing. A truth about life — the truth is that no truth is enough to give us a sense of security, enough for us to rest the whole meaning of our lives upon. Every truth is just a float, letting us rest and catch our breath for a while. When I have the strength, I can only keep paddling forward. The continent of ultimate meaning, that legendary continent — when will I ever catch a glimpse of it? Or perhaps the truth of life is this vast sea, a boundless ocean, with the endless sky above and mysterious waters below. Whichever direction I go, what awaits me will be endless surprises, and endless void. So what? Cowards never set out, the weak die along the way; only we are left moving forward, and we cannot stop for a moment.
