The Professor's Questions What is the "melting iceberg" situation facing the IA division? What are the key changes affecting IA's product line, sales, competition, or other business activities? What is the status of the IA division in the overall business and financial structure of Belden? What are the implications for initiating and sustaining any changes at IA? Consider the ESD initiative. What has changed in Belden's marketing, sales, pricing, staffing, incentive, and account-management processes? What has not changed? Why? What should Chand do about the three decisions described at the end of the case? What lessons do you take away from this case about selling solutions? Managing growth and/versus profitability? My Answers Q1. The "melting iceberg" The "iceberg" is IA's core business: selling hardware — cables, switches, connectors — to plant managers and buyers. It is still big and still profitable. The ground under it is melting from below. What is changing Hardware is becoming a commodity. Margins on OT devices are falling. Customers want products customized to their industry, which pushes suppliers into narrower niches. IT and OT are merging (Industry 4.0). Value moves from "the wire" to "the data": monitor, diagnose, control with AI. The Industry 4.0 market is projected from about $102B (2020) to $337B (2028). Competition comes from above. Cisco, IBM, later Google Cloud and Microsoft talk to the CIO, CTO and CEO about what the customer's data can do. Belden talks to the maintenance director about part numbers. Chand: Belden was being "relegated to a widget supplier." IT vendors want to own the whole data pipeline — Belden only owns pre-ingestion. Wrong buyer. Product sales meet people with a parts list and a target price. The real budget and long-term decisions sit with the C-suite; those decisions are CapEx, not OpEx. Growth was bought, not grown. 16 acquisitions since 2007; 15 brands. Acquired sales teams kept selling legacy brands; distributors kept brand-restricted rights. "One Belden solution" was structurally hard to sell. Incentives pointed the wrong way. Cost-plus pricing; revenue-only quotas; profit did not factor into bonuses. None of this shows up as a crisis in today's P&L. That is the point of the melting-iceberg metaphor (Kotter): by the time the numbers scream, the ice is already gone. Q2. IA's place in Belden Where IA stands 2019: almost half of Belden revenue, 54% of EBITDA — the profit engine. 2019 → 2022: revenue $1.0B → $1.4B; EBITDA beat budget by $84M (despite ~10% dip in 2020 from COVID). ESD has been self-funded , mainly by a pandemic boom in SPMRO (small projects, maintenance, replacement, overhaul). ESD itself is still tiny: 69 customers, $7.7M revenue / $16.3M bookings — under 1% of IA. Goal: half of IAS revenue by 2026. New consultants alone: 7 × $230K + 51 × $190K ≈ $11M/year , already more than ESD revenue. Implications for change Room to act, almost no room to fail. A hit to IA's core hits the whole company and the stock. Chand cannot "burn the boats." Old business pays for new. Product sales and the channel fund ESD — that is why pay still leans product and the channel cannot be casually upset. The cash cow sets the speed limit. The funding cushion is temporary. SPMRO fades; edge-to-cloud R&D bills are coming. The $26M decision is the first time ESD must compete for capital with hard ROI. Strong results are political capital. Use them now to lock in structure (single P&L, pay redesign) while numbers look good. Prove ESD in board language : bookings, pull-through product sales, solution-level EBITDA — not story alone. Q3. ESD: what changed, what didn't, why Area Changed Not changed (yet) Organization 9 product P&Ls → 2 → 1 ; direct sales from region/product → vertical Channel managers' jobs stayed the same Marketing CICs (Stuttgart, Santa Clara; more planned), use cases, VR demos Partner tiers (Elite/Premier/Pro/Authorized); brand-restricted distribution rights Sales process 5 → 8 stages; MEDDICC; sell to C-suite EBIs; cycle 6+ months No formal handover between SAM / consultants / implementers Pricing Value Calculator; paid network audit; pricing moved from product mgmt to sales; CapEx buyers Still one-time solution price (no recurring); products still cost-plus Staffing SAMs; 7 digital automation consultants + 51 solution consultants; 6-week vertical training; new hiring funnel Talent still scarce (tech + industry); "Oh, the cable company" stigma Incentives 70% revenue / 30% ESD bookings ; credit at booking (not invoice) Still mostly revenue; profit not in quota ; product KPIs unchanged; 50/50 planned but no date Why not change the rest Channel ≈ 70% of revenue and owns 5-day fulfillment Belden cannot replace. Leadership: no resources, infrastructure, or desire to replace partners. If pay flipped to 50/50 overnight, reps lose income during a 6-month ramp and leave. Side effect already visible: SAMs hit product quota first, then ESD. Pilot logic: start CPG, learn, expand. New partner category and handover rules wait for volume. Brand rights came with acquisitions — contractual legacy. Cost of half-change: every one of Chand's three end-of-case decisions is a symptom of what did not change (channel conflict, brand rights, revenue-heavy pay). People follow the pay plan, not the strategy speech. Q4. What should Chand do about the three decisions? Underneath all three: how does a channel built to sell parts absorb selling solutions? Turn exceptions into rules. ① NTE + French materials-handling / self-driving vehicle client — hybrid Belden delivers the network audit and services (solution consultants / CIC). The client already expects to deal with Belden directly. NTE keeps all product fulfillment at standard margin (it can meet the 5-day spare-parts window) + a finder's fee of ~5–10% of services, not 20% of $28K. Do not bring in the German partner: punishes the lead source, adds language risk, teaches every distributor "bring us leads and we cut you out." Codify as a lead-registration policy so this is not renegotiated deal by deal. $28K is small; the signal to 70% of revenue is not. ② City Transport Authority + Magenta — both, in order Now: one-time exception for Magenta on this ESD deal only, labeled "ESD-validated project." Mass transit is IAS's largest serviceable market ( $504M ). Forcing a flagship customer across multiple distributors is a terrible first impression. Do not make Magenta buy-and-resell from other Belden distributors (stacked margin, pushes Magenta to competitors). Next: build the ESD partner category ($300K, ~6 months). Solutions cross brands by nature; this conflict will recur. $300K ≈ one ESD deal — cheap insurance that turns today's exception into a rule other distributors can see. ③ $26M — ~60% go-to-market / ~40% R&D , and set a pay date Do not simply hire ~104 SAMs ($26M ÷ $250K) against today's 281 salespeople. Ramp ≈ 1 year; talent scarce; diminishing returns as accounts/verticals saturate. Put a large share of GTM into consultants (the real bottleneck), placed near CICs and existing SAMs where synergies work. R&D only for edge-to-cloud software tied to CIC-proven use cases . Window closing: Google Cloud launched a manufacturing unit May 2022. Reading Table B: sales hire $2.7M EBITDA over 5 years vs R&D $2.15M — but sales figure ignores turnover; R&D ignores the 70% channel multiplier . Over ~10 years R&D usually wins. Mix is right. Also: set a calendar date to move pay toward 50/50. Otherwise new hires will still sell cable first.

The Professor's Questions The founders of Nantucket Nectars are trying to decide whether, to whom, and how to sell their company. What are the pros and cons of staying independent? If management decides to sell a majority stake (but not all of) the business, what would be their role afterwards? Is this a good outcome? How should they identify and work with prospective buyers? Which of the potential acquirers listed in Exhibit 6 looks best? How should they orchestrate the process? Do they need an investment banker? How much is Nantucket Nectars worth? To whom? Why? What should Tom and Tom do? My Answers Q1. Pros and cons of staying independent Short answer: staying independent is a real option, but it is a bet that two young founders with a 30% gross margin and no buying power can win the supermarket shelf against Coke, Pepsi and Seagram — in a category whose growth is slowing from ~38% a year to ~9%. The upside is theirs alone; so is the risk. Pros The company works. Revenue $233K (1991) → $29.5M (1996), +92% last year. 1995 was the first profitable year; 1996 EBITDA $969K. Standalone, Exhibit 7 already values it at $34–58M. Huge untapped channels. Supermarkets sell 55% of New Age beverages but only 1% of Nantucket Nectars. Midwest and West are 9% each. If they can get in, the runway is long. They keep what makes it special : the story, the no-dress-code culture, the two Toms on the radio, "eye to thigh" merchandising, 27 flavors in three years. All of this is hard to copy and easy to kill. Control. No one tells them to swap cane sugar for corn syrup. Egan has shown that a 50% outsider can be hands-off; they already live with that. No acquirer stock risk. They said they do not want to hold the stock of a different company. Independence avoids that. Cons Margins are the worst in the category. Gross margin 30.5% vs the 34.3% the model needs; EBITDA 3.3%. Four times the juice, cane sugar, no futures contracts. In the bad 1995 cranberry harvest they got zero cranberries because Ocean Spray controlled the supply. That does not get better by staying small. The supermarket needs scale they do not have. Supermarkets want multi-serve (the 36oz bottle), shelf power and slotting money. Big players compete by blocking small brands off the shelf. 57 salespeople cannot buy their way in. The Cola Wars are coming to New Age. Coke, Pepsi, Seagram want to be "total beverage companies." Pepsi just dropped Ocean Spray to enter juice itself. Over 100 companies have launched New Age drinks. Consumers have no switching costs. Growth is decelerating. Exhibit 4: alternative fruit drinks grew ~38%/yr 1991–95 and are projected at ~9%/yr 1995–2000. The standalone case still assumes 20–25% growth — that means taking share, not riding the wave. Capital. They were undercapitalized for four years, employees unpaid for a year, founders unpaid for three and a half. Going national needs money. Raising it now means another Egan-style dilution, at a moment when strategic buyers would pay ~3x the standalone number. Concentration. The two founders' entire net worth is in one juice brand in a segment some analysts call a fad. Egan, 50% owner, also has no liquidity. The window is external and short. Interest exists today because of a magazine mistake and because Ocean Spray loses Pepsi in May 1998. Next year the buyers may have solved their problems another way. Q2. Majority sale: their role afterwards — a good outcome? Their role : after selling a majority stake, Tom and Tom become minority shareholders who are also employees . On paper they still "run the company." In reality, the big decisions move upstairs: capital, distribution, pricing, product formula, hiring budgets, where the brand sits in the acquirer's portfolio. Their day-to-day job becomes keeping the story, the culture and the 57-person sales force alive inside someone else's organization. Whether this is a good outcome depends on three things, and all three are written in the contract, not in the handshake: Why the buyer is buying. If the buyer wants the brand, the story and the 18–34 access (things it cannot build), the founders are the asset and will be given room. If the buyer wants to plug a distribution hole or kill redundancy (Triarc with Snapple/Mistic), the founders are a transition cost. Quaker–Snapple is the warning: new ads, new distributors, CEO fired, $1.4B gone in under three years. What they keep. A meaningful minority stake only has value if there is a way out : a put/call at a formula price (say, a fixed multiple of EBITDA in years 3–5), not "we'll see." Otherwise they hold illiquid paper in a company they no longer control — the exact thing they said they did not want. Cash for most of the stake today, a rollover for the "second bite." What they are promised in writing. An autonomy charter: brand and marketing control, keep the Nantucket office and the dress code, a say over distributor changes for a fixed period (anti-Snappleization), a committed growth budget, a retention pool for the 100 employees. Plus a defined role and title, and the right to leave with the put intact. Is it good? Yes — if the buyer is one that needs them (Ocean Spray fits best: private, culturally similar, needs youth and single-serve, has an Egan-like hands-off history to point to). They have lived with a 50% outside owner for four years and it worked because Egan did not meddle. A majority sale is Egan 2.0 with a distribution network attached. Not good if it is Pepsi (history of "downscaling" quality, Lipton Brisk) or any buyer whose plan is to fold them in. Then they should sell 100%, take cash, and leave with the story intact. The honest cost: they will not be the boss anymore. Their list of fears — losing the entrepreneurial spirit, departmentalizing, "will consumers still enjoy the story if a big public company owns it?" — is real. A contract can slow that down; it cannot stop it forever. Q3. Identify and work with buyers; who looks best; orchestrate; banker? Who to talk to. The right list is not "who is big" but " who has a problem this company solves right now ": Ocean Spray — loses ~$200M of Pepsi-handled single-serve distribution in May 1998 (19% of $1.05B). Needs a single-serve sales force and a younger brand. Private. Knows the Toms. Biggest berry buyer in the world (the cranberry problem disappears). Five captive bottling plants. Pepsi — just dropped Ocean Spray to enter juice itself; insiders think it used the deal to learn single-serve New Age. Deepest pockets. Needs a brand to enter with. Risk: downscales quality for volume. Triarc — just bought Snapple ($300M) and owns Mistic and RC; "best platform to grow the business over the next two years." Risk: redundancy → distributor purge → Snappleization; and it just spent $300M. Tropicana (Seagram) — a juice company that wants juice cocktails without risking its own brand equity. That is literally item 5 on the founders' own asset list. Keep a fifth and sixth in the room for tension (Coke, Cadbury, Quaker's other brands) even if they are unlikely to win. Which looks best? On fit, Ocean Spray . Three reasons, all structural: Highest urgency = highest willingness to pay. A $200M hole with a May 1998 deadline is the best thing that could happen to a seller. Complementary, not redundant. Ocean Spray is strong in supermarkets, especially the Northeast; Nantucket Nectars is 93% in "other" small outlets and 1% in supermarkets. Each has what the other lacks. Fewer overlaps means fewer distributors fired, fewer people cut, less Snappleization. Private, culturally close, hands-off history possible. Less disclosure, less quarterly pressure. The founders can actually stay. Triarc is the best growth platform but the worst integration risk ; Pepsi is the best pocket but the worst cultural fit . Use both to make Ocean Spray pay for its urgency. How to orchestrate. Today they are improvising — splitting up to meet Ocean Spray and Pepsi on the same afternoon, hiding meetings from employees. That is a leak waiting to happen (employees, distributors, retailers). Replace it with a controlled, confidential auction : One short information memorandum; one data room; NDAs before anything is shared. A timetable: indicative bids in ~4 weeks, management presentations with 3–4 bidders, final bids with mark-ups of a draft contract. Set the clock around Ocean Spray's May 1998 deadline — that is the seller's leverage. Ask bidders to bid on structure as well as price : cash vs stock, % acquired, founders' role and autonomy, employee retention, distributor commitments, put/call on the rollover. Keep Egan (50%) aligned in advance on price floor and on whether he exits fully. A split cap table at the final hour kills deals. Founders keep the relationship conversations — the buyers are buying their story — but not the price conversations. Investment banker? Yes , for this one. Reasons: (a) a $100M+ deal with four or five bidders is a process, and two founders running a company growing 90% a year cannot run it part-time; (b) a banker lets the Toms stay "good cop" and keep their future bosses as friends; (c) confidentiality and discipline — bankers know how to keep five bidders in the dark about each other; (d) they know the bidders' corporate development people and what each can pay; (e) Egan is a one-time 50% investor, not a process manager. Cost: typically 1–2% of value — ~$1–2M on $100M — a bargain if competition moves the price 10% (~$10M) or protects the structure. Pick a boutique with beverage M&A experience , pay mostly on success, keep a short tail, and make sure the banker is the founders' banker, not Egan's. Q4. How much is it worth? To whom? Why? There is no single number. Exhibit 7 gives two, and the gap between them is the whole case. Standalone (stay independent, 20–25% growth, 34.3% gross margin flat): $34M–$58M ; midpoint at 14% / 10× ≈ $47M . That is ~1.6× 1996 revenue and ~48× 1996 EBITDA — the value is almost entirely in future growth, not in today's earnings. Strategic sale (25–30% growth from supermarket access, gross margin to 37.3% from 10–20% COGS savings, operating margin to 13%): $106M–$176M ; midpoint ≈ $144M . About 3.1× the standalone number. The ~$97M gap is synergy. It does not belong to Nantucket Nectars; it only exists inside a buyer. The negotiation is about how much of it the seller can take. A buyer's opening anchor will be "standalone plus a little." The seller's job is to make competition push the price into the synergy zone. A realistic target: capture half or more of the gap — $90M–$110M for 100% of the equity (before adjusting for the small debt behind the $301K of interest). To whom is it worth the most? Buyer What NN is worth to them Why Ocean Spray Highest Fills a $200M, May-1998 hole in single-serve distribution; adds a youth brand; biggest berry buyer → largest COGS synergy on a product that is 4× juice; private, can pay for strategy not quarters. The founders' own list ("last good access to single-serve distribution", "vehicle to expand into juice cocktails without risking own brand") was written for them. Pepsi High on paper, but discounted Could pay the most in absolute terms, but it can also build or buy elsewhere, and NN would be a rounding error ($30M in a company whose brands are measured in billions). Its downscaling history lowers what the founders are worth to it — it wants the shelf, not the story. Triarc Medium-high National single-serve network means fast growth, but Snapple/Mistic overlap means part of the value is cannibalized and distributors get cut. Just paid $300M for Snapple; may push stock, not cash. Tropicana (Seagram) Medium Clean brand-extension logic into juice cocktails; less urgency than Ocean Spray. Useful bidder for tension. Why the numbers swing so much. This category reprices violently: Snapple went $1.7B (1994) → $300M (1997) on roughly the same brand. Value here is not an attribute of the company; it is a function of who needs it on the day they sign . Which is exactly why the time to sell is when a buyer's need is at its peak, not when the founders feel ready. What this means for the owners. Egan holds 50%, the Toms 50% together. At $100M of equity, Egan turns $600K into ~$50M (≈83×) and each founder's ~$8,500 half of the $17,000 becomes ~$25M. Those are the stakes on the table. Q5. What should Tom and Tom do? Sell a majority stake now, to Ocean Spray, through a short competitive process — and keep a minority stake with a contractual way out. Concretely: Decide to sell. The buyers' need peaks now (Pepsi–Ocean Spray split, May 1998). The category is slowing (38% → 9%). Margins are a structural disadvantage only scale fixes. The strategic value is ~3× what they can build alone, and the biggest part of that 3× — procurement, bottling, supermarket shelf — is exactly what they cannot do themselves. Hire a boutique banker and run a 3–4 month confidential auction with Ocean Spray, Triarc, Pepsi and Tropicana. Price target: north of $100M for 100% of equity (i.e., more than half the synergy gap). Let Pepsi and Triarc be the pressure; let Ocean Spray win on fit. Structure : cash for Egan's 50% and most of the founders' shares; the Toms roll ~20–25% combined into the new structure; a put/call in years 3–5 at a fixed EBITDA multiple ; no public-company stock (they said they don't want it, and Ocean Spray is private anyway). Governance in writing : the Toms run the brand as a separate unit from Nantucket; control of marketing and formula (no corn syrup); a 24–36 month moratorium on involuntary distributor changes; a committed growth budget; a retention pool for the 100 employees, especially the 57 salespeople who are the distribution asset. Prepare for the day after. Say the honest sentence out loud: they will be rich, and they will not be the boss. Plan their own next chapter so the put is a choice, not a trap. Cost of this choice : they give up the small chance that they alone build a $200M brand and keep all of it. They accept a slower, more corporate second act. Some of the culture will go. Why not the alternatives: Stay independent and raise growth money — possible, but they would be fighting Coke, Pepsi and Seagram for supermarket shelf with 30% gross margins and no procurement power, in a slowing category, with capital that dilutes them anyway. Snapple shows what the big players do to even the category leader. Sell 100% for cash and walk — clean, but leaves the "second bite" on the table and makes the 100 employees' fate entirely someone else's problem. Right answer only if the winning bidder is Pepsi or a buyer who plans to fold them in. Sell to Triarc for the growth platform — the growth is real, but so is the distributor purge. Their 57 salespeople and their distributors are the asset; Triarc is the buyer most likely to destroy it.

The Professor's Questions What should Cynthia Carroll do about the safety issues at Rustenburg? What should Cynthia Carroll do to achieve her goal of "Zero Harm" for all of Anglo American employees, taking into account all relevant stakeholders? My Answers Q1. What should Carroll do about safety at Rustenburg? Shut Rustenburg — all nine shafts — now, as her own decision, and use the stoppage to retrain every one of the 30,000 workers before anyone goes back underground. Not a speech, not a task force, not a new procedure. A stop. Why a stop and not something softer: The baseline itself is the problem. 29 deaths by June 27, 16 of them at Rustenburg. Anglo averaged 46 deaths a year from 2002 to 2006. South Africa as a whole was losing a miner every 44 hours. Anglo is not worse than its peers — and that is the point. If "no worse than the industry" is acceptable, 46 deaths a year is acceptable. Rustenburg is getting worse, not better. Exhibit 8: Rustenburg's LTIFR went from 1.84 (2006) to 2.28 (2007). Group LTIFR went from 0.94 to 1.16. Potgietersrust, an open pit, sits at 0.26 with zero deaths. Depth explains the gap; it does not excuse it. Words have already been tried. The 2003 industry summit promised a 20% cut in fatalities every year; by 2007 it was 20–25% behind target. The board's own language was that procedures were in place "but the attitude was not where it needed to be." Front-line supervisors were "the most resistant to change." One more message from a four-month-old CEO is one more sentence in a language that only speaks downward. Only a decision that costs money is believed. Rustenburg makes about $8M of revenue a day. Fixed costs are large, so the loss "flows right to the bottom line." A week ≈ $56M; a month ≈ $240M. Rustenburg is 35% of Platinum's steady-state operating profit; Platinum earned $2,398M in 2006, so Rustenburg is roughly $840M a year, or about $2.3M of profit a day. A month of that is about 2.4% of the group's 2006 operating profit ($9,832M). It hurts. It is survivable. And it turns "unacceptable" from an adjective into a number that every tribal chief understands. If she doesn't stop it, the government can. Section 54 of the 1996 Mine Health and Safety Act lets an inspector halt a mine or part of a mine. A CEO who stops her own mine owns the story; a CEO who gets stopped looks like every other South African miner. The problem is low-tech, which means it is people. Moody-Stuart: "We had made a lot of progress using technology... Where we were still having problems was with low-tech incidents." Mud rush, conveyor belt, blasting barricade. You can't engineer your way out of these in a week — you have to change what 30,000 people and their supervisors do every shift. That takes everyone's attention at the same time. A shutdown buys exactly that. How to do it, so the stop is a test and not just silence: Decide it with Havenstein, announce it herself. Anglo Platinum is majority-owned and separately listed; Havenstein is the CEO. Going around him at month four is a governance cost. So: tell him first, insist on the outcome, let him execute. But the public message is hers — "I will not support operations that are killing people." Pay the workers through the stoppage. 70% illiteracy, many migrants, many paid by shift. An unpaid shutdown is a strike you started. The wage answer has to exist before the announcement, not after. Keep the mine alive while it is idle. The case is clear: an idle deep mine can get more dangerous because rock conditions change while no one is watching. So the stop is short, planned, with skeleton crews on ventilation, pumping and ground-support inspection. Restart is shaft by shaft, each one signed off against written criteria. Retrain every person — supervisors first. Supervisors are the resistance and the bottleneck. Retraining is not a new rulebook read aloud in Fanagalo. It is: every worker has the right and the duty to stop unsafe work; every supervisor is accountable for using that information rather than punishing it. Train in the workers' own languages (Setswana for two-thirds of Rustenburg), visually, not in 2,000 words of commands. Bring the union and the government to the table during the stop. NUM, Solidarity, the Department of Minerals and Energy. Not after the restart — during. The shutdown is the one moment when all three have a reason to sit down. Publish the numbers. Fatalities and LTIFR, mine by mine, every month. Define in advance what "the shutdown worked" looks like: no fatalities in the first N months after restart, LTIFR back under 2006 levels, supervisor turnover, and whether the dialogue became two-way. The honest costs: lost production in a record platinum market; shareholders in Johannesburg who want dividends and institutions in London who want to know why a first-year CEO is burning cash on a problem "everyone has"; Havenstein's authority; and the risk that supervisors simply wait it out. She should name all four in her own announcement. A leader who names the costs before her critics do is harder to argue with. Q2. How does she get to "Zero Harm" across Anglo American, with all stakeholders in view? Rustenburg is the shock. Zero Harm needs a system: one standard for the whole group, personal accountability at every level, a workforce that is allowed to say no, and three parties — company, unions, government — owning the same number. The stop buys attention for perhaps six months. What she builds in those six months decides whether the deaths come back. Start with a fact about the organisation: Anglo is "a collection of mining businesses that operated independently." The business heads "don't" meet. "If they were asked to do something around safety... they would tell you to get lost." Zero Harm is impossible in a federation. So the first move is structural, not motivational. 1. The board — get the mandate in writing, then spend it. The board told her safety "had improved but that I might want to attend to it." Mild. She should go back and make them say the hard version: Zero Harm is a group goal, the CEO owns it, and the board will accept the production cost of getting there. Peter Woicke's safety and sustainability committee becomes the place where this is reviewed first, every meeting, before the numbers. Tie her own pay and every business-unit CEO's pay to safety outcomes — fatalities and LTIFR — not as a small modifier but as a gate. 2. The business heads — end the federation on safety. One Anglo American safety standard, written at group level, mandatory in all 40 countries. Fatal-risk standards for the handful of things that actually kill people (fall of ground, transport, machinery, blasting, mud rush). Non-negotiable. Local rules can be stricter, never looser. Make the "tribal chiefs" meet. A quarterly safety review where every business CEO presents his own numbers to his peers. Public comparison does what memos cannot. Replace people who won't comply. The case says senior management was "on board"; the test is whether a chief who misses the standard and shrugs keeps his job. One visible exit does more than ten speeches. 3. Middle management and front-line supervisors — the real battlefield. Ndlovu: "It was our front line supervisors that were the most resistant to change." Woicke: procedures were in place, attitude was not. So: supervisor KPIs change — a share of their evaluation is safety, including leading indicators (near-misses reported, stop-work calls honoured), not just whether anyone died this month. Train supervisors to lead a two-way conversation, and give workers something to say back. The "visible felt leadership" she brought from Alcan — executives underground, asking questions — only works if the people above the supervisor model it first. 4. The workers — turn the language around. Fanagalo has 2,000 words, "most of them commands," and operates "in the imperative. The dialogue is one way." You cannot build Zero Harm in a language that cannot carry a question. Shift training and safety communication into workers' own languages; retire Fanagalo as the safety language over time. Give every worker the right to refuse unsafe work, protected from retaliation, and make supervisors report how often it was used. If the number is zero, the right doesn't exist. Use what already works. The HIV/AIDS programme — free anti-retrovirals, 110,000 people tested voluntarily — proves that this workforce will trust the company when the company acts first and visibly. Safety can borrow that trust; it should also borrow the method: voluntary, peer-led, in the community. 5. Unions and government — from adversaries to co-owners of the number. NUM and Solidarity: invite them into writing the standard, not just reviewing it. Solidarity's McMaster has already named the problem ("the human element was rarely if ever addressed"); he is a potential ally. The South African government: the relationship is strained; the board will judge her on fixing it; Section 54 is their weapon. Turn it around — propose a tripartite safety agreement: company, unions, Department of Minerals and Energy, one target, one scoreboard, published together. The 2003 summit failed because it was companies promising to each other. Three parties watching the same number is harder to let slide. The PIC — the government's own fund is a shareholder. A safety agenda the government co-owns is also a shareholder relations move. 6. Shareholders and analysts — make the business case explicit. Three kinds of shareholders: old South African holders who want dividends; London institutions holding Anglo because it's in the FTSE 100; emerging-market investors. Citigroup says Anglo could cut $560M–$1.1B of costs. None of these groups will applaud lost production. Her argument, said the same way every time: "business performance follows safety performance." Then prove it: every fatality is a stoppage, an investigation, a Section 54 risk, supervisor turnover in a hot labour market, and a licence-to-operate question in a country that already distrusts the industry. Report safety alongside the financials, every quarter. Shareholders accept a cost they can see and a plan they can track. 7. The industry and the communities — lead outward. Carroll's own framing: "this was not just about Anglo American; it was about the responsibility of the mining industry as a whole to the communities in which its companies operated." Share the standards with competitors. Being first non-South African, first woman, four months in — she has no history to defend. That is what lets her say what the industry hasn't said about itself. 8. Herself — be the standard. 20-day tours, 14 countries, "she gets energy from other people." Keep going underground. Make the first question on every site visit a safety question, in front of the general manager, every time. Culture is what the CEO asks about first. Keep "Zero Harm" as the stated goal even though an executive told her "it will never happen in our lifetime." The moment she accepts a non-zero number, she has named how many deaths are fine. Sequence and timeline. Months 0–2: Rustenburg stop, retraining, tripartite talks begin. Months 2–6: group standard written and signed by every business CEO; pay changed; right-to-refuse policy issued; monthly public reporting starts. Months 6–18: tripartite agreement signed; first full-year numbers; first consequence for a non-compliant leader. The test: fatalities under 46 (the 2002–2006 average) in year one, and falling every year after, with LTIFR moving the same way. Where it can fail. Supervisors wait it out; production pressure in a record platinum market pulls everyone back; the government uses the opening to tighten rather than partner; Havenstein and other unit heads treat group standards as London interference. Her mitigation for all four is the same: make the number public and make the consequences personal.

The Professor's Questions (These are the key points of the questions as jotted down in my notes, not the professor's original wording.) Compete with Amazon? Decisions that made digitalization work Customer-focused? Are customers loyal? Takeaways and what I will do My Answers Q1. Compete with Amazon? Yes. Compete as the credit layer, not as a second Amazon. If the choice is "mine the wallet" or "rush into smaller towns," I would do both, in that order, and I would refuse a third option the case keeps flirting with: turning the app into a general store. Amazon wins the next tap. BFL wins the credit decision and the repayment. Those are different games. BFL should not spend its 13.9% net interest margin fighting a price war it cannot fund. Why yes BFL already sits at the checkout. The case says it moves 30% of electronics and 15% of smartphones in India. By August 2021 it had $21.2 billion of assets and 50.5 million customers. Amazon Pay Later had 2 million customers. Online is still a thin slice. In 2020, e-commerce was 5.8% of Indian retail, and Amazon had 36% of that e-commerce. 0.36 × 0.058 ≈ 2% of all retail. The other 98% still runs through stores, which is where BFL's 114,000-point network lives (Exhibit 5, June 2021: 114,450). The profit pool is the spread, not the shelf. Exhibit 8: BFL's NIM is 13.9%, against 4.25% at HDFC Bank and 3.5% at HDFC Ltd. Market cap was $42 billion on $16 billion of advances. HDFC Ltd's market cap was $62 billion on $78 billion of advances. Investors were paying for the franchise, not for book size. Lending is a regulated, capital-heavy business. An NBFC cannot take demand deposits, so BFL's funds are already expensive. That is a weakness on price and a moat on skill: underwriting, collections, and fourteen years of cleaning a book. Net NPA went from 7% in FY2008 to 0.12% in FY2012, and was 0.75% in FY2021 even after the overdue definition tightened from 6 months to 3 months. What I would do, in order Protect the moment of purchase. Make a half-finished application continue from the store counter to the app and back. The person already standing at a BFL counter should not finish the next purchase inside Amazon. Treat the 10% wallet as profit, not as a substitute for growth. These 50.5 million customers account for 45% of India's mortgage book, 65% of its credit cards, and $100 billion of personal loans, while BFL holds about 10% of their wallet. That gap is real. It is not the whole growth plan. Cross-sell franchise only grew from 24.1 million to 27.4 million in two years (Exhibit 6, Q1 FY2020 to Q1 FY2022), while the firm adds 6 to 7 million new customers a year. Durables are replaced slowly. Panchal is right: cross-sell will not replace new acquisition. Enter the uncovered 38% of households with the urban risk engine, not with franchisee enthusiasm. Distribution covers 62%. Rural points are already mostly franchised: 1,218 of 1,745 rural locations in June 2021, about 70%. No credit bureau, weaker franchisee service, and customers new to formal repayment can replay 2008. That year they shut 330 locations and dropped 14,500 dealers. Urban durable stores fell from 19,000 (FY2008) to 2,000 (FY2010). I would cap franchisee-originated credit until its delinquency matches owned branches. Keep shopping, bill pay, and travel as reasons to open the app. They are frequency, not businesses. Exhibit 11: 52% of online durable buyers come for low price, 46% for convenience, and 90% prefer an aggregator to a brand's own app. BFL loses a price war. It can win "0% credit + next-day delivery + a warranty" on the purchase that needs finance. Pamnani's rule still applies: try things, do not collect hobbies. If an add-on cannot clear the same bar as a real product line, shut it. The cost of this choice Amazon may plant a flag in some small towns while BFL moves second. Wallet-deepening will look slow, because a refrigerator is not bought every quarter. I would rather lose a town for a year than buy FY2021's lesson twice: provisions rose from $519 million to $816 million, and ROE fell from 20.2% to 12.8%. In FY2019 it had been 22.5%. The operating ratio actually improved, to 30.7% of net interest income. Credit cost, not overhead, is what broke the year. What I would not do I would not try to out-Amazon Amazon on assortment, logistics, or price. A marketplace that fights Amazon also fights BFL's own retailers. And I would not "only mine existing customers." Six to seven million new customers a year are the growth math. Cutting that off hands the next town to whoever shows up with a phone. Q2. Decisions that made digitalization work The app in 2019 was the last chapter, not the start. Seven decisions made the earlier years work. Each one had a trap next to it. BFL missed the traps because it had already been burned, and because it paid people to cooperate instead of ordering them to. Clean the book before you scale it. After the crisis, net NPA was 7%. They shut 330 locations, stopped 14,500 dealers, fired several hundred people, stopped sharing the manufacturer's subsidy with retailers, and killed personal-computer loans — borrowers were selling the computers and disappearing. The trap is to grow your way out of bad credit. They did not, because Nanoo Pamnani said he would shut the business, and a newly spun-out firm had to show shareholders a clean win. Urban durable stores went from 19,000 to 2,000, then were rebuilt to 26,900 by June 2021. The cut was the strategy. Change the game to same-day joy, not to a lower price. Loan approval took 3 to 5 days; rivals did it the same day. Project WOW cut it to 3 hours. Bajaj's line: if parents can tell their children the television will be installed that day, word of mouth does the rest. By March 2008 they were booking 621,000 durable loans a year across 19,000 dealers. The trap is speed without rules, which is how the book had reached 15% non-performing assets, three times the industry. They put the rules in software. Later, a rule change could go out to the whole merchant network with one click. On Diwali the system flags red if point-of-sale processing is down for five minutes, because they originate 300,000 applications that day. Add only businesses large enough to deserve the effort, and kill the rest. "A Mercedes, not a Ferrari or a Ford." Pamnani: try everything, avoid hobbies. They ended above 50 products, but they also exited infrastructure lending — repayment depended on the government paying on time, not on the customer's own risk — and they wound down life-insurance sales through the field force when productivity failed. A young business had to grow 100% a year. A mature one had to grow at least 20%, or fix the model, or close. The trap is Olay's trap: a pile of products and no kill rule. Make customer data a company asset, and pay the team that collected it. In 2015 Jain forced every system into one warehouse. "Giving up customer data was like giving away the crown jewels." The trap is the silo. Two things blocked it. It was top-down: people who said "our market is different" were told to join the competition, and Mody says nobody left. And there was a price: the business that uses another unit's customer pays an internal fee. Durable and mobile-phone finance originated 90% of customers and earned 35% of its profit from that fee. Sharing became revenue, not a favor. Let vendors supply the limbs. Keep the brain. Technology partners provided software and hardware. BFL's own people owned process design and underwriting rules. The trap on one side is a vendor's process you cannot change. The trap on the other side is building everything yourself and spending years on capital projects. They wanted the brain without the heavy capex. Split origination, risk, and collections, then give risk and collections joint ownership of losses. Day-to-day approval is not the same job as watching the portfolio. If losses rise, risk tightens the rules and collections gets better at the same time. They call a customer right after a check bounces, "when he still feels a bit ashamed." Retailers' approval rates are published and auto-cut when their customers go bad, so the dealer sends better people to the counter because he wants larger, faster approvals. A home-loan customer, they found, has one-fourth the delinquency of someone without one, and gets a better price or a larger line. The trap is the sales team owning the growth number and hiding the bad loans. Digitize the process only after you have deleted steps, and put the designers inside the business. In November 2019 they framed an "omnipresent" model because income and cost were both growing in a straight line, and they feared cost would soon outrun income. The history does not yet show that: rupee operating expenses compounded at 29% for the fourteen-year span, income at 36%, profit after tax at 51%, and operating expenses fell from 58% of net interest income to 31%. The fear was about the next chapter. Covid made it urgent. Jain told his top 100 leaders to imagine they had a billion dollars of capital and a smaller economy, and to redesign their function. The CTO's admission matters: as a B2B company they had never really built the B2C layer. They plotted every offline process, cut what did not add value, then put it on the app. User-experience people sat inside the businesses, because "business originates ideas." The trap is a digital lab next to an unchanged company. They had three different adults in the room: Sanjiv Bajaj, the owner; Pamnani, a retired chairman of Citibank Asia; Jain, the operator. They also had a scar. A firm that has already seen 15% bad loans does not treat risk as a slide in the appendix. Q3. Customer-focused? Not yet. BFL is excellent at the customer's moment of purchase. It is not organized around the customer. It is organized around products, risk, and ROE. What looks customer-focused WOW was designed around a parent's same-day joy, not around a rate card. The Rs 1 scheme, against a normal 33% down payment, pulled 2,000 people to one southern retailer on the first weekend. People walked out with a 43-inch television instead of a 32-inch, or a double-door fridge instead of a single-door. The customer spent more because the entry fee collapsed. "People who are not desperate for loans seek good service." That is why they pushed salaried personal loans up to Rs 2 million at the front line with the algorithms in the back, and became the number-two player in a business owned by banks. The app was built so a dropped journey can resume on another channel. On the durables marketplace a customer can pick from over a million items, take a 0% loan, and get delivery in 24 hours. What the organization actually is Each product is its own business unit. The head is a mini-CEO for profit, sales, risk, and people. Technology and operations are the only things they must share. That is a product company with a common data pipe. Cross-sell is a push. A separate, highly paid team sells the next product to people risk has pre-approved. Existing customers cannot walk up to that team and ask for another loan. The firm decides when the customer is allowed to buy more. The CTO said they had been a B2B company and had not focused on the B2C layer. After Covid, Jain told the top 100 that the answer was to accelerate digital and "become a consumer-focused company." You do not announce that you are becoming one if you already are. The sharpest line in the case is Jain's: the stupidest thing a company focused on ROE can do is pay twice for the same customer. That is an acquisition-cost sentence. The customer is an asset you should not buy twice. It is not a person whose next need you are organized to hear. Collections are effective and not warm. They call when the customer is still ashamed. I would not romanticize this. It is one reason the book survived. It is also not what "customer-focused" usually means. My line in class: BFL is customer-competent, not customer-centered. Amazon calls itself the earth's most customer-centric company. BFL calls its ambition omnipresent, and manages itself to ROE. The 2019 app is an attempt to close that gap. It is not evidence that the gap was never there. Q4. Are customers loyal? No. They are loyal to the offer, and some of them are loyal to access. They are not loyal to the firm. The 10% wallet share is the evidence. Where repeat behavior is real The EMI card, from about Rs 5,000 (around $70), lets a repeat customer check out like a credit-card holder without new paperwork. For people who cannot get a bank card, it is often the only card they have. That creates repeat purchase. I would call this access loyalty: they come back because the other doors are closed. The cross-sell pool is large in absolute terms: 27.4 million of 50.5 million customers, about 54%, sat in the cross-sell franchise in June 2021. Something is being sold twice. Where loyalty fails The front door is a 0% loan. The case says even people who can pay in full do not mind taking it. That is deal loyalty. The day another counter offers the same 0%, the reason to choose BFL is gone. The wallet number is decisive. These customers already hold 45% of India's mortgages, 65% of its credit cards, and $100 billion of personal loans. BFL's share of that wallet is about 10%. Where the customer has a real alternative, nine rupees in ten sit somewhere else. Exhibit 8 puts home finance at only 12% of BFL's own loan mix. BFL is not the mortgage lender behind that 45%. New relationships do not become second relationships at the same speed. The firm adds 6 to 7 million customers a year. The cross-sell franchise grew by about 3.3 million over two years (24.1 to 27.4). Total franchise grew from 42.6 to 50.5 million in that same window, about 7.9 million net. Gross adds and net adds are not the same series, so I would not call the gap "churn" in class. I would say the direction is clear: most new customers are not showing up in the cross-sell pool. About 30% of customers added each year are new to credit, mostly from smaller markets. That is a good acquisition machine. It also means the book is constantly refilled with strangers. A loyalty compound would not need that high a share of first-timers to keep growing. Online, the customer is loyal to price and convenience. 52% and 46% in Exhibit 11. Rewards, travel, and bill pay are there so the app gets opened. The loan itself does not create a habit. A durable sits in the house for years. Class line: people repeat what is easy and unavailable elsewhere. The moment it is easy elsewhere, the repeat stops. BFL's loyalty is real at the locked door. It is unproven at the open door. Q5. Takeaways and what I will do What I take Winning the transaction is not the same business as winning the gap between two transactions. A digital app on top of siloed customer data is just the silo, moved online. The warehouse in 2015 mattered more than the app in 2019. Speed and standards have to be separate jobs, and both have to own the loss. People share customers when sharing pays them. A speech about "one firm" does not do it. The 35% profit from transfer pricing did. You can be very good at the customer's moment and still not be a customer-centered firm. Look at whether the customer can pull the next product, or only receive a push. Do not fight a platform on the shelf it already owns. Fight on the decision it cannot yet make. For BFL that decision is credit. For us it is judgment and trust. Near term — this quarter Write down where a client's truth actually sits today. In our own language, the failure mode is an empty platform: the memory lives in one person's head, and when the person leaves, the client leaves. Before any new interface, I want one client record, one owner, and a rule that the person who brought the family in is credited when someone else does the next piece of work. That is BFL's transfer price, translated. Success looks like this: a second colleague can brief the family without re-collecting the story, and the originator is not punished for the handoff. Mid term — this year Draw the current client journey on one page. Delete the steps that do not change a decision. Only then put what remains into a system. BFL plotted the offline process before it coded the app. I also want origination speed and judgment standards split, the way approval was split from risk. Publish a short quality gate the front line can see, so people select better work instead of being told no at the end. And write the kill rule before a new service launches. Pamnani's "no hobbies": if it is not large enough to deserve a real effort, it does not get a team. Success looks like fewer steps in the journey, and at least one service we stop because it missed a standard we wrote in advance. Long term Omnipresence for a family office is not an app with extra products on it. It is being present at the moments that actually move a family — a liquidity event, a succession, a cross-border decision, a next generation coming in — in person and in the system. The natural cycle is generational, which is even longer than a refrigerator. If we do not design frequency on purpose, quarterly reviews, governance, education, the relationship goes dormant, and the next platform meets the family at the next event. The product rule stays the one in our own blueprint: the product serves the allocation, the allocation does not serve the product. Success looks like a rising share of the family's important decisions made with us, not a longer menu. How these do not stay as intentions One metric for "the second decision with us," next to new names. BFL had 10,000 metrics. I do not want that. I want a few that would have shown the 10% wallet early. A person whose job is to stop the thing if trust or quality slips. That was Pamnani on Tuesday at 8:00. Without that chair, the franchisee expansion will always have a reason. Economics for the originator. If sharing a client cuts someone's number, the warehouse will stay a speech. A date. Belden's lesson still applies here: a pay mix and a kill rule that have no date will not happen.

The Professor's Questions To achieve success in today's volatile economy is viewed by many as simply looking for avenues for survival. … Spurred by visions of a dismal future and haunted by intense competition, companies are rushing to cut costs across the board. At the same time there are others who view this time as opportune to break away from the pack. While others are hunkering down, these few are running forward. How do such organizations deal with the seemingly competing sets of demands of cutting back and investing in the future? What do they do to expand while others contract? What tangible and intangible assets do they leverage to create advantage? Identify and explore the essential foundations for building competitive advantage in turbulent markets Investigate how firms in a range of industries use creative strategies to build and sustain profitable market positions with top and bottom line growth in difficult markets Cultivate an understanding of how these firms actually implement some of these changes to ensure success My Answers Q1. What are the essential foundations for competitive advantage in turbulent markets? Short answer: the foundation is not a bigger cost cut and not a bolder bet. It is a specific combination — cut selectively through operating efficiency, invest comprehensively in markets and assets, and use the customer as the filter for both — carried by leaders whose mindset lets them do both at once. The evidence from the 4,700-company study: The downturn is a sorting machine. 17% of companies did not survive. Of the survivors, 80% had not regained their pre-recession growth rates three years later and 40% had not regained even their absolute sales and profit levels. 85% of pre-recession growth leaders were toppled. Only about 9% came out stronger and beat their industry by 10%+ on sales and profit growth. So "surviving" is not the bar; the bar is being in the 9%. Pure defense loses. Prevention-focused companies — the ones that cut everything and invest in nothing more than peers — have a 21% chance of breaking away. Their post-recession sales grow 6% a year and EBITDA 4%. Among the 200 largest companies after 2000, their profits rose by $600 million on average; progressive companies' rose by $6.6 billion — eleven times more. Sony cut headcount 11%, R&D 12% and capex 23% in 2000–02; margins went from 8% to 12%, but sales growth went from 11% to 1%, and it lost e-readers, consoles and OLED TVs to Amazon, Microsoft/Nintendo and Samsung. Pure offense also loses. Promotion-focused companies have a 26% chance. They cannot bring their cost-to-sales ratio down at all (prevention companies cut it by 3 points), their optimism blinds them to early warning signs, and when they finally must cut, every function believes it is essential and decisions seize up. HP "doubled down" with a $25B Compaq deal, +9% R&D, $200M on branding, $1B on IT in developing countries — and by 2004 its EBITDA margin was 8.4% against IBM's 16.8% and Dell's 9.3%. The winning foundation has three parts. 1. Selective defense : cut cost of goods sold by rethinking how the business runs — supply chain, structure, processes — rather than by cutting people. Only 23% of progressive firms laid people off versus 56% of prevention firms. Companies that relied on workforce cuts alone had an 11% chance of breaking away. Efficiency cuts are permanent; layoffs come back as rehiring costs, lost morale and late scale-up. 2. Comprehensive offense : spend more than rivals on both market development (SG&A, R&D) and assets (capex, PP&E, bought cheap). The best cell of the 3×3 matrix — operational efficiency plus both kinds of investment — delivers 13.0% sales and 12.2% EBITDA growth. The worst cell is layoffs plus both kinds of investment : 3.3% sales and −5.2% EBITDA. You cannot invest your way out after you have removed the people who would execute. 3. Customer need as the filter : "Progressive companies stay closely connected to customer needs — a powerful filter through which to make investment decisions." Target read that "wants" spending was collapsing and doubled its food floor space; food became a $1.8B business. The 2023 article adds the human foundation. Strategy alone did not explain why so few manage it. Three mindsets do: sensemaking (act first, then learn — "when you're lost, any old map will do"), a bootstrap ethic (frugal everywhere except where it makes you more effective for the customer), and stakeholder balance (spread the pain, do not dump it on one group). Alaska Airlines did all the defensive things in 2020 — hiring freeze, pay cuts, no dividends — and was still the only major U.S. airline to order 68 Boeings that December. Both at once is the whole point. Caveat worth saying in class: the four groups only include companies whose resource shifts were in the top or bottom third relative to their industry; the 21–37% odds are within those groups, which is why they are higher than the 9% headline. Q2. How do firms across industries use creative strategies to grow top and bottom line in difficult markets? Short answer: the winners in both articles do the same three things in different clothes — they cut where the customer will not notice, they invest where the customer is going, and they buy what rivals are dropping . Here are the patterns, with the cases behind each. Cut the model, not the people — then use the savings to fund the offense. Staples (2000–02) closed underperforming stores but added 10% to headcount to staff new high-end categories and services, while holding operating costs flat. Sales doubled from $7.1B (1997) to $14.6B (2003); Office Depot, which cut 6% of staff but could not lower operating costs, went from $8.7B to $13.4B and saw sales growth fall from 19% to 8%. Staples was about 30% more profitable in the three years after. Firefly (2020) cut sales and support headcount, took a 20% company-wide pay cut, renegotiated fleet contracts and moved engineering to Turkey — then used the money to hire a chief revenue officer and keep building the forecasting and optimization tools customers were asking for. Read the customer's new "need" and move the whole business toward it. Target in 2008 saw same-store sales fall as Wal-Mart's everyday-low-price message landed. Instead of discounting across the board, it noticed "wants" were collapsing and "needs" were not, doubled floor space for food, extended Market Pantry (+30% sales by 2008) and Archer Farms (+13%), reworked operations behind it and leaned the slogan "Expect more, pay less" toward the second half. Food became a $1.8B business. Panera read that store-manager turnover was destroying the customer experience and raised baseline pay, added training, and tied pay to store results so the best managers earn six figures — funded by above-inflation menu pricing plus demand-stimulators like flatbread pizzas and a $10.99/month Sip Club. Revenue growth beat the industry and turnover fell 10%. Buy assets while they are cheap — but only if you also change how you make money. Alaska Airlines placed a 68-aircraft Boeing order in December 2020 when every rival was cancelling, took the 52 options and then locked in 105 more through 2030 — and used the order to simplify from a mixed Airbus/Boeing fleet to Boeing only, which lowers operating cost permanently. It also locked in five labor deals in 2022 so it would have crews when demand returned. Target in 2000–02 raised capex 50% (947 → 1,107 stores, SuperTarget 30 → 118) and changed the model: Amazon partnership instead of building e-commerce alone, designer collaborations (Graves, Starck, Oldham) for "cheap chic," co-founding the WorldWide Retail Exchange to cut procurement cost, folding Dayton's and Hudson's into Marshall Field's. Result: +40% sales, +50% profit through the recession. The counter-example is TJX: +300 stores on a base of 1,350, +25% square footage, capex nearly doubled — sales 4 points above peers, but bottom-line growth 9% below peers three years later, because it only scaled the old model. Keep investing in the long-term transformation, but change the pace, not the destination. Edward Jones started its "human-centered complete wealth management" transformation in 2019 and let investment outrun revenue growth through the pandemic. In 2022–23, with peers cutting, it postponed hiring 1,000 associates but strengthened FP&A so every investment carried a business case and success metrics, and sequenced projects by value — fixed-income IT before equity IT. Pennington: "We invest when times are good, and we invest when times are hard." Share the pain across stakeholders so you keep the relationships you will need later. Levi Strauss in 2020 suspended dividends and cut 15% of staff ($100M saved) — but extended health benefits to the departing, added benefits for those who stayed, gave vendors nearly $2M in grants and helped them find financing, and kept its sustainability programs running. It could have saved more; it chose to keep the people and suppliers it would need in the recovery. What is common: every one of these moves starts from a sentence about the customer — what they stopped buying, what they still need, what they will want when the storm passes — and works backward to what to cut and what to buy. Q3. How do these firms actually implement the changes? Short answer: implementation is where most companies fail, and Gulati's 2023 article is really an answer to this question. Both articles together give a five-step playbook , and each step has a named obstacle. Pressure-test first, then look for the edge. Resilience "requires both pressure-testing your firm's operational and financial health (its P&L and balance sheet) in worst-case scenarios and staying alert for measures you might take, even amid chaos, to find a winning edge." Alaska Airlines did the stabilizing moves (hiring freeze, pay cuts, vendor terms, no buybacks or dividends, lower capex) before it placed the aircraft order — and it placed the order because it was "confident that its balance sheet was strong." Offense is earned by defense, not instead of it. Act before the picture is complete, then correct. Weick's lost soldiers walked out of the mountains with a map of the wrong range. Resilient leaders "define their ultimate goals and then make thoughtful initial moves, adjusting and pivoting when necessary." Gulati noted in 2010 that "few progressive business leaders have a master plan when they enter a recession. They encourage their organizations to discover what works and combine those findings in a portfolio of initiatives." Edward Jones kept the destination fixed and changed the route: postpone 1,000 hires, strengthen FP&A, sequence fixed-income before equity. Use one filter for every cut and every investment: does this make us more effective for the customer we serve? This is the bootstrap ethic — efficiency in tandem with effectiveness, Drucker's "doing things right" and "doing the right things" together. If yes, keep and invest; if no, cut. It is also the answer to the organizational obstacle: budget reallocation causes internal strife, and a customer focus "provides a clear basis for making the right mix." Firefly cut sales staff but kept engineering because customers were demanding better planning tools; Panera raised manager pay because managers are the customer experience. Make bravery a norm, not a mood. The cultural obstacle is loss aversion — the same psychology that makes prevention-focus the default in a crisis. The fix is to "explicitly nurture bravery as a cultural value, adopting courageous behaviors as cultural norms and exemplifying those behaviors themselves." Minicucci's "we wanted to be aggressive to enable our recovery" and Pennington's "it would be riskier not to invest" are the CEO saying the brave sentence out loud so the organization can. Give decision-makers one overarching purpose, and balance the stakeholders who bear the cost. The strategic obstacle is reconciling short-term efficiency with long-term investment and then communicating it. The fix is "an overarching purpose or business intent that gives decision-makers clear direction and helps them make painful trade-offs." Then practice practical idealism : extract short-term concessions but limit the pain. Levi's cut 15% and still extended health benefits and funded vendors; Edward Jones cut spending but still paid (reduced) adviser bonuses and funded financial-fitness programs. Singh's test — "if I can sleep well at night" — is the honest version of "there is no formula." Two implementation traps from the 2010 data worth naming: Centralized across-the-board cuts. When finance cuts every line equally, it "pays little attention to initiatives that may be the nuclei of postrecession growth," and pessimism and disempowerment spread. Cuts have to be made by people who can tell the nucleus from the frill. Investing after you have gutted execution. The worst cell in the matrix (−5.2% EBITDA) is layoffs plus full investment. Sequence matters: protect the people who will deliver the offense before you launch it. Case Summary Article one (2010): a study of 4,700 companies. In December 2008, with the Great Recession in full swing, Gulati, Nohria and Wohlgezogen launched a year-long project to answer a question with almost no empirical research behind it: what strategy should you use during a recession in order to win after it? They took 4,700 listed companies from Compustat through the three previous recessions (1980–82, 1990–91, 2000–02), and for each one looked at the 3 years before, the recession itself, and the 3 years after, using six balance sheet items to measure changes in resource allocation: headcount, cost of goods sold/sales, R&D spending, SG&A, capital expenditure, and the stock of fixed assets. Only changes in the top or bottom 33rd percentile relative to the industry average counted as a "significant increase or decrease." The results were stark. 17% of companies didn't survive the recession. Among the survivors, 80% hadn't returned to their pre-recession growth rates three years later, and 40% hadn't even returned to their absolute pre-recession levels. Only about 9% did better after the recession than before, outpacing peers by more than 10% in both sales and profit growth. Of the growth leaders before the recession, 85% were knocked off their perch during it. Borrowing Columbia University psychologist Tory Higgins's theory of "promotion focus / prevention focus," the authors sorted companies into four types: prevention-focused (only cut, and invest more than rivals in nothing), promotion-focused (invest more than rivals in at least one item, and cut no item more than rivals), pragmatic (lay off staff or cut COGS, while investing more in at least one of SG&A / R&D / capex / fixed assets), and progressive (cut COGS but lay off no more than peers, while out-investing rivals both on the market side — SG&A / R&D — and on the asset side — capex / fixed assets). The probabilities of each type breaking away after the recession were 21%, 26%, 29% and 37% respectively. Then come a set of contrasting stories. In the 2000 recession, Sony cut headcount by 11%, R&D by 12% and capex by 23% within two years; its profit margin rose from 8% to 12%, but sales growth fell from 11% to 1%, and it was subsequently overtaken in e-readers, game consoles and OLED TVs by Amazon, Microsoft and Nintendo, and Samsung respectively; in December 2008 it again announced US$2.6 billion in cost cuts, 16,000 layoffs and the postponement of an LCD plant in Slovakia. HP went the other way in the same recession: Fiorina said, "In blackjack, you double down when the odds are in your favor," and so it bought Compaq for US$25 billion, raised R&D by 9%, spent US$200 million on brand advertising and US$1 billion on IT in developing countries — management attention was spread thin, and in 2004 its EBITDA margin was 8.4%, against IBM's 16.8% and Dell's 9.3%. Office Depot and Staples are the cleanest pair. Office Depot cut 6% of staff, failed to bring operating costs down, and saw sales growth fall from 19% to 8%; Staples closed underperforming stores but increased headcount by 10% to support newly launched premium categories and services, while keeping operating costs in check — sales doubled from US$7.1 billion in 1997 to US$14.6 billion in 2003, while Office Depot went from US$8.7 billion to US$13.4 billion, and in the three years after the recession Staples' profit margin was about 30% higher. Target and TJX are another pair: Target raised marketing by 20% and capex by 50%, grew its stores from 947 to 1,107, partnered with Amazon, and hired designers for "cheap chic," while building a B2B procurement exchange and consolidating its department store brands — during the recession, sales rose 40% and profits 50%; TJX added 300 stores in the same period, expanded floor space by 25% and nearly doubled capex, with sales 4 points above peers, but three years later its profit growth was 9% below peers — because it had simply scaled up the old model without changing the business model. The article concludes with a nine-box grid: defensive moves (layoffs / operational efficiency / both) × offensive moves (market development / asset investment / both). The best box is operational efficiency × investing in both market and assets , with sales at 13.0% and EBITDA at 12.2%; the worst box is layoffs × investing in both market and assets , with sales at 3.3% and EBITDA at −5.2%. Progressive companies are "selective in defense and comprehensive in offense," and "closely connected to customer needs — the most powerful filter for making investment decisions." Article two (2023): thirteen years later, the same author returns to talk about mindset. The article opens with Alaska Airlines. In early 2020 its passenger traffic plunged 96% year on year, and it did everything its peers did — froze hiring, cut executive pay, renegotiated supplier payments, suspended buybacks and dividends, slashed capex — but in December 2020, as rivals were cancelling aircraft orders, it ordered 68 Boeings plus 52 options, the only major US airline to place a big order that year, and used the moment to consolidate its fleet from Airbus + Boeing to all Boeing. CEO Minicucci said: "You can't grow in this business without airplanes." In 2021–22 it exercised the 52 options, locked in another 105 through 2030, and in 2022 concluded 5 labor agreements. In 2022 its pre-tax margin was among the highest in the industry. Gulati says the 2010 study only answered "what to do," not "what kind of mindset makes leaders dare to do both at once." He offers three mindsets: sensemaking , the bootstrap ethic , and stakeholder balance . Sensemaking draws on a story told by Karl Weick: a unit of soldiers lost for days in snowstorm-swept mountains; someone found a map, morale soared, and they made their way back to base — only later did they discover the map was of a different mountain range. "When you are lost, any old map will do": the map's role isn't to show the way, it's to get people moving; once they move, the terrain starts giving feedback. Edward Jones is the example: it launched a transformation in 2019, and both during the pandemic and amid the economic clouds of 2022–23 people asked whether to pause; CEO Pennington's answer was that "not investing is more dangerous," but the approach was step by step — postponing 1,000 hires, strengthening FP&A, requiring evaluation metrics for every investment, upgrading the fixed-income system before the equities system. "We invest in good years, and we invest in bad years." The bootstrap ethic begins with a line from Nietzsche: "The most common stupidity consists in forgetting what one is trying to do." Drucker, for his part, said efficiency is doing things right and effectiveness is doing the right things. Frugality should be like an early-stage startup's: obsessive about customer value, stingy about everything else, filtering every expense through one question — "Does this make us better able to serve our target customers?" If yes, keep it and invest more; if no, cut it. When Firefly's revenue went to zero, it cut sales staff, reduced everyone's pay by 20% and moved engineering to Turkey, then used the savings to hire a CRO, keep investing in engineering, and make acquisitions at low valuations in 2021 and 2022. Panera, amid labor shortages and rising costs, went the other way, raising pay, adding training and tying store managers' performance pay to six figures, funded by above-inflation price increases, new products and the US$10.99 Sip Club; as a result revenue growth outpaced the industry and turnover fell 10%. In between is a section on why attacking and defending at once is hard in three ways — organizational (additions and cuts happen simultaneously, and budget reallocation sparks infighting; the solution is to use customer focus as the basis), cultural (loss aversion makes people afraid to move; the solution is to explicitly cultivate courage as a cultural value and lead by example), and strategic (balancing the short and long term makes it hard to form and communicate a coherent strategy; the solution is an overarching purpose, or business intent). Stakeholder balance uses a metaphor from Sumantra Ghoshal: the best leaders are like Chinese chefs who can cook sweet-and-sour — able to look after stakeholders with completely different demands at the same time. In a crisis, the various parties become tribal; the solution is "practical idealism": ask certain groups for short-term concessions, but limit their pain while attending to longer-term needs. In 2020 Levi Strauss suspended its dividend, cut 15% of staff and saved US$100 million, but extended health coverage for departing employees, gave suppliers nearly US$2 million in assistance, and maintained its sustainability programs. CFO Harmit Singh said: "There's no right answer, no formula, and I'm sure someone could find fault with it. But if I can sleep at night, I think we're in the right place." The article ends on a question — borrowing Vivian Greene's words: would you rather crouch down and wait for the storm to pass, or learn to dance in the rain?
