Core Tensions The fastest way to save money (layoffs) vs the ability to recover after the recession : layoffs work fastest — 56% of prevention-focused companies cut staff, and their cost ratio fell 3 points over three years; but companies relying only on layoffs had an 11% chance of breaking away, and rehiring during recovery is costlier and slower. Only 23% of progressive companies laid people off, yet they posted 13% / 12%. The professor's first theme (the foundations of competitive advantage) lands on this one. Defense vs offense, or defense × offense : treat the two as opposite ends of a single line (cut a bit more or invest a bit more) and the conclusion is "compromise"; the article says they are two independent dimensions to be pursued simultaneously — and laying people off and then investing across the board is the worst combination (−5.2%), because the people who would carry out the investments are gone. An optimistic culture vs seeing reality : promotion-focused companies attract people with optimism, and because of that optimism they ignore early signals of shrinking customer budgets; when they finally have to cut costs, every department thinks it matters, and decision-making seizes up. HP is the example. Scale vs model : TJX and Target both expanded during the recession; the difference is that TJX only scaled up its old model, while Target changed its procurement, brands and channels. Cheap assets don't mean you should buy. Acting vs thinking it through : Weick's old map says get moving first; but Edward Jones's approach was stepwise and metric-driven. "Any old map" doesn't mean no map — it means don't wait for the map to be perfect. Short-term stakeholders vs long-term stakeholders : Levi's could have saved more by laying off another 1,000 people, but it chose to share the pain — a dimension new in the 2023 article and absent from the 2010 study. The author's position in 2010 vs 2023 : the first article says "a few had a master plan; most discovered as they went"; the second calls for an overarching purpose. The two are actually complementary — purpose sets the direction, sensemaking sets the steps.

The Professor's Questions The Axel Springer (A–C) case series explores the radical transformation of a legacy German media company into a global digital force. Under the leadership of CEO Mathias Döpfner, Axel Springer evolved from a conservative postwar tabloid empire into a billion-dollar player in digital journalism and online classifieds. The case spans nearly two decades of strategic reinvention through M&A, cultural change, and governance restructuring. How has Axel Springer changed under Mathias Döpfner's leadership? What are the strategic, financial, and cultural implications of acquiring Business Insider vs. Huffington Post? What should Döpfner do in 2015? Why? My Answers Q1. How has Axel Springer changed under Döpfner? Short answer: in 13 years Döpfner turned a loss-making, Germany-only, print-only, founder-shadowed publisher into a profitable, majority-digital, pan-European media-and-classifieds group that grows by buying founders and leaving them alone. He did it with the plan he announced on day one — "strengthen the core, digitize it, internationalize it" — and he kept the one thing that was not allowed to change: the Essentials. 1. From losing money to making money. 2002: losing €200M a year, unstable governance. He cut 40% of jobs — "brutal, radical, and fast" by German standards — sold or closed unprofitable assets, and went from −€200M to about +€200M in one year. That cash is what paid for everything after. 2. From print to digital — by selling the family silver. By 2014 more than half of revenue was digital (≈52%). The hard part was not launching websites; it was selling. In 2013 he sold the regional papers — including titles Axel Springer himself founded in 1948 — to Funke for €920M, about 10× EBITDA (€95M EBITDA on €512M revenue). Bayer called it "probably the last potential exit." Friede Springer said yes immediately. The same year Bild finally put up a paywall (BildPlus), which went from 0 to 680,000 digital subscribers by 2016. 3. From a newspaper company to a classifieds company. Döpfner saw early that job, real estate and car ads were moving to Craigslist and Zillow. So he bought the marketplaces: StepStone ($110M), aufeminin ($367M), Seloger ($634M), Totaljobs ($175M), Immoweb ($155M), Immonet, N24 — over $1.4B disclosed — and rolled them into horizontal groups by vertical. Analysts called Axel Springer one of the most aggressive classifieds buyers in Europe. That is where the digital profit actually lives. 4. From Germany to Europe, now aiming at English. France, UK, Belgium through classifieds; then the realisation that "you can't really grow with German or French content." FT was the first English-language attempt. It failed, so now the US. 5. From integrating to "United Artists." Growth switched from launching titles in-house to M&A, and M&A switched from control to autonomy: founders keep a stake, run their company, use Axel Springer "like a buffet," and exit later through a put/call — 12× EBITDA if they beat plan, 8× if they miss. "If a founder wants to sell 100% upfront and leave, we're skeptical." Bayer's image: a jazz band — improvisation inside a clear frame. 6. From founder's shadow to a stable governance pair. A professional CEO with a 13-year run, backed by a majority shareholder who "always looks forward, never back." That pair is what let the company sell the founder's own newspapers without a family fight. 7. Setbacks became accelerators. ProSiebenSat.1 (2004–05, blocked by antitrust) pushed the company toward digital and abroad. FT (2015, lost to Nikkei's +10%) pushed it toward the US. Döpfner: "both setbacks were in retrospect healthy, because they radicalized and accelerated our shift." What did not change : the Essentials (democracy, Israel, the transatlantic alliance, free markets), Bild and Welt as the two national flagships, and Friede Springer's majority. The core was strengthened, not abandoned — which is exactly what the first of his three verbs said. Q2. Strategic, financial, cultural implications: BI vs HuffPost One line : HuffPost is 3.4× the revenue at 2.5× the price — but one-fifth the growth, 100× EBITDA, no paid product, no founders, and a political identity opposite to the owner's. Business Insider is small and noisy, but it is growing 2× a year, has a subscription seed, has founders who would stay, and Axel Springer already sits on its board. Strategic Business Insider HuffPost What you buy A business & tech news brand with ~90M monthly uniques, ~$50M revenue (~75% ads), a small B2B research subscription (BI Intelligence), early international editions A general-interest news brand with ~$168M (2015E) revenue, 13 international editions + Arabic, HuffPost Live video, thousands of unpaid bloggers Fit with "paid digital journalism" (BildPlus logic) Yes — BI Intelligence is a seed you can grow; business readers pay No — 100% advertising, no paid consumer product, competing for the same programmatic dollars as Buzzfeed/Vox Fit with Welt / Bild Business/tech is adjacent to Welt's audience; the traffic-and-headline DNA is close to Bild's General news in the US — no adjacency except scale International Still small — Axel Springer can be the platform that takes it to Europe (that is a job it knows how to do) Already everywhere — but through partnerships with local media, which you manage rather than own; the "internationalize" box is ticked on paper, not in ownership Growth stage $20M (2014) → $42–50M (2015): doubling $146M → $168M: +15%; the international build-out is already paid for and already slowing Platform risk High: SEO/social traffic, clickbait reputation High: same model, plus heavy video and newsroom costs Information advantage Axel Springer owns 9% and a board seat since Jan 2015 — six months of looking inside None — a corporate orphan inside AOL, now Verizon Financial Price. BI: Series G post-money $191M (Feb 2015); Axel Springer's $20M for 9% implies ~$222M. A control deal for the other 91% at 7–9× ~$50M revenue = ~$350–450M total , so roughly $320–410M of new money . HuffPost: Verizon is reported to want ~$1B = 6–7× revenue = ~100× 2015E EBITDA of $10M. On revenue multiples the two are similar; on growth-adjusted terms BI is far cheaper (doubling vs +15%). On EBITDA, HuffPost is priced like a growth stock without the growth. Budget. FT was >$1B. HuffPost spends the whole FT budget on an ad-only asset; BI spends ~40% of it and leaves a war chest for classifieds — where the actual digital profit is. Downside. If BI fails, Axel Springer loses ~$400M on a company it already knows from the inside. If HuffPost fails, it loses $1B at the top of a cycle Mediashift was already calling "valuations gone wild." Structure. BI lets Axel Springer use its own playbook: founders and management roll a stake, put/call at 8–12× EBITDA, earn-out aligned to plan. HuffPost is a 100% purchase from a telecom — no founder to align, no earn-out logic, and Arianna is an employee, not an owner. Process risk. Verizon will run a process; Axel Springer would be one bidder among many — the FT movie again. With BI, Axel Springer is already in the room. Cultural United Artists needs artists. The whole model — "a home for entrepreneurs," put/call, autonomy — assumes founders who stay. BI has them (Ryan as chairman, Blodget as CEO). HuffPost has been a corporate division since 2011; the entrepreneurs left or became executives of someone else's company. Essentials. Axel Springer's constitution is conservative, pro-Israel, free-market. Döpfner calls himself "a non-Jewish Zionist." HuffPost's identity is liberal-leaning political commentary. Editorial independence can be promised, but the headline "German conservative buys America's progressive flagship" writes itself, in both newsrooms. BI's beat — business and tech — does not collide with any of the five Essentials; and Essential 3, the transatlantic alliance, is literally the reason to go to America. Reputation. BI brings Blodget's SEC history and a clickbait reputation; the case quotes one critic at length. Axel Springer owns Bild — "read by businessmen and workers" — it knows how to live with a tabloid reputation and monetize it. HuffPost brings a different risk: a contributor model built on unpaid bloggers, and a brand that is inseparable from one person who does not own it. Integration. BI: keep it separate, give it Europe through the group, resist the urge to "synergize." HuffPost: 13 partner-run editions, one of them in Germany — you would inherit partnerships with other publishers, and a video studio with cost structure Axel Springer would have to decide to keep or cut. Q3. What should Döpfner do in 2015? Why? (and how to make the deal go through) Buy Business Insider — the other ~91% — at a full but capped price, in weeks not months, with a United Artists structure. Walk away from HuffPost at $1B. Why BI It is the only target that fits all three of Döpfner's verbs. Digitize: BI is digital-native with a paid B2B seed (BI Intelligence) that matches the BildPlus thesis. Internationalize: English-language, US-based, and still small enough for Axel Springer to be the platform that scales it into Europe. Strengthen the core: business and tech sit next to Welt's readers, and the headline-and-traffic DNA is something Bild understands. It fits the United Artists playbook; HuffPost does not. Founders in place, stake to roll, put/call at 8–12× EBITDA, autonomy. Noth's own rule — be skeptical of anyone selling 100% and leaving — disqualifies HuffPost, where the seller is a telecom and the face of the brand is an employee. It is the better-priced growth. ~$400–450M total for a company doubling revenue, vs ~$1B for one growing 15% at ~100× EBITDA. The money saved (~$550M+) stays available for classifieds, which is where Axel Springer's digital profit actually comes from. No collision with the Essentials. A conservative, pro-Israel German owner buying America's progressive flagship is a culture war on day one. Business and tech news is not. Axel Springer already knows what it is buying. Six months on the board. The "foot in the door" was designed for exactly this moment — use it. How to make sure it closes (the FT lessons) Speed and certainty are the currency, not price. FT was lost after a year of negotiation to a bidder who copied the contract and added 10%. This time: a short, bilateral negotiation with the BI board and the lead investors, not a year-long process. Sign in weeks. Offer no financing condition and minimal regulatory risk (a US digital-only site raises none of the German antitrust issues of ProSieben). Pre-wire the people who can say yes. Ryan, Blodget, and the VCs (IVP, RRE, Bezos, Andreessen) — their alternative is another VC round at ~4.5× revenue; a strategic exit at 7–9× with a rollover is a better deal for them than for anyone else. Lock the founders' rollover and management terms before the price conversation becomes public. Set a walk-away price that already contains the "Nikkei buffer." Decide the number including a 10% topping-bid cushion; then do not move. A bruised buyer is the most likely to overpay — Döpfner should write the ceiling down before the first meeting. Ask for exclusivity and a break fee in exchange for speed and certainty; use the board seat to keep the process from turning into an auction. Protect the asset through the deal. Retention for the newsroom and sales leadership; a public commitment to editorial independence (United Artists in writing); no "integration into Bild" talk. Cost of this choice Scale: ~$50M revenue is small for a €3B group. BI must be a platform, not an endpoint — the plan has to include Europe and Asia editions and more "foot in the door" bets (Mic, Ozy, Retale show the pipeline exists). Reputation: Blodget's history and the clickbait critique will be in every German article about the deal. Axel Springer has to own that, not hide it. Economics: still loss-making or thin; ad-dependent; platform risk from Google and Facebook. BI Intelligence has to grow from "a small slice" into a real second leg. Pride: the FT was a trophy; BI is not. Döpfner has to be willing to buy the less glamorous asset after losing the glamorous one. Why not HuffPost — it violates every rule Axel Springer wrote for itself: no founders to back, no paid product, 100× EBITDA at the top of a cycle, a political identity that contradicts the Essentials, and a seller (Verizon) that will run an auction where Axel Springer would again be the slow, careful European bidder. The only argument for it is instant scale and 13 editions — and that scale is leased through partnerships, not owned. Why not wait — the print cash flows that fund all of this are shrinking; Bayer already called 2013 "the last potential exit" for the regional papers. The US window is open now and valuations are high but financeable; in two years BI will either be bigger and more expensive or sold to someone else. Case Summary July 23, 2015, Tegel Airport, Berlin. Mathias Döpfner was sitting at the gate waiting for a phone call. He was about to fly to London to sign the agreement to buy the Financial Times (FT) from Pearson, a deal worth more than US$1 billion — the core step in Axel Springer's strategy of "internationalizing the media business and entering the English-speaking world." Everyone wanted to board; he said no, wait for final confirmation from Pearson's board. The call came: during the board meeting another offer had arrived, and they had no choice but to accept it. The FT went to Nikkei. A contract negotiated for a year had been taken by the other side and bid up 10% — "take it or leave it." Deputy CEO Jan Bayer recalled that the two of them talked about it all summer, then met in Berlin and said: the international direction is right; we're going to America. Rewind seventy years. Axel Springer was founded in Hamburg in 1946 by the journalist-entrepreneur of the same name. Hamburger Abendblatt in 1948, Bild in 1952, the acquisition of Die Welt in 1953, the acquisition of the Ullstein publishing house (including the Berliner Morgenpost ) in 1959. By the 1960s it was Germany's most important news publisher. The company put its headquarters beside the Berlin Wall at Checkpoint Charlie, and in 1967 it set down the "Essentials" — five editorial principles still in use today: freedom and democracy, Israel's right to exist, the transatlantic alliance between the US and Europe, the free market, and opposition to extremism. In the 1960s this made it a target of left-wing protest; the street leading to its headquarters was later named after the protest leader Rudi Dutschke. Bild is the most-read newspaper in Europe, and was still running topless pin-up photos as late as 2012; Schröder said "all you need to govern Germany is Bild , Bild am Sonntag and television." Welt has a far smaller circulation and is the group's intellectual flagship. In 1985 Axel Springer listed 49% of the shares and died the same year, leaving control to his widow, Friede Springer. From then on, day-to-day management was handed to professional CEOs and an executive board (Vorstand) of 3–5 people, with Friede sitting behind them as a supervisory board member and major shareholder. In 2002, Döpfner took over. He was 39, had studied musicology, had spent 16 years in journalism, the last four as editor-in-chief of Welt . Friede acknowledged the doubts at the time: "They said he was too young, a music critic with no business experience... I said, I want him. And I have the majority of votes." His plan was simple: strengthen the core business, digitize, internationalize. He said that when he saw his first news website he understood "this will replace newspapers." The company was losing €200 million a year at the time, governance was unstable, and the culture needed to change — "there was nothing to lose and a lot to win." He cut 40% of the jobs, sold or shut down unprofitable assets, and within a year went from a €200 million loss to a profit of about €200 million. Almost everyone was against it: "This young man is destroying our business." 2004–2005: the first wall. They tried to buy ProSiebenSat.1, Germany's largest private TV group — bigger than Axel Springer was at the time. The team designed a multi-step deal of "tender offer for preferred shares + capital increase + merger"; the structure worked, but the German antitrust authority blocked it. Bayer called it a turning point: Döpfner concluded that they had to drastically accelerate digitization and internationalization, and use the print business to fund it while it was still making money. Over the next decade, three tracks moved in parallel. First, digitizing news: Bild only launched its paywall, BildPlus (Bundesliga highlights, sweepstakes and slot-machine games plus news), in 2013; the same year, they sold a group of regional newspapers and magazines — including the paper the founder himself started in 1948 — to Funke for €920 million. Those assets had 2012 revenue of €512 million and EBITDA of €95 million, roughly 10x EBITDA; Bayer said it was "probably the last chance to exit," and Friede "understood immediately and agreed decisively — she always looks forward, never back." Second, classifieds: Döpfner saw early on that newspapers' real estate, jobs and car ads were being replaced by the Craigslists and Zillows, so he went shopping worldwide — StepStone, Immonet, aufeminin, Seloger, Totaljobs, Immoweb — merging them into horizontal groups for jobs, real estate and autos; analysts called Axel Springer "one of the most aggressive buyers of classifieds in Europe." Third, by 2014 more than half the group's revenue came from digital businesses. The way it bought companies became a philosophy in itself. Döpfner didn't do deep integration; he called it the "United Artists model" — after the film company Chaplin and others founded in 1919 to protect their creative independence: "I respect entrepreneurs, and I want Axel Springer to be their home. As long as they deliver the plan and the results, let them go their own way." Bayer's metaphor was a jazz band: improvising within a clear framework, with no preset direction. "We don't believe in top-down synergies. You can treat Axel Springer as a buffet — knowledge, technology, product, legal, M&A — but you don't have to." The deal structure became standardized as a result: founders keep a substantial stake and later exit via a Put/Call — 12x EBITDA if they beat the plan, 8x if they miss. Deputy head of M&A Andreas Noth said: "When founders want to sell 100% at once and walk away, we're usually suspicious — they may not believe in the company's potential." The industry was running in the same direction at the same time. Nikkei bought the FT; News Corp bought Myspace, Move and REA; Schibsted bought Blocket and Leboncoin; Bertelsmann integrated Gruner + Jahr; in the US, Gannett, the New York Times and Tribune bet on digital subscriptions; PE firms like Alden bought distressed newspapers to restructure them. The US digital media market was hot in 2015: NBCUniversal invested a combined US$400 million in Buzzfeed and Vox; Buzzfeed was valued at US$1.5 billion, about 13x revenue; Hearst and Disney bought 10% of Vice at a US$2.5 billion valuation, about 5x revenue; none was profitable. Forbes sold to a Hong Kong investor group in 2014 for US$475 million, about 3x revenue and 22x EBITDA. Two candidates. Business Insider: founded in 2007 by former DoubleClick CEO Kevin Ryan and Henry Blodget (Blodget had a history from his Wall Street analyst days of being investigated by the SEC, barred from the industry and fined US$4 million), purely digital business and tech news, known for high output, SEO and social distribution, and also criticized for "clickbait headlines, more ads than content, and slideshows to farm clicks"; about 75% of revenue from advertising, plus a small B2B subscription research product, BI Intelligence; venture-backed, with shareholders including Bezos and Andreessen; in 2013 AOL offered about US$100–150 million and the board rejected it, asking around US$250 million at the time. In January 2015, Axel Springer led its Series G, US$20 million for 9% and a board seat — Noth called it "a foot in the door": invest a small amount first, get to know the management and founders, understand the culture. By mid-2015 BI had nearly 90 million monthly unique visitors and revenue approaching US$50 million. Huffington Post: founded in 2005 by Arianna Huffington, Kenneth Lerer, Jonah Peretti and Andrew Breitbart, a liberal-leaning news and commentary site that became a large general-interest site through aggregation, original content and a high-output model built on thousands of unpaid bloggers; by 2015 it had 13 international editions (UK, Canada, France, Germany, Spain, Brazil, India, Japan, Korea, Australia) and had just launched an Arabic edition. AOL bought it in 2011 for US$315 million, when annual revenue was about US$30 million. Its business model relied entirely on advertising, with no paid product; in 2012 it invested in the video platform HuffPost Live. 2014 revenue was estimated at US$146 million, still loss-making (international expansion, newsroom, video); 2015 revenue was expected to be US$168 million, with EBITDA over US$10 million. In 2015 Verizon bought AOL for US$4.4 billion and was rumored to be spinning off HuffPost for about US$1 billion — roughly 6–7x revenue. The case stops here : Döpfner and his team, recovering from the FT setback, have to decide — buy Business Insider or HuffPost? And this time, how do they make sure the deal doesn't fly away at the last minute? News vs. classifieds : The money is in classifieds (US$1.44 billion in disclosed acquisitions); news is the identity and the mission. Spending US$1 billion on a news brand — is that paying for identity or for returns?
Now Is the Time for Courage

The Professor's Questions What does courage mean to you? Can we learn to be courageous and if so, how? How can organizations become more courageous and what role can leaders play in doing so? My Answers Q1. What does courage mean to you? My one-line answer: courage is paying a real price, while I am still afraid, for something I have decided is worth it. Three parts matter to me — the price, the fear, and the decision. The price has to be real. Gulati's definition is "a willingness to take bold, risky action to serve a purpose you perceive to be worthy, in the face of an abiding fear." I would underline risky . CVS gave up $2 billion of sales to stop selling tobacco. Haugen gave up a lucrative job. If nothing is at stake, it is not courage — it is just an opinion. This is also why I distrust "bold" statements that cost the speaker nothing. The fear stays. Mandela: courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it. The article is careful here — the goal is not to stop being afraid but to act with the fear still in the room. Foulkes said walking away from a business that size was "a very scary thing," and they did it anyway. So for me courage is not a feeling. It is a behaviour you can observe: did the person act, or not? It is a decision, not a trait. Knight's distinction matters: when the odds can be calculated, what you need is good analysis, not courage. Courage starts where the spreadsheet stops — in uncertainty, where the outcomes themselves are unknown. At that point the brain's default is freeze or flight, and courage is the choice to take back agency and move. The article calls this reclaiming agency; I would call it taking responsibility for a decision nobody can prove right in advance. Two things courage is not , for me. It is not recklessness — Aristotle put courage between cowardice and rashness, and Gulati agrees that "leaders should not take outsize risks." And it is not loud. Most of the courage I have seen in business is quiet: a founder going to survival salary for the fourth time (Bajpai), a plant manager sending a team to inspect a damaged reactor with a whiteboard as the only tool (Masuda). In my own writing, long before this course, the three words I kept coming back to were being brave, caring, and being serious. Reading this article I would now reorder them: caring comes first — it is what makes something worth a price — and courage is what you do about it. Q2. Can we learn to be courageous, and if so, how? Yes — and the article's strongest evidence is not the research, it is the structure of the playbook: five strategies, each broken into three concrete, repeatable moves. Fifteen things you can practise. Nothing on the list requires a special personality. Why I believe it is learnable: The science says so. From Socrates to Mencius the question was open; modern research across psychology, sociology, neuroscience and healthcare lands on the side of "learnable." People who never thought of themselves as brave became so when the situation called for it. The stories say so. Sully's training never covered a double engine failure, yet "my entire life had been preparation to handle that particular moment." The Taj staff were not hired for heroism; they went through 18 months of onboarding and then "fell back on that training." Courage looked like character from outside, but it was built by repetition. The 9% says so. In the 2008 study, the companies that invested while cutting were not a different species. They had different habits. How — my own ordering of the fifteen moves, from easiest to start with to hardest: Start with the body (Stay calm). Sleep, food, water; a ritual before the hard moment (Jobs' mirror question, Bernanke facing the clock); and the reframe: write down the pessimistic, realistic and optimistic version of what you face. Fink's line — "we have lived through moments like this before" — is a reframe you can borrow on day one. Hunt the risks (Positive narrative). Make a list of what you are actually afraid of. The point is not to get risk to zero; it is to turn a fog into a list. Fink built a whole company (Aladdin) on this; a founder can do it with one page. Name the purpose. Ask what this decision is for . CVS's $2 billion became bearable because 25,000 pharmacists could be proud of it. A moral quest is not decoration — it is what makes the price payable. Train deliberately in your own craft (Cultivate confidence). Competence is the raw material of confidence. Bandura's self-efficacy is not "I am brave," it is "I know what I can do with the skills I have." Pick the core skill of your role and drill it until it is second nature; then widen the tool kit (delegation, transparent debate, mental endurance). Focus on what you control. Break the big fear into small, ownable problems — "tariffs" into "change suppliers faster, tweak pricing." Saban: "We're not going to talk about what we're going to accomplish. We're going to talk about how we're going to do it." Take small steps, through two-way doors (Take small steps). Evaluate objectively, let meaning emerge, interpret in motion. Masuda's team never made one big decision at Daini; they made a sequence of small, reversible ones and corrected twice. This is the move that most changes what "bold" means: bold is not big; bold is early and reversible. Build the team around the fear (Find connection). One ally who believes in you (Nair's aunts, Nooyi), one source of tangible resources (Ixigo's bridge money), and at least one honest critic ("listen to the complainer"). Courage is a team sport; design the team before you need it. The hardest of the fifteen, in my view, is "accept feedback" — because it means letting someone else judge the decision you are already afraid of. The easiest is self-care, and it is the one most leaders skip. Q3. How can organizations become more courageous, and what role can leaders play? An organization becomes courageous the same way a person does — through the same five strategies — except that in an organization every one of them can be designed into a system, and the leader has one job nobody else can do: go first, and pay visibly. Mapping the five strategies onto organizational design: Strategy What it looks like as a system Example in the article Positive narrative A shared risk map everyone can see (not a risk register that only legal reads); a stated purpose that the hard decisions are explicitly tied to Aladdin; Fink's annual letter; CVS tying $2B to 25,000 pharmacists Cultivate confidence Long, serious onboarding and drilling of the core craft; a wide tool kit taught, not assumed; "focus on process" as a management language Taj's 18-month onboarding; Nick Saban; Schultz and Knudstorp going back to basics Take small steps A decision taxonomy: which decisions are two-way doors (fast, delegated, reversible) and which are one-way (slow, senior, deliberate); whiteboards before plans Amazon's two-way doors; Masuda's whiteboard Find connection Safety nets (bridge capital, reserves, legal/medical support) so people can afford to act; institutionalized dissent — transparent debate, gemba walks, "listen to the complainer" Ixigo's investors; Luminate; Foulkes' debate culture; Culp; Lego Stay calm Rest treated as operational necessity, not weakness; rituals before high-stakes moments; a habit of writing the pessimistic / realistic / optimistic case Nair's oxygen mask; Bernanke's clock; Fink's reframe What only the leader can do: Define courage as a value out loud, then behave as if it costs something. Gulati's own conclusion is that bravery "must be learned and taught to others." In the 2023 article he said the cultural barrier — loss aversion — is overcome by "explicitly cultivating courage as a cultural value, making courageous behaviour the norm, with leaders modelling it." Pennington's "not investing is riskier" and Minicucci's "we want to be aggressive" are the leader saying the sentence first, in the quarter when it was hardest to say. Pay first. Foulkes' team debated for a long time and did not all agree. The decision became a source of pride only after it cost $2 billion. A leader who asks for courage while taking none is asking for compliance. Lower the cost of being brave for everyone else. Most people in an organization are not afraid of the market; they are afraid of their boss. Two-way doors, honest post-mortems without blame, and a visible safety net make bold action cheap enough that ordinary people will take it. The Taj employees were brave because the organization had made "guests first" the default, not an exception. Hunt risks in public. Put the fears on the whiteboard. Masuda did not tell his team "stay calm"; he gave them data to write down. An organization that names its risks is less frightened than one that whispers about them. Build dissent into the calendar. Gemba walks, complainer sessions, red-team reviews of the leader's own narrative. The point of accepting feedback is not humility — it is that validated interpretations produce more confident action. Protect the body of the organization. Sleep, pace, recovery. A team running on fumes will default to freeze. The leader sets the pace, and most set it too fast to be brave. The cost: an organization that practises courage will make more visible mistakes. Two-way doors mean walking back through some of them in public. The leader has to absorb that — which is itself the courage the organization is learning from. Link to this unit: Roaring Out of Recession (10-14) said what progressive companies do; this article says how their people find the nerve. And Cynthia Carroll (10-10) is the whole playbook in one person — a moral quest (zero harm), a visible price (shutting the mines), allies and critics, and small steps after the big one. Case Summary The article opens with a discovery the author never saw coming. During the 2008 financial crisis, Gulati, Nitin Nohria and Franz Wohlgezogen studied how 4,700 public companies came through the three previous recessions (this is Roaring Out of Recession , which we read for the October 14 class). They found that roughly 9% of companies emerged from each recession stronger than they went in — not just because they cut costs cleverly, but because at the same time they took calculated risks to invest in growth. As the author puts it, they had "inadvertently documented the enormous difference that courage makes in business." For the next decade and more he turned to a different question: facing the same hard circumstances, why do some leaders dare to move while others don't? He starts by defining courage. Courage is "the willingness to take bold, risky action in the face of persistent fear, for a purpose one considers worthy." It might mean taking on a physical challenge, making yourself emotionally vulnerable, staking your social or financial standing on a moral conviction, or publicly championing a new, unorthodox idea. He quotes Mandela: courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it. From Socrates, Plato and Aristotle to Mencius, philosophers have long argued over whether bravery is an innate virtue or something that can be taught; modern research in psychology, sociology, economics, neuroscience and medicine backs the latter — plenty of people who never thought of themselves as brave have acted bravely when the situation demanded it. Yet almost no one has systematically studied "how a person can become braver." So he pulled together the existing literature, archival research and more than 200 in-depth interviews to distill a playbook for how "anyone can be more fearless at work." Then he draws a line: courage is for the part that risk management can't solve. Many experts say the way to overcome the anxiety of uncertainty is risk management — Kathleen Reardon calls courageous action a "smart gamble," built on "careful weighing and preparation." Running a cost-benefit analysis does lower the odds of a bad outcome. But the economist Frank Knight long ago distinguished "risk," whose probabilities can be estimated, from "uncertainty," which can neither be fully enumerated nor estimated. Under VUCA conditions, the possible outcomes themselves are unknown; most people feel a loss of control, which triggers fear, and they then either freeze or take flight. What sets courageous leaders apart is that they can seize back the initiative and choose the third response — fight. At the time of writing, 76% of S&P 500 companies had mentioned "uncertainty" on their earnings calls, up from 37% three months earlier. Next come five strategies, each with three concrete practices, illustrated with stories. Strategy one: build a positive narrative. The first practice is "risk hunting": not driving risk down to zero, but identifying the unknowns one by one so the world looks more orderly. BlackRock's Larry Fink built his whole career on this — his first employee, Charlie Hallac, was tasked with developing a comprehensive risk-assessment platform, later called Aladdin, which became the gold standard of the financial industry. In his 2025 annual letter, he pointed out that US$25 trillion was sitting idle in US bank accounts and money-market funds, while global public and private infrastructure would need about US$68 trillion over the next 25 years — figures like these, and finer-grained analysis, gave management the confidence to make three big acquisitions in late 2024: Global Infrastructure Partners (US$170 billion in assets, more than 100 countries), private-markets data firm Preqin, and private-credit manager HPS. The second practice is "find a moral mission": reframe the work as the pursuit of some value. Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen said she "did what I believed was necessary to save the lives of people" endangered by Facebook putting profits first. In 2014, CVS's Helena Foulkes and her team decided to stop selling tobacco, giving up US$2 billion in sales and risking a backlash from consumers and investors — "We debated it for a long time, and not everyone agreed... walking away from such a big piece of business was scary," but "we had 25,000 pharmacists at the time, and for them and for all of us, working at a company that made such a bold decision really created a sense of pride." The third practice is "draw on faith": research shows entrepreneurs spend more time praying than the general population and are more likely to believe in a God who responds to them; people who believe they'll be lucky feel a stronger sense of agency. Cadbury, Rockefeller, Sam Walton and Aflac's Dan Amos have all spoken publicly about the role of faith; former PepsiCo CEO Indra Nooyi kept a statue of the elephant-headed god Ganesha in her office — "when the stress was unbearable... I'd close my eyes and think of a temple... and suddenly feel I could take on the whole world." Strategy two: cultivate confidence. Confidence comes from what Bandura called self-efficacy — "your belief in what you can do with the skills you have, under a variety of circumstances." The first practice is "deliberate training": practice best practices until they become second nature. Sully Sullenberger's pilot training had no lesson on "how to ditch in the Hudson after a dual engine failure," but he said, "I'd been preparing for that moment my whole life." Bernanke's academic career studying the Great Depression equipped him to handle 2008; GE's Larry Culp carried out GE's complex restructuring on the lean expertise he built over 25 years at Danaher, 13 of them as CEO. Staff at Mumbai's Taj Mahal Palace hotel stayed at their posts through the days-long siege of the 2008 terrorist attacks; every one of them had gone through 18 months of onboarding, learning not just the job but a "guest first" culture — during the attack they saw themselves as guardians of the company and its guests. The second practice is "build a big toolkit": meta-tools of all kinds for thinking, solving problems and staying resilient. NASA's Terry Virts said boot camps on mental endurance were as useful as technical and physical training; Foulkes's personal tool was delegation and her team tool was transparent debate — "deep conversations about paradox and complexity... letting people say what excites them and what makes them nervous... and turning those competing emotions into a new, creative solution." The third practice is "focus on what you can control": break a big question like "how do we respond to changing tariff policy" into small ones like "switch suppliers faster, fine-tune pricing"; or simply get the operational basics right. In sport it's called "focus on process, not outcome" — Nick Saban told his players, "We don't talk about what we're going to achieve; we talk about how we're going to do it." Starbucks' Howard Schultz got through 2008 by going back to the core coffeehouse experience; LEGO's Jørgen Vig Knudstorp engineered a turnaround by returning to the mission of bricks and creativity; Ixigo's Aloke Bajpai ran the company out of money at least four times — "Most companies would have shut down, but each time the founders put money back in and took subsistence salaries, investors gave bridge funding, many employees took big pay cuts, and most importantly, we kept shipping one of the most innovative products in the world." Strategy three: take small steps. Many people equate boldness with big moves, but the leaders and organizations the author studied probe with small steps before they leap — what Karl Weick calls sensemaking. You let go of the need for a perfect plan and trust that the path will appear as you walk it. Step one is "assess objectively": the trigger is often a disruptive event that creates uncertainty, and the instinct is to freeze or flee, but you need to practice mindfulness, observing both the external situation and your own emotional reaction, and ask: What am I facing? Whom can I call on for help? What can I do right now to understand the situation? When the 2011 tsunami hit Fukushima, Naohiro Masuda, head of the Daini (No. 2) plant, gathered his team around a whiteboard, wrote down the data they knew, and analyzed what might go wrong and how to stop it — a 55-foot wave had struck a plant designed for only 17 feet. Step two is "let meaning emerge": gather every clue you can, however trivial it seems, piece them into an explanation, form hypotheses, pick the most plausible one, then keep gathering and revising. As Weick says, "Sensemaking is not about truth and getting it right. Instead, it is about continued redrafting of an emerging story so that it becomes more comprehensive, incorporates more of the observed data, and is more resilient in the face of criticism." When the main control panel went dark, Masuda sent people out at personal risk to inspect the damaged equipment on site, and from that hypothesized that the cooling systems had lost power and that they needed to bring materials to repair them and find an alternative energy source. Step three is "interpret through action": act on the hypothesis, expose yourself to new clues, and carry on or change course. The key is to take steps that keep options open — what Amazon calls "two-way doors": you can walk through, and you can walk back out. Masuda's team first tried to draw power from the only building on site that still had electricity; that proved technically too hard, so they switched to the one generator still working, and redirected their efforts after judging that another reactor was in greater danger. Small steps, observation, learning, iteration — in the end they averted disaster, which Fukushima Daiichi (No. 1) did not. Strategy four: find connection. Contrary to the popular story, lone heroes are rare. Courage is a team sport; behind every brave leader there is usually a group of less visible but vitally important supporters, plus a set of constructive critics. The first practice is "seek emotional support from allies": when the people around you believe you're capable of courage, you start to believe it too; relationships also affirm your identity and your obligations to others, making you feel more responsible for acting. Chanel CEO Leena Nair says that when people doubted her abilities as a woman, or as an HR leader from a "soft skills" background, she would think of the older women in her family whose own ambitions had been stifled but who had complete faith in her — "they'd say, give Leena that chance, she's smart, she's talented." Her mentor Nooyi told her not to think about her limitations but about the key strengths she could bring to the role. The second practice is "secure resources": money and people are a safety net. Bajpai's bridge funding; Luminate (the organization of eBay founder Omidyar) and Whistleblower Aid behind Haugen. Nooyi: "You can't know everything. Bring in the experts and let them teach you." The third practice is "accept feedback": you can't surround yourself only with cheerleaders; you need critics who assess you honestly. One of Knudstorp's mottos at LEGO was "listen to the people who complain"; Culp is known for "gemba walks" — managers walking the shop floor to hear directly from frontline workers. Strategy five: stay calm. What psychologists call "emotion regulation" is the ability to influence how you feel when the "freeze, flight, fight" response is triggered. The first practice is "self-care": sleep, nutrition, hydration — "you can't think clearly when your tank is empty." Nair says, "Put on your own oxygen mask first, so you have the energy to play all your roles." The second practice is "embrace rituals": Japanese samurai and Norse Vikings had pre-battle rituals; every morning Steve Jobs made his bed, showered, then looked in the mirror and asked, "If today were the last day of my life, would I be happy with what I'm about to do today?"; some entrepreneurs wear a lucky sweater or recite a mantra before every fundraising or customer pitch; Bernanke, following Greenspan's habit, always sat facing the clock at Fed meetings; Schultz relies on regular meditation. The third practice is "reframe the situation": redefine what the uncertainty means in the long run for you and your organization, thinking through pessimistic, realistic and optimistic versions in turn — fully acknowledging the danger while dialing down your reaction to it. Fink wrote in his annual letter: "We've been through moments like this before. Somehow, over the long run, we always figure things out." Foulkes: "My mind sometimes goes to 'what could go wrong' — that's probably the benefit of business school training — but it's just as important to ask, 'What good could happen?'" Bajpai reframed the Covid pandemic as yet another crisis that forced him to conserve cash, while it also pushed the company to explore new growth, including acquiring train and bus ticketing businesses — which laid the groundwork for Ixigo's successful IPO in 2024. It closes with a judgment. As change and disruption accelerate, courage — or its absence — will make or break careers, organizations and societies. That doesn't mean leaders should take excessive risks, "but most of us tend to be too timid rather than too reckless." After hundreds of interviews, the author is convinced that bravery is a skill every businessperson today must learn and teach to others; solving big problems like climate change, economic inequality and political polarisation will require summoning a kind of collective courage. "A little more boldness can go a long way." The Professor's Questions David Jacobs founded a high-end ski apparel company in 1978. In 1996, he sought external financing to support further growth of the company and structured a financial deal with CHB Capital Partners, a private equity firm in Denver that began in September, 1997. By 2004, Jacobs was ready to consider alternative types of equity transactions that would provide a source of liquidity to him and his family, including sale of Spyder to another apparel company and sale of a large block of stock to a private equity firm. How, if at all, does the value of Spyder depend on its ownership structure? What are the (other) primary determinants of value? Prepare estimates of the company’s value based on DCF and trading and transaction multiples presented in the case. How well do these estimates reflect the considerations for a sale that you believe are most important? Compare the alternative transactions on the last page of the case. Which one would you choose if you were David Jacobs? Which one would you choose if you were CHB? Who else is affected by your choices and how? My Answers Q1. Does value depend on ownership? Other determinants Yes. Spyder does not have one price. It has a price for each next owner, because the owner changes the cash flows, the people who stay, and the brand that remains. A DCF that ignores ownership is a DCF of a company that may not exist after the closing. Ownership moves value in four concrete ways. Who the owner is, changes the cash flows. A strategic buyer (Columbia, VF, Nike, Adidas-Salomon) can put Spyder through its own sourcing and its own stores. That is extra EBITDA the standalone model does not have — a synergy premium. A financial buyer cannot. It pays for the business as it is, plus the governance it will add, minus the extra debt and the 3–5 year exit clock. CHB itself said this in 1997: the CEO who is retiring to France does not care what the PE firm brings; the CEO who will still be there cares what the firm and he can make the company worth in three to five years. In 2004 the question flips: what can the next owner make it worth. Control is not the same asset as a 37.9% stub. A 100% trade sale or a PE buyout of everyone is a control deal. CHB selling only its minority piece is not. Buyers pay less for stock they cannot steer, cannot take public, and cannot easily resell. The case is explicit: if Jacobs keeps control, CHB's exit shrinks to a minority sale to another PE — the worst version of an already illiquid asset. Add a marketability discount on top of a minority discount. The people stay, or the forecast dies. Morris's sentence is the whole valuation: Jake and Walbrecht are "the creative engine of that company." Exhibit 5's path — $61M to $166M in four years, EBITDA $9.6M to $27.9M — is a Jake-and-John model. A strategic that folds Spyder into a portfolio and loses them should not pay for that path. A PE that rolls their equity and keeps Jacobs as coach can. The 11.3% option pool is not a rounding error; it is how you keep the engine. The wrong owner can erase the thing being sold. Jacobs's original bet was "own that little spot at the top." Half of the board's time is already spent keeping channels clean so a $600 jacket at Christy's is not killed by a $300 sale at Gart. A fashion conglomerate that pushes department stores too hard, or a PE that chases the $100M brand with the wrong mix, does not buy Spyder. It buys a brand that used to be Spyder. Hilfiger on the pages of Men's Health was the warning in 1995. Snappleization, from the Nantucket class, is the same movie in a different aisle. Other primary determinants of value — the ones that sit in the spreadsheet even before you pick an owner: Growth that just inflected. $10M (1997) → $61.4M (FY04), seven-year CAGR ~30%. Last year +52%. That is rare in technical apparel. Buyers pay for the slope, then argue about whether FY05's +39% is real. Margin that just appeared. Gross margin 39% → 49.5%; EBITDA 4.9% → 15.6%. Europe going direct, scale, and mix. Trailing sales multiples (~1.1× → $69M) miss this; trailing EBITDA multiples (~10× → $100M) catch it. The brand, made scarce on purpose. U.S. / Canadian / Austrian teams. Sell-through above the 80% industry average. "Always sell one less jacket than the market demanded." Scarcity is why specialty shops defend it, and why a strategic will overpay. Seasonality and working-capital violence. June sales $22M, January almost zero; revolver $0 to $23.4M, average $8M. This is why there is no IPO, why a small-company discount belongs in the WACC, and why a buyer with a weak treasury function will stumble. Market timing. Exhibit 8: trading and deal multiples were crushed in 2000–02 (CHB tried to leave and could not) and are back. "Huge amounts of cash that people wanted to put to work." The window is the buyer's dry powder, not Jacobs's readiness. Key-person and family risk. Jacobs is 70 and still the conductor. Jake is the product. Walbrecht is the market. Shimokubo is Japan. None of this is diversified. The short classroom line: ownership is not a footnote on the DCF. It is an input that rewrites the cash flows. Q2. DCF and multiples; do they capture what matters? Center of gravity: about $100 million of enterprise value on trailing EBITDA. Sales multiples say ~$70 million. Management's DCF says $170–200 million. I would walk into the room with $90–110 million for a financial buyer and $100–130 million for a strategic, and treat anything built on Exhibit 5's hockey stick as the seller's story, not the buyer's check. Do these numbers capture what matters for a sale? Partly, and the part they miss is the part that will decide the deal. What they get right: The EBITDA multiple is the right center . Margin just appeared. A 1.1× sales number ($69M) values Spyder as if it were still the 5–10% EBITDA company of FY01–03. It is not. The gap between financial ~9× and strategic ~10–11× is exactly the ownership point from Q1: synergies and control on one side, a sponsored hold on the other. Exhibit 8 says now is a better year to sell than 2002 . Multiples are an input, not just an output. What they miss, and these are the sale considerations I would actually underwrite: Who stays. No multiple knows if Jake and Walbrecht sign. A $186M DCF that loses them is fiction. A $100M check that keeps them and rolls 11.3% may be the better deal. Who the buyer is, in the brand sense. Channel integrity, the "one less jacket" scarcity, the race-suit halo. A strategic can pay 11× and destroy the asset; a PE can pay 9× and keep it. Price and value part ways. Minority vs control. None of the Exhibit 9 deals (except TNF 81% and Helly Hansen 70%) is a 37.9% stub. Applying 10× to CHB's slice without a discount overstates what CHB can get if Jacobs will not sell. Forecast credibility. Exhibit 5 is the offering memorandum talking. FY04 is unaudited. FAS 133 already showed $1M of noise in FY03–04. Seasonality means one warm winter changes the trailing year. The DCF is a story about a $400M brand; CHB told them to install the ERP for that brand. A buyer will not pay for the ERP's ambition. Jacobs at 70, CHB's fund clock, two sons, Shimokubo's Japan line. None of this is in WACC. All of it is in the term sheet: rollover, put/call, employment, non-compete, channel covenants, who sits on the board. Classroom close: use $100M as the number you can defend without blushing; use the DCF as the ceiling you put on the board to keep the auction honest; decide the deal on who owns it next, not on which cell in the spreadsheet is largest. C protects a control Jacobs says he no longer wants, and traps the partner who made the last seven years possible. Case Summary David Jacobs founded Spyder in Boulder, Colorado, in 1978. A Canadian downhill champion and national team coach, he had already crashed twice as an entrepreneur: Lange ski boots, after going public, recalled 25,000 pairs over their liners and was eventually sold; Jacobs Corp. sold 45% to venture capitalists and the rest to García, which went bankrupt in 1978. He turned down an offer from Hong Kong's Auyang family to stay on as a vice president and started two more companies of his own, one of which was Spyder: high-end racing sweaters, sold by mail order, made in Hong Kong, positioned with a "powerful, slightly menacing" logo. The first twenty years are the story of a family workshop growing into a brand. For the first two years it ran out of the family kitchen, with his two teenage sons, Bill and Jake, helping mail out catalogues. To raise money, Jacobs sold stock to Hanson Industries in exchange for $75,000 in cash and a warehouse; when Hanson hit a financial crisis in 1982, he had to either buy it back for $50,000 or lose the company. Having no money of his own, he brought in his Osaka manufacturer, Tsunehisa Shimokubo: Shimokubo put in $50,000 for 50,000 shares, Jacobs took 25,000 shares, and they agreed he would get another 25,000 shares when sales reached $2.5M — he was convinced he had to own at least 50% of any business he was part of. The target was hit in 1986, and the two became 50/50 partners. The brand claimed that "small spot at the top." Fabrics came from Japan and Switzerland, insulation from 3M, snaps from Italy, and together with suppliers it developed proprietary materials such as X-static, Thermaweb and Spylon. In 1988 it won the U.S. Ski Team sponsorship, and Picabo Street and Tommy Moe appeared at World Cups and Olympics in spiderweb-patterned race suits. Sales grew from $3.4M in 1987 to $7.9M in 1990, and the channel shifted from mail order to specialty ski shops. In Jacobs's words: the market wasn't big, but "if I can hold that small piece at the top, there aren't many people fighting me for it." Jake represents another life running through this story. International business at the University of Colorado, top honours in fashion design at FIDM, a year at Ono Trading's factory in Japan, then managing production in Hong Kong, before Nike poached him to do apparel development in Singapore and Hong Kong. In 1995 his father called him back as vice president of design and manufacturing. In 1995 the company hit a midlife crisis. Sales were stuck at $10–15M, Jacobs was nearly 65 and had always kept his money in the company; Tommy Hilfiger, Nautica, Prada and Armani had begun making ski fashion, and Hilfiger ran a two-page ski ad in Men's Health. Jacobs said: "This is my turf." His advisers concluded: either sell the whole company or find a minority partner — "selling 51% is the same as selling everything." In February 1997 he hired Robertson Stephens to take it to market, approaching both strategic and financial buyers; Nike was at one point rumoured to want a majority stake, but it went into skateboarding and hockey instead, and that was that. CHB Capital Partners is a local Denver PE firm, and its name literally means Closely Held Businesses. Tad Kelly and John Flanigan (both Harvard MBAs), plus Blake Morris. Low volume, high touch: they look at hundreds of deals a year and do only 2–3; they don't buy whole companies but want to "partner" with the CEO; Kelly said equity capital had become as commoditised as debt, so "we have to offer more than money." Their sweet spot: revenue of $10–50M, stakes of 20–80%, holding periods of 3–5 years. They were willing to put in about $5M and take a minority stake, but required a minimum 30% return. After due diligence they felt the projections in the memorandum were high, and proposed a sliding stake based on cumulative 1998–2002 EBITDA: hit the memorandum's $20.5M and they would hold 35%; above $26.5M, it would fall to 25%; below $10.5M, it would rise to 60%. Jacobs rejected the sliding scale and insisted on a fixed percentage. The final deal: on September 25, 1997, CHB first invested $2.5M for convertible preferred stock, a 22% stake; by no later than the end of 1998 it could invest another $2M (of which $1M could have gone to Jacobs and Shimokubo as cash-out, and $1M to working capital). If both tranches were invested, the fully diluted stake would be 37.9%. Once the money came in, the company was switched over to a different operating system. The board went from "we meet when I'm in Japan and toss a page into the minutes" to formal quarterly meetings, with Kelly and Flanigan joining the board and Morris watching day-to-day operations. CHB pushed them onto J.D. Edwards ERP — "If you want to be a $100M brand, don't install a $10M system, install a $400M one." It cost about $1M. In May 1998 they brought in John Walbrecht, 31–32 years old and from outside the industry (global head of sales and marketing at Dr. Martens, previously at Gloria Vanderbilt and Timberland), as vice president of global sales and marketing. They rolled out fixtures / concept shops, landing 1,500 square feet at Marshall Field in Chicago. Flanigan chaired the annual strategy meeting. At the end of 1998 CHB exercised the second $2M tranche; Jacobs and Shimokubo chose not to take the $1M in cash. Ownership became: CHB 37.9%, employee options 11.3%, Jacobs and Shimokubo 25.4% each. Growth meant losing money first and making it later. Walbrecht took sales meetings, which under Jacobs had never cost more than $25,000, and turned them into a $150,000 Hollywood-style launch in Vail with 75 dealers invited; the industry's view of the company went from "sleepy little firm" to "player." He himself spent 250 days a year on the road, working out for retailers how to display the merchandise, what music customers should hear and what prices to charge. Blake Morris boiled the industry statistics down to a one-page chart: third in insulated jackets, being crushed by The North Face in shells — and only then did people react. Jake moved his father out of the design seat, expanded the product and buying teams the Nike way, and within 18 months was promoted to vice president of merchandising. Products expanded from tight race suits and the $300–$1,000 core line into Venom, Kyds, Stryke and a snowboard line, with prices reaching down to $100, and distribution into Sports Authority, Dick's and Macy's. In Europe they switched from multiple distributors to selling direct, starting in 2001 with Germany, Australia and Benelux, then France and Switzerland — more profitable on the books. In 2000 the books showed a loss of $972,000 and the bank got nervous; Kelly and Jacobs stripped out the one-off investments, the bank accepted two sets of numbers, "before investment / after investment," and the relationship was saved. By spring 2004, the report card had turned a page. Net sales went from $27.3M in FY01 to $61.4M in FY04, and net income from $83K to $5.1M. The Canadian and Austrian national teams were added. Retailers valued the high margins and high sell-through; Spyder's principle was "always sell one fewer — one fewer than the market wants." Bill was also called back to run Northern California. CHB tried to exit in 2002, but the market wasn't there; by the end of 2003, this was the only unrealised investment left in one of CHB's funds, held for seven years, longer than the expected 3–5. Jacobs said there was a great deal of cash out there with nowhere to go — "smart money is looking for brands." They hired two investment banks to split the fees and the responsibilities: Financo (retail) and Wachovia (consumer products, handled by Joe Pellegrini from the 1997 round). An IPO was ruled out: the company was relatively small and highly seasonal. The last page of the case lays out three workable structures: sell to a strategic buyer (an apparel company); sell a large block of equity to another PE firm; or Jacobs keeps control and CHB can only sell its minority stake to another PE firm. Jacobs was 70. He said that in recent years he had stepped back a little from the day-to-day, and that being fairly rewarded for decades of entrepreneurship mattered more to him than continuing to control the company's direction. But Jake and Walbrecht were "the company's creative engine," and an acquisition would rewrite their positions and those of the whole executive team. He had to balance himself, CHB, his two sons, and the company he had built, all at once.
