The Professor's Questions Why did Pearson feel the need to roll out NWOW to begin with? Reviewing the B case – which is an interactive NWOW playbook what do think are its strengths? Its weaknesses? Why? The firm claims it has achieved significant performance improvements. Which elements of the NWOW approach contribute most to the enhanced results? Why? Do you think NWOW would have succeeded had COVID not happened when it did? If yes, why? If no, why not? Should Pearson and Hurd continue to push for 100 percent adoption of NWOW in the firm? If yes, why? IF no, why not? What do you recommend Pearson and Hurd do with the pockets of resistance? Should they leave them be? Should they pull adoption and acceptance through metrics and oversight? Going ahead, does it make sense for Equitable to only recruit leaders who will embrace NWOW and the firm’s operating model? Is it a viable approach? Or, will the firm miss out on talent by using such a stringent condition? My Answers Q1. Why roll out NWOW Pearson rolled out NWOW because the IPO gave Equitable a new scoreboard and an old metabolism. The scoreboard was quarterly, public, and unforgiving. The metabolism was still a mutual-company subsidiary's: two accounting cycles a year, a 50-day close, a $200 million error threshold, a 61% not-in-good-order rate on enrollment forms, and 1,500 registrars in group insurance. He did not need a new product idea. He needed the firm to move at the speed the new owners would measure. Three pressures stacked on top of that. The house was new; the habits were not. After the 2018 IPO ($2.8 billion raised), Pearson said they wanted to "move out of AXA mother's house" and build their own. Five years of preparing the spin, the IPO, and the rebrand had exhausted people. The internal line was: the old ways worked, why change. Raju's diagnosis: no urgency, no sense of disruption, strategy aimed at policies not revenue. The board approved the 2020 targets and then asked the only question that mattered: do you have the culture to hit them? The industry was slow in a market that was not. U.S. life insurers grew earnings at 2.7% a year against 5.5% for the S&P 500. Their NPS was 4.5 against USAA's 77. Life insurance ownership among U.S. adults fell from 63% in 2011 to 52% in 2023. Meanwhile 10,000 Americans were turning 65 every day (Pearson later says 11,000), the retirement income gap was on a path from $28 trillion in 2015 to $137 trillion in 2050, and 67% of retirees worried their money would not last. Equitable's largest unit already threw off $1 billion of cash a year, with the market peaking around 2030 at 90 million people. A slow firm in a shrinking-window market is a strategy problem, not an HR problem. Talent would not come for the old story. By 2025 millennials would be 50% of the workforce; 4% were interested in working for a U.S. life insurer. Pearson had seen in Asia that scarce resources force innovation. In New York, abundance had produced the opposite. What he copied was not a slogan. He read Doerr on OKRs, sat in a Stanford d.school studio, studied Spark, ING, and USAA. The 61% NIGO rate is the tell: ordinary process improvement asks how to cut the ratio; design thinking asks how to get to zero returns. NWOW was the operating system that would let a newly public firm publish targets and actually hit them — faster, cheaper, with the people closest to the work allowed to decide. The five pillars (OKRs, adaptive leadership, design thinking, enterprise agile, dynamic enablers) are just the kit. The need was: we cannot run a NYSE company on a twice-a-year close. Q2. Playbook strengths and weaknesses The playbook is unusually honest about why , unusually clear about who does what , and unusually heavy on when we meet . Its strengths are the spine. Its weaknesses are that the spine got buried under a calendar. Strengths It starts with a burning platform and a burning aspiration, signed by the CEO. Pearson's letter puts 10,000 Americans turning 65 each day and a retirement gap compounding by trillions next to "we need people who love to come to work." Menard's note says one-third of the firm is already on NWOW as of early 2021, and the playbook itself is an MVP. Most corporate agile decks skip the why. This one does not. It is a kit, not a law — at least on page 4. "Not a how-to. Building blocks you hand-pick for the Mission." That sentence is the best sentence in the document. It is also the sentence the rest of the document keeps violating. It names five questions, not five slogans. How do we aim teams at the biggest aspirations? How do the people closest to the work get to decide? How do we make a place that grows skill and autonomy? How do we prototype what customers want rather than what we assume? How do we unleash teams? Adaptive leadership, design thinking, enterprise agile, OKRs, and dynamic enablers are answers to those questions. It distinguishes Squads from Self-Managing Teams, Tribes from CoEs from Delivery Units. Cross-functional 6–10 for end-to-end product work; same-function 6–15 for sales desks and wholesalers; Tribes of 70–150 with a Tribe Lead; CoEs of 30–100; Delivery Units of 100–1,000 running repeatable client-facing work. The architecture admits that a call center is not a feature team. The role cards then do something rare: they list I do not — do not micromanage, do not play the boss, do not skip the ceremonies, do not assume you must have the answers. It separates moonshots from commitments. Hit 70% of a moonshot (onboard 200k educators; NPS of 50) and it counts as success. Hit 100% of a commitment (50–60% capital payout; 40% diversity in leadership). That single distinction keeps OKRs from becoming a second budget. It measures four things, not one. Maturity, efficiency (lead time, velocity, defects), culture (eNPS), and business impact (NPS, net flows, first-year premium). A playbook that only tracks story points would have been a ritual. This one at least aims the instruments at the P&L. Weaknesses Page 4 says kit; pages 40–48 issue a timetable. Daily 15-minute stand-up, sprint planning, backlog refinement, sprint review, retro, PO sync every sprint, monthly macro-unit review, quarterly Big Room Planning, QBR. Schirripa's wholesalers were right: this is a heavy cadence. The playbook never writes a page titled "when not to run this ceremony." That missing page is why ops and distribution later called it a time sink. The Delivery Unit — the archetype that matches call centers, advisors, and branch work — had not been mobilized by February 2021. The playbook says so in plain language. The later resistance in Chandler's and Fafian's shops is not a surprise. The kit was designed, then left empty, in the exact places the A case later struggles. Being is declared more important than Doing, then given two slides. The iceberg drawing (mindset under the waterline; stand-ups and trackers above) is the right picture. The next 30 pages are agendas, Betterworks, Azure DevOps, Thrive, Yammer. A new hire will learn the calendar before they learn "from analyze-and-perfect to act-and-iterate." It still smells like the consultants they later fired. Tribes, Squads, Chapters, CoEs is the Spotify model as McKinsey packaged it. Pearson was right to burn the boats. The vocabulary stayed. A 25-year claims processor hearing that her Tribe Lead is "the start-up founder" will not feel seen. "Interactive PowerPoint, click around" is a 2021 format, not a living system. Ownership of updates is unnamed. By 2025 the firm has 36 months of scars the playbook does not contain: 130-touchpoint collections, seven systems timing out on one screen, wholesalers who will share upstream information but will not sit in a daily stand-up. A living playbook would have added a "regulated operations" chapter and a "field sales" chapter. This one froze in February 2021. Co-location was a premise; remote was a patch. The A case says teams were assumed to sit in one room. The B case adds seven remote practices and a day-in-the-life of a PO. Useful. Still a patch. The original design did not contemplate the world that actually arrived. Net: I would keep the first 20 pages and the role-card I do nots . I would cut the ceremony calendar down to a menu, and I would write the two missing chapters — Delivery Units and field distribution — before I used this document to push the last 20%. Q3. Which NWOW elements drive results The results are real, and they are not mainly from the stand-up. The pieces that moved numbers are: a named Mission with a team that does nothing else; the functions that used to hand off sitting in one squad; OKRs that made "3% growth" look like the wrong sport; and permission to ship an unfinished MVP. The ceremonies are how those pieces stay visible. They are not the engine. I would rank them. Dedicated teams against a Mission, not borrowed evenings. Scanlon gave Mitchell one month to turn 1,200 registrars into phone-and-online enrollment. She came back in two weeks. His line is the whole theory: "In the past I had to pull people off other work and have them do this in their spare time. Now this is the squad's mission. They are highly focused." Group Retirement then saw online service clicks +400%, 13,000 extra outbound calls, and $70 million of extra sales. Raju: "Double the speed and you can double the revenue." That is not a standup metric. That is what happens when the work stops being a side hustle. Cross-functional squads that kill handoffs. In Individual Retirement, product, IT, and pricing used to live in silos. NWOW put them in one team. New products moved faster. The 10-person cap (Raju: above 10 you cannot move fast) is a constraint that forces the right people into the room and the wrong meetings out of it. Layers falling from 26 to 5 is the same idea at enterprise scale: fewer places for a decision to die. Moonshot OKRs, not incremental targets. Scanlon had to stop hearing "your numbers are fine" and start hearing "you are here for exponential growth, not 3% or 10%." The playbook's 70%-equals-success rule matters: it makes a stretch target safe to declare. Without that, people sandbag. Design thinking's question on the 61% NIGO rate — how do we get to zero returns, not a better ratio — is the same muscle. MVP as a cultural permission, not a software trick. They shipped an enrollment app with pieces still missing, collected advisor feedback, and built the missing panel. Scanlon: "We would never have launched an unfinished product before." COVID made that permission urgent. The method made it legal. That is design thinking earning its keep. Ceremonies as the accountability layer, second. Daily stand-ups meant you could not hide. Scanlon: when you are in the work and being held to account, you cannot escape what you own, because there are so many rituals that update completion. Useful. But the wholesalers who refused the stand-up still created value once they shared upstream demand with the back office. The information flow mattered more than the 15 minutes. What I would not credit first. The full ceremony calendar. The Spotify nouns. The dashboards. Those are how HQ sees the work. Chandler's eNPS going from 0.7 to 29.5 happened after she listened for months, ran a 90-day control group, and had IT extend a timeout so people stopped losing work across seven systems. That is adaptive leadership and a bottleneck removed — NWOW as a license to fix the work, not NWOW as a meeting. On TSR. Since IPO, Equitable's TSR is 175.5% against core peers at 86.1% and the S&P 500 at 116% (Exhibit 5c, through 2024-12-31; 1-year 45% vs peers 24.7%). Raju is right that if culture change does not show up in TSR it does not count. I would still not draw a straight line from stand-ups to the stock. GAAP net income jumps around with derivative marks (2019 −$1.76B, 2022 +$2.07B). The cleaner story is operating: faster product, more calls, fewer layers, a workforce that will recommend the place (ops eNPS 29.5; TAP 33 vs firm 27). Those are NWOW. The multiple is also a decade of rates, AB, and the RILA book. Hold both. Q4. Would NWOW have succeeded without COVID Yes, it would have succeeded — as a slower, shallower, more political program. No, it would not have succeeded as the thing in the case: a 36-month march to 80%, with an unfinished app in market and a COO who had sat next to a clerk for an hour. COVID was not the idea. It was the deadline that made the idea expensive to refuse. Why it would still have lived: Pearson had already tied it to a public scoreboard. Quarterly reporting, 2020 targets on the whiteboard, a board that had asked about culture. That pressure does not need a virus. He had already burned one boat in principle: IDO staffed internally, Menard (his former chief of staff) in charge, five-day boot camp that rips the Band-Aid off. Scanlon had already been tapped as the first line of business. The first tribe was going to run even in an office. The 61% NIGO rate, the 1,500 registrars, the 50-day close — those bottlenecks were not created by COVID. A patient CEO who had rebuilt a balance sheet after 2008 would have kept pushing. Why it would not have looked like this: MVP permission arrived because the alternative was 20–40% less sales and 1,200 registrars who could not enroll anyone from home. Scanlon would not have launched an unfinished product "before." Without COVID there is no "before." Design thinking stays a workshop. Co-location was a premise. Raju asked, do we pause. Hurd said accelerate. If the office had stayed open, NWOW would have been "the new meeting in the same room," easier to fake, easier to wait out. The field would have kept playing golf. The headquarters-versus-line gap Schirripa describes would have stayed comfortable. They fired McKinsey because they could not wait. Pearson: once the people driving the culture change are not Equitable's, it dies. A non-crisis rollout keeps the consultants in the building longer. The playbook would have stayed theirs. George Floyd and TAP used the same operating system in a second crisis. That chapter does not exist without 2020. The diversity pipeline (24 people, 54% promoted, eNPS 33 vs 27) is a COVID-era child. The 2025 irony is the proof. Scanlon now hears: "Why bother, COVID is over, there is no burning crisis, we are doing fine." If the program needed a crisis to get to 80%, the last 20% will not move on nostalgia. That is why Q5 is not optional. A method that only works in a pandemic is a wartime habit, not an operating model. Pearson's job is to show that the Mission-and-squad logic still pays when people can go back to golf. Q5. Push for 100% adoption? No to 100% of the 2021 playbook. Yes to 100% of the operating principles. Pearson should not declare victory at 80%, and he should not force every wholesaler into a daily stand-up. He should make it impossible to opt out of four things: a Mission, OKRs, a team that owns the work end to end, and the customer's voice in the room. How they meet can vary by archetype. Why not "leave it at 80%": Scanlon is right about the social physics. If it is optional, it becomes a philosophy, then a preference, then a memory. Wealth management's "very high preference for the status quo" is the canary. Retirement throws off $1 billion of cash a year and peaks around 2030. A split firm — agile in Group Retirement, 1990s in wealth — will leak the next decade through the unconverted half. Pearson already spent the sentence he cannot take back: "This is a culture change. This is not a test, not a pilot." Walking it back teaches the organization that the next transformation is also a test. The 20% is not random. It sits in distribution, operations, and wealth — the market-facing and the regulated. Leaving them be is leaving the client-facing edge on the old OS. Why not "100% of the ceremonies": The playbook itself said pick building blocks. Delivery Units were never mobilized. Hurd watched a junior employee do an inefficient hour of work and concluded NWOW was not the most efficient way in that case . Fafian has 130 touchpoints and 25-year specialists who will not trust a toggle. Schirripa's wholesalers will give you upstream signal; they will not give you 15 minutes every morning. Forcing the calendar is how you turn a good OS into cargo-cult agile. They already have the counter-example. Chandler got ops eNPS from 0.7 to 29.5 by listening, running a 90-day cell, and fixing a timeout — not by winning the stand-up argument. Scanlon: "I don't care what page 35 of Turn the Ship Around! says. I care about output." What I would tell the room: 100% on Mission / OKRs / end-to-end ownership / customer in the loop. A menu of ceremonies by archetype — Squads run the full sprint set; SMTs and field sales run a weekly sync plus a monthly review; Delivery Units run Kanban, SLAs, and a weekly bottleneck review. Publish the menu so "we adapted" is not a euphemism for "we ignored." Pearson keeps saying it is not a pilot. Fine. The thing that is not a pilot is the OS, not the Tuesday agenda. The cost: purists will say we blinked. Some of the 20% will hear "adapted" as permission to wait. That is why Q6 cannot be "leave them be." Adaptation is for the work. It is not a hiding place for the leader. Q6. What to do with pockets of resistance Do not leave them be. Do not only pull them through metrics. Sort the pocket before you treat it. There are three kinds of resistance in the case, and they need three different moves. Kind 1 — the playbook does not fit the work. Ops (Chandler, Fafian), wholesalers (Schirripa), and the still-empty Delivery Unit. Treatment: rewrite the last mile with them in the room. Hurd already did the right diagnostic — sit for an hour and watch. Fafian's turning point was not a dashboard. It was new business growing exponentially, headcount not being enough, and the NWOW team arriving as people who "are here to hear our ideas and make our lives easier." Pull that through: map the seven systems that time out, extend the timeout, cut the 130 touchpoints, give the field a weekly demand signal instead of a daily stand-up. Then put two or three metrics on the wall that they already believe — cycle time, error rate, eNPS, first-year premium — not a maturity score from IDO. Oversight yes; HQ's scorecard as the only lever, no. Kind 2 — the leader will not own it. Hurd's own question: "If they will not fully embrace it, are we willing to replace that leader?" For this kind, yes. A Tribe Lead who is an "un-enabler" (Pearson's word) taxes every squad under them. Scanlon's method is usable: two meetings to explain why, the third to say this is how we work. After that, it is a selection decision, not a change-management problem. Do it in the 20%, not as a purge of the 80%. Kind 3 — people two or three years from retirement. Hurd already saw them leave. Let them. Do not spend coaching inventory on someone whose rational strategy is to wait you out. Offer a clean exit. Spend the seats on TAP-like people who want the new game (54% of that 24-person pipeline already promoted). What I would not do. A single firm-wide adoption KPI that treats Wealth Management's status-quo preference the same as a claims team's timeout problem. That metric will be gamed, and it will poison Kind 1. I also would not hold a third offsite with another Marquet chapter. They are past inspiration. They are in the last mile, where Pearson's burning aspiration (11,000 people turning 65 each day, Social Security in deficit since 2016, a market that peaks in 2030) has to be translated into this week's bottleneck, not into another letter. A practical 90-day pack: Publish the archetype menu (Q5). Name which pocket is which kind. For every Kind 1 pocket: one Hurd-style observation day, one bottleneck kill, one metric the team chose, one IDO coach who reports to the line leader, not the other way around. For every Kind 2 leader: a decision in the quarter — in, or out. No third meeting. Do not announce 100%. Announce: no team without a Mission and OKRs by quarter-end. That is the non-optional floor. Q7. Only hire leaders who embrace NWOW? Yes for leaders. No as a blanket filter on all talent. The operating model is the job description of anyone who sets a Mission, owns a budget, or coaches a squad. It is not the job description of the best actuary, the 25-year claims specialist, or the advisor who holds the client relationship. Use the role cards' I do not list as the leadership screen. Do not use "loves daily stand-ups" as the talent screen. Why the leadership bar should be hard: Hurd already framed the risk: a hire with ambition who is not 100% on NWOW may become an un-enabler. In a tribe model one such person is not a diversity of thought. They are a tax. Pearson flattened 26 layers to 5. The remaining five have more leverage, not less. A skeptic in a 26-layer stack could be waited out. A skeptic in a 5-layer stack runs a fifth of the firm. They have evidence that selection works. Raju: one response to resistance was "this may no longer be the best organization for you." TAP built a pipeline instead of hoping the old one would convert (24 people, 54% promoted). Scanlon drafted under-used talent into the first squads the way a team uses a first-round pick. That is hiring for the OS. The playbook is explicit. Tribe Lead, Area Lead, PO, Coach — every card says coach, do not micromanage, do not skip ceremonies, do not play the boss. If a candidate cannot sign that, they are applying for a job Equitable is trying to delete. Why a firm-wide purity test will cost them people they need: Dynamic enablers were supposed to be skills-first, not title-first. A skills-first firm that then filters for cultural enthusiasm in every specialist is contradicting itself. Fafian's 25-year operator is the person who knows which of the 130 touchpoints actually breaks a client. Chandler needed those people in the 90-day cell. The field wholesaler is, in Hurd's words, "the voice of the customer" even when they hate the ritual. Life insurance is a shortage market on the talent side. 4% of millennials want in. Equitable cannot afford to add a second filter — "and also please love Agile nouns" — on scarce technical skill. The 2021 playbook will itself keep changing. Hiring for "this version of NWOW" locks the firm to February 2021. Hiring for "you will run a Mission, publish OKRs, put the customer in the room, and not hoard decisions" stays true if the ceremonies move. How I would write the rule. For Tribe Lead, Area Lead, PO, SMT Lead, Chapter Lead, NWOW Coach: must demonstrate they have run or will run the OS. A live case in the interview: here is a 130-touchpoint process and a wholesaler who refuses stand-ups — what do you keep, what do you drop, what do you measure. If they say "full playbook, no exceptions," they fail. If they say "my team, my rules," they fail. If they can separate principle from ritual, they pass. For specialists and producers: hire for craft and for not poisoning the OS. They do not have to love it. They do have to live with a Mission and a number. The cost of the hard leadership bar: you will lose a rainmaker who wants a personal fief. Good. The cost of applying it to everyone: you will lose the person who can take NIGO from 61% toward zero because they have sat the process. Not acceptable. Case Summary Equitable is an American life insurer founded in 1859. Originally called The Equitable Life Assurance Society, it was already one of the largest life insurers in the US by the early 20th century, and still the fifth-largest in the early 1990s. In 1992, France's AXA committed to invest US$1 billion on condition that it demutualize and go public; the company did so, raised a further US$450 million, became AXA's main investment outside Europe, and was renamed AXA Equitable. In CFO Robin Raju's words, after going from a mutual to a subsidiary of a large overseas conglomerate, "the culture was relaxed and comfortable, but there was very little accountability." The books were closed twice a year, with a 50-day turnaround and a US$200 million error threshold. The group insurance business relied on 1,500 policy enrollers. Many products were still promoted by phone and in person. In 2011, Mark Pearson was moved to New York from his post as CEO of AXA Japan. He was born and raised in Zimbabwe during its war of independence, couldn't afford university, went abroad at 17 to join the insurance industry, and drove growth in Hong Kong and Japan. America was a post-financial-crisis turnaround job: rebuild the balance sheet, stabilize earnings. He describes himself as having "the patience to get things done," not the type who tears everything down and then leaves. The industry itself is mature and low-growth, but society's need for retirement products is huge: people are living longer, employers are shifting retirement responsibility onto individuals, and people want a more active retirement. In 2018, AXA spun off Equitable through an IPO, raising US$2.8 billion. The new company was Equitable Holdings, with Athena on a blue shield. Pearson became CEO. Five divisions: Individual Retirement, Group Retirement, Investment Management and Research, AllianceBernstein, and Protection Solutions. He later said: "How many people get to design everything from scratch — the brand, the core principles, the organizational structure, the key goals?" But at the time almost nobody wanted big changes. Five years of preparing for the spin-off, the IPO and the rebrand had left employees exhausted. Chief Innovation and Design Officer Hillary Menard: "We needed a period to catch up and recover." The internal refrain was: "We've done things the same way for a long time. They work. Why change?" After the IPO, Pearson had to publicly announce targets that had to be met by 2020. Reporting moved from twice a year to quarterly. When the board approved the targets, it asked one question: "That's fine, but do you have the culture to deliver these results?" That question struck a nerve with Pearson and COO Jeff Hurd. They went to look at Spark, ING and USAA; Pearson read John Doerr on OKRs and was invited by Stanford's d.school to a design thinking workshop. One specific number stopped him in his tracks: the "not in good order" rate for enrollment forms was 61% — 61% of forms had to be sent back and filled in again. Ordinary improvement asks how to bring that rate down; design thinking asks "how do we get to zero returns?" In 2019, Pearson launched New Ways of Working (NWOW), and at year-end set up the Innovation and Design Office (IDO), handing it to Menard, his former chief of staff. Five pillars: OKRs, adaptive leadership, design thinking, enterprise agile, and dynamic enablers. A new structure: tribes (70–150 people), delivery units, centers of excellence, squads (6–10 people, cross-functional), and self-managed teams. He insisted that the IDO be staffed with internal people, bringing in McKinsey only to accelerate capability-building. Menard designed a five-day boot camp that rolled out all five pillars at once — "Doing it all at once is exhausting and scary. But if we asked people to keep coming back to learn more, we'd lose them." Once the boot camp ended, teams had to operate under NWOW. No squad could exceed 10 people. In early 2020, Pearson took his top 30 leaders to an offsite in New York. The pre-read was David Marquet's Turn the Ship Around! . Steve Scanlon, head of Group Retirement, walked in thinking it was "another meeting to make us better managers that will evaporate afterwards." When it broke up, most people were still in "wait and see" mode. Pearson pulled Scanlon aside: you'll be the first to put this approach into practice in a business line. Scanlon figured he had no choice. Right after the boot camp ended and squads were chosen in a single day, the world shut down because of COVID-19. The original assumption was that everyone would be in the same room. Hurd's decision was the opposite — to accelerate, because agile and design thinking were exactly the capabilities needed in uncertain times. At the same time, Pearson ended the engagement with McKinsey: "You have to burn the proverbial boats… the moment the cultural transformation is no longer being driven by Equitable's own people, it dies." Wholesalers, used to in-person visits and rounds of golf, were sent home and faced sales declines of 20%–40%. Group Retirement had 1,200 enrollers and no technology for enrolling by phone or online. Scanlon gave Bernadette Mitchell's squad a month to produce a transformation roadmap — they delivered in two weeks. They launched an MVP with some features still under development, then iterated on advisor feedback. "We would never have launched an unfinished product before." After George Floyd's murder in May 2020, they used NWOW principles to build a talent acceleration program, TAP. By 2023, five cohorts and 24 people had completed it; 54% were promoted, and diverse employees' eNPS was 33, above the company average of 27. Resistance appeared at the same time. Wholesalers' calendars were already full, and they refused daily stand-ups. Operations teams' work was highly standardized, manual and subject to compliance review — a single payment interaction involved more than 130 touchpoints. When Christy Chandler joined in 2023, her operations team's eNPS was just 0.7. Michael Fafian said the NWOW people were at first "a bit idealistic," unwilling to admit that operations was different. Hurd himself sat with a junior employee for an hour, watching her do something obviously inefficient and still not give up on it, before realizing that in this situation NWOW wasn't the most efficient approach. Some people with 30 years on the job and only a few left before retirement chose to leave early. Raju acknowledged that one response is: "This may no longer be the best organization for you." The Professor's Questions Service Excellence by Design. The case takes place as a technological breakthrough made it possible for customers to bank without visiting a physical branch. Commerce Bank was one of the fastest-growing banks in the United States by deposit growth, and had launched a pilot called Retailtainment . Analyze Commerce Bank's service delivery system before Retailtainment. How well did its operating model support its competitive strategy? Which design choices were most critical to the bank's success? What problem was Retailtainment designed to solve? How successful was it? What, if anything, would you change? How should competitors have responded to Commerce Bank's market entry? What lessons from the rise of online banking are most relevant to the age of AI? My Answers Q1. Operating model vs strategy The operating model and the strategy fit tightly — better than almost any retail bank in the case. Commerce does not try to be a nicer version of Citibank. It is a retailer that happens to take deposits. Every major design choice feeds one job: get people to walk in, open a core deposit, and stay. The strategy in one line: win on service and convenience (the 62%), not on rate (the 3%). Pay about 50 bp less on deposits. Spend the savings on hours, people, and small delights — and give cost wins back to the customer (free ATM and debit, NYC surcharge rebate up to $5/month) instead of dropping them to the bottom line. The design choices that actually matter, in order: The store is the product. 7:30 a.m.–8 p.m., weekends, midnight drive-through, the 10-minute rule. Average 40,000 visits a month, 100,000 at the busy ones — more than a McDonald's. Hill is explicit: even if nobody banked on Sunday, Sunday hours would still work, because they say "I am always there." One prototype, copied. ~$1 million, built from scratch, same white brick, black roof, marble, lollipops, dog biscuits. "We know every screw." Break-even in 12–18 months versus three years for the industry. Consistency cuts customer learning cost and makes training, mystery shopping, and hiring scalable. A short menu. Four checking products, not a dozen. After a merger, other banks force customers into unfamiliar products. Commerce never creates that mess. Simplicity is what lets a "wack job" hired for warmth still get the transaction right. Incentives face the same way as the strategy. Deposits and loans both credit the store. No deposit, no loan. The loan officer is the branch manager. WOW shops (14,000 a year) drive raises. Retailer of the Year is scored on core deposit growth, WOW shops, losses, and turnover — not on calls handled. Fleet's healthcare team keeps the deposit credit while the branch does the work; Commerce inverted that, and the politics flipped. People system, not posters. Commerce University, 41 people. Traditions teaches the handshake and "smiles have teeth." 2,000 interviews for 40 Manhattan jobs. Mystery shoppers ding you for saying "can" instead of "may." Kill-a-stupid-rule pays $50. This is how the cult survives growth. Credit is conservative on purpose. Loan-to-deposit 45.5% versus the industry's 87%. Non-current loans 0.38% versus 1.44%. They do not earn enough spread to buy credit risk. The deposit franchise is the asset; securities are 42.5% of assets versus 18% for the industry. They are a deposit gatherer that happens to lend, not a lender that happens to have branches. Do not push people off the expensive channel. Industry: advertise the ATM, sometimes charge $3 to see a teller. Commerce: every channel should be excellent. Online usage still lands at 34%, above Wells Fargo. The cheap channel is a complement when the expensive one is loved, and a rejection when it is used as a dump. Fit is visible in the P&L. Efficiency ratio 70.3% versus 59.7% — they are more expensive, as promised. Cost of interest-bearing deposits 2.37% versus 5.35%. ROE 15.0% versus 12.4%. Net income doubled from 1998–2001 while the industry grew 20%. Deposit growth in 2001 was 37.5% against the industry's 5.1%. The operating system is not a decoration on a bank. It is the strategy, running. The critical few: hours + identical stores + four products + store-level deposit credit + the WOW people system + "we do not push you out." Take any one away and the 62% story starts to leak. Retailtainment is not on this list. Q2. Retailtainment: problem, results, what I would change Retailtainment was designed to solve a next-move problem, not a waiting-line problem. Competitors had started copying the easy layer of Commerce's offer — evening and weekend hours, "human" ads, a café, TVs in the queue. Pauls says it out loud: "We need the next penny arcade." The bank pays less on deposits on purpose; if the service gap closes, the 50 bp discount becomes a reason to leave. Friday-afternoon experiments were a search for a new, visible wow, plus a bet that local managers know their fans better than Cherry Hill does. It was not successful, on the evidence in the case. We get no lift in deposits, no cut in perceived wait, no mystery-shop scores. We get: a greeter problem ("too many greeters standing around"), a friend who would rather the greeter get behind the counter, and a hot-dog cart that catches fire, takes the juggler with it, and makes the local news. The one thing Commerce had been religious about — one bank, one brand, every screw the same — is the first thing Retailtainment relaxes. What I would change: kill it as a local variety show. Keep the search for the next penny arcade, but run it the way they already know how to run a store. Standardize delight; do not freelance it. Penny Arcade, umbrellas, the 10-minute rule, check images the next day, a phone on the ATM — these are designed once, copied everywhere, and they solve a real job (coins, rain, "are you open?", "did my check clear?"). A guitarist on Friday solves none of those jobs and cannot be mystery-shopped. If you must prototype, prototype like a retailer, not like a talent show. One idea, designed by marketing and operations together, piloted in a handful of stores, with a script, a safety check, and a kill rule. The hot-dog cart had marketing approval and still burned. Approval without a playbook is not control. Put the greeter back on the value stream. The friend's complaint is the real operations issue: peak-load capacity. 40,000–100,000 visits a month means the constraint is tellers, not atmosphere. A Friday juggler while the line is stuck is a strategy–ops contradiction. Flex staff into the queue before you flex staff into costume. Measure it or it is theater. Add Retailtainment to WOW-shop items only if there is a single expected behavior. If there isn't, it does not belong in a system whose raises already hang on 14,000 shops. Do not spend the "next penny arcade" budget on copying WaMu's children's corner. The next penny arcade should be another job-to-be-done that rivals refuse (they already refused coins). It should not be a louder lobby. The honest sentence for Jacovelli: Retailtainment is a symptom that the leadership team is anxious about imitation. The cure is to go deeper on the uncopyable system — hiring 50-to-1, four products, store-level P&L, Sunday hours — not to go louder on the copyable theater. Q3. How competitors should have responded They should not have copied the lobby. That is what they did — WaMu's un-bank, ING's espresso, Bank of America's TVs — and it is the weakest possible reply, because it copies the one layer Commerce can replace next Friday. Three better replies, depending on who you are: If you are a money-center bank (Citi, BofA, Fleet): do not get on Commerce's field. You cannot retrofit a cult. Hill is right about the direction even if he overstates the history: "You can only build a delivery model like this from scratch." Mergers already wrecked your service (34% of leavers cite fees, service, errors; Robbins walks across the street at 8:15 a.m.). Adding a juggler on top of a merger integration is how you become a punchline. Pick a different excellence and say it: best rate, best digital, best for companies, best for the top 5% of balances. Then design down to that — including the things you will be bad at. Charge for tellers if you mean it. Close on Sunday if you mean it. Stop running ads that claim Nordstrom while the operating system still pays on call volume. If you insist on fighting for the 62%: copy the trade-offs, not the mascot. Match hours. Cut the product list to a handful. Give the branch the deposit credit. Build a university. Shop yourself 14,000 times. Interview 50 people for every teller. Pay less on deposits and publish it as the price of the experience. Accept a 70% efficiency ratio. Stop merging for cost saves in the same metro where Commerce is opening. The $5,000 Commerce pays its staff when you close a branch is a clue: your exits are their marketing. None of this is a campaign. It is a five-year rebuild. Most boards will refuse it. That refusal is the response — concede the service segment and harvest the 3% who want rate. Use the two leakages Commerce is already fishing. 34% of bank leavers move house; 34% leave because of fees and bad service, often right after a merger (Exhibit 8). A competent incumbent would: keep surplus branches for 18 months after a merger instead of "rationalizing" them into Commerce's lap; waive the surprise fees that create the 34%; and staff the remaining stores on Saturday. You do not need Mr. C to stop a geographic and a post-merger leak. Do not try to win New York by out-promoting $500,000 of hot dogs. Commerce broke even in half the time at 4× cost because the model was already loved. A copycat without the model is just a more expensive me-too, which is what Hill founded the bank not to be. The response that looks aggressive and is actually weak: match Sunday hours and install a coffee machine. The response that looks passive and is actually hard: choose a different axis of excellence, and stop pretending you compete on service when your economics require pushing people to the VRU. Q4. Lessons from online banking for the age of AI The online-banking story in this case is not "digital won." It is: banks used a new technology to push customers where the bank wanted them to go, and Commerce used the same technology to go where customers already were — and got more digital use, not less. The industry logic in 2002: teller is expensive, so advertise the ATM, the VRU, the website; pay people to move; sometimes fine them $3 for coming in. Commerce's logic: you cannot name a retailer that survived by driving people where they do not want to go. Offer the best of every channel. Result: 34% online usage, above Wells Fargo, and 40,000–100,000 store visits a month. That is the AI lesson. Four specifics: Do not confuse a cheaper channel with a better offer. AI will make self-service, chatbots, and "digital-only RMs" look free at the margin, the way the website looked in 2002. If you push clients there to save on the human, you are Fleet charging $3 for a teller. The clients who can leave, will. Commerce's 34% says the opposite: people adopt the new channel when the old one still loves them . Use the new tech to make the expensive channel excellent, not empty. Commerce put a phone on the ATM so you could reach a human; showed the cheque image the next day; let you opt out of the VRU without a hunt. That is High Tech in service of High Touch. The AI analogue: prep the meeting, remember the family, draft the memo, sit in the room as a second memory — do not replace the room. Gimmicks arrive first; systems arrive late. Retailtainment is the 2002 version of "we should have an AI demo on Friday." Penny Arcade is the 2002 version of a real workflow (count the coins, print a receipt, no fee). In the age of AI, refuse the juggler. Fund the coin machine: one job, same in every "store," mystery-shoppable. You still cannot be great at everything. Frei's class title is Service Excellence by Design. Design means trade-offs. Commerce is great at convenience and average-to-poor at rate and at credit risk. AI does not lift that constraint. If you use AI to try to be the cheapest and the warmest and the most complete, you will get a chatbot that apologizes in four products' jargon. Pick the 62% you serve, and let AI deepen that, including the parts you will stay bad at. Consistency scales; personality-as-exception does not. 185 stores, one greeting, 14,000 shops. AI makes it tempting to let every RM (or every model) improvise. That is Retailtainment at software speed. The lesson is: write the playbook first, then let the machine copy it. Kill the stupid rule remains a human job. One sentence for class: the banks that "won" at online were not the ones that moved customers online; they were the ones customers still wanted to visit — and then followed online. AI will rhyme. Case Summary Halloween 2002, Cherry Hill, New Jersey. A pumpkin, a Dalmatian and a masked avenger run past Deborah Jacovelli's office door. This is Commerce University — Commerce Bank's full-time training center. The giant letter C outside has been draped in a cape. Jacovelli is the dean here. She is used to this culture that looks nothing like a bank's, but something new this year makes her uneasy: headquarters has just launched a pilot called Retailtainment , which lets branch managers experiment freely on Friday afternoons with ways to entertain waiting customers — free hot dogs, guitarists, jugglers, someone in a giant C costume on roller skates. Some stores have already had incidents: a hot dog cart caught fire, a juggler got burned, and it made the local news. Vernon W. Hill II opened this community bank in southern New Jersey in 1973 with $1.5 million. His judgment: the world did not need another me-too bank. He had no capital and no brand, so he had to find a way to be different. Over the next thirty years Commerce made no acquisitions, opening its own stores into Pennsylvania, Delaware and New York. Hill called his branches stores , and benchmarked against Starbucks and Home Depot, not the bank next door. He asked: why will Starbucks get you to pay $6 for a cup of coffee? Because of the retail experience. Since 1990 the stock had risen 20-fold. CFO Douglas Pauls's words are on the cover: "The hardest thing about becoming a big bank is not becoming a big bank." — the hardest part isn't growing up, it's growing up without turning into a big bank. Around 2001, the industry was solving a different problem. Deposits and loans were both commodities. From 1998 to 2001, industry deposits grew about 19% cumulatively, and nearly 90% of deposits were lent out; the outsized growth of the big banks came almost entirely from acquisitions. Two trends: pushing cross-selling up from 1.5–2.5 products per customer; and leaning on fees — non-interest income +27%, interest income only +11%. On service, banks began tiering customers by profitability; satisfaction was chronically low, with 79% "very satisfied" at credit unions versus only 53% at retail banks. Attrition at the worst could reach a third of customers a year, and even the best lost 15%. Of those who left, 34% did so because of fee surprises, poor service or errors, 34% because they moved outside the branch network, and 15% because somewhere else was more convenient or open longer. On channels, the total number of branches kept rising even as the number of banks fell; ATMs went from cost centers to fee-generating profit centers; almost every bank had a 24/7 call center and online banking. Because electronic channels had low marginal costs, most banks actively pushed customers from the teller window to self-service — through advertising, rewards, and occasionally penalties: $3 to see a teller. Front-line hiring targeted people who could do repetitive work and accept low wages; performance was measured by call volume and transaction counts. Commerce turned this whole logic on its head. Stores were open 7:30–20:00 on weekdays and on weekends too; busy drive-through lanes could stay open until midnight. There was also a 10-minute rule: open 10 minutes early, close 10 minutes late. There were only 4 kinds of checking accounts, and opening one came with a gift. In Hill's words: other banks, because branches are expensive, try to push people out and online; "You can't find a successful retailer that survives by pushing people to where they don't want to go." Their model was to be the best in every channel, and to assume you'd use all of them. The result was not only the fastest deposit growth in America, but an online usage rate of 34% — higher than Wells Fargo's. An average store had 40,000 visits a month and a busy one 100,000 — McDonald's gets about 25,000. Hill said: I don't have to resell you every day; once you've opened an account, your balance is making me money. Big banks saw customers as a cost. He didn't. Growth was organic, and New York was organic on steroids. Others said New York was the most crowded banking market in America; Hill said it was the most underserved — there was $500 billion in deposits there. Each store got a $500,000 promotion, five times the usual: direct mail, subway ads, phone booths, plus street vendors handing out 10,000 hot dogs wrapped in Commerce napkins. Costs were four times those of other regions, but the payback period was cut in half. Hill was adamant about not growing through acquisitions: "No power retailer in this country was built by acquisition. This delivery model can only be built from scratch. Acquisitions are at heart about cutting costs; culture and brand get diluted. It's a formula for failure. Every big bank merger in this country has failed." "It's easier to build a bank than to fix one." It took the company 18 years to reach $1 billion in deposits; now it could exceed that in a single quarter. The goal was $100 billion in deposits and 1,000 stores, from Washington to Boston. Net income doubled from 1998 to 2001, versus +20% for the industry. When Pauls joined in 1994 he thought the projections were aggressive; later the whole plan was left in the dust. What they sold wasn't loans — it was core deposits. Hill: a bank's value isn't in its loan book, it's in deposits that didn't come for the interest rate. They were typically the lowest payer in the market, often 50 basis points lower. The consumer business contributed more than half of deposits, versus about a third for the industry. In the '80s and '90s the big banks gave up on gathering retail deposits, funding themselves in wholesale markets while cutting back their retail networks. Pauls said Vernon wasn't afraid of competition — rivals were fighting an air war, while they fought a ground war in the stores. Longer hours are of course more expensive, and the expense ratio would look ugly. Hill's reversal: "A low expense ratio is a negative, not a positive. People with low expense ratios are draining capital from their business every day." Asked why they opened a new account, 3% of customers said they wanted the highest rate, and 62% said service and convenience. Rivals fought over the 3%; Commerce fought for the 62%. Money saved didn't go to the income statement — it went back to customers. Switching ATM contracts saved several million, which they used to abolish card fees and transaction fees company-wide; in New York, when someone else's machine charged you $1.50, they reimbursed you (up to $5 a month). Hill said this is how a power retailer operates: use your competitive advantage to make yourself stronger, not to fatten your margins. Loans were a supporting act, and designed to pull in yet more deposits. Loans were credited to the store serving that customer, and so were deposits. Dennis Falese contrasted this with Fleet: deposits brought in by the medical lending group were credited to the group, while the branches still had to service them and got no credit, so branch managers hated the lending group; at Commerce it was the reverse — branch managers loved the lending people. The loan-to-deposit ratio was well below the industry's. Falese: "The spread we earn doesn't cover the credit risk. Whether the customer can repay comes first. Some of our best loans are the ones we didn't make." The policy was no deposit, no loan . Loan delivery was pushed down to the stores; at some point you had to come into the store to sign, and the loan officer was the store manager — who used that moment to persuade you to bring your deposits over as well. Stores were built as replicable retail machines. Floor-to-ceiling windows, plenty of parking, built from scratch for about $1 million — "we know every screw in the model." White brick, black metal roofs, black-and-white marble, no-frills checking and savings, lollipops and dog biscuits — nearly every store was identical. Marketing chief John Cunningham: whichever store a customer walks into, they know exactly what to expect. Hill decided on locations himself — he also owned 45 Burger Kings in the Philadelphia suburbs — busy but not too congested, with the right mix of residential and commercial, and often right in a competitor's backyard. If a rival closed a branch, nearby Commerce employees got a $5,000 bonus. Payback was 12 to 18 months, versus three years for the industry. When it rained, staff walked customers to their cars with umbrellas; 300,000 pens were given away each month. Phones next to the ATMs dialed straight into the call center; online, you could see images of the front and back of your checks the next day. When Hill noticed other banks starting to refuse large amounts of coins or charge for them, he spent $10 million on the Penny Arcade : in 2001 it handled 750,000 transactions and took in $71.7 million in coins, free for customers and non-customers alike. Falese called it Marketing 101: once people come in, keep working with them. At a new store in Manhattan, meeting planner Carole Robbins had finished her banking by 8:15 a.m.; across the street was the Citibank that had swallowed her old bank. She said this was old-fashioned service, "like we're all in the same boat. But time will tell. Every restaurant is good at the start." Mergers were Commerce's deposit engine — whenever others merged, Commerce's deposits tended to jump. WOW! was an operating system, not a slogan. In 1994, nine people wrote the SMART principles (Exhibit 9): say Yes to the customer, make everyone feel taken care of, keep your promises, know how to recover, think like the customer. Internal and external service quality were measured, and hitting the targets was celebrated. WOW! stickers could be exchanged for sweatshirts, mugs and radios. The WOW! Awards began in 1997; the most dazzling, "Retailer of the Year," came with a Porsche Boxster for a year; for the 30th anniversary in 2003 they planned to rent out Radio City Music Hall. Commerce University had 41 full-time staff. New employees attended Traditions: half games, half training, half common sense, teaching how to smile ("smile with your teeth showing"), shake hands and greet people. Hill told employees: in a sense you have joined a service cult. Hiring looked for people who would get addicted to giving great service; as John Manning put it, "we hire wack jobs." New hires were given a stack of cards to hand out whenever they saw someone giving good service at another bank, a restaurant or a gas station. There were Red Fridays, the WOW! Patrol, mascots Mr. C and Buzz, and a Dr. Wow whom nobody had ever seen, who replied to letters and gave out prizes. With Drexel, they ran Camp Business for high school students. Mystery shops (WOW! shops) were the hard core of evaluation: 5 employees managed 100 mystery shoppers doing 14,000 visits a year; staff had to shake hands, use the standard greeting (Hi, my name is . How may I help you today? — "can" could not substitute for "may"), walk customers to their seats, follow the manual, and act like they meant it. Raises depended on shop results; scores were posted on the intranet, and regions competed in leagues. They also opened accounts at competitors to test their service. Suggestions to "kill a stupid rule" earned $50 if adopted. At the call center you could easily escape the phone tree to reach a person, and agents' dress code was far stricter than the industry's — DiSabatina said you never know who might walk in: Hill, shareholders, the press. The vans were painted blue and red as free advertising; in New York some drove around empty. Hill said rivals didn't dare paint their vans for fear of being robbed, but the vans carried checks, not cash, and there hadn't been a robbery since 1945. Hiring was always the bottleneck. For 40 positions in Manhattan they interviewed 2,000 people. Falese reviewed new hires at three months, six months and a year; in ten years, only one executive was found to be a bad fit within four months. He was willing to hire retirees part-time; what he wanted was thirty years of local experience — knowing which entrepreneurs could survive a cycle. Mergers created talent pools at competitors, and he had their org charts in hand, from loan officers to secretaries. Retailtainment was the next step in 2002. Competitors had started copying the basic service: evening and weekend hours, ads playing up the personal touch. Washington Mutual (WaMu) came into New York as the "un-bank": roving tellers, kids' areas, no desks. The Dutch bank ING opened café-style branches in Manhattan, with espresso alongside savings accounts and free internet. Bank of America was experimenting with TVs for people waiting in line. Pauls said: we need the next penny arcade. Commerce deliberately didn't compete on price, using lower deposit rates to pay for better service. The question was how far service differentiation should go. A friend of Jacovelli's said: it was nice to be greeted and handed a pen, but she'd rather that person got behind the counter and moved the line along. Another customer complained of "too many greeters standing around." Some stores had already botched it with the hot dog cart and the juggler and ended up in the news. On one side: managers know their customers best and should be encouraged to delight them; on the other: total freedom is dangerous. Some thought it could work with training and guidelines; others thought attention and resources shouldn't be spent on it at all, and the existing service model should simply be executed well. Jacovelli's conclusion: Commerce is one bank, one brand, and its success depends on whether its service is better than its rivals'. The question is what role Retailtainment plays in that mission.
