The Professor's Questions The Role of Auditors, Law Firms, and Management. If you were an investor in Lehman Brothers, how would you evaluate the riskiness of Lehman’s business? Why did Lehman use the repo 105 transactions? What institutions, if any, were at fault for Lehman’s use of repo 105's and how would you go about improving the institutions? My Answers Q1. Investor view of risk I would not start with the net leverage they advertised. I would start with how the firm dies. Lehman had no stable retail deposits. It rolled short-term loans every day. In 1998, a rumor after LTCM already showed how fast that funding can run. After Bear Stearns in March 2008, that was not a theoretical risk. It was the whole business. Then I would look at what sat on the thin equity. From 2004 to 2007, assets grew about $300 billion; equity grew $6 billion. That is 50 times leverage on the new dollar. The 2007 record — $19.3 billion of revenue, $4.2 billion of profit — came from packing and trading exotic mortgage paper, the high-margin stuff. Fuld said smart risk management is never putting yourself where you cannot fight another day. The portfolio said the opposite: they had switched from moving assets for clients to holding them. Then I would distrust the ratio itself. Callan told the market net leverage was 15.4, down from 16.1. Lowitt later said 12 times, "low double digits," "we will operate conservatively." Einhorn had been short since July 2007 and said they were about 40 times on tangible equity, holding things that should not be levered at all. By June 2008 Lehman was the most shorted firm on the Street. He was looking at the right object. Matthew Lee, who signed the balance sheet for a thousand entities, gave the inside version in May 2008: on the last day of each month the books held about $5 billion more net assets than management actually ran; tens of billions of accounts were unsubstantiated; tens of billions of inventory probably could not be bought or sold at the marks, in that size, in that market. That is not a footnote. That is the risk: a confidence business, financed overnight, sitting on sticky marks. If I had also seen Exhibit 2, I would have done one more piece of arithmetic. Ernst & Young’s own papers said a 0.1 move in net leverage was material, typically $1.8 billion. So tangible equity was about $18 billion. Repo 105 at Q2 2008 was $50.4 billion — 28 times that threshold, about 2.8 turns of net leverage. The "12.1" was closer to 14.9 without the quarter-end sale. The "15.4" in Q1 was closer to 18. The rating agencies were shown the cleaned number. S&P still praised the "strong funding/liquidity profile" on June 2, then the firm pre-announced its first quarterly loss as a public company one week later. So my scorecard as an investor: (1) funding model — overnight confidence, no deposits; (2) asset quality — sticky, levered, marked in an illiquid market; (3) governance of the number — if the ratio only looks right on the last day of the quarter, it is not a risk metric, it is a press-release metric. Repo 105 is the proof of (3). Even without knowing its name, Einhorn and Lee were already pointing at it. Q2. Why Repo 105 They used it because they needed the leverage ratio to fall, and they did not want to sell the sticky inventory at a real loss. From mid-2007 the market stopped staring at revenue and started staring at the balance sheet. Rating agencies, analysts, and short sellers were all reading one number: net leverage. Fuld made McDade "balance sheet czar." Businesses were ordered to cut the ratio to avoid a downgrade. McDade wanted them to sell inventory. Traders found the assets hard to sell, or did not want the discount. So they "rented the balance sheet": Repo 105 moved inventory off for a few days, cash paid down other liabilities, equity sat still, and the ratio printed lower. King said there was always quarter-end pressure, but from mid-2007 it jumped. "To the powers that be, Repo 105 counted as a balance sheet reduction." McDade’s own phrase: "another drug we are on." The accounting trick is small and specific. A normal repo is financing: 2% haircut, asset stays, cash and a liability both go up. SFAS 140 says that at 98–102% collateral you still have effective control, so you cannot call it a sale. Lehman took a 5% or 8% haircut, claimed it had surrendered control, and booked a sale. Exhibit 4: the same $50 billion, treated as financing, leaves net leverage at 17.6 after you repay; treated as a sale, it falls to 15.6. That two-turn cosmetic is the whole product. They then hid the product. No public disclosure. The obligation to buy tens of billions back in a few days did not appear. The trades were dumped into the derivatives footnote. US law firms would not call them sales. Linklaters would, if the securities were "sited" in the UK and done under English law. So American paper was walked through LBIE in London and walked back after the reporting date. Watch the dose. $24.5 billion at end-2006. $38.6 billion at end-2007. $49.1 billion in Q1 2008 — the Bear quarter, a $10.5 billion jump. $50.4 billion in Q2. Sum of the last three quarter-ends: $138 billion. They had told Ernst & Young the cap would be $20–30 billion. They blew through it. They used more of the drug in the days just before reporting dates. They took the cleaned ratio to S&P, Moody’s, and Fitch in May–June 2008 and argued that no negative action was justified. Repo 105 was not in the deck. The Fed and the SEC did not know either. So the motive is not "we found a clever way to finance ourselves." Ordinary repo already did that. The motive is window dressing under pressure: hit the number the agencies and the earnings call were going to read, without taking the loss McDade said they should take. Richards, in the prison letter, describes the same slope from the other industry: once you start managing the number, even small changes in procedure leave you exposed. Lehman’s small change was 3 extra points of haircut and a London opinion letter. After that, every quarter needed a bigger dose. Q3. Who was at fault, and how to improve I would not pick one villain. I would say the system passed a form and failed a function. Management designed the drug and raised the dose. The law firm made the form legal in a jurisdiction that would say yes. The auditor blessed the policy, knew what it was for, heard $50 billion from a whistleblower, and still did not say the words "Repo 105" to the Audit Committee. The Audit Committee had every SOX chair in the room and never heard the fact. Rating agencies and the Fed were shown the cleaned ratio. Lee followed the Code of Ethics and was fired in about two weeks. Management. They are first. Goldfarb is alleged to have invented it. Fuld set the growth model, pushed leverage, and pushed Antoncic out of the room when risk got tense. They told E&Y the cap was $20–30 billion, then printed $50.4 billion. They never disclosed. They took the number to the agencies. McDade at least named it a drug and wanted real sales; the traders were rewarded for the cosmetic. That is tone at the top: the ratio was the goal, the inventory was not. Linklaters, and the US firms that refused. This is the session title. US counsel would not call Repo 105 a sale. That refusal was information. Lehman shopped the answer to London, then walked American securities through LBIE so the opinion would attach. A legal opinion that is "legalistic" and "form-driven" — Kelly’s words — is not a control. It is a ticket. Improving law firms: opinions should state what the structure is for , not only whether a haircut clears a paragraph. If the only commercial purpose is to print a quarter-end ratio, the letter should say so, or not be written. Forum-shopping a true-sale opinion for US paper should itself be a disclosure event. Ernst & Young. They approved the Policy in 2001. Smith’s 2001 memo told them, in words, that the point was to net down the balance sheet. Jain flagged reputational risk in 2006 and it died in the hierarchy. Kelly told Schlich the justification was form-driven and that volumes spiked at quarter end. Materiality in their own papers was 0.1 of net leverage, about $1.8 billion; $50 billion is not a rounding of 31 times to 32 times. Most damning: on June 12 Lee told them about $50 billion coming off and going back. Cruikshank had ordered them to report every assertion, in the letter or not. Schlich was silent on June 13, silent on July 8, silent on July 22. On July 10 they issued an unqualified review on the 10-Q. The engagement letter said fraud involving senior management goes straight to the Audit Committee. They measured GAAP comfort — process. They did not measure "did the board hear the ugly fact" — outcome. Turley’s later line, "we feel very good about the work we did," is the paper talking. How to improve auditors: (1) materiality for leverage window-dressing is the move in the ratio the market is using, not net income; (2) a whistleblower interview is not closed until every new fact is in the Audit Committee minutes, in the whistleblower’s words; (3) alumni moving from the audit firm into the CFO chair should trigger extra skepticism, not extra comfort; (4) "the accounting wasn’t challenged" cannot be the end of the disclosure analysis. The Audit Committee. Independent members, a financial expert as chair, private sessions with the engagement partner — the process inputs of Sarbanes-Oxley were all green. They still did not know Repo 105 existed. You cannot oversee a number you have not been told is synthetic. Improve: the committee should receive, as a standing paper, quarter-end vs mid-quarter balance sheet, and a list of all true-sale opinions in use. If the auditor says a whistleblower letter is "pretty ugly" but "shouldn’t result in significant issues," that sentence is itself an issue. Rating agencies, the Fed, the SEC. They are downstream. They were not told. Still, a 73% price drop, a first-ever quarterly loss, and Einhorn’s 40-times claim were already on the tape. An agency that praises "de-leveraging" without asking "sold or rented?" is measuring the press release. Improve: for broker-dealers who live on wholesale funding, require a gross and net leverage before quarter-end window dressing, or simply forbid calling a 5% haircut repo a sale. The Code of Ethics, as an institution. This is where Soltes’s preface belongs. Lee did exactly what the paper asked. Outcome: dismissal, a gag, unpaid severance. Ninety percent of people say they would report; fewer than half did. Lehman is that gap in one career. Improving speak-up is not a new hotline. It is: the reporter still has a job, the board heard the fact that was not in the letter, and the next quarter’s ratio is published two ways. Those are outcomes. Training completion would have changed nothing. Richards is the human version of the same slope. He also had a Big Four comfort letter. He also had an internal GC investigation that found nothing. He also told himself it was "just timing, two or three days." Repo 105 is timing, two or three days. The gray is where senior managers live, he wrote, and it is a dangerous place. The fix is not to pretend the world is black and white. The fix is what Soltes calls uncomfortable dissonance: a person outside the quarter-end huddle who can still kill the trade. Antoncic was that person, and she was asked to leave the room. Lee was that person, and he was fired. Jain was that person, and the email stopped at his manager. If I have to put it in one classroom sentence: no single institution invented the lie; each institution certified a piece of the form, and so nobody owned the function. Improve them by changing what they count as success — not "was there a policy, an opinion, an independent committee, an audit fee, a code of ethics," but "did the number the CEO said on the call match the number without the drug, and did the person who said otherwise still work there." Case Summary In May 2008, Matthew Lee had been at Lehman for fourteen years. A senior vice president in the finance division, he was responsible for the balance sheets of more than a thousand legal entities around the world. He read the company's Code of Ethics over and over: anyone who discovers a possible violation has a duty to report it immediately; there will be no retaliation for good-faith reports. He hesitated for a long time, and after seeing a lawyer he concluded that this was his duty. On May 16 he handed his letter to Controller Martin Kelly, head of capital markets product control Gerard Reilly, CFO Erin Callan, and Chief Risk Officer Christopher O’Meara. The letter made six points: at month-end the books carried roughly US$5 billion of net assets that no one was really managing; billions of dollars of accounts across global entities did not reconcile; billions of dollars of inventory were nearly unsellable at their marked prices; systems and staff had not kept pace with the expansion since the 1994 IPO; the finance function in Mumbai might be efficiently distributing wrong numbers; and some internal audit executives lacked the skills to audit what had become a complex business. The words Repo 105 did not appear anywhere in it. About two weeks later, his boss called him in and told him he had been laid off as part of a broader downsizing. No other reason was given. He fought it, then accepted a severance agreement with a confidentiality clause. Lehman went bankrupt in September 2008, and he never received all the money in the agreement. E&Y later said that Lehman had investigated the letter itself, and that in July 2008 management reported to the audit committee that the allegations were unfounded and there were no material issues; E&Y's own review was never finished, because the company had gone bankrupt. Founded in 1850, Lehman was one of Wall Street's oldest investment banks, and once one of its most profitable. It was sold to Shearson/American Express in 1984 and spun off in a 1994 IPO. Richard Fuld, who came up as a trader, became chairman and CEO. Its historic strengths were fixed-income underwriting and trading. Investors worried that its fixed-income exposure was too large, so the firm diversified: fixed income fell from 55% of revenue in 1995 to 39% in 2007, with equities and advisory filling the gap. In the mid-2000s it deliberately chased faster growth, shifting from a low-risk brokerage model to a high-risk banking model — the balance sheet went from "moving" assets to "holding" them, with the risk staying on its own books. From 2004 to 2007, assets grew by about US$300 billion while equity grew by only US$6 billion. Fortune 's Shawn Tully described Wall Street's game bluntly: take shareholders' small pile of cash, lever it up enormously, and use the debt to stack up securities; as long as interest rates fall, the portfolio swells, and a thin layer of equity can carve out huge returns. The high profits came from riskier stuff. Like its peers, Lehman went ever deeper into packaging and trading exotic mortgage-backed securities. These high-margin products helped it post record profits of US$4.2 billion on revenue of US$19.3 billion in 2007. In Fuld's own words: smart risk management means never putting yourself in a position where you can't fight another day. But it had no retail deposits underneath it; it relied on short-term loans that had to be rolled over again and again. Once creditors panicked, the funding would stop. When LTCM nearly collapsed in 1998, rumours had already gone round that Lehman was in trouble; Fuld put down that crisis of confidence, and it was seen as the defining performance of his career. In March 2008, the equally highly levered Bear Stearns collapsed. Since mid-2007, analysts and rating agencies had been watching investment banks' leverage; after Bear, it became an urgent task: the market had to see leverage going down. CFO Callan said she was fighting "hand-to-hand combat" against the rumours. On the March 18 first-quarter earnings call she said: we have deliberately brought leverage down; net leverage is 15.4x, versus 16.1 at year-end. On June 2, S&P cut the rating from A+ to A but still praised its funding and liquidity profile. Less than a week later, Lehman pre-announced its first quarterly loss since going public, US$2.8 billion, replaced its CFO, and announced its third capital raise of the year, US$6 billion. The new CFO, Ian Lowitt, said on June 16: gross leverage has fallen from 31.7 to 24.3, and net leverage from 15.4 to 12; the appropriate level of leverage right now is the low double digits; we will run the business conservatively. Not everyone believed it. Hedge fund manager David Einhorn had been short since July 2007 and particularly distrusted the published leverage numbers: the problem was overall leverage and the loan portfolio; on tangible equity they were levered about 40 times, and they held things that should never be levered at all. By June 2008, Lehman was the most heavily shorted investment bank on Wall Street. Over the summer Moody's moved its outlook to negative while still writing that it was actively adding capital and deleveraging, and that its liquidity management remained sound. In August it cut 1,500 jobs, about 6%. In the first eight months of the year the share price fell 73%. On September 10 it reported another loss, of US$3.9 billion, and planned to sell most of its investment management business. Fitch put the rating on negative watch. Three days later, New York Fed president Geithner called Wall Street together and made it clear the government would not bail it out. That weekend there was no buyer. On September 15, Lehman filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, citing "significant liquidity problems." With more than US$600 billion in assets, it was the largest bankruptcy in US history. Repo was a form of short-term financing everyone in the industry used. In 2007 the US and European repo markets were worth about US$11 trillion, double their 2002 size. The standard deal has two steps: first, borrow cash using assets on the books as collateral (a typical haircut is 2%, i.e. Repo 102); then repay the loan, take the assets back and pay a little interest. In accounting terms this is a financing: cash and short-term liabilities both increase, and the collateral stays on the balance sheet. SFAS 140 says that with collateral between 98% and 102%, the borrower retains effective control and the deal cannot be treated as a sale. To be a sale, it must meet three conditions for surrendering control — and the standard itself notes that most repo market participants are not used to treating these transactions as sales. Lehman invented Repo 105: raise the haircut to 5% or 8%, claim that it had surrendered control, and therefore book the deal as a sale. Booked as a sale, assets on the balance sheet fall (by the amount lent plus the haircut), the cash received goes to pay down other liabilities, equity is unchanged, and leverage looks lower. Exhibit 4 illustrates it: the same US$5 billion, treated as a financing, leaves net leverage at 17.6 after paying down debt; treated as a sale, net leverage drops to 15.6. From the fourth quarter of 2007 to the end of the second quarter of 2008, the practice removed more than US$138 billion of net assets in total. Volumes were ramped up in the days before each reporting date to push down net leverage. It was never publicly disclosed. The financial statements counted it as derivatives, mixed into the note on "more traditional" derivatives; readers could not see an obligation to repurchase tens of billions of dollars of securities within days. From mid-2007, what the market watched shifted from revenue to the balance sheet. Chief Risk Officer Madelyn Antoncic had already urged caution, pulling back and more study at the executive committee in late 2006; in 2007 she was sidelined — whenever a tense risk topic came up, Fuld had her leave the room along with the deal team. At the same time, senior executives pushed every business to sell assets and push down net leverage, to avoid a downgrade. When traders found sticky assets hard to sell, or didn't want to sell them at a discount, they could "rent the balance sheet": use Repo 105 to move inventory off temporarily and still hit their net leverage targets. Trader Mitchell King recalled that there had always been quarter-end pressure, but it rose noticeably from mid-2007; the goal was to be profitable and shrink the balance sheet at the same time; to the people in charge, Repo 105 counted as balance-sheet reduction. In March 2008 Fuld appointed veteran Bart McDade as "balance sheet czar." McDade wanted traders to be disciplined, and in an email called Repo 105 "another drug we are on." His position was: sell the inventory. E&Y's 2007 walk-through workpapers noted that net leverage was an important ratio in rating agency analysis and was also included in Lehman's earnings press releases. On its calls Lehman repeatedly stressed deleveraging and never said how much of the number came from Repo 105. In May and June 2008 it met Fitch, Moody's and S&P and used the balance-sheet reduction and deleveraging it had achieved, and was about to achieve, to argue against negative rating action; Repo 105 appeared nowhere in the materials. The New York Fed and the SEC didn't know either. E&Y had been Lehman's auditor since it became independent in 1994, and also did other accounting, advisory and tax work. From 2001 until the bankruptcy its fees exceeded US$150 million; one analysis put the decade's total at over US$185 million, an average of about US$31 million a year. For seven years running Lehman was one of E&Y's fifteen largest clients, ranking eighth by US audit fees in 2007. Quite a few accountants worked on this one account alone. Several of Lehman's senior finance executives were E&Y alumni: CFO Christopher O’Meara (2004–2007) had been a senior manager in E&Y's financial services practice and jumped ship while auditing Lehman in 1994; the CFO before him, David Goldfarb (2000–2004), had been a senior partner in E&Y's financial services business from 1979 to 1993, and some pointed to him as the person who invented Repo 105 internally. On paper it complied with Sarbanes-Oxley: E&Y reported directly to the audit committee, the members were independent, the chair was a financial expert, and the committee met the engagement partner alone without management present. The engagement letter stated that any fraud involving senior management, or fraud causing a material misstatement of the financial statements, would be reported directly to the audit committee. In 2001, Lehman showed its internal accounting policy statement to the then engagement partner Kevin Reilly, as well as Matthew Kurzweil and William Schlich, hoping to use Repo 105. E&Y approved the policy. It did not help draft it and did not advise on the transactions. But the audit partners knew perfectly well what it was for. On August 19, 2001, Lehman's Kristine Smith sent the three of them a memo: this accounting treatment lets Lehman turn repos into inventory transactions, giving it greater capacity to net down the balance sheet. Lehman also told E&Y that no US law firm would characterise Repo 105 as a "sale," but that the UK firm Linklaters had given an opinion that, under strict conditions, it could be characterised as one — the securities had to be "located" in the UK, and the transactions had to be done in the UK under English law. Later Lehman put billions of dollars of US fixed-income government securities into Repo 105 as well: a US entity would first transfer the securities to its UK affiliate, LBIE, which then did the transaction. Schlich later said he was unaware of such transactions; Smith and Kelly insisted in testimony that they had explicitly told Schlich US securities were included. In September 2006, Bharat Jain, a member of the E&Y audit team, worried that this could be a reputational risk and wrote to his superior Jennifer Jackson: what do we think about how much Lehman should be doing? Have we compared it to competitors, are there industry publications, is there regulatory guidance? Jackson later said that raising reputational risk was not an everyday occurrence and she couldn't immediately think of another example; but she couldn't recall whether she had raised the matter with Schlich. Lehman had initially told E&Y by email that it planned to cap volumes at roughly US$20–30 billion. It began exceeding the cap in 2007, and by the end of the second quarter of 2008 it had reached US$50.38 billion. E&Y received many internal documents stating the volumes. Kelly, who had just become financial controller in December 2007, told Schlich that volumes spiked at every quarter-end, and that the accounting rationale for sale treatment was "legalistic" and "form-driven," so Lehman had to rely on the Linklaters opinion. Kelly later said that E&Y was still "comfortable with the GAAP treatment, for the same reasons Lehman was comfortable." The 2007 audit workpapers defined materiality as anything that, individually or in aggregate, moved net leverage by 0.1 or more (typically US$1.8 billion). That was Lehman's own threshold; E&Y never expressed a separate view on the materiality of Repo 105. In 2009 Schlich admitted to the bankruptcy examiner that E&Y had no "bright-line" materiality rule, and that in a balance-sheet context it depended on facts and circumstances. E&Y's chief executive, Jim Turley, later defended the firm: every institution manages its balance sheet, and managing it is not in itself window dressing; what matters is that investors have an accurate picture of leverage; these repos — and the accounting was never challenged — would probably have changed leverage only from 31 times to 32 times, and Lehman would still have been the bank with the third-highest leverage. Lee's letter reached E&Y. Schlich immediately told the chair of the audit committee and insisted that management inform the SEC and the New York Fed. He later said he had discussed the whistleblower letter with the committee at least three times in June and July 2008. The letter itself did not mention Repo 105, but it raised a series of possible accounting irregularities. The committee chair, Thomas Cruikshank, asked E&Y to assist the company's internal audit investigation, to meet Lee, and to report every allegation that came up during the investigation — whether or not it was in the letter — to the committee. Schlich wrote to colleagues: we are also dealing with a whistleblower letter that "on its face is pretty ugly," and it will take a great deal of time; based on what he had seen so far, he was confident it would not turn into a material issue for the financial reporting; that, plus some very difficult off-balance-sheet accounting issues, had everyone under a lot of pressure. On June 12, 2008, Schlich and another partner, Hillary Hansen, interviewed Lee. On the spot, Lee added an allegation that wasn't in the letter: at the end of the second quarter of 2008, Lehman had used Repo 105 to take US$50 billion of fixed-income securities off the balance sheet, and put them back a few days later. The next day, June 13, Schlich briefed the audit committee on the investigation's progress and did not mention Repo 105. At the July 8 committee meeting, and when internal audit reported its findings to the committee on July 22, he still said nothing. Internal audit's conclusion: "no material issues identified." The audit committee never knew about Repo 105, never knew it was undisclosed, never knew US securities were being shifted to a UK affiliate to do it, and never knew that its size, its growth and its quarter-end timing had been flagged as problems. Meanwhile, on July 10, E&Y issued an unqualified review report on Lehman's 10-Q — less than a month after interviewing Lee. In the epilogue, Turley said in the summer of 2010: at the end of the day, we feel good about the work we did at Lehman. He argued that the partners "took some comfort in the fact that the issue was a disclosure issue around Repo 105," since the accounting was aligned with US rules. Later, on television, he placed Lehman's failure in the context of a global financial meltdown, mortgage defaults, falling asset prices and a liquidity crisis, and said that without governments stepping in, many financial institutions would have filed for Chapter 11. He acknowledged that the system needed reform. Taiwan, Semiconductors, and a "Cold New War"?

The Professor's Questions The United States and China competed over dominance of the global semiconductor industry in the 2020s. Beijing’s Made in China 2025 initiative aimed to achieve 70 percent self-sufficiency in semiconductor technology. Meanwhile, the U.S. Congress debated a bill authorizing $52 billion in support for the semiconductor industry. The so-called “tech war” posed pressing questions for Taiwan, the world’s leading manufacturer of semiconductors. Would the competition between the United States and China erode the “silicon shield” that Taiwanese leaders counted on to preserve their island’s autonomy? And what consequences could the world expect from the seeming deglobalization of the semiconductor industry? Assess the effects of government policies on the development of the semiconductor industry in the United States, Taiwan, and China. How should Taiwan navigate the rise of Sino-American tensions? Is its semiconductor industry a source of protection or vulnerability? Does the competition over Taiwan and the global semiconductor industry indicate a world of deglobalization? Why or Why not? If so, what likely consequences might follow from deglobalization? My Answers Q1. Government policy and the industry Government policy built this industry in all three places. It just built three different kinds of power. In the United States, the state created the science, then stepped back from the factory. Bell Labs needed wartime purification work at MIT. The Pentagon paid for transistors, set standards, and financed plants. The Justice Department forced AT&T to open its patents. That open IP cadence, plus venture capital, produced Fairchild, Intel, and later the fabless model. When Japan’s share jumped from 28 percent in 1978 to 46 percent in 1986, Washington did not stay liberal: it threatened anti-dumping duties, taxed $300 million of Japanese electronics, and stood up SEMATECH at about $200 million a year. The later U.S. edge is not in making wafers. Exhibit 11: America still takes 38 percent of value added and 74 percent of EDA and core IP. What it lost is the leading-edge factory. Intel missed EUV. Nvidia, a U.S. design firm that does not own a fab, became the most valuable chip company — and it is a TSMC customer. The CHIPS Act’s $52 billion is an attempt to buy the factory back. BCG’s own math in the case: $50 billion of subsidy lifts the U.S. production share from 12 to 14 percent. Morris Chang called it an expensive exercise in futility. Policy can seed an industry. It cannot, in one bill, rebuild a work culture that fixes a tool at 2 a.m. In Taiwan, policy chose a narrow bet and stuck to it. Land reform, export zones, vocational schools, and a 30 percent engineering share of university students built the human base. ITRI did applied research, not basic science, and leaked 12,000 engineers into firms. ERSO bought RCA’s obsolete seven-micron node, beat RCA’s own yields, and spun out UMC. Chang then refused to become another integrated device maker. He used the state to build a pure-play foundry, licensed Philips technology only nine months off the frontier, and let design houses bloom in Hsinchu — more than forty in a year. That single institutional choice created the global fabless industry. Apple, Qualcomm, and Nvidia exist in their current form because Taiwan’s government absorbed manufacturing risk. By 2019 Taiwan held 92 percent of wafer capacity for logic below 10 nanometers. The developmental state did not pick “electronics” in the abstract. It picked the one slice of the chain that matched what Taiwan could do, and what it could not. In China, policy has been bigger, broader, and less precise. The National IC Plan aimed at $150 billion. China supplied 86 percent of worldwide state equity support for chip firms from 2014 to 2018. SMIC’s government stake rose from under 15 percent to over 45 percent. Made in China 2025 wrote down a 70 percent self-sufficiency target. The toolkit included forced joint ventures, $35 billion of outbound chip M&A in a single year, talent programs, and civil-military fusion. The result, by the case’s own scoreboard, is mixed. About 200 new chip firms were registered per day in early 2020. SMIC announced 7-nanometer chips. Tsinghua Unigroup went bankrupt. Chinese-owned firms still made only 5.9 percent of the chips China used. Huawei’s Mate 60 raised the China-origin share of components from 29 to 47 percent — real progress, still without EUV, still on a process analysts called unreliable. Money created activity. It has not yet created TSMC. The comparative lesson: policy is not a on/off switch. U.S. policy created an open knowledge system and then offshored the plant. Taiwanese policy created a specialist plant and invited the world to use it. Chinese policy is trying to buy the whole chain at once, under a security clock. The first two worked because they chose a slice. The third is still paying for wanting every slice. Q2. How Taiwan should navigate Taiwan should treat the silicon shield as a wasting asset. Keep the leading edge on the island. Put just enough capacity in the United States to keep Washington’s skin in the game. Build a porcupine. Do not declare a new republic. Do not bet the island on “one country, two systems.” The industry is still protection. It is becoming vulnerability faster. Why it is still protection. In 2019 Taiwan held 92 percent of wafer capacity for logic below 10 nanometers. Only three firms on earth could do 5 nanometers. A war that breaks TSMC is not a local war. It is a shutdown of phones, clouds, cars, and AI training. That is why Tsai wrote to Foreign Affairs , why Liu told 60 Minutes the world would not let war happen, and why Lai, on the night he won, called the industry “a common asset of the world.” The shield is real in one direction: it raises the cost of a kinetic war for everyone who uses chips. Why it is becoming a vulnerability. Both patrons are now paying to stop needing Taiwan. Beijing’s target is 70 percent self-sufficiency. Washington’s CHIPS Act and the October 2022 export rules are designed so that advanced logic does not have to live in one strait. Every successful Arizona tool-install makes the sentence “the world can only make this chip in Taiwan” a little less true. The customer base is already political: Huawei was TSMC’s second-largest customer, more than 15 percent of revenue, and disappeared by regulation, not by the market. China still takes 44 percent of Taiwan’s exports. That is not a diversified book of business. It is a single counterparty that has already used pineapples as a sanction. The military numbers make the vulnerability worse. Conscription is four months. Headcount is about 80 percent filled. Defense spending fell from roughly 5 percent of GDP around 1990 to about 2 percent (Exhibit 8a). Half the public says it would fight; most believe it will never have to, because America will come. Pentagon war games often have the red team win. Buying 66 F-16s for $8.1 billion is the opposite of a porcupine. High-prestige platforms die in a first strike. Anti-ship missiles, mines, and air defense do not look like a silicon shield. They are what you buy when you stop using TSMC as a substitute army. So the navigation is a portfolio, not a slogan. Keep N-2 and below, and the yield knowledge, on the island. That is the last piece of leverage that is actually scarce. Do not let CHIPS money relocate the frontier. Accept a costly, limited U.S. footprint. Arizona at four times Taiwan’s construction cost is an insurance premium paid to Congress and to TSMC’s American customers. Chang already said the quiet part: globalization is almost dead, so you build there anyway. The point is political entanglement, not cost. Lengthen conscription, fill the ranks, and buy the ugly weapons. The shield cannot remain the only defense. A four-month summer camp plus a $8.1 billion fighter deal is how a rich island pretends a foundry is a navy. Hold the political status quo in words and in law. Exhibit 6 is the mandate. Immediate independence invites the invasion the case says Beijing has promised. Immediate unification on Hong Kong’s formula is what Taiwanese voters rejected after 2019. Ambiguity is not weakness here. It is the product the median voter already bought. Slowly reduce the 44 percent. Not a sudden decoupling — Taiwan is the world’s second-most exposed economy to global value chains. A multi-year shift of assembly and final demand toward Europe, Japan, Southeast Asia, and the U.S. makes the pineapple episode harder to repeat at chip scale. The cost of this package is explicit. Arizona raises TSMC’s cost base. A porcupine raises the defense budget. Diversifying away from the mainland costs exporters. The cost of the alternative is larger: a shield that Washington and Beijing are both working to make obsolete, sitting on an island whose young men binge McDonald’s to fail the physical, while 92 percent of the world’s most advanced wafers wait in one typhoon path. Q3. Deglobalization or not No. This is not deglobalization. It is the same global chain, with permission to ship now treated as a weapon. A deglobalized semiconductor world would look like three complete stacks: American design plus American fabs plus American tools; a Chinese stack that can live without EDA, EUV, and Nvidia; a Taiwanese or Korean stack that does not sell to either. The case does not show that world. It shows a fight over a still-shared chain. The evidence against the word. In 2019 the United States still did 74 percent of EDA and core IP. The only EUV firm is Dutch, and Washington can block a shipment only because American parts sit inside the machine. TSMC’s customers are American fabless firms. China still bought near-record volumes of chips and tools in 2023. Nvidia did not leave China; it redesigned cards to sit just under the threshold. The Netherlands and Japan joined export controls — that is alliance politics, not autarky. Chip 4 is a club inside the old network, not a breakup of the network. Taiwan remains the world’s second-most exposed economy to global value chains. A world that was deglobalizing would be reducing that score. It is arguing about who is allowed to use the same scoreboard. The evidence that looks like deglobalization is real, and it is narrower. CHIPS money tries to pull leading-edge capacity onto U.S. soil. CFIUS now reviews deals with almost no U.S. footprint, like Magnachip. The Foreign Direct Product Rule claims jurisdiction over chips that contain no U.S. atoms. Chang said globalization is almost dead and free trade is almost dead. He is describing the political overlay, not the production graph. Wafers, software, and talent still cross borders. What no longer crosses freely is permission . If we still want a word, use weaponized interdependence , or securitized globalization . The frontier is being recoupled along alliance lines. Mature nodes are still global, and may become more global in the wrong way: TSMC’s CEO said in 2024 there might be too much capacity being built for mature nodes, exactly what you get when every capital dumps subsidy into the easy part of the chain. Consequences, even without full deglobalization: Higher costs, forever. Arizona is about four times Taiwan. That cost will sit in every iPhone and every server, or in a government budget that never quite sunset. A glut at the trailing edge, a shortage at the frontier. Duplicate mature fabs plus Chinese subsidy is how you get dumping. The scarce thing — EUV, yield, 5-nanometer discipline — stays scarce longer, because you cannot subsidy-clone a 700-step process. A slower Moore’s Law. The old model socialized manufacturing risk in one specialist island so that a hundred design firms could iterate. Three half-copies of that island waste capital on concrete instead of nodes. Two permission regimes, not two planets. A China-accessible stack and an America-accessible stack will share tools and older nodes, and diverge on AI accelerators and anything that looks like a military input. Families, carmakers, and cloud firms will keep two bills of materials. The bill lands on small open economies first. Taiwan’s 44 percent, Korea’s memory plants, Dutch export licenses. Deglobalization talk in Washington is paid for, in the first round, by places that actually live inside the chain. So if someone in class says “the chip war proves globalization is over,” the reply is: globalization of atoms is still running. Globalization of permission is being rewritten. Those are different sentences. The first one is why a war over Taiwan still crashes the world. The second one is why both superpowers think they can, in time, afford to care less. Case Summary In autumn 2021, Tsai Ing-wen addressed the world in Foreign Affairs . Chinese military aircraft were entering Taiwan's air defence identification zone in record numbers. Defence Minister Chiu Kuo-cheng judged that by 2025 China would be able to attack Taiwan "at the lowest possible cost and losses." Tsai wrote that if Taiwan fell, it would be a catastrophe for regional peace and the democratic alliance, tantamount to authoritarianism prevailing over democracy in the contest of values. She also knew that ideals often dissolve in international relations, so she offered another reason — TSMC, and Taiwan's semiconductor industry more broadly, was a "silicon shield." Chairman Mark Liu told 60 Minutes that the whole world needs Taiwan's high tech, and therefore "will not let a war happen in this region." Yet Beijing and Washington were both pouring in money to break their dependence on Taiwan — and on each other. Some began calling it a "new Cold War." What Taiwan is, is itself contested. An island of 13,826 square miles, with about 23.5 million people in 2021, more than 95% Han Chinese. It meets Weber's functional definition of a "state," yet since the 1970s has struggled to maintain external recognition. The mainstream view on the island is that the Republic of China is "already independent," and that the ambiguous status quo beats the alternatives. Mainland China regards Taiwan as a breakaway province; its military has built a scale model of the Presidential Office in Inner Mongolia to rehearse "decapitation." Over thirty years, identity has shifted heavily towards "Taiwanese" (Exhibit 7), while positions on unification versus independence are heavily concentrated on "maintaining the status quo" (Exhibit 6). The island's modern history is a crossroads of empires. Dutch and Spanish outposts, the Ming loyalist Zheng regime, annexation into Fujian by the Kangxi Emperor in 1684 (he had originally said "a ball of mud beyond the sea, of no great consequence"), cession to Japan in 1895. Japan made it a "model colony": primary school enrolment for boys rose from 39% to 80%, while dissent was suppressed. In 1945 the Kuomintang took over; the popular saying was "the dogs left and the pigs came." In the February 28 Incident of 1947, at least 10,000 people were killed. In 1949 about 1.5 million soldiers and civilians retreated to Taiwan and imposed decades of martial law and White Terror on the roughly 6 million islanders. Meanwhile, "Free China" received US$4.2 billion in American aid between 1949 and 1968. Land reform cut the share of tenant farmers from 64% to 10%, and the surplus capital and labour fed import substitution, which then pivoted to export orientation in the late 1950s. In 1966 the world's first export processing zone opened. Upstream state-owned enterprises supplied cheap raw materials, and downstream small and medium-sized firms did contract manufacturing — in Toy Story , Buzz Lightyear finds Made in Taiwan stamped on his wrist. Semiconductors were the next stop on this upgrading path. A 1966 plan aimed to make Taiwan an "electronics industry centre." The share of vocational education rose from 40% to 60%, and in 1990, 30% of university students studied engineering (India 5%, South Korea 20%). The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) was founded in 1973 to do applied rather than basic research; in 1974 its Electronics Research and Service Organization (ERSO) bought RCA's already outdated 7-micron process and trained 40 engineers. The pilot line's yields soon exceeded those of RCA's plant in the US. In 1980 it spun off UMC, the first company in the Hsinchu Science Park, which three years later was the most profitable company in Taiwan. Hsinchu deliberately copied Silicon Valley: the government could hold up to 49% of equity, with tax exemptions, low-interest loans, matching R&D funding, plus housing, schools and hospitals. ITRI staff turned over at 10–15% a year, and from 1973 to 2000 about 12,000 engineers moved into industry; in 1999, 110 of the park's 284 companies had been founded by engineers who had returned from the United States. In the summer of 1985, Morris Chang put down the phone. Born in Ningbo, he went to Harvard to escape the civil war, felt that "in the early fifties, the only career a Chinese American could seriously pursue was technology," transferred to MIT, and spent 25 years in semiconductors at Texas Instruments, rising to group vice president, before leaving in 1983 feeling he had been "put out to pasture." He saw two things: the cost of building a fab was roughly doubling every five years, reaching US$250 million by 1985; and a crop of fabless design companies had begun renting idle capacity from IDMs. Premier Sun Yun-suan asked him to lead Taiwan's semiconductor push. He accepted the presidency of ITRI and proposed spinning off from ERSO a pure-play foundry — one that only manufactures for others, with no design and no brand of its own. This used Taiwan's strengths in manufacturing and engineering while sidestepping its weaknesses in IP-intensive design and marketing. He signed with Philips, bringing in technology only nine months behind the frontier, and founded TSMC. Within a year, more than forty design companies sprang up in Hsinchu. In 1992 AMD's Jerry Sanders was still saying "real men have fabs." In 2009 AMD sold off its own fabs. By 2020 TSMC held half of global foundry capacity, and the overwhelming majority of capacity for the most advanced chips. This industry has never grown out of the market on its own. Bell Labs produced the germanium transistor in 1947; the Pentagon provided money, set standards and built plants; the Justice Department's antitrust action forced AT&T to open up its patents. Shockley, the "Traitorous Eight," Arthur Rock and venture capital grew Fairchild and Intel in the Stanford Industrial Park. Moore's Law became the metronome. In the 1970s American companies moved assembly and testing to developing economies including Taiwan; Japan's MITI coordinated R&D, subsidised loans and restricted competition, and its share rose from 28% in 1978 to 46% in 1986 while the US fell from 55% to 40%. The Reagan administration forced Tokyo to set export price floors, raise foreign companies' share of the Japanese market from 8% to 20%, and imposed tariffs on US$300 million of Japanese electronics. In 1987 the Defense Science Board said dependence on foreign microelectronics was "unacceptable." Hence SEMATECH, with an annual budget of about US$200 million, split evenly between DARPA and industry. America's share later came back — some credit the consortium, others say it was really the PC and Intel's microprocessors, while the consortium was still focused on already commoditised DRAM. In 2014, Beijing switched to a bigger industrial policy. The Snowden affair convinced the leadership that core technologies could not be in other people's hands. Xi Jinping's words in 2016: core technology is our greatest vital weakness, and being controlled by others is our greatest hidden danger. The National Integrated Circuit Industry Development Guidelines aimed to reach "advanced international levels" by 2030; Made in China 2025 set a ten-year self-sufficiency target of 70%. This round differed from the 1980s and 1990s: it was about 40 times larger in scale, the strategy was to build national champions through overseas acquisitions plus technology transfer, and execution was handed to local private equity funds. The Big Fund, provincial and municipal funds, and the Phase II fund together added up to the hundred-billion-dollar range. From 2014 to 2018, 86% of the world's state equity support for semiconductors came from China. The government's stake in SMIC rose from under 15% in 2004 to over 45% in 2018. Alongside this came mandatory joint ventures, US$35 billion of outbound acquisitions in 2015 alone, the Thousand Talents Plan, and poaching Richard Chang and over a hundred former employees from TSMC — TSMC's litigation ultimately won it a 9% stake in SMIC and a US$325 million settlement. In the first ten months of 2020, about 200 new semiconductor companies were registered in China every day. SMIC announced a 7-nanometre breakthrough, though analysts still said it was "years behind"; Tsinghua Unigroup went into bankruptcy in 2021. Chinese-owned companies still produce only 5.9% of the chips China uses. In the 2010s, Washington rewrote Beijing from "responsible stakeholder" into strategic competitor. The export control Entity List, the extraterritorial reach of the Foreign Direct Product Rule (FDPR), and CFIUS's expansion to minority stakes step by step removed Huawei from TSMC's customer list. In September 2022, Jake Sullivan said that it used to be enough to stay a generation or two ahead, but for advanced logic and memory the US now had to maintain "as large a lead as possible." In October, the Commerce Department imposed sweeping controls on advanced chips at roughly 14 nanometres and beyond, manufacturing equipment, IP and support from "US persons," and through the FDPR reached all the way to the EUV machines of the Netherlands' ASML — the only company in the world that can make them. Some analysts called it "a full-blown techno-economic cold war." The results were mixed: the Netherlands and Japan followed in 2023, and Chip 4 took shape; China's imports of semiconductors and equipment that year were still near record highs; Nvidia modified its chips to sit just below the thresholds; Huawei's Mate 60 brought domestic components up to 47%. Romney, who had once attacked Obama for wasteful subsidies to Solyndra, turned to supporting CHIPS: the CHIPS and Science Act authorised US$278 billion, more than US$52 billion of it for semiconductors. Intel, TSMC and Samsung planned fabs in Ohio, Arizona and Texas respectively. Conditions included childcare, sharing of excess profits, no buybacks, and no new high-end investment in China. Boston Consulting Group estimated that US$50 billion in subsidies would only lift the US share of production from 12% to 14%. Morris Chang called it "an expensive exercise in futility." Building in Arizona costs about four times as much as in Taiwan. He said: if a machine breaks at 1 a.m., in the US it gets fixed the next morning; in Taiwan it's fixed by 2 a.m. He also said: globalisation is almost dead, free trade is almost dead. That's why he was still optimistic about Arizona. The silicon shield theory is being used both on the island and in politics. In 2020 Taiwan was the world's 22nd-largest economy, with exports often exceeding half of GDP, 40% of them semiconductors, and China absorbing 44% of exports. It is the economy with the second-highest exposure to global value chains. Only 13 countries still have formal diplomatic relations with it; the US supplies defensive weapons under the Taiwan Relations Act and "strategic ambiguity," and in Pentagon war games the red team often beats the blue team. Compulsory military service was cut to four months, which some called summer camp, with "strawberry soldiers"; units were filled to only about 80% of establishment, and military spending fell from about 5% of GDP to about 2%. Around half the population says it is willing to fight, and most believe they will never have to and can count on the US. Procurement favours expensive platforms like the F-16 — the Tsai government bought 66 for US$8.1 billion in 2020 — while analysts would rather see a "porcupine": anti-ship, anti-tank and air defence, to fight a survivable war of attrition. In the winter of 2024, Lai Ching-te, whom Beijing calls a "troublemaker," won the presidency, while the Kuomintang won a majority in the legislature. After his victory he said: Taiwan's semiconductors are a shared asset of the world, and he hoped both China and the international community would cherish them. The silicon shield narrative is still there. The case ends on a question: is it alive and well, or slowly and painfully dying? The Professor's Questions This case follows the entrepreneurial journey of Janan Knust, founder and CEO of KLog.co, a Chile-based logistics company that has grown from a traditional freight forwarder into a technology-enabled logistics platform serving over 1,500 clients across Latin America. In a highly fragmented and commoditized industry, KLog has defied structural limitations by combining a high-touch freight operation with a proprietary SaaS platform and a distinctive organizational culture defined by its AFIRE values: Alegría (Joy), Foco (Focus), Incomodidad (Discomfort), Resiliencia (Resilience), and Estudio (Study). Is the freight forwarding industry attractive? Why? What are the most innovative features of Klog’s business model? Is Klog solving the problems in the freight forwarding industry? What is Klog’s competitive advantage? Is it sustainable? Provide an assessment of the growth trajectory of Klog. What are its strengths? Its weaknesses? What growth strategy would you recommend Janan Knust to follow? Why? Should Klog finance the proposed growth strategy using external funds? Explain your answer. My Answers Q1. Is the freight forwarding industry attractive? No. As an industry, freight forwarding is structurally ugly. It is a place you enter only if you can change the game. Five facts from the case: No barriers, no loyalty, price is the product. Knust: "The entry barriers are basically zero; anyone can do this." Customers use different forwarders on different routes and pick the cheapest. Switching is easy. Services look the same, so the industry is treated as a commodity. Fragmented, and the giants still do not own it. The market is ~$176B in 2024, growing a dull ~4.1% to 2029. DHL is 6%, Kuehne + Nagel is 4%. Small players are 60%. The big two grow by buying local winners, not by inventing a better product. The P&L is thin and people-heavy. Exhibit 3: average COGS 82%, gross profit 18%, EBIT 5% (range 1–11%). Almost all trade documents are still paper. COVID showed what that means: Bills of Lading could not move, cargo sat. Rates, not skill, swing the top line. Exhibit 5: industry revenue +30% in 2021, +15% in 2022, then -11% in 2023 — a 41-point drop from the peak. KLog's own ticket size went from $7,819 to $2,764. That is not a strategy problem. That is the industry. Big shippers bypass you. Large enterprises already talk to the shipping lines. SMEs are the ones who need a forwarder — and they are the most price-sensitive. The only attractive reading is as a disruption target . Paper, fax, no visibility, low trust: that is why Flexport once printed an $8B valuation and why KLog's software found a job. But "the industry is broken" is not the same as "the industry is a good business." A good strategy starts by admitting the first sentence. Q2. Innovative features — is KLog solving the industry's problems? The innovative piece is not "they built a TMS." Many people built a TMS. The innovative piece is that the same operating system runs the freight shop and the customer's desk — and it still works when the freight is not KLog's. The features that actually change the game: A dual product with one OS. Freight (ocean, air, land, rail, plus warehouse, insurance, customs, dangerous goods, last mile) plus a platform built with the ops team, not by a separate software company. Knust: the two products "merge into one." Employees use what customers use. That is how you get labor efficiency and fewer errors, and how you stop the software from becoming a demo. Forwarder-agnostic system of record. Customers can add and track shipments handled by other forwarders. Documents live in one place even when KLog did not move the box. That is a very different job from "please use our booking tool." It is a bid to become the customer's memory. K4All as a wedge. One KLog shipment in a window, and the platform is free. Most of the 26% "platform users" are almost certainly here, not in the paid SaaS column. $500k ARR ÷ ~$24,000 per SaaS client ≈ 21 paying software accounts. The free layer is doing the retention work Exhibit 10 shows. They attacked their own information advantage. Traditional FF pricing lives on relationships, negotiation, and opacity. KLog put a rate engine on the table and a three-click Book & Pay that skips the sales team. That is not a feature. That is a choice to give away the old profit logic in exchange for trust and volume. Hospitality DNA plus AFIRE, and they hire outside the industry on purpose. The innovative "feature" customers feel is service in a business that is not customer-centered. Culture is written as an operating system, not a poster. Is it solving the industry's problems? For a slice of their clients, yes. For the industry, not yet. Visibility, documents, quotes, free days, internal dashboards: yes. Bencuya and Gomez say so in plain words. Paper Bills of Lading across the whole trade lane: no. One firm cannot fix that. Commodity pricing and churn: only partly. Platform users stay (~80–93%, 100% by year 7). Everyone else still looks like the industry (~20% retained by year 5–7). Blended churn is still ~40% in 2023. Low margins: only partly. Their FF gross margin is ~22% vs the industry 18%, operating margin ~11% vs industry EBIT 5%. SaaS is 90% / 35% — and $500k. Large forwarders are already copying the tech. The case says hopes dimmed. So: KLog is solving the customer's problem of blindness and clutter. It has not yet made freight forwarding a good industry. The 26% number is the honest scoreboard. Q3. Competitive advantage — is it sustainable? KLog's advantage is a freight shop, a software layer, and a culture that were grown together — not software, and not "better service" as a slogan. It is sustainable only if they finish the job they started: get far more than 26% of clients onto the platform, without breaking AFIRE. What is actually hard to copy: Culture as the operating system. Knust calls culture "the single most important factor" in the company's success. AFIRE is specific: joy as a working climate, focus as anti-distraction, discomfort as the growth rule, resilience as the permission to be wrong, study as the ban on improvisation. They hire people who did not grow up in freight. That is a real filter. It is also the most fragile piece under capital and geography. Software written from live operations. Serrano stayed because "technology alone wasn't going to cut it." The platform was iterated with the logistics team. Customers say other tools are "too basic and rigid" and take forever to change. That learning sits in the people and the workflows, not in a feature list. Exhibit 10 is the moat, if they can spread it. Platform users stay. Non-platform users leave like the rest of the industry. A competitor can copy a screen. Copying seven years of "this is where my documents and my history live" is a different problem — but only for the 26% who already live there. Service from hospitality, in an industry that does not do hospitality. That is why a large retailer stayed through COVID volumes, and why Gomez talks about the account executive in the same breath as the tracker. What is not a durable advantage on its own: The TMS features (quote, track, POM, dashboards). Large FFs are integrating the same tools. Flexport and Nowports already ran this play at much larger valuations. Price. Ticket size just collapsed 60%. Nobody wins a price war in a 5% EBIT industry. Personal networks. "I have known most of my C-level since I was three" is an asset at 200 people. It is a risk at 2,000. Sustainable? Conditionally, and not yet at full scale. The combination is hard to copy. The combination is also unfinished. A 40% blended churn rate means the advantage is still sitting in a minority of the book. Raise the wrong capital, open three countries before the platform travels, or let automation hollow out the "joy" side of AFIRE, and the advantage becomes a mural. Q4. Growth trajectory — strengths and weaknesses The honest trajectory is: volume and clients are compounding, revenue is not, and the software is still a seedling sitting on top of a cash cow that just halved. Strengths They take share when prices fall. TEUs 30%+ CAGR 2020–2023; FCL 5,256 → 14,718 (41%). Transactions 5,695 → 13,834, +35% in the year the ticket fell 60%. 2024 budget $50M on 15,000 shipments is a recovery plan, not a moonshot — and it is still a share-gain story. They survived without a patron. Profitable, no outside equity, no bank debt. $15M of expected excess cash over two years is real strategic freedom. The Kerry near-death in year three is in the muscle memory. The retention split is the best number in the case. Exhibit 10 is a strategy slide, not an HR slide. Once the platform is the customer's system of record, seven-year retention goes to 100%. That is the only path out of a 40% churn industry. Unit economics already lean their way. FF 22% / 11% versus industry 18% / 5%. SaaS 90% / 35%. The direction of the mix is right. They professionalized before they had to. New C-level in 2021, offices in three more countries, Endeavor / EY recognition, a fundraising process they walked away from — and kept the learning. Weaknesses The P&L is a rate chart. $78.1M → $38.8M. Anyone who reads only revenue will say the company shrank. Anyone who reads only 2021 will over-value it. $200M pre-money is the second reading. Churn is still industry-like for most of the book. 40% blended. 74% of active clients are not on the platform. Paid SaaS is ~21 accounts. The "tech company" sentence on page 6 is ahead of the mix. Geographic density is thin. Four countries, Chile-heavy, 200 people. AFIRE, beer on tap, and a founder who hires from kindergarten do not travel as a kit. The two cultures still clash. Serrano almost left in 2020. Tech is now eating workflows. Knust can already see a world where, without exponential growth, "employees will not have work to do." That is a strategy risk and a culture risk at the same time. The bench is intimate. Most C-level known since age three is speed in a bootstrap. It is a blind spot when the next hires are CMO, CRO, and a fintech credit function. SaaS go-to-market is unbuilt. They say so themselves: different timeline, different buyer, different contract. Freight sales are Sandler and aggressive. That muscle does not sell a $24k software implementation. Net: a strong regional compounder with one unfinished transformation. The next two years decide whether they become a platform that happens to move boxes, or a nicer forwarder with a website. Q5. What growth strategy? Deepen the platform first. Do not pave Latin America, and do not build a bank, until more than half the clients live inside the software. Fund digital platform + SaaS sales ($12M) and the executive bench ($2M) from the $15M of cash. Sequence geography. Park fintech. Why this order — four numbers: Exhibit 10 is the only escape from the industry. Non-platform clients leave. Platform clients stay. Spending $20M to stand up Brazil, Colombia, Panama, China, and Miami while 74% of today's book still behaves like a commodity forwarder is how you export a 40% churn rate. DHL and K+N can buy local winners. KLog should not copy their path until it has something those winners do not have. $12M + $2M = $14M, and cash is $15M. The two initiatives that actually compound the advantage fit inside the bootstrap. The two that look like "growth" do not. SaaS is not the business yet; it is the lock. ~21 paying accounts and $500k ARR do not justify a software-company strategy. They do justify a two-year push: move platform adoption from 26% toward 50%+, turn K4All from a free gift into a funnel, and build a sales motion that can talk to a different buyer. Every extra platform client is a freight client who stops shopping every route on price. Fintech is a third business. Trade credit, inventory finance, payments, insurance: $11M, and none of the current muscle is credit risk. They just lived through a 60% ticket collapse. Do not put a loan book on a rate cycle you do not control. Revisit with a partner after the data and the volume sit in one system. How to grow geography anyway, later: enter with the software, not with a warehouse. Sell the platform to a Brazilian importer who still uses three local forwarders. Become their system of record first. Stand up KLog freight only where the platform has already made you the default. That is the opposite of "open five flags and hope AFIRE boards the plane." The cost of this choice: they will look smaller than a funded competitor in São Paulo for a while. Some term sheets will go cold. Isaac Cañas-type hires in new countries wait. The cost of the other choice: they become a nicer regional DHL, on someone else's clock, before the 26% becomes 60%. Q6. Should they finance with external funds? No — not for this strategy, and not on this term sheet. The growth plan I want (platform + bench = $14M) fits inside the $15M of cash. The term sheet is built for a different company: a funded land-grab that has to justify $200M by year seven. Read Exhibit 14 as a strategy document, not a compliment: $50M at $200M pre / $250M post, 20% out. 5.2× 2023 revenue, 4.0× 2024 budget. SaaS at a generous 10× ARR is $5M. Investors are underwriting a freight book that just fell from $78M to $39M, plus a story. That is the 2021 Flexport tape, after the case itself said hopes dimmed. 1.5× non-participating pref = $75M off the top. Common — Knust — does not see a dollar in a sale until that clears. Redemption or a forced sale after year seven. This is not patient capital. It is a calendar. AFIRE's "discomfort" and a redemption clock are not the same kind of urgency. One board seat with veto on audit and compensation. The first place culture gets rewritten is how people are paid and what gets measured. That veto sits exactly there. They already took the useful part of fundraising once: the process professionalized the company, built relationships, and confirmed the story. They walked away. That was the right trade in the boom. It is still the right trade after the bust, if they are willing to sequence. When would I say yes? Three conditions, none of which are in Exhibit 14: a smaller check that only funds a later geo push ($10–15M, not $50M); no redemption / no sale right on a seven-year fuse; a partner who brings Brazil or China operations, not just a multiple. Until then, outside money is not cheaper than the $15M they already have. It is more expensive in the one asset the case keeps naming: the thing that made KLog special. The cost of "no": a slower flag count; a funded competitor who can outbid them on a few lanes; some pride. The cost of "yes" on this paper: they will be asked to become the company on the mural's next panel in someone else's handwriting. Case Summary December 2023, Santiago. Janan Knust, espresso in hand, stares at the mural by the headquarters entrance. It depicts KLog's eleven years so far, and employees are proud of it. He hopes the mural will have room for the next eleven years too. The company has grown from an analog freight forwarder into a digital platform providing both software and freight to more than 1,500 importers and exporters across Latin America: over 10,000 forwarding transactions a year, a SaaS product that reached US$500,000 in ARR just over a year after launch, consistently profitable, never externally funded. There are already several term sheets on his desk, with more to come. He and his team keep asking the same set of questions: keep growing on their own cash, or take their first outside money? How should resources be split between forwarding and SaaS? Will each decision damage "the layer that makes KLog KLog"? Knust's path doesn't look like a freight forwarder's. Born in Israel, with dyslexia and ADHD, he was cut from the Universidad Católica football team at 17, went to Switzerland to study hotel management, and worked his way up from dishwasher to head of food and beverage at a global luxury hotel chain. He brought the hospitality industry's obsession with service and culture into an industry that "isn't customer-centric." In 2012, his father Werner, who ran fish-export logistics in Chile, asked him to join a meeting with Kerry Logistics. During the meeting he found forwarding simple; when his father turned down the Chinese company's proposal, he cut in: I'll represent Kerry in Latin America. That's how KLog began — initially just Kerry's agent in Chile. The two key early hires he kept — first salesperson Anthony Asp (later CCO) and first operations hire Marianela Catalán (later head of customer service in Chile) — are both still there. The first crossroads was survival. The business was expanding, and the brand and relationships were there, but it didn't make money for the first three years, and its debt to Kerry piled up to the brink of bankruptcy. Knust flew to China and secured a line of credit. As he said later: good relationships aren't enough in a low-margin, highly commoditized industry; the new management principle had to be "who we are," not "what we do." He gradually replaced people from traditional industry backgrounds, brought in industry veteran Marcelo Delgado to run finance, and wrote resilience and passion into the culture. Once the company recovered, he began to feel that a mature industry was mature enough to be unbundled by technology. The second crossroads was becoming a tech company. In 2017 KLog made a strategic investment in a local startup, whose CTO, Álvaro Serrano, stayed on and built the platform from scratch. It started as an internal TMS: purchase orders, instant quotes, sailing schedules, tracking, reports and centralized documents. Technology was a "nice to have" at the time — six developers, almost all in their first jobs, with no product, design or marketing. At the end of 2020 Serrano said he couldn't keep going. They wrote a plan to "make technology the core value proposition," kept the CTO, and made "the clash between analog DNA and tech DNA" the management team's top agenda item. Customers started voting with their feet. William Bencuya, purchasing and freight manager at a large Latin American home-goods retailer, said: we switched to KLog because the platform can adapt to our operations — with others, a single change takes forever, and their platforms are thin and rigid; the freight itself is good too, and they handled the volume during the pandemic. Felipe Gomez, CEO of a Chilean sporting-goods distributor, said: beyond the freight, what we like is being able to track, store documents, see historical costs, compare prices and talk to our account manager. The third crossroads was whether to take money. The pandemic drove freight rates to unprecedented highs, and importers often didn't know where their goods were or when they'd arrive. KLog's tech investment proved right amid the chaos: new clients and volume came in, and on top of the rates, revenue soared. Platforms like Flexport and Nowports raised money at record valuations. Knust knew that revenue, gross margin and EBITDA had all been lifted by freight rates, and that the tide would go out; he also knew that he'd grown the company for ten years as sole owner with zero bank debt, and that raising money would mean changing both mindset and transparency. He strengthened the team: Igal Meirovich as head of finance and strategy, early tech advisor Gabriel Gurovich as CPO, and Fernando Varetto as COO; commercial offices opened in Peru, Bolivia and Mexico; and Isaac Cañas came over from Rappi to be CEO of Mexico. By 2024, KLog saw itself as Latin America's leading technology company in international freight and integrated logistics. Four countries, 200+ people, annual sales of over US$40 million. Revenue had fallen from a pandemic peak of about US$80 million, but TEU grew at a CAGR of over 30% from 2020 to 2023. Knust was named an Outlier Entrepreneur by Endeavor two years running and was included in EY's 2024 World Entrepreneur awards. The product comes as a pair: freight forwarding by sea, air, road and rail, plus warehousing, insurance, customs brokerage, dangerous goods and local transport; and a platform grown out of the operations team's and clients' pain points — centralized documents (even for shipments not moved by KLog), remaining free container days, real-time tracking and alerts, reports, and dashboards for sales and inventory, integrated with clients' WMS, ERP and purchase orders. To get people using it, they created K4All: ship at least one load with KLog during the period and the platform is free. Software-only clients pay by the number of containers tracked, with unit prices falling as volume rises, plus an implementation fee. The platform also offers transparent quotes and three-click "Book & Pay," letting clients bypass sales and book directly — the information asymmetry forwarders live on, dismantled by KLog itself. Clients range from large Chilean companies such as CasaIdeas and Arauco to Crocs, Tommy Hilfiger, Makita and Lee. Forwarding sales use the Sandler method — aggressive and focused; SaaS has entirely different sales cycles, decision-makers and contracts, and building a separate commercial team for it is a management priority. Churn is inherently high in forwarding. KLog cut overall churn from about 55% in 2017 to about 40% in 2023 while still growing its active client count; clients on the platform retained significantly better, and by mid-2023 platform users made up 26% of active clients. In Knust's words: clients who switch forwarders will also become SaaS clients, because they contribute profit and ship frequently; competitors are still moving freight with pen and paper, and the platform will make people stick. Internally, the same operating system is used by employees, complex manual work is being automated, and AI has begun reading documents and extracting data. He's already worried: if the company doesn't grow exponentially, employees will run out of work. The culture is codified as AFIRE. Joy, focus, discomfort, resilience, study. Hiring is extremely selective and deliberately avoids people from the forwarding industry; at the same time, most of the C-level comes from a personal network of people he's known since he was three. The office feels like a Silicon Valley startup: nap areas, on-site massages, draft beer; an annual all-staff getaway, KFunFest; and underneath it, KPEOPLE (interest-free loans, the Semillero intern incubator), KLEARNING and KGIVING. Knust says: culture is by far the most important success factor. Money has always been sufficient, and always carefully thought through. During the pandemic valuation bubble they met all kinds of VCs and received term sheets, but ultimately decided to keep rolling forward on excess cash. The fundraising process itself forced them to professionalize operations. Now, with an expected US$15 million in excess cash for 2024–2025, four things are on the table: geographic expansion at about US$20 million, the digital platform at about US$12 million, fintech at about US$11 million, and executive hires at about US$2 million — about US$45 million in total. The case ends at his desk: should he keep expanding into more countries? Double down on SaaS or on forwarding? How much engineering capacity should go to new products? How will employees feel about technology continuing to replace jobs? If he takes outside money, which of the things that got the company here would be put at risk — and does he even want to take it?
