Core Tensions Make the platform sticky first, or expand the map first (where the professor's Q5 / Q6 land) : the four-year growth menu totals $45M, but two-year cash is only $15M. Platform + team = $14M, just covered by cash; geography $20M + fintech $11M must be financed or dropped. Exhibit 10 says the stickiness lies in the platform; 26% penetration and roughly 21 paying SaaS clients say the platform is still a seedling. Geographic expansion is the DHL / K+N playbook and would replicate the 40% churn rate in Brazil. Take $50M @ $200M, or keep rolling on its own cash : the terms carry a 1.5× preference, 7-year redemption/sale, and veto over audit and compensation. A 5.2× revenue valuation rests almost entirely on forwarding and the story; SaaS alone isn't worth that price. Taking it would allow all four things at once, at the cost of culture and control; not taking it means prioritizing. Forwarding cash cow vs. SaaS option : 98%+ of revenue is still forwarding, and SaaS operating profit is roughly $180,000. The platform's real job today is reducing forwarding churn, not becoming a standalone software company. But forwarding revenue per shipment has just crashed from $7,819 to $2,764. Dismantling the information asymmetry it lives on : Book & Pay and fully transparent quotes attack the profit source of traditional forwarding. Short term, this hurts the sales intermediary; long term, it buys trust and scale. Can AFIRE scale with the company? : culture is written up as the number-one success factor; yet the C-level is mostly childhood friends, and technology is replacing employees' manual work. Fundraising, going multinational and continued automation will all touch this layer. Industry window : big forwarders are catching up on tech, and the high valuations of Flexport / Nowports have receded. "If we don't do it, someone else will" still holds, but "we must raise now at unicorn prices and pace" is no longer the 2021 refrain.

The Professor's Questions AI and the Ideas Economy. In March 2024, The Atlantic announced a strategic content and product partnership with artificial intelligence giant OpenAI. OpenAI would license The Atlantic’s content to train its models and respond to user queries, while The Atlantic would receive a fee, privileged access to OpenAI’s technology, and “premium” positioning within the tech giant. At the time, over 70 similar deals had been struck between publishers and AI companies. The Atlantic’s journalists, however, were incensed, concerned that partnering with OpenAI was “a devil’s bargain.” The New York Times had also just sued the tech giant for allegedly using 16 million pieces of the Times’ copyrighted content without permission to train its large language models. For Laurene Powell Jobs, the billionaire owner of The Atlantic, was it in the magazine’s best financial interest to continue the OpenAI partnership? What impact might a continued partnership have on the magazine’s journalism, or on the ideas landscape as a whole? What responsibility did Powell Jobs have – if any – to protect creativity and expression? Was Jobs undermining The Atlantic’s reputation, or was she bringing a new business model to bear on an industry facing major headwinds? What is the ideas economy? In what ways does it impact the world in which a business leader operates? Why did Laurene Powell Jobs and her Emerson Collective buy The Atlantic? Should The Atlantic have partnered with OpenAI? Why or Why not? What impact might a continued partnership with OpenAI have on the magazine’s journalism, and on the ideas landscape more broadly? My Answers Q1. The ideas economy The ideas economy is the market that produces, distributes, and prices original thought — journalism, literature, science, argument, design, and the other things a society uses to decide what is true, what is worth paying for, and what is allowed. It has three layers. Production is the scarce human work: a 168-year magazine, a novel that took three decades, a Pulitzer investigation that can force a resignation or free a wrongly convicted man. Distribution used to be printing, then the open web, then a search box. It is now also a chatbot that answers without sending the reader to the source. Capture is who gets paid. For most of The Atlantic’s life, capture was weak: culturally indispensable, rarely profitable, losing $4 to $8 million a year even after Bradley had put in more than $100 million. The 2024 P&L finally worked — $100 million of revenue, nearly two-thirds from 1 million paying subscribers — just as a new buyer of ideas appeared: model trainers who treat the archive as fuel. This is the world a business leader already operates in, with or without a media P&L. First, leaders live inside other people’s sentences. Regulation, talent, customers, and permission to operate are downstream of what magazines, courts, and now models say is legitimate. Powell Jobs bought a magazine because she wanted a voice in that layer, not because the 1990s P&L was pretty. Second, every firm is now both a consumer and a supplier of ideas. Consultants using ChatGPT beat those who do not, but the gains sit mostly with low-baseline people and the variance across a team collapses. A 2025 MIT study in the case has ChatGPT users at the lowest brain engagement, sliding toward copy-and-paste. The leader who treats the model as a free intern is quietly thinning the firm’s own judgment. Third, the legal design of this market is unfinished, and it is global. U.S. fair use has four factors and no formula. One Delaware judge said training a competing product on Thomson-Reuters headnotes was not transformative. Another judge said Anthropic’s use of seven million books was. Anthropic still paid $1.5 billion, about $3,000 a title. OpenAI’s own argument is national: training is “critical for U.S. competitiveness.” A 2022 AAAS study found text-and-data mining more common in countries with weaker copyright control. So a CEO in Boston, Shenzhen, or Singapore is already choosing a copyright regime when she chooses a model vendor. Fourth, platforms have become the clearinghouse. Google’s AI Overviews cut referral clicks by more than 34 percent. Chatbots have replaced search for more than 25 percent of Americans. The FTC’s 2023 warning in the case is the industrial-organization sentence: firms that control the data may “wield outsized influence over a significant swath of economic activity.” That is not a media problem. It is a market-structure problem that happens to show up first in sentences. The Global Markets point is simple. Ideas used to cross borders as magazines, books, and graduates. They now also cross as tokens in a training run. Whoever sets the price of those tokens — license, lawsuit, or “fair use” at $0 — is writing the trade rule for the next decade of knowledge work. Q2. Why they bought The Atlantic They bought a civic instrument that had finally learned how to lose less money, not a growth asset. The sentence Powell Jobs used in 2017 is the reason: a “critical mission at this critical time” — equality, the American idea, American culture and literature, and “our marvelous and sometimes messy democratic experiment.” Three facts make this more than a press release. One, the magazine had never been a financial prize. Bradley paid $10 million in 1999, put in more than $100 million, and still lost $4 to $8 million a year until a digital and events turnaround produced $1.8 million of profit in 2010. He sold because his adult children wanted nothing to do with it. A 70 percent stake for more than $100 million, paid by a woman then worth about $18.2 billion, is a stewardship check, not a PE entry multiple. Emerson is an LLC on purpose: venture, activism, and philanthropy at one table. It had already put money into Gimlet and Axios “for serious journalism for its own sake,” Bradley’s phrase. The name is Ralph Waldo Emerson, who opens the case: the poet and inventor who “unlocks our chains.” She said Emerson invites us “to transcend limitations that are placed on us by society.” Buying the magazine his circle founded is the most literal way to fund that sentence. Two, she did not want to be a distant check-writer. A director at an Emerson-backed group said a philanthropist at her level can operate from a comfortable distance. She wanted to be “an active participant.” She added more than 100 people, about 30 percent of headcount, put in a paywall, rebuilt the typeface and nameplate, and told Bradley the magazine should operate on the frontiers of technology — after he had said its gift was not that. The expansion made the P&L red again. She still hired Thompson in 2020 with a different order: dig the company out and make it self-sustaining. Mission without a going concern is a subsidy. A going concern without a mission is just another website. She has been trying to hold both. Three, the Silicon Valley habit came with the check. She runs Emerson like a start-up and sends sector leads out to “disrupt” their spaces. She takes “tech tours.” The same woman who promised — and kept — editorial independence also sat in OpenAI’s world through AI start-ups and the Jony Ive partnership. That is not a contradiction she hid. It is the marriage the case names on page 1: tech titans and award-winning journalists, under one owner. So the purchase is not explained by the 2010 $1.8 million, and not contradicted by the later $20 million hole. She bought the right to keep an American ideas institution alive, to keep her hands off the edit page, and to push the business side toward technology. The OpenAI deal is where those three wishes stop being able to live in separate rooms. Q3. Should they have partnered Yes. They should have signed. They should renew. They should not renew the same deal. The first deal was a price discovery, not a marriage. Thompson’s sentence is the right frame: the models “scraped without permission”; there are “a whole bunch of ways you can get paid for that”; you weigh what they offer against what a suit would cost and what it might return. That is not cynicism. That is the only adult arithmetic once the archive is already inside GPT-3. The financial case for signing is clearer than the newsroom letter admits. The Atlantic in 2024 had $100 million of revenue and had only just climbed out of a $20 million hole. Exhibit 3’s visible prices run from the AP’s “single-digit millions a year” to News Corp’s $250 million over five years. The cluster that looks like The Atlantic — FT at $5 to $10 million a year, Axel Springer at $25 to $30 million over three years — is 5 to 10 percent of the magazine’s revenue. That is enough to fund most of the 2025 hiring wave: 30 editors at $200,000 to $300,000 is about $6 to $9 million. The lawsuit path is not free. The Times spent $10.8 million in year one, before any judgment. Statutory damages of $150,000 an article against a $10 license sound like a jackpot until you remember Anthropic got a mixed ruling and still settled books at about $3,000 a title, and until you remember OpenAI’s public line that any single source “didn’t meaningfully contribute.” A just-profitable magazine with one million subscribers should not be the test case that funds a decade of discovery. The strategic case is the one Goldberg already made, accidentally. They moved off day-to-day news toward fewer, deeper stories. Commodity news is what a chatbot replaces first. A Pulitzer investigation that can oust a network chief, or free a prisoner, is what a model cannot originate and what a subscriber will still buy. Licensing the archive while thickening the newsroom is coherent: sell the past, raise the price of the next original piece. The later suit against Cohere — alleged full-article reuse and fake Atlantic bylines — shows they already know the difference between a paying counterparty and a parasite. That hybrid is the strategy, not a wobble. The “no” side is real, and it should write the next contract, not kill the relationship. Beres is right that OpenAI’s history is messy and that hallucinations at nearly 30 percent can smear a brand the magazine just spent years making worth $67 a subscriber. Lessin is right that a cheap license can fund the product that keeps the reader from ever arriving. Google Overviews already took more than 34 percent of referral clicks; chatbots already replaced search for more than a quarter of Americans. If “premium source” becomes a substitute for the site, Thompson’s “potential traffic source” is a story he tells himself. Powell Jobs’s silence is not editorial virtue on this file. Emerson’s AI book and the Ive–OpenAI hardware deal mean she must be able to show that renewal terms were set as if she had no other chip on the table. So renew, on terms a seller writes: Split the rights. Training is one license. Retrieval, quotation, and answer-generation are another. Do not sell both as a bundle at FT prices. No verbatim regurgitation, and working citations only. Hallucinated links were the newsroom’s first exhibit. Technical controls belong in the contract, not in a blog post. A most-favored reset. If the Times judgment or the next Anthropic-scale settlement sets a higher floor, this deal reopens. $3,000 a book is now a public number. A traffic cap in the opposite direction. Never let AI referral become a material acquisition channel. The magazine already learned this with programmatic ads; it should not relearn it with chatbots. Keep suing the ones who do not pay. Cohere is the deterrent that makes the OpenAI check mean something for the rest of the ideas market. Keep the owner’s other bets off the term sheet. Recuse, disclose, or put an independent director on the renewal. The newsroom cannot be asked to trust a deal the owner also sits on the other side of. The cost of this package is a smaller check, a slower product roadmap, and a colder relationship with a lab that likes to move fast. The cost of a blind renewal is the sentence Lessin already wrote, printed in The Atlantic, about The Atlantic. The cost of walking away is to spend like the Times without the Times’ balance sheet, while the archive stays in the model and the hiring spree is paid for by subscribers alone. Powell Jobs bought the magazine to defend an American idea. Paying writers $200,000 to $300,000 with money the models now have to acknowledge is a defense. Giving the models a quiet, perpetual feed is not. Q4. Impact on journalism and the ideas landscape A continued partnership, on seller’s terms, buys time for the newsroom and sets a price for the rest of the market. A continued partnership on the first contract’s terms subsidizes replacement and flattens the ideas landscape. The variable is the contract, not the logo on the press release. On journalism, the near-term effect is already visible and mostly good. The magazine is hiring while peers cut. Thirty editors at $200,000 to $300,000 in a single half-year is not “billionaire benevolence” as a mood. It is a bet that human reporting is the scarce input — the same bet the case floats at the end when it asks whether AI labs need writers to avoid model collapse. Goldberg’s shift to fewer, deeper stories is the right editorial answer to a chatbot that can summarize yesterday. Three Pulitzers, a cover that can exonerate a man, a story that can move a network chief: that is the product a subscriber still cannot get from a 30 percent hallucination engine. The medium-term effect is the one the newsroom fears, and it is not imaginary. If ChatGPT answers with a polished paraphrase plus a dead link, the subscriber never arrives. Overviews at minus 34 percent of clicks, and chatbots at more than 25 percent of U.S. search, are already that world. Incentives inside the magazine will tilt, quietly, toward being cited by the model: shorter explainers, more evergreen explainers, fewer expensive investigations that a model cannot use cleanly. That is how a hiring spree becomes a content farm with better furniture. Brand risk sits on the same page. A hallucinated “Atlantic” claim is not a traffic problem. It is a defamation problem wearing the magazine’s typeface — which is why the Cohere suit matters as much as the OpenAI check. On the ideas landscape, scale is the tell. By April 2025 OpenAI had twenty publisher partnerships covering more than 160 outlets; about seventy-two licenses existed across AI firms. That sounds like a market. It is a market only for people who can hire Nick Thompson. Min Jin Lee’s Instagram note in the case is the other half: three decades, a legal career left on the table, and then a model that “stole my stories.” If the going rate is a low-seven or mid-seven figure check to a masthead, and $0 to everyone else, two things follow. First, the training corpus concentrates around a few English-language institutions that can litigate or bargain. Second, the next Pachinko does not get written, or it gets written by someone who already has a trust fund. The FTC’s worry about outsized influence is this, in prose. Adobe’s Content Credentials are a useful patch for attribution. They do not create a living. Creativity research in the case is the third effect, and it is the one business leaders will feel even if they never buy a magazine. AI lifts the floor and sands the ceiling. Divergent-thinking scores beat all but the best humans. Stories written with ChatGPT were more useful for weak writers and more like each other as a set. Consultants got better together and more alike. MIT’s ChatGPT users got lazier. Kaufman and Beghetto’s Four-C model (Exhibit 4) is the vocabulary: mini-c and little-c everyday work will be automated and homogenized; Big-C and Pro-C work — the steam engine, the choreopoem, the investigation that takes a year — become more valuable and harder to fund if the distribution layer no longer sends a reader, or a royalty, back. A partnership that only dumps The Atlantic into the blender accelerates that flattening. A partnership that forces citation, forbids regurgitation, and recycles the fee into $300,000 reporters is one of the few ways a private owner can put sand in the gears. Powell Jobs’s responsibility is not to freeze the technology. Ive already said the quiet part: if you make something new, some consequences will be harmful, and responsibility is “a determination to try to be useful.” Her version of useful, given why she bought the magazine, is narrower than OpenAI’s. She does not owe Altman a cheap corpus. She owes the next Emerson a world in which a new thought still has a payer. Renewing without terms fails that. Walking away and letting fair use stay at $0 for everyone smaller than the Times also fails that. The owner who sits in both rooms has to set a price that other rooms can copy. Case Summary In March 2024, The Atlantic announced a two-year content and product partnership with OpenAI. OpenAI got a licence to use the magazine’s content to train its models and answer user queries; the magazine got a licensing fee, privileged access to OpenAI’s technology, and a place inside the tech giant as a “premium news source.” What CEO Nicholas Thompson cared about wasn’t only the money, but “a potential traffic channel” and the chance to “help shape the future of AI.” The newsroom exploded. Journalists wrote an open letter to Thompson and editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg: AI cannot replace journalists, and no outlet that still wants to live up to this magazine’s century-and-a-half of standards can allow that to happen. Editor Damon Beres called it “a devil’s bargain” in the magazine’s own pages. Jessica Lessin, founder of The Information, also wrote in The Atlantic : these deals amount to settling without suing, trading hard-won credibility for a bit of cash, while the other side undervalues you and builds products plainly designed to replace you. From day one, this magazine was more an American idea than a good business. In 1857, a group of abolitionist intellectuals — Emerson, Longfellow, Holmes — founded The Atlantic Monthly in Boston to talk about slavery, and about the tensions pushing the country toward civil war. It went on to publish Hemingway, Einstein and Booker T. Washington, as well as early work by Mark Twain, Henry James and Louisa May Alcott. Former editor Cullen Murphy put it this way: it advanced something you might call “the American idea.” Culturally indispensable, it rarely won on the books. In the 1990s it could lose as much as US$500,000 a year. In 1999, David Bradley — owner of National Journal and HBS MBA 1977 — bought it for US$10 million, and reportedly poured in more than US$100 million afterwards: better paper, dinners with advertisers, new subscription prices. The magazine still lost US$4–8 million a year. In 2004 “Monthly” came off the cover. Only when Bradley started running it like a startup — digital advertising rose from 9% to 45%, it launched city coverage and a digital edition, and the business expanded into events and marketing consulting — did it turn a US$1.8 million profit in 2010. His children didn’t want the magazine. He began looking for an exit. In 2017, Laurene Powell Jobs, Steve Jobs’s widow, bought 70% through the Emerson Collective for more than US$100 million. Her net worth at the time was around US$18.2 billion. Bradley kept a minority stake and stayed on to run it for another three to five years. He told staff that Powell Jobs had always been at the very top of his list: Emerson was already investing in serious journalism “for journalism’s sake.” She described the magazine as having “a critical mission at a critical time” — fostering equality for all, articulating and defending the American idea, celebrating American culture and literature, and covering this wonderful and often messy experiment in democracy. The collective is named after Emerson. She said Emerson invites people to move beyond the limits society places on them. The organisation itself, though, is pure Silicon Valley: an LLC rather than a traditional foundation, putting venture capital, activism and philanthropy at the same table; it invested in Gimlet and Axios; it helped Iñárritu make a VR piece on immigration; its climate action and College Track work run at billion-dollar scale. She encouraged the heads of each area to “disrupt” their fields, and regularly made her own Silicon Valley “tech tours.” She rarely speaks publicly and prefers to give anonymously, but she is willing to get her hands dirty rather than write cheques from a comfortable distance. After taking over, she promised not to touch the editorial side. Bradley said that line went down “very well” in the newsroom — the question everyone was asking then was whether the magazine would acquire a party line on “her issues.” At the same time she hired heavily: headcount grew by more than 100, about 30%; a paywall went up; design talent was brought in to redo the logo, create a custom typeface and simplify the layout; and she pushed the whole company to use technology more deeply. Bradley’s words at the time: The Atlantic’s core competence is not operating at the frontier of technology. Her reply: it should be. The expansion was expensive. Profits of roughly US$10 million a year when she arrived turned back into losses. Ta-Nehisi Coates and other star writers left. The conservative writer Kevin Williamson was hired and fired in quick succession, rattling the newsroom. When the pandemic hit in March 2020, subscriptions rose, yet the magazine still laid off 17% of its staff. For those who had hoped “billionaire benevolence” could shield it from the industry’s headwinds, the layoffs were a sign that the inevitable obstacles had already arrived. At the end of 2020, former Wired editor-in-chief Nick Thompson became CEO. Powell Jobs’s brief to him: dig the company out of its hole and make it a business that could support itself. He inherited a US$20 million deficit, and traffic was sliding as the pandemic eased. He immediately raised subscription prices by 50% and launched a dynamic paywall that targets readers by their likelihood to convert. Editor-in-chief Goldberg shifted the magazine away from daily news toward fewer, more deeply reported pieces. He said that Powell Jobs and the team all believed there was still a large, untapped audience willing to pay for the highest-quality journalism. By 2024 the magazine was profitable again, with more than 1 million subscribers and US$100 million in revenue, nearly two-thirds of it from subscriptions — up from less than half before. What advertising remained moved from programmatic toward events and direct brand relationships. The editorial scorecard looked just as good: three Pulitzers under Thompson, two of them won by Jennifer Senior and Caitlin Dickerson, freshly poached from the Times ; the almost headline-free October 2024 cover won ASME’s best cover of 2025; a story on then-CNN chief Chris Licht led to his resignation, and a cover story helped exonerate a wrongly convicted man. Goldberg’s words: we treat it almost as an ideology, an idealism — what we make is worth paying for. Over the same period, OpenAI turned the tech industry upside down. It started in 2015 as a non-profit backed by Musk, Thiel and Hoffman. Altman became CEO in 2018, and a capped-profit subsidiary was later added. ChatGPT launched in 2022, passed 30 million users in two months, and became one of the fastest-growing software products in history. Microsoft’s investment reached US$14 billion. Google, Meta and Amazon rushed to build the same thing. In 2023 the non-profit board tried to oust Altman and failed; a year later he dismantled the original non-profit structure. The models need enormous amounts of text. Convinced that scale buys performance directly, AI companies tested the limits of copyright and swallowed the internet whole: code from GitHub, homework from Quizlet, subtitles from YouTube, almost every English-language book, essay, poem and news story they could find. Meta executives even discussed buying Simon & Schuster purely for the data. Altman himself admitted that the usable data online would run out. One NIH-linked study found ChatGPT-4’s hallucination rate was close to 30%. In December 2023, The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft, the first major American media outlet to do so. The complaint said they had copied and used millions of the Times ’s copyrighted works without permission to train their models; in Common Crawl, a “copy of the internet,” there were 16 million unique pieces of Times content alone. GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 were estimated to have been trained on 45 TB of data, roughly a 3.7-billion-page Word document. The Times sought billions of dollars in statutory and actual damages and demanded the destruction of models and data built with its copyrighted material. OpenAI mounted a fair-use defence and said that only weeks earlier, talks with the Times about a strategic partnership had been “progressing constructively”; it also wrote that any single source like the Times does not meaningfully contribute to the training of existing models and would not have sufficient impact on future training. It called training “fair to creators, necessary for innovators, and critical for US competitiveness.” Sarah Silverman, the Authors Guild (including Franzen and Grisham) and Getty (alleging Stability AI copied more than 12 million images) sued one after another. By May 2025 there were about 40 pending copyright cases. Condé Nast’s CEO once said content must not be stolen, distorted and trafficked — he later signed a deal with OpenAI himself. Frank Pine of Alden’s newspapers put it more bluntly: they pay their engineers, they pay for servers, they have astronomical valuations, but they don’t want to pay for the content without which there is no product. That isn’t fair use, and it isn’t fair. There is no one-size-fits-all formula for fair use. Copyright law lists four factors: the purpose and character of the use (commercial or not, “transformative” or not), the nature of the work, the amount and substantiality of what is used, and the effect on the existing or potential market for the original. The Supreme Court once called the fourth “undoubtedly the single most important.” Experts are split. Stanford’s Lemley argues that models learn uncopyrightable ideas, facts and linguistic structures, not creative expression. Berkeley’s Samuelson argues courts have generally been lenient toward copying done to extract information and thereby advance the public interest. Loyola’s Hughes argues that if we accept models are “learning, training, memorising,” then that ingestion is quasi-expressive. The case law is split too. In February 2025, Delaware judge Bibas sided with the copyright holder in Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence: using the other side’s lawyer-written headnotes to train a competing research product was not transformative, and the potential market was “obvious.” A few months later, Judge Alsup granted partial summary judgment in the Anthropic case: using 7 million books was transformative — “everyone reads books and then writes new text” — but Anthropic would still have to go to trial over alleged piracy for not having bought a single legitimate copy. In September 2025 Anthropic settled for US$1.5 billion, about US$3,000 per book, split between authors and publishers. It is the largest settlement in US copyright history. The Times , for its part, maintains that ChatGPT “regurgitates” articles verbatim, so readers no longer need to visit the Times ; that Google’s AI summaries have already cut outbound clicks by more than 34%; and that chatbots have already replaced search for more than 25% of Americans. OpenAI counters that the Times manipulated prompts to coax out the original sentences, which is not how most users use it; it also says it helps journalists work more efficiently and sends readers back via links. Thompson chose a different road from the Times . He acknowledged that the big models had “obviously scraped without permission.” Then he did the maths: there is a whole range of ways to get paid, so put what the other side offers on the same scale as the cost of suing and the damages you might win, and then choose. The exact terms were not disclosed. OpenAI was signing deals at a furious pace, and industry estimates of annual fees ranged from a few million to US$50 million (Exhibit 3: News Corp US$250 million over 5 years; FT US$5–10 million a year; Axel Springer US$25–30 million over 3 years). Thompson said the magazine would not become overly dependent on AI traffic; it would keep “telling stories in the best way possible” and then “distribute like crazy.” Another line of his: if content like The Atlantic’s goes into these models, the world will be a better place. The journalists weren’t buying it. They pointed out that ChatGPT hallucinates links, invents allegations, and steers readers to aggregator pages rather than the original site; they also worried about partnering with a company that, in litigation, was demanding to see all of Times reporters’ notes — which pushes right up against the limits of journalistic ethics. Powell Jobs never spoke publicly about the deal. She kept her promise of editorial non-interference: she didn’t meddle in planned candidate endorsements, nor did she bend editorial policy to be Trump-friendly; when Goldberg was mistakenly added to a classified Signal group where the Trump administration discussed war plans, she stood by her editor. But her interest in AI is public. Emerson has invested in several AI startups and played a key role in the roughly US$6.4 billion hardware tie-up between OpenAI and Jony Ive, a long-time friend of the Jobs family — the collective took part in the US$225 million round in Ive’s company before OpenAI acquired it, and had also backed Ive’s design firm LoveFrom. The Professor's Questions What were the strengths of AMD during its rise and into the 1990s and early 2000s? What were the root causes of AMD’s struggles? If you were Lisa Su, taking over AMD in 2014, what would be your first three steps to turn around the company? My Answers Q1. What were the strengths of AMD during its rise and into the 1990s and early 2000s? AMD combined a credible alternative to Intel with real engineering strength and customer value. Its advantage changed as the company grew. A trusted second source. Customers wanted supply options. AMD could enter an established market by providing a reliable alternative. That gave it access to customers and the x86 ecosystem. [S1] Compatibility and value. Customers could use familiar software while gaining another price and performance choice. AMD64 later offered a path to 64-bit computing that protected existing software investments. [S2、S4] The ability to lead in selected technologies. Athlon and Opteron showed that AMD could develop important products of its own. This was more than a low-price position. [S3、S5] Partners that helped turn chips into usable systems. Support from computer makers and software companies mattered because customers buy a working system, not just a processor. [S5] A strong challenger identity. AMD's people-first tradition and engineering ambition could help attract commitment. I would treat this as a cultural asset, not proof that the company always executed well. [S16] My conclusion: AMD's early opportunity came from offering choice; its stronger position came from making that choice technically valuable. Q2. What were the root causes of AMD’s struggles? AMD's struggles came from a mismatch between its ambitions, its resources, and its ability to deliver competitive products consistently. External pressure made that mismatch more costly. An uneven competitive position. Intel had greater scale and strong influence over the PC ecosystem. AMD also faced disputed commercial practices; the 2009 settlement shows that market access was a real issue. But external pressure cannot explain every product and investment decision. [S2、S15] Product choices that did not serve enough customer workloads well. The FX-8150 tests showed a weakness in single-thread performance. My management inference is that a promising design idea must be tested against how customers actually use the product. [S8] Large financial commitments reduced room for error. ATI added valuable graphics capabilities, but its acquisition also used cash and debt. A strategically useful asset can still be acquired with a financial burden that is hard to carry. [S6] The cost and complexity of manufacturing. AMD had to fund design and production while competing at a smaller scale. The foundry separation reduced direct ownership of fabs, but it did not remove supplier, process or delivery risks. [S2、S7] Too much to execute with limited resources. Weak PC conditions, several product lines and a need to rebuild CPU competitiveness competed for attention and funding. My diagnosis is that AMD needed sharper priorities and more reliable execution. This is an interpretation of its business position, not a documented claim that employees were unwilling to cooperate. [S9–S12] The cycle I would worry about is: weaker products lead to pricing pressure and lost business; lower financial flexibility makes sustained investment harder; further delays then weaken customer confidence. This is a causal framework, not a claim that every link happened in every quarter. Q3. If you were Lisa Su, taking over AMD in 2014, what would be your first three steps to turn around the company? I would establish the facts and protect cash, choose a focused product path, and rebuild execution with customers and employees. These steps would overlap; I would not wait for one to finish before starting the next. First, find out what can keep the company alive and what must be protected. In the first month, I would review cash needs, debt maturities, inventory, supplier commitments and customer payments with the CFO. I would meet key customers and technical leaders to learn which promises were at risk and which capabilities were still strong. I would build a 13-week cash forecast and a longer product-funding plan. I would stop low-priority spending while protecting critical engineers and customer commitments. The cost is that some projects lose funding and some restructuring may be necessary. An equal percentage cut across every team would be a poor starting point. Second, put the best people and funding behind a few connected priorities. I would make high-performance computing the main direction, with a competitive CPU core and graphics as key capabilities. I would maintain useful semi-custom and embedded business to help support the transition, while judging each contract on cash, margin and engineering effort. I would review the CPU work already under way rather than pretend to start it from nothing. Projects outside the main direction would need clear customer evidence, a small budget and a stop rule. The cost is fewer options and greater dependence on a limited number of bets. Third, make delivery credible again. I would give each major product one accountable leader, connect engineering, sales and operations in a weekly review, and use shared milestones for performance, power, quality and delivery. I would ask people to report problems early and make it safe to challenge the plan. With key customers, I would agree on realistic validation and launch steps. With the board, I would agree on the funding and evidence needed across more than one product generation. The cost is that problems become visible and some public promises may need to be reduced. By the end of the first 90 days, I would want three things: a funded survival plan, a clear list of product priorities and cancellations, and a delivery plan owned jointly by the teams and key customers. I would judge early progress by cash visibility, talent retention, engineering milestones and customer validation—not by expecting a new chip to appear in one quarter. AMD's strength was that it offered a credible alternative to Intel, backed by real engineering. Its weakness was that it could not turn that strength into consistent product and financial performance. If I were Lisa Su in 2014, I would first understand the cash position and protect the people and projects that mattered most. Second, I would focus the roadmap on high-performance computing, while using valuable existing businesses to support the transition. Third, I would rebuild trust through clear ownership, honest reporting and realistic customer commitments. The difficult leadership choice is deciding what to stop, while keeping people committed to a plan whose results will take years to appear. Case Summary When AMD first entered the microprocessor market, it held an important position: a credible second source of supply for customers. The Computer History Museum's oral history with Intel insiders records IBM's requirement for a second supplier, and also AMD's reputation at the time as a reliable supplier. That let it enter a market that already had software, PC makers and users, without having to build all the demand on its own. [S1] In the 1990s, AMD steadily strengthened its own processor design capabilities. After the K6, the Athlon, which began shipping in 1999, became an important product; in 2000 AMD launched an Athlon that reached 1 GHz. In 2003, Opteron brought 64-bit capability to x86 servers while keeping the ability to run existing 32-bit software. This let customers keep their software investments and upgrade their systems gradually. Ecosystem partners such as IBM and Microsoft provided product or software support when Opteron launched. [S2–S5] AMD also faced bigger rivals, R&D and manufacturing businesses that required constant investment, and pressure to keep iterating its products. When it completed the ATI acquisition in 2006, the announced deal value was about US$5.4 billion, including about US$4.3 billion in cash, with a new US$2.5 billion term loan. The acquisition brought GPU, chipset and other capabilities, but also added financial and integration burdens. Afterwards, in 2009, AMD put its wafer manufacturing business into the newly formed GLOBALFOUNDRIES, gradually moving to a model that relied on outside manufacturing. [S6–S7] The difficulties on the product side did not end with the manufacturing spin-off. The Bulldozer architecture reached the market in 2011; benchmarks of the FX-8150 at the time showed its single-threaded performance was uncompetitive in some common applications and games. This is evidence about a specific product and specific test scenarios, and can't be written up as "every AMD product lagged at every task." At the same time, weakness in the consumer PC market hurt the traditional business. [S8–S10] The transformation had already begun before 2014. Jim Keller returned in 2012, reporting to CTO Mark Papermaster and leading CPU core design; Lisa Su joined AMD the same year. In 2013 Sony and Microsoft announced that their next-generation game consoles would use AMD semi-custom chips. In a 2017 interview, Lisa Su said directly that the new high-performance CPU core had been in development for about four years. So the new CPU roadmap, the team and the console business can't all be credited to the period after she became CEO in 2014. [S11–S14] On October 8, 2014, Lisa Su succeeded Rory Read. Quarterly data from around the handover show a company with divergent business performance: the traditional Computing and Graphics segment was under pressure, while the Enterprise, Embedded and Semi-Custom segment was profitable. What she had to work out was how to get cash, talent, product direction and customer commitments all supporting the same long-term path. Core Tensions Short-term survival and long-term R&D must both hold. Cash is limited, and developing a new core takes years; cutting spending evenly across the board might improve immediate outgoings but damage competitiveness in the next round. There are opportunities in several markets, but only one engineering team. CPU, GPU, consoles, embedded and other directions can't all get equal priority; focusing means giving up some potential revenue. Recognise the value left by predecessors while changing resource allocation. The manufacturing spin-off, the console customers and the CPU team already exist; the new CEO has to judge what to continue and what to scale back. The technology is worth investing in, but customers may not be willing to adopt it right away. Customers still need to validate software, quality, supply and the future roadmap; R&D and commercial trust have to be built together. A long-term direction needs patience; project management needs timely course correction. Sticking with a direction can't become an excuse for tolerating hidden problems or endless delays.

The Professor's Questions Analyze S&G’s “No Win—No Fee” business model. Does S&G’s consolidation strategy create value? Will it continue to create value as it grows? Does it make sense for growing entrepreneurial businesses to go public? What are the plusses and minuses? Should law firms and other professional service companies such as accounting firms be publicly owned? How much is S&G worth as a company? Use the financial model and assume WACC = 11%. Would you invest in this deal? My Answers Q1. Analyze S&G’s “No Win—No Fee” business model. Does S&G’s consolidation strategy create value? Will it continue to create value as it grows? S&G combines legal expertise with financing and case selection. Consolidation can create value, but only if the firm keeps its discipline as it grows. Clients can pursue valid claims without paying the legal fee upfront. S&G takes the risk of not earning a fee and pays expenses before collecting cash. In the case example, it funds A$12,750 before receiving payment. A successful case produces A$4,500 in pre-tax profit, but that profit is not available as cash during the case. Some clients may still have to repay disbursements even if they lose, so “no fee” does not always mean “no cost.” WIP makes this timing easy to miss. It reflects the expected fee, completion percentage, and probability of success. It is an accounting asset, not cash in the bank. Faster growth can raise reported revenue and profit while increasing the funding gap. Management must monitor collections, case duration, and changes in WIP estimates alongside earnings. At 11%, the worksheet values a successful case at about A$1,408 and an unsuccessful one at about minus A$8,940. Using the historical 95% success rate as a scenario gives expected NPV of about A$890. The break-even success rate is about 86.4% under those assumptions. Extending each period from six to nine months roughly halves the successful-case NPV to A$701. Good selection and timely resolution are central to the economics. These calculations assume the worksheet's cost, recovery, and tax treatment; the 95% historical rate is not a guarantee for new cases. Consolidation can improve client acquisition through a shared brand and referral network. Central systems, training, specialist knowledge, and administration can improve productivity and service consistency. A larger pool of cases can reduce some case-specific volatility, although changes in law or common defendants can affect many cases together. S&G's consumer brand also makes client relationships less dependent on an individual lawyer. The financial test is whether these benefits exceed the acquisition price, integration costs, and additional funding needs. In the supplied model, the acquisition plan adds about A$6.83 million to enterprise value compared with no further acquisitions, with other assumptions unchanged. That is positive value, but most of the company's value comes from the existing business and organic growth. The base model assumes no annual margin improvement, so its acquisition value cannot be presented as proof of realized cost synergies. I would continue selective acquisitions, with limits on price and integration capacity. As S&G expands, attractive targets may become scarcer, prices may rise, and local legal work may be harder to standardize. I would measure acquired firms by cash returns, lawyer and client retention, case outcomes, and cash collection. Revenue growth or EPS growth alone would not justify another deal. Q2. Does it make sense for growing entrepreneurial businesses to go public? What are the plusses and minuses? Should law firms and other professional service companies such as accounting firms be publicly owned? Going public makes sense when permanent outside capital supports valuable growth and the firm can accept the demands of public ownership. For S&G, I support the IPO, subject to strong professional governance. The main benefits are access to capital without a fixed repayment date, a broader investor base, liquidity for early owners, and shares that may help recruit staff or fund acquisitions. Public reporting can also improve discipline. These benefits matter for a firm that pays costs long before it collects fees. The costs include dilution, issuance and continuing compliance costs, disclosure burdens, market volatility, and pressure to produce short-term results. Liquid shares do not make the underlying cases liquid. A public valuation can also tempt management to overpay for acquisitions in order to meet growth expectations. For S&G, the alternatives had real limits: employee shareholders could not or would not supply enough capital; additional debt was risky given irregular cash flows and limited collateral; and private equity investors wanted unacceptable changes to the business model. The IPO therefore addresses a funding need. The case does not show that an IPO is the only reasonable choice for every growing firm; slower growth and more selective acquisitions remain alternatives. I would separate the company's financing from the founders' liquidity. Of the A$35 million offering, A$17.3 million goes to selling shareholders and A$2.3 million to issuance costs. The remaining A$15.4 million reduces net debt. The company does not receive a fresh A$35 million acquisition budget. The transaction improves its financing capacity, but future growth still requires a cash plan. Law and accounting firms should not be ruled out merely because they sell professional expertise. A transferable institutional brand, repeatable processes, diversified clients, and durable incentives can support outside ownership. A practice that depends almost entirely on a few partners is less suitable. However, the source of capital must not determine professional advice. S&G's stated duty order is court first, client second, then other corporate obligations and shareholders. I would protect independent case and settlement decisions, maintain clear escalation procedures, and reward quality and cash outcomes rather than short-term reported earnings alone. For audit firms, public-interest and independence duties also require their own safeguards. Listing eligibility depends on the jurisdiction; the case's Australian rules are not a statement of today's rules everywhere. Q3. How much is S&G worth as a company? Use the financial model and assume WACC = 11%. Would you invest in this deal? The supplied worksheet gives enterprise value of A$151.03 million, equity value of A$145.63 million, and A$1.35 per diluted share. At the A$1 offer price, I would make a small investment, subject to checking WIP quality and the funding plan. I use the model's 10% organic growth through FY2015, 3% thereafter, 24% EBIT margin, and 30% tax rate. It assumes A$10 million of annual acquisitions in FY2009–11 at 1.2 times revenue. NWC is 30% of revenue, and WIP equals PI revenue, or 75% of total revenue. Project litigation is excluded. Free cash flow is after-tax operating profit plus depreciation and noncash taxes, less capital expenditure, acquisition spending, and increases in NWC and WIP. Noncash taxes equal 30% of the increase in WIP. Since capex equals depreciation, those two terms offset. WIP must still be deducted; otherwise the value is materially overstated. The model discounts FY2008–16 cash flows to FY2007 year-end. The final-year FCF is A$24.89 million. Terminal value at the end of FY2016 is 24.8876 × 1.03 ÷ (11% − 3%) = A$320.43 million. The present value of forecast cash flows is A$25.76 million, and the present value of terminal value is A$125.26 million. Subtracting A$5.4 million of post-IPO net debt and dividing by 107.78 million diluted shares gives A$1.3512 per share. The model value is 35.1% above the offer price; equivalently, the offer price is 26.0% below the model value. This is a valuation gap, not a promised investment return. About 83% of enterprise value comes from the terminal value. At a 20% EBIT margin, value falls to about A$0.96 per share. A combined downside of 22% margin, 5% organic growth, and a 1.5-times acquisition multiple produces about A$0.90. The acquisition years also require financing: FY2009–11 FCF totals minus A$21.64 million. A positive DCF does not establish that the company can fund each year. I would check committed credit, collection schedules, interest and dividend plans, and management's ability to slow acquisitions. The A$5.4 million net debt figure is a valuation input, not a measure of unused borrowing capacity. My class vote is a small yes, not an unconditional endorsement of the growth story. I would need evidence that WIP turns into cash, that the forecast margin is achievable, and that professional standards survive expansion. If those checks failed, I would pass despite the A$1.35 estimate. The case does not supply enough portfolio information to choose a precise position size. Case Summary In 1935, William Slater and Hugh Gordon founded S&G in Melbourne, starting out with workers' compensation work for unions and working people. Years of representing individuals against larger institutions helped the firm build a consumer brand. As of the case date, the firm had nearly 400 staff, more than 140 lawyers and 21 offices across six states; total revenue in 2006 was about A$44.37 million. The headcount and office numbers in the text are as of the case date, while Exhibit 2's 2006 historical data show 114 professional legal staff FTE and 19 offices — the two should not be treated as the same year or the same basis. (pp.1–2; Exhibits 1–3) The firm's core business splits into personal injury litigation and non-personal-injury legal services, at about 75% and 25% of core revenue respectively. The former relies heavily on No Win—No Fee: legal fees can be charged only if the case succeeds. The firm also runs project litigation/class actions, which can bring sizeable revenue and brand impact but irregular cash collection. An ordinary personal injury case usually takes 6–24 months, with a typical legal fee of about A$15,000. (pp.2–3) While a case is under way, S&G pays for staff, offices, outside experts and so on, while recognising revenue based on the expected fee, stage of completion and probability of success, booked as a work-in-progress (WIP) asset. Exhibit 5 shows one successful case: A$4,250 spent in each of the first three periods, A$17,250 recovered in the fourth, for a final pre-tax profit of A$4,500. Book profit appears period by period, but cash keeps flowing out first. (p.3; Exhibit 5) S&G's growth comes from client acquisition and M&A. Its telephone advice line receives about 30,000 calls a year, and its brand and referral network bring in clients. Since 2002 it has acquired and integrated eight small law firms; in the most recent year it acquired four, paying A$9.3 million, expected to contribute more than A$8 million of revenue in FY2008. Personal injury law becoming more complex has put pressure on smaller firms lacking systems and expertise, creating consolidation opportunities. (pp.3–4) Growth needs capital — both to pay acquisition prices and to fund the outlays on new cases. The original shareholders could not or would not keep putting in enough capital; more debt would worsen the strain on cash flow and the shortage of collateral; and the business changes proposed by private equity investors were not accepted. As Australian rules changed at the time to allow outside ownership, S&G began planning an IPO, and its prospectus set out a clear order for handling conflicts: duty to the court first, then duty to clients, then the firm's other obligations and shareholders' interests. (pp.4–5) The offer proposes to sell 35 million shares at A$1 each, comprising about 17.3 million sold by existing shareholders and about 17.7 million new shares. After the deal, fully diluted shares are about 107.78 million and net debt about A$5.4 million. Rosen must decide whether to participate, how to assess the growth, valuation and governance risks, and how much to buy. The case text gives differing dates for the listing timetable; this analysis uses only the decision point "before the 2007 IPO" and does not depend on the specific first trading day. The Professor's Questions How does India’s past inform its future? Will India successfully reach its Viksit Bharat2047 goals? Why or why not? What is the relationship between democracy and economic growth? My Answers Q1. How does India’s past inform its future? India’s past explains both its strengths and its bottlenecks. It shapes the choices India faces, but it does not fix the outcome. India has a long history of gaining from global exchange. The case’s Golden Road connected trade, knowledge, and culture. This is a useful reminder that national strength can grow through openness. It does not prove that ancient success will return automatically. For the future, India needs access to customers, technology, capital, and ideas. Colonial rule helps explain the demand for economic autonomy. The colonial state focused on extraction and order, while broad education and health remained weak. After independence, planning and import substitution were understandable responses. But a policy can make sense at its starting point and later become a constraint. The License Raj protected firms and made entry and expansion difficult. Early investments created strong capabilities, but they reached too few people. Elite engineering schools and research institutes helped build technical talent. The separation of research from universities and industry limited its spread. In the rural learning survey cited in the case, only 48.7% of fifth-grade children could read a second-grade text in 2024. The next stage requires better basic learning and stronger links between research and everyday production. 1991 shows that policy change can alter the growth path. A foreign exchange crisis opened the way to trade, investment, and industrial reforms. Services then expanded, but many workers could not enter skilled jobs. India should retain global openness while making it easier for workers and smaller firms to move into more productive activities. It should not need another crisis to reform. Democracy and digital infrastructure are cumulative assets. India adopted universal suffrage before becoming rich. The 1977 election corrected a period of concentrated power. Digital identity began before the change of government in 2014, and later governments built on it. Long-term development depends on institutions that can learn and on public systems that survive changes in political leadership. My conclusion is that India should preserve openness, technical talent, and democratic participation, while changing the parts of the state that still control activity better than they deliver services. History is a guide to reform, not a reason to treat today’s problems as inevitable. Q2. Will India successfully reach its Viksit Bharat2047 goals? Why or why not? If I must vote today, I would vote no on full achievement by 2047 under the current path. I expect substantial progress, but the complete promise requires a faster and broader change in productive capacity. First, I would separate the goals. A $30 trillion economy, high-income status, and universal quality services are different tests. High-income classification uses GNI per person and the World Bank’s Atlas method. It is not based on total GDP. Even passing an income threshold does not establish that every family has good healthcare, schooling, and a secure livelihood. [S2] The arithmetic is demanding. Moving from $4 trillion in 2025 to $30 trillion in 2047 requires about 9.59% annual growth in nominal US-dollar GDP . This is not the same as real GDP growth. Domestic inflation and the exchange rate matter. The case’s statement that growth must be at least 9% does not fully specify the price and currency assumptions. Separately, the World Bank’s 2025 high-income scenario requires about 7.8% average real growth . These figures should not be treated as competing forecasts. [S1] There are strong reasons for optimism. India has a large domestic market, technical talent, a global diaspora, and proven digital public infrastructure. The case reports that e-KYC cut customer onboarding costs from about $15 to $0.25. Services also earn foreign exchange: the 2024 services surplus of $178 billion partly offset the goods deficit of $280 billion. Better infrastructure and firms’ search for additional production locations could support new investment. These are opportunities, not guaranteed orders or jobs. The main obstacles are connected: Jobs and skills: Informal employment was 88.3% in 2024. The rural fifth-grade reading result was 48.7%. More people of working age will not create a dividend unless firms can employ them productively. Participation: Female labor force participation was 32.4% in the case’s 2024 series. Safe transport, childcare, health, and workplace access can expand opportunity as well as output. The growth model: High-skill services cannot employ everyone. AI may increase productivity while reducing some entry-level tasks. Manufacturing can help, but advanced factories also need skills and may create fewer jobs than expected. India needs productive services, labor-absorbing manufacturing, and better agriculture together. Execution and innovation: A digital transfer cannot supply a missing doctor or teacher. Low R&D spending and weak research–industry links limit technology diffusion. Implementation also depends on states and local institutions. Fiscal, social, and climate pressures: Public debt in Exhibit 6 is about 81.64% of GDP. Heat, water stress, exclusion, and policy uncertainty can reduce returns on investment and make reform harder to sustain. I would prioritize basic learning and primary health; remove practical barriers to labor-intensive exports and growing small firms; make women’s participation easier; and link research and training to employers. I would fund climate resilience as part of development. I would judge industrial support by productivity, exports, and durable jobs, with a clear end to support that does not work. The cost is real: less room for permanent subsidies and prestige projects, disruption for protected firms, and visible results that may take longer than an election cycle. I would manage that cost through transition support, transparent measures, and phased state-level implementation. I would become more optimistic if learning, real earnings, productive employment, private investment, and local service quality improved together over several years. A high GDP growth number alone would not change my vote. Q3. What is the relationship between democracy and economic growth? Democracy can support long-term growth, but it is neither a sufficient condition nor a requirement for every period of rapid growth. State capacity and political accountability matter together. Democracy and state capacity are different. Elections decide who governs and allow people to remove leaders. Capacity determines whether the state can teach children, deliver health services, enforce contracts, and carry out policy. A democracy can have weak delivery. A non-democratic state can have strong delivery in some areas. Neither observation settles the long-term comparison. Democracy can help growth through several channels. Public debate reveals failures. Political competition gives governments a reason to serve a wider population. Courts, scrutiny, and predictable procedures can limit arbitrary decisions. Peaceful changes of power make it possible to correct policies without destroying the political system. These channels work only if the institutions function in practice. It also has costs and failure modes. Elections can encourage short-term giveaways. Organized interests can block reform. Majority rule can exclude minorities. Federal bargaining may delay projects. But removing checks can also increase policy mistakes, favoritism, and the time needed to reverse a bad decision. Faster decision-making is valuable only when the decisions and implementation are good. India offers useful evidence, but not a controlled experiment. It grew slowly under democracy before 1991 and faster after reforms while retaining elections. This suggests that policy and institutions matter beyond the label. The 1977 election reversed an abuse of concentrated power. The 2004 election showed that strong headline growth did not satisfy enough voters. Neither episode proves a precise effect on GDP, but each shows a channel for correction and inclusion. A useful external study by Acemoglu, Naidu, Restrepo, and Robinson estimates that democratization raises long-run GDP per person by about 20% relative to its counterfactual. This is a cross-country estimate of the income level, not annual growth, and not a promise for India. It offers evidence against the simple claim that democracy necessarily obstructs development; the size and application of the effect still depend on research assumptions and context. [S3] The relationship also runs the other way. Growth changes education, tax capacity, expectations, and demands for accountability. It can also strengthen incumbent power or patronage, so growth does not automatically produce democracy. For India, I would strengthen delivery and preserve correction at the same time. Rights and political voice also have value beyond their effect on GDP. Case Summary The case opens with a scene from everyday life: in the Delhi heat of 2025, a white-collar worker with a fever can order food delivery, see a doctor remotely and have medicine brought to the door; a delivery worker who is just as sick finds the public clinic closed. This is the author's opening device for presenting India's development gap: digital services are already quite advanced, but stable jobs, basic healthcare and a decent life still don't reach most people. (p.1) The case then takes us back to ancient times. India was once connected to the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia and China through monsoon trade, commercial networks, the spread of religion and the exchange of knowledge. After the Mughal Empire, the East India Company gradually turned from a trading participant into a tax collector and ruler, and the British colonial government then put taxation, order and resource extraction at the center of the administrative system. The case stresses that this period left behind damaged industries, inadequate basic education and public health, and an elite bureaucracy. Both ancient prosperity and colonial trauma later became important historical resources for how India understands its national identity and economic self-reliance. (pp.2–5) Independence in 1947 came with Partition, mass migration and violence. The new state had to integrate the former British provinces and the princely states, and build a shared political order across religious, linguistic and caste differences. The 1950 constitution established a democratic republic; the first general election faced 176 million eligible voters, nearly 85% of them illiterate. India chose to establish universal political rights first, while keeping and reshaping the colonial administrative skeleton. The union and the states share power, with development tasks such as education, agriculture and health assigned to different levels. (pp.5–7; Exhibits 3–5) The post-independence government drove industrialization through planning, state-owned enterprises and import substitution, and also carried out land reform and the Green Revolution and set up research institutions and elite engineering education. The licensing system, meanwhile, subjected investment, output and expansion to approvals. Food security and technical capability grew, but competition among firms was constrained, links between research, university teaching and industrial application were weak, and grassroots education and healthcare remained inadequate for a long time. From 1970, Operation Flood connected smallholder farmers to urban markets through dairy cooperatives. The 1975–1977 Emergency suspended civil liberties; when elections resumed, voters threw out the ruling party. (pp.7–9) By 1991, foreign debt, an oil price shock and financing difficulties had produced a balance-of-payments crisis, with foreign exchange reserves enough to cover only a few weeks of imports. Prime Minister Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh pushed through a rupee devaluation, opened up trade and foreign investment, and dismantled most industrial licensing restrictions. Afterwards, software and business process outsourcing grew rapidly on the back of global demand, and financial services and private companies expanded. But agricultural workers didn't necessarily have the language and technical skills needed to enter high-skilled services, and many moved into low-productivity informal work. The government also faced new capability requirements as it shifted from running businesses to regulating markets. (pp.9–11) After the 2004 election, the Congress-led coalition government continued market reforms while expanding employment, education and health protections. The digital identity system Aadhaar launched in 2010, and in 2013 e-KYC lowered the cost of identity verification. After the BJP came to power in 2014, Jan Dhan bank accounts, mobile communications and UPI instant payments were further linked together, and digital infrastructure expanded into education, vaccination, health records, microcredit and e-commerce. The pandemic exposed the vulnerability of informal workers and public health on the one hand, and demonstrated the ability of digital systems to organize delivery at scale on the other. (pp.11–13; Exhibit 15) The case ends by returning to Viksit Bharat 2047: becoming a developed, high-income country by the centenary of independence, with a vision of a US$30 trillion economy, manufacturing and exports, green growth and high-quality public services. At the same time, informal employment, weak foundational learning, low female participation, low R&D spending, political and social polarization, extreme heat and water stress all remain. Generative AI is also beginning to change the outsourced service jobs that once helped India grow. The case stops at a choice of development path: how to expand high-productivity employment so that technological strengths, state capacity and social inclusion reinforce one another.
