The Professor's Questions (The following are the key points of the questions as recorded in my notes, not the professor's original wording.) Does GeBBS in 2017 have an attractive and viable business model? What changes did Thakor implement to address the key critiques of the investment bankers following the 2012 “beauty contest”? Do you think such changes were successful? Why or why not? Regimental Technologies and ChrysCapital valued GeBBS at $150 million and $145 million, respectively. Do you think these were fair valuations? Why or why not? What should Thakor do: Sell 100% of GeBBS to Regimental Technologies? Sell 80% of GeBBS to ChrysCapital? Reject both offers and continue growing the company with the existing management team? My Answers Q1. Does GeBBS in 2017 have an attractive and viable business model? Yes. By 2017, GeBBS had an attractive, viable healthcare services model with growing technology support. Its moat was improving, but it was not a pure software business. It solved an expensive, recurring problem. U.S. providers had to code care correctly, submit claims, appeal denials and collect cash. GeBBS combined healthcare knowledge with lower-cost delivery. A billing error could delay revenue, so accuracy and reliability mattered as well as price. FlexSource let a client start with U.S. delivery and move work offshore when comfortable. (pp.3–6) The model had demonstrated demand and profits. FY2017 revenue was $35.3m, up 36.1%. Adjusted EBITDA was $5.755m, a 16.3% margin. Direct revenue reached $14.1m, or 39.9% of revenue. These are actual results available for judging 2017. FY2018 revenue of $49.3m is later evidence, not information I would assume was known in 2017. (Exhibits 5, 11b) It had a credible way to expand. A small initial contract could lead to more services for the same customer. iCode helped automate workflows and make data useful. Direct relationships with major hospitals improved access to customer needs. MG and the expanded team made delivery less dependent on Nitin alone. (pp.7–9) The risks were still material. Channel revenue was 60.1% of FY2017 revenue. Selling directly could conflict with those channel partners. Large customers could switch, bring work in-house or use another provider. Privacy, service quality, wage costs and dollar–rupee exchange rates mattered. Software helped the service; the case does not establish high-margin recurring software subscriptions. (pp.8, 10; Exhibit 5) I would verify the unit economics before paying for a strong moat. I would ask for customer retention, concentration, contract terms, gross margin by client and service, coding error rates, sales payback and cash collection. The case does not supply enough evidence to claim low churn, predictable subscription revenue or an unbreakable moat. Classroom line: “I like the business in 2017. It solves a costly problem and already makes money. But I would value it as a technology-enabled service company, with a moat it still has to prove.” Q2. What changes did Thakor implement to address the key critiques of the investment bankers following the 2012 “beauty contest”? Do you think such changes were successful? Why or why not? The changes were largely successful. Thakor used the five critiques as an operating plan, and accepted lower short-term earnings to improve the business. The strongest evidence is better revenue mix and a stronger team, not just a higher sale price. Bankers’ critique Change Evidence and remaining limit Weak management team Used Korn Ferry; hired MG in late 2013, Stein in 2017, and stronger sales, HIM and operating leaders More experienced people owned delivery, sales and new products. The later bids specifically praised the management team. Succession was still important. Little differentiated technology / IP Invested in iCode; required customers to work with the company during software development Technology improved workflows, visibility and decision support. The case does not isolate software revenue or measure how hard competitors would find it to copy. No marquee direct clients Won major hospital systems and expanded direct selling Direct revenue rose from $7.1m in FY2015 to $28.8m in FY2018. Direct share rose from 31.5% to 58.3%. Commodity labor arbitrage Added more complex services, cross-selling, patient contact and payer solutions By FY2018, revenue included RCM 45%, HIM 41%, patient contact 7% and payer solutions 7%. The company remained people-intensive. Too dependent on Thakor Delegated real operating authority to MG; used Vision 2020 and a broader leadership team Thakor stopped managing every detail of India operations. Both final buyers still wanted Thakor and MG involved, so key-person dependence was reduced, not eliminated. The financial evidence supports the change. Revenue rose from $11.6m in 2012 to $49.3m in FY2018. Adjusted EBITDA rose from $5.755m in FY2017 to $10.760m in FY2018, about 87%. In FY2018, direct revenue grew about 104%, while channel revenue declined 3.1%. This was a meaningful change in where growth came from. (pp.6–10; Exhibits 5, 6, 11b) There are three limits to my conclusion. First, the later $145–150m headline offers also reflect a larger business and an active M&A market; I would not attribute the whole increase from the 2012 $30m indication to management improvements. Second, gross margin was still below the case’s healthcare IT benchmark, and some buyers questioned revenue per employee. Third, customers and cash collection remained risks. FY2018 pre-tax cash flow was only $4.8m after working-capital investment and capital expenditure, against about $10.8m adjusted EBITDA. (pp.9–10; Exhibit 11c) Classroom line: “He made the company less dependent on cheap labor, intermediaries and himself. That is why I call the changes successful. But the transition was incomplete.” Q3. Regimental Technologies and ChrysCapital valued GeBBS at $150 million and $145 million, respectively. Do you think these were fair valuations? Why or why not? Both were defensible headline enterprise values. I would treat them as a reasonable negotiating range, not as two equally certain cash prices or a precise measure of intrinsic value. First, use consistent earnings. The table below uses the precise FY2018 adjusted EBITDA from Exhibit 11b and the newer figures in Exhibit 12. All calculations are EV / EBITDA; they are not P/E ratios. EBITDA denominator Regimental $150m ChrysCapital $145m FY2018 actual adjusted EBITDA $10.760m 13.94× 13.48× LTM June 2018 adjusted EBITDA $12.1m 12.40× 11.98× Fully ramped adjusted EBITDA $14.7m 10.20× 9.86× FY2019 forecast adjusted EBITDA $13.638m 11.00× 10.63× The latest actual LTM figure is my starting point. Fully ramped earnings require execution, and forecast earnings are not already earned. GeBBS’ growth, direct clients and technology can support a premium to the case’s broad 2018 North American M&A median of 9.7×. But that broad median is only a rough reference. (Exhibits 8, 11b, 12) Second, public peers give a noisy check. Exhibit 10 implies EV/EBITDA multiples of 54.6×, 39.9×, 23.9×, 55.8× and 13.9× for its five peers. Weak EBITDA can produce a very high multiple. The businesses differ in scale, software mix and profitability; two have net losses. I would not apply the simple average to GeBBS. Also, the exhibit is dated December 31, 2018, after the November decision. It is a classroom reference supplied by the case, not a quotation known on the decision date. Third, cash flow supports a range rather than an exact number. Exhibit 11c provides pre-tax cash flow. It is not ready-to-use after-tax free cash flow. The illustrative DCF below uses the supplied annual forecast, a 12% tax assumption and no depreciation tax shield because the case does not provide a complete D&A schedule. At a 15% discount rate and 3% terminal growth rate, the FY2018 year-end benchmark is about $139.6m. Holding terminal growth at 3%, the value ranges from $108.6m at 18% to $191.9m at 12%. About 73.6% of the base value comes from the terminal value. These assumed rates test the price; they do not prove it. The benchmark is not a precise November 2018 valuation. Fourth, compare the actual deal economics. Regimental offers $120m at closing plus a conditional $30m. With full payment assumed, a 12% illustrative discount rate and year-end timing, the headline $150m has a present value of about $144.71m before escrow, costs and tax. If expected payments were half of each earn-out amount, it would be about $132.36m. The probabilities and rate are assumptions, and the contract’s catch-up provision makes actual timing more complicated. ChrysCapital’s $145m is the value of the whole business. Selling 80% does not produce $145m of seller cash. In a simplified cash-free/debt-free bridge, before working-capital adjustments, incentive dilution, escrow, fees and tax, the 80% sale is $116m and the 20% retained interest is marked at $29m. Retained equity is risky and illiquid. Acquisition financing must be analyzed separately from existing target debt. My judgment: the competitive process and the business improvement make both offers credible. Regimental’s higher headline does not establish a better offer. I would negotiate the consideration, governance and funding details rather than reject both simply because a favorable forecast produces a higher DCF. Q4. What should Thakor do: Sell 100% of GeBBS to Regimental Technologies? Sell 80% of GeBBS to ChrysCapital? Reject both offers and continue growing the company with the existing management team? I would choose ChrysCapital’s 80% acquisition as the preferred path and grant exclusivity after agreeing the main funding and governance terms. This is a choice to sell control while retaining a smaller economic stake. The choice fits four needs. First, it lets the family realize much of its concentrated wealth. Second, it keeps exposure to future growth through a minority stake. Third, ChrysCapital offers sector knowledge, an operating partner, healthcare relationships and experience scaling companies toward the revenue level GeBBS wants. MG has worked successfully with the firm before. Fourth, the structure offers a route to meet management’s liquidity and incentive needs. None of these benefits guarantees future returns. (pp.7, 12–13) Regimental is a credible alternative. It has a large balance sheet, a respected name, acquisition capacity and possible cross-selling benefits. But the $30m earn-out depends on performance after control has shifted. Both executives would have three-year employment commitments. This is not a clean, immediate retirement. The negotiation over earn-out timing is useful evidence of how difficult future decisions could become, without proving the buyer would behave badly. I would not choose continued independence as the base case. It preserves control and all upside, but leaves the family’s concentration, management liquidity, founder fatigue and funding constraints unresolved. Growing from $100m to $300m needs more than repeating the earlier operating model. A future sale also depends on the market, not just the company’s earnings. Independence remains the fallback if the final terms destroy the benefits of the PE option. The cost of my choice is real: ChrysCapital would hold four of seven board seats. Thakor’s two seats and chairman title do not preserve control. The retained interest is illiquid and can be affected by leverage, future dilution and exit timing. A warmer negotiation does not replace written rights. Before signing, I would settle: Funding and distributions: reconcile the “debt-free” narrative with the $35m debt in Exhibit 12; identify the borrower, guarantees, dividend obligations, covenants and limits on later acquisition debt. Operating authority: put budgets, senior hiring and removal, acquisitions and material strategy changes into a clear decision framework. Define ordinary management authority and the matters requiring board or minority consent. Minority economics: document incentive-pool dilution, new share issues, related-party transactions, information rights and how retained shares rank economically. Clarify the NWC peg and the EV-to-equity bridge. Exit and commitments: agree tag-along and drag-along terms, liquidity routes, lockups and management vesting. Confirm the time commitment and succession plan for both Thakor and MG. These are proposed negotiation points, not rights the case says the family already has. Classroom vote: “I would sell 80% to ChrysCapital. It gives the family liquidity and brings useful capabilities for the next stage. But I would be clear that I am selling control, and I would protect the remaining stake through the agreement.” Case Summary Nitin Thakor's father, Vijay Singh, had founded a computer monitor company, which closed after India's economic environment changed. Thakor then returned to the US and in 1997 founded GeBBS Consulting from his home, outsourcing American software development work to India. By 2000 the company's revenue reached $20m, but after the tech bubble burst its main clients cut back. By 2003 he had cut costs and restored profitability, handed day-to-day management to the team, and started looking for his next venture. (Case text pp.4–5) From that earlier experience, Thakor concluded: with no client focus, no differentiated intellectual property and competing mainly on low price, it was hard to retain talent and clients. He spent about $100,000 exploring opportunities and chose US healthcare back-office services. In 2005 he and his father founded GeBBS Healthcare. With limited capital and brand at first, they began as subcontractors to US medical billing companies before developing direct hospital clients. Professionals in India handled medical coding and billing, while the US team could serve clients unwilling to offshore work; once clients built trust, they could choose whether to move delivery offshore. (Case text p.5) The business expanded from RCM (revenue cycle management) into HIM (health information management), and gradually came to cover patient engagement and services for government healthcare payers. FlexSource let clients choose the technology, workflow and delivery location; Land and Expand meant entering through one service a client was willing to buy, then cross-selling more. (Case text pp.5–8; Exhibit 6) In 2010, with revenue of $8m and EBITDA of $2.8m, an Indian BPO company made a $20m acquisition offer, but the deal fell through at the last stage. In 2012 revenue rose to $11.6m, with more than 1,000 employees. Thakor invited investment banks to pitch for a sale mandate; the "beauty contest" refers to banks competing to be hired, not buyers bidding. The bankers pointed to problems in five areas — the management team, differentiated technology, marquee direct clients, the value-add of the services, and dependence on the founder — and thought it might only sell for about $30m. (Case text pp.6–7) The family decided to keep investing and accept short-term pressure on profits. At the end of 2013, MG joined to run Indian operations and professionalize the organization. Thakor promised him real room to run the business and to deliver on his equity within about five years. The company strengthened its sales, HIM and operations teams, drew up Vision 2020, developed iCode with client participation in its design, and landed well-known hospital system clients. In 2017 Gabe Stein joined and drove sales and the payer business. FY2017 revenue was $35.3m, reaching $49.3m in FY2018, with direct sales becoming a major source of growth. (Case text pp.7–9; Exhibits 5, 11a) From 2017 the company revisited a sale and hired Houlihan Lokey. In May 2018 it launched a broad outreach covering 185 potential buyers; 119 requested confidential materials, 17 submitted preliminary indications of interest, it narrowed to four in July and two remained in November. Regimental offered an outright sale; ChrysCapital offered a PE deal acquiring up to 80%. The company was seeking the capabilities and capital needed to get to $300m in revenue; the family wanted to reduce its wealth concentration, and Thakor had borne thirteen years of continuous operating pressure. The case stops at the decision point: which party to grant exclusivity to, or whether to walk away from both offers. A Marshall Plan for Africa: Equity Group

The Professor's Questions (What follows are the key points of the questions as recorded in my notes, not the professor's original wording.) How effective has the Kenyan government been since independence in reducing poverty? What past and present circumstances have shaped the country’s conditions, and the government’s policies? What role has Equity Bank played in reducing poverty in Kenya? Why has Mwangi been so successful? Is the Africa Recovery and Resilience Plan a good idea or a bad idea? For whom? My Answers Q1. How effective has the Kenyan government been since independence in reducing poverty? What past and present circumstances have shaped the country’s conditions, and the government’s policies? The record is mixed: early growth did not reach enough people, poverty worsened under Moi, and later progress remained incomplete. I would judge the government by living standards, access to services and opportunity, not GDP growth alone. The starting point was unequal. Independence in 1963 did not remove the colonial pattern of unequal access to land, work and resources. Kenyatta supported private enterprise and GDP grew by roughly 5%–8% a year. Yet population growth was about 3.8%–4%, and gains were concentrated. By the later Kenyatta years, the poorest 40% of households received only about 9% of income, while the richest 10% received nearly half. Growth and broad poverty reduction were different tasks. (p.3) Political incentives weakened distribution and accountability. Ethnic patronage and concentrated power shaped who received opportunities. Under Moi, repression and corruption combined with higher oil prices and lower agricultural prices. The case reports poverty rising from 45% in 1992 to 57% in 2000. Cold War alliances had supported the state; after the Cold War, aid conditions became a stronger constraint. Donors suspended US$250 million in 1991. The government faced both domestic political incentives and external financial pressure. (pp.3–4) There were real public contributions. Education received nearly two-thirds of social-sector public spending. Mwangi himself benefited from government scholarships. After 2002, Kibaki supported universal primary education, privatization and some deregulation. Later, regulators permitted agency and mobile banking, while courts helped settle entry disputes. These actions enabled private innovation, even though corruption and uneven public capacity persisted. (pp.3, 7–10) The later improvement was meaningful but fragile. The case reports poverty falling from 45.2% in 2009 to 34.3% in 2021, a decline of 10.9 percentage points. This is not evidence that government alone caused the decline. Banks, mobile money providers, households, donors and public policy all mattered. Election-related insecurity and COVID-19 exposed how easily incomes and essential supplies could be disrupted. (pp.9, 11–12) The policy challenge changed. Basic services remained necessary, but people also needed affordable savings, payments, productive credit and routes to markets. By 2022, the state needed to improve public delivery and coordinate private capacity. It should preserve fair competition and customer protection while addressing infrastructure and cross-border barriers. It could not hand its responsibility for inclusion to one bank. Classroom line: “Kenya did achieve growth and later poverty reduction, but its institutions did not consistently turn national progress into broad access to opportunity.” Q2. What role has Equity Bank played in reducing poverty in Kenya? Equity made it cheaper and easier for ordinary people to participate in the economy, then added services that helped them use that access. Its contribution is broader than lending, although the case cannot measure its exact share of Kenya’s poverty reduction. It removed barriers to everyday money management. Minimum balances, high charges, withdrawal restrictions and intimidating treatment made banking unsuitable for people with small, irregular incomes. Equity removed key barriers and taught customers how banking worked. Safe savings and accessible payments could help households manage school fees, business purchases and emergencies. This matters before a person borrows. (pp.5–7) It used savings to support more informed lending. The model described in the case waited for six months of savings history before providing credit. That history helped the bank learn about a customer while the customer built a buffer. Loans could then support productive activity. But this also has a limit: the poorest people may be unable to save consistently and may need grants, social protection or basic services first. (p.8; final point is my inference) It lowered the cost of reaching customers. Automation reduced transaction time from about 30 minutes to 5. Agency and mobile banking reduced dependence on expensive branches and long trips. By 2021 the group had 61,061 agents and 16.2 million customers across six countries. These are group figures, not the number of Kenyans lifted out of poverty. (p.8; Exhibit 5) It addressed constraints that credit alone could not solve. EGF used the bank’s network for education, healthcare, enterprise training, agriculture and social protection. Exhibit 8 reports 47,009 scholarships, 391,887 MSMEs trained and more than 1.12 million cumulative patient visits. These are reported outputs. They are consistent with a broader approach to development, but are not independent proof of lasting income gains. (pp.23–24) It strengthened resilience and changed the market. During COVID, loan relief and access to development finance helped the bank support customers through disruption. Its commercial success also challenged the belief that low-income customers could not be served profitably. Other banks, mobile money providers and regulators remained essential parts of this change. (pp.9–12) My test would be whether clients have more stable income, stronger businesses, fewer harmful debt burdens and more choice. The 2021 FinAccess survey distinguishes formal financial access from bank usage; neither measure alone establishes poverty reduction. We need household outcomes and a credible comparison group. Classroom line: “Equity widened economic participation through savings, payments, credit and capability building. Access was the mechanism; better lives are the result we still need to verify.” Q3. Why has Mwangi been so successful? Mwangi combined first-hand customer knowledge with a workable business model, a capable team and access to outside resources. His purpose helped him see the market; execution made that purpose sustainable. He understood a neglected customer. His mother’s experience showed him that poor households already saved and managed money carefully. The problem was that formal products did not fit their lives. He designed around small balances, frequent transactions and personal dignity. (pp.5–7) He translated that insight into economics. A high-volume, low-margin model needed low costs, trust and repeated use. Savings-led relationships supplied information and deposits; automation and agents made small transactions more practical. A reduction from 30 to 5 minutes mattered because the model had to work for many people. (pp.6–9) He attracted people with different skills. Warui helped build customer relationships and education. Wamae handled legal and organizational barriers to becoming a bank. Africap, private investors and Helios supplied capital for successive stages. Helios’s US$178.7 million investment made expansion more credible than purpose alone could. (pp.7–9) He adapted while keeping a clear customer focus. Equity moved from competing with mattresses to banks, telcos, fintech and big tech. It worked with Safaricom, competed when interests diverged, and later cooperated again. It also diversified its actual operations across countries when political risk became more visible. (pp.7–10) He built trust through costly actions. His early pay cut and personal investment made his commitment visible. Customer education, staff development and crisis support reinforced that commitment over time. The foundation then gave partners an existing delivery system rather than just a fundraising story. (pp.6–12) His success also depended on public education, regulatory openings, mobile infrastructure and available partners. It was not a one-person achievement. He described political neutrality as a way to avoid dividing the customer base, while still working with public institutions. That distinction becomes harder to maintain as the bank takes on public functions. The next risk is that confidence in the founder substitutes for independent review. The board must test the new plan’s assumptions, build successors and allow staff to challenge the CEO. Classroom line: “His strength was turning empathy into a repeatable operating model. His next test is whether the institution can question and outlast him.” Q4. Is the Africa Recovery and Resilience Plan a good idea or a bad idea? For whom? I would vote yes to a phased, jointly governed plan. I would not approve its full scale on the evidence in the case. Equity should lead financing and coordination where it has proven strengths, while sharing execution and risk with capable partners. Why the idea is strong. Small firms often face several problems at once: finance, skills, inputs, logistics and customers. Lending alone may leave the other constraints untouched. The plan connects these parts across regional markets. Equity already has bank distribution, business relationships and a foundation that implements programs. Its response to PPE shortages provided a useful example of organizing local production. This is a plausible extension of its mission, but the example does not prove it can coordinate every industry. (pp.11–12; Exhibit 9) Why scale is the concern. Exhibit 9 targets 100 million online customers by 2025, compared with 16.2 million group customers in 2021. If the definitions and dates were aligned, that would mean about 6.17 times the base, or 57.6% annual growth over four years. The target of 25 million direct jobs across 5 million borrowing businesses implies an average of five direct jobs per business. We still need timing, job quality, survival and attribution assumptions. Neither a signed MOU nor a large lending target supplies that evidence. The Marshall Plan analogy has limits. The original program was established through US legislation in 1948 and funded through congressional appropriations. Equity's proposal is a bank-led financing and partnership framework. The shared idea is coordinated recovery; public authority, funding and responsibility for losses are different. A powerful name cannot turn repayable loans into public grants or confer a public mandate on a private institution. (Historical context: US National Archives ; comparison is my analysis.) For whom? Agriculture linked to processing and logistics is a reasonable starting candidate, subject to local demand and risk checks. Let specialist operators run factories and health facilities. Separate funding commitments from cash disbursed; identify currency, tenor and loss-sharing. Use grants for noncommercial needs and appropriately structured finance for repayable investments. Match long-lived projects with long-term funding. Do not assume excess liquidity is loss-absorbing capital. Give the board independent risk review and explicit stop/go authority. Set country, sector and borrower concentration limits; examine how drought, devaluation or trade disruption could affect several exposures together. Protect depositors and maintain capital and liquidity buffers. The case’s roughly 17.71% capital-to-risk-weighted-assets ratio does not establish unlimited capacity. Publish partner roles, procurement rules, conflicts of interest and community complaint channels. Keep services accessible beyond the bank’s own borrowers. Public partners should set and supervise public priorities rather than simply endorse the CEO’s choices. Scale only when both commercial and social evidence supports it: repayment and arrears, business survival, household income stability, net new jobs and distribution of benefits. Verify outcomes independently and avoid counting existing jobs or the same job twice. Revise the target if the evidence is weaker than the promise. The cost of my vote: slower expansion, more coordination expense, less short-term control and potentially lower returns. Some people would wait longer for service. But a stable bank and a credible partnership are more useful than a fast launch followed by retrenchment. If not Equity, who? Governments, EAC, development institutions, other banks and local businesses could form the coalition. Equity has a strong claim to be a lead participant because it already has delivery capacity. That does not make it the sole legitimate architect or justify an exclusive mandate. Classroom line: “The plan is a good idea if Equity expands opportunity and shares accountability. It becomes a bad idea if one bank’s balance sheet and one leader’s judgment carry the region’s development promise.” Case Summary When Kenya won independence in 1963, the inequalities in land, employment and resource distribution formed under colonial rule remained in place. The Kenyatta government pursued pro-market policies, the overall economy grew fairly quickly, and the state invested in education; but rapid population growth, concentrated incomes and ethnic politics meant many households did not share in the gains. After Moi took over in 1978, political repression, corruption and price shocks in oil and agricultural commodities deepened the hardship. The poverty rate cited in the case rose from 45% in 1992 to 57% in 2000. James Mwangi was born in rural Kenya in 1962. His father died during the independence struggle, and his mother raised seven children on her own. As a boy he sold firewood and vegetables, kept studying on scholarships, went on to study business, qualified as an accountant, and became a senior executive at Trade Bank. His mother hid her small savings under the mattress, and even put them in a tin can buried beside a banana tree — an experience that became his starting point for understanding financial exclusion. In 1993, Peter Munga, founder of Equity Building Society, invited him to join. The central bank had deemed the institution technically insolvent; non-performing loans made up 56% of its book, and only about 12,000 customers remained. Mwangi took a 94% pay cut and mortgaged his own house again to inject capital. Drawing on the experience of Indonesia's BRI and Bangladesh's BRAC and Grameen, he chose an integrated financial model driven by individual savings, scrapped barriers such as minimum balances, trained staff, and went into rural markets to teach people about banking and saving. As customers grew, funding, technology and licensing became the new constraints. Equity replenished its capital through customer shareholdings, an investment from Africap and private placements, and automated transactions, cutting processing time from about 30 minutes to 5. Mary Wangari Wamae helped handle legal and compliance requirements; the institution converted into a commercial bank in 2004, listed in 2006, and in 2007 received an investment of about US$178.7 million from Helios. Its lending model required customers first to show a savings record of about six months before receiving corresponding credit. Equity then expanded through agent outlets, basic mobile banking and digital systems. Its relationship with Safaricom went through cooperation, conflict over who owned the customer, competition and renewed cooperation; in 2014 Equity obtained a mobile virtual network operator license and partnered with Airtel to launch Equitel. Electoral violence in Kenya also prompted the group to extend its operating assets into other countries. By 2021 the group operated in six countries, with 16.2 million customers, 337 branches and 61,061 agent outlets. Equity Group Foundation (EGF) was founded in 2006 and uses the bank's network to deliver programs in education, health, entrepreneurship, agriculture, the environment and social protection. It uses a commercial network to deliver social programs, while the bank in turn benefits from customers' improved capabilities and more stable lives. During the pandemic, Equity offered loan relief and secured liquidity through development finance institutions. In organizing local production of personal protective equipment, Mwangi saw further possibilities for collaboration across business, government and social institutions. In 2022, Equity launched the Africa Recovery and Resilience Plan, and in July signed a memorandum of understanding with the East African Community (EAC). The plan links six pillars — agriculture and extractives, manufacturing and logistics, trade and investment, MSMEs, social and environmental, and technology — and sets out a US$6 billion financing framework, with targets of 100 million online customers, 5 million borrowing businesses, 25 million borrowing consumers and 50 million direct and indirect jobs. The story stops at a new capability frontier: can the bank's existing financial and social delivery network take on the coordination, risk management and public accountability of a cross-border development plan? Unspeakable: The Taboo Topics We Avoid

The Professor's Questions Read the HBS note "Note on Difficult Conversations in the Family Enterprise," and the introductory chapter of Unspeakable (PDF attached). Before our session, think of one conversation you've been avoiding with a colleague, a family member, a business partner, or a successor. Write down who it's with, why you haven't had it yet, and what waiting is costing you Case Summary In the introduction to Unspeakable , Luis Garcia founded a successful dry-cleaning business, yet for years was unwilling to talk about money, succession or death. The arrangements he made twenty years earlier had their reasons at the time: his elder daughter lived locally and was well placed to take over the business; his son was just starting a career in education and needed help with housing; his younger daughter's finances were unstable and called for the restrictions of a trust. Over the next twenty years, the elder daughter and the son moved out of state, while the younger daughter stayed in the business and looked after her father — but the arrangements were never updated, nor discussed with the children. The documents revealed after the funeral took all three children by surprise. According to the author, within a year they were no longer speaking to one another. The introduction also describes Alex and Maya. Alex, ashamed of being unable to find a job, was unwilling to ask for help; Maya's manager, out of consideration for her having just returned from parental leave, let her miss a promotion opportunity without asking her. The author uses these stories to show that silence can come from shame, kindness or concern about boundaries, yet still shapes decisions and relationships. The HBS note offers three sample conversations. Steve wants to take over, but his mother assumed he didn't want to join the business; John, the other candidate his mother had in mind, had never been asked what he wanted either. After the conversation, they agree to hold a third-generation meeting in two weeks. Jason doesn't know how much longer his father can keep supporting him; through the conversation he learns about his own spending, and the two agree on budgeting coaching and a follow-up in a month. Crystal took a suddenly proposed prenuptial agreement as a sign that her father didn't trust her partner, and only later learned it was a family-wide arrangement; they agree that her father and the lawyer will take part in explaining it. The materials don't portray these conversations as solving everything in one go. The HBS note emphasises follow-up meetings, a neutral third party when needed, and reflection and rescheduling after a conversation goes off the rails. The appendix covers nine categories of questions: family, governance, the operating company, education, the family office, estate planning and inheritance, philanthropy, legacy, and open communication. Mercado Bitcoin: M&A, IPO, or Series B?

The Professor's Questions How does Mercado Bitcoin make money, and what is the potential for growth? How have they positioned themselves within the market, and how does this influence which of the options on the table makes the most sense for them? Why and how do the valuations differ between the M&A, IPO, and Series B options? What does this reflect about the objectives of each of MB’s counterparties? How does this influence your decision if you are Dagnoni? Which elements of the SoftBank term sheet would you consider renegotiating if you were Dagnoni? Why? What argument would you make in your renegotiation? Taken as a whole, and assuming each deal is final, would you advocate as CEO to take the M&A, IPO, or Series B route? What are the most important financial considerations? What are the most important non-financial considerations? My Answers Q1. Business model, growth and positioning How does Mercado Bitcoin make money, and what is the potential for growth? How have they positioned themselves within the market, and how does this influence which of the options on the table makes the most sense for them? MB is a financial platform built around a crypto exchange. Its strongest asset is the ability to earn trust and process transactions safely, but its revenue is still exposed to the crypto cycle. It has three revenue buckets. In 2020, Services-Exchange produced $11.041m, or 52.0% of gross revenue. This includes crypto trading, custody, OTC and other exchange services. Financial produced $9.731m, or 45.8%, from treasury, float and several financial and content activities. Tokens produced $0.482m, or 2.3%. Total gross revenue was $21.254m; EBITDA was $8.095m. We should not label the whole business “trading fees.” [Ex.5] Trading activity is the main growth engine, but price increases alone do not equal revenue. A useful model is active customers × trading frequency × average trade value × effective fee, plus other services. The case does not disclose a complete fee schedule or consistent enough volume data to calculate a precise take rate. Customer assets held in custody are not MB’s own expansion cash. [pp.7–8, Ex.5, Ex.9] Growth can come from deeper use of the existing platform and adjacent services. The company had 2.125m users at the end of 2020. It wanted more customers, more products, tokenized assets, institutional services, and expansion in Latin America and Europe. Its 2025 targets were 20m customers, about $86bn of trading volume and $822.230m of gross revenue. That revenue target implies about 108% annual growth from 2020. This is an ambitious plan, not a proven market outcome. [p.8, Ex.5, Ex.8, Ex.10] Customer acquisition looks attractive, but retention needs work. Estimated LTV/CAC improved from 14.91x in 2020 to 19.34x in Q1 2021. Yet estimated LTV fell from $138.70 to $77.15. Cheap new customers during a boom do not prove lasting loyalty. The reported 2018 contraction is another reason to use a down-cycle budget. [pp.5,8] MB positions itself as a trusted bridge to traditional finance. Its own technology, security focus, voluntary KYC, custody verification and regulated-market leadership support this position. They help attract institutions and strategic buyers. My preference is Series B because it funds the next stage while preserving a broad, independent platform. A bank is stronger if regulatory access and distribution are the binding limits; IPO is stronger if the business is ready to support public reporting and needs much more primary capital. [pp.4–8,10–13] Q2. Valuation and counterparties Why and how do the valuations differ between the M&A, IPO, and Series B options? What does this reflect about the objectives of each of MB’s counterparties? How does this influence your decision if you are Dagnoni? These are prices for different claims on the business. We must compare cash, control and downside rights before comparing the headline valuations. Bank M&A: up to $1.5bn. Banks wanted control and considered earn-outs and put/call arrangements. They preferred EBITDA multiples and worried about regulatory and custody risk. They were buying access to a new market and potential distribution synergies. A strategic buyer can pay a control premium, but here uncertainty and conditional payments can offset that premium. The quoted value is not necessarily cash paid at closing. [p.11] IPO: $1.1–2bn indicative value, with $220–350m expected proceeds. Public investors would price growth, comparable firms, earnings quality and liquidity. Underwriters also want a deal they can sell successfully. The estimate is not a guaranteed clearing price. The case does not specify the valuation basis, final primary/secondary split or fees, so net company cash and exact dilution cannot be calculated. Existing holders also face potential lock-ups. [pp.9–10] Series B: a $1.5bn price for secondary shares and a separate note. SoftBank wants exposure to a large regional platform, with protection if growth disappoints. The $2bn cap limits its conversion price; it is not a guaranteed valuation floor. It also receives a 20% discount, preferred shares on conversion, information rights, a board seat and an IPO ratchet. A higher headline value can coexist with a lower effective price per unit of risk. [pp.12–13] Different horizons matter. A bank wants strategic integration and tolerable regulatory exposure. Public investors need a business they can understand and value continuously. SoftBank seeks large future equity value while protecting its downside. A-round investors may also prefer an early exit: their short holding period makes annualized IRR very sensitive. That is not the same objective as maximizing the company’s long-term value. [pp.10–12] My decision would focus on the common shareholders’ outcomes across scenarios. I would compare company cash, immediate secondary proceeds, retained equity, control, and the payout to each class at a weak, normal and strong exit. A lower all-cash acquisition can be worth more to a seller than a higher price dependent on earn-outs; a higher VC price can become expensive if additional shares or preferences absorb the upside. Q3. Renegotiating SoftBank’s term sheet Which elements of the SoftBank term sheet would you consider renegotiating if you were Dagnoni? Why? What argument would you make in your renegotiation? I would first reduce the terms that could damage a later financing or exit. I would not start by asking for an even higher headline valuation. The case gives a summary, not the full term sheet. The requests below are my proposals, not terms already agreed. IPO ratchet — remove it, or cap it tightly and let it expire. The exact trigger and formula are not disclosed. It could transfer more dilution to common shareholders at a weak IPO, making a sensible exit harder. My argument: “You already receive a conversion discount and cap. A separate open-ended IPO adjustment can discourage new investors and harm both of us.” At minimum, define its base price, maximum extra shares, scope and expiry, and prevent double protection for the same price decline. Preferred economics — specify them before signing. Request a 1x non-participating liquidation preference on the actual primary investment, no cumulative guaranteed return, and clear conversion at a qualifying IPO. Clarify the class of purchased secondary shares; do not assume that $100m of common shares bought from founders also receives a new liquidation preference. My argument: “A modest priority can protect your capital without destroying incentives for the team or creating an excessive preference stack.” The case does not disclose a liquidation multiple, participating rights or a guaranteed return. Note mechanics — lower the discount, or trade it for a simpler priced round. A lower discount or a higher cap can reduce founder dilution, but asking for a higher cap alone may not help in a down round. Specify the fully diluted share base, treatment of the option pool and other notes, conversion on sale/IPO, and valuation if no qualified transaction occurs by month 18. I would ask to extend that period to 24–36 months as a proposal. The case says the note converts; it does not say cash repayment is automatically due at maturity. My argument: “Let the timetable match product and regulatory milestones, not an arbitrary financing deadline.” Qualified transactions — prevent an isolated secondary trade from setting the price for everyone. The current definition includes a primary or secondary transaction of at least $100m, as well as IPO or company sale. A secondary can occur at a liquidity discount and bring no new company cash. Request an arm’s-length financing definition, exclusion of the simultaneous $100m secondary from unintentionally triggering the note, and clear separate treatment of change of control. My argument: “A price set for one seller’s liquidity should not automatically price the entire company’s capital structure.” Primary versus secondary — preserve liquidity, but size company funding from a budget. Only half the $200m goes to MB. Keep a meaningful founder/employee sale to reduce personal concentration, but consider shifting part to primary if a downside operating plan shows $100m is insufficient. Use staged spending, not an assumption that every expansion project begins at once. My argument: “Your return comes from the company we can build with the primary cash, not only from the shares you can buy today.” Board and information rights — accept oversight, define boundaries. A board seat, budgets and audited accounts are reasonable. Define reserved matters so minority protection does not become day-to-day control. Require confidentiality, information barriers and recusal for competitor-sensitive matters, because SoftBank was also involved with Bitso. Do not demand total blindness or assume SoftBank has already misused information. My argument: “Good governance should improve decisions while protecting the company’s competitive position.” Deadline and closing conditions — ask for a short, defined review window. The 24-hour deadline limits our ability to model dilution and reconcile existing shareholder agreements. Request several business days, a dated diligence plan, a clear closing timetable and limited exclusivity tied to progress. Make waivers of preemptive rights explicit. My argument: “Our existing audit work and real IPO/M&A alternatives support a quick process, but a rushed signature can create avoidable conflicts.” Q4. Final choice Taken as a whole, and assuming each deal is final, would you advocate as CEO to take the M&A, IPO, or Series B route? What are the most important financial considerations? What are the most important non-financial considerations? I would advocate Series B on the disclosed terms, even if all three deals are final and my renegotiation requests fail. IPO is my second choice, and bank M&A is third. This is a judgment based on the disclosed terms; the case does not provide enough detail to calculate an exact risk-adjusted winner. Dagnoni is chairman in the case and Rabelo is CEO; I answer this question from the requested company-level CEO perspective. Why Series B: MB wants to build a broad financial infrastructure business. Series B puts $100m into the company, gives existing holders $100m of liquidity and keeps the business independent of a bank parent. It also postpones the recurring burden of being public while revenue mix, controls and several adjacent businesses develop. Its funding is smaller than the indicative IPO proceeds, but the case does not prove MB needs all the IPO capital immediately. I would prioritize the core platform and phase expansion. This reasoning does not depend on IPO failure, a slow M&A process or better SoftBank terms. Financial considerations, in order: Usable company cash and downside runway. Build a cash budget after fees, capex, working capital and regulatory capital needs. Customer custody assets cannot fund operations. The case gives no full cash-flow statement or expansion budget, so $100m cannot honestly be called “enough for X years.” Annual forecast expenses of $55.889m in 2021 and $124.177m in 2022 are not cash burn. [Ex.5] Dilution and exit payout. Model the note, secondary transfer, future primary rounds, option pool and every preference/ratchet. In the illustrated $2bn next-round valuation, SoftBank would hold about 12.16% before that round’s new capital and other adjustments—not simply $200m/$2bn = 10%. Under the $1bn scenario, management’s illustrative share falls to 48.30%. Quality of earnings across a cycle. Separate transaction services from treasury and other Financial income. Stress lower volumes, lower fees, lower LTV and sticky security/compliance costs. The Financial forecast inconsistency must be resolved before using the forecast as a financing plan. Liquidity for shareholders and its governance. Limited secondary sales can reduce pressure to sell the company too early. But allocations must be transparent and employee incentives preserved. Company needs come first; selling shareholders’ preferences should not decide the transaction by themselves. The cost of future capital. A high private valuation can make the next round difficult. Preferred terms and a ratchet can leave common shareholders worse off even if the headline value remains high. We are accepting that risk, not assuming it can be negotiated away. Non-financial considerations, in order: Strategic independence and culture. The independent platform can serve different banks and institutions and prioritize new products without a bank parent’s approval. The cost is giving up the bank’s ready-made distribution and regulatory relationships. Custody, security and governance. Capital and a recognized investor do not themselves validate custody or make the platform safe. Independent checks, clear client-asset records and reliable operations remain central. Management capacity. Moving from 200 to 750 people while entering countries, launching products and making acquisitions is a major execution risk. Financing should support staged milestones rather than reward simultaneous expansion everywhere. Investor fit and conflicts. Test SoftBank’s practical contribution, growth expectations and competitor information boundaries. “Smart money” is a hypothesis to verify. Future choice. Remaining private preserves the possibility of later IPO or M&A, but the note and ratchet make those options more constrained than they were before the deal. The strongest objection to my choice: IPO could deliver much more company capital, a tradable acquisition currency and less dependence on one preferred investor’s contract. With every deal final, execution risk cannot be used to dismiss it. I still prefer Series B because the company’s current challenge is to turn a cycle-sensitive exchange into durable infrastructure, while founders obtain partial liquidity. I would switch to IPO if a verified downside budget showed the $100m primary could not finance that stage. That threshold states the limit of my judgment; it does not change my vote on the facts supplied. Case Summary In 2013, brothers Gustavo and Mauricio Chamati founded Mercado Bitcoin in Brazil, initially letting customers buy and sell bitcoin in reais. The team put its money first into security audits, built its own trading platform, and — at a time when regulatory requirements were still incomplete — voluntarily verified customer identities, kept customer records and issued service invoices. It needed to earn the trust of customers, banks and future investors all at once. When the crypto market rallied in 2017, MB's full-year gross revenue topped US$24 million, customers approached 871,000, and the team grew from 8 to 85 people. The brothers brought in Roberto Dagnoni and Reinaldo Rabelo, both with experience at the B3 exchange; the two bought out some early shareholders' stakes and joined the governance. In 2018 the market cooled, revenue fell and expenses rose, the EBITDA margin dropped to about 33%, and the company cut half its staff. Management then broadened the business goal to financial market infrastructure. 2TM became the holding platform, covering trading, wallets, custody, asset tokenization, education and other businesses. From 2019 the company began tokenizing real-world assets, including assets tied to Brazilian government court-ordered debts. The core team hoped to turn the exchange's customers, technology and credibility into a more complete financial services system. The 2020 Series A took about a year. After some potential lead investors dropped out, GP Investments and Parallax Ventures led the round, with other investors joining. In December 2020 the company raised nearly US$20 million at a US$64 million pre-money valuation. The deal included fairly strong shareholder rights and required a Big Four audit and verification of custody. Management felt the price didn't fully reflect the year-end growth, but the new shareholders also brought institutional recognition. In early 2021, trading activity surged. MB prepared for an IPO in Brazil, led by JP Morgan, expected to raise US$220–350 million at a valuation of US$1.1–2 billion. At the same time, two large banks were negotiating a controlling acquisition, with offers capped at about US$1.5 billion and arrangements such as earn-outs and put/calls under consideration. CEO Rabelo valued the regulatory, distribution and organizational support a bank would provide; Dagnoni and adviser Cunha worried about the valuation, integration and the deal process. On April 10, 2021, SoftBank made a new offer valid for only 24 hours: invest US$100 million in the company through a zero-coupon convertible note, and spend another US$100 million buying existing shares. The secondary shares would trade at a US$1.5 billion valuation; the note would convert at a 20% discount at the next qualified transaction, with a US$2 billion pre-money valuation cap and an 18-month term. SoftBank also asked for information rights, a board seat and an IPO ratchet. Dagnoni had to recommend a path to the board. Key Data Amounts are in US dollars by default; in the table below, m means million and bn means billion. Gross revenue is revenue before deductions — not trading volume, and not gross profit. Get the terms straight first: A primary offering / primary capital means the company issues new equity or financing securities, and the money goes into the company; a secondary sale means existing shareholders sell their holdings, and the money goes into the sellers' pockets. An IPO is the initial public offering/listing route, and can include both new and existing shares. So "primary" and "IPO" are not mutually exclusive categories; the Series B in this case also includes both primary and secondary. The Professor's Questions What are the key resources and capabilities behind Golden Goose’s success? Are they scalable? What challenges or constraints does Golden Goose face in growing its business, especially given its luxury positioning? Should Golden Goose deepen its focus on sneakers and Co-Creation, or pursue new directions for growth? Think about the potential and trade-offs of each of the three strategic paths: a. Sneakers & Co-Creation b. Ready-to-wear and accessories c. Geographic expansion Which of these options best balances growth potential with brand coherence and executional feasibility? What would need to be true for your chosen strategy to succeed? My Answers Q1. What are the key resources and capabilities behind Golden Goose’s success? Are they scalable? Golden Goose's advantage is a connected system: recognizable shoes, a personal experience, direct customer access and the ability to learn from customers. Parts of it scale more easily than others. The distressed look and a small set of recognizable styles give the product a clear identity. Italian craftsmanship and a disciplined price position make that identity credible. Co-Creation lets customers participate, so the value is partly in the experience and attachment, not only the physical shoe. Stores and CRM connect the company directly to customers. Staff collect information that helps with recommendations, inventory and store location decisions. These activities reinforce one another. (pp.3–8) The results support the system: FY2024 revenue was €654.6m, with a 74.4% gross margin. There were 215 stores at year end. However, a margin alone does not prove that competitors cannot copy the model. Nor does a customer buying 1.8 pairs a year establish the retention rate of the full customer base. (Exhibits 2, 12; p.4) Core designs, data systems and inventory rules can scale through repeatable processes. Friendly staff, skilled artisans and meaningful customer interaction need training, time and local judgment. The academy helps, but it cannot instantly create experienced artisans. I would scale the operating standards and training while leaving room for individual expression. The scarce resource is consistent human attention, not simply more store space. Q2. What challenges or constraints does Golden Goose face in growing its business, especially given its luxury positioning? Growth must preserve the reason customers pay a premium, while funding a more complex operation. I see four constraints. First, wider distribution can weaken distinctiveness if customers see the same product and experience everywhere. Exclusivity need not mean hostility or very few stores, but the company must preserve craft, recognizable design and personal service. Second, Co-Creation consumes space and skilled labor. More demand can produce queues and uneven quality if artisan capacity does not grow with it. Third, category expansion adds sizes, design decisions, inventory and markdown risk. Sneakers still represented about 87% of 2024 sales, so customer permission to become a broad lifestyle brand remains a question. (pp.4–9; Exhibit 7) Fourth, growth is already placing demands on profit and working capital. FY2024 revenue rose 11.5%, while EBIT fell slightly from €132.5m to €131.7m. Inventory rose 29.5%, to €147m. These figures warrant investigation; they do not by themselves prove weak stores or obsolete stock. (Exhibits 1–2) I would therefore watch full-price sell-through, store contribution, service quality, inventory aging and cash payback together. A store that looks successful in revenue can still tie up cash or dilute the experience. Q3. Should Golden Goose deepen its focus on sneakers and Co-Creation, or pursue new directions for growth? Think about the potential and trade-offs of each of the three strategic paths: a. Sneakers & Co-Creation b. Ready-to-wear and accessories c. Geographic expansion I would put sneakers and Co-Creation first, use selective geographic expansion second, and keep apparel and accessories as measured experiments. This is a sequence, not a permanent rejection of the other routes. Path Growth potential Trade-off and evidence needed Sneakers and Co-Creation More value from a proven product and customer relationship; Co-Creation starts at $150 Larger space and more artisans must create enough incremental contribution; measure waiting time, extra margin and later repeat purchases Ready-to-wear and accessories More purchases per customer and less dependence on footwear Awareness is not demand; check full-price purchases, returns, stock turns and whether the brand has a distinctive product advantage Geographic expansion Serve customers who already buy online or while traveling New countries bring duties, operating complexity and opening delays; use CRM demand evidence, local economics and management capacity For apparel, Exhibit 10 shows €22m in 2021, €33m in 2022 and €38m in 2023; €11m for 2024 is only Q1. I would not annualize that quarter mechanically. For geographic expansion, the company's targets are a payback below two years and a 30% EBITDA margin. Neither should be replaced by a revenue-growth target. (pp.8–9; Exhibits 10–11) The opportunity cost of my choice is slower diversification. I accept it because expanding every dimension at once would make it harder to diagnose what works and harder to protect execution quality. Q4. Which of these options best balances growth potential with brand coherence and executional feasibility? What would need to be true for your chosen strategy to succeed? A staged expansion of Co-Creation in proven stores offers the best balance. It strengthens the existing customer promise and uses capabilities already present, though it still needs proof of profitable scale. Four assumptions must hold. Customers must pay for the experience without simply moving spending from other products. Extra contribution must cover rent, staff, training and working capital. The company must train artisans without losing service quality. Finally, the deeper experience must improve repeat purchase or customer advocacy, not just the first transaction. I would test comparable stores with and without the added service, account for differences in location and customer mix, and track contribution per customer, contribution per square meter, wait time, rework, satisfaction and repeat purchases over a full buying cycle. My proposed decision rule is to expand only where the extra cash supports the investment and the experience remains strong. The case does not supply a validated numerical hurdle for a store expansion, so I would agree that hurdle before the test rather than invent a proven return. If demand is strong but labor is the constraint, invest in training before adding more locations. If customers enjoy the experience but incremental economics are weak, keep it in selected flagship stores. If the concept succeeds, use CRM to identify the next geography. My classroom vote is: deepen first, replicate selectively, broaden categories after evidence. Case Summary Golden Goose was founded in 2000, initially combining the artisanal craftsmanship of the Venice region of Italy with the casual style of California to sell high-end lifestyle apparel. After it launched the Super-Star sneaker in 2007, footwear became the centre of business growth. The distressed finish made the product feel less like a showpiece that needed careful protection and more like something that already belonged to the wearer. (pp.2–3) The brand later went through several rounds of private equity investment. DGPA came in in 2013, Ergon in 2015 and Carlyle in 2017, and Permira acquired it in 2020. As capital came in, the organisation also gradually professionalised: functions such as HR, merchandising, marketing and legal were built, and responsibilities once concentrated in the hands of a few managers were split up. From 2017, the company accelerated the build-out of its own stores and brought e-commerce operations in-house; at the time it had only six directly operated stores. (p.3) Silvio Campara joined as commercial head in 2013 and became CEO in 2018. Through a small number of core sneaker styles, constantly changing colours and materials, Made in Italy, a distressed aesthetic and a pricing policy of rarely discounting, the company built a recognisable product system. What management wanted to create was a sense of belonging for customers, not just the distance of traditional luxury. (pp.3–4) In 2019, the brand launched Co-Creation in Milan. Customers design details together with in-store artisans, turning a purchase into participation in creation. Later, Forward Stores offered repair, re-creation, resale and recycling services, and in 2024 it opened HAUS, adding community, events and artisan training. At the same time, CRM information fed into store location, product design, customer contact and inventory allocation, and sales staff also took on the job of accurately collecting customer feedback. (pp.5–8) The business extended from sneakers into ready-to-wear, accessories and kidswear, but footwear still accounts for the vast majority of revenue. At the end of 2024 there were 215 stores in total, and full-year revenue in the exhibits was €654.6m. Greater scale did not remove the growth choices: keep expanding stores to deliver the sneaker co-creation service; double down on ready-to-wear and accessories; or open stores in new countries and cities. All three paths could deliver growth, and each draws on different resources: space, design and inventory capability, and cross-border operating capability. The Professor's Questions What are your favorite personal and professional uses of AI? How do you expect AI to change your business over the next 6-18 months? How would you like your employees' use of AI to change? What could you do to accelerate that change? My Answers Q1. What are your favorite personal and professional uses of AI? My most useful personal use is turning learning material into something I can understand, discuss, and revisit. For OPM, I use AI to connect the assigned readings with the professor's questions, prepare answers in English and Chinese, and organize my reflections into an article. I also use it to develop illustrations and a preview that I can review. This is a connected learning workflow, not only a search for a quick summary. I value the ability to compare interpretations and practice explaining an idea in simple English. But I still need to return to the source, check numbers, distinguish a case fact from an inference, and decide what I actually think. A polished answer is not proof that I have learned the material. For professional work, my preferred direction is assistance with knowledge organization, research synthesis, drafts, and comparing alternatives. Those are proposed priorities here, not a claim about current staff practices. The goal is to free attention for judgment, relationships, and difficult exceptions, while retaining responsibility for what is delivered. My test is whether the entire task becomes more useful and reliable. I would count checking and revision time, not only generation speed. I would also be explicit when input is missing—as with the class data file—rather than ask the tool to produce a plausible-looking result. Q2. How do you expect AI to change your business over the next 6-18 months? Over the next 6–18 months, I expect the most useful change to come from redesigning selected workflows around AI assistance. This is a working hypothesis, not a technology forecast or an internal operating plan. Drafting, retrieving information, comparing documents, and preparing explanations may become faster. Whether that improves the business depends on the quality of inputs, verification, and handoffs. I would start with one repeated, bounded task using material appropriate for the tool and the task. First define the output standard and measure a manual baseline. Then compare AI-assisted work on similar tasks, including review and rework. If it performs well, turn the useful instructions, examples, and checks into a shared method. Only then expand its scope. In a trust-based service, speed is valuable only when the explanation is accurate and the promise can be delivered. I would expect people's work to move toward framing problems, interpreting evidence, handling exceptions, and maintaining relationships. I would not assume a specific headcount reduction, revenue increase, or autonomous service capability without evidence. I would track cycle time, important errors, first-pass acceptance, and recipient usefulness. If drafts are faster but verification consumes the gain, I would narrow the task or improve the inputs. If evidence remains weak, I would stop that use case. The business change I want is more dependable judgment and service, not merely more generated content. Q3. How would you like your employees' use of AI to change? What could you do to accelerate that change? I would like employees to move from occasional prompting to accountable use within a real task. A good user can explain the objective, provide relevant context, check the result, disclose uncertainty, and know when to ask a person. This is my desired direction; I do not have a verified baseline for current employee use in this preparation. To accelerate learning, I would select one task with the team, give protected practice time, and provide an approved set of tools and suitable sample materials. Pair a domain expert with a curious user. Show both a strong result and a failure, including how the error was found. A short weekly demonstration should focus on what changed in the work, not who wrote the cleverest prompt. For a four-week pilot, week one sets the baseline and quality rubric; week two tries assisted drafts; week three tests unfamiliar but comparable examples and exceptions; week four compares total effort and quality. These are suggested stages, not commitments already made. One named owner should decide whether to expand, revise, or stop. I would reward useful outcomes and honest reporting of problems. I would not make message counts or tool usage a performance target. Employees need to know they can reject an output and escalate an exception without being treated as resistant to change. Keep reference material current, make successful methods reusable, and retain human approval for consequential commitments. The cost is time for learning and review; leadership must actually allocate that time. Case Summary This session asks students to bring their own experience of using AI into the classroom, then practise together using a designated data file and their preferred LLM. Preparing well means more than knowing the names of tools: it also means being able to explain what work a tool has changed, and which judgements you still have to own yourself. This process links input, analysis, expression and delivery — and it also shows that checking against the original, consistency in how numbers are defined, personal stance and final review cannot be skipped. The professor's second question shifts the lens to how the business will change over the next 6–18 months. This calls for conditional scenarios and experiments, not claims that the organisation has already transformed. Gathering materials, producing first drafts and repetitive processing may be the first parts of work to change; judgement standards, knowledge updates, accountability and exception handling determine whether that change can become a reliable service. The third question is about employees' usage habits and how leaders can encourage them. There is a gap between one person occasionally getting a good answer and a team consistently delivering verifiable results. Bridging it takes use cases, time, reference examples, feedback and clear accountability for judgement. The data file hasn't arrived yet, so I can't choose fields, aggregate metrics or announce classroom conclusions in advance. I've prepared the workflow below for checking the file, clarifying the question, verifying calculations and interpreting results; once the file is in hand, I can go straight through it for the actual exercise.
