The Professor's Questions What is Breezm’s value proposition, and how is it different from incumbents like Luxottica or newer players like Warby Parker? Does Breezm have a competitive advantage? If so, what is it, and how sustainable is it? What are Breezm’s key internal bottlenecks or constraints for growth? Evaluate the three growth strategies Breezm faces: operational optimization in Seoul, domestic expansion within Korea, and international entry. What are the trade-offs associated with each option? What should Breezm do next? Why? What are the assumptions behind your recommendation? How would you test those assumptions? My Answers Q1. What is Breezm’s value proposition, and how is it different from incumbents like Luxottica or newer players like Warby Parker? Breezm sells a better fit, not just a printed frame. It combines facial measurements, an eye exam, frame adjustment, custom production, and aftercare. A customer should feel less pressure, less slipping, and better lens alignment. The product is the whole service, including a 45-day redo or return policy. Luxottica combines brands, lenses, manufacturing, and retail at scale. Breezm also integrates activities, but uses that control to solve an underserved fit problem. Warby Parker initially challenged price and shopping convenience with $95 prescription frames and then built stores and labs. Breezm is not simply another cheaper online brand: its Korean model relies on licensed opticians and in-person consultation. The trade-off is time and cost. Customers wait 10–14 days and staff spend substantial time on consultation. I would target people with persistent fitting problems first, rather than claim every buyer values customization equally. Q2. Does Breezm have a competitive advantage? If so, what is it, and how sustainable is it? Yes, it has an emerging advantage, but not a proven permanent moat. The strongest asset is the linked system: fitting data, optician software, manufacturing know-how, and customer feedback. Digital Fitting reduced a designer's 1–2 hour task to roughly ten minutes for a trained optician. That is a concrete improvement in the economics of customization. The 31% cumulative repeat purchase rate and 12.5 inventory turns support customer acceptance and a leaner stock model. Neither proves exceptional profitability: 2022 operating loss was $2.901 million on $4.448 million revenue. Nor does collecting 1,200 data points automatically create a network effect. More data matter only if they improve fit, reduce remakes, or make staff more productive. Equipment and many suppliers are accessible to rivals. Patented hinges protect some designs, not the entire business. I would defend the advantage through measured fit outcomes, faster learning, reliable optician training, and ownership of the customer relationship. It is strongest where these activities reinforce each other. Q3. What are Breezm’s key internal bottlenecks or constraints for growth? The immediate constraint is profitable throughput across the whole system. Printing capacity exists, but more output helps only when stores can attract, fit, and retain customers at a sound contribution margin. Eight stores and 15,000 annual pairs imply a simple average of 1,875 pairs per store, but store opening dates and mix must be checked before calling any location inefficient. There are four internal bottlenecks. First, consultation and optician skills can limit daily capacity; customers spend about 90% of store time in consultation. Second, the two manufacturing processes need different quality controls, including dye consistency and finishing. Third, broad in-house functions create a high fixed expense base. SG&A alone was slightly above annual revenue in 2022. Fourth, the founders must manage retail, software, design, factories, and expansion at once. The old $313 cost table includes R&D and SG&A, not just manufacturing. I would rebuild current economics by product, store cohort, and customer channel before deciding that scale alone solves the loss. Missing data include remake rates, customer acquisition cost, mature-store contribution, cash runway, and unused capacity by material. Q4. Evaluate the three growth strategies Breezm faces: operational optimization in Seoul, domestic expansion within Korea, and international entry. What are the trade-offs associated with each option? Seoul optimization offers the lowest learning cost. Existing stores can test appointments, consultation design, optician training, product mix, and factory utilization. Its weakness is a ceiling: Korean prices are highly competitive, and many customers may see less need for customization. Optimization must have a deadline and clear targets. Domestic expansion tests whether the model can travel without adding another country. Regional cities can fill existing factories and broaden demand. But new stores still require licensed partners, training, marketing, and cash. It may replicate weak economics, and a small market share does not mean every new location is attractive. International entry offers larger markets and potentially stronger willingness to pay for fit. The US market was about $42 billion in the case, compared with Korea's $2 billion. But market size is not accessible demand. Local service, prescriptions, returns, distribution, regulation, and acquisition costs must be validated. I would use a tightly bounded pilot rather than a multi-country launch. My ranking is Seoul economics first, a small domestic replication test second, then an overseas pilot when evidence supports it. This sequence has an opportunity cost: rivals may move sooner. I would still run low-cost overseas demand interviews in parallel, without committing a full store network. Q5. What should Breezm do next? Why? What are the assumptions behind your recommendation? How would you test those assumptions? I would authorize a 90-day operating proof in Seoul and reserve a small budget for overseas customer discovery. The operating work would measure contribution after actual service labor, remake cost, and customer acquisition cost; it would compare mature stores and products rather than only group gross margin. I would also test whether better scheduling and digital fitting increase completed, satisfactory orders per optician hour. My assumptions are that demand can grow without a damaging price cut, fit remains consistently better as volume rises, existing factories can absorb more orders, and current cash can fund the test. I would test price with limited offers and real bookings, quality with 45-day return and remake outcomes, capacity with controlled batches, and demand with repeatable acquisition cohorts. Any numerical success thresholds should be approved after baseline measurement; they are not supplied by the case. If mature stores show positive contribution after all local costs, and a second location can reproduce it without founder intervention, open one domestic test store. If interviews and paid commitments show that an overseas niche offers enough extra contribution to cover service and acquisition costs, test one city with a qualified local partner and legal review. Stop or redesign if remakes rise or acquisition costs consume the extra margin. I would not make the 2027 IPO date the decision rule. The price of this choice is slower headline growth and possible delay of the IPO. The benefit is learning whether a customized product can support a repeatable business before multiplying its fixed commitments. Case Summary Park had previously built the eyewear brand ALO and brought experience of the industry, consumers and retail; Sung moved from accounting and investment banking into manufacturing entrepreneurship, and saw how well small, high-value eyewear suited 3D printing. The two met in 2016 and, drawing on Humax Optics' manufacturing capabilities, spent a year on research before founding Breezm in 2017. Its point of entry was the problem that traditional standard frames don't properly fit every face. In 2018 the company tested demand with ten pop-up stores, selling 25 pairs on the first day. At the end of the year it opened its first permanent store. It linked face scanning, style recommendations, eye exams, digital fitting, made-to-order production, and a re-check at pickup; customers were buying comfort and optical fit, with 3D printing as the means of delivery. In 2019 it introduced Face Ruler and AI Fit Finder; in 2021 its digital fitting system turned work that used to take a designer 1–2 hours into roughly ten minutes for an ordinary optometrist after one day of training. The company kept expanding its polymer styles and in 2022 launched a titanium line. Metal 3D printing was too costly, so the team switched to laser cutting and proprietary hinges. This shows that its core promise is custom fit; not every product has to use the same manufacturing technology. Design, R&D, the factory and in-store service are run by the company, while lenses are bought from outside suppliers. By 2022, Breezm had eight stores and annual sales of about 15,000 pairs. Revenue grew from US$1.7 million in 2020 to US$4.448 million in 2022 (exhibit basis), with gross margin of about 60.5%; but operating losses widened from US$1.64 million to US$2.901 million. The factory had idle capacity, stores were built around one-on-one consultations, about 90% of customers' time in store went to consultation, and delivery took 10–14 days. The two founders hope to break even in 2024 and go public in 2027, and face three paths: first improve the efficiency of existing operations in Seoul, replicate stores in other Korean cities, or enter larger overseas markets with different pricing environments. Korea accounts for only about 1.4% of the global market, but overseas opportunities come with the costs of brand-building and customer acquisition, local service and regulatory adaptation. The case stops at the moment of choosing the sequence of growth. Note on the Starbucks Case We will not be discussing the Starbucks case in class. If you have a few minutes, please skim the case text and Exhibit 1. You do not need to prepare the case or discuss it in your living groups, though I would be delighted if you did. Case Summary According to the case, Starbucks Korea launched a promotion for large-capacity stainless steel tumblers on May 18, 2026, using the name "Tank Day" and an onomatopoeic Korean slogan. To the team, these words seemed to convey capacity, sturdiness and memorability; to many consumers, the date and the words connected to historical trauma in Korea. May 18 is linked to the commemoration of the Gwangju Democratization Movement; the slogan was in turn associated with official cover-up rhetoric from another historical incident. The problem came from the combination of words, date, region and public memory — it can't be caught just by checking whether a single line of copy is grammatical or obviously offensive on its own. The case cites reports and company statements saying the team consulted AI tools while drafting the copy, that the approval chain involved seven managers, and that some approvers reportedly did not open the attachment. The materials do not provide the full prompts, model versions or each person's actions, so we cannot conclude that AI independently created all the content, nor precisely allocate each individual's responsibility. The campaign was pulled within hours, but screenshots had already spread. The case describes apologies, management changes, boycotts and investigations, followed by nationwide early store closures for training on historical and social sensitivity. The fallout from a headquarters marketing mistake also landed on store employees. Training can fill knowledge gaps, but it does not automatically change who needs to see what, who can stop something, and who bears final responsibility. Exhibit 1 places AI uses across twelve marketing-mix elements, covering activities such as demand insight, product, pricing, brand, channels, sales, advertising, promotion, packaging, display, service and fulfillment. So the case is not only about writing copy, but about how AI takes part in the entire market-facing decision chain. As generation gets faster, human judgment and organizational design matter no less. More layers of approval do not necessarily mean more effective judgment; responsibility can also get diluted layer by layer. My Answers Q1. Was this mainly an AI failure or a management failure? It was a failure of an AI-assisted organizational workflow. The tool may have generated or helped refine inappropriate material, but people selected it, paired it with a date, approved it, and released it. The case does not provide enough records to isolate each contribution. Calling it only an AI failure would hide the decisions that allowed the output to become a public campaign. The failure was contextual. A product name, sound, date, and local history jointly changed the meaning. A generic grammar check or a second model asked whether the copy was “good” would not reliably test that combination. A reviewer needed the complete campaign, the intended market, and the release calendar. Seven names in a chain do not prove seven meaningful reviews. If everyone assumes someone else checked the issue, another approval can add delay without protection. I would ask what each approver had to inspect, whether the exact final asset was visible, and whether anyone could stop the launch without penalty. Training can improve knowledge, but it should support a redesigned workflow. I would assign a campaign owner, specify cultural review triggers, require local review for sensitive material, and record approval of the final version. I would also protect staff who raise uncertainty. These are proposals; the case does not show that such changes have already been implemented or proved effective. Q2. Where can AI help across the customer journey, and where is judgment needed? Exhibit 1 is a map of possible applications, not a claim that every application should be automated. I would group the twelve elements by the decisions they support and the cost of error. One model can contribute to several stages, but responsibility stays with the relevant business owner. At discovery, AI can organize reviews, service conversations, and demand signals. Humans must check whether the sample represents customers and whether a pattern supports a causal claim. At design, it can propose products, positioning, packaging, and prices. Managers must test feasibility, actual benefits, and customer understanding. At acquisition and purchase, it can draft campaigns, prioritize leads, personalize offers, and improve product discovery. Review must cover context, factual claims, authorized prices and terms, and whether the firm can fulfill its promise. A high click rate does not establish a good customer outcome. At delivery and service, it can help forecast stock, retrieve policy, draft replies, and route cases. Decisions involving exceptions, conflicting policies, or distress need a clear human path. Finally, analytics should connect conversion to returns, complaints, retention, and delivery quality. Begin with a narrow use case and a measured baseline; expand when quality and net benefit are demonstrated. Q3. What would you change immediately, and how would you know it works? Immediately, stop the offending assets across channels, preserve records for review, explain the error accurately, and support front-line staff. Engage affected groups with listening and a concrete repair process. Do not imply that store employees created the headquarters campaign. Do not claim that lack of intent cancels impact. Before the next campaign, require the owner to review a one-page release packet: final wording and visuals, date, audience, geography, evidence for claims, and any sensitive references. Add an independent local reviewer when a trigger is met. Give that reviewer stop authority and a rapid escalation path. Avoid adding seven generic signatures to every routine item. Over the next month, pilot this process on a limited campaign set. Keep useful AI support for drafting and organizing information. Log model-assisted work and material edits enough to reconstruct the decision, without creating unnecessary data collection. Maintain a versioned calendar and reference set, but do not assume a sensitive-date list can replace local judgment. Measure serious errors escaping review, meaningful issues caught before launch, review time, rework, complaints, and recovery outcomes. A rise in near-miss reports may initially reflect better reporting rather than worse behavior. Review samples independently and adjust thresholds. The cost is reviewer capacity and slower approval of some campaigns; prioritize it where harm is hard to reverse.

The Professor's Questions What were the most critical challenges facing Mudo when Karakullukcu joined the firm? What is your assessment of Karakullukcu’s performance to date? How should Karakullukcu interact and build trust with the founder and his son? What goals should she try to achieve with each of them? What immediate actions should she take next? My Answers Q1. What were the most critical challenges facing Mudo when Karakullukcu joined the firm? Mudo faced a connected strategy and governance problem. Its model had outgrown a single decision-maker. The owners wanted professional management but had not fully separated ownership, board oversight, and daily operations. Managers had responsibility without enough authority, and several key roles were vacant or weak. The retail proposition also needed repair. Apparel had lost its price-to-value appeal as competition intensified. Furniture and apparel served different customers and purchase cycles; one estimate put customer overlap at only 3%. Blended mall stores constrained furniture display and created storage costs. Personal lease relationships and exit penalties made closing weak stores difficult. Finally, the operating base was unreliable: poor inventory control, about 200 monthly complaints, high loss rates, weak information systems, and employee retention problems. The family chose to undertake a private-equity-style transformation without the new equity capital. I would therefore rank cash, the apparel proposition, and decision rights ahead of an ever-longer project list. The challenge was not just to install systems, but to decide which stores and products deserved resources. Q2. What is your assessment of Karakullukcu’s performance to date? Her performance is mixed but valuable enough to support a focused second phase. Complaints fell by about 90%, apparel stock losses dropped from 7% to below 1%, and home EBIT improved from minus TL5.7 million to plus TL7.7 million. She built leaders, improved access to management, and applied accountability even to her own CIO hire. She also shifted real decision authority away from the founder. However, transformation activity cannot substitute for commercial outcomes. Apparel EBIT fell from plus TL10.7 million to minus TL1.6 million between 2012 and 2014. Filling support functions before the key business roles delayed commercial learning; the apparel leader arrived only in late 2013. Fifty projects in 18 months and 54 ongoing projects in the later exhibit suggest attention was spread thin. Recruiting capable people without retail experience added a learning cost. I would give her a strong score for institution building and an incomplete score for economic delivery. I would not endorse her near-perfect self-assessment. Nor would I dismiss all progress because group profitability disappointed. The owners also retained decision friction, and a clothing cycle takes about 15 months. Continue her mandate, narrow it to a few cash and customer outcomes, and agree a transparent review schedule. There is no clean causal estimate of what would have happened without her. Q3. How should Karakullukcu interact and build trust with the founder and his son? What goals should she try to achieve with each of them? With Mustafa, I would start from continuity: his product judgment and supplier relationships remain assets. Invite him to a regular product and location review, ask him to explain the signals behind his intuition, and test a few ideas. Discuss weak stores privately and preserve dignity when renegotiating leases. The goal is to turn his experience into an input that others can use, while ending direct instructions that bypass accountable managers. With Ömer, I would acknowledge that his caution reflects past losses and his responsibility as the next-generation owner. Agree in advance what evidence is sufficient, the downside limit, a decision date, and which decisions the CEO can make alone. Give him a concise weekly cash and risk dashboard. The goal is a chairman who challenges assumptions and then supports a decision, rather than becoming a second operating CEO. For all three, create a written authority matrix: routine decisions, material capital commitments, store closures, hiring, and brand choices. Set thresholds jointly rather than invent numbers from the case. Separate the advisory board's advice from the formal board's authority. Record exceptions and give staff one final instruction. Trust should grow through predictable behavior and admission of mistakes, not promises of certainty. Q4. What immediate actions should she take next? At the next board meeting I would present one page that separates home improvements, apparel deterioration, cash needs, and unresolved owner decisions. I would ask for a temporary hold on uncommitted new-store obligations, not an automatic rejection of all 50 locations. Existing binding commitments must be reviewed individually. In the first 30 days, build a rolling 13-week cash forecast and store-level contribution after rent, labor, logistics, markdowns, and inventory cost. Compare continue, resize, renegotiate, and close alternatives, including exit penalties and landlord relationships. Resolve the definitions behind inconsistent revenue figures before using them to set targets. Over 30–90 days, concentrate on three workstreams: apparel assortment and conversion; furniture inventory losses and profitable formats; cash and store portfolio decisions. Pause low-value projects. Give each one a business owner, observable milestones, and a review date. Test apparel marketing only where product quality and availability can support the promise; a controlled campaign can learn, but a broad relaunch before product repair risks paying to disappoint customers. Approve selected new stores only when the site economics, funding, management capacity, and downside case are clear. Preserve the founder's scouting role and require the same approval criteria for every idea. The cost is slower visible expansion, possible exit expenses, and difficult family discussions. The benefit is making the next phase accountable to cash and customers rather than to the number of initiatives. Case Summary Mustafa Taviloğlu founded Mudo in 1964, growing it from a small record and gift shop into a well-known Turkish retailer. Relying on his feel for trends and his network of relationships, he successively developed apparel, home and mixed store formats. After going through economic crises and difficulties with the franchise model, the company switched to company-operated stores. His son Ömer formally joined after graduating in 2005, working on the youth brand, e-commerce and the apparel business, and at one point served as interim CEO. As the business grew, the founder still directly influenced a large number of day-to-day decisions; managers were used to carrying out instructions, and responsibilities didn't match authority. Father and son wanted both to keep control and to build a professional management system. Rather than taking private equity investment, they hired Accenture to design a transformation roadmap, and in March 2012 invited Barış Karakullukçu, the partner on the project, to become CEO. She had consulting and cross-cultural project experience, but had never before held operating responsibility at a retail company. When she took over, the company had 119 store/channel counting points, 2,436 employees and annual turnover of about US$199 million. Apparel and furniture serve different customers with different purchase cycles, yet mixed stores accounted for a very high share of revenue. Apparel faced international and local competition, with pressure on value for money and positioning; furniture was more attractive in dedicated large street-front stores, but in mixed stores in shopping malls it was held back by space, storage and logistics. The CEO first pushed forward operations and organisation-building: performance metrics, IT, supply chain, project management, renewal of staff. Fifty projects were implemented within 18 months. Monthly complaints fell from about 200 to 20, and inventory shrinkage improved markedly. The head of home cut redundant SKUs, improved pricing and delivery, and controlled store openings, achieving positive EBIT in 2014. The head of apparel arrived later and needed to go through a merchandise cycle of about 15 months; the business's financial performance was still declining. The father's intuition and the son's caution made different demands. The CEO gradually won trust by admitting she didn't know retail, respecting existing staff, and proving her ability through real improvements. After two and a half years, she and the management team were independently handling about half of decisions, about 40% were discussed with Ömer, and the remaining 10% still needed the founder's approval. The three still met for three hours every week; the formal org chart had not entirely displaced relationship-based governance. By the end of 2014, the capital budget was already tight. The founder still wanted to open 50 stores over the next three years, while the CEO's analysis supported only a few of them. She had to explain to the advisory board: the processes and the team had changed, so why hadn't profitability followed, and in the next stage what should be stopped, what should be done first, and who should decide. Opening 50 new stores would add cash and organisational burdens. The founder's experience should be preserved, and the professional manager's authority must also be real and effective. Building systems requires up-front investment, but customer positioning and merchandise quality can't wait until all processes are perfected to be fixed. Home and apparel belong to the same brand, but have different paths to profit, shopping contexts and turnover cycles. Respecting the successor's risk awareness, and avoiding the decision paralysis caused by repeated proof, need shared rules.

In addition to A Letter from Prison, please read the Preface of Eugene's book, Paper to Practice: Why Compliance Programs Fail and How to Build Programs That Work. You will receive this book at the beginning of the program. The Professor's Questions How serious were Stephen Richards’s actions? If Computer Associates achieved the same financial results through GAAP flexibility, does your answer to Question 1 change? Suppose you were placed in Stephen Richards’s position at Computer Associates and were under pressure to extend the fiscal quarter. How would you have handled the situation differently? What would be the expected consequences of those actions? My Answers Q1. How serious were Stephen Richards’s actions? His actions were very serious. The fact that contracts and cash were genuine does not make the timing immaterial. Investors were told that business had been completed in a quarter when the recognition conditions had not been met. In FY2000 Q2, improperly accelerated revenue was about $558 million, roughly 53% of correctly recorded revenue. Reported EPS of $0.60 beat the $0.59 estimate; without the improper revenue it was $0.05. This changed the apparent operating result, not just the presentation of a minor item. As global sales head, Richards could influence deadlines and what finance was told about contracts. He was not a passive recipient of an accounting choice. The repeated extension of quarters also taught teams that hitting the number could override the rule. The investigation adds a further concern: the case describes misleading responses by senior executives and an internal counsel who later admitted coaching such behavior. Concealment prevents governance from correcting the original conduct. I would distinguish explanation, responsibility, and harm. Analyst pressure, compensation, and fear of losing status help explain the behavior. They do not remove responsibility. The case supports serious distortion and damage to trust, but it does not provide a defensible total dollar measure of investor loss. The $2.115 billion sum is accelerated revenue across six quarters, not stolen cash. Nor does the seriousness depend on whether the company later went bankrupt. I can take his experience and suffering seriously while rejecting the claim that a few days made the conduct unimportant. His letter is especially useful because an intelligent manager can describe the pressures clearly and still understate his own choices. Q2. If Computer Associates achieved the same financial results through GAAP flexibility, does your answer to Question 1 change? Yes, my assessment can change, but the answer depends on what “GAAP flexibility” means. If the company uses a genuinely permitted, supportable, consistently applied estimate, with appropriate disclosure and no false contract dates, that is different from deliberate misstatement. The same reported earnings do not make two processes equally wrong. I would not call a legitimate accounting judgment fraud merely because it helps meet a target. However, an accounting choice still needs evidence and economic meaning. I would ask whether the estimate reflects new information, whether assumptions are applied consistently in good and bad quarters, and whether material effects are transparent. A technically arguable treatment used to obscure deterioration raises a different ethical concern from a neutral estimate. The case alone cannot resolve every hypothetical GAAP treatment, and auditors' acceptance is not a substitute for accurate underlying facts. Real business actions also deserve separate scrutiny. Delaying useful R&D or an economically sound project may lawfully increase current earnings while destroying long-term value. That can be a poor or harmful management decision without being the same legal category as falsifying the reporting period. Conversely, a sound business decision that improves earnings is not suspicious merely because it improves earnings. My test has three parts: are the facts and method valid; does the report allow a fair understanding; and does the decision serve sustainable business value? Outcome, intent, process, and disclosure all matter. I would reduce the severity judgment for a genuinely legitimate choice, while still examining any deception or value destruction. Q3. Suppose you were placed in Stephen Richards’s position at Computer Associates and were under pressure to extend the fiscal quarter. How would you have handled the situation differently? What would be the expected consequences of those actions? I would refuse to change the reporting period and make that position operational. I would tell the team: keep selling after quarter end, but preserve actual signature and delivery dates and book each deal in the period supported by the evidence. I would ensure finance has the original contract history rather than a target-driven summary. A shortfall should be reported as a shortfall. Before escalation, I would clarify the facts and the proposed treatment with the controller or CFO, state my objection in a factual record, and request an independent review. If senior finance or internal counsel is implicated, I would go to the audit committee or an independent board channel, with appropriate independent professional advice. Preserve records and do not coach employees on a common story. Disclosure or external reporting obligations would need qualified advice; the classroom plan is not a claim about today's legal procedure. I would also offer a business response: revise the forecast, explain late contracts honestly, examine excessive end-quarter concessions, and reduce incentives that make a single cutoff decisive. Separate bookings, recognized revenue, cash collection, and customer value in management reporting. Reward accurate forecasting and verified contracts, and protect people who flag concerns. Do not simply add another annual training slide. Expected consequences are not painless. Earnings could miss expectations, the share price could fall, bonuses could decline, and I might lose influence or my job. The board could initially resist. The 42% share-price reaction in the case shows why the pressure felt real, but it does not forecast the exact reaction to my alternative. The benefit is avoiding further distortion and allowing the company to confront its actual business problem. If the organization insists on continuing and I cannot stop participation, I would be prepared to leave after seeking independent advice and addressing any reporting duties. Leaving alone would not erase what I already knew or did. Case Summary Computer Associates (CA) was founded in 1976 in enterprise software and grew into a large software company through acquisitions and global expansion. Stephen Richards joined the Sydney office in 1988, rose quickly, and became head of worldwide sales in 2000. The sales organization revolved around quarterly targets: strong results brought large bonuses and stock options, while missing targets brought pressure. Customers typically bought three- to ten-year licences. Under the accounting treatment of the time as described in the case, once a contract was signed, the software delivered and collection reasonably assured, the present value of the licence fee could be recognised in that quarter; usually at least 80% of the fee was allocated to the licence. So the signing date of a few large contracts could significantly change a quarter's revenue. Customers knew they had negotiating leverage at quarter-end and often pushed signing to the last minute. Some managers effectively extended the fiscal quarter, booking contracts signed after quarter-end into the previous quarter. The products, contracts and cash could be real, but the reporting period was not. After an earnings warning in July 2000, the share price fell 42%, showing the capital-market pressure the company faced; that does not establish the pressure as sufficient justification for illegal conduct. After media scrutiny and regulatory investigations emerged, the initial internal investigation did not uncover the problem. In 2003 the board asked an independent law firm to investigate further, which found 23 boxes of previously missed documents and more electronic evidence. The investigation involved finance executives and ultimately implicated Kumar, Richards and others. The case describes executives misleading the investigation, and the head of internal legal later admitted to directing executives to mislead it. "We already asked the company's lawyers" cannot be treated as sufficient for an effective independent review. Richards pleaded guilty in 2006 and was sentenced to seven years in prison. In 2008 he wrote from prison to Eugene Soltes, then a student. He explained how analyst expectations fed into internal targets, and how targets shaped teams, organizational structure and incentives; he also discussed how self-identity and recognition for performance can be stronger drivers than money, and stressed that managers often operate in grey areas. The letter preserves his explanations and self-understanding; it is not an independent conclusion about his conduct. The professor asks us to assess how serious the conduct was, then to judge whether that changes if the same numbers were achieved through flexibility GAAP allows, and finally to put ourselves in his shoes and propose a different course of action and its consequences. The focus of the class is not only recognising the wrongdoing, but whether you can adopt a workable arrangement at the moment of greatest pressure. The short-term cost is real and cannot be eliminated by rewriting the facts. A real transaction and truthful reporting are requirements at two different levels. Legitimate room for judgement and intent to mislead must be distinguished item by item; "everyone does it" cannot substitute for analysis. Understanding the pressure and holding people accountable can both hold true; explaining the mechanism does not absolve individual choice. There is a gap between control responsibilities on paper and whether they are carried out in the face of real incentives.

Please read the foreword (pages 7-15) by Arthur Schlesinger and the main book (pages 19-98) for a total of 88 pages. The Professor's Questions How did we get into this mess? Please consider the pros and cons of the airstrike vs. blockade options. Think about how our assumptions might impact our analysis. Think about the decision-making and other process points that President Kennedy Employed during the crisis. What are some of the generalizable lessons we might draw for our own use? What lessons around closing the deal might be useful and generalizable? My Answers Q1. How did we get into this mess? We got here through interacting security fears, risky choices, and misread signals. The Bay of Pigs and US efforts against Castro helped make Cuba fear another invasion. Khrushchev sought to protect Cuba and improve the Soviet position by placing missiles nearby. The secrecy and false assurances then made the deployment a direct test of US security and credibility. Understanding that chain does not excuse the deception or remove Soviet responsibility for the deployment. US missiles in Turkey also mattered. They made the Soviet proposal for a reciprocal removal intelligible, even though the circumstances were not identical. Kennedy had wanted the obsolete missiles removed earlier, but implementation had stalled. A decision that was not followed through became a bargaining problem during the crisis. Intelligence and political assumptions made the surprise worse. Past Soviet restraint was treated as evidence that this move would not occur. Once evidence arrived, US leaders also faced public commitments, domestic critics, and alliance obligations. The parties were bargaining with each other and with their own constituencies. My general lesson is to map the interaction, not search for one villain or one communication error. What does each side fear? Which action looks defensive to us and offensive to them? Which belief is based on evidence, and which is merely based on habit? The foreword's later revelations also warn that no participant had a complete risk picture. Q2. Please consider the pros and cons of the airstrike vs. blockade options. Think about how our assumptions might impact our analysis. I favor quarantine as the initial choice under the information available, combined with diplomacy, credible preparation, and explicit review points. It offers more opportunities to pause and revise than an airstrike. This is a comparative judgment under uncertainty, not a claim that blockade is peaceful or guaranteed to work. An airstrike could act quickly against an immediate threat and demonstrate resolve. But its value depends on locating and destroying all relevant capabilities. Military advice did not support that certainty. A limited strike could expand into a larger operation and invasion, kill Soviet personnel, leave surviving weapons, and provoke action in Berlin or Turkey. It also carried moral and alliance costs. Even a militarily successful first step could produce a disastrous next step. Quarantine restricts additional shipments, creates time, permits gradual pressure, and can mobilize broader support. Its weaknesses are equally real: it does not remove missiles already in Cuba; construction continues; ships or submarines may clash; and delay may reduce future options. It therefore needs a negotiating offer and a way to assess whether the threat is actually declining. Key assumptions are that leaders can still control their forces, the opponent values avoiding war, communications are understood, and there remains enough time. I would challenge each assumption. Ask what happens if an officer acts locally, if a ship cannot turn promptly, if a weapon survives, or if a public threat prevents retreat. Later information about tactical nuclear weapons makes the potential cost of invasion clearer, but it was not available to justify every decision at the time. I would not assign precise probabilities unsupported by the reading. Q3. Think about the decision-making and other process points that President Kennedy Employed during the crisis. What are some of the generalizable lessons we might draw for our own use? Kennedy made disagreement possible before making the decision. He brought departments and people with direct expertise into the discussion, sometimes stayed away so advisers could speak more freely, and asked competing groups to develop complete alternatives. Challenging an option was easier when the group had to explain implementation and consequences, not only state a preference. Yet he retained final responsibility; this was not decision by unanimous vote. He repeatedly asked about the opponent's response and the steps after that. This shifted analysis from the appeal of the first move to the escalation path. He also treated execution as part of strategy: interception instructions, communication delays, and authority to respond to incidents could determine whether the chosen policy remained limited. When the U-2 was shot down, he sought confirmation and reconsidered implications rather than letting retaliation become automatic. The same discipline appeared in allowing ships time to turn. Restraint was active management of a dangerous process, not absence of a decision. For a business decision I would use six practices: write the objective and constraints; separate facts from assumptions; obtain independent proposals before the leader speaks; compare second and third responses; specify who may pause or escalate; and record review triggers. Give specialists direct access while preserving a clear decision owner. Time-box the debate so consultation does not become evasion. There are limits to copying the example. The memoir is written by the president's brother and emphasizes his judgment. Informal trusted circles can improve speed but also exclude affected parties. A successful outcome does not prove every intervention was optimal. The transferable lesson is disciplined inquiry and control, not that a charismatic leader should personally manage every detail forever. Q4. What lessons around closing the deal might be useful and generalizable? First, define a limited outcome that both parties can implement. The core US aim was removal of the threatening weapons, not public humiliation or regime change. The Soviet side needed a way to protect Cuba and preserve an acceptable explanation for retreat. The public package linked withdrawal with assurances against invasion and the lifting of quarantine, with proposed verification arrangements. Second, distinguish the public formula from the full bargain. The memoir emphasizes replying to the earlier Khrushchev letter and says there was no quid pro quo under threat. But Schlesinger's foreword explicitly describes the secret Turkey missile trade. Reading only the memoir can turn a reciprocal settlement into a story of unilateral victory. My conclusion is that closing required both pressure and substantive accommodation. Third, use authorized private channels to clarify a feasible package. Robert Kennedy and Dobrynin could convey urgency and the president's position. Such channels are useful only if they connect to real authority and their meaning is understood. They can also create accountability and third-party trust costs. In ordinary organizational negotiations, confidentiality should not become a pretext to bypass required approvals or make incompatible promises. Fourth, address sequencing, verification, and delivery. Who stops which activity, when does pressure ease, how is compliance checked, and what happens if a message or action is delayed? The proposed UN arrangements in the letter were part of the offer; the memoir's endpoint should not be mistaken for proof that every implementation detail had already been completed. Finally, protect the agreement after acceptance. Avoid triumphal language that makes the other side unable to defend compliance. Do not assume an apparently conciliatory leader controls every subordinate. Keep monitoring and communication open. A deadline can concentrate minds, but in this case the shrinking time was a real danger, not a sales tactic to imitate. A good close makes the desired behavior possible and credible; a dramatic announcement alone does not. Case Summary In October 1962, the United States discovered that the Soviet Union was deploying nuclear missiles in Cuba. US intelligence had previously judged that the Soviets would not take this step, and the Soviet Union had given assurances that it would not deploy offensive weapons. Photographic evidence overturned the earlier assessment. Kennedy had to decide how to eliminate the threat while keeping his actions from triggering a war between the US and the USSR. The crisis did not arise in a vacuum. The foreword connects the Bay of Pigs, US operations against the Castro regime, Cuba's security fears and Khrushchev's decision to deploy. US missiles in Turkey also form part of the backdrop. Understanding these factors does not mean endorsing the Soviet secret deployment and deception; it explains why each side could call its own actions defensive while making the other side feel threatened. Kennedy convened cross-departmental discussions, in which his advisers compared an airstrike, an invasion, a naval quarantine and a diplomatic arrangement. An airstrike looked direct, but could not guarantee destroying every missile, and might provoke a Soviet response in Berlin or Turkey. A quarantine offered time and room to apply pressure step by step, but could not by itself remove the missiles already on the island, and construction was continuing. The President ultimately chose a naval quarantine, combined with military preparations, allied support, public disclosure of the evidence and negotiation. He repeatedly stepped into the details of execution: when to stop ships, how to give ships turning back the chance to carry out their orders, and how to reduce the chance that an accident would trigger escalation. On October 27, a US U-2 was shot down, and the pressure rose further. Even so, he did not let the pre-planned retaliation scenario automatically decide the next step. Khrushchev put forward proposals in differing terms, one after another. The US publicly responded to an arrangement that traded the withdrawal of the missiles from Cuba for a no-invasion pledge and other conditions; at the same time, Robert Kennedy held private talks with Dobrynin that touched on the missiles in Turkey. The foreword states explicitly that this exchange was played down in the memoir, and that the outcome cannot be attributed solely to toughness and the blockade. On October 28, the Soviet Union accepted a settlement based on removing the missiles, and the most urgent confrontation eased. The result does not prove that the process was safe and error-free. Information disclosed in the foreword, such as that about tactical nuclear weapons, shows that the decision-makers at the time did not know the full extent of the risks. The value of this case lies in studying how to bring uncertainty, the other side's interests and execution risk into decision-making, rather than in finding a negotiating posture that is sure to win. Public support is needed, and so is room for discreet communication; secrecy cannot automatically erase questions of allies and accountability. Leaders should listen to differing views, yet must make — and own — decisions when information is incomplete.

The Professor's Questions What strikes you most about Ohtani's approach to goal setting? What enabled him to turn an audacious goal into sustained world-class performance? Ohtani tracked both performance metrics (e.g., lower-body strength, pitch volume) and character behaviors (e.g., respect umpires, clean his room). Why do you think he included both? What role, if any, do character and karma play in achieving elite performance? The Harada Method translates long-term ambition into structured daily practices. What are its greatest strengths? What are its potential limitations? If you were creating a Harada chart today, what would you put in the center square? My Answers Q1. What strikes you most about Ohtani's approach to goal setting? What strikes me is the distance between the ambition and the daily action—and how deliberately he connects them. His chart moves from an elite draft ambition to strength, control, mental habits, and even how he treats other people. The eight support areas and 64 actions force him to ask what the goal requires today. He also separates the result he wants from the kind of person and environment that can sustain the work. His father's notebook made reflection a habit before the more elaborate chart existed. The chart therefore builds on feedback rather than replacing it. I would not treat the exact teenage age schedule as the key achievement. He changed the route, including staying in Japan and adapting after injury. The strength is serious commitment with a revisable path. The risk is reading his success backward and assuming every item caused it. Q2. What enabled him to turn an audacious goal into sustained world-class performance? Several conditions worked together. He had exceptional ability and years of practice, but also a feedback system: specific observations, written reflection, and repeated adjustments. Strength work and technical skills were connected to performance rather than pursued as isolated tasks. The environment mattered. His father and high-school coach gave feedback and structure. The Fighters offered a credible path to pitch and hit, so he did not have to abandon one capability prematurely. Later teams provided opportunities and support. Choosing an environment that fits the goal is part of execution. He sustained focus through daily routines and adapted to constraints. In 2024, he could not pitch while recovering from surgery and concentrated on hitting and baserunning. The 54 home runs show an exceptional outcome that year, but they do not prove the chart alone caused it. Talent, coaching, resources, teammates, health, and chance remain part of the explanation. For my own work, I would copy the feedback cycle and environment design, not his training volume. High effort without recovery, prioritization, or evidence can become counterproductive. Q3. Ohtani tracked both performance metrics (e.g., lower-body strength, pitch volume) and character behaviors (e.g., respect umpires, clean his room). Why do you think he included both? What role, if any, do character and karma play in achieving elite performance? Performance metrics tell him whether his capabilities are improving. Character behaviors help shape the conditions in which improvement is possible. Respect for umpires can support emotional control; caring for equipment can reduce preventable disruption; gratitude and consideration can strengthen cooperation. These are plausible mechanisms, not causal estimates established by the case. Some behaviors also have value even if they never improve a statistic. Treating others respectfully should not depend on whether it produces a win. “Karma” can be understood as a personal reminder to contribute, notice his surroundings, and act with care. I do not interpret the case as scientific evidence that good deeds cause favorable events. I would track a few observable commitments and invite honest feedback, while avoiding moral scorekeeping. A lost game does not show poor character, and excellent results do not prove virtue. The important combination is technical standards plus a way of living and working that people can sustain together. Q4. The Harada Method translates long-term ambition into structured daily practices. What are its greatest strengths? What are its potential limitations? Its greatest strength is translation. A distant ambition becomes support areas, specific behaviors, and a basis for reflection. The chart exposes missing conditions: a goal may need technical skill, relationships, attention, and an environment, not just more hours. It also gives a coach a concrete starting point for feedback. Its limits are false precision and overload. Sixty-four actions can compete for limited time. The chart may look complete while omitting a critical assumption. It may reward checking boxes instead of learning. Some goals depend heavily on other people or luck, and a teenage life schedule should not become a rigid contract with the future. I would treat the chart as a living hypothesis. Use one center goal, identify the most important constraints, choose a small active set of actions each week, and review evidence monthly. Keep a stop-doing list and room for rest. Change the actions when conditions change, and revise the goal if its purpose no longer holds. Finally, one celebrated athlete is not a controlled study. The framework can organize effort; it cannot promise elite performance or eliminate uncertainty. Q5. If you were creating a Harada chart today, what would you put in the center square? Provisional classroom draft, pending my own confirmation: “Over the next 12 months, turn my OPM learning into 12 well-documented decisions or practice experiments, and build a sustainable cycle of learning, action, and clear writing.” This is a proposed center goal based on the current learning task, not an established personal commitment. I would prefer evidence of use over a volume target for articles. For each selected lesson, record the original idea, the situation where I tried it, the choice I made, what happened, and what I changed. A decision that overturns an attractive idea can count as useful learning. An article without any new understanding should not count merely because it was published. The eight supporting areas could be source reading, problem selection, small experiments, reflection, feedback, writing, time boundaries, and integrity. I would start with one case and one modest action, then review after four weeks whether the target and workload make sense. The number 12 and the deadline are suggestions for discussion. Joyce should replace the center square if a different purpose matters more. Case Summary Shohei Ohtani was born in 1994 in Iwate Prefecture, Japan. His father had played in Japan's corporate baseball league, and his mother was a skilled badminton player. He tried many different sports as a child, and his father also coached him for a time. After practices and games, father and son exchanged little notebooks, recording both the good plays and the mistakes. The point was to help him understand his own actions in words, rather than just looking at whether he won or lost. His high school coach, Hiroshi Sasaki, required players to write down their dreams and introduced the Harada Method. Through goals, purpose, analysis, plan and action, it turns a long-term aspiration into behaviors that can be practiced. Ohtani's chart centered on becoming a draft prospect coveted by multiple teams as a first-round pick, and branched out into eight supporting areas — body, control, pitch sharpness, mindset, velocity, breaking balls, character and luck — each with eight specific actions. The chart included technical items such as strength, range of motion and pitching, but also gratitude, courtesy, respecting umpires, tidying his room, picking up trash and reading. So the goal was not only an athletic result; it was also about the kind of everyday life through which he wanted to become an athlete. The coach also stressed helping one another, which placed individual practice inside a supportive social environment. He originally wanted to go straight to the US after high school, but later chose the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters, because the team offered a development path that let him keep both pitching and hitting. The design of his environment and opportunities helped him preserve a rare ability. After deciding to move to the US in 2017, he joined the Angels and later moved to the Dodgers. The case describes his elite performance, but also records injuries and outside turbulence. In 2024, recovery from elbow surgery meant he could not pitch, so he shifted that season's focus to hitting and baserunning, and reached the goal of at least 50 home runs and 50 stolen bases in a single season. The exhibit shows 54 home runs and a .310 batting average that year; in 2025 it was 55 and .292. The case also mentions back-to-back World Series titles and four MVPs, but a team championship cannot be guaranteed by one person's habits alone. What is most worth discussing about this method is that it helps bring a grand aspiration down to today, yet must also allow a person to adjust the path after injury, a changing environment, and growth in ability. His high-school list of age milestones was not achieved item by item as planned; later achievements should not be treated as proof that every early plan was right. Injuries and changing environments change which actions fit best. Controllable behaviors help performance, but cannot fully control injuries, opponents, selection or team results. Structured record-keeping can deepen self-knowledge, but can also become a burden of filling in charts. Character has value in itself and should not be treated merely as a tool for winning. A success story is inspiring, but on its own cannot prove that the method is sufficient to produce the same achievement.

The Professor's Questions What factors account for Jean-Claude Biver’s success at Blancpain and Omega? What professional and personal challenges did he face? How would you assess Biver as a leader? What lessons can we learn from Biver? My Answers Q1. What factors account for Jean-Claude Biver’s success at Blancpain and Omega? What professional and personal challenges did he face? At Blancpain, Biver changed the basis of value. Mechanical watches could not beat quartz on low-cost accuracy, but they could offer craft, heritage, scarcity, and identity. He made those claims credible through watchmakers, a workshop setting, limited inventory, customer orders, and a focused collection. Piquet's technical capabilities and Biver's industry relationships were essential complements to the message. He also built a community rather than relying only on advertising. Collectors, younger buyers, displaced watchmakers, and other industry leaders found a reason to support the revival. Sales rose from 97 watches and $75,000 in the first year to about 3,000 and $9.4 million five years later. That supports a successful change in demand and value capture, without proving every element was causal. At Omega, the task was different. He worked inside a large group, restored a coherent message to a diluted brand, and connected its heritage to current consumers. Long-term work with Cindy Crawford and the Bond franchise gave Constellation and Seamaster distinct routes to relevance. Hayek's sponsorship and the group's manufacturing, distribution, and capital helped turn the idea into scale. Revenue rose from $350 million in 1995 to over $900 million in 1999. His professional challenges were scarce skills, an industry rejecting his view, building a team, and later operating under a powerful boss. Personal challenges included insecurity, marital crisis, loss of purpose after selling, serious illness, and a changing family life. These shaped his choices. They do not excuse harmful conduct toward employees. The industry revival also included Swatch's successful quartz business and consolidation; it was not one man's victory over technology. Q2. How would you assess Biver as a leader? He was an exceptional creator of meaning and commitment, and an inconsistent steward of other people's working experience. He gave people a convincing purpose, challenged conventional assumptions, debated ideas intensely, and recognized contribution through personal attention and generosity. Several employees developed into industry leaders, which suggests real talent development and exposure to ambitious work. But the case describes public humiliation, repeated threats, and physical expressions of anger, including the pen incident. I would assess those as leadership failures. Later apologies and generous gifts do not cancel them. A person who is afraid to deliver bad news may hide problems; a talented employee who dislikes confrontation may be screened out. These are risks inferred from the behavior, not measured outcomes supplied by the case. His own reflection links early anger to insecurity. That creates an opportunity for change, not a fixed personality diagnosis. I would ask whether he can receive dissent without punishment, apologize with changed behavior, delegate decisions, and let others succeed without his constant presence. Independent feedback and clear conduct standards should apply even to a commercially successful leader. I would want his strategic imagination and ability to mobilize people on a team. I would not copy his intimidation or make it a hiring criterion. Testimonials from people who stayed and later succeeded may miss people who left. The fair question is which strengths created value and which behaviors imposed avoidable costs. Q3. What lessons can we learn from Biver? First, when a technology loses one competition, ask whether customers still value something it uniquely provides. Biver did not restore mechanical superiority in accuracy; he built a credible reason to buy a mechanical watch. This requires evidence of customer willingness to pay and a product that supports the claim. It does not justify rescuing every old technology. Second, align the whole system around a clear promise. Product design, production, distribution, communication, and employee behavior should reinforce it. Omega's message mattered because partnerships and execution made it visible. A slogan alone would have been weak. Third, combine complementary people and institutions. Craft partners, employees, collectors, group resources, and a supportive boss were part of the result. Charisma is easier to see than this infrastructure, but both must be examined. Fourth, separate ambition from harmful conduct. Set high standards while protecting truthful disagreement. Generosity is welcome, but it is not a substitute for consistent respect or professional boundaries. Finally, define success beyond position and money. At the end of the case I would complete the agreed recovery period, clarify family and workload constraints, and explore Hublot in stages rather than commit immediately. Before choosing, I would need its economics, product promise, decision rights, cash needs, and the owner's agreement on leadership behavior. Returning to Swatch should depend on a meaningful mandate, not an assumption that succession is owed. This is a personal recommendation under uncertainty, not a prediction based on what happened later. Case Summary Quartz technology offered timekeeping that was more accurate, cheaper and easy to mass-produce, and it hit the Swiss mechanical watch industry hard. Large numbers of companies went under, jobs disappeared, and traditional craftsmen's skills were for a time seen as having no future. Biver learned watchmaking and sales at Audemars Piguet, then moved to Omega, and gradually came to a different view: the mechanical watch could be a vessel for craftsmanship, culture and identity, rather than continuing to compete head-on with quartz on accuracy and price. In 1982, Biver and his watchmaking partner Jacques Piquet bought the Blancpain brand, dormant for years, for US$16,000. They tracked down craftsmen who had left the trade, turned an old farmhouse into a workshop, and built a consistent promise out of brand heritage, mechanical craftsmanship, low inventory and made-to-order production. Through bold communication and industry relationships, Biver made mechanical watches attractive again to young consumers, and showed craftsmen that their skills still had value. In the first year they sold 97 watches, for revenue of US$75,000; five years later it was about 3,000 watches and US$9.4 million. The growth came not only from volume but also from higher realised prices and product mix. Other brands began adopting a similar positioning. Biver's enthusiasm, recruiting and community-building helped the business, but employees also described his rages, humiliations and threats — behaviour that cannot be automatically justified by commercial results. A crisis in his marriage affected his work, and friends warned him to change his behaviour or sell the business. In 1992 he sold Blancpain for US$43 million. After leaving, he found that wealth did not replace work, a team and meaning, so he asked to come back to the Swatch Group; Hayek let him stay involved with Blancpain and gave him the task of reviving Omega. At Omega, Biver repaired the brand's positioning, connected historical assets such as the moon landing to contemporary consumers, built a long-term partnership with Cindy Crawford, and partnered with the James Bond films. He stressed that every action revolved around a unified brand message, not personal whim. From 1995 to 1999, Omega's revenue grew from US$350 million to more than US$900 million. The group's manufacturing efficiency, distribution, capital and Hayek's backing were also important conditions. A serious illness in 2000 and a new stage in his family life led him to rethink his life; at the same time he felt his influence at Hayek's side was waning. In 2001 the two agreed on a one-year sabbatical. Then a possible opportunity at Hublot came up, but the company had about 20 people and was losing US$2.5 million a year, and its founder was also worried about Biver's management style. He faced a choice between returning to the group, retiring, or starting something new, and the case does not offer one inevitably right ending. Results do not prove that rage was causally necessary. Traditional skills need to stay credible, and they also need new meaning for consumers and a new business model. A strong personal vision can bring people together, but can also make an organisation overly dependent on the leader's moods and presence. Gaining access to group resources requires cooperation; personal autonomy and organisational politics have to be balanced. There is a real trade-off between the next career opportunity and recovery, family and meaning in life.
Whether people trust you rests on three legs — authenticity, logic, empathy. Find the one that wobbles under pressure

Frances Frei describes trust as a triangle: authenticity (do they experience the real you?), logic (do they trust your judgment and competence?) and empathy (do they believe you care about them?). When all three legs hold, trust holds. When one wobbles, trust starts to leak. Most of us, she says, wobble on one leg under pressure, and usually the same one every time. Empathy is the most common, and the cause is usually distraction. Logic problems are more often about how we explain than how we think. Authenticity is the hardest to spot and the slowest to rebuild. So the first step in rebuilding trust isn't to improve everything. It's to find the leg you wobble on most , and work on that one. This page has two things: An assessment : think of one specific relationship, respond to twelve statements, and see your trust triangle: which leg is weakest, and one small thing to try this week. Customer analysis with Frances Frei's frameworks in the room — it makes you think first, then tells you where you went wrong

Of everything in Frances Frei's operations class, what I come back to most is a very plain chart. Down the left side: what the customer cares about, most important at the top. Across the top: five steps, from "worst in class" to "best in class." Mark how you perform on each one and join the dots. The chart is not hard to draw. It is hard to draw honestly. A line that is "pretty good" everywhere usually means there is no position at all. The line worth having is slanted: all the way right on what the customer cares about most, and willingly back to the left on what they care about least. This skill turns her frameworks (the attribute map, trade-offs, funding, managing employees and customers, culture) and my class notes into an AI coach. It has one rule: it won't do the first three steps for you. Who the customer is, what they care about and in what order: you say it first, and then it probes, pushes back and adds. One line from class stuck with me: if you let AI do the first three steps, AI makes you dumber. What it does Asks one question at a time, starting from one specific customer, through the attribute map and on to funding, employees, customers and culture. Reads your map: is there a wedge, are your strengths in the wrong rows, are you trying to win everything? Leaves you a one-page summary and three hypotheses to take to real customers. How to use it 1. Download the zip and unpack the frei-customer-analysis folder. 2. Put it in your skills folder: .claude/skills/ for Claude Code, .cursor/skills/ for Cursor, or upload the zip on the Skills page of the Claude app's settings. 3. Tell the AI "help me with a customer analysis" or "let's discuss this case the Frei way." It answers in whatever language you use. The frameworks come from Uncommon Service by Frances Frei and Anne Morriss (HBR Press, 2012). The skill only contains my paraphrase and notes; please buy the book for the original. It is not affiliated with the authors. The attribute map: draw one yourself first Enter your company and target customer, rank what the customer cares about from top to bottom, and rate yourself. The map draws itself, with a short reading underneath. Try it on your own company or on a case from class.

From case PDF to a publishable prep article: bilingual Q&A, article and illustrations, all in one go

Before every class at Harvard, I prep with this skill: I hand the case text and the professor's questions to the AI. It first helps me lay out the case clearly and answers each question in both Chinese and English (the English plain enough that I can say it out loud in class), then writes it up as a prep article with a fixed structure, and finally adds hand-drawn, pencil-style illustrations. Every piece in the "HBS Prep" series on this site was written this way. What it delivers A prep Q&A: a breakdown of the case, key data, the relationships between the people, the Tensions, and bilingual answers to each question — for my own use in class; An article you can publish: title, summary, "My Thinking," Takeaways and Before Class, in a fixed structure; Prompts for the header image and in-text illustrations, plus a method for choosing among them. How to use it 1. Download the zip file below and unzip it to get the harvard-case-preview folder; 2. Put it in your skills directory: for Claude Code, under the project's .claude/skills/ ; for Cursor, under .cursor/skills/ ; in the Claude app, you can upload the zip on the Skills page in Settings; 3. Open SKILL.md and, following "Personalization" at the end, change a few placeholders (storage directory, author name, school); 4. Send the case PDF and the professor's pre-class questions to the AI and say, "Help me prep this Harvard case." It works for non-Harvard classes too: just swap the title prefix and the buildings in the illustrations for your own school's.
